fix(ravel): return view for ravel('F') of F-contig source — eliminates 3000× copy

Audit V2 finding (Section 1.6 / src/NumSharp.Core/Manipulation/np.ravel.cs:30-34):
np.ravel(a, 'F') unconditionally routed through a.flatten('F'), which allocates
fresh F-contiguous memory and runs NDIter.Copy over the source. NumPy, in
contrast, returns a 1-D view sharing the underlying buffer whenever the source
is already F-contiguous (np.shares_memory(np.ravel(aF, 'F'), aF) == True).

The audit reports a 3000× performance regression on the hot F-order path
(np.arange(12).reshape(3,4).copy('F') -> np.ravel(.,'F')): an O(1) shape-only
aliasing was replaced with an O(N) buffered copy.

Root cause
----------
ravel's F-branch had no fast path for the IsFContiguous case. flatten('F') is
documented to "ALWAYS return a copy" by design, so calling it from ravel forced
materialization even when the linear memory walk would already reproduce the
column-major read-out.

Why a 1-D view is correct for F-contiguous sources
--------------------------------------------------
An F-contiguous array has strides[0] == 1 and strides[i] == dims[i-1] *
strides[i-1] for i > 0, with no broadcast/stride-0 dimensions. Walking the
underlying buffer linearly from `offset` for `size` elements visits values in
F-order (first axis varies fastest), which is exactly what ravel('F') is
specified to produce.

For non-F-contig sources we still fall back to flatten('F') — a strided / C-
contig / sliced source needs the column-major copy to reproduce F-order
correctly.

Implementation
--------------
ravel(a, 'F') with NDim > 1 and size > 1:
  * a.Shape.IsFContiguous → build Shape(new[]{size}, new[]{1}, a.Shape.offset,
    a.Shape.bufferSize) and return new NDArray(a.Storage.Alias(vec)). offset and
    bufferSize are preserved so sliced F-views remain correct; size becomes the
    1-D shape's logical and physical extent.
  * Otherwise → existing flatten('F') copy path (unchanged).

The new shape's flags are recomputed by ComputeFlagsStatic over the 1-D
dims/strides, which trivially marks the result as both C- and F-contiguous and
writeable (a 1-D dense vector is both orders). Storage.Alias chains _baseStorage
to the ultimate owner, so view tracking and the @base property continue to work.

Test coverage
-------------
* AuditV2_ManipulationApis.Ravel_FContiguous_FOrder_ReturnsView is no longer
  marked [OpenBugs(audit-v2-ravel-fcont-fview)] — the documented NumPy
  np.shares_memory invariant is now asserted directly in CI.
* test/Manipulation/np.ravel.Test.cs gains 10 new tests:
    - Ravel_FOrder_FContig2D_IsView                — write-through verifies aliasing.
    - Ravel_FOrder_FContig2D_ValuesMatchColumnMajor — read-out sequence matches NumPy.
    - Ravel_FOrder_FContig3D_IsView                — 3-D F-flat-index decomposition.
    - Ravel_FOrder_CContig_IsCopy                  — C-contig source still copies.
    - Ravel_FOrder_Transpose2D_IsView              — a.T (F-contig view) also aliases.
    - Ravel_FOrder_KOrder_FContigSource_IsView     — 'K' resolves to 'F' for F-source.
    - Ravel_FOrder_AOrder_FContigSource_IsView     — 'A' resolves to 'F' for strict F.
    - Ravel_FOrder_FContig_DtypeFloat              — dtype preserved across the view.
    - Ravel_FOrder_FContig_EquivalentToFlattenF_Values — values match flatten('F').
    - Ravel_FOrder_FContig_PreservesSize           — 2-D / 3-D / 4-D size invariants.

Verified

perf(np.clip): scalar-bounds fast path + fix latent ClipScalar min>max bug

Benchmarking np.clip against NumPy 2.4.2 revealed a 48-80× slowdown on
the common case `clip(arr, lo, hi)` with scalar literal bounds. Root
cause: the engine was materializing every scalar bound via
`np.broadcast_to(scalar, lhs.Shape).astype(outType)`, which for a 10M
int32 input allocated and memset two 40MB bound arrays per call (then
ran an element-wise array-bounds kernel that re-read both buffers).

Investigation also surfaced a pre-existing kernel bug exposed once the
new fast path routed scalar-bound calls through ClipScalar / ClipStrided
/ ClipScalarTail: the integer scalar fallbacks used `if / else if` to
apply the two clamps, so when `minVal > maxVal` values below `minVal`
incorrectly stuck at `minVal` instead of capping to `maxVal` (NumPy
guarantees `min(max(x, lo), hi)` — i.e. `maxVal` wins when bounds are
inverted). SIMD paths and Math.Min(Math.Max,...) float paths were
already correct.

Changes
=======

src/NumSharp.Core/Backends/Default/Math/Default.ClipNDArray.cs
- Add scalar-bounds fast path: detect 0-d min/max (or null) and
  dispatch directly to ClipUnified / ClipMinUnified / ClipMaxUnified
  (the kernel family that broadcasts the scalar inside the vector loop).
  Skips broadcast_to + astype materialization entirely.
- ClipNDArrayScalarBounds: type-switch on outType to call the right
  generic kernel; uses a small delegate-based helper (ClipScalar<T>) so
  the dispatch logic isn't duplicated 12 times.
- ClipNDArrayScalarBoundsFallback: Half and Complex still go through
  the array-bounds path — their scalar SIMD kernels aren't wired and
  Complex has lex-ordering NaN semantics already implemented there.
  Cost is just the 0-d→shape broadcast (stride-0 view, O(1)) plus a
  1-element astype.
- Array bounds (any non-0-d min or max) flow into the existing path
  unchanged.

src/NumSharp.Core/Backends/Kernels/ILKernelGenerator.Clip.cs
- ClipScalar<T> (generic integer fallback, called by ClipHelper): replace
  `if (val > maxVal) val = maxVal; else if (val < minVal) val = minVal;`
  with two sequential `if`s. Now matches NumPy semantics when min > max.
- ClipScalarTail<T> (non-float tail after SIMD bulk loop): same fix.
- ClipStrided<T> (coordinate-iterated path for non-contiguous arrays):
  same fix.
- Added comments explaining why two sequential clamps are required.

src/NumSharp.Core/Backends/Default/Math/Default.ClipNDArray.cs

1. PrepareBound(bound, targetShape, outType) helper:
   When the bound is already same-shape, same-dtype, contiguous, offset
   zero, return it directly instead of running broadcast_to + astype
   (which clones via UnmanagedStorage.Clone). Wins for the common case
   where users pass arrays that already match the input layout.

2. ClipNDArrayFusedScalarBounds: new fast-fast path for the dominant

src/NumSharp.Core/Backends/Kernels/ILKernelGenerator.Clip.cs

Discussion of the user's two questions
──────────────────────────────────────

1. Vector<T> vs Vector256<T> — measured both on this CPU; identical
   wall time (5527 vs 5559 µs/10M int32 in micro-bench, see
   $CLAUDE_JOB_DIR/clip_micro.cs). Vector<T> picks the widest hardware
   register at JIT time, so on AVX-512 hardware it'd be 512 bits = 2×

   Vector256<T> kernels to Vector<T> is a low-risk forward-compat move
   for AVX-512 hosts but no measurable win here. Not changed in this
   commit (would touch the whole kernel file ecosystem; out of scope).

   enough that hand-unrolling doesn't help and can hurt. IL emission
   for this op would add significant complexity for ~no perf win.
   Not pursued.

   skipping redundant clones) — not from instruction-level tuning.

refactor(np.clip): all kernels via IL-generated DynamicMethods, width-adaptive

Per the user's directive, the entire clip code path now goes through a
single ILKernelGenerator entry point that dispatches internally and
emits all loops as DynamicMethod IL using the runtime-detected vector
width (V128 / V256 / V512). No hardcoded Vector256 references remain;
no hand-written C# loops remain in the engine or kernel files.

=====

src/NumSharp.Core/Backends/Kernels/ILKernelGenerator.Clip.cs
  Rewritten from scratch (~1900 → ~360 lines, -81%).
  Public surface — what the engine actually calls:

      public enum ClipMode      { BothBounds, MinOnly, MaxOnly }
      public enum ClipBoundsKind { Scalar, Array }
      public unsafe delegate void ClipKernel(
          void* src, void* dst, long size, void* lo, void* hi);

      public static unsafe void Clip(
          NPTypeCode dtype, ClipMode mode, ClipBoundsKind kind,
          void* src, void* dst, long size, void* lo, void* hi);

  All dispatch happens inside ILKernelGenerator:
    - Cache key = (dtype << 16) | (mode << 8) | kind
    - On first miss, Generate(dtype, mode, kind) builds a DynamicMethod
      and stores the resulting delegate in a ConcurrentDictionary.

  The IL emitter:
    - Uses GetVectorContainerType() / GetVectorType() / GetVectorCount()
      so the SIMD loop body adapts to V512 on AVX-512 hosts, V256 on
      AVX2, V128 on SSE2. There is no `Vector256` or `Vector128` token
      anywhere in the kernel file.
    - Hoists the scalar bound load and Vector.Create() out of the SIMD
      loop (one broadcast per kernel call, not per iteration).
    - Computes `byteOff = i * sz` once per iteration into a local and
      reuses it for src/lo/hi/dst pointer arithmetic — avoids the
      O(N × pointer_count) multiplications the prior C# kernels had.
    - Falls back to a pure scalar IL loop for dtypes without
      Vector<T>.Min/Max (Char, Decimal, Half, Complex). Half and
      Complex delegate the per-element clamp to static helper methods
      (NaN-aware / lex-order); the loop is still IL.

feat(unique): add 5 missing NumPy 2.x keyword arguments

Implements full NumPy 2.x API parity for np.unique / NDArray.unique:

  np.unique(ar, return_index=False, return_inverse=False,
            return_counts=False, axis=None, equal_nan=True)

Previous signature accepted only the array — five keyword args were
silently missing, blocking ports of any code that relied on them.

Implementation:
- Returns NDArray[] = [values, index?, inverse?, counts?] with positions
  shifting based on which flags are set; matches NumPy's tuple ordering.
- Flat path (axis=None): single-pass walk with Dictionary<T,long> to track
  first-occurrence index + count, then sort, then build inverse via
  second pass with value→sorted-rank lookup.
- Axis path: moveaxis to position 0, lex-compare slabs with NaN-aware
  ordering, dedup adjacent equal slabs after sort, gather output slabs
  into contiguous result, then moveaxis back.
- equal_nan: when true (default) all NaNs collapse to a single entry
  via default float equality (.NET's EqualityComparer<double>.Default
  already treats NaN==NaN); when false, NaN bypasses the dict and each
  occurrence becomes its own unique entry.
- Index/inverse/counts always returned as Int64 (matches NumPy on Win64).
- Inverse keeps input shape when axis=None (NumPy 2.x behavior), is
  flattened to 1-D when axis is specified.
- Negative axis values are normalized via axis += ndim; out-of-range
  axis raises ArgumentOutOfRangeException.

Int64/UInt64/Char/Half/Single/Double/Decimal/Complex) — NaN-aware
overloads for Half/Single/Double/Complex, generic path for the rest.

perf(unique): switch flat path from Dictionary to sort+mask — up to 43× faster

Replaces the Dictionary<T,long>-based dedup loop in the kwargs path with
NumPy's two-pass algorithm:

  1. Array.Sort(keys, perm) with NaN-aware comparer for floats
  2. mask[i] = (keys[i] != keys[i-1]) using IEEE != (NaN != NaN is true)
  3. For equal_nan=true + floats: collapse trailing NaN run (CollapseNaNTail)
  4. Emit values/index/inverse/counts from mask + keys + perm

Matches numpy/lib/_arraysetops_impl.py::_unique1d structure. Float types
get specialized inline mask construction using IEEE `!=` (operator) so
equal_nan=false semantics work — generic Equals() collapses NaN==NaN
which is wrong for that mode.

Index uses min(perm) within each unique-key run for first-occurrence
semantics, since .NET's Array.Sort is unstable. One extra pass over n,
no extra allocations.

perf(unique): NaN-partition + default sort — eliminates Comparer overhead

Profiling revealed the float sort path's bottleneck wasn't the sort
itself, it was the delegate-dispatched Comparer<T>:

    Array.Sort<double>           plain (no Comparer) : 10.4 ms / 100K
    Array.Sort<double,long>      no Comparer         : 11.3 ms
    Array.Sort<double,long>      with struct Cmpr    : 18.4 ms (+62%)
    Array.Sort<double,long>      with delegate Cmpr  : 22.3 ms (+97%)

The NaN-aware comparer was nearly doubling sort cost just to push NaN
to the end of the array. Solution: do an O(n) two-pointer partition
that moves NaN entries to the tail FIRST, then call Array.Sort on the
non-NaN prefix with no comparer. The NaN tail's perm is then stabilized
with a tiny secondary sort (NaNs are all equal, so ordering by perm
recovers NumPy's mergesort-stable semantics for return_index).

PartitionNaN_<T> is type-specialized for Double/Single/Half/Complex and
uses AggressiveInlining. Tested alternatives that did NOT help:
  - Hand-written unsafe quicksort with inlined Cmp: 13.7 ms vs Array.Sort 11.3 ms
    (.NET's introsort/heapsort hybrid is already optimal — no IL emit win)
  - struct IComparer<T> (no delegate): 18.4 ms — still 60% overhead

Added CheckSortableLength gate: n > Array.MaxLength (~2.1B) throws
NotSupportedException with a clear message pointing to the no-kwargs
hash-based path (Hashset<T> in NumSharp is long-indexed and handles
any size). In practice n > int.MaxValue requires >16 GB for doubles,
so this is a theoretical limit.

  100K float64 NaN eq=T unique(all)   12 ms    16 ms    13 ms    parity ⬆ NEW
  100K float64 unique(all)            12 ms    23 ms    15 ms    1.2× ⬇ much closer
  100K int32 high-card unique(all)    7 ms     10 ms    7 ms     parity ⬆ NEW

feat(unique): add long-indexed fallback for n > Array.MaxLength

Previous: kwargs path threw NotSupportedException for n > Array.MaxLength
(~2.1B elements) because managed T[] is bounded by that limit.

This adds an unmanaged fallback path that handles any size:

  - struct KeyPerm<T> packs (T Key, long Perm) into 16 bytes, implements
    IComparable<KeyPerm<T>> so the existing LongIntroSort utility can sort
    them directly without writing a parallel-array sort.
  - struct ComplexKeyPerm for Complex (which doesn't implement IComparable);
    sorted with explicit lex Comparison<> delegate.
  - All buffers allocated via UnmanagedMemoryBlock<T> with long count.
  - Mask is UnmanagedMemoryBlock<byte> (1 byte per element, ~2 GB for 2.1B).
  - PartitionNaN works on KeyPerm<T>* (NaN to tail), then sort non-NaN prefix.
  - StabilizeNaNTailLong re-sorts the NaN tail by Perm ascending to match
    NumPy's mergesort-stable order for return_index.

Routing: every uniqueFlatSorted* method now checks IsManagedSortableLength(n)
and dispatches to the long path when needed. The fast managed path
(n ≤ Array.MaxLength) is unchanged — verified by benchmark, no regression.

- ~30-50% slower than the managed Array.Sort path (LongIntroSort is a
  port of .NET's introsort, but our managed Array.Sort uses tuned
  native code).
- 2× memory for the packed key+perm struct (16 bytes vs 8+8 separate);
  same total bytes, slightly worse cache density.
- Worth it: this path only activates when n > 2.1B which requires
  16+ GB just for the input array. The slowdown is dwarfed by I/O
  and memory bandwidth at that scale.

feat(searchsorted): full NumPy API parity — side, sorter, multidim validation, shape-preserving v

Closes audit T1.27 (misnamed binarySearchRightmost), Issue #436 follow-up, and Batch 7
selection/sorting gaps. NumSharp.searchsorted now matches NumPy 2.x behavior on all four
documented gaps and several previously-undetected bugs surfaced during the work.

## API changes

  searchsorted(NDArray a, int v,    string side = "left", NDArray sorter = null) -> long
  searchsorted(NDArray a, double v, string side = "left", NDArray sorter = null) -> long
  searchsorted(NDArray a, NDArray v, string side = "left", NDArray sorter = null) -> NDArray

Both new optional parameters preserve the existing call sites (NumPy defaults: side="left",
sorter=null). The misnamed private helper `binarySearchRightmost` (which actually implemented
bisect-LEFT — bug T1.27) is gone, replaced by a single `BinarySearch(arr, target, leftSide, sorter)`.

## Behavior matrix

| Aspect | Before | After (matches NumPy 2.x) |
|---|---|---|
| `side='right'` | unsupported | bisect_right (a[i-1] <= v < a[i]) |
| `sorter` | unsupported | reads arr[sorter[mid]] during the bisect |
| Multi-dim `a` | silently flattened | ArgumentException("object too deep for desired array") |
| Multi-dim `v` | flattened + memory corruption from `GetValue(long)` partial-dim indexing | output preserves v.shape; reads via GetAtIndex |
| Sliced `v` (strided view) | wrong values + Debug.Assert "Memory corruption expected" | iterates by linear index through TransformOffset |
| Invalid `side` | n/a | ArgumentException("search side must be 'left' or 'right' (got '<x>')") |
| Wrong-size / multi-dim sorter | n/a | ArgumentException matching NumPy |
| Duplicates with default side | bisect_left (1 for [1,2,2,2,3], target 2) — same | unchanged; now also explicit |

## Bugs found and fixed (in addition to T1.27)

1. `Storage.GetValue(long i)` on multi-dim `v` interpreted `i` as a partial first-dim index,
   returning out-of-bounds buffer memory (the old code returned `[0, 2, 5, 0]` for searching
   `[[1,2],[3,4]]` instead of NumPy's `[[0,1],[2,3]]`). Now uses `GetAtIndex(i)` which
   linearizes via TransformOffset.
2. Constructing `new NDArray(NPTypeCode.Int64, v.Shape, false)` propagated v's slice
   offset/stride into a new contiguous buffer, producing wild reads. Now builds a fresh
   `new Shape(v.shape)` (contiguous, offset=0, computed strides) for the output.

perf(searchsorted): IL-emitted typed binary-search kernels (5–25× over baseline, faster than NumPy on 20/22 benchmarks)

## What changed

`ILKernelGenerator.Search.cs` (new) emits one specialized DynamicMethod per
`(NPTypeCode, side, has_sorter)` tuple — up to 56 kernels, cached by key on first use.
Each kernel mirrors NumPy 2.4.2's `binsearch.cpp` template:
  - typed inner loop with `ldind.<T>` and `clt`/`clt.un` (no boxing, no double conversion)
  - NumPy-style monotonic key tracking: when consecutive keys ascend per the side's cmp,
    L_prev carries across iterations; when they descend, L resets to 0 and R bumps by 1
  - sorter path emits a second indirection inside the bisect (sort_idx = sorter[mid])

`np.searchsorted.cs` orchestrator:
  - Validates (unchanged): side ∈ {left, right}, a is 1-D, sorter is 1-D and size==a.size
  - Normalizes v to contiguous of a's dtype (NumPy's `PyArray_CARRAY_RO`)
  - Normalizes sorter to contiguous int64
  - Looks up the right kernel, calls it with raw pointers
  - Scalar overloads go through a stackalloc 1-element buffer + the same kernel

## Type-specific paths

| Type | Load opcode | Compare |
|---|---|---|
| Int8/16/32/64 | Ldind_I[1-8] | clt / cgt+negate |
| UInt8/16/32/64 | Ldind_U[1-4]/I8 | clt.un / cgt.un+negate |
| Char | Ldind_U2 | clt.un / cgt.un+negate |
| Boolean | Ldind_U1 | clt.un / cgt.un+negate |
| Single | Ldind_R4 | clt / cgt+negate (signed float) |
| Double | Ldind_R8 | clt / cgt+negate |
| Half | Ldobj Half | Half.op_LessThan / op_LessThanOrEqual |
| Decimal | Ldobj decimal | decimal.op_LessThan / op_LessThanOrEqual |
| Complex | Ldind_R8 (Real only) | clt on double — preserves legacy Real-part comparison |

Complex memory layout (m_real, m_imaginary) puts Real at offset 0, so Ldind_R8 fetches Real
directly. Element stride remains 16 bytes (full Complex), only the *read* width narrows.

## Algorithmic parity items adopted from NumPy

1. **Monotonic key tracking** — when v is sorted, L_prev carries between bisects. This is where
   the 25-30× wins on sorted-key cases come from. NumPy comment: "Updating only one of the
   indices based on the previous key gives the search a big boost when keys are sorted".
2. **Contiguous v** (and contiguous int64 sorter) before the kernel call. Strided/typed v is
   copied via astype/copy. This is why strided-v benchmark went 0.76ms (NumPy) -> 0.40ms (us),
   beating NumPy because we copy once + tight loop instead of paying stride per access.
3. **Per-(dtype, side, sorter) specialization** with native compare. No boxing or conversion in
   the hot loop.

Doubles the kernel cache key (dtype × side × sorter × contiguousA) so that when a is

The JIT can then fold the stride into scaled-index addressing (mov reg, [base + idx*N])
instead of emitting a separate imul per bisect iteration.

perf(np.copyto): 0-d where-mask short-circuit, matching NumPy's nditer optimization

NumPy's array_assign_array.c:433-446 short-circuits a 0-dimensional boolean
wheremask before broadcasting:
  - where=True (0-d):  drop the mask, fall through to the unmasked fast path.
  - where=False (0-d): return immediately with no writes.

NumSharp previously broadcast every mask to dst.Shape and ran the per-element
CopyWithMask loop, which was catastrophically slow for the scalar False case:
copying nothing still scanned the entire destination.

This commit mirrors NumPy: a leading "shape is 0-d OR size == 1" check peeks
the single mask byte and either no-ops or hands off to NDIter.Copy.

refactor(np.copyto): centralize cross-dtype SIMD casts via ILKernelGenerator (replaces hardcoded SimdCast.cs)

Replaces ~700 lines of hardcoded typed SIMD methods (SimdCast.ByteToUInt16,
Int32ToInt64, SingleToInt32, etc.) with one IL-emitted DynamicMethod cached
per (src, dst) NPTypeCode pair. Same SIMD semantics, centralized in the
existing ILKernelGenerator partial-class architecture (joins 28 sibling files).

Architecture
------------
ILKernelGenerator.Cast.cs adds:
  - CastKernel delegate: void(void* src, void* dst, long count)
  - CastKernelKey struct: (NPTypeCode src, NPTypeCode dst)
  - ConcurrentDictionary cache + per-key "unsupported" memo (so unsupported
    pairs don't repeatedly re-attempt IL gen)
  - TryGetCastKernel(src, dst) public API — returns null for unsupported
    pairs (Boolean/Char/Half/Complex/Decimal involved)
  - ResolveStrategy(src, dst) — maps to one of 12 strategies:
      MemoryCopy, ScalarOnly, WidenInt, NarrowInt, WidenIntChain2,
      Int32ToSingle, Int32ToDouble, SingleToInt32, SmallIntToSingle,
      SingleToDouble, DoubleToSingle, (None)
  - 9 per-strategy IL emitters that call into Vector{128,256}.{Load, Store,
    WidenLower, WidenUpper, Narrow, ConvertToSingle, ConvertToDouble,
    ConvertToInt32, AsXxx} via reflection-resolved MethodInfo
  - Loop skeleton: SIMD body + scalar tail (when count is not a multiple
    of the vector step), or pure scalar loop when no SIMD path applies

Width selection mirrors the old hardcoded code:
  - WidenInt: V256 for src >= 4 bytes (Int32->Int64), V128 otherwise
  - NarrowInt: V128 (two loads -> one Narrow -> one store)
  - WidenIntChain2: V128, 4 stores per V128 input
  - Int32ToSingle / SingleToInt32: V256 (1:1 SIMD convert)
  - Int32ToDouble / SmallIntToSingle / SingleToDouble / DoubleToSingle: V128
    (forced by ConvertToDouble(V<long>) requiring AVX-512DQ above V128)

AVX-512-only conversions (UInt32<->Float, UInt64<->Float, Long<->Double,
Single->UInt32, Single->Int64, Double->Int32, Double->Int64, Double->UInt64)
emit pure scalar IL — same fallback as the hardcoded code, since
Vector256.ConvertToInt64/UInt64/UInt32 etc. require AVX-512.

NDIter.Copy hook
-----------------
NDIter.Copy was updated to call TryGetCastKernel + invoke when the cross-
dtype contiguous path is selected. Same gate as before
(state.IsContiguousCopy + size > 0); pairs that return null fall through
to the existing NDIterCasting.CopyStridedToStridedWithCast scalar dispatch.

Removed
-------
- src/NumSharp.Core/Backends/Kernels/SimdCast.cs (~700 lines, ~80 hardcoded
  methods). All cases are covered by IL gen with identical SIMD semantics.

Tests
-----
- All 8429 tests pass on both net8.0 and net10.0 (no regressions).
- 19 IL-cast smoke tests cover: V256 widen (Int32->Int64), V128 widen
  (Byte->UInt16, Int16->Int32, Single->Double), V128 narrow
  (Int16->Byte, Double->Single), 2-step widen (Byte->UInt32), ConvertTo
  paths (Int32->Single, Single->Int32, Int32->Double, Int16->Single,
  UInt16->Single), MemoryCopy same-size (Int32->UInt32), scalar tail
  on non-vector-multiple counts, AVX-512 scalar fallback (UInt32->Single),
  unsupported-pair null returns (Boolean, Decimal), sign extension
  (SByte->Int16), and negative-value Int32->Double.

Performance
-----------
10M-element bench on AVX-2 hardware (VectorBits=256):
  Int32->Int64:    8.0 ms  (NumPy: 6.0 ms)
  Byte->UInt16:    2.0 ms  (NumPy: 2.0 ms)
  Int16->Int32:    4.7 ms  (NumPy: 3.0 ms)
  Int32->Single:   6.8 ms  (NumPy: 3.7 ms)

ConvertTo*}). The DynamicMethod call site costs ~1.3x vs inlined static

perf(np.copyto): add IL StridedCastKernel for broadcast/strided cases (1.3-1.6× of NumPy, was 14-72× slower)

Extends the IL cast generator to handle non-contiguous source/dest layouts.
Previously the only fast path was contig→contig; everything else (broadcast,
strided slices, outer-strided-inner-contig) fell through to a scalar
coordinate-iterated loop ~14-72× slower than NumPy.

New StridedCastKernel
---------------------
Signature: void(void* src, void* dst, long* srcStrides, long* dstStrides, long* shape, int ndim)

IL emission per (srcType, dstType) pair, cached. The emitted IL:

1. ndim == 0: single scalar conversion; return.

2. Outer loop walks all dims except innermost via coord array (stackalloc/localloc).
   At each outer position the IL checks at runtime:

   2a. If srcStrides[innerAxis] == 1 AND dstStrides[innerAxis] == 1:
       - Same-type (MemoryCopy strategy): emit Buffer.MemoryCopy for the inner row.
       - Cross-type: emit the same SIMD body used by the contig kernel
         (WidenLower/Upper, Narrow, ConvertTo*) over shape[innerAxis] elements.

   2b. Else (inner is strided): emit a scalar inner loop with incremental
       offset advance (innerSrcOff += innerSrcStride, no mod/div).

3. Outer coord advance is also incremental:
   - coords[axis]++ ; offsets += strides[axis]
   - On carry: coords[axis] = 0 ; offsets -= strides[axis] * shape[axis]
   No mod/div per element per axis.

Architecture changes
--------------------
SIMD body emitters refactored to take `Action pushSrcBase` / `Action pushDstBase`
lambdas instead of hardcoded Ldarg_0/Ldarg_1. The contig kernel passes
() => Ldarg_0 / () => Ldarg_1; the strided kernel passes ldarg + outerOffset + add.
This lets both kernels share the same SIMD body emission code.

NDIter.Copy integration
------------------------
- Same-type contig: existing CopyKernel.Contiguous (cpblk) — fastest possible.
- Same-type strided/broadcast: routes through StridedCastKernel (Int32→Int32 etc.
  → MemoryCopy strategy → Buffer.MemoryCopy per inner row). Replaces
  CopyGeneralSameType which did mod/div per element per axis.
- Cross-dtype contig: existing CastKernel.
- Cross-dtype strided/broadcast: new StridedCastKernel.
- Last resort (Decimal/Complex/Half/Char/Boolean): scalar coord iter.

perf(np.copyto): IL MaskedCastKernel for where= masked copies (1.0-1.2× of NumPy, was 7-13×)

Replaces the fully scalar CopyWithMask coord-iter (3 muladds per element per
axis + ConvertValue switch + double round-trip) with a centralized IL kernel.

New MaskedCastKernel
--------------------
Signature: void(void* src, void* dst, void* mask,
                long* srcStrides, long* dstStrides, long* maskStrides,
                long* shape, int ndim)

One DynamicMethod per (srcType, dstType) pair, cached. The emitted IL:

1. ndim == 0: single conditional element (if mask, convert-and-store).

2. Walk outer dims via stackalloc coord array; offsets advance incrementally
   (no mod/div).

3. At each outer position the IL checks at runtime:

   3a. If srcStride[innerAxis] == 1 AND dstStride[innerAxis] == 1
       AND maskStride[innerAxis] == 1:

       3a-i.  For 1:1-lane strategies (MemoryCopy, Int32ToSingle, SingleToInt32):
              SIMD masked path. Per iteration:
                vNew      = strategy(V.Load(src+i*srcSize))
                vOld      = V.Load(dst+i*dstSize)
                vMaskBits = expand vstep mask bytes to V<int> of dstSize width
                            (WidenLower chain + zero-subtract for 0→0, 1→-1)
                result    = V.ConditionalSelect(vMaskBits.AsT(), vNew, vOld)
                result.Store(dst+i*dstSize)
              Scalar tail when count is not a vector multiple.

       3a-ii. For widen/narrow/multi-lane strategies (Int32→Int64, Int16→Int32,
              Byte→UInt16, etc.): scalar inner with mask gate + inline IL
              conversion. SIMD per-store mask expansion was deemed too complex
              for the gain on these paths (still 10-13ms vs NumPy 8-12ms).

   3b. Else (one or more inner strides non-unit): scalar inner loop with
       mask gate + incremental offset advance.

Architecture notes
------------------
The masked kernel reuses ResolveStrategy() and CastKernelKey from the contig
cast kernel. The kernel cache (_maskedCastCache) is separate to allow distinct
IL bodies; both kernels share the same Vector method lookup helpers
(GetVectorLoadMethod, GetWidenLowerMethod, etc.) in ILKernelGenerator.Cast.cs.

For the SIMD masked path, mask bytes (1 per element) are expanded to V<dst>
width via Vector128.WidenLower chains, then `V<int>.Zero - V<int>` converts
0→0 and 1→-1 (all-bits-set). The reinterpret-as-V<dst> step uses the existing
GetAsMethod helper.

JIT note: DynamicMethod calls run interpreted in tier 0 until the JIT promotes
them to tier 1 (typically ~25-50 calls). The bench needed WARM=50 to capture
steady-state performance; with WARM=10 the masked kernel measured ~11× slower
purely from interpretation overhead. Real workloads naturally warm up.

perf(np.copyto): broadcast convert-once + memcpy fast path (int32->float32 broadcast: 7.53→2.31ms, matches NumPy)

Closes the last remaining gap in the IL strided cast kernel: when the source
is broadcast across all outer dims (all outer srcStrides == 0) and the
innermost axis is contiguous for both src and dst, we now convert the source
row ONCE and memcpy the result into every outer dst position.

Previously the strided kernel re-ran the SIMD conversion body for each outer
row, doing M conversions for an M-row broadcast. NumPy does the same trick
(see numpy/_core/src/multiarray/dtype_transfer.c get_unindexed_setrange_loops
which detects stride-0 srcs and uses the row-tiling path).

Detection in EmitStridedCastBody (runtime, at IL kernel entry)
--------------------------------------------------------------
1. outerNdim > 0          (must have outer dims to broadcast across)
2. innerSrcStride == 1    (inner src is contig)
3. innerDstStride == 1    (inner dst is contig)
4. srcStrides[d] == 0 ∀ d ∈ [0, outerNdim)
                          (every outer dim is fully broadcasted)

If all four hold, branch to the fast path. Otherwise fall through to the
existing outer-coord-iter (which handles strided outer / strided inner /
mixed cases identically to before).

Fast path body
--------------
Step 1: Convert one source row → dst[0..innerN].
        - Same-type: Buffer.MemoryCopy(src, dst, innerN*srcSize, ...).
        - Cross-type: SIMD loop + scalar tail for innerN elements
          (reuses EmitSimdLoopAndTail with srcBase=arg0, dstBase=arg1).

Step 2: For each remaining outer dst position, memcpy dst[0..innerN] →
        dst[outerDstOffset..]. Outer coord advance is the same incremental
        pattern as the regular outer loop — no mod/div per row.

The outer iteration walks ALL non-zero outer dst positions; the first row
(coords all 0) is already filled by step 1 so the loop starts after the
first coord advance.

perf(np.copyto): IL-emitted any-true mask prescan inside MaskedCastKernel (all-false: 10.3ms→1.1ms; 2D-broadcast all-false: 0.001ms)

Closes the where=array all-false 11× gap vs NumPy without leaking the
optimization out of the IL kernel architecture — the prescan is emitted as
part of each (srcType, dstType) MaskedCastKernel DynamicMethod, sitting at
the top of the kernel body. No C# pre-scan helper in np.copyto.cs.

IL prescan structure (emitted at kernel entry, after the ndim==0 branch)
------------------------------------------------------------------------
Phase 1: Compute the unique-byte length of the mask buffer at runtime.
  Walk dims inner→outer; for each axis:
    - stride == 0 : broadcast dim, skip (bytes repeat)
    - stride == expected_contig_stride : contig dim, unique *= shape[d]
    - else : non-contig pattern, branch to lblSkipPrescan (prescan disabled)
  Result: unique_size = bytes that uniquely cover the mask buffer's
  reachable byte set. For (1,K)→(M,K) broadcast this is K, not M*K.

Phase 2: SIMD scan unique_size bytes starting at maskBase.
  V256<byte> when VectorBits>=256, V128<byte> when 128, scalar tail.
  Per chunk: V.EqualsAll(chunk, V<byte>.Zero) returns bool.
    - true  (all bytes zero) -> next chunk
    - false (any non-zero)   -> branch to lblSkipPrescan (found a true)
  Reaching the end of unique_size without finding a non-zero byte
  branches to lblRet (caller's "return" label) — kernel work is skipped.

Phase 3 (fall-through label lblSkipPrescan): existing masked kernel body.

Behavior matrix
---------------
mask pattern              Phase 1 detects      Phase 2 outcome          Effect
all-false contig          unique = total       no true → goto lblRet    skip kernel
all-false broadcast       unique = inner row   no true → goto lblRet    skip kernel (tiny scan)
all-true contig           unique = total       first chunk → skip       proceed (~0.3ms scan overhead)
sparse contig             unique = total       early chunk → skip       proceed (~ns scan)
strided mask              non-contig → skip    (skipped)                proceed without prescan

Helpers added
-------------
- EmitMaskAnyTruePrescan(ILGenerator, Label): emits the full prescan IL,
  branches to the passed lblRet on all-false.
- GetEqualsAllMethod(simdBits, elementType): reflects Vector{N}.EqualsAll<T>,
  matches by (genericArity=1, paramCount=2, returnType=bool).

perf(np.nonzero): IL-emitted SIMD kernel — closes 8-241x gap to NumPy

The np.where(cond) index form (= np.nonzero) was routed through
FindNonZeroStridedHelper unconditionally, even for contiguous arrays.
That helper does N multiplies per element to compute elemOffset and
allocates a fresh long[ndim] per non-zero hit (huge GC pressure for
dense data). The contig SIMD helper that existed was never reached.

Three new IL-emitted kernels (DynamicMethod via System.Reflection.Emit,
cached as delegates):

  IsAllZeroBoolKernel:      bool(byte* mask, long size)
    SIMD any-true prescan. Vector{256,128}<byte>.EqualsAll(load, Zero)
    short-circuits on the first non-zero chunk. Matches NumPy's all-false
    short-circuit. Builds the kernel specialized for the detected
    VectorBits at startup — no V128/V256 if/else in the JIT'd code.

  NonZeroCountBoolKernel:   long(byte* mask, long size)
    SIMD popcount of non-zero bytes. PopCount(~ExtractMostSignificantBits)
    per chunk + scalar tail. Used to pre-size the output buffer to exact
    count — avoids the pathological "alloc 80MB max-size buffer to discard"
    case for dense masks. NumPy does the same two-pass approach.

  NonZeroFlatBoolKernel:    long(byte* mask, long* outBuf, long size)
    SIMD bit-scan that materializes flat indices via BitOperations.
    TrailingZeroCount per set bit. For ndim==1 writes directly into
    result[0].Address (no temp buffer). For ndim>1 writes to a buffer
    sized exactly to count, then BuildCoordinatesFromFlat converts to
    per-dim coords in a single pass.

Refactored nonzeros<T> in Default.NonZero.cs to route:
  * Empty                  → tuple of empty index arrays.
  * Contig + T=bool        → IL kernels (prescan → count → scan).
  * Contig + other dtypes  → existing NonZeroSimdHelper<T> (generic V*<T>).
  * Non-contig             → FindNonZeroStridedHelper (unchanged).

Removed the dead comment claiming "strided helper handles all cases".

Benchmark (10M / 1M elements, after 100 warmup, 200 iterations):

  where(1pct 10M)          ~50 ms    2.1 ms  2.2  ms     0.95x (faster)
  where(2D 1Kx1K 50pct)  18.18 ms   6.21 ms  5.9  ms     1.05x
  nonzero(int32 1M)        ~10 ms   8.48 ms  2.3  ms     3.7x

perf(np.where): IL-emitted scalar-broadcast Where kernels

np.where(cond, scalar, arr) and np.where(cond, arr, scalar) were 6.5x
slower than the same-shape contig path because asanyarray(scalar)
produces a 0-d array, broadcast_arrays expands it to a stride-0 view,
and the IsContiguous gate in np.where_internal drops to NDIter.

Three new IL-emitted kernels (DynamicMethod via System.Reflection.Emit,
cached per T):

  WhereScalarXKernel<T>(bool* cond, T scalarX, T* y, T* result, long count)
  WhereScalarYKernel<T>(bool* cond, T* x, T scalarY, T* result, long count)
  WhereScalarXYKernel<T>(bool* cond, T scalarX, T scalarY, T* result, long count)

Each kernel hoists the scalar into V<T>.Create(scalar) ONCE before the
SIMD loop via a typed local. Inside the loop we Ldloc the pre-broadcast
vector instead of loading from memory each iteration.

GetVectorCreateBroadcast prefers the type-specific Create(T) overload
(e.g. Vector256.Create(double)) over the generic Create<T>(T) — the
JIT folds the non-generic overload to a single vbroadcastsd/vpbroadcastd
instruction, while the generic version routed through a runtime helper
that added ~30-50% per call on .NET 8.

The IsGenericParameter check is the precise discriminator when picking
the broadcast overload — Vector256 has 5 single-arg generic Create
overloads (T, T[], ReadOnlySpan<T>, Vector128<T> for concat, Vector64<T>
for concat) and only the first has a parameter that IS the generic
parameter T itself.

Routing in np.where_internal:
  * Pre-detect xIsScalar/yIsScalar on user-supplied operands BEFORE
    broadcast_arrays expands them into stride-0 views.
  * After dtype promotion, if cond is contig + at least one operand was
    a scalar, cast the 0-d original to outType (1-element NDArray) and
    dispatch the scalar IL kernel.
  * Fall back to the existing NDIter path when no IL kernel is available
    (no SIMD, unsupported dtype).

Benchmark (1M elements, after 100 warmup, 200 iterations):

  Dtype     Test            Before    After    NumPy   Ratio AFTER/NumPy
  float32   scalar-x       6.69 ms   0.78 ms  0.86 ms      0.91x (faster)
  float32   scalar-y       6.65 ms   0.85 ms  0.83 ms      1.02x
  float32   scalar-x-y     6.77 ms   0.73 ms  0.85 ms      0.86x (faster)
  int32     scalar-x        ~7 ms    0.77 ms     n/a       n/a
  int32     scalar-y        ~7 ms    0.86 ms     n/a       n/a
  double    scalar-x       ~7-10 ms  1.60 ms  1.50 ms      1.07x
  double    scalar-y       ~7-10 ms  2.51 ms  1.54 ms      1.63x (residual gap)

Closed the 2.1-2.3x scalar gap to ~1x for float/int32 and most double
cases. Double scalar-y has a 1.6x remaining gap — JIT codegen difference
between Ldloc-first-then-Load and Load-first-then-Ldloc that's not yet
understood. Net win is still >3x vs the original NDIter path on every
dtype.

All 8429 tests pass on net8.0 / net10.0.

refactor(IL): consolidate Vector* reflection into VectorMethodCache

Before this change the IL kernel partials each owned a slice of the
Vector{128,256,512} reflection surface:

  * Top-level ILKernelGenerator.cs had GetVectorContainerType /
    GetVectorType for runtime width dispatch.
  * Cast.cs had its own file-private VType / ContainerType + 9 Get*Method
    helpers (Load, Store, WidenLower/Upper, Narrow, ConvertTo{Single,
    Double,Int32}, As).
  * Cast.Masked.cs had GetConditionalSelectMethod, GetCreateFromTwoMethod,
    GetEqualsAllMethod (duplicated against Cast.cs's helpers).
  * NonZero.cs had GetEqualsAllMethodNZ, GetVectorEqualsMethodNZ,
    GetExtractMostSignificantBitsMethodNZ (NZ-suffixed because the same
    helpers already lived as private statics elsewhere in the partial
    class).
  * Where.Scalar.cs had GetVectorCreateBroadcast.
  * Binary / Comparison / Reduction / Reduction.NaN / Unary.Vector /
    Shift / MixedType all had ~30 inline ad-hoc lookups of the shape
    `containerType.GetMethods(BF.Public | Static).Where(m.Name == "X" &&
    m.IsGenericMethod && paramCount == N).Select(MakeGenericMethod(T)).
    First(...)` — same pattern, six places.

Single source of truth now lives in
src/NumSharp.Core/Backends/Kernels/VectorMethodCache.cs:

  * Container(int simdBits) -> typeof(Vector{128,256,512})
  * V(int simdBits, Type elem) -> Vector{N}<T>
  * Generic ops cached as CLOSED MethodInfo (so callers don't allocate a
    fresh closed generic per IL emission): Load, Store, ConditionalSelect,
    Equals (vector-returning), EqualsAll (bool-returning), GreaterThan,
    LessThan, ExtractMostSignificantBits, CreateScalar, GetLower, GetUpper,
    GetElement, OnesComplement.
  * Multiply / Divide disambiguated into MultiplyVectorVector vs
    MultiplyVectorScalar (the (V, T) scalar overload is distinct from
    (V, V) and the cache makes that explicit).
  * Non-generic-by-arg-type: WidenLower, WidenUpper, Narrow,
    ConvertToSingleFromInt32, ConvertToDoubleFromInt64,
    ConvertToInt32FromSingle.
  * CreateBroadcast — prefers the non-generic Create(T) over generic
    Create<T>(T) (JIT folds the non-generic to a single vbroadcastsd /
    vpbroadcastd; the generic routed through a runtime helper on .NET 8
    for double and added 30-50% per call).
  * CreateFromHalves — V256.Create(V128 lo, V128 hi).
  * As(simdBits, fromElem, toElem) — tries AsX<from> first, falls back
    to the two-type-parameter As<from, to>.
  * Operator(simdBits, elem, "op_Addition" / "op_Multiply" / etc.) for
    Vector{N}<T> operator overloads (used by MatMul, Binary, Unary).
  * Zero / One — Vector{N}<T>.{Zero,One} property getters.
  * ShiftByScalar — non-generic (V<T>, int) overload used by left/right
    shifts.
  * Generic(simdBits, name, elem, paramCount?) — escape hatch for the
    less-common ops.

Cache layout: one ConcurrentDictionary<Key, MethodInfo> for ops, one for
operators, one for the (simdBits, from, to) As family, one for property
getters. The Key bit-packs paramCount + discriminator into one slot so
the same struct serves all op families.

Files migrated (all switch their helpers to thin delegates or replace
inline lookups):
  * ILKernelGenerator.cs — top-level GetVectorContainerType/Type now
    delegate to the cache. Inline lookups in EmitVectorLoad / Store /
    Create / MinOrMax / Operation replaced.
  * Cast.cs — VType / ContainerType / Get{Vector,WidenLower,WidenUpper,
    Narrow,ConvertTo*,As}Method now one-liners over the cache. Cast.Masked.cs
    helpers (ConditionalSelect, CreateFromTwo, EqualsAll) the same.
  * NonZero.cs — drops the NZ-suffixed helpers entirely; call sites use
    VectorMethodCache.{Load,Zero,Equals,EqualsAll,ExtractMostSignificantBits}
    directly.
  * Where.Scalar.cs — drops GetVectorCreateBroadcast; call sites use
    VectorMethodCache.CreateBroadcast.
  * Binary.cs, Comparison.cs, Reduction.cs, Reduction.NaN.cs,
    Unary.Vector.cs, Shift.cs, MixedType.cs, Clip.cs — inline GetMethods
    lookups replaced with cache calls (Generic + Operator + MultiplyVV +
    OnesComplement + Equals + ExtractMostSignificantBits + GetLower /
    Upper / Element + ShiftByScalar).

Side benefit: the new cache caches CLOSED MethodInfo, while several of
the old call sites recomputed MakeGenericMethod on every emission. On
the np.where benchmark, double scalar-y dropped from 2.51ms to 1.77ms
post-migration (~30% faster) — fewer reflection allocations per IL
kernel build. No regressions on the other dtypes.

feat(np.expand_dims): NumPy 2.x tuple-axis support

np.expand_dims now accepts a tuple/sequence of axes in addition to a
single int, matching NumPy 2.x's full surface:

    np.expand_dims(np.arange(6).reshape(2,3), (0, 2)).shape == (1, 2, 1, 3)
    np.expand_dims(a, (-1, -2)).shape == (2, 3, 1, 1)
    np.expand_dims(a, (2, 1, 0)).shape == (1, 1, 1, 2, 3)
    np.expand_dims(a, ()).shape == a.shape  # no-op

Surface additions
- np.expand_dims(NDArray, int[])               -- canonical tuple-axis API
- np.expand_dims(NDArray, IEnumerable<int>)    -- sequence overload, delegates
- Shape.ExpandDimensions(int[])                -- reusable multi-axis builder

Semantics (NumPy parity)
- Each axis is normalized against the FINAL output ndim
  (out_ndim = inputNdim + axes.Length), not against the input ndim.
- Duplicate normalized positions raise ArgumentException("repeated axis")
  -- matches NumPy's `ValueError: repeated axis`. Detected after
  normalization so e.g. (0, -4) for ndim=2 collides at position 0.
- Out-of-range axes raise
  ArgumentException("axis N is out of bounds for array of dimension M"),
  the .NET analog of NumPy's AxisError.
- Empty axis list (and null) returns the input unchanged.
- Result is a view (Storage.Alias of the new shape) -- no copy.

Implementation
- Shape.ExpandDimensions normalizes + validates + sorts ascending, then
  iteratively calls the existing single-axis ExpandDimension. Sorting
  ascending guarantees each insert sees a stable "earlier dims already
  inserted" view so axis indices stay correct against the partial output.
- The single-int overload is untouched; behavior unchanged.

Testing
- 16 new unit tests in np.expand_dims.Test.cs covering: positive/negative
  axes, mixed signs, unsorted input, empty tuple, duplicates (direct and
  via negative normalization), out-of-range positive/negative, the
  IEnumerable overload, null axis, view semantics.
- AuditV2 ExpandDims_TupleAxis_Implemented is now a passing test (no
  longer [OpenBugs]).
- Existing 3 single-int tests preserved.
- Full manipulation/shape/audit suite: 810 passed, 0 failed.

Reference: numpy/lib/_shape_base_impl.py:516 (expand_dims).
Audit ref: docs/plans/audit_v2/06_manipulation_apis_logic.md (Section 1.3).

feat(np.concatenate): full NumPy 2.x parity + fast paths

NumPy signature now matched in full:
    np.concatenate(arrays, axis=0, out=None, *, dtype=None, casting='same_kind')

Bugs fixed
- T1.8: dtype promotion now uses np.result_type (NEP50). Previously
  used NPTypeCode.CompareTo (enum-ordinal ordering) which mis-promoted
  e.g. float32+int64 -> float32 instead of float64; half+float -> half
  instead of float (Half=16 ranks above Single=13 in the enum);
  int8+uint8 -> byte instead of int16.
- T1.9: mixed-dtype copy now routes through ILKernelGenerator cast
  kernels (no astype intermediate). Previously crashed on certain
  SByte/Half/Complex pairs via NDIterCasting; the IL kernel path
  handles every (src,dst) pair in the cross-product.
- Single-array `np.concatenate([a])` now returns a fresh copy (NumPy
  parity); the previous `arrays.Length == 1 -> return arrays[0]`
  short-circuit aliased caller storage.

New parameters (NumPy 1.20+ surface)
- axis: int? (default 0). Passing null flattens every input to 1-D and
  concatenates along axis 0, matching NumPy's `axis=None` flatten mode.
- out: NDArray (default null). When provided, writes into the
  destination and returns it. Shape must match what would have been
  allocated without out. Cannot combine with dtype.
- dtype: NPTypeCode? (default null). Forces the output dtype,
  overriding NEP50 promotion. Cannot combine with out.
- casting: string (default "same_kind"). One of 'no', 'equiv', 'safe',
  'same_kind', 'unsafe'. Validated up-front (NumPy raises ValueError
  on unknown values); per-input cast feasibility checked via
  np.can_cast, raising InvalidCastException with the NumPy-style
  "Cannot cast array data from dtype('X') to dtype('Y') according to
  the rule 'Z'" message.

Edge cases brought into line with NumPy
- 0-D arrays raise ArgumentException("zero-dimensional arrays cannot
  be concatenated").
- Negative axis is normalized against input ndim (ArgumentOutOfRangeException
  if still out of bounds).
- Mismatched ndim raises IncorrectShapeException with the NumPy
  "same number of dimensions" message.
- Non-axis dimension mismatch raises IncorrectShapeException with the
  NumPy "must match exactly" message.
- Empty input along the axis is now skipped rather than mishandled.
- F-contiguity preservation: when ALL inputs are F-contig, output is
  F-contig. Earlier check rejected (1,N) inputs that are both C- and
  F-contig (ambiguous layout); the new check votes them as F.

Performance — two new fast paths
1. TryDirectMemcpyConcat — when every source is same-dtype as the
   result and C-contig (and dst C-contig), compute byte offsets per
   outer slab and call Buffer.MemoryCopy directly. Bypasses NDIter
   slicing and view machinery.
2. TryDirectCastConcat — same shape/layout assumptions but mixed
   dtypes. Drives the IL contig cast kernel per source with computed
   pointer offsets. Bypasses NDIter.Copy state construction and any
   intermediate astype temp.
   Same-dtype slabs within the mixed call still use Buffer.MemoryCopy.

Output buffer no longer zero-initialized (`fillZeros: false` on
allocation) since every byte is overwritten -- saves ~20us for an
80KB allocation; scales with output size.

Bench vs NumPy 2.4.2 (median of 100 after 20-iter warmup, Windows 11)
  1D int32 contig (1M+1M)         NS 0.89 ms  vs  NP 1.01 ms   0.88x (faster)
  1D float64 contig (1M+1M)       NS 1.91 ms  vs  NP 2.08 ms   0.92x (faster)
  2D contig axis=0 (1000x100 x2)  NS 0.15 ms  vs  NP 0.01 ms   12x  (per-call overhead)
  2D contig axis=1 (1000x100 x2)  NS 0.12 ms  vs  NP 0.02 ms   7x   (per-call overhead)
  Mixed int32+float32 (1M+1M)     NS 3.43 ms  vs  NP 2.56 ms   1.34x (bandwidth-bound widening cast)
  8 arrays x 100k int32           NS 0.60 ms  vs  NP 0.62 ms   0.98x (par)
  100 arrays x 10k int32          NS 0.74 ms  vs  NP 0.78 ms   0.96x (par)
Bandwidth-bound paths (>=1M elements) now match or beat NumPy. Small
2D arrays remain slower than NumPy's tightly-coupled C dispatcher.

Tests

docs(np.concatenate): justify custom fast paths over NDIter.Copy

A reviewer asked: why have TryDirectMemcpyConcat/TryDirectCastConcat
when NDIter.Copy already handles same-dtype copies, IL contig cast
kernels, IL strided cast kernels, and the scalar fallback?

I tested the simplification (removing both fast paths and routing
everything through NDIter.Copy(dst[axis_range], src)). Results:

  Scenario                            Fast path   NDIter-only   Delta
  layout_f_contig_2d_axis0            1.47 ms     22.94 ms       16x worse
  layout_transposed_2d_axis0          1.36 ms     23.92 ms       18x worse
  layout_c_contig_2d_axis1            1.29 ms      2.16 ms       1.7x worse
  prom_int32_float32                  2.44 ms      4.00 ms       1.6x worse
  prom_int32_int64                    2.38 ms      3.43 ms       1.4x worse
  count_1024 (1024x 100k int32)      78.85 ms    122.13 ms       1.5x worse

Root cause: for an F-contig dst, slicing `dst[0:M, :]` produces a
shape with strides (1, full_M) and dim (M, N) -- the inter-column
stride still points to the ORIGINAL full-height column boundary, so
the slice is neither C- nor F-contig. NDIter.Copy's IsContiguousCopy
fast path bails, the IL contig cast kernel doesn't apply, and the
copy falls into the strided path with a coordinate iterator.

The custom fast paths sidestep this by computing per-outer-slab byte
offsets directly against dst.Storage.Address, never materializing a
sliced view. Each outer iteration of the for-loop emits a single
memcpy (or IL cast kernel call) per source -- exactly what the
strided path *should* devolve to but doesn't, because NDIter has no
"all-sources-same-layout-as-dst-cluster-write" detection.

Fixing this inside NDIter would benefit every np.* function that
slices into an F-contig dst, but it's a much larger change. The
~250 LOC of bookkeeping here pays for itself with the 16-18x F-contig
speedup that callers depending on F-contig output (numerical linear
algebra, BLAS-aligned interop) rely on.

This commit just expands the inline justification block at the call
site and updates the XML doc comments on the two helpers so future
readers don't repeat the same simplification attempt.

perf(NDIter): K-order axis permutation in CreateCopyState

NDIter.Copy previously fell into the strided slow path for F-contig
and transposed dst views because CreateCopyState built the iterator
state in raw axis order, leaving the unit-stride axis at the OUTER
position (axis 0) instead of innermost (axis NDim-1). The IL strided
cast kernel's inner-contig fast branch only fires when innermost has
unit stride for both src and dst -- otherwise it falls through to a
scalar inner loop, ~17x slower than per-row memcpy.

Example -- F-contig dst (2000, 1000) sliced as dst[0:1000, :]:
  Before permutation:
    shape=(1000, 1000), src strides=(1, 1000), dst strides=(1, 2000)
    Innermost axis stride: src=1000, dst=2000 -> strided scalar loop
  After permutation (descending by min stride):
    shape=(1000, 1000), src strides=(1000, 1), dst strides=(2000, 1)
    Innermost axis stride: src=1, dst=1 -> inner memcpy per outer row

The permutation infrastructure already existed in NDIterCoalescing
(ReorderAxesForCoalescing, used by the full NDIter constructor for
K/A/C/F orders) -- CreateCopyState just wasn't calling it. One-line
fix: invoke with NPY_KEEPORDER + forCoalescing=false (descending sort)
after CoalesceAxes. Skipped when NDim <= 1.

Bench impact (1M+1M int32, fresh dst, median of 100):
  NDIter.Copy F-contig slice:    22.94 ms -> 0.29 ms   (79x faster)
  NDIter.Copy transposed:        23.92 ms -> 0.30 ms   (80x faster)
  NDIter.Copy 1D contig:          0.21 ms -> 0.21 ms   (unchanged)
  NDIter.Copy cross-dtype 1D:     2.00 ms -> 2.00 ms   (unchanged)

This is a GENERAL improvement to NDIter -- every np.* function that
copies into an F-contig or transposed slice (numerical linear
algebra, BLAS interop, manipulation APIs) benefits.

np.concatenate keeps its custom TryDirect{Memcpy,Cast}Concat fast
paths because they still win ~50-90% on workloads they cover by
skipping the dst[axis_range] slice creation and per-source NDIter
state construction -- savings that amortize over many small calls
(count_1024) or compound across many copies. Updated the in-source
comment to reflect the layered structure (fast paths first, then
the improved NDIter.Copy as fallback).

All other callers of NDIter.Copy (np.copyto, NDArray view writes,
stack/vstack/hstack, etc.) get the fix transparently.

perf(NDIter): skip np.broadcast_to in CreateCopyState when shapes match

Add a tight inline check (ShapesMatchExactly) in NDIter.CreateCopyState
that bypasses np.broadcast_to entirely when src and dst already have
identical dimensions. In that case the broadcast result is just src.Shape
unchanged, so we reuse it directly — skipping ValidateBroadcastTo,
Shape.Broadcast dispatch, and the (already hash-shortcut) allocation path.

ShapesMatchExactly compares NDim and dimension values position-by-position.
Strides are intentionally NOT compared because the iterator walks each side
with its own strides regardless of layout — same-dim is sufficient to
guarantee no broadcast stretching is required. This covers the very common
"copy into a same-shape destination" case (concatenate slices, ascontiguous
copy, astype, np.copy, etc.).

Falls through to np.broadcast_to for the genuine broadcast cases:
  - Different NDim (e.g. src=(N,) → dst=(M,N) requires dim prepend)
  - Any axis where src=1 but dst>1 (broadcast stretch → stride 0)
  - Any axis where src!=dst (validation throws)

Microbenchmark: saves ~13 ns/call vs the hash-shortcut path through
np.broadcast_to. Small per-call, but compounds in tight loops
(concatenate's count_1024 = 1024 NDIter.Copy calls).

feat(memory): atomic reference counting (ARC) + IDisposable on NDArray

Replaces the prior bool-Disposed pattern with full atomic refcounting on
UnmanagedMemoryBlock<T>.Disposer so unmanaged buffer release happens
deterministically when the last logical owner releases — no more waiting
on the CLR finalizer queue.

L1: Refcounted Disposer (UnmanagedMemoryBlock`1.cs)
- _refCount: long, starts at 0, encoded -1 = released
- TryAddRef: CAS-driven add; returns false on released blocks
- Release: Decrement + CAS 0→-1 to claim free transition atomically;
  stray Releases self-heal one-for-one via Increment
- _freed: int guard so ReleaseUnmanagedResources runs exactly once even
  when finalizer races concurrent Release/Dispose
- Wrap allocations bypass refcount entirely (immortal non-owners)
- Finalizer remains as safety net for the user-forgot-Dispose path

L2: NDArray IDisposable (NDArray.cs)
- _disposed: int (not byte — Interlocked.Exchange's narrowest type)
- Idempotent Dispose() via single CAS — multiple calls safe
- ~NDArray() finalizer drops the ref if Dispose was missed
- InitializeArc() called from every concrete ctor; bumps refcount via
  IArraySlice.TryAddRef on the underlying MemoryBlock

Interface additions
- IUnmanagedMemoryBlock: TryAddRef, Release, IsReleased
- IArraySlice: same (forwards to underlying MemoryBlock struct)
- ArraySlice<T>: passthrough implementation

perf(np.concatenate): use `using` on internal intermediates for atomic release

np.concatenate allocates two kinds of owning NDArray intermediates that
previously rode the finalizer queue until GC:

1. **`workArrays` from ravel (axis=null path)** — Every input is ravel'd
   into a new NDArray wrapper, even when ravel returns a view of the
   caller's storage. Without explicit release each wrapper sits on the
   finalizer queue holding an ARC ref to the caller's buffer.
2. **`dstSlice` inside the general loop** — `dst[dstAccessor]` produces
   a fresh sliced view per source. N-source concatenates queue N dead
   wrappers per call; under tight loops these compound.

Refactor:
- Track ravel'd workArrays in `disposableWorkArrays` and dispose them
  in a finally that wraps the body. Caller's `arrays[]` are never
  touched (Rule 1 — the ravel wrappers always alias, never re-bind).
- Add `using` to `dstSlice` inside the per-source copy loop. The
  storage is kept alive by `dst` (the return value), so the using on
  the slice wrapper only drops the wrapper's local ARC ref.

Safety:
- Inputs (`arrays`, `@out`) and return value (`dst`) untouched
  (Rule 1 + Rule 2).
- `disposableWorkArrays` is null whenever axis != null, so the
  finally is a no-op on the common path.
- `dstSlice` is unambiguously an owning intermediate (new wrapper
  via Slice indexing, never returned).

perf(np.allclose): use `using` on the np.isclose intermediate

DefaultEngine.AllClose is a one-liner: np.all(np.isclose(...)). The
np.isclose result is a bool NDArray with the shape of broadcast(a, b)
— a strictly transient buffer that np.all collapses to a single bool.

Before this commit the closeness array dropped to the finalizer queue,
which in a tight comparison loop (e.g., per-step convergence checks
in iterative solvers) accumulated hundreds of dead wrappers each
holding an ARC ref to a fresh unmanaged buffer.

Adding `using var closeness = np.isclose(...)` releases the buffer
atomically as soon as np.all has finished consuming it. The wrapper
is unambiguously owning (np.isclose always allocates a new result
NDArray) and unambiguously not the return value (this function
returns `bool`), so no Rule 1 or Rule 2 risk.

perf(np.random.shuffle): use `using` on swap temps in SwapSlicesAxis0

SwapSlicesAxis0 is called per pair from the multi-dim Fisher-Yates
loop in shuffle(). It allocates three NDArray intermediates per call:

  var sliceI = x[i];           // view wrapper
  var sliceJ = x[j];           // view wrapper
  var temp   = sliceI.copy();  // fresh owned row-buffer

A shuffle on an N-row array calls this up to (N-1) times, so without
explicit release each shuffle queued (N-1) * 3 NDArray wrappers plus
(N-1) unmanaged copy buffers onto the finalizer queue.

The intermediates are unambiguously owning (the views participate in
ARC; the .copy() always allocates a fresh buffer) and unambiguously
not returned (this is a void helper). Add `using` to all three.

- Caller's `x` and the per-row slices' shared storage are kept alive
  by x's outer reference (Rule 1).
- Helper is `void` (no Rule 2 risk).

perf(np.random.exponential): use `using` on the log intermediate

np.random.exponential(scale, size) is computed as:

    log(1 - uniform(0, 1, size))   →  x

The `x` buffer (a Double NDArray the size of `size`) is consumed
exactly once by np.negative; the multiplication by `scale` then
produces the returned NDArray. With ARC available there's no reason
to leave `x` on the finalizer queue.

Safety:
- Pure local intermediate; no caller-owned alias (Rule 1 N/A).
- Return value (`np.negative(x) * scale`) is a fresh NDArray
  produced by two more operations; it does NOT alias `x`'s buffer

perf(boolean-mask indexing): `using` on per-iter view wrappers

NDArray.Indexing.Masking.cs walks the mask row-by-row and allocates
view wrappers per iteration in two helpers:

- BooleanMaskAxis0 (getter):

    var destSlice = result[destIdx]; // view of result
- SetBooleanMaskAxis0 (setter):

On an N-row array these loops can allocate 2N (getter) or N (setter)

immediately consumed by np.copyto. With ARC, each can be released
atomically at iteration end.

(return value), so disposing the view wrappers only drops the
wrappers' ARC refs — Rule 1 safe.

`v` chains through caller-owned `value`, so it stays NOT `using`-bound
(Rule 1). The added comment in the source makes the asymmetry explicit.

perf(np.eye): use `using` on the flat view wrapper

np.eye walks the diagonal via:

`flat` is an owning view wrapper into `m`'s storage, used only to
drive the diagonal write and then discarded. Scope it via

left untouched — `m` is the return value on the C-order path, so it
can't be `using`-bound here without splitting the return logic
(would be a Rule 2 risk for the simple case).

- `flat` is unambiguously owning; storage outlives it via `m`.

perf(np.tile): `using` on promoted/broadcasted/contiguous intermediates

np.tile's general case (multi-axis broadcast-then-reshape) allocates
three owning intermediates before the final reshape:

    var promoted   = A.reshape(new Shape(interleaved));         // view or copy
    var broadcasted = broadcast_to(promoted, broadcastTarget);  // stride-0 view
    var contiguous  = broadcasted.copy();                       // fresh buffer
    return contiguous.reshape(new Shape(outShape));

`contiguous` carries the full output-sized unmanaged buffer; without
release it queued on the finalizer queue alongside `promoted` and
`broadcasted` (both small wrappers).

The returned NDArray (`contiguous.reshape(...)`) shares storage with
`contiguous` and holds its own ARC ref via InitializeArc — so disposing
`contiguous` only drops one ref, never frees the live storage.

All three are unambiguously owning (each operation allocates a new
wrapper; `promoted` may be a view or copy but is always a fresh
wrapper). None are returned (Rule 2 satisfied by the final reshape
producing a new wrapper).

perf(NDArray.flatten): `using` on the F-order copy intermediate

NDArray.flatten('F') always materializes a fresh F-contiguous buffer:

    var fcopy = this.copy('F');
    return new NDArray(new UnmanagedStorage(fcopy.Array, Shape.Vector(size)));

The returned NDArray shares the ArraySlice (and therefore MemoryBlock)
with `fcopy` and bumps the refcount via InitializeArc. After
construction the local `fcopy` wrapper is no longer needed — its ARC
ref can drop atomically, leaving the storage alive through the returned
wrapper.

- `fcopy` is unambiguously owning (copy('F') always allocates).
- The returned NDArray's InitializeArc takes its own ref before the
  using disposes fcopy, so the storage refcount is always ≥ 1 while
  any wrapper is live (see Flatten_FOrder_ResultSurvivesSourceDispose
  for the explicit regression guard).

perf(NDArray.flatten): `using` on the F-order copy intermediate

NDArray.flatten('F') always materializes a fresh F-contiguous buffer:

    var fcopy = this.copy('F');
    return new NDArray(new UnmanagedStorage(fcopy.Array, Shape.Vector(size)));

The returned NDArray shares the ArraySlice with `fcopy` and bumps
the shared Disposer's refcount via InitializeArc (verified by runtime
trace — refcount goes 1 → 2 → 1 across the new NDArray ctor and the
fcopy dispose). After construction the local `fcopy` wrapper is no
longer needed; its ARC ref can drop atomically.

Refcount math:
  1. copy('F') → fcopy refcount = 1
  2. new NDArray(new UnmanagedStorage(fcopy.Array, ...))
       → InitializeArc bumps the shared Disposer → refcount = 2
  3. fcopy.Dispose() at scope exit → Release → refcount = 1
  4. Returned NDArray keeps storage alive at refcount = 1

The `UnmanagedMemoryBlock<T>` struct is value-copied into the new
storage, but the inner `_disposer` field is a class reference shared
by both struct copies — that's where the refcount lives.

Safety:
- `fcopy` is unambiguously owning (copy('F') always allocates).
- The returned NDArray's InitializeArc takes its own ref before
  using disposes fcopy.

feat(np.all, np.any): tuple-axis, out=, where= (NumPy 2.x parity)

Brings np.all / np.any up to the full NumPy 2.x signature:
  np.all(a, axis=None, out=None, keepdims=False, *, where=True)
  np.any(a, axis=None, out=None, keepdims=False, *, where=True)

Previously only `bool all(a)` and `NDArray<bool> all(a, int axis, bool keepdims)`
existed (audit_v2/06: tuple-axis, out=, where= missing).

New overloads
- `all(NDArray, int[], bool)` / `any(NDArray, int[], bool)` — tuple-axis.
  - axis=() returns the input cast to bool with shape unchanged (matches NumPy).
  - Negative axes are normalised; duplicates raise ArgumentException
    ("duplicate value in 'axis'"); out-of-range raises AxisError.
- `all(NDArray, bool keepdims)` / `any(NDArray, bool keepdims)` —
  axis=None reduction that keeps the dims as size-1 when requested.
- `all(NDArray, int?, NDArray @out, bool, NDArray @where)` and the int[] variant —
  the full kitchen-sink overload covering out= and where= with single or tuple axes.

Implementation
- DefaultEngine.ReduceLogicalMultiAxis (Default.LogicalReduction.cs) drives the
  tuple-axis path with three tiers:
    1. All axes reduced  → falls through to the 1-D SIMD All/Any (~10× faster
                           than chained axis reductions for that case).
    2. Contiguous run of axes on a C-contig input → reshape fuses them into a
       single axis so we hit one strided reduction instead of N.
    3. Otherwise → chain single-axis reductions in descending order with
       keepdims=true, then squeeze if !keepdims (axis indices stay valid).
- ApplyWhereForAll / ApplyWhereForAny build the effective bool array:
    all: !mask | bool(a)   (skipped elements contribute the identity True)
    any:  mask & bool(a)   (skipped elements contribute the identity False)
  Both compose through existing NDArray operators (broadcast handled there).
- WriteToOut copies the bool reduction into the user's out= via np.copyto with
  casting="unsafe", so an int/float out= receives 0/1 — matches NumPy's "out
  dtype is preserved" rule. Shape mismatch throws ArgumentException.

Inner-axis SIMD fast path
- NDAxisIter.ReduceBool now detects SourceAxisStride == 1 and dispatches each
  row through the existing ILKernelGenerator.AllSimdHelper / AnySimdHelper SIMD
  helpers. TKernel.Identity is a static-abstract bool, so the All vs Any branch
  is JIT-constant-folded. Speeds up axis=ndim-1 reductions by ~5× (e.g.
  all(float64 128×64×64, axis=2): 2.40ms → 0.46ms; within ~1.5× of NumPy).

feat(np.repeat): add axis parameter with IL-emitted 3-loop kernel

NumPy parity: np.repeat(a, repeats, axis=None) — adds the `axis` parameter
to all three NDArray overloads. Mirrors NumPy 2.x PyArray_Repeat semantics
(numpy/_core/src/multiarray/item_selection.c).

API additions:
  - np.repeat(NDArray a, int    repeats, int? axis = null)
  - np.repeat(NDArray a, long   repeats, int? axis = null)
  - np.repeat(NDArray a, NDArray repeats, int? axis = null)

Behaviors covered for full parity:
  - axis=None: flattens the input then per-element repeat (existing behavior).
  - axis=int: normalizes negative axis, validates bounds (AxisError on OOB).
  - 0-d input with axis=0/-1 promotes silently to a 1-d size-1 array.
  - Non-contiguous / F-contig / transposed / sliced inputs are materialized
    to C-contig (NumPy's PyArray_CheckAxis(... CARRAY)) before the kernel.
  - Scalar / 0-d / size-1 repeats array broadcasts along the axis
    (or whole input for axis=None) — fixes a pre-existing gap where
    size-1 repeats arrays were incorrectly rejected.
  - Per-element repeats: ValueError-shaped message on size mismatch,
    matches NumPy's "operands could not be broadcast together" wording.
  - Empty arrays preserve shape with axis dim set to 0.

Implementation — ILKernelGenerator.Repeat.cs (new partial):
  All loops now live inside IL-emitted DynamicMethods. Two kernel families
  per chunk-bytes size, cached by ConcurrentDictionary<int, delegate>:

    RepeatBroadcastKernel — scalar / size-1 repeats. Five args, no count load
                            in the j-loop (broadcastCount lives in arg4).
    RepeatPerJKernel      — per-element repeats. Loads counts[j] each j.

  Splitting by kind lifts the broadcast/per-j branch out of the inner loop —
  measurable on axis-innermost paths where the j-loop runs 100K+ times.

  Inner-copy specialization (size-bucketed, dtype-agnostic — the byte-level
  copy is independent of dtype, only on the slab width):
    chunk = 1, 2, 4, 8  — preload the slab into a typed register once per j,
                          then emit Stind_I[1/2/4/8] in the k-loop. Saves a
                          load on every k iteration vs. repeated cpblk.
    chunk = 16          — same idea via Vector128<byte> Load/Store.
    chunk >  16         — `cpblk dst src chunkBytes` with the constant size
                          baked into the IL so .NET 7+ specializes the memcpy.

  No C# switch over NPTypeCode / dtype anywhere — both the dispatch and the
  inner copy come out of the IL emitter. The chunk-size buckets are keyed on
  bytes (which collapses Int32/UInt32/Single into one kernel, Int64/UInt64/
  Double into another, etc.).

Geometry — the canonical NumPy 3-loop is preserved:
    n_outer = ∏ dims[0..axis)
    n       = dims[axis]
    nel     = ∏ dims[axis+1..ndim)
    chunkBytes = nel * elsize
  axis=None reduces to the degenerate (n_outer=1, n=size, chunkBytes=elsize)
  case so both paths go through the same kernel emitter.

perf(np.repeat): SIMD-broadcast inner loop with cnt-gated three-stage k-loop

Extends the IL-emitted repeat kernel with the codebase's standard width-adaptive
SIMD primitives — scalar pre-broadcast + Vector{N}.Store in a three-stage k-loop
(SIMD body + scalar tail) — for chunks where a single primitive lane covers the
slab. Hits >= 1.5x faster than NumPy at every workload where r >= lanes per
vector.

Techniques newly applied (referencing the codebase rulebook):
  C/Scalar pre-broadcast — Vector{N}.Create(val) is hoisted into a per-j local
                           before the k-loop. The SIMD body then issues one wide
                           store per `lanes` k-iterations instead of `lanes`
                           scalar stores.
  C/Width-adaptive emit — Vector{N} resolves to V128 / V256 / V512 through
                          VectorMethodCache.{V, CreateBroadcast, Store, CreateFromHalves}
                          and the startup-baked VectorBits. No runtime width
                          branch — the IL targets exactly the host width.
  B/Three-stage loop — SIMD body + scalar tail. The wide stage drains
                       `lanes` k-iterations at a time; the tail picks up the
                       remaining < lanes via the existing Stind_I{1,2,4,8} or
                       Vector128.Store emit.
  E/Type-promotion-aware path skip — When `cnt < lanes` the entire SIMD setup
                                     (Vector.Create + loop) is gated behind a
                                     single `blt` so r=2 workloads pay only the
                                     scalar tail. No regression vs. the
                                     pre-SIMD kernel for small r.

Chunk-size dispatch in EmitRepeatBody:
  1, 2, 4, 8  → broadcast scalar into Vector{N}<byte|ushort|uint|ulong>;
                lanes = VectorBytes / chunkBytes (e.g. 4 for chunk=8 V256).
  16          → pack two copies of the V128 slab into Vector{N}<byte> via
                Create(v128, v128) when VectorBits >= 256; lanes = VectorBytes/16
                (= 2 for V256). Falls back to plain V128 store when V128 only.
  > 16        → unchanged cpblk path (the size is already baked in as constant).

Both kernel families (RepeatBroadcastKernel, RepeatPerJKernel) share the same
EmitRepeatBody emitter, so per-j workloads also pick up the SIMD body when an
individual count exceeds `lanes`.

Tests: 67 repeat tests + 8705-test full suite pass on net8.0 + net10.0.
Decimal (chunk=16) and Complex (chunk=16) outputs verified bit-exact via
runtime probe — exercises the V256 Create(v128,v128) broadcast path.

feat(np.median, np.percentile, np.quantile): full NumPy 2.x parity

Adds the entire percentile/quantile/median family in one shot — they share
the same machinery (median == quantile(a, 0.5), percentile == quantile with
q/100) so a single sort-and-interpolate engine backs all three.

Engine — src/NumSharp.Core/Statistics/QuantileEngine.cs (new)
---------------------------------------------------------------
- 13 interpolation methods (all of NumPy 2.4.2's _QuantileMethods table):
  linear (default), lower, higher, nearest, midpoint, inverted_cdf,
  averaged_inverted_cdf, closest_observation, interpolated_inverted_cdf,
  hazen, weibull, median_unbiased, normal_unbiased. Each method's
  virtual-index + gamma formula mirrors numpy/lib/_function_base_impl.py.

  numpy's _ureduce.

  no q axis out" rule).

- overwrite_input: parameter accepted; the partition runs on a scratch
  copy either way (matches NumPy's docs: "Treat the input as undefined").

  methods, preserved for discrete (lower/higher/nearest/inverted_cdf/
  closest_observation). float dtypes preserve themselves. Half stays Half
  via float promotion internally. decimal stays decimal via decimal lerp.

  be an array of real numbers"), matching NumPy.

  q-output for that slice becomes NaN — matches NumPy's "NaN sorts to

  means partitioning around just (n/2-1) and (n/2) instead of a full
  sort. Net cost O(n + k·n) average, far below O(n log n).

feat(np.argwhere): add NumPy 2.4.2 argwhere with IL-kernel two-pass scan

Adds np.argwhere(NDArray) — the NumPy-aligned (N, ndim) int64 result of
np.transpose(np.nonzero(a)), with the special 0-d handling NumPy gives:
truthy scalar → (1, 0), falsy → (0, 0). Empty input shape (0, d1, ..., dn)
returns (0, ndim). Covers all 15 NumSharp dtypes.

Implementation
==============

* `np.argwhere(NDArray)` routes through `TensorEngine.Argwhere` (new
  abstract) → `DefaultEngine.Argwhere` (`Default.Argwhere.cs`). Mirrors
  the np.nonzero structure but writes the (N, ndim) result row-major in a
  single expand pass, avoiding the per-dim column materialization +
  transpose that the textbook `transpose(nonzero(a))` route would pay.

* Contig bool fast path reuses the existing IL kernels:
  - `GetIsAllZeroBoolKernel` prescan (all-false short-circuit, NumPy parity)
  - `GetNonZeroCountBoolKernel` SIMD popcount for exact-size allocation
  - `GetNonZeroFlatBoolKernel` SIMD bit-scan into the result buffer
  When ndim == 1 the scan writes directly into the (count, 1) result; for
  ndim > 1 it writes into a temp long[] which is then expanded via
  `ExpandFlatToArgwhere`.

* Contig non-bool path uses two new generic SIMD helpers added to
  `ILKernelGenerator.Masking.cs`:
  - `NonZeroCountHelper<T>(T*, size)` — V256/V128/scalar popcount that
    JIT-specializes per dtype (drops to scalar on Decimal/Half/Complex
    where Vector<T> isn't supported).
  - `NonZeroFlatHelper<T>(T*, size, long*)` — V256/V128/scalar bit-scan
    that writes flat indices to a pre-sized buffer.
  Replaces the List<long>-based `NonZeroSimdHelper` path that was the
  dense-case bottleneck (~5–10 ns/elt of List.Add overhead → tight SIMD
  scan + pointer store).

* `ExpandFlatToArgwhere` uses incremental coord advance (delta-based
  carry chain) instead of per-element divmod. For dense outputs
  (delta == 1) it's a branch-predictable increment + one carry check
  per row; for sparse delta > 1 the divmod only applies at carry
  boundaries, not per element. Drops the ndim > 1 expand pass from
  ~10 ns/elt (divmod) to ~1 ns/elt (carry chain).

* Non-contig inputs (sliced / transposed / negative-stride / broadcast)
  materialize via `np.ascontiguousarray(x)` before routing through the
  SIMD path — one extra O(N) memcpy buys a 4–6× speedup vs the scalar
  coord-iter `FindNonZeroStridedHelper`. The flat indices into the
  contig buffer map back to user-facing coordinates through the shape
  dims, so C-order traversal semantics are preserved.

* 0-d input is routed through `np.atleast_1d` + the existing NonZero
  IL path to dispatch the truthiness check without re-routing dtype at
  the argwhere layer; the result shape (truthy ? (1,0) : (0,0)) is
  built directly.

Tests
=====
35 new tests in `Indexing/ArgwhereTests.cs`:
* 1D / 2D / 3D / 4D predicate and bool-mask shapes vs NumPy reference
* 0-d truthy/falsy for int + bool + float
* Empty input (0,), (0, 3), (2, 0, 4)
* Non-contig: strided, transposed, negative-stride, broadcasted
* All 15 dtypes (sbyte, byte, short, ushort, int, uint, long, ulong,
  char, half, single, double, decimal, complex, bool)
* Result dtype == Int64 invariant
* Large-array bool fast paths (1M all-ones, 1M all-zeros, sparse 2D)

Full suite: 8753 passing on net8.0 and net10.0 (no regressions).

The previous QuantileEngine had two rule violations:

---------------------------------------------------------------------
- `ILKernelGenerator.Quantile(srcType, outType, method, ...)` is the
  single entry point. First call for a `(srcType, outType, method)`
  tuple emits a `DynamicMethod` and caches it; subsequent calls hit
  `ConcurrentDictionary.GetOrAdd` and invoke the cached delegate.
- The emitted body IS the outer row-loop in pure IL: load i, compute

  the JIT-specialized generic helper, increment, branch. No managed

- Per-row helper `ProcessQuantileRow<T, TOut>` uses `typeof(T) ==
  typeof(X)` JIT-folded branches for the NaN prescan and lerp body.
  Each `(T, TOut)` specialization collapses to straight-line dtype-
  specific code — no runtime dispatch.
- Cache key: `(NPTypeCode src, NPTypeCode out, QuantileMethod)`. About
  ~50 reachable tuples in practice (15 src × 3-4 out variants per
  src × 13 methods, but most src+method combinations map to one
  fixed out-type).

-------------------------------------------------------
- Drops the 15-arm switch + ComputeForType<T> + ComputeForHalf +

- Becomes a thin orchestrator: validates input, resolves output dtype,
  stages the array so the reduction axis is innermost, computes the
