fix(nditer): exact NumPy parity for NDIterCasting.CanCast (safe + same_kind)

Aligns NDIterCasting.CanCast with NumPy 2.x byte-for-byte across the full
13x13 dtype matrix under both the 'safe' and 'same_kind' rules. Verified
programmatically against np.can_cast: 338/338 cells identical.

Motivation: np.copyto(int32_array, float64_dst) — and other valid casts —
threw InvalidCastException, because the casting rule tables diverged from
NumPy. The default copyto casting is 'same_kind', and int32->float64 is a safe
(hence same_kind) cast in NumPy, but NumSharp rejected it. Conversely some
casts NumPy forbids were being allowed.

same_kind (IsSameKindCast rewritten): now a strict superset of safe, matching
NumPy's NPY_SAME_KIND_CASTING:
  - int -> float is now ALLOWED (was rejected) — e.g. int32->float64.
  - signed -> unsigned is now REJECTED (was allowed) — e.g. int32->uint32.
  - int/float -> bool is now REJECTED (was allowed for int).
  Rule = safe || float->float || int->int(except signed->unsigned)
              || int->float || real->complex.

safe (IsSafeCast, pre-existing divergences closed):
  - unsigned -> strictly-wider signed is now safe: uint8->int16/int32/int64,
    uint16->int32/int64, uint32->int64 (the full unsigned range fits).
  - int64/uint64 -> complex128 is now safe (NumPy treats real->complex128 as
    safe across the board, consistent with int64->float64 being safe).
  - bool/uint8/int8 -> float16 is now safe (float16's 11-bit mantissa holds
    integers exactly to +-2048; wider ints and float narrowing stay unsafe).

("same-kind should not allow int -> float"). Renamed to ..._Allowed and

perf(dot): fused single-pass 1-D inner product — 3.5–9× faster, zero GC

Replace the 1-D·1-D branch of DefaultEngine.Dot (numpy.dot vector·vector)
with a fused single-pass kernel that computes sum(a[i]*b[i]) directly,
instead of materializing a full n-element product array (`left * right`)
and then walking it again in ReduceAdd.

Motivation
----------
The previous path did `var product = left * right; return ReduceAdd(product, ...)`.
That allocates an n-element temporary every call and traverses the data twice
(write product, then read it back to reduce) — roughly 2× the memory traffic
plus heavy gen0 GC churn under repeated calls.

Implementation
--------------
- SimdDot.cs (Backends/Kernels): SIMD multiply-accumulate for contiguous
  float/double, 4 independent Vector256 accumulators + FMA (falls back to
  mul+add when FMA is absent) + scalar tail. Accumulates in the element type
  so the result dtype mirrors numpy.
- Default.Dot.Fused.cs (DotInner1D): same-type dispatch, all stride-aware
  (reads strides[0]+offset, so sliced / reversed `a[::-1]` / stepped `a[::2]`
  views are consumed in place — no copy):
    * float/double  -> SimdDot (contiguous) or scalar strided loop
    * int/uint8..64, Half, Decimal -> INumber<T> scalar accumulator
    * bool    -> OR over k of (a[k] AND b[k]), short-circuiting
    * Complex -> Complex accumulator (no conjugation)
  Mixed dtypes fall through to the original `left*right` + ReduceAdd, which
  already applies NEP50 promotion. Char (no INumber<char>) also uses the
  fallback.

NumPy 2.4.2 parity (verified)
-----------------------------
- same-type result PRESERVES the input dtype (int32·int32 -> int32, NOT the
  widened int64 that np.sum yields; float16·float16 -> float16);
- integer products wrap in the element dtype before accumulating
  (int8 [100,100]·[100,100] -> 32);
- bool dot -> bool (OR-of-ANDs); complex dot has no conjugation;
- empty -> scalar 0 of the input dtype (not the widened sum dtype);
- shape mismatch -> "shapes (n,) and (m,) not aligned: ..." (was a Debug.Assert
  that vanished in Release).

Benchmark (net10.0 Release, double, same harness before/after)
--------------------------------------------------------------
  n            before            after           speedup   GC(before->after)
  1,000        760.0 ms / 54 GC  219.2 ms / 15   3.5x      54  -> 15
  100,000      445.3 ms / 446    57.4 ms / 0     7.8x      446 -> 0
  1,000,000    1001.9 ms / 498   111.3 ms / 0    9.0x      498 -> 0
  10,000,000   1218.6 ms / 60    328.9 ms / 0    3.7x      60  -> 0
For n>=100k the fused np.dot is within ~3% of the raw SIMD ceiling; the
remaining n=1000 cost is the per-call result-scalar NDArray allocation
(inherent to returning an array). Large-n speedup is memory-bandwidth bound
(the old path moved ~2x the bytes); small-n speedup is fixed-overhead bound.

  mixed-type promotion, shape-mismatch message).

  matmul paths unchanged).

perf(where): migrate non-contiguous np.where to an NDIter multi-operand per-chunk kernel

Move np.where's broadcast/strided path off the scalar NDExpr.Where fallback and
onto a dedicated multi-operand per-chunk kernel driven by NDIterRef.ForEach — the
"selection" item on the NDIter migration priority list (NPYITER_PERF_HANDOVER §8).

WHY THE OLD PATH WAS SLOW
  WhereImpl already iterated on NDIter, but compiled its inner loop through
  NDExpr.Where, which is structurally wrong for where:
    * WhereNode.SupportsSimd == false  -> scalar only, and
    * NDExpr gates SIMD on AllEqual(inputTypes, outputType), which is ALWAYS
      false for where (cond is Boolean, x/y are the output dtype). The DSL's
      "load every input at the output dtype" rule therefore casts cond -> T on
      EVERY element, then does a float compare-to-zero, before the branch.

WHAT CHANGED
  * New Backends/Kernels/ILKernelGenerator.Where.cs (the target per-chunk class):
    GetWhereInnerLoop(outType) emits a cached NDInnerLoopFunc that, per chunk,
    runtime-dispatches on the inner strides:
      - cond stride==1 && x/y/result stride==elemSize  -> 4x-unrolled SIMD
        Vector.ConditionalSelect over an expanded bool mask + 1-vec remainder;
      - otherwise (broadcast cond/x/y, transpose, ::k, and all non-SIMD dtypes
        Bool/Char/Half/Decimal/Complex) -> raw-bool scalar walk (Ldind_U1, no cast).
    The SIMD mask expansion reuses the proven IL from the whole-array kernel, so
    SIMD output is bit-identical to the contiguous Direct WhereKernel.
  * APIs/np.where.cs: WhereImpl drives the existing 4-operand iterator with
    ForEach(GetWhereInnerLoop(dtype)) instead of NDExpr.Where + ExecuteExpression
    (method marked unsafe for the ForEach default void* arg).
  * Direct/DirectILKernelGenerator.Where.cs: EmitInlineMaskCreation promoted
    private -> internal so the per-chunk kernel reuses one source of the
    bool-mask-expansion IL (EmitLoadIndirect/EmitStoreIndirect were already
    internal and cover all 15 dtypes for the scalar path).

  The contiguous and scalar-operand fast paths (DirectILKernelGenerator.WhereExecute
  and WhereScalarX/Y/XY) are deliberately UNTOUCHED — they already hit a fused
  whole-array SIMD kernel; routing them through NDIter only ties at large N and
  risks a small-N setup-tax regression (HANDOVER §4.1/§4.7).

MEASURED (clean same-binary A/B; ms/call + GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread)
  Every non-contiguous shape faster, GC down, small-N improved (no setup-tax hit):
    cond-row-bcast  f32 2.06x  i32 1.67x  f64 1.23x      (now hits SIMD select)
    cond-col-bcast  f32 1.54x  i32 1.34x  f64 1.39x      (faster raw-bool scalar)
    strided-transp  f32 1.34x  i32 1.52x  f64 1.26x
    strided-1d ::2  f64 1.31x  (GC -48%)
    small (1K) row  f32 1.38x  i32 1.46x  f64 1.19x      (cached kernel, no NDExpr alloc)
  GC bytes/call reduced 7-48% (NDExpr tree + ExecuteExpression machinery removed).

CORRECTNESS
  * Focused matrix: 7023/7023 checks across all 15 dtypes x {row-broadcast SIMD,
    col-broadcast scalar, transpose strided} + vector-aligned/tail sizes + NaN/Inf.
  * Full suite (CI filter): 9458 passed / 0 failed / 11 skipped.
  No public API or behavioral change; NumPy parity preserved.

Follow-ups documented in docs/MIGRATE_NPYITER.md: cond-broadcast SIMD-copy path
(closes the col-broadcast gap), np.place/masked-assign reuse, and full unification
(after the setup-tax phase).

    np.multithreading(false);      // back to single-threaded (default)

work-size gate:
  DegreeOfParallelism(n) = (enabled && n >= MinTotalWork)
                           ? min(MaxThreads, ProcessorCount, n / MinWorkPerThread)
                           : 1
with MinTotalWork=50k, MinWorkPerThread=32k. So tiny/medium dots stay on one
thread (thread fan-out costs more than it saves — the POC showed 32 threads
*regressing* at n=100k), and only large vectors are split.

Parallel dot (Default.Dot.Fused.cs)
-----------------------------------
DotContiguousF64/F32 consult DegreeOfParallelism; when >1 they partition [0,n)
into p contiguous chunks, run SimdDot on each via Parallel.For, and sum the
partials in chunk order (deterministic). Partials are padded to a cache line to
avoid false sharing. Summation regrouping means results can differ from the
single-threaded path in the last few ULPs — the same reordering NumPy's threaded
BLAS shows; tests assert agreement to tolerance.

DISABLED BY DEFAULT: default behavior and exact summation order are unchanged
unless the caller opts in. Only contiguous float/double dot is parallelized;
strided views and the other dtypes stay single-threaded.

----------------------------------------

  n=10M  : 5350  -> 2783 us  (1.9x)  -> ~matches NumPy default (2527us); RAM-bw bound
At 1M (cache-resident) throughput scales with per-core cache bandwidth and beats
NumPy; at 10M it converges with NumPy at the memory-bandwidth wall (~55-63 GB/s).
Net effect: np.dot goes from ~2x behind NumPy-default (single-thread, prior
commit) to parity-or-better on large vectors.

perf(reduction): widening-SIMD axis reductions for narrow ints — 230-390x faster, at/beyond NumPy; fix uint32 axis-sum corruption

Phase 2b of the NDIter performance migration (docs/NPYITER_PERF_HANDOVER.md).

Problem
- sum/prod/mean over an axis for byte/sbyte/int16/uint16 (NEP50: accumulate
  in int64/uint64/double) fell to CreateAxisReductionKernelScalar - a
  per-element loop with a runtime op-switch and a double round-trip per
  element: sum(int16 10M, axis=0) = 1068 ms vs NumPy 4.55 ms (235x).
  mean(int16, axis=0) = 1354 ms. SByte pairs missed even the typed scalar
  table and fell to the ReadAsDouble conversion path.
- Bisect vs benchmark snapshot 6038990f (handover sec.13) proved this was
  NOT a regression: the snapshot commit measures identically (int16 axis0
  1137 ms). The snapshot report's "58 ms" NumSharp numbers are pipeline
  artifacts (~19.5x off); its NumPy column matches reality.
- BUG: sum(uint32, axis=0) silently returned WRONG VALUES. The widening
  kernel zero-extended via Avx2.UnpackLow/UnpackHigh, which interleave per
  128-bit lane: accumulator slots held columns (0,1,4,5)/(2,3,6,7) but were
  stored to (0..3)/(4..7), swapping columns 2,3 <-> 4,5 in every group of
  eight. No test covered >=8 distinct uint32 columns, so 9447 tests stayed
  green.
- Secondary: even the covered int32->int64 kernel was 4.6x off NumPy
  (24.2 vs 5.27 ms): its column-tiled accumulator walked all rows per
  32-column tile at a page-crossing stride, defeating the prefetcher
  (latency-bound, ~1 miss per 128B segment).

Design (rewritten DirectILKernelGenerator.Reduction.Axis.Widening.cs)
Three tiers:
1. Concrete Sum kernels (hot tier) - per-pair, zero abstraction:
   - Leading axis: blocked row-streaming. The output slab IS the
     accumulator; an 8192-element block stays L2-resident across all axis
     rows while input rows stream sequentially. 8/16-bit inputs accumulate
     into an int32/uint32 scratch (VPMOVSX/ZXWD|BD: 8 lanes/instr, half the
     accumulator traffic), drained into the 64-bit output every CHUNK rows
     with overflow-proof chunk sizes (int16 16384*32768 < 2^31; uint16
     32768*65535 < 2^32; int8/uint8 8M rows). 32-bit inputs widen directly
     (VPMOVSX/ZXDQ + VPADDQ).
   - Innermost axis: per-output flat reduce with per-chunk int32/uint32 lane
     accumulation + drain; 4-way unrolled direct widen for 32-bit.
2. Generic tier (Prod/Min/Max + all ->double pairs incl. Mean): static-
   abstract IWidenLoad/IWAccOp structs over the same blocked row-streaming
   structure. Mean accumulates as Sum into double and post-divides
   (DivideOutputByCount), gated to double accumulators.
   Widening loads are element-order-correct by construction (exact-width
   PMOVSX/PMOVZX/CVT loads of 4 elements) - the UnpackLow/High bug class is
   structurally impossible. uint32->double uses the exact bias trick
   (cvt(i32(u xor 0x80000000)) + 2^31).
3. Typed scalar fallback for non-contiguous layouts (unchanged helper); the
   general table in Reduction.Axis.cs gains the missing SByte/Boolean/Char
   typed-scalar rows so non-AVX2 machines and odd layouts no longer hit the
   ReadAsDouble path.

Why concrete loops in the hot tier (measured, int16 axis-0 sum, 10M):
   fully concrete:                                  6.5 ms
   + int32-chunked accumulation:                    3.6 ms
   one interface hop (static abstract OR instance): 10-11 ms
   two interface hops (op + load):                  14.5 ms
   generic struct / static generic with typeof:     23-45 ms
The JIT neither folds typeof(T) chains nor fully inlines interface dispatch
at one-widen-per-4-elements call density (4x the density of the same-T
kernels where ITypedReductionOp is tolerable). Confirms and extends the
Add256<T> post-mortem in Reduction.Axis.Simd.cs.

Coverage added to TryGetAxisReductionWideningKernel:
   sbyte/short/int -> long; byte/ushort/uint -> ulong (also Int64-accum
   aliases); bool->byte and char->ushort routes; sbyte/byte/short/ushort/
   int/uint/float -> double; ops Sum/Prod/Min/Max + Mean (double accum).
   (u)long -> double stays scalar (no AVX2 64-bit-int <-> double convert).

Results (10M elements, 1000x10000, vs NumPy 2.4.2 same machine)
   sum(int16,  axis=0)  1068.6 ms -> 4.61 ms   (232x; 1.01x NumPy)
   sum(int16,  axis=1)  1058.1 ms -> 2.72 ms   (389x; 0.84x NumPy - faster)
   sum(uint8,  axis=0)  1046.4 ms -> 4.03 ms   (260x; 0.91x NumPy - faster)
   sum(uint8,  axis=1)  ~1050  ms -> 2.90 ms   (362x; 0.88x NumPy)
   sum(int32,  axis=0)    24.2 ms -> 7.78 ms   (3.1x; 1.48x NumPy)
   sum(int32,  axis=1)    12.0 ms -> 5.23 ms   (2.3x; 1.36x NumPy)
   sum(uint32, axis=1)    22.9 ms -> 4.98 ms   (4.6x; 1.29x NumPy)
   mean(int16, axis=0)  1354.5 ms -> 40.6 ms   (33x; generic tier)
   sum(int16, axis=0) 3162x3162: 1136 -> 3.47 ms (327x; 0.76x NumPy)

Also fixes parity: prod with int64 accumulator now multiplies in exact
int64 (NumPy-identical wraparound, e.g. prod of 70 twos -> 0) instead of
rounding through double.

Tests
- New Backends/Kernels/AxisReductionWideningTests.cs (13 tests): uint32
  column-order regression, all six pairs vs scalar reference with negatives,
  chunk-drain boundaries (axisSize/rowLength > 16384), 3-D slab path,
  inner-slab slice, scalar-fallback slice, mean dtype+values, prod
  wraparound.

  independent reference) during development.
- Full suite: 9477 passed, 0 failed (TestCategory!=OpenBugs&!=HighMemory).

Known remaining gaps (documented, not blockers): int32/uint32 axis sums at

->double sums possible later); innermost int16/uint8 could use

ROOT CAUSE OF THE 'GAPS' — Debug-build benchmark invalidator
============================================================
'dotnet run file.cs' (file-based apps, incl. the dotnet_run helper) compiles
BOTH the script assembly AND the #:project-referenced NumSharp.Core in Debug
with DebuggableAttribute(DisableOptimizations) (flags=263). RyuJIT honors it
even over [MethodImpl(AggressiveOptimization)]. Measured effect:
  - hand-written C# hot loops ~2x slower (the POC strided kernels),
  - NDIterRef construction ~40% slower (H 0.69 -> 0.40 us/call),
  - DynamicMethod-emitted kernels IMMUNE (emitted IL is always optimized) —
    which is exactly why only aspects C/D/E looked slow while A/B/F/G/H looked
    fine, and why the cause survived E-core/scheduling, GC-drain, 4K-aliasing,
    chunking-census, and runtime-vs-const-stride investigations (all ruled out
    empirically; census: 1 call, count=1M, strides [8,8,4], 64B-aligned ptrs).
Fix rule: '#:property Optimize=true' fixes only the script; '#:property
Configuration=Release' changes output paths but binaries stay debug; ONLY
command-line 'dotnet run -c Release' optimizes both. The POC now asserts
IsJITOptimizerDisabled==false on both assemblies at startup and refuses to
mislead. Rule + diagnostic signature documented in benchmark/CLAUDE.md (new
top warning section) and handover section 4.12.

NUMPY GROUND TRUTH (read from src/numpy, not guessed)
=====================================================
- C strided binary: NumPy has NO SIMD path for non-unit strides at all —
  loops_arithm_fp.dispatch.c.src 'goto loop_scalar' (plain scalar C loop).
- D strided unary: hardware gather npyv_loadn_f32 = _mm256_i32gather_ps,
  4x unrolled (loops_unary_fp.dispatch.c.src + simd/avx2/memory.h).
- E strided reduce: scalar 8-accumulator pairwise loop (loops_utils.h.src),
  no SIMD for non-unit strides.
So NumPy's strided floors are beatable with fast gather hardware.

KERNEL UPGRADE — AVX2 hardware gather
=====================================
PocKernels.AddF32/SqrtF32/SumF32 strided branches now use
Avx2.GatherVector256 (vgatherdps, scale=1, byte-offset index vector hoisted
out of the loop — hot loop is stride-agnostic; guard: Avx2.IsSupported and
|7*stride| <= int.MaxValue; insert-gather Vector256.Create fallback kept).

binary 2x (334us), unary 4x (203us, NumPy's own shape), reduce 4 accumulators
(121us). Also re-settled the technique record: stride-2 vshufps/vpermd
compaction = 314us (the earlier 'compaction loses 2x to gather' verdict was a
Debug artifact — retracted in handover 4.12/12.1); hw-gather chosen for

=================

  contig 1.04x, broadcasts 0.96-1.01x, neg-stride 1.00-1.11x, F-order 0.91x,

  ALLOCATE, COMMON_DTYPE, order K/C/F/A + neg-stride flip, coalescing,

feat(nditer): COPY_IF_OVERLAP — overlapping operands no longer silently corrupt (roadmap Wave 1.1)

Implements NumPy-parity memory-overlap protection for NDIter, fixing the
proven silent-corruption bug where add(a[:-1], a[:-1], out=a[1:]) produced
[1,2,4,6,8,16,32,64] (kernel reads its own freshly written values, cascading
at the vector boundary) instead of NumPy's [1,2,4,6,8,10,12,14].

THE SOLVER — NDMemOverlap.cs (new, ~600 lines)
===============================================
Faithful port of numpy/_core/src/common/mem_overlap.c (Pauli Virtanen,
3-clause BSD): the overlap question reduces to a bounded linear Diophantine
equation with positive coefficients (negative strides mapped positive by
x -> shape-1-x; itemsize as an extra stride-1 term), solved by GCD-pruned
depth-first search with extended-Euclid precomputation:
- memory-extent fast path (offset_bounds_from_strides): disjoint ranges
  answer NO without any GCD work — the common case for fresh outputs.
- maxWork semantics identical to NumPy: 0 = bounds-only
  (NPY_MAY_SHARE_BOUNDS), -1 = exact (NPY_MAY_SHARE_EXACT), N = candidate cap
  (nditer uses 1, exact for all practical slicing patterns).
- NumPy's 128-bit helper arithmetic (npy_extint128.h) maps to System.Int128;
  products of two int64 stay < 2^126 so only the 64-bit narrowing is
  range-checked, as in the original.
- solve_may_have_internal_overlap ported too (stride-0 broadcast dims answer
  YES immediately; doubled-bounds require_ub_nontrivial formulation).
Validated 14/14 against np.shares_memory / np.may_share_memory on the
curated matrix (interleaved even/odd, gcd-incommensurate offsets, 2-D
row/col slices, reversed, broadcast, touching/adjacent ranges).

THE ITERATOR — NDIter.cs construction + Dispose
================================================
Port of the COPY_IF_OVERLAP block of npyiter_allocate_arrays
(nditer_constr.c:3083-3311):
- For each WRITE operand, check against every READ operand (skip
  already-copied, skip iterator-allocated nulls) with maxWork=1.
- OVERLAP_ASSUME_ELEMENTWISE pair short-circuit: exact aliasing (same base
  address, ndim, dims, strides, dtype, no internal overlap) needs no copy —
  add(a, a, out=a) stays zero-copy like NumPy.
- On overlap: FORCECOPY the WRITE operand — fresh C-order temporary, copy-in
  only if the operand is also READ, iterate over the temp, write back to the
  user's original on Dispose (NumPy WRITEBACKIFCOPY resolved at
  NDIter_Deallocate). Op-itflags FORCECOPY|HAS_WRITEBACK set for DebugPrint.
- Write-back resolves in Dispose regardless of state ownership; callers must
  consume results after the using scope (documented on the field, the
  probe, and the tests).

PRODUCTION WIRING (NumPy ufunc parity, ufunc_object.c:1070)
===========================================================
DefaultEngine Binary/Unary/Compare NDIter routes now pass
COPY_IF_OVERLAP + per-op OVERLAP_ASSUME_ELEMENTWISE. Outputs there are
freshly allocated, so the cost is one extent comparison per input — measured
zero regression (P15 small-N 1.37 us, P1/P9/S1 unchanged; the 1K path exits
via the trivial bypass before reaching the iterator anyway).

BONUS BUG FOUND WHILE TESTING (collected per instructions, now guarded)
=======================================================================
Pre-existing, unrelated to overlap: the Layer-2 typed helpers
(ExecuteBinary/ExecuteUnary/ExecuteComparison/ExecuteScan) bridge to legacy
whole-array Direct kernels that IGNORE output strides — a strided/offset
write operand (e.g. out=c[::2]) was silently written CONTIGUOUSLY:
  add(a[::2], a[1::2], out=c[::2]) -> wrote [3,7,11,15,...] to c[0..3].
The Tier-3B per-chunk route (ExecuteElementWise*, what production uses) was
always correct. New RequireContiguousOutput guard throws
InvalidOperationException with guidance instead of corrupting (offset-contig
outputs like a[1:] still pass; FORCECOPY temps always pass). Real fix is the
Phase 3 per-chunk migration. No production caller was affected (only
POC/probe scripts call these helpers, all with contiguous outputs).

BEHAVIOR MATRIX (all expected values from live NumPy 2.4.2)
===========================================================
B1 add(a[:-1],a[:-1],out=a[1:])   -> [1,2,4,6,8,10,12,14]   (was corrupted)
B2 add(a[1:],a[1:],out=a[:-1])    -> [4,6,8,10,12,14,16,8]

perf(nditer): AVX2 hardware-gather strided SIMD in the Tier-3B shell + strided reductions (Phase 2a / roadmap Wave 3)

Closes the last large performance hole from the gap analysis: genuinely
strided shapes ran scalar inside the Tier-3B inner-loop shell (S1 strided
binary 3.0x behind NumPy, S2 strided 2-D unary 7.1x behind, S3 strided
reduce 1.8x behind). The POC-proven hardware-gather kernels are now emitted
by the production IL shell itself.

WHAT SHIPPED
============
1. Gather dispatcher + EmitSimdGatherLoop in DirectILKernelGenerator.
   InnerLoop.cs: when a same-dtype SIMD kernel's contig/broadcast stride
   checks fail, control falls to a gather block instead of the scalar loop.
   Per-input AVX2 vgather (Avx2.GatherVector256, scale=1) with the BYTE-
   OFFSET index vector built once from the runtime stride — the hot loop is
   stride-agnostic and advances only base addresses. The caller's vectorBody
   (the same IL emitted for the contiguous path) runs unchanged between
   gather-loads and the store. Structure mirrors EmitSimdContigLoop: 4x
   unroll + 1-vector remainder + scalar-strided tail (reuses
   EmitScalarElement). Runtime guards: |stride| <= int.MaxValue/8 per
   operand (negative strides sign-extend correctly; stride-0 broadcast
   gathers are valid — SL/SR still catch the common binary broadcasts
   first).
2. Scatter-store variant (roadmap 3.3): when the OUTPUT is strided too,
   the result vector is stored per-lane (Vector256.GetElement + scalar
   store — NumPy's npyv_storen shape; AVX2 has no scatter instruction), so
   NCONTIG->NCONTIG shapes vectorize their compute.
3. Strided flat reductions (roadmap 3.4): gather section in
   EmitReductionStridedLoop's ndim==1 fast path — 4 independent vector
   accumulators, tree-merge, horizontal reduce, then the existing scalar
   loop finishes the tail from the advanced position. Gated to
   Sum/Min/Max/Prod with same-type accumulation; reuses EmitVectorIdentity/
   EmitVectorBinaryReductionOp/EmitVectorHorizontalReduction so float
   min/max NaN semantics are bit-identical to the contiguous SIMD path.
4. GATHER_ELIGIBLE wired in UpdateContiguityFlags (roadmap 3.2):
   informational (the kernels self-dispatch at runtime; one layout-
   polymorphic kernel per cache key beats key-splitting).
Dtype coverage: i32/u32/f32/i64/u64/f64 (NumPy's gather set) at
VectorBits==256 + Avx2; all other dtypes/widths keep the existing scalar-
strided fallback (documented; insert-gather fallback is follow-up work).

BONUS BUG FOUND & FIXED — NDIterFlags alias collision
======================================================
The four NumSharp-extension flags (0x10000..0x80000) ALIASED the NumPy-
parity flags shifted to bits 8-20:
  CONTIGUOUS==GROWINNER, GATHER_ELIGIBLE==ONEITERATION,
  EARLY_EXIT==DELAYBUF, PARALLEL_SAFE==REDUCE.
Setting CONTIGUOUS has silently set GROWINNER since the extensions were
added (latent: GROWINNER only matters with BUFFER). The first time
GATHER_ELIGIBLE was actually set, IsSingleInnerLoop() saw ONEITERATION and
ForEach ran ONE inner loop: 2-D strided ops computed row 0 and silently
skipped every other row (np.sqrt(a[::2,::2]) 'finished' in 10us with
garbage rows 1+). Extension flags renumbered to genuinely free bits 3-6;
NDIterFlags_ExtensionFlags_DoNotAliasNumPyFlags pins pairwise alias-
freedom across the whole enum. Handover section 4.13 documents the bug
class.

==========================================

  strided add  1M f32 [::2]+[::2]   318 us  (POC hand-written: 334)
  strided sqrt 1M f32 [::2,::2]     201 us  (POC: 203; pre-wave3 IL: 2654)
  iterator route incl MultiNew      354 us  (raw kernel + ~36us)
Production end-to-end, same-run vs NumPy (both sides allocate results):
  S1 strided binary   1080 vs 1033 us  -> parity      (was 3.0x behind)
  S2 strided 2-D sqrt  941 vs 1282 us  -> 1.36x FASTER (was 7.1x behind)
  S3 strided sum       117 vs  259 us  -> 2.2x FASTER  (was 1.8x behind)
The residual S1/S2 e2e component is the result-allocation tax (fresh 4MB
per call; GC-deferred frees keep pages cold) — Wave 2.4 scope, measured
independently: kernel+iterator with preallocated out beats NumPy's out=
numbers.

feat(nditer): windowed buffered iteration + DELAY_BUFALLOC + buffered-cast Advance fix (roadmap Wave 4 + 1.2)

Implements NumPy's buffered-iterator machinery end-to-end and fixes three
pre-existing correctness bugs it exposed. The headline discovery: buffered
NON-REDUCE iteration never worked for IterSize > BufferSize — there was no
buffered iternext at all. Construction did ONE eager fill (8192 elements) and
the plain advancers (Standard/External/SingleIteration) neither refilled nor
wrote back, so everything past the first window was silently skipped; the
Phase-4 execution bridge avoided it by construction (small-N tests only).

THE WINDOWED MACHINERY (NDIter.cs / NDIterBufferManager.cs / Execution.cs)
=============================================================================
- BufferedNext (EXLOOP protocol): flush WRITE operands -> IterIndex jumps to
  window end -> GotoIterIndex repositions into the arrays -> fill next window.
  Mirrors NumPy npyiter_buffered_iternext (nditer_templ.c.src).
- BufferedElementNext (no EXLOOP): NumPy's user-facing nditer protocol — one
  element per iternext, walking the buffer via BufStrides, refilling at the
  window edge. The two protocols are NOT interchangeable: kernel drivers
  (ForEach/ExecuteGeneric/ExecuteReducing/RunBufferedBinary) consume whole
  fills, so they window-advance via BufferedWindowAdvance() regardless of
  EXLOOP.
- ComputeTransferSize: fills capped at BufferSize and row-aligned for
  NDim > 1 — matches observed NumPy behavior (a (100,100) strided source with
  buffersize=4096 fills 4000/4000/2000, with and without GROWINNER; verified
  against numpy 2.4.2 nditer).
- FillBufferWindow / FlushBufferWindow: per-operand window copies decomposed
  into inner-axis runs driven through the SIMD IL cast kernels
  (TryGetCastKernel / TryGetStridedCastKernel; memcpy + typed strided loop for
  same-dtype; scalar ConvertValue only as the exotic-dtype fallback). Fills
  swap buffered operands' DataPtrs to their buffers and record the array
  write-back positions; flush is idempotent (BufFlushed) and runs from
  iternext, Reset, the single-fill fast paths, and Dispose (before
  COPY_IF_OVERLAP write-backs, NumPy NDIter_Deallocate order).
- NumPy buffering criterion ('buffered' buffers only when REQUIRED): operands
  needing cast/CONTIG or whose layout is not one linear walk are buffered;
  linear operands (contiguous, constant-stride 1-D, fully-broadcast) keep
  their TRUE inner byte stride exposed through BufStrides — so same-dtype
  strided operands keep Wave-3 gather kernels instead of paying copies.
  Buffered REDUCE keeps its historical criterion + double-loop machinery
  untouched.
- DELAY_BUFALLOC implemented: construction is allocation-free; Reset() or
  EnsureBuffersReady() (auto-called at every execution entry point)
  materializes buffers + primes the first window. NumPy raises if iterated
  without reset; NumSharp auto-ensures (documented divergence).
- State: new BufTransferSize (NumPy NBF_SIZE) + BufFlushed fields; Copy()
  duplicates them; GetInnerLoopSizePtr/ResolveInnerLoopCount expose the
  window size for non-reduce buffered iterators (BufIterEnd stays the legacy
  reduce semantic).

THREE PRE-EXISTING BUGS FIXED
=============================
1. Bug (b) (handover Phase-0 leftover, now gated): Advance/GotoIterIndex/
   ExternalLoopNext/GotoIndex/GotoMultiIndex multiplied source-element strides
   by ElementSizes — the BUFFER dtype size — making every reposition 2x under
   an int32->float64 cast. All five sites now use SrcElementSizes (identical
   values when no cast: zero behavior change otherwise).
2. NDIterRef.GetDataPtr recomputed the buffer position as
   IterIndex - (BufIterEnd - BufferSize): correct ONLY for full windows; the
   final PARTIAL window (e.g. 3621 of 8192) read stale data from the previous
   fill (20005-element walk returned arr[12763] at index 16384). DataPtrs —
   maintained by fill/advance — is the single source of truth now.
3. IsSingleInnerLoop's 'EXLOOP && NDim<=1' shortcut fired for coalesced 1-D
   BUFFERED iterators, so ForEach ran one kernel call over the first window
   and dropped the rest. Windowed iterators now decide single-vs-multi purely
   by 'first window covers IterEnd'.

PRODUCTION ROUTES — MEASURED, NOT ASSUMED (A/B, i9-13900K, Release)
===================================================================
NumPy's ufunc config (EXTERNAL_LOOP|BUFFERED|GROWINNER|DELAY_BUFALLOC|
COPY_IF_OVERLAP, op_dtypes=compute dtype, unsafe casting) was wired into all
three element-wise routes, A/B-measured against the existing fused
per-element-convert IL bodies, and kept ONLY where it wins:
- binary mixed (add contig 2M: buffered 2.20 ms vs fused 1.49; strided 1M:
  3.18 vs 2.98; div: 1.72 vs 1.61) -> KEEP FUSED. The extra L2 buffer
  round-trip (~16 B/element) outweighs the SIMD gain on cheap ops. NumPy
  buffers because its AOT C loops cannot fuse casts into the op loop; our
  runtime IL can — and the fused path beats NumPy itself (mixed add 4M:
  6.0 ms vs NumPy 7.6 = 0.79x).
- comparison mixed -> KEEP FUSED (same cheap-op class).
- promoting unary math (sqrt 2M: buffered 1.65 ms vs fused 2.25 = 1.36x)
  -> BUFFERED-CAST ROUTE SHIPPED: sqrt/exp/log(int)-class ops now cast via
  SIMD windows and run the same-dtype vector body. End-to-end sqrt(i32) 4M:
  14.0 ms vs NumPy 17.3 = 0.81x. Predicates (IsNan/...) and Complex-Abs keep
  their input-dtype semantics (excluded).
The A/B table is documented in-code at the binary route so the next session
does not re-litigate without new evidence.

End-to-end vs NumPy 2.4.2 (4M, both sides allocating): mixed add 0.79x,
mixed mul 0.88x, sqrt(i32) 0.81x, mixed cmp ~parity, strided mixed 1.00x.

fix(nditer): size-1 stride-0 invariant, op_axes OOB, bug-(b) sites #6/#7, write-broadcast validation, PARALLEL_SAFE wiring, unit-axis absorption (roadmap Wave 1.4)

The hygiene wave's size-1-axis stride audit found the root divergence behind
the suspicious relaxed coalesce rule, plus two more real bugs. All three were
reproduced against NumPy 2.4.2 ground truth before fixing, and all are fixed
by adopting NumPy's structure (nditer_constr.c / nditer_api.c) rather than
patching symptoms. A post-commit review pass (A/B-measured) then hardened the
axis-ordering interaction and removed a pre-existing (N,1) pathology - see
"Review pass" below.

BUG 1 - missing fill_axisdata invariant corrupted RemoveMultiIndex iteration.
NumPy forces stride 0 for EVERY operand on any size-1 iterator axis and on
broadcast-stretched dims (nditer_constr.c:1594-1615). NumSharp copied raw
operand strides instead, and compensated by RELAXING npyiter_coalesce_axes'
trivial branch (accept any size-1 axis) while keeping NumPy's merge rule
("take stride1 when stride0==0") - which is only correct UNDER the invariant.
A size-1 axis carrying a nonzero stride could therefore win a merge with the
wrong stride: RemoveMultiIndex on a (1,4) view with element strides (1,2)
(base.reshape(4,2)[:, 0:1].T) iterated [0,1,2,3] where NumPy reads [0,2,4,6].
The constructor's all-contiguous coalesce guard masked the bug on every path
except RemoveMultiIndex.
Fix (root): stride normalization at fill time in Initialize - both standard
broadcast branches (sameAsIter + broadcast_to) and the op_axes branch force
stride 0 where Shape[d]==1 - and CoalesceAxes' condition reverted to NumPy's
exact strict form ((shape==1 && stride==0) || stride0*shape0==stride1).
Contiguous size-1 shapes ((2,4,1)/(1,4)/(4,1)) still fully coalesce to 1-D.

BUG 2 - op_axes fill walked out of bounds for stretched size-1 operand axes.
The op_axes stride fill used the RAW array stride when the operand's mapped
axis has length 1 but the iter dim is larger (broadcast stretch):
op_axes=[[0],[0]] over [(3,), (1,)] read heap garbage ((1, -1.35e-310)
instead of (1, 10.0)). Now stride 0 per NumPy (op dim==1 -> 0; iter dim==1
-> 0), REDUCTION_AXIS-encoded entries are decoded via NDIterUtils.GetOpAxis
(previously they fell into the zero branch only by accident of their huge
encoded values), and ApplyOpAxes applies the same reduce-validation to
stretched dims as to op_axis=-1 entries (NumPy nditer_constr.c:1653-1661).

BUG 3 - bug-(b) family sites #6/#7: buffer dtype size on source strides.
FlipNegativeStrides (NDIterCoalescing.cs) and GetAxisStrideArray (NDIter.cs)
multiplied source-element strides by ElementSizes (buffer dtype size) instead
of SrcElementSizes (source dtype size). K-order + BUFFERED + int32->float64
over negative strides landed the flip base offset 2x too far and read garbage
([4390958, 7077999, ...] for NumPy's [0..9]). Production np.* routes were
immune - the unary buffered route forces C/F order, so the flip never ran
there - but the bug was reachable through the public K-order iterator API.
GetInnerFixedStrideArray's non-buffered branch also switched to
SrcElementSizes for semantic consistency (sizes are equal on that branch:
casts require BUFFER, which takes the BufStrides branch).

Review pass (A/B-measured against the pre-wave tree):

- The normalization makes GetMinStride return 0 for size-1 axes, and the
  DESCENDING (iteration-order) reorder sorted key-0 axes INNERMOST - inner
  loop of one element + linearity lost (needless buffering) on K-order paths.
  Fixed: in descending mode all-stride-0 axes sort OUTERMOST. Sequence-
  neutral (a size-1 axis has exactly one coordinate value) and NumPy-outcome-
  equivalent (NumPy's ambiguous stride comparison keeps them out of the way,
  then its coalesce absorbs them). Ascending (pre-coalesce) mode keeps key-0
  first - the strict trivial branch absorbs those axes immediately.

- The review exposed a PRE-EXISTING pathology (slow on both trees): the
  forced-C/F non-coalesced branch never sorts, so a TRAILING size-1 axis sat
  innermost and EXLOOP degenerated to one-element inner loops - (N,1)-strided
  ufuncs ran N kernel invocations of count 1 (4M f32: add 30 ms, sqrt 23 ms).
  Root divergence: NumSharp gates coalescing on all-operands-contiguous;
  NumPy coalesces UNCONDITIONALLY after order resolution and its strict
  trivial branch absorbs every stride-0 size-1 axis. Fixed with
  NDIterCoalescing.RemoveUnitAxes - absorbs size-1 axes on the non-coalesced
  branch (only where no multi-index/flat index is tracked; index
  reconstruction needs original axes, NumPy likewise skips coalescing there).
  Removal is provably sequence-neutral. Measured: (4M,1) strided add
  30.0 -> 5.4 ms, sqrt 23.0 -> 5.2 ms (4.5-5.6x faster than the PRE-wave
  tree; the absorbed axis re-enables the linearity test and Wave-3 gather).

Also shipped:

- NumPy write-broadcast validation (fill_axisdata 1601-1611 parity): a WRITE
  operand with a broadcast-stretched dim (stride 0, iter dim > 1) is a
  reduction. Without REDUCE_OK -> ArgumentException with NumPy's message
  ("output operand requires a reduction along dimension N, but the reduction
  is not enabled..."); write-only -> "...flagged as write-only, not
  read-write"; with REDUCE_OK + READWRITE -> REDUCE flags set and per-element
  accumulation works (probed W1/W3/W5/W7 against NumPy 2.4.2). Previously
  NumSharp filled stride 0 silently and let the colliding writes race.

- PARALLEL_SAFE wired (was declared, never set or read): construction sets it
  when there is no REDUCE operand and either no WRITE operands, or exactly
  one WRITE operand whose potential overlap with inputs was resolved by
  COPY_IF_OVERLAP - i.e. it reuses decisions the Wave-1.1 overlap machinery
  already made, at zero added construction cost. Exposed as
  NDIterRef.IsParallelSafe; the consumer is Wave 6.2's parallel ForEach.

- EARLY_EXIT flag deleted: early exit is a KERNEL property
  (INDBooleanReductionKernel.ShouldExit / ReductionOp.SupportsEarlyExit),
  not iterator state - the iterator-level flag was dead since introduction.
  Bit 5 documented as unassigned; the alias-freedom test updated to the three
  remaining extension flags.

- Dead code removed: CalculateGrowInnerSize + PrepareBuffers +
  FinalizeBuffers (zero callers since the Wave-4 windowed machinery replaced
  them). CalculateGrowInnerSize carried the flagged latent bug: its
  expectedStride accumulator was declared outside the per-operand loop, so
  operand 2+ was validated against operand 1's accumulated stride product.
  The BUF_REUSABLE reuse helpers stay (relevant to REUSE_REDUCE_LOOPS /
  Wave 5.2).

- CA2014 fixed: the keyStrides stackalloc in ReorderAxesForCoalescing's
  insertion sort hoisted out of the loop (stack growth per iteration matters
  here - NumSharp has no NPY_MAXDIMS cap).

Compatibility notes:
- IsOperandIterLinear / IsOperandContiguous / CheckAllOperandsContiguous all
  skip size-1 dims already (and the coalesce guard reads ORIGINAL array
  strides, not state strides), so the normalization does not disturb
  coalescing decisions; RemoveUnitAxes removes the size-1 axes from the
  non-coalesced internal representation entirely.
- GetAxisStrideArray now reports source byte strides under buffered casts
  (NumPy NAD_STRIDES semantics); with MULTI_INDEX, size-1 axes report
  stride 0 (the invariant made observable); without index tracking the
  internal NDim shrinks by the absorbed axes (NumPy-equivalent post-coalesce

feat(nditer): WRITEMASKED/ARRAYMASK execution + VIRTUAL operands (roadmap Wave 1.3)

Masked iteration now EXECUTES instead of validating-and-ignoring: a buffered
WRITEMASKED operand's window flush writes back ONLY the elements whose
ARRAYMASK byte is nonzero. Before this, the mask was construction-time
decoration — a buffered+cast masked write landed 99s in every slot where
NumPy 2.4.2 preserves the unmasked values (silent corruption of the exact
elements the caller asked to protect). VIRTUAL operands (null op slots) now
construct with NumPy 2.x semantics instead of throwing.

Architecture was settled by probing NumPy 2.4.2 BEFORE any code (new
handover lesson §4.16 "Probe WHERE a semantic lives"):

* Masking is enforced in exactly ONE place — the buffered copy-back
  (npyiter_copy_from_buffers, nditer_api.c:2001-2026). Unbuffered
  WRITEMASKED operands write the array directly (kernel contract), and
  NumPy 2.x BUFNEVER means flags=['buffered'] with contiguous same-dtype
  operands ALSO skips enforcement ('buffered' is a permission, not a
  promise). Both NOT-enforced cases are pinned as parity tests; the
  execution drivers/Tier-3B needed ZERO changes — the roadmap's assumed
  "masked write contract in ForEach" does not exist in NumPy either.

* VIRTUAL is allocate-equivalent in NumPy 2.x: npyiter_allocate_arrays
  allocates a real backing array for EVERY null operand (NEP-12's
  buffer-only design never landed; NPY_OP_ITFLAG_VIRTUAL's sole consumer
  is DebugPrint). Unlike ALLOCATE, the requested dtype is DISCARDED
  (npyiter_prepare_one_operand nulls op_dtype on the non-ALLOCATE branch)
  and the common dtype of the real operands is used; a null ARRAYMASK
  defaults to bool; virtual+allocate -> ALLOCATE wins (dtype honored).
  All verified by Python probes (operands[0].dtype == float32 despite an
  int32 request) before porting.

Implementation:

* NDIterBufferManager.FlushBufferWindow dispatches WRITEMASKED WRITE ops
  to CopyWindowFromBufferMasked: the same run-decomposed window walk with
  a mask cursor riding the flat window counter. Mask source follows
  NumPy's BUFNEVER switch (nditer_api.c:2009-2014): the mask's buffer
  when it was buffered, else its window-start ARRAY pointer
  (ArrayWritebackPtrs — FillBufferWindow already saved it for every
  operand); mask byte stride is BufStrides[maskop] (tight element size
  when buffered, the TRUE single linear stride when unbuffered — valid
  across the whole window because unbuffered implies IsOperandIterLinear,
  including stride 0 for a fully-broadcast mask).

* CopyRunFromBufferMasked decomposes each inner run into contiguous TRUE
  stretches and hands them to the unmasked CopyRunFromBuffer — NumPy's
  _strided_masked_wrapper structure — so memcpy/SIMD-cast kernels keep
  working for dense masks; a stride-0 mask gates whole runs.

    WRITEONLY" (was: silently accepted READONLY+WRITEMASKED)

feat(ufunc): out= and where= parameters across the elementwise np.* API (roadmap Wave 2.1)

The ufunc out=/where= kwargs — present on every NumPy ufunc, absent from
the entire NumSharp API until now — land on the elementwise core:

  binary: np.add, np.subtract, np.multiply, np.divide, np.true_divide,
          np.mod, np.power, np.floor_divide
  unary:  np.sqrt, np.exp, np.log, np.sin, np.cos, np.tan, np.abs,
          np.absolute, np.negative, np.square

All semantics probed against NumPy 2.4.2 BEFORE implementation; every
rule and error text below is pinned verbatim by tests:

* out joins the broadcast but never stretches: inputs broadcast UP to a
  larger out (add((4,),(4,),out=(2,4)) repeats rows, verified); a
  mismatched out raises "operands could not be broadcast together with
  shapes (4,) (4,) (5,) " (every operand listed, NumPy's trailing space
  included); a stretchable out raises "non-broadcastable output operand
  with shape (1,) doesn't match the broadcast shape (4,)".
* The loop dtype is resolved from the INPUTS (NEP50) — out only needs a
  same_kind cast from it: add(f64,f64,out=i32) raises "Cannot cast ufunc
  'add' output from dtype('float64') to dtype('int32') with casting rule
  'same_kind'" (ufunc names matched: np.mod reports 'remainder', np.abs
  'absolute', np.negative 'negative', np.divide 'divide');
  i32+i32->i16 and f64+f64->f32 work (same_kind within a kind).
* The provided out instance is returned (reference identity).
* where must be exactly bool — NumPy casts the mask under the 'safe'
  rule: "Cannot cast array data from dtype('int64') to dtype('bool')
  according to the rule 'safe'". It broadcasts over the operands AND
  participates in the output shape (probed: add((4,),(4,),
  where=(2,4)-mask) returns (2,4)). Mask-false slots keep the prior out
  contents; 'where' without 'out' produces an uninitialized fresh result
  (NumPy warns; the unmasked values are unobservable).
* out aliasing an input is well-defined — the Wave-1.1 COPY_IF_OVERLAP
  machinery makes add(x[:-1], x[:-1], out=x[1:]) produce NumPy's exact
  result with zero extra plumbing.

Architecture (mirrors NumPy's ufunc layer, ufunc_object.c:2169-2251):

* DefaultEngine.UfuncOut.cs (new): validation with exact texts +
  ExecuteBinaryUfuncInto / ExecuteUnaryUfuncInto. The kernel bodies and
  cache keys are IDENTICAL to the existing Tier-3B routes — both routes
  share compiled kernels; only the iterator wiring differs:
  - provided out rides as the write operand (no result allocation);
  - a dtype-mismatched out becomes a CAST operand: the kernel writes the
    loop dtype into the out operand's buffer and the Wave-4 windowed
    flush casts on write-back (BUFFERED|GROWINNER|DELAY_BUFALLOC,
    iterator casting UNSAFE — the same_kind gate already ran, same as
    NumPy where the iterator runs after loop resolution);
  - where rides as a trailing ARRAYMASK operand with the out flagged
    WRITEMASKED (NumPy: op[nop] = wheremask, ufunc_object.c:2221), and
    the unary promoting buffered-cast config (Wave 4) composes with both.
* NDIterRef.ForEach masked inner loop (NumPy execute_ufunc_loop
  masked=1 structure): when a WRITEMASKED operand with a 1-byte mask is
  present, each inner chunk is decomposed into mask-TRUE runs and the
  unmasked kernel is invoked per run with run-adjusted pointers — SIMD
  survives dense masks; a stride-0 (scalar-broadcast) mask gates whole
  chunks. Non-1-byte masks keep the plain nditer kernel contract.
  Under a buffered cast the masked flush (Wave 1.3) is the second line
  of defense — kernel and flush masking compose.
* ExecuteElementWise accepts operandTypes of NOp-1 when the trailing
  operand is the ARRAYMASK (the kernel compiles over data operands only).
* TensorEngine: 16 signatures gain trailing `NDArray @out = null,
  NDArray where = null` (house pattern from ReduceAdd/ClipNDArray;
  breaking for external engine implementers — accepted per NumPy-parity
  policy). DefaultEngine overrides thread them into
  ExecuteBinaryOp/ExecuteUnaryOp, which branch to the Into paths AFTER
  dtype promotion (the loop dtype must be input-resolved first) and
  skip the trivial bypass exactly like NumPy disables its trivial loop
  for masked/provided-out execution. Power skips its scalar-exponent
  fast paths when out/where given; FloorDivide's dtype post-cast is
  bypassed (out's dtype governs); Abs routes unsigned inputs through
  the iterator instead of the Cast shortcut when out/where given.

perf(alloc): open the buffer-pool window + live-state GC pressure + finalizer suppression (roadmap Wave 2.4 + 2.2-partial)

THE measured finding of the wave: the allocator tax was the window, not
the machinery. SizeBucketedBufferPool existed but its 4 KiB-1 MiB window
missed BOTH hot patterns: the small-N ufunc result (1000 x f32 = 4000
bytes) sat 96 bytes under the floor, and every 4M-element output
(16-32 MiB) sat above the cap - so the dominant benchmark and real-world
shapes paid a fresh VirtualAlloc + demand-zero page faults on every call
while the pool idled.

Wave 2.4 changes:

* Pool window opened to 1 B - 64 MiB; buckets at >= 1 MiB hold at most 2
  buffers (MaxBuffersPerLargeBucket) so resident memory stays bounded -
  realistic workloads keep one or two hot output shapes warm, exactly
  the glibc-tcache pattern NumPy gets for free.
* GC memory pressure moved POOL-SIDE, tracking the buffer's LIVE state:
  AddMemoryPressure on every Take, RemoveMemoryPressure on every Return
  (pooled or freed). The first attempt kept pressure registered while
  buffers idled in the pool ("pressure follows native residency") and it
  measurably backfired: the GC saw ~100-200 MB of phantom live memory
  and ran near-constant gen2 collections - every probe row degraded
  30-50%. Pressure is a GC-scheduling signal about collection-reclaimable
  memory; idle pooled buffers are not collection-reclaimable. The
  Disposer no longer does pressure accounting for Native allocations
  (the issue #501 protection lives at the pool layer now, same pairing).
* GC.SuppressFinalize(Disposer) the moment the buffer is freed
  (ReleaseUnmanagedResources): after _freed flips, the finalizer is a
  guaranteed no-op - pulling the object out of the finalizer queue saves
  the churn on every released buffer whether the release came from
  Dispose or from ~NDArray's refcount drop. UnmanagedMemoryBlock
  create+Dispose: 121 -> 70 ns.

Measured (Release, i9-13900K, IN-PLACE toggle A/B - same directory, same
binary cache, cap flipped 1 MiB <-> 64 MiB with rebuild between, both
directions confirmed twice):

  P1  contig add 4M f32      3.37 ms -> 1.74 ms   (~2x)
  P9  mixed i32+f64 4M       6.4-6.9 -> 3.4-4.2 ms
  S2  strided 2-D sqrt 1M    790-807 -> 432-538 us
  P2-P4 broadcast rows       ~3.0    -> ~1.48 ms
  full grid record run: P1 1.84, P2 1.49, P3 1.48, P4 1.48, P5 1.84,
  P6 2.60, P7 2.13, P8 2.33, P9 4.25, P10 3.75, P11 2.06, P14 1.37 ms;

  WELL ahead of NumPy's class (P1 NumPy ~2.4-2.7 ms) on the

mixed trees, and the EXTERNAL_LOOP foot-gun (~40x) was one missing flag away
for every caller.

== np.evaluate(expr[, operands][, out]) ==

* ArrayNode leaves + implicit conversions: (NDExpr)a * b + 2 builds a tree;
  one cast lights up the operator set. Binding rewrites array leaves to
  positional inputs with REFERENCE deduplication - (a-b)/(a+b) iterates

  list) kept for the Tier-3C style.
* Iterator config: EXTERNAL_LOOP | COPY_IF_OVERLAP; out= joins via the
  ufunc rules (same_kind validation with the ufunc error text, never
  stretched, reference identity, overlap-safe aliasing through the Wave-1.1

  (BUFFERED|GROWINNER|DELAY_BUFALLOC + UNSAFE, NumPy ufunc-layer shape).

  default so alternative engines opt in); per-arity flag arrays cached

== NumPy result_type PER NODE (NDExpr.Typing.cs) ==

The old contract computed every node at the output dtype - documented as
"mirrors NumPy", actually wrong for any mixed tree: (i4*i4)+f8 must WRAP the
multiply in int32 (1410065408) before promoting; the old model gave 1e10.
A typing pass now resolves every node to its NumPy 2.4.2 dtype (all rules
probed first, pinned in tests):

* strong-strong NEP50 incl. the int/float tier crossing (i4+f4 -> f8,
  i2+f2 -> f4) - note the iterator's PromoteTypes gets this WRONG
  ("float always wins"); divergence recorded in the roadmap matrix
  (COMMON_DTYPE/VIRTUAL-common paths only; engine routes + evaluate use
  correct tables). Left unfixed pending a COMMON_DTYPE consumer.
* weak python-scalar literals: i4+2 -> i4, f2+2.5 -> f2, u1+2 -> u1,
  bool+2 -> i64, i4/2 -> f8, with the exact OverflowError ("Python integer
  300 out of bounds for uint8"). Weakness never propagates past a literal:
  every operator node materializes (np.add(2,3) -> i64), matching ufunc
  semantics.
* special resolvers: true_divide ints/bool -> f64 (flat); arctan2 -> tier
  float (i1 -> f16, i2 -> f32, i4+ -> f64); power/remainder/floor_divide
  bool -> int8; power with a NEGATIVE INTEGER LITERAL exponent raises
  NumPy's "Integers to negative integer powers are not allowed." at typing
  time (array exponents stay a documented runtime divergence); unary math
  tiers bool/i8 -> f16, i16 -> f32, i32+ -> f64, floats preserved;
  comparisons/logical_not/isnan-family -> bool; bool add=OR, multiply=AND
  (True+True is True, not byte 2); abs/floor/ceil/trunc identity on
  ints/bool (Math.Floor has no int overload - previously a latent crash);
  invert(bool) = XOR 1; boolean negative/subtract and invert/bitwise-on-float
  raise with NumPy's texts.
* emission converts at node edges; the kernel reads each operand at its
  NATIVE dtype (no iterator casting for inputs - the Wave-4 lesson applied:
  fused in-register converts beat buffered casts). SIMD engages when the
  whole tree resolves homogeneous. Legacy Compile() is byte-preserved:
  with no typing table every node falls back to OutputType (the existing
  146 Tier-3C tests pass unchanged).
* C# gotcha encoded as exact-match operators (handover lesson 18): with
  NDArray->NDExpr and numeric->NDArray implicits both live, expr + 2.5
  bound to the (NDExpr, NDArray) overload (better conversion target) and
  silently strong-typed the weak literal - f4+2.5 promoted to f8. The
  scalar/NDArray operator overloads on NDExpr are correctness, not sugar.

== Fused reductions (root-only ReduceNode) ==

NDExpr.Sum/Prod/Min/Max/Mean compile a one-pass raw inner loop
(CompileRawInnerLoop): evaluates the child tree per element, folds into a
host aux accumulator slot, 4-way unrolled with 4 accumulators (acc0 carries
across EXLOOP chunks; lanes init to the per-chunk identity, min/max lanes to
the carry - idempotent). sum(a*b) reads a and b once and never materializes
the product. Dtypes per NumPy: sum/prod bool/int -> i64, uint -> u64, floats
preserved; min/max preserve; mean ints -> f64. f16/f32 sums accumulate in
f64 and cast back once - a DOCUMENTED divergence from NumPy's pairwise
(usually more accurate; sum of 70000 f16 ones -> inf identically). Min/max
NaN-propagate via Math.Min/Max, And/Or for bool, double-roundtrip for Half.
Empty inputs: sum=0, prod=1, mean=NaN at the result dtype, min/max raise
"zero-size array to reduction operation minimum which has no identity".
Complex min/max -> NotSupported (documented).

== EXTERNAL_LOOP guard ==

ExecuteExpression now throws InvalidOperationException when the iterator
lacks EXTERNAL_LOOP (unless single-chunk ONEITERATION or IterSize <= 1):
without it the driver advances per element and the compiled kernel runs
with count==1 - silently correct, catastrophically slow (the measured ~40x
foot-gun). np.evaluate configures the flag automatically.

feat(ufunc): ONE NumPy-shaped overload per elementwise ufunc — dtype= joins out=/where= (Wave 2.1 follow-up)

Follow-up to 5962a5e: the out=/where= wave left the 18 elementwise ufuncs
without a single overload matching NumPy's actual signature. sqrt (and 11
peers) split the surface across an out-REQUIRED overload and separate
positional-dtype overloads, so NumPy call forms like np.sqrt(x, where: m)
or np.sqrt(x, out, dtype: f32) had no C# equivalent, and np.power dropped
the dtype request entirely whenever out/where was given.

Every ufunc from that commit now exposes exactly one NumPy-shaped overload
mirroring f(x1[, x2], /, out=None, *, where=True, dtype=None):

    f(x[, x2], NDArray out = null, NDArray where = null[, NPTypeCode? dtype = null])

  unary:  sqrt, exp, log, sin, cos, tan, abs, absolute, negative, square
  binary: power, floor_divide
  (add/subtract/multiply/divide/true_divide/mod already had the merged
   (x1, x2, out, where) shape from 5962a5e; their dtype= needs typeCode
   plumbing through TensorEngine.Add/Sub/Mul/Div/Mod — separate wave.)

out sits in NumPy's positional slot (2nd/3rd arg IS out — NumPy raises
'return arrays must be of ArrayType' for a positional dtype, probed);
where/dtype are reachable by name without out. Legacy positional-dtype
overloads remain for source compat, demoted from (x, NPTypeCode? = null)
to (x, NPTypeCode) where the optional form would make f(x) ambiguous
against the merged overload (C# betterness rule: a no-defaults candidate
beats a defaults-filling one, so bare f(x) overloads stay safe).

dtype= semantics — ALL probed against NumPy 2.4.2 before implementation
and pinned verbatim by tests (the loop-SIGNATURE rule, not post-cast):

* dtype selects the LOOP and composes with out=: computation runs at the
  requested precision even into a wider out — np.sqrt([2.], out=f64,
  dtype=f32) stores 1.41421353816986083984 (the float32 value) in the
  float64 out; power(10,8,out=f64,dtype=f32) stores float32(1e8); the
  out-cast gate validates against the dtype-overridden loop ('Cannot cast
  ufunc "power" output from dtype("float32") to dtype("int32")...').
  Fixes Default.Power/Default.FloorDivide silently DROPPING typeCode when
  out/where was given (their 'NumPy ignores a dtype request when out is
  given' comments were disproven by probe).
* dtype-without-out runs the loop in dtype too — power(10, 11, dtype=f64)
  = 1e11 EXACTLY (was: int32 loop wraps to garbage, then cast). The
  compute-promoted-then-Cast post-step in Power/FloorDivide is gone;
  ExecuteBinaryOp takes an NPTypeCode? dtype override that replaces the
  promoted resultType after NEP50 resolution, exactly where NumPy's loop
  resolution sits. Power's scalar-exponent fast paths (x**0/1/2/0.5/-1
  substitute whole other ufunc loops) are skipped under an explicit dtype.
* the negative-integer-exponent ValueError follows the RESOLVED loop:
  power(2, -1, dtype=f64) = 0.5 is legal; power(2, -1, dtype=i64) still
  raises 'Integers to negative integer powers are not allowed.'.
* inputs must reach the dtype loop via same_kind casts, NumPy texts
  verbatim: binary errors are indexed ('Cannot cast ufunc "floor_divide"
  input 0 from dtype("float64") to dtype("int32") with casting rule
  "same_kind"'), unary errors name no index ('...ufunc "negative"
  input from...'). New ValidateUnaryInputCast/ValidateBinaryInputCasts
  beside the existing ValidateOutCast in DefaultEngine.UfuncOut.cs;
  applied in Default.Negate/Abs/Square and ExecuteBinaryOp's override.
* float-only ufuncs (sqrt/exp/log/sin/cos/tan) reject int/bool dtype with
  'No loop matching the specified signature and casting was found for
  ufunc sqrt' — each now names ITS ufunc: ResolveUnaryReturnType/
  ResolveUnaryFloatReturnType gain a ufunc-name parameter, fixing the
  hardcoded 'ufunc Sin' that every op's error reported (pre-existing).
* negative follows NumPy's loop rule for bool: TensorEngine.Negate gains
  NPTypeCode? typeCode (house signature; breaking for external engines —
  accepted per NumPy-parity policy) and Default.Negate rejects a BOOLEAN
  LOOP rather than a boolean input: negative([True,False], dtype=f64) =
  [-1., -0.] now works; negative(f64, dtype=bool) raises the same
  boolean-negative TypeError as plain negative(bool) — all probed.
* abs(complex): dtype names the loop's OUTPUT (D->d) — float kinds select
  the magnitude dtype, int/bool/complex requests raise the no-loop error
  for ufunc absolute (probed: abs(c128, dtype=c128) raises in NumPy).

* floor/ceil/trunc have IDENTITY loops for every bool/int dtype

  PRESERVED. np.round's integer path is an identity COPY (round_(i4) ->

  ints). Implemented as an identity arm in EmitUnaryScalarOperation
  (emit nothing -- the loaded value IS the result) + engine loop-dtype
  preservation; fixes trunc(i4)/round_(i4) -> f64 and floor(bool) -> f64
  divergences (NumPy: int32/int32/bool).
* np.round/np.around accept out= ONLY (function, not ufunc -- where=/
  dtype= raise TypeError in NumPy; probed). decimals==0 routes to the
  rint path (cast errors name 'rint'); decimals!=0 is NumPy's

    numeric loop; the INPUT must reach it same_kind ("Cannot cast ufunc
    'floor' input from dtype('float64') to dtype('int32') with casting

    was found for ufunc <name>" -- each op now names ITSELF via the
    ResolveUnaryFloatReturnType ufunc-name parameter 6a566e49 added.

== ExecuteComparisonUfuncInto (UfuncOut.cs) ==

Mirrors ExecuteBinaryUfuncInto with the comparison deltas, all probed:
* loop dtype is Boolean; the kernel compares at result_type(lhs, rhs)
  INSIDE the body (fused per-element converts -- the Wave-4 measured
  winner for cheap ops) and emits bool. Pinned by the 2^53 precision
  probe: greater(int64 2^53+1, float64 2^53) -> False, equal -> True
  (both operands cast to f64 first).
* out of ANY numeric dtype is valid -- bool casts same_kind to all ten
  (probed A1 incl. complex128); True -> 1 at the out dtype through the
  windowed bool->X flush (scalar CopyWithCast fallback; bool pairs have
  no SIMD cast kernel -- correct, perf-only). ValidateOutCast stays for
  structural parity (unreachable for NumSharp's 15 dtypes).
* the scalar body and npy_cmp_{op}_{lhs}_{rhs} cache key are SHARED
  with TryExecuteComparisonOpViaNDIter -- the first out= call on an
  already-used comparison triple hits the warm kernel cache; vector
  body stays null (bool output breaks the Tier-3B same-dtype
  invariant, unchanged from the no-out route).
* flag arrays REUSED from the binary configs (identical operand layout
  [in, in, out(, mask)]) -- zero new statics (Wave-2.2 discipline).
* NO F-layout post-step: NumPy returns the provided out untouched --
  the ladder's ShouldProduceFContigOutput/copy('F') steps would clone
  and break reference identity, so the Into-path never runs them.

non-bool out engages the same windowed flush, and the overloads do NOT
call MakeGeneric<bool> (the plan's trap -- out may be f64). Zero new
engine machinery.

refactor(ufunc): merge the comparison/predicate bare+out overload pairs into ONE NumPy-shaped overload each

Follow-up to eb2abd6c (out/where plan slice 3), applying the merged-overload
convention from 6a566e49 to the families that shipped with the additive
required-out pattern. np.isinf — the reported example — had:

    public static NDArray<bool> isinf(NDArray a)
    public static NDArray       isinf(NDArray a, NDArray @out, NDArray where = null)

i.e. two overloads, neither matching NumPy's isinf(x, /, out=None, *,
where=True, dtype=None): out was REQUIRED on the second form, so the
NumPy-legal call np.isinf(x, where: m) did not compile, dtype= did not
exist, and the same split was repeated 9× across three layers.

Merged — 9 duplicate pairs collapsed at each layer (18 members removed):

  TensorEngine   : Compare/NotEqual/Less/LessEqual/Greater/GreaterEqual +
                   IsFinite/IsNan/IsInf are now ONE abstract member each,
                   house parameter order (inputs, NPTypeCode? typeCode = null,
                   NDArray @out = null, NDArray where = null) — same shape as
                   the unary-math family (Sqrt/Abs/...).
  DefaultEngine  : CompareOp + Default.Is{Finite,Nan,Inf} overrides merged;
                   the bare path keeps the existing trivial/SIMD ladder, the
                   out/where path keeps the Into-route (no behavior change on
                   either route — same bodies, one entry point).
  np layer       : np.equal/not_equal/less/less_equal/greater/greater_equal
                   (np.comparison.cs) and np.isfinite/isnan/isinf (np.is.cs)
                   are now f(x[, x2], out = null, where = null, dtype = null),
                   1-to-1 with the NumPy ufunc signature. The (NDArray, object)
                   / (object, NDArray) scalar conveniences stay (they ride the
                   operators and are not signature duplicates).

Return-type rule (the reason the split existed) resolved per NumPy:

* The merged member returns plain NDArray because with out= NumPy returns
  the PROVIDED array as-is whatever its dtype (np.less(a, b, out=f64)
  returns the f64 out, True→1 — bool casts same_kind to every numeric).
* A plain call (out==null, where==null) still returns an NDArray<bool>
  INSTANCE — now an explicit TensorEngine contract — so the typed wrapper
  is one zero-alloc cast away. The C# comparison operators (==, !=, <, <=,
  >, >=) keep their NDArray<bool> static type via AsGeneric<bool>(), which
  is a free downcast on the contract-conforming path (no new allocation:
  Default's bare path already produced the typed instance).
* Breaking (accepted per NumPy-parity policy): the np.* bare forms'
  STATIC type changes NDArray<bool> → NDArray. Runtime instances are
  unchanged, so '(NDArray<bool>)np.isnan(x)' and boolean-mask indexing
  keep working; only typed assignments need the cast.

dtype= added with NumPy's exact validate-only semantics (probed 2.4.2
before implementation — comparisons and these predicates have bool-output
loops ONLY, unlike sqrt&co where dtype selects a computation precision):

    np.equal(a, b, dtype=bool)    → no-op, normal result
    np.equal(a, b, dtype=float64) → TypeError 'No loop matching the
        specified signature and casting was found for ufunc equal'
    np.isnan(x, dtype=float64)    → same text, 'ufunc isnan'

  ValidateBoolLoopDtype (DefaultEngine.UfuncOut.cs, beside the existing
  ValidateOutCast/ValidateUnaryInputCast) raises the verbatim text with
  each ufunc's NumPy name: equal, not_equal, less, less_equal, greater,
  greater_equal, isfinite, isnan, isinf.

feat(ufunc): close the 1-to-1 signature sweep — dtype= on the binary six + bitwise, np.positive full ufunc surface, NumPy round shape

Completes the single-NumPy-shaped-overload audit across 5716f864 (slice 2)
and 6a566e49 (merged-overload wave). A reflection audit over every np.*
member those commits touched found four remaining gaps; all are closed
here, every rule probed against NumPy 2.4.2 BEFORE implementation and
pinned verbatim by tests.

1) dtype= on add/subtract/multiply/divide/true_divide/mod
   The 6a566e49 wave deferred these because the loop-dtype machinery
   didn't exist; it does now (ExecuteBinaryOp's dtype override from the
   power/floor_divide work), so the deferral was stale. TensorEngine
   gains the house (lhs, rhs, typeCode, out, where) signature on the
   five members; np.* adds the trailing dtype= param.
   * the loop COMPUTES in dtype: subtract(300_i64, 5_i64, dtype=i16) =
     295 in the int16 loop; add(0.1, 0.2, out=f64, dtype=f32) stores
     float32(0.3) = 0.30000001192092896 in the f64 out (probed).
   * BUG FIX (ordering): the bool add/multiply remap (+ = logical OR,
     * = logical AND) keyed off the PROMOTED dtype and ran before the
     dtype= override — add(True, True, dtype=i32) would have run the
     BitwiseOr loop and returned 1. NumPy runs the i32 add loop and
     returns 2 (probed). The remap now keys off the FINAL loop dtype:
     moved after the dtype override in ExecuteBinaryOp.
   * divide/true_divide are float-only ufuncs: integer/bool dtype=
     raises 'No loop matching the specified signature and casting was
     found for ufunc divide' (probed; same gate family as sqrt&co).
   * mod reports 'remainder' with indexed input-cast errors (probed:
     mod(f64, f64, dtype=i32) → "Cannot cast ufunc 'remainder' input 0
     from dtype('float64') to dtype('int32') ...").

2) dtype= on bitwise_and/or/xor
   Loop selection among the bool/int loops: dtype=i64 widens,
   dtype=i16 narrows under same_kind (300 & 300 = 300_i16, probed).
   A float/complex/decimal dtype= raises the NO-LOOP text — distinct
   from the float-INPUT coercion text ValidateBitwiseLoop produces
   ('ufunc not supported for the input types...'); both texts probed,
   the first implementation reused the wrong one and the probe caught it.

3) np.positive — full ufunc surface (was: bare copy only)
   Slice 2 prepared UnaryOp.Positive (identity emit, UfuncName mapping,
   Round uses it as the masked-copy vehicle) but never exposed the np
   surface. New TensorEngine.Positive + Default.Positive:
   * positive(x, out=) returns the provided instance; where= masks
     (false slots keep prior contents); both ride the unary Into-path
     with the identity kernel.
   * dtype= selects the loop: positive(i32, dtype=f64) widens (the
     no-out path is a cast-copy); positive(f64, dtype=i32) raises the
     unary same_kind input-cast error naming 'positive'.
   * bool rule probed precisely: positive has NO bool loop — plain
     positive(bool) raises "ufunc 'positive' did not contain a loop
     with signature matching types <class 'numpy.dtypes.BoolDType'> ->
     None" and dtype=bool raises the two-sided variant naming the
     input's DType class (new NumPyDTypeClassName helper maps
     NPTypeCode → numpy.dtypes.* names); positive(bool, dtype=f64) is
     LEGAL → [1., 0.] — the guard keys off the loop, not the input.

4) round_/around — NumPy's round(a, decimals=0, out=None) shape
   Slice 2 shipped TWO out-overloads each ((x, out=null) + (x, decimals,
   out=null)); NumPy has ONE signature whose 2nd positional is DECIMALS
   (np.round(x, out_array) raises 'only integer scalar arrays can be
   converted to a scalar index' — probed). Merged to
   (x, int decimals = 0, NDArray out = null); positional-out callers
   migrate to @out: (3 test sites updated). Legacy positional-dtype
   conveniences unchanged.

bench(nditer): iterator-core benchmark — NDIter machinery itself vs NumPy + standalone decomposition

New matched-id benchmark pair (npyiter_core_bench.{cs,py}) measuring the ITERATOR,
not the kernels: construction across 13 flag configurations, traversal/orchestration
across chunk profiles (w=4..1024 strided rows, transposed, row/col broadcast),
buffered cast/mixed windows, per-element protocol (+C_INDEX/+MULTI_INDEX), full-
reduce, and small-N pipeline scaling N=8..2M. All kernels trivial and matched to
NumPy's loop families (memcpy / scalar-strided / V256-contig) so iterator cost
dominates. Both scripts correctness-check before timing and refuse Debug JIT.

Headline results (i9-13900K, NumPy 2.4.2, Release — full tables in
benchmark/poc/NPYITER_CORE_BENCH_RESULTS.md):
- Construction beats np.nditer 1.4-3.7x in every multi-operand config
  (3-op 308 vs 622 ns; ufunc config 343 vs 1000 ns; 8-op 385 vs 1140 ns).
- Full-iterator vs full-iterator (strided-row ADD through NumPy's real ufunc
  nditer): parity at w=4 (10.1 vs 10.3 ns/chunk), 2x faster at w=1024.
  The 4 ns/chunk machine in np.copyto is NumPy's stripped raw-copy walker,
  NOT nditer — and production NDIter.Copy matches it exactly (T2c).
- Buffered mixed add 0.86x, broadcast adds 0.74-0.81x, transposed copy 0.84x,
  reductions 0.64-0.85x, contig copy at DRAM roofline parity.
- Raw iterator pipeline tracks NumPy's whole ufunc dispatch within +-8% at every
  N; production np.add(out=) carries ~200 ns of glue above it (648 vs ~440 ns).
- REUSED iterator (Reset+ForEach) at N=512: 54.7 ns/call — 7x under NumPy's
  e2e floor; the structural small-N lever NumPy cannot reach from Python.

Bugs/gaps surfaced (quantified in the results doc):
1. GROWINNER is hollow — NDIter.cs:751 sets the bit, ComputeTransferSize never
   reads it: same-dtype BUFFERED iterators chunk into 512 needless 8192-elem
   windows, +8.4% on 4M f64 add (G-series). One condition fixes it.
2. Broadcast construction pays +388 ns over same-shape (C5 696 vs C3 308 ns):
   rank-mismatched operands miss the same-shape fast path and allocate through
   np.broadcast_to; NumPy's delta is +97 ns.
3. Chunked-callback overhead decomposed: delegate ~1.3 ns/chunk (ForEach vs
   ExecuteGeneric), element-stride imul per op/axis/step in ExternalLoopNext
   (NumPy stores byte strides), mask-resolution branch — 7 vs 4 ns/chunk against
   raw-walker workloads only; already parity against NumPy's real nditer.

'How NDIter becomes the best' (prioritized, measured headroom): iterator
reuse/state pooling (54.7 ns floor proven), cut the 200 ns production glue,
implement GROWINNER, broadcast-ctor fast path, byte-stride axisdata +
specialized iternext, tiny-chunk whole-array lowering, parallel ForEach.
Roadmap doc links the new bench in its verification harness section.

bench(nditer): size-tier sweep (scalar/1K/100K/1M) — the official-report tiers, for the iterator core

Adds a parameterized size-sweep that runs the SAME six NDIter operation
families at each of four element-count tiers (scalar=1, 1K, 100K, 1M), so the
iterator's NumSharp-vs-NumPy story can be read per cache tier the way the
official benchmark report presents whole-op throughput. Prior NDIter rounds
used per-aspect ad-hoc sizes; this fixes a clean 6x4 matrix on both sides with
identical ids.

Files:
- npyiter_sizesweep_bench.cs  — NumSharp side. Six matched-kernel families:
    add   contiguous binary V256        copy  contiguous copy (memcpy chunk)
    sqrt  contiguous unary V256 Sqrt    sadd  strided a[::2]+b[::2]
    sum   4-acc V256 reduction          bcast stride-0 a+b1(1)
  Same Release-only Debug-JIT guard, best-of-rounds timing, and per-size iter
  counts as npyiter_core_bench.cs. All 24 correctness checks pass.
- npyiter_sizesweep_bench.py  — NumPy side, identical ids. copy uses
  np.positive (a REAL ufunc nditer) not np.copyto (a stripped raw-array
  walker), so the copy row is an honest iterator-vs-iterator comparison.
- npyiter_sizesweep_chart.py  — renders the speedup bar chart (NumPy/NumSharp,
  >1.0 = NumSharp faster) in the official-report axis style, grouped by size
  tier and by operation, plus a per-cell matrix. Self-contained: the settled
  clean run is embedded as (NumSharp_ms, NumPy_ms) per id; pass two recorded
  output files as argv to re-chart a fresh run (the bench .txt outputs are
  gitignored artifacts). The first C# run after a build is noise-tainted
  (machine not quiesced — sqrt@100K read 248us vs the true 57us); embedded
  numbers are the settled re-runs.

Result (geomean NumPy/NumSharp): scalar 2.29x, 1K 2.08x, 100K 1.33x, 1M 1.19x;
ALL 1.66x (20 win / 4 lose). The shape is the MIRROR of the full-API report:
NDIter is strongest at small N (construction beats np.nditer + ufunc dispatch
setup) and converges to parity at 1M where the kernel saturates memory
bandwidth and the iterator contributes ~nothing. The four sub-1.0 cells
(add@1M 0.88x, sqrt@1M 0.98x, sqrt@100K 0.99x, sadd@100K 0.99x) are all parity
within run-to-run bandwidth variance (add@1M measured 380-453us across runs vs
NumPy 398us). Standout: sum is 2.35-10.11x faster at every tier — NumPy's
reduce carries a ~1.5us fixed setup (sum@1: NS 151ns vs NumPy 1.53us) and a
slower large-N pairwise pass (sum@1M: NS 89us vs NumPy 209us).

bench(nditer): canonical NDIter benchmark — one section-addressable harness, one results sheet

Promotes the exploratory poc/npyiter_* rounds into a single MAINTAINED
NumSharp-vs-NumPy benchmark under benchmark/nditer/. Every distinct NDIter
aspect the poc rounds surfaced now lives in one place, swept across cache tiers,
rendered into ONE sheet (nditer_results.md): 162 measured pairs.

Pieces:
- nditer_bench.cs / .py  — identical-id NumSharp + NumPy benches, SECTION-
  ADDRESSABLE via the NPYITER_SECTION env var. Ten sections:
    operations x size : elementwise/reductions/selection/copycast/indexmath/
                        dtypes/dividends — 33 families x {scalar,1K,100K,1M}
    construction      : 9 iterator flag configs vs np.nditer build
    chunkwidth        : per-chunk dispatch overhead across inner widths 4..1024
    pathology         : the regression canaries (bcast-reduce, allocate,
                        overlap-copy, F-order-out, 0-d)
  Iterator-isolation rows drive NDIterRef directly with trivial NumPy-loop-
  matched kernels; production rows call np.* both sides; copy compares to
  np.positive (a real ufunc nditer), never np.copyto.

  kernels, positive-not-copyto), section table, and the findings ledger.
- nditer_results.{md,tsv}  — the rendered sheet + raw (id, ns_ms, np_ms) pairs
  from the 2026-06-13 run (i9-13900K, NumPy 2.4.2, Release).

fix(bench): op-matrix report ranked measurement artifacts as the "Top 15 Best"

The op/dtype/N matrix report (benchmark-report.md, rendered into the site as
benchmark-matrix.md) showcased garbage: every "Top 15 Best" row was np.copy(float64)
and np.searchsorted at "0.0 / 0.0x". Three distinct bugs, all fixed.

BUG 1 — searchsorted benchmark measured nothing (both sides)
  SortingBenchmarks.cs and numpy_benchmark.py issued a SINGLE scalar lookup
  (np.searchsorted(sorted, N/2)) — one O(log N) binary search, ~18ns at EVERY N,
  pure call overhead. Against NumPy's ~1µs Python overhead that manufactured a
  meaningless 50–1000x "win". Fixed: both now query the N-element array (a) into the
  sorted target → N binary searches, real work that scales with N. (Verified the C#
  benchmark project still compiles.)

BUG 2 — normalize_op_name collapsed a slice-copy onto np.copy
  The Slicing suite's "np.copy(a[100:1000])" (a fixed 900-element slice copy, ~3.6µs
  at every N) was normalized by stripping ALL "[...]" — including the array-index
  "[100:1000]" — yielding "np.copy", which COLLIDED with the Creation full-array
  "np.copy(a)" in csharp_index (last-write-wins) and overwrote the real float64
  measurement. THAT was the bogus "copy float64 = 0.0036ms" (not a copy bug at all;
  the op is fine — archived raw float64 copy@10M = 11.04ms). Fixed: only strip a
  space-separated " [annotation]" (\s+\[ instead of \s*\[), never index brackets
  attached to an identifier. Incidentally also de-collides concatenate/stack/slice
  variants. copy(float64) now reads its real values across all sizes (10M → 11.04ms,
  ratio 0.60 = a genuine win).

BUG 3 — the report ranked/averaged non-credible rows as wins
  merge-results.py sorted "Top Best" by ratio with only a `ratio is not None` guard,
  so a sub-resolution NumSharp time (ratio rounding to 0.0) sorted to #1, and CSV
  blanked legit 0.0 via `r.ratio or ''`. Fixed with a credibility gate (classify()):
  a row is "negligible" (new ▫ status) when either side did <1µs of work OR the
  speedup exceeds 20x (NumSharp >20x faster ⇒ artifact: a view, a lazy alloc, or a
  dead-code-eliminated kernel). Negligible rows are EXCLUDED from Top Best/Worst and
  from the per-size geomean, but still listed (▫) in the per-suite tables — nothing
  hidden. Also: store ms at 4 / ratio at 3 decimals, show 3-decimal ms + 2-decimal
  ratio in the showcase (no more "0.0/0.0x"), fix the `or ''` falsy-zero in CSV, add
  the ▫ legend row + summary/size-table counts, and a header note stating how many
  rows were excluded and why.

Result (regenerated from the on-disk run archive with the fixed merge):
  * Top Best is now real reductions/statistics wins (np.nansum 0.08x, np.percentile
    0.10x, np.average 0.10x) — genuine ms on both sides.
  * 1233 ops → 305 faster / 255 close / 169 slower / 103 much-slower / 275 NEGLIGIBLE
    (the artifacts, previously ~all counted as "faster") / 126 n/a.
