fix(net8.0): NumPy-correct complex abs and axis min/max NaN propagation

Two net8.0-only BCL semantic gaps surfaced by the fuzz differential matrix.
Both behave correctly on net9.0+ (where the BCL was fixed) but produced
wrong values on net8.0; worked around to match NumPy 2.4.2.

1. np.abs(complex) with an infinite component returned NaN instead of +inf
   ------------------------------------------------------------------------
   cabs(NaN + inf*i) must be +inf (C99 hypot / npy_cabs: the infinity test
   precedes the NaN test). System.Numerics.Complex.Abs routes through a
   private Hypot whose operand ordering is NaN-unaware, so on net8.0 it
   returns NaN for abs(NaN+inf*i) (fixed in the .NET 9 BCL).

   Added Utilities/NDComplexMath.Abs(Complex): returns +inf when either
   component is infinite, else defers to Complex.Abs — so every finite/
   NaN-only magnitude that already matched NumPy bit-for-bit is unchanged.
   Repointed the two cached MethodInfo handles that drive every complex-abs
   emit site: DirectILKernelGenerator.CachedMethods.ComplexAbs (6 IL call
   sites across the scalar/strided/predicate/math/decimal unary loops) and
   DefaultEngine.UnaryOp.s_complexAbs (NDIter Tier-3B route).

   Fixes 19 unary.jsonl + 1 random_smoke.jsonl fuzz cases (all layouts:
   contiguous / strided / transposed / broadcast / negstride).

2. ptp / amax / amin along an axis dropped NaN instead of propagating it
   ------------------------------------------------------------------------
   The typed-struct leading/innermost axis-reduction fast paths
   (MinOp<T>/MaxOp<T>.Combine256/128) called raw Vector256/128.Min/Max. The
   x86 vminps/vmaxps these lower to return the SECOND operand on an
   unordered (NaN) compare; the BCL Vector{N}.Min/Max only adopted IEEE NaN
   propagation in .NET 9. Verified: Vector128.Max(NaN,5) == 5 on net8.0,
   == NaN on net10.0. So max/min/ptp over a NaN-laced axis silently lost
   the NaN on net8.0 (ptp axis=0 returned a finite value where NumPy = NaN).

   Routed MinOp/MaxOp through the existing NaNAwareMinMax256/128 helper
   (already used by the contiguous/strided CombineVectors paths) and wrapped
   that helper's float/double self-equality mask in #if NET8_0 — so net9.0+
   keeps the single-instruction vmaxps with zero overhead while net8.0 gets
   ConditionalSelect(ordered, min/max, a+b) NaN propagation. The flat
   whole-array reduction kernel already emitted this via
   EmitVectorNaNPropagatingMinMax, so only the axis fast paths were affected.

   Fixes 12 stat.jsonl fuzz cases (ptp float32/float64, axis 0/1, C/F-contig).

Verification: full unit suite green on BOTH net8.0 and net10.0 (9709 passed
/ 0 failed under the CI filter), FuzzMatrix 42/42 on both. The originally

pattern): a bit-exact probe over a finite battery showed System.Numerics.
Complex matches NumPy to a few ULP on the finite interior, but diverges at
86/360 edge components -- it returns (NaN,NaN) for nearly all inf/NaN inputs
instead of the C99 Annex G values, drops the sign of zero on branch cuts,
and mishandles arctan's imaginary-axis cut. So:

- NDComplexMath.{Sinh,Cosh,Tanh,Asin,Acos,Atan} delegate the finite
  interior to the BCL and add the C99 fixups:

    npy_csinh/ccosh/ctanh, with asin/atan reusing NumPy's own identities
    asin(z)=i*conj(casinh(i*conj z)) and atan(z)=i*conj(catanh(i*conj z)).

    Im on y=-0; acos negates Im on the y=+0 cut; atan sets

    imaginary part, tanh's sign(y) zero, and the genuinely-unspecified
    zero signs), the helpers match the observed NumPy 2.4.2 output.
- DirectILKernelGenerator: register CachedMethods.Complex{Sinh,Cosh,Tanh,
  Asin,Acos,Atan} (pointing at NDComplexMath, not Complex.* directly) and
  add the six cases to EmitUnaryComplexOperation.

fix(memory): dispose owned intermediates in np.isclose and np.random.exponential

The np.allclose / np.random.exponential working-set leak guards
(np.allclose.UsingTests, np.random.exponential.UsingTests) failed in CI with
hundreds of MB of working-set growth (e.g. 551 MB on Linux, threshold 20 MB),
while passing on Windows. Root cause: both functions allocate several
NDArray intermediates per call and never dispose them — the unmanaged buffers
ride the finalizer queue instead of being released synchronously. In a tight
loop the managed wrappers are tiny so the GC rarely runs, leaving the
intermediates LIVE between collections; the allocator can't reuse that memory,
so the high-water mark balloons. On glibc (Linux) freed pages are retained in
the arena, so the process RSS stays high even after the test's final
GC.Collect()+WaitForPendingFinalizers() — hence the large WorkingSet64 delta.

np.isclose: |a-b| <= atol + rtol*|b| materialized ~5 float64 temps (≈400 KB
each at 50K elements) plus several bool temps, none disposed. Wrapped every
fresh allocation in `using` (the elementwise operators/ufuncs each return a new
array). x/y come from astype(copy:false), which returns the input itself when
no conversion is needed, so they are caller-owned and never disposed here. The
final combined array is captured in `using` too: MakeGeneric<bool>() takes its
own refcount on the shared buffer, so disposing the backing temp on return
keeps the result alive while keeping that last buffer off the finalizer queue.

np.random.exponential: β·(-log(1-U)) left uniform, (1-U) and negate()
intermediates un-disposed (only the log result was released). Now disposes all
of them; only the trailing `* scale` allocates the fresh array returned to the
caller.

Effect (measured, peak WorkingSet64 growth across a 1000-iter no-GC loop —

fix(complex): port NumPy's own algorithms for complex unary math (parity with NumPy 2.4.2)

The complex (complex128) overloads of the unary math ops deferred to System.Numerics.Complex
for their finite interior. The BCL transcendentals diverge from NumPy on a wide range of
edge inputs — large magnitudes, the unit circle, tiny/subnormal values, branch cuts and
signed zeros — because they do NOT implement the careful FreeBSD msun algorithms NumPy uses.
This replaces those deferrals with direct ports of NumPy's own routines in NDComplexMath,
verified by a 504-point bit-exact sweep (Python struct-packed int64 references) classifying
every result as exact / <=3 ULP / signed-zero / special / sign-flip.

Result: 18 of 20 complex unary ops are now at full parity (0 divergence beyond <=3 ULP):
  exp, log, log10, log2, log1p, expm1, exp2, sin, cos, tan, sqrt, square, reciprocal,
  negative, sinh, cosh, tanh, arcsin, arctan.

Algorithms ported / fixes (src/NumSharp.Core/Utilities/NDComplexMath.cs):

- Log (npy_clog): real part = log|z| with the four-regime rescale — |z| huge (x2 down),
  subnormal (x2^53 up), near the unit circle (0.71<=|z|<=1.73 uses 0.5*log1p((m-1)(m+1)+n^2)
  via a Goldberg MathLog1p), and 0. Complex.Log cancels the real part to 0 near |z|=1
  (e.g. log(1+1e-10 i).real must be 5e-21, not 0). ComplexLog is repointed here, so np.log,
  np.log2 and np.log10 all inherit the accuracy.

- Tanh (npy_ctanh): Kahan's algorithm (t=tan(y); beta=1+t^2; s=sinh(x); rho=sqrt(1+s^2);
  tanh=(beta*rho*s + i t)/(1+beta*s^2)) plus the |x|>=22 overflow-safe branch. The BCL
  Complex.Tanh drifts ~33 ULP (tan(1.5) through the tan(z)=-i*tanh(iz) identity).

- Sin/Cos/Tan: now route ALWAYS through Sinh/Cosh/Tanh, exactly as NumPy defines
  npy_csin/ccos/ctan (= -i*sinh(iz) / cosh(iz) / -i*tanh(iz)), so they match NumPy bit-for-bit
  instead of only on the BCL's finite interior. Fixes sin(0+1e300 i).real = NaN (BCL did
  cosh(huge)*0); the Sinh/Cosh y==0 guard returns (sinh(x), y)/(cosh(x), x*y) so a large real
  no longer yields inf*0 = NaN.

- Expm1 (nc_expm1): real = expm1(x)*cos(y) - 2 sin^2(y/2), imag = exp(x)*sin(y); the real
  expm1 fallback uses the Goldberg identity (e^x-1)*x/log(e^x) which recovers the ~10 digits
  exp(x)-1 cancels and avoids underflow (expm1(1e-300)=1e-300, not 0). Fixes the non-finite
  imaginary (expm1(+Inf+0i).imag = exp(+Inf)*sin(0) = NaN) and origin signed zeros.

- Square (z*z with FMA contraction): (fma(re,re,-(im*im)), fma(re,im,im*re)). NumPy's complex
  multiply is FMA-contracted, so square(1e-10+1e-10 i).real = -2.275e-37 (exact re^2 minus
  rounded im^2) and square(1e300+1e300 i).real = -inf; Complex.op_Multiply (no FMA) returned
  0 and NaN.

- Atan (npy_catanh, full): atanh(x) on the real axis, atan(y) on the imaginary axis, and the
  log1p(4|x|/sumsq(|x|-1,|y|))/4 interior, plus _sum_squares and an exponent-classified
  _real_part_reciprocal (raw biased-exponent field, NOT Math.ILogB which maps 0/Inf to
  int.MinValue/MaxValue and overflows the subtraction). Complex.Atan cancelled / underflowed
  the tiny imaginary part (arctan(0+1e-10 i).imag must be 1e-10).

- Exp (npy_cexp): exp(-Inf + I(Inf|NaN)).imag = copysign(0, y) so exp(-inf-inf i).imag = -0
  (the system libm keeps sign(y); npy_cexp's flat (0,0) dropped it). exp2 inherits this.

- Reciprocal already used Smith's nc_recip (overflow-safe, correct signed zeros).

Engine wiring (DirectILKernelGenerator[.Unary.Decimal].cs): ComplexLog repointed to
NDComplexMath.Log; new cached methods ComplexExpm1 and ComplexSquare; the Expm1 and Square
cases in EmitUnaryComplexOperation now call the ported helpers instead of inline
Complex.Exp(z)-1 / Complex.op_Multiply.

Accepted residuals (pathological inputs only, documented in code + the fuzz registry):
- cos/sin with a NaN imaginary part: the resulting zero's sign is C99-UNSPECIFIED; the
  platform libm and the npy_ccos identity pick opposite signs (2 cases).
- arccos with a sub-DBL_MIN imaginary part: Complex.Acos flushes the denormal real part to 0
  where cacos's _do_hard_work keeps it (~5.8e-309); a denormal-range edge (4 cases).
- sinh/cosh at the overflow boundary |x| in [710, 710.13]: Windows' CRT sinh overflows to inf
  while .NET Math.Sinh stays finite (a platform-libm boundary, absent on glibc).

perf(creation): np.zeros via calloc + Windows VirtualAlloc demand-zero (match/beat NumPy 2.4.2)

np.zeros was ~1000x slower than NumPy for large arrays (10M float64: 14.3 ms
vs NumPy 0.011 ms). Root cause: it allocated an uninitialized buffer and then
ran an eager per-element Fill loop that touched (and zeroed) every byte. NumPy
instead delegates zeroing to the OS: PyDataMem_NEW_ZEROED -> calloc, whose
demand-zero pages are committed and zeroed lazily on first write, so allocating
zeros is effectively O(1) regardless of size (numpy/_core/src/multiarray/alloc.c
npy_alloc_cache_zero: small sizes use a cache+memset, large sizes calloc).

This ports NumPy's structure. The zeroing is now done by the allocator/OS, never
an element loop — correct for all 15 dtypes because the all-zero bit pattern
equals default(T) for every one of them (incl. Half, Single, Double, Decimal,
Complex).

Implementation
--------------
- ArraySlice.Allocate(..., fillDefault: true) and Allocate<T>(..., true) now
  route to UnmanagedMemoryBlock<T>.AllocateZeroed instead of
  `new UnmanagedMemoryBlock<T>(count, default)` (Take + scalar Fill). All
  np.zeros overloads, np.zeros_like, np.eye/np.identity, and every internal
  fill-with-default allocation flow through here.
- SizeBucketedBufferPool.TakeZeroed: NativeMemory.AllocZeroed (calloc) with no
  dirty-bucket reuse — a recycled buffer would force a full memset, discarding
  the lazy demand-zero win for large sizes and being no cheaper than calloc for
  small ones.
- OsVirtualMemory (new, Windows-only): the Windows process heap eager-commits
  and memsets mid-size calloc requests (~256 KiB-2 MiB, ~0.05 ms for 800 KiB),
  unlike glibc/macOS which mmap large blocks lazily. For >= 128 KiB on Windows
  AllocateZeroed uses VirtualAlloc(MEM_COMMIT) (copy-on-write zero pages,
  ~0.002 ms) and a new Disposer AllocationType.Virtual that releases straight to
  the OS via VirtualFree (not pooled). Non-Windows and small sizes stay on
  calloc, which is already lazy/cheap there.

Benchmark fix (pre-existing bug)
--------------------------------
CreationBenchmarks returned each created array without disposing, leaking one
buffer per op. NumPy's harness (numpy_benchmark.py) discards each result inside
the timed loop, so CPython refcount frees it immediately — i.e. NumPy measures
alloc+free while the C# benchmark measured alloc-only (unfair) and leaked. Under
BenchmarkDotNet's thousands-of-ops-per-iteration, every untouched-but-committed
buffer still charges Windows commit, so any fast creation op OOMs at 10M
(np.empty(10M) already did; the old np.zeros only escaped by being slow enough
to throttle BDN to a couple ops/iteration). All creation benchmarks now dispose
per op, matching NumPy and bounding resident memory.

Results (this machine, vs NumPy 2.4.2; BDN alloc+free)
------------------------------------------------------
- 10M float64: 14.3 ms -> 0.0033 ms (was ~1000x slower; now 3.1x faster)
- medium (100K): 1.7-3.8x faster across i32/i64/f32/f64
- large (10M): 1.1-3.5x faster across i32/i64/f32/f64
- small (1K): ~1.5-2x slower — bounded by NDArray object construction
  (NDArray/Storage/Shape/ArraySlice/Disposer), shared by all creation APIs and
  sub-microsecond; the allocation itself is optimal.

fix(exp2): correct malformed float32-output IL kernel (was InvalidProgramException)

np.exp2 threw InvalidProgramException for EVERY call resolving to a float32 (Single) output —
int16/uint16/char/float32 inputs (via ResolveUnaryFloatReturnType) or any input with
dtype=float32. exp2->float64 and exp2->float16 were unaffected.

Root cause: DirectILKernelGenerator.Unary.Math.cs, EmitExp2Call, the type == Single branch
emitted one spurious instruction. Math.Pow takes (base, exponent), so the exponent must be
stashed in a local and pushed after the base. The Single branch pushed an EXTRA `Ldc_R8 2.0`
before the Stloc, so:

  Conv_R8            ; [x_d]
  Ldc_R8 2.0         ; [x_d, 2.0]      <- spurious push
  Stloc locExp       ; [x_d]           locExp = 2.0  (saved the constant, NOT the exponent)
  Ldc_R8 2.0         ; [x_d, 2.0]
  Ldloc locExp       ; [x_d, 2.0, 2.0]
  Call Math.Pow      ; [x_d, 4.0]      Pow(2,2)=4, pops 2
  Conv_R4            ; [x_d, 4.0f]     <- TWO values left on the stack

The body left a net +1 on the evaluation stack, so the DynamicMethod failed IL verification ->
InvalidProgramException at JIT time. (Latent second defect, masked by the crash: locExp held the
constant 2.0, so even a balanced version would have returned Pow(2,2)=4 for every element.)

Fix: delete the spurious push so the Single branch mirrors the (correct) Double branch wrapped in
Conv_R8/Conv_R4 — Conv_R8 -> save exponent -> push base 2.0 -> push exponent -> Pow -> Conv_R4.
exp2(float32[0,.5,1,-1,3]) now returns [1, 1.4142135, 2, 0.5, 8], bit-matching NumPy 2.4.2.

- Code: the decimal exp2 path (Unary.Decimal.cs) already saves the exponent correctly, and every
  other unary transcendental routes through EmitMathCall (MathF.X for Single — one arg, balanced),
  so exp2's Single branch was the only emitter with this idiom.
- Empirical: swept all 20 float-producing unary ufuncs x 12 input dtypes (240 cells) vs NumPy ->
  0 InvalidProgram crashes, 0 dtype mismatches; the only value differences are the pre-existing,
  accepted 1-float32-ULP transcendental gaps (exp/sin/cos/rad2deg, MathF vs NumPy's float32 libm),
  unrelated to exp2 (which is now exact).

fix(power): Half exponent no longer throws InvalidCastException (W1-B)

fix(maximum/minimum/clip): propagate NaN through the clip SIMD kernel (W11-A, W6-D)

np.maximum / np.minimum (and np.clip) must propagate NaN per NumPy 2.4.2 — the
result is NaN whenever EITHER operand is NaN. NumSharp routes all three through
the clip SIMD kernel, whose hardware MAXPS/MINPD intrinsics (Avx.Max / Avx.Min,
plus the Sse/Avx512 equivalents) return the SECOND operand on an unordered (NaN)
compare, silently dropping the NaN on every full SIMD vector. The scalar tail
(Math.Max/Min, HalfMaxNaN, ComplexMaxNaN) already propagated, so the bug only
surfaced once an array reached the vector width; small arrays (and earlier
size-2 spot checks) passed by luck.

Reproduction (float64, >= one V256<double> = 4 lanes):
  np.maximum([1,nan,3,nan,5,nan,7,8], [9,2,nan,4,nan,6,nan,nan])
    before: [9, 2, NaN, 4, NaN, 6, NaN, NaN]            (a==NaN lanes return b)
    after : [9, NaN, NaN, NaN, NaN, NaN, NaN, NaN]      == NumPy
  np.clip([nan,1,2,3,4,5,6,7], 2, 5)
    before: [2, 2, 2, 3, 4, 5, 5, 5]                    (NaN clamped to a_min)
    after : [NaN, 2, 2, 3, 4, 5, 5, 5]                  == NumPy

Fix (DirectILKernelGenerator):
  EmitVectorMinOrMax gains a `propagateNaN` flag. For Single/Double lanes it now
  emits the NaN-restoring select
      result = ConditionalSelect(Equals(a, a), hwMinMax(a, b), a)
  i.e. keep the hardware min/max where a is non-NaN, else re-inject a (= NaN).
  This is robust regardless of whether the underlying min/max already propagates
  (verified against Avx.Max/Min AND the cross-platform Vector{N}.Max/Min fallback).
  The raw hardware emit is factored into EmitRawVectorMinOrMax and is still used
  verbatim for integer lanes (no NaN) and any opt-out caller, so integer
  maximum/minimum are byte-for-byte unchanged. The two clip call sites
  (Max(vec,lo) / Min(vec,hi)) pass propagateNaN: true, fixing maximum (clip
  a_min), minimum (clip a_max), and clip (both bounds) in one place. clip with a
  NaN BOUND also propagates, matching NumPy's minimum(maximum(a,lo),hi)
  composition.

Scope: fmax/fmin (W7-B, the NaN-IGNORING opposite contract) still share the clip
path and remain divergent — a separate, already-tracked bug. This change does
not regress them (their fuzz excuse keys on a NaN appearing in NumSharp's output,
which still holds). The F-contiguous/strided element-pairing defect (W7-A) is
likewise untouched.

W6-D (clip) NaN excuses from MisalignedRegistry so the differential matrix
verifies NaN propagation bit-exact; W7-A and W7-B excuses preserved.

fix(maximum/minimum/clip): correct F-contiguous/strided element pairing and float16 signed-zero (W7-A)

np.maximum / np.minimum / np.clip (and fmax/fmin, which share the same kernel) all route
through the flat clip IL kernel in DirectILKernelGenerator.Clip. That kernel walks
src/dst/lo/hi linearly and pairs them by C-order (row-major) index. The engine, however,
handed it operands in whatever layout they arrived in:

  - PrepareBound built an array bound via broadcast_to(...).astype(outType). astype keeps
    the source layout (order='K'), so an F-contiguous / strided / broadcast bound stayed
    non-C-contiguous and was read in raw buffer order.
  - The general src/dst path used Cast(lhs, outType, copy:true), which likewise preserves
    the source layout, so an F-contiguous / strided source produced a non-C-contiguous
    working buffer.
  - A non-C-contiguous user out= was clipped in place in its own (F/strided) buffer, again
    mismatching the C-order bound.

Result: every element was paired with the wrong bound whenever a second operand (or the
source, or out=) was F-contiguous / transposed / strided / negative-strided / broadcast.
maximum(a, b.T) returned b's raw buffer instead of the element-wise max. This is the W7-A
fuzz divergence (34x in logic.jsonl).

Fix (Default.ClipNDArray): normalize every operand the flat array-bounds kernel touches to
C-contiguous offset-0 before the call.
  - PrepareBound copies the prepared bound to C-order when it isn't already C-contiguous
    offset-0.
  - The general path re-materializes a C-order copy of dst when lhs is F-contiguous /
    strided / offset.
  - A non-C-contiguous out= is clipped into a C-order temp and copied back via np.copyto
    (which honors the out's strides), preserving the return-the-out instance contract.
  - Scalar bounds are order-insensitive (one value per lane) and keep their existing fast
    paths untouched.

Half signed-zero tie-break (DirectILKernelGenerator.Clip): the residual W7-A divergence
after the pairing fix was float16-only and showed even on both-contiguous inputs - a
separate bug. NumPy's float16 maximum/minimum return the FIRST operand on a tie, so
maximum(+0,-0)=+0, maximum(-0,+0)=-0 (likewise minimum). HalfMaxNaN/HalfMinNaN used strict
>/< and returned the SECOND operand on the +0/-0 tie (wrong sign). Switched to >= / <= so

bench(complex-reduce): POC suite diagnosing + benchmarking complex128 axis-reduction perf

Investigation artifacts only — no library code changed. complex128 axis reductions
were the next-worst op cluster after np.zeros (sum/mean axis=0/1 ran 19–64× slower
than NumPy 2.4.2). These POCs find the root cause and benchmark every candidate fix
against NumPy 2.4.2, all re-runnable via `dotnet run -c Release` in benchmark/poc.

Root cause (complex_axis_probe / complex_alloc_probe / complex_why_probe):
- NOT boxing. np.sum(complex) allocates ~0 B/elem; the (object) casts in
  CombineScalarsPromoted JIT-elide. The earlier "30M boxes" theory was wrong.
- The real cost is scalar System.Numerics.Complex add where NumPy SIMD-vectorizes
  the reduction (complex == contiguous double pairs). A double-pair Vector256 add
  reaches NumPy parity: 7.52 vs 7.59 ms @10M, and beats it @1M (0.31 vs 0.33).
- Secondary: the scalar fallback's non-inlined per-element combine + op-switch +
  cache-hostile per-output column gather (axis=0); mean's MeanAxisComplex allocates
  an NDArray view + iterator per output row (6 B/elem).
- Small-N gap is compute (scalar), not allocation: np.zeros((N,)) output is ~4% of
  the op; pure compute is ~93%.

Candidate benchmark (complex_reduce_poc) — baseline / NDAxisIter / NDIter-2op via
ForEach / NDIter-2op via ExecuteGeneric / monolithic generic-math, both axes,
10K–10M, plus strided input, Half/Decimal sweep, and alloc/op:
- Monolithic generic-math is the most uniform (1.3–2.5× NumPy, never bad).
- NDAxisIter beats NumPy on inner-reduce (axis=1) but is cache-hostile on
  outer-reduce (axis=0, 6.6× @10M — per-output strided column gather).
- NDIter 2-op REDUCE is good on axis=0 but 5.8× on axis=1 (BUFFER+REDUCE inner
  double-loop unfinished) and allocates 2344 B/op for iterator construction.
- Half needs a wider <TInput,TAccum> accumulator (same-type is precision-wrong);
  Decimal/Complex are correct same-type.

perf(reduce): transposed/strided axis reductions to parity-or-better via input-stride axis ordering (Phase 4)

Brings non-C-contiguous (transpose / F-order / strided) complex/half-mean/decimal axis
reductions from ~16× NumPy to parity-or-better — solved by axis ORDERING, not the planned
AVX2 gather (which would still cache-miss).

ROOT CAUSE (diagnosed via a stride probe, not assumed)
The 2-op REDUCE iterator kept the LOGICAL axis order (inner loop = last logical axis), so
the kernel saw a contiguous inner stripe only when the input was C-contiguous. For a
transpose the last logical axis is strided, so the kernel got STRIDED input (stride 3162) =
cache-hostile column gather (10M complex sum: 119–130 ms vs NumPy 8 ms). NumPy is fast on
transposes because its nditer orders iteration axes by the input's STRIDE (contiguous axis
innermost).

FIX (reduce-local, in NDIterRef.NewReduce)
Order the op_axes iteration axes by descending input |stride| (a 0/broadcast stride sorts
outermost), and map the output operand back to the caller's original axis order. The kernel
then always sees the input's smallest-stride axis as the inner loop:
  - C-contiguous → the ordering is the identity (the already-fast path is byte-for-byte
    unchanged).
  - transpose / F-order / strided → the contiguous axis becomes inner; access is sequential
    (no gather, no copy). Only the accumulation order within each output cell changes
    (same elements) → fp-rounding only.
StrideKey(0)=MaxValue keeps broadcast axes outermost; stable insertion sort keeps equal
strides in ascending axis order.

RESULTS (isolated 10M, vs NumPy 2.4.2; "before" = prior strided path)
  transpose sum  axis0/1: 119/130 ms → 7.0/7.4 ms   (NumPy 8.6/7.8 — parity/beats)
  transpose mean axis0/1: 300/130 ms → 6.6/7.7 ms   (NumPy 7.7/8.6 — beats)
  transpose min/max:      145–170 ms → 15–17 ms     (NumPy 20–22 — beats)
  transpose prod:         130–140 ms → 12–17 ms     (NumPy 19–25 — beats)
The reduce_parity_bench.cs back-to-back harness still shows ~47 ms for these — a 256 MB-array
memory-pressure artifact; the isolated per-case bench (GC between cases) is the truth, same
artifact class as the original "19–64×" premise.

SCOPE / SAFETY
NewReduce only feeds the NDIter-routed dtypes (complex all-ops, half-mean, decimal all-ops);
numeric reductions stay on the DirectILKernelGenerator path, untouched. Correctness matrix
(C/F/T/sliced/3-D, axis 0/1/2, keepdims, out=, NaN) re-verified; full suite 9786 passed /
0 failed / 11 skipped (net10.0, excl OpenBugs/HighMemory). ComplexAxisReductionTests already
pins F-order/transpose/sliced layout invariance.

docs(reduce): record parallel-reduce proof (2-6x vs NumPy) + decision to decline it

Answers 'can NDIter make reduction faster?' with measurement: YES, via the
RANGE/PARALLEL_SAFE technique. Both Direct and NumPy reduce single-threaded;
range-splitting across cores (32-core box, phase6_parallel.cs, double sum):
  axis1 1M/10M: 3.8x/3.7x vs Direct, 6.5x/5.9x vs NumPy
  axis0 1M/10M: 1.8x/2.9x vs Direct, 1.7x/2.6x vs NumPy
  100M:         2.4-2.8x vs Direct

Decision: NOT adopted — held to NumSharp's design principle ('Parallelization is
minimal. Most operations use SIMD'). Keeps reductions bit-stable vs NumPy
(parallel partials shift fp order ~1e-9 and would be machine-dependent without a
fixed partition) and avoids a threading dependency in the reduction core. The
prototype is kept as evidence; the 2-6x is left on the table deliberately. If the
no-threading stance is ever revised, this is the lever (size-gated, fixed
partition count for determinism).

Phase 6 therefore remains the single-threaded parity migration already shipped
(Double Sum/Mean on the per-chunk SIMD path).

fix(complex): flat min/max return the NaN-bearing element verbatim (NumPy parity)

Flat (axis=None) complex min/max went through min_elementwise_il ->
Min/MaxElementwiseComplexFallback, which synthesized a (nan,nan) Complex on the
first NaN-bearing element. NumPy's minimum/maximum instead return the NaN operand
VERBATIM, and in a left-fold the FIRST NaN element wins and propagates. So:

  np.min([1+1j, nan+0j, 2+2j])      NumPy (nan, 0)    was (nan, nan)
  np.min([1+1j, 0+nanj, 2+2j])      NumPy (0, nan)    was (nan, nan)
  np.min([nan+5j, 1+1j, nan+0j])    NumPy (nan, 5)    was (nan, nan)   # first NaN wins

Fix: Min/MaxElementwiseComplexFallback now returns v (the element) on the first
NaN instead of new Complex(NaN, NaN). Returning v on the first NaN matches NumPy's
left-fold exactly (once the accumulator is NaN it stays, so the first NaN element
is the result). Verified against NumPy 2.4.2 across 8 cases (real-NaN, imag-NaN,
two-NaN first-wins, genuine (nan,nan), and the non-NaN lexicographic path).

The axis path (ILKernelGenerator LexFold) was already correct (ar=br; ai=bi).

(8 cases). Corrected NewDtypesCoverageSweep_Reductions_Tests.B8_Complex_NaN_
PropagatesThroughMin, which had pinned the old buggy (nan,nan) - it now asserts the

feat(reduce): pairwise summation on NDIter — bit-exact NumPy sum/mean, unblocks float32

Ports NumPy's pairwise_sum (loops_utils.h.src) onto the per-chunk REDUCE path so
float32/float64 sum and mean match np.add.reduce BIT-FOR-BIT, and routes float32
(previously deferred because a flat 8-accumulator diverged from NumPy by >float
tolerance, e.g. 10M axis1 maxdiff ~24).

Why NDIter is the right substrate: the two reduce orientations map onto NumPy's
two summation behaviors exactly.
  - PINNED (reduced axis is the contiguous inner loop): NumPy folds the stripe with
    pairwise_sum. NewReduce's stride-ordering makes the contiguous reduced axis
    inner; EXTERNAL_LOOP delivers the full stripe as (ptr, count, stride); the +0
    identity seed + slot-accumulate reproduce NumPy's `*acc += pairwise_sum(...)`.
  - SLAB (kept axis inner): NumPy accumulates rows sequentially; the existing
    Vector256 streaming add already bit-matched that orientation.
So only a kernel was needed; the iterator contract is unchanged.

Implementation (ILKernelGenerator.Reduction.cs):
  - PairwiseFold<T>: NumPy's algorithm 1:1 — n<8 naive (seed -0 to preserve signed
    zero); n<=128 eight independent accumulators unrolled by 8 + Sse.Prefetch0 +
    the exact tree-combine ((r0+r1)+(r2+r3))+((r4+r5)+(r6+r7)); n>128 split
    (n2 -= n2%8) and recurse. stride in elements.
  - PairwiseSumSameType<T> (renamed from SimdSumSameType): PINNED -> *out +=
    PairwiseFold(stripe); SLAB -> unchanged Vector256 streaming add.
  - Route Double AND Single Sum (CreateReduceInnerLoop); MeanDivideByCount gains a
    Single case; UseNDIterReduce re-enables float32 sum/mean (now exact).

Validation:
  - Bit-for-bit vs np.add.reduce across 13 sizes (n<8, the 128-block, >128
    recursion, non-mult-of-8 tails) for f32+f64 — benchmark/poc/pairwise_parity.{cs,py}.
  - Live np.sum/np.mean axis0/1 bit-identical to NumPy for f32+f64.
  - Tests: PairwiseSumParityTests (4, incl. the large-value float32 case that
    diverged before the fix). Full suite 9795 passed / 0 failed / 11 skipped
    (net10.0, excl OpenBugs/HighMemory).

Perf: PINNED axis at 10M is 0.88-0.92x NumPy (faster); the exact recursive
structure costs vs a flat pass only at cache-resident 1M (~1.3x NumPy, sub-ms) —
the accepted price of bit-exactness. An explicit Vector256-lane leaf (same
summation order) measured identical on the routed axis case (recursion-bound, not
inner-loop-bound), so the simpler scalar leaf is kept. SLAB unchanged.

Generalizes: PairwiseFold is the same core NumPy reuses for mean/var/std/average/
nan* (all funnel through add.reduce); mean already rides it here. Flat axis=None
float sum still uses sum_elementwise_il (could be routed onto the leaf later).

perf(reduce): IL-emit SIMD pairwise sum per dtype — bit-exact NumPy, fixes f32/f64 PINNED regression and beats NumPy

WHAT REGRESSED
--------------
Commit d3733159 ("pairwise summation on NDIter") made float32/float64 sum &
mean BIT-EXACT with NumPy on the contiguous-reduced-axis (PINNED) path, but the
PairwiseFold<T> it shipped was SCALAR. A before/after sweep (pre = 0eeef0f1,
post = d3733159) proved the contiguous reduce got SLOWER than the prior NumSharp:

  PINNED sum f64 1M  : 0.139 -> 0.267 ms  (1.92x slower)
  PINNED sum f32 1M  : 0.054 -> 0.249 ms  (4.65x slower)
  PINNED sum f32 10M : 1.21  -> 3.12  ms  (2.58x slower)

Root cause: the .NET JIT does not auto-vectorize an 8-accumulator reduction the
way GCC vectorizes NumPy's pairwise_sum, so the scalar fold forfeited the
Vector256 throughput the old (non-bit-exact) flat accumulator had. Every other
reduction (prod/min/max/var/std/arg*/all/any/cumsum, and int/complex/half sum)
was byte-identical across the two commits and unaffected.

THE FIX — IL-emitted SIMD pairwise, mimicking NumPy
---------------------------------------------------
New ILKernelGenerator.Reduction.Pairwise.cs emits, per dtype, a self-recursive
DynamicMethod that reproduces NumPy's pairwise_sum (loops_utils.h.src) EXACTLY:
n<8 naive (seed -0), n<=128 the eight-accumulator unrolled block then the exact
tree-combine ((r0+r1)+(r2+r3))+((r4+r5)+(r6+r7)), n>128 split (kept a multiple of
8) and self-recurse via Emit(Call, dm). Because NumPy's 8 accumulators each take
elements {k, k+8, k+16, ...}, they map 1:1 onto SIMD lanes and the result is
width-independent (V128/V256/V512 give identical bits) — so the contiguous leaf
runs in vector registers and stays bit-for-bit equal to np.add.reduce. The load/
add use the x86 intrinsic path (Avx.LoadVector256/Avx.Add, ~1.8x tighter JIT
codegen than cross-platform Vector256.*). A strided reduced axis uses the scalar
8-accumulator leaf (also bit-exact); the SLAB orientation streams a 4x-unrolled
width-native vector add.

CreateReduceInnerLoop now prefers the emitted kernel for Single/Double Sum (Mean
rides on Sum + MeanDivideByCount), falling back to the generic scalar pairwise
fold only when IL generation is disabled. The 8-accumulator block divides cleanly
into lanes for double at V128/V256/V512 and float at V128/V256; float on V512 is
capped to 256-bit so the 8 accumulators still map 1:1.

MEASURED (AVX2 host, vs NumPy 2.4.2)
------------------------------------
  PINNED sum f64 1M : 0.267 -> 0.144 ms  (1.85x vs regressed; 1.43x FASTER than NumPy)
  PINNED sum f32 1M : 0.249 -> 0.100 ms  (2.48x vs regressed; 1.61x FASTER than NumPy)
  PINNED sum f64 10M: 4.83  -> 3.98  ms  (1.34x FASTER than NumPy)
  PINNED sum f32 10M: 3.12  -> 2.08  ms  (1.54x FASTER than NumPy)
  SLAB sum f64 10M  : recovered to 3.70 ms (0.98x NumPy) after the 4x unroll

All bit-exact with NumPy. Full suite 9795/0/11 (unchanged). Added strided-leaf
bit-equality tests for f32/f64 (strided 8-accumulator leaf must match the
contiguous SIMD leaf, since pairwise depends only on values/order/n).

Scope: this covers the IEEE binary floats (Single/Double) that the regression
hit. Integer sum already runs IL+SIMD via the Direct widening path (NumPy does
not pairwise integers). Half/Complex/Decimal still use their existing kernels and
are the next dtypes to migrate onto this emitter.

perf(reduce): IL-emit Vector128 pairwise sum for Complex128 — bit-exact NumPy

Extends the IL pairwise emitter to complex128, the second NumPy pairwise dtype.
Previously complex sum used the hand-written flat ComplexSumKernel (a single
Vector256<double> accumulator), which is NOT NumPy's pairwise order and diverges
in the low bits.

A complex is two contiguous doubles [re,im], so ONE Vector128<double> per complex
carries (re,im) in lockstep. EmitComplexPairwiseFold emits a self-recursive
DynamicMethod returning Vector128<double> = [reSum, imSum] that reproduces NumPy's
CDOUBLE pairwise_sum (loops_utils.h.src) EXACTLY: 4 accumulators (v0..v3, one per
complex-mod-4), the (v0+v1)+(v2+v3) tree-combine — which componentwise equals
NumPy's (r0+r2)+(r4+r6) real / (r1+r3)+(r5+r7) imag — and the n2-=n2%8 recursion
split. Because Load128 of a complex is [re,im] regardless of the stride BETWEEN
complexes, ONE code path is bit-exact for both contiguous and strided reduced axes.

The kernel: PINNED folds the stripe and accumulates with a single Vector128 add;
SLAB streams out[k]+=in[k] — contiguous uses a full-width (Vector256) 4x-unrolled
double-stream add over the 2*count interleaved doubles (bit-identical to per-complex
add), strided uses Vector128 per complex. CreateReduceInnerLoop prefers the emitted
kernel for complex Sum, falling back to ComplexSumKernel only if emission fails.

Validated bit-exact vs np.add.reduce(complex128) across sizes 3..3162 (Python
replica + live), contiguous and strided. Measured (AVX2 host): complex sum SLAB
1M 0.46->0.32 ms and 10M 9.77->7.39 ms (now BEATS the old kernel's 0.35/7.90 and is
~parity with NumPy 7.42); PINNED 1.05-1.13x NumPy, now bit-exact. Full suite
9797/0/11. Added Complex128 sum axis + strided bit-exactness tests.

fix(reduce): bool axis min/max identity + NDIter reduce Shape.offset handling

Two reduction correctness bugs, both surfaced while auditing min/max parity
against NumPy 2.4.2.

1) Boolean amax/amin along an axis (FUZZ_FINDINGS #13)
   np.max(bool_2d, axis=k) returned True at every all-False reduction group
   ([[T,F,T],[F,F,T]] -> amax(axis=0) gave [T,T,T] vs NumPy [T,F,T]).
   Root cause: CreateAxisReductionKernelScalar<bool,bool> seeded its accumulator
   from GetIdentityValueTyped<bool>, which built a double identity
   (Max -> double.NegativeInfinity) and routed it through ConvertFromDouble<bool>
   (value != 0). NegativeInfinity != 0 is True, so the Max accumulator started
   True and Math.Max(1.0, <=1.0) never dropped below 1 -> every group reduced to
   True. amin was coincidentally correct (PositiveInfinity->True is the correct
   Min seed); int/byte/char were correct (their NegInf casts are valid Max seeds)
   -- only bool's "!= 0" test corrupted the seed. Fixed with an explicit bool
   identity block (Max->false, Min->true) in GetIdentityValueTyped.

2) NDIter reduce path ignored Shape.offset (FUZZ_FINDINGS #23) -- the larger bug
   Every reduction routed through the NDIter REDUCE path (NDIterRef.NewReduce:
   double/single sum+mean; complex & decimal sum/prod/min/max/mean; half sum+mean)
   read from the buffer base instead of the view's logical origin for any input
   whose offset lives in Shape.offset -- sliced views (a[1:3,1:3]) and
   negative-stride views (a[::-1], a[:,::-1]). It silently produced wrong cells,
   and once FlipNegativeStrides moved the (already wrong) pointer it read/wrote
   out of bounds (garbage / NaN / denormals).
   Root cause: in NDIter.cs the op_axes operand base-pointer branch set
   basePtr = arr.Address WITHOUT adding arrShape.offset * elemBytes, while the
   standard-broadcast branch did add it. Contiguous / transpose / F-order /
   positive-strided views all have Shape.offset == 0, so they were unaffected --
   which is why this hid for so long. Fixed by adding the offset in the op_axes
   branch (matching the standard branch), using NPTypeCode.SizeOf() (1 byte for
   bool, never arr.dtypesize).
   Example: np.sum(np.arange(12).reshape(3,4)[::-1], axis=0) now [12,15,18,21]
   (was [0,1,2,3] = a single mis-located stripe).

perf(reduce): SIMD-route non-C-contiguous int-widening axis sum (kill the F-order/transpose cliff)

The int->int64/uint64 (and ->double Mean) widening axis-reduce kernel only routed
to its SIMD paths for C-contiguous inputs: fast path 1 (leading C-contig / axis-0
inner slab) and fast path 2 (innermost axis + C-contig). Every other 2-D layout —
F-order, transposed, sliced-along-the-strided-axis — fell to the scalar
AxisReductionScalarHelper. Result: a layout cliff measured in the reduction×layout
matrix — int32 sum on F-order/transposed ran 14-20× SLOWER than NumPy while
C-contiguous won ~10×.

Root cause was routing, not kernels: WideningLeading already handles an arbitrary
axisStride over a contiguous inner slab, and WideningInnermost already handles
consecutive contiguous blocks — the F-order/transposed memory patterns are exactly
those, the gates just never reached them (they keyed off C-contiguity / axis
position instead of the actual strides).

Fix: a stride-driven "fast path 3" for ndim==2 before the scalar fallback:
  - SLAB  (inputStrides[other] == 1): the non-reduced axis is the contiguous inner
    slab; stream the reduced axis with its stride. Covers F-order reduce-last-axis.
    axisStride may be 0 (broadcast reduce) — folded correctly.
  - PINNED (inputStrides[axis] == 1 && inputStrides[other] == axisSize): the reduced
    axis is contiguous AND tiles into consecutive blocks → each output cell reduces a
    contiguous run. Covers F-order reduce-axis0 and a.T reduce-axis0. The
    block-consecutive guard rejects sliced/negative-stride views (block gaps /
    reversed order) so they stay on the correct scalar path.
Both reuse the existing concrete-sum and generic WideningLeading/WideningInnermost
kernels, so they cover sum/prod/min/max/mean alike.

  1M|i32|F|sum|ax0   4.139 -> 0.059 ms  (70× faster; vs NumPy now ~5.5× faster, was 0.05×)

  100K|i32|F|sum|ax0 0.408 -> 0.005 ms  (80×)
  F/T axis1 likewise 46-50×.

perf(reduce): materialize broadcast views in flat reduction (bcast-reduce 50x→11x)

The flat (axis=None) reduction of a BROADCAST view (a stride-0 axis with dim>1)
was the worst reduction pathology — the `bcast_reduce` canary
(np.sum(broadcast_to(a,(1024,8192)))) ran ~50× slower than NumPy. The non-contig
coordinate-walk kernel visits all D×N logical elements computing coordinates per
element, even though only N are unique and the inner axis is contiguous.

Fix: in ExecuteElementReduction (the shared flat sum/prod/min/max chokepoint),
materialize a broadcast input to a contiguous copy once, then take the fast
contiguous kernel. NumPy reduces the same element multiset as the materialized
copy, so the result matches (bit-exact on the canary; the residual is ULP-level
summation-order divergence — NumPy itself reduces a broadcast in stride order, not
C-order, and the codebase already accepts such ULP differences in its pairwise
reductions). min/max are order-independent → exact regardless. mean (= sum/count)
benefits via the sum path.

Measured (1024×8192 f64 broadcast, this machine):
  sum   61.6 → 13.5 ms   (4.6×)
  min   62.0 → 14.4 ms   (4.3×)
  max   62.0 → 14.3 ms   (4.3×)
  mean  ~62  → 13.6 ms
Canary vs NumPy: 0.02× → ~0.09× (NumPy stays cache-hot at ~1.2 ms; closing the
remaining gap needs an order-preserving cache-hot kernel or a stride-0-aware
axis-collapse — follow-up).

perf(reduce): bool/char/half min/max-along-axis — kill the scalar double-bridge (~90× / ~250× / ~7×)

bool, char and half amin/amax along an axis were catastrophically slow: 6× to
250× the equivalent SIMD reducer, and for half ~6× slower than NumPy itself.

Root cause
----------
All three fall through CreateAxisReductionKernel's `!CanUseSimd` branch into
CreateAxisReductionKernelGeneral -> CreateAxisReductionKernelScalar ->
AxisReductionScalarHelper, whose per-element combine (CombineScalarsPromoted)
round-trips EVERY element through double: ConvertToDouble -> Math.Min/Max ->
ConvertFromDouble. No SIMD, and half pays an extra Half<->double pair on top.
Confirmed NOT boxing — GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread was identical
(1,416 B/call) for the fast and slow dtypes, so the (T)(object) casts are
JIT-elided (same-type box/unbox). The cost is pure scalar conversion + Math.Min
dispatch per element.

Fix — per-dtype specialization
------------------------------
* bool -> reinterpret to byte, route to the existing SIMD MinOp<byte>/MaxOp<byte>
  reducer (vpminub). bool min/max is bit-identical to byte min/max over {0,1}. ~90×.
* char -> reinterpret to ushort, route to MinOp<ushort>/MaxOp<ushort> (vpminuw).
  char is unsigned 16-bit; the UNSIGNED order is the correctness invariant
  (0x8000 and 0xFFFF must out-rank 'A'=0x41 — a signed reinterpret would invert
  the top half of the range). ~250×.
  Both reinterprets are injected at the top of CreateAxisReductionKernel, gated on
  (Op in {Min,Max} && InputType==AccumulatorType). The cache identity stays
  (Boolean/Char, Op): CreateAxisReductionKernelTyped reads only key.Op and its
  type argument, never key.InputType, so passing <byte>/<ushort> is safe.
* half -> boxing-free direct-Half loop (new AxisReductionHalfMinMaxHelper). Half
  has no Vector<Half> arithmetic in the BCL but exposes a hardware-backed total
  order via its comparison operators, so a direct Half scan with no double bridge
  is ~7× faster (9.99 ms -> ~1.45 ms at 1000×1000) and beats NumPy's f16 loop
  (1.7–2.1 ms, which widens to float per element). Half CANNOT reinterpret to
  ushort: IEEE-754 ordering != uint16 bit ordering for negatives/NaN. Min/Max
  only — Sum/Mean/Prod keep the double-intermediate path for accumulation
  precision. NaN propagates (seed from element 0; a NaN input is taken on sight,
  matching Math.Min/Max and NumPy's reduce).

Two loop-shape details inside the half helper:
* inner-contig dispatch — with a runtime axisStride the JIT can't prove unit
  stride, so axisStart[i*axisStride] (or p += axisStride) emits a variable-stride
  load plus a per-element 64-bit multiply that alone doubled the loop; branching
  on axisStride==1 into axisStart[i] lets the JIT treat the row as the sequential
  stream it is. The strided/negative-stride branch uses pointer increment.
* the body is a static AggressiveOptimization helper behind a thin lambda, matching
  AxisReductionSimdHelper/ScalarHelper. ~1.45 ms is the floor for this delegate
  path: pointers arrive as method parameters (not fixed-block locals), so the JIT
  emits a slightly more conservative inner loop than a ~0.85 ms standalone scan —
  still well ahead of the double-bridge and ahead of NumPy.

Measured (1000×1000 amin/amax along axis, ms; NumPy 2.4.2):
            before     after    NumPy
  bool       1.19      0.013    0.011–0.024
  char       6.05      0.020    0.030–0.034
  half       9.99      ~1.45    1.7–2.1
NumSharp now beats or matches NumPy on all three dtypes (previously 6–250× behind
the SIMD path; half was ~6× behind NumPy).

perf(reduce): fold broadcast axes in place instead of materializing (bcast-reduce 50x→0.9x, now beats NumPy)

Supersedes the arr.copy() materialize from 3fadd113. copy() was a workaround with a
real downside: it allocated an O(D×N) temp (64 MB for the bcast_reduce canary, ~7.6 GB
for a 1e9-element broadcast) — an OOM regression, since the slow coordinate walk it
replaced was O(1) memory. It also stayed ~11× behind NumPy and did not match NumPy's
structure (NumPy never copies a broadcast to reduce it).

Proper fix: in the shared flat-reduction chokepoint (ExecuteElementReduction), fold each
broadcast (stride-0) axis in place with the fast per-chunk axis kernel, then flat-reduce
the small contiguous remainder. Folding a stride-0 axis with the same op collapses its D
identical copies (sum→×D, prod→^D, min/max→identity-exact); accumType already carries the
op's accumulator (widened for sum/prod, preserved for min/max), so the fold dtype is
correct. ArgMin/ArgMax opt out — their index must address the full broadcast.

Measured (this machine):
  canary 1024×8192 f64: sum 61.6 → 1.07 ms (was 13.5 with copy) — now FASTER than NumPy (~1.2 ms)
                        min 62.0 → 1.72 ms
  1e9-element broadcast sum: 0.01 MB managed alloc (copy ≈ 7600 MB), 127 ms, exact 4.9995e12 — no OOM

O(unique) memory and cache-hot, matching NumPy. Residual vs NumPy is ULP-level
summation-order (the codebase's pairwise reductions already accept this); min/max
order-independent → exact. Verified: Flat_Reduce_OverBroadcastView_MatchesMaterializedCopy
+ full suite green on net10.0 (9810/9810; the net8.0 UnaryExtra failure is the pre-existing
complex-log1p ULP, unrelated), reduce parity 1616/1620 (4 = pre-existing prod(char)), minmax 1132/1132.

perf(copy): strided/broadcast same-type clone for the Vector-less dtypes — kill the per-element div/mod (char/half ~30×, complex ~7×)

Non-contiguous same-type clones of Char/Half/Decimal/Complex/Boolean ran
16–33× slower than NumPy's typed strided copy. This is the path taken by
np.positive(v) and v.copy() on any sliced/strided/transposed/broadcast view:

    Storage.Clone() → CloneData() (non-contig branch) → NDIter.Copy
        → TryCopySameType → (StridedCastKernel rejects) → CopyGeneralSameType

ROOT CAUSE
Same-type strided copy piggybacks on the *cast* kernel via
TryGetStridedCastKernel(tc, tc). That kernel's strategy resolution returns
null whenever Boolean/Char/Half/Complex/Decimal is involved — they have no
Vector<T> conversion lanes. But a same-type copy needs no conversion at all;
it is pure byte movement. The five rejected dtypes therefore fell through to
CopyGeneralSameType, which reconstructed the full N-dim coordinate from a flat
index with a div + mod per axis PER ELEMENT (ndim divisions + ndim modulos +
2·ndim muls for every single element). The other 10 dtypes use the fast
StridedCastKernel (Buffer.MemoryCopy per contiguous row + incremental coord).

Measured 1M, ratio = NumPy_ms / NumSharp_ms (>1 = NumSharp faster), per-cell
strided/sliced/negstride/bcast BEFORE:
    char  0.03 / 0.06 / 0.06 / 0.06   (NS 7.5 ms vs NumPy 0.22 ms)
    f16   0.03 / 0.06 / 0.06 / 0.06
    c128  0.57 / 0.63 / 0.65 / 0.58
This also slowed v.copy() of an F-order/transposed char/half/complex array,
which must reorder F→C through the same fallback (40× / 17× vs positive()'s
layout-preserving whole-buffer memcpy).

FIX
Rewrote CopyGeneralSameType<T> to walk the outer axes by incremental
stride-add + carry (no div/mod) and move each contiguous inner run with
Buffer.MemoryCopy — dtype-agnostic byte movement that matches the fast
kernel's wall time. Edge layouts handled explicitly:
  • unit-stride inner on both sides  → one memcpy per row (the hot path);
  • negative-stride inner (a[:,::-1]) → not contiguous → scalar inner walk;
  • negative-stride outer (a[::-1,:]) → per-row memcpy marches backwards;
  • broadcast stride-0 axis           → add 0 / carry 0, falls out naturally;
  • 0-d scalar and ndim==1            → handled without an outer walk.
Strides are element-based (NDIter.cs:1508 multiplies by elemSize for bytes),
so the byte count is inner·sizeof(T) and pointer math stays in T* units.

RESULT (1M, non-contiguous geomean, NP/NS):
    char  0.050 → 1.504   (~30×)
    f16   0.051 → 1.430   (~28×)
    c128  0.605 → 4.210   (~7×)
13 of 13 comparable dtypes now beat NumPy on the copy path (was 11 of 13).
char/f16 now track their 2-byte int siblings exactly (char 1.50 ≈ i16 1.43);
the only residual sub-1.0 cell is [:, ::2] strided-inner, shared by ALL small
dtypes (i16 0.75, u16 0.61) — no longer anything special about char/half.
c128 leaps to 5.36× overall because memcpy-per-row moves 16 B/element far
better than NumPy's complex strided copy.

SCOPE
Only the same-type General fallback changed. The fast 10 dtypes
(StridedCastKernel) and the contiguous cpblk path are untouched. Bonus:
Boolean and Decimal non-contiguous clones take the same fast path now.
NDIter.cs comments refreshed to state CopyGeneralSameType is row-memcpy +
incremental-coord (the old "mod/div per element" note was stale after this).

TESTS
New StridedCopySameTypeParityTests: 15 dtypes × 8 awkward layouts (F, T,
strided, sliced, negrow, negcol, negboth, bcast) assert the clone is a
bit-exact, contiguous, source-independent materialization of the view's
logical order — covering the negative-stride-inner (scalar walk) and
negative-stride-outer (backward memcpy) branches. 30 tests pass.
Full suite: 9840 pass / 0 fail (net10.0). net8.0 unchanged — only the
pre-existing UnaryExtra log1p/complex128 ULP divergence (.NET8 libm), which
is transcendental unary math, unrelated to copy.

perf(reduce): flat char/half min/max — reuse the per-dtype trick on the axis=None path (~110× / ~4×)

The bool/char/half axis min/max fix (c79ce606) killed the scalar double-bridge
on the AXIS reduction path. The FLAT (axis=None) path dispatches separately —
min_elementwise_il / max_elementwise_il route Char and Half straight to dedicated
fallback methods before ExecuteElementReduction is ever consulted — so it still
carried the catastrophe. Measured (4M elements): flat char amin/amax 12.5 ms,
flat half 13.7 ms, vs double's ~1 ms. Same two root causes, same two fixes.

char (T1 — unsigned reinterpret)
--------------------------------
Max/MinElementwiseCharFallback ran a scalar `arr.AsIterator<char>()` loop (legacy
NDIterator, virtual MoveNext/HasNext per element). char is unsigned 16-bit with a
total order bit-identical to its UTF-16 code unit, so the char buffer reduces
bit-for-bit through the ushort SIMD reducer. The fix is one line each:

    arr.view(typeof(ushort))  ->  ExecuteElementReduction<ushort>(.., Max/Min, UInt16)  ->  (char)

view(ushort) is a zero-copy byte reinterpret (char and ushort are both 2 bytes, so
shape/strides/offset survive every layout — verified on contig/reversed/sliced/
transposed views), and routing through ExecuteElementReduction reuses the whole
machinery for free: contiguous SIMD reduce, broadcast-axis folding, and NDIter
strided routing. 12.5 ms -> 0.11 ms (~110×), now at NumPy parity (0.12 ms).

half (T3 — boxing-free direct-Half scan)
----------------------------------------
Max/MinElementwiseHalfFallback bridged every element through (double):
`(double)iter.MoveNext()` + the same per-element iterator. Half has no Vector<Half>
in the BCL, but its comparison operators are hardware-backed, so for the contiguous
buffer we now scan the raw Half* pointer with Half's own ordering — no double
round-trip, no iterator. 13.7 ms -> 3.2 ms (~4.3×), and 2.4× FASTER than NumPy
(7.9 ms — NumPy widens f16->float per element; the direct-Half scan beats it).
Non-contiguous / empty inputs keep the existing iterator fallback. NaN propagates
(seed from element 0; once acc is NaN, `x > acc` is false and only another NaN
re-sets it) — matching the prior fallback and NumPy.

clip half — investigated, NOT the same bug
------------------------------------------
half clip is also ~5× double (13 ms), but its per-element clamp helpers
(HalfMaxNaN/HalfMinNaN) ALREADY use direct Half comparison — no double-bridge.
Its cost is inherent: scalar (Half has no SIMD) × two clamps (lo and hi) per
element. "The trick" yields nothing there; a separate loop-shaping pass could win
~2× but is out of scope for this change (and riskier — it lives in the clip IL
emitter, not a dispatch fallback). Left as-is.

------------

  axis=None (and 0/1/-1/2) across C/F/transpose/strided/negative-stride/offset views.

* 1183 reduction/minmax/clip/char/half unit tests pass.

fix(reduce)+perf: half flat sum/prod/mean — boxing-free contiguous scan; fix mean Half-accumulation overflow bug

Continuing the per-dtype reduction sweep to the half sum/prod/mean flat path, which
shared the same legacy AsIterator fallback the min/max paths did — and uncovered a
silent correctness bug in mean.

CORRECTNESS BUG (half mean) — FIXED
-----------------------------------
np.mean(float16) accumulated the sum in Half via ExecuteElementReduction<Half>(arr,
Sum, Half). Half saturates at 65504, so on any array whose running sum exceeds that
the accumulator corrupted and the mean came out garbage:

    mean([2.5] * 100_000)  ->  0.0819   (NumPy: 2.5)

NumPy upcasts float16 for the mean accumulation; the fix accumulates the sum in
double and narrows the final mean to Half. sum() itself is unchanged in spirit — it
still narrows the double accumulator to Half, so a too-large sum saturates to ±inf
exactly like NumPy's float16 reduce (sum([2.5]*100k) -> inf, matching NumPy). The
small-array reduce fuzz never reached the overflow regime, so this hid behind green
tests; pinned now by Half_Mean_LargeArray_AccumulatesInDouble_MatchesNumPy.

PERF — half flat sum/prod/mean
------------------------------
SumElementwiseHalfFallback / ProdElementwiseHalfFallback ran arr.AsIterator<Half>()
(legacy NDIterator: virtual MoveNext/HasNext per element) and mean ran the even-slower
Half-accumulating IL kernel. Replaced the contiguous case with a boxing-free Half*
pointer scan widening each element to double (new TryHalfAccumulateContiguous helper;
double is the accumulation precision these reductions already used). Non-contiguous /
empty inputs keep the iterator. Offset-contiguous (sliced) views honored via Shape.offset.

Measured (4M elements, ms):

  prod       13.8      3.2     ~4.2×
  mean       32.6      3.3     ~10×
(half is still ~3× the double path — scalar Half->double widening, no Vector<Half> in
the BCL; a SIMD F16C widen could close that but is a separate, larger change.)

* This is the FLAT (axis=None) path. min/max flat were fixed in 158ccc50; axis in
  c79ce606. sum/prod here narrow the double accumulator to Half (unchanged); only mean's

perf(cast): typed strided cross-dtype cast for the Vector-less dtypes — kill the per-element coordinate recompute + type dispatch (astype ~2×)

Opportunity ① of the strided-fallback audit. astype / any cross-dtype cast of
Boolean/Char/Half/Decimal/Complex (and even CONTIGUOUS casts of them, since the
SIMD cast kernels reject these types on both the contiguous and strided sides)
funnels into NDIterCasting.CopyStridedToStridedWithCast. That fallback was
doubly slow:
  (a) it recomputed Σ coords[d]·strides[d] for BOTH operands on every element
      (O(ndim) muls/element) — paid even on fully contiguous data; and
  (b) ConvertValue dispatched a ~3-deep type-switch per element.
Measured astype->f64 on a 1M strided view, ratio = NumPy_ms / NumSharp_ms
(>1 = NumSharp faster): char 0.37, f16 0.34, bool 0.37, c128 0.54.

FIX (two parts)
1. Addressing: walk the innermost axis as a tight pointer run (advance by the
   per-axis byte step) and advance outer axes by incremental stride-add + carry —
   no per-element coordinate reconstruction. Mirrors the same-type copy fix.
2. Dispatch hoist: for primitive↔primitive pairs, resolve a typed
   Converts.FindConverter<TIn,TOut> delegate ONCE (a non-boxing
   Converts.{Src}To{Dst} method group) via a 13+13-arm two-level switch and run a
   typed inner loop — zero per-element type dispatch. Complex/Decimal endpoints
   keep the box-free scalar ConvertValue path: it encodes their exact NumPy
   semantics (complex real-part drop / truthy-bool) and their FindConverter
   converters can box; both are 16-byte so the scalar cost amortizes.

   (Probed Converts.ChangeType<TIn,TOut> called directly — faster for bool/char
   (~0.86×) but it FALLS TO A BOXING DEFAULT for Half inputs (~0.23×, worse than
   scalar). The resolved FindConverter delegate is uniform and landmine-free, so
   that is what shipped.)

perf(reduce): migrate non-contig Half/Complex reduction fallbacks from per-element AsIterator to NDIter chunked ForEach (~2.5×)

AsIterator<T>() returns NDIterator<T>, which is just NDIter driven in PER-ELEMENT
mode — a Func<T> MoveNext delegate invoke plus an Advance for every single element.
That dispatch was the entire cost of the strided/non-contiguous reduction fallbacks.
Switching them to NDIter's chunked EXTERNAL_LOOP via the public ForEach(kernel, aux)
amortizes the iterator over a whole inner-loop chunk and lets NDIter normalize the
layout (it coalesces/permutes strided & transposed views to contiguous-inner chunks),
so strided now runs at contiguous speed.

Measured (4M elements):
  non-contig (transposed) Half sum   ~15.5 ms -> ~6.1 ms   (~2.5×)
  non-contig Half prod/mean/min/max  similar ~6 ms
  Complex sum  (all layouts)         ~AsIterator -> 6.4-6.7 ms (~2.2×)
  Complex prod (all layouts)         -> ~9.8 ms (complex mul is 4mul+2add/elem)
Contiguous Half stays on the direct-pointer scan from ebd50cd8 (3.3 ms) — that still
beats ForEach (5.9 ms), because ForEach hands the kernel a RUNTIME byte-stride (the
i*stride variable-stride penalty) plus a per-chunk delegate call, whereas a direct
p[i] loop knows the stride is sizeof(Half) at compile time. Complex had no contiguous
fast path, so ForEach is a pure win there on every layout.

Migrated (order-INDEPENDENT reductions — safe under NDIter's stride-magnitude axis
permutation):
  * Half sum / prod / mean — non-contiguous tail (contig keeps TryHalfAccumulateContiguous)
  * Half min / max         — non-contiguous tail (contig keeps the direct-pointer scan)
  * Complex sum / prod     — all layouts (Complex had only the AsIterator path)
sum/prod are commutative (permuted order is value-equivalent modulo float rounding,
which the f16/complex fuzz tolerances accept); min/max VALUE and NaN-propagation
(any NaN → NaN) are order-independent.

Deliberately NOT migrated (their result is POSITIONALLY specific, so NDIter's permuted
traversal would change it):
  * argmin / argmax (Half, Complex) — return a C-order FLAT INDEX; a permuted walk yields
    a different index. (Same reason ExecuteElementReduction already opts argmax/argmin
    out of its NDIter routing.)
  * Complex min / max — on a NaN they return the FIRST NaN-bearing element verbatim
    (NumPy parity); "first" is order-dependent, so these stay on the C-order AsIterator.

New helpers in DefaultEngine.ReductionOp.cs: HalfReduceViaNDIter (sum/prod → double),
HalfMinMaxViaNDIter (+ HalfExtremaAccum state: best/seen/nan; empty → ±inf, any NaN →
NaN), ComplexReduceViaNDIter (sum/prod). Each drives ForEach with a non-capturing
kernel and a stack accumulator passed through auxdata (no closure/per-call alloc).

------------

  — both exercise Half & Complex over contiguous / F / transpose / strided / negative-stride

* Full suite (net10.0, minus OpenBugs/HighMemory): 9859 passed, 0 failed, 11 skipped.

perf(unary): float16 negate via sign-bit flip, not the BCL float roundtrip (~10×)

Opportunity ② of the strided-fallback audit. np.negative on float16 was the worst
cell in the entire elementwise matrix: 0.14× NumPy contiguous, 0.16× strided —
while f16 ABS, a structurally identical scalar kernel, was 1.6×. The difference was
the BCL method each emitted:
  Half.Abs(h)               => bits & 0x7FFF        (sign-bit MASK, ~0.37ms/1M)
  Half.op_UnaryNegation(h)  => (Half)(-(float)h)    (float ROUNDTRIP, ~2.74ms/1M)
Microbenchmarked: the operator is 7.3× slower than a sign-bit flip and 7.3× slower
than Half.Abs. NumPy negates float16 with exactly the bit flip (npy_half: h ^ 0x8000).

FIX
Added DirectILKernelGenerator.NegateHalf — BitConverter.HalfToUInt16Bits → ^0x8000 →
UInt16BitsToHalf — and pointed CachedMethods.HalfNegate at it instead of
Half.op_UnaryNegation. The emitted f16 negate kernel now flips the sign bit per
element (same shape as the abs kernel), with no float conversions.

RESULT (NP/NS, 1M, >1 = NumSharp faster):
    f16 neg  C       0.14 -> 1.47   (~10×)
    f16 neg  strided 0.16 -> 1.04
now on par with f16 abs (1.52 / 1.02). The 10 SIMD dtypes and f32/f64 negate are
untouched.

CORRECTNESS
The bit flip is the DEFINING NumPy operation: bits(-x) == bits(x) ^ 0x8000 across
normals, ±0, ±inf, and NaN (sign flips, payload preserved). It also produces results
identical to the old float-roundtrip operator (-(float)NaN flips the float sign too,
then narrows back), so this is a pure perf change — no value moved. Validated bit-exact
vs NumPy on ±0/±inf/normals/subnormals; the only "diff" in the raw probe was the NaN
cell, explained entirely by .NET float.NaN being sign-negative (0xFFC0…) vs NumPy
np.nan sign-positive (0x7FC0…) — the inputs differ, both negates flip the sign bit
correctly.

NOT addressed here (documented residual): f16 add/mul stay ~0.57× — Half binary ops
genuinely need the Half→float→op→Half compute (no Vector<Half>); matching NumPy needs
F16C vector widening, a separate kernel.

TESTS

reversed views, double-negate identity, and an abs-clears-sign-bit guard so a future
change can't alias the two ops. 4 tests pass; 952 unary/half tests pass; full suite
9863 pass / 0 fail (net10.0).

fix(reduce): complex nansum axis reduction read uninitialized memory for ndim>=3 (B28)

NanSumComplex's axis branch wrote the per-slice sum with
    ret.SetAtIndex(sum, iterIndex[0])
using only the FIRST coordinate of the result incrementor as a flat index into the
output. iterIndex (ValueCoordinatesIncrementor.Index) is the full output COORDINATE,
not a flat index — so for a >=3-D input (multi-D reduced output) only the positions
whose flat index equals the first-axis coordinate were ever written. Every other
position kept the uninitialized bytes of `new NDArray(NPTypeCode.Complex, axisedShape,
false)` — observed as ~6.95E-310 denormal junk. The 2-D->1-D case happened to work
because the single output coordinate IS the flat index.

Not broadcast-specific: reproduced on a plain contiguous 3-D complex array (the
materialized copy went through the same path, so both the broadcast and the copy were
wrong — differently).

Fix: resolve the FULL output coordinate to its C-order flat offset, matching how the
slice/coordinate incrementors already advance in lockstep:
    ret.SetAtIndex(sum, ret.Shape.GetOffset(iterIndex))
ret is freshly C-contiguous (offset 0), so GetOffset(coord) is exactly the flat element
index SetAtIndex expects.

Full-optimization follow-up to the typed-cast commit. The cross-dtype strided cast

  double->int  4M:  direct/IL 4.56ms   Func 8.11ms  (1.77× slower)

docs(cast-plan): PROVE float→narrow-int kernel by benchmark — correct the saturate-pack error

Empirically validated the float→narrow-int cast (the matrix's worst cliff, f32→i8 = 0.09×
vs NumPy) by benchmarking FIVE implementations of the worst cell plus per-dtype variants —
for both correctness (0-diff vs the NumPy-faithful Converts scalar) and speed. Two plan
errors corrected as a result:

ERROR 1 (semantic, would have shipped WRONG results): §0.1/P1′ instructed the back-end as a
vector "pack (vpackssdw/vpackuswb)". Those SATURATE. NumPy float→narrow-int WRAPS (low bits):
oracle f32→i8 128.5 → -128 (wrap), a saturating pack gives +127. Benchmarked head-to-head at
4M: the cvtt+saturate kernel was the FASTEST (0.31 ms, 34×) and the WRONGEST (3.9 M diffs).
The correct primitive is cvtt + TRUNCATING narrow = mask-to-width (&0xFF / &0xFFFF) +
unsigned-pack (saturation becomes a no-op because masked values are already in-range) +
cross-lane permute.

ERROR 2 (framing): §0.1 claimed "NumPy does cvttps2dq + vector pack". NumPy does NOT vectorize
these casts — its generic cast loop is scalar-speed (measured 4M: f32→i8 1.31 ms, f64→i32
3.26 ms). That scalar baseline IS the headroom a SIMD kernel exploits.

PROVEN (4M, best-of-7, all 0-diff vs NumPy):
  f32→i8  cvtt+&0xFF+2×vpackuswb+vpermd   0.33–0.38 ms   NPY/NS 3.45–3.95×
  f32→u8  (same kernel — bit-identical)    0.33–0.38 ms   NPY/NS 4.14–4.74×
  f32→i16 cvtt+&0xFFFF+vpackusdw+vpermq    0.42–0.60 ms   NPY/NS 3.55–5.04×
  f32→u16 (same kernel)                    0.42–0.60 ms   NPY/NS 3.37–4.79×
  f64→i32 cvttpd2dq+store                  1.56–1.75 ms   NPY/NS 1.86–2.09×
  f64→i16 cvttpd2dq+128-bit vpackusdw      1.32–1.56 ms   NPY/NS 1.69–1.99×

Per-dtype optimization is real and measured: 8-bit targets (2-level pack) interleave at 4-byte
granularity → need vpermd ([0,4,1,5,2,6,3,7]); 16-bit targets (1-level pack) interleave at
8-byte granularity → need only the cheaper vpermq (0xD8). Permute4x64 on the 2-level result is
insufficient (1.99 M diffs — cannot split a quadword holding two operands' bytes). i8≡u8 and
i16≡u16 each share one kernel. f64 source uses cvttpd2dq (INT_MIN sentinel for out-of-i32
range, matches NumPy 3e9→i16→0) with 128-bit packs (no lane crossing). Win is memory-bound
(~52 GB/s at f32→i8) — near the bandwidth floor, so the kernel is already optimal.

AVX-512 confirmed UNAVAILABLE on this host (Avx512F=False) → no vpmovdb truncating-move and no
cvttpd2qq; the AVX2 mask+pack+permute path is the production design.

inner chunks additionally get Vector256<double> SIMD (Complex sum) or a 4-way

    Min/Max (+ lexicographic Complex compare, NaN-verbatim), Half/Complex
    ArgMin/ArgMax (running C-order index), Half/Complex Any/All (early-exit),

    Sum/Prod/Min/Max/Mean/SquaredDeviation (mirrors the existing Float/Double).

    Half min/max + arg, Half sum/prod/mean non-contig; bool max/min now delegate
    to Any()/All() (the SIMD ReduceBool path).

    the two-iterator two-pass, matching the Float/Double paths).
  - Default.All.cs / Default.Any.cs: Half + Complex non-contiguous branches.

Order contract
  - Value reductions (sum/prod/mean/min/max/any/all/nan*) -> NPY_KEEPORDER
    (cache-friendly; also the correct NaN order, see fix below).
  - Index reductions (argmin/argmax) -> NPY_CORDER (the returned flat index must
    be the C-order first occurrence, even for transposed/strided views).

BUG FIX (found via NumPy 2.4.2 probe): np.min / np.max on a non-C-contiguous
COMPLEX array (e.g. a transpose) returned the C-order-first NaN-bearing element,
but NumPy's reduce propagates the MEMORY-order-first NaN. The old AsIterator
forced C-order; the new min/max run in KEEPORDER and now match NumPy. Example:
a = [[1+1j, nan+5j, 3+3j], [nan+7j, 2+2j, 4+4j]] -> np.min(a.T) now (nan,5)
(was (nan,7)). argmin/argmax stay CORDER, so their indices are unchanged.

perf(cast): SIMD float->narrow-int (cvtt+truncating-Narrow) — kills Phase-0's worst cliff

P1' of CAST_BEAT_NUMPY_PLAN.md — the dominant cast cliff. Phase 0 found
float/complex->narrow-int (->bool/u8/i8/i16/u16/char) owned 45 of 46 reds;
f32->i8 bottomed the whole matrix at 0.09x NumPy (2.6ms vs 0.24ms, 10.8x
slower). Cause: ResolveStrategy gives every srcFloat->dstInt pair EXCEPT
Single->Int32 the ScalarOnly strategy (a per-element EmitConvertTo loop),
while the narrowing conversion is heavy (float->double->ToInt32->narrow per
element). NumPy's own cast loop is scalar-speed here — pure headroom.

MECHANISM (DirectILKernelGenerator.Cast.FloatNarrow.cs), bit-exact with the
Converts reference (hence NumPy 2.4.2):
  Converts.To{Narrow}(double) == unchecked((narrow)ToInt32(value)), and
  ToInt32 is the truncating convert with the int.MinValue NaN/overflow
  sentinel. So the faithful SIMD chain is:
    cvtt (VCVTTPS2DQ / VCVTTPD2DQ: trunc-to-zero, INT_MIN on NaN/overflow)
    -> truncating Vector.Narrow i32->i16[->i8]   (low-bits extract).
  Vector.Narrow is TRUNCATING, not the saturating vpackssdw (proven:
  0x80000000->0, 0x12340041->0x0041) — so it matches unchecked((narrow)int)
  incl. WRAP (NumPy oracle: f32->i8 128.5->-128, 256->0, 300->44, NaN->0).
  For f32, cvttps2dq(f) == ToInt32((double)f) for ALL inputs (exact in-range,
  INT_MIN out-of-range/NaN), so the double-intermediate is elided losslessly.
  Signedness doesn't change the body (truncating narrow gives identical low
  bits for i8/u8 and i16/u16/char); only the scalar-tail Converts call differs.

  Contig (TryGetFloatToNarrowIntKernel): f32 32-wide via Vector256, f64
  16/8-wide via Vector128 lanes (cvttpd2dq yields a 4-wide Vector128<int>
  directly — no Vector256.Create vinsertf128 combine, which stalled the
  memory pipeline: f64->i8 0.47x -> 0.99x after that change).

  Strided (TryGetFloatToNarrowIntStridedKernel): the generic strided emitter
  gave float->narrow ScalarOnly AND excludes char entirely. New driver:
  inner-contig rows (sliced, negrow: inner stride 1) run the Bulk directly;
  strided/reversed rows ([:, ::2], [:, ::-1]) STAGE the strided source into a
  contig chunk buffer with a tight typed strided load, then vectorize the
  convert (the per-element COST was the conversion, not the load). Outer dims
  walk the proven incremental-coord odometer (element strides).

feat(broadcast): live index cursor + iteration + reset() — align np.broadcast with NumPy

Previously np.broadcast.index threw ("NumSharp does not model a live cursor") and
the object was not iterable. NumPy's np.broadcast IS its own iterator (iter(b) is b):
it carries a single live cursor (index), yields one per-operand value tuple per step,
and reset() rewinds it. NumSharp now matches.

Broadcast is now IEnumerable<object[]> + IEnumerator<object[]>:
  - index: live flat position — 0 before iterating, +1 per step, == size once exhausted
    (was a property that threw; same int return type, so no source break).
  - GetEnumerator() returns the broadcast itself (NumPy's iter(b) is b), so iteration
    shares the one cursor; a fresh pass needs reset().
  - MoveNext()/Current: reads each operand's value at the cursor (C-order) into an
    object[] of length numiter and advances; Current is the step's per-operand tuple.
  - reset(): rewinds the cursor to 0 (NumPy's broadcast.reset()).
  - 0 operands iterate exactly once yielding an empty tuple (NumPy: list(np.broadcast())
    == [()], index 1); the parameterless ctor (no operands) stays non-iterating.
  - Operand views are now built once (cached) and shared by iters and the cursor.

advances; reset() rewinds; 1-op -> (v,), 3-op -> (a,b,c), 0-op -> [()].

and INDEPENDENT of the cursor, whereas NumPy's flatiters are one-shot and share the
cursor (after two next() calls NumPy's iters[0] would start at index 2). Reading iters
does not move NumSharp's cursor — kept deliberately as the idiomatic, less footgun-y
behavior.

tuples and advances index to size; MoveNext exposes Current; reset re-iterates;

perf(cast): SIMD float->narrow-int + complex->int (Waves 1-2) — kill the two worst cliffs

casting refactor) and adds the complex->int deinterleave kernel, both correctness-gated

WAVE 1 — float|double -> {i8,u8,i16,u16,char} (DirectILKernelGenerator.Cast.FloatNarrow.cs):
Phase-0's worst cells (f32->i8 was 0.09x; live baseline this branch 0.13x). NumPy doesn't

(VCVTTPS2DQ/VCVTTPD2DQ, trunc-to-zero, INT_MIN sentinel on NaN/overflow) + truncating
Vector.Narrow i32->i16[->i8]. Vector.Narrow is TRUNCATING (low-bits, == unchecked((narrow)int)),
NOT the saturating vpackssdw — matches NumPy's WRAP (128.5->-128, 300->44, NaN->0). Contig +
strided (inner-contig rows run the Bulk; inner-strided rows stage to a contig buffer then

perf(cast): SIMD Half->int via Giesen bit-fiddle widen (Wave 3)

f16->narrow was Phase-0 geomean 0.48 (f16->i32 ~0.69x). There is NO F16C in this .NET
(verified: Avx512FP16 absent, no Vector256<Half>, no vectorized ConvertToSingle(Half)), and
scalar (float)half is a TRAP (double-converts, measured slower than the current scalar). So
widen with a vectorized IEEE bit-fiddle.

MECHANISM (DirectILKernelGenerator.Cast.Half.cs), bit-exact with Converts.To{X}(Half):
  widen 8 halves (vpmovzxwd) -> 8x i32 bit patterns
  GIESEN half->float (branchless, exact for finite incl. subnormals): expmant<<13 as f32 *
    MAGIC rescales the exponent / reconstructs subnormals; inf/nan (expmant>0x7bff) OR in the
    f32 inf/nan exponent; sign = (bits&0x8000)<<16
  cvttps2dq -> i32 (INT_MIN sentinel on the built inf/nan; Half max 65504 never overflows i32)
  truncating Vector.Narrow i32->i16[->i8] for narrow targets (WRAP, matches NumPy:
    f16->i8 65504->-32, NaN->0).

inner-strided rows stage to a contig u16 buffer then vectorize). Covers f16->{i32,i8,u8,i16,
u16,char}. f16->f32/f64 intentionally stay on the scalar path — Giesen's NaN payload bits
differ from the BCL's (harmless for ->int, user-visible for ->float), and those are already ~1.0x.

conversion is very slow — large headroom). 0-diff contig + strided.

Phase-0's worst dst COLUMN (*->bool 0.82-0.94x this branch). bool is byte-per-element 0/1 =
(v != 0); the scalar path didn't vectorize the compare.

MECHANISM (DirectILKernelGenerator.Cast.ToBool.cs), bit-exact with Converts.ToBoolean(T):
  boolByte = AndNot(CompareEqual(v, 0), 1)   // 1 where v!=0 else 0
    int:   integer vpcmpeq* (==0), sign-agnostic bit compare (covers u32/u64/u16/u8 too)
    float: OrderedEqualNonSignaling so -0.0==0 -> False, NaN unordered -> True (bit-exact !=0)

  then truncating Vector.Narrow the 0/1 lanes to bytes (i8/u8 are 1-byte already: compare+&1).
Contig + strided (reuses StridedNarrowDriver, dstSize=1). Covers Single/Double/Int16/UInt16/
Int32/UInt32/Int64/UInt64/SByte/Byte/Char/Half -> bool. Complex/Decimal -> bool stay scalar
(Complex needs re|im OR; Decimal has no SIMD compare) — correct, unchanged.

perf(cast): fused VPGATHER whole-array kernels for f32/f64->narrow strided (Wave 7a)

Kill the inner-strided ([:, ::2]) and reversed-inner ([:, ::-1]) lag for
float|double -> {i8,u8,i16,u16,char}: every such cell flips from 0.41-0.65x
NumPy to a clean win (f32->i8 1.35x, f32->i16 1.54x, f64->i8 1.37x, f64->i16
1.37x, f64->u16 1.30x; f64->u8 ~parity). 0-diff vs the Converts.* reference
across strided/negcol/negstr/sliced/negrow incl. Inf/NaN/overflow (18150 checks).

WHY THE OLD PATH LAGGED
  The strided narrow cast staged each strided source row into a contiguous
  buffer then ran the contig Bulk on it. Two costs dominated, NOT the strided
  load: (a) the staging buffer roundtrip (write buf, read buf = 2x traffic),
  (b) a per-row indirect bulk/conv call. Geomean stuck at ~0.45x.

WHAT REPLACES IT
  For inner ss!=1 && inner ds==1 (contig dst row, the real astype shape) && AVX2,
  the Strided* entry points now dispatch to whole-array FUSED-GATHER kernels:
  VPGATHERDD/VPGATHERQQ loads the strided inner lanes straight into cvtt ->
  truncating Vector.Narrow -> contiguous store, in ONE pass (no staging buffer).
  Gather is bit-agnostic (raw 4/8-byte word), so it feeds f32/f64 cvtt identically
  to the contiguous Vector256.Load -> bit-exact with the contig Bulk.

  CRITICAL: the kernel walks EVERY row inside one function with the gather index
  vector hoisted OUTSIDE the outer odometer. The intermediate design called a
  per-row gather helper through a function pointer; that call boundary blocked the
  JIT from pipelining gathers across rows and rebuilt idx per row, pinning f32->i8
  at 0.70x. Proven in isolation: identical body, idx hoisted single-call 1.68x vs
  per-row NoInlining call 0.70x. Folding the row loop in lifts the direct kernel to
  1.89x (matches the standalone prototype). Three-stage row body: wide main
  (32/16-wide) + 8/4-wide gather mop-up + scalar drain.

CORRECTNESS PITFALL FIXED (caught by the Inf probe before commit)
  The scalar drain must use (narrow)Converts.ToInt32(val), the SAME audited
  NumPy-faithful convert as the contig tail. A (narrow)(int)val shortcut is NOT
  equivalent: C#'s float/double->int SATURATES since .NET Core 3.0 (Inf/overflow
  -> int.MaxValue 0x7FFFFFFF, low byte 0xFF) while the vector cvttps2dq/cvttpd2dq
  and Converts.ToInt32 give the INT_MIN sentinel (0x80000000, low byte 0x00 ==
  NumPy). They diverge exactly on Inf/NaN/out-of-int-range; f32->u8 of +Inf gave
  255 instead of NumPy's 0. The vector body + GetElement mop-up already use cvtt
  (correct); only the final scalar loop needed the Converts fix.

Reversed inner ([:, ::-1], ss<0) rides the same signed-stride gather. ss==1
(inner-contig sliced/negrow), strided dst, and no-AVX2 keep the unchanged
StridedNarrowDriver bulk/staging path. The per-row gbulk delegate that was
briefly threaded through StridedNarrowDriver is removed; its signature is back
to the original (bulk, conv).

Verification: 75 cast parity tests + 801 cast/astype/convert tests green on
net8.0 + net10.0; 18150-check Inf/NaN/overflow x 5-layout probe 0 failures.

Extend the Wave-7a fused-gather model to the *->bool strided cells. Every
gatherable source flips from a 0.32-0.50x NumPy lag to a clean win:
f32->bool 2.30x, i32->bool 1.82x, f64->bool 1.58x, i64->bool 1.23x. With 7a the

0-diff vs Converts.ToBoolean / (v!=0) across strided/negcol/negstr/sliced incl.
-0.0, +/-0.0, NaN, +/-Inf, int min/max (5704 checks).

MECHANISM

  VPGATHERQQ loads the strided 4/8-byte lanes straight into the (v!=0) compare ->
  0/1 -> Vector.Narrow pack -> contig bool bytes, in one pass with the gather index
  hoisted outside the outer odometer. Reuses the EXACT BulkXToBool compare so it's
  bit-exact with the contig kernels:
    float  -> AndNot(OrderedEqualNonSignaling(v,0), 1)   (-0.0->False, NaN->True)

  stage row: 32-wide main + 8/4-wide GetElement mop-up + scalar (Converts.ToBoolean
  / !=0) drain. i32/u32 and i64/u64 share a kernel (!=0 is signedness-agnostic).

  Same rationale as 7a: a per-row function-pointer gather blocked the JIT from

MECHANISM

  odometer), but INTEGER -> no cvtt: the gathered int IS the value and a truncating

perf(cast): drop stale signed->UInt64 SIMD-widen rejection (Wave 9)

is STALE: the WidenInt / WidenIntChain2 emit widens through the SOURCE-typed

bit-identical to the (already-enabled, already-winning) signed->Int64 widen. So

overhead.

  i16->u64 C 0.49ms / strided 0.32ms
  i32->u64 C 0.52ms / strided 0.35ms

([:, ::2]) / reversed-inner ([:, ::-1]) was 0.17-0.24x NumPy (the StridedComplex
Driver ran the UnpackLow deinterleave Bulk only for ss==1; every ss!=1 row fell to
the scalar Converts loop). Now a whole-array gather-real kernel: the real part of
the strided complex[i] lives at double-offset i*(2*ss), so VPGATHERQQ over the
reals (double stride 2*ss) feeds cvttpd2dq -> truncating Narrow directly, idx
hoisted outside the odometer.

  negcol   0.47-0.70x

16-byte gather is bandwidth-bound and NumPy's complex cast is well-tuned, so the
ss!=1 rows reach ~parity rather than a clean win (contig c128->narrow already won
~1.38x and is unchanged). negcol's backwards gather is the weakest; a forward
load + lane-reverse fast path (as in the double->i32 strided kernel) is the

perf(cast): SIMD Giesen float->f16 narrow for {bool,u8,i8,i16,u16,char,i32,f32}->Half (Wave 11)

f16 (Half) was the ONLY losing DST column in the cast matrix (geomean ~0.78):
every X->Half cast fell to the scalar generic emitter because this .NET has no
