the f16->X direction). Wave 11 adds the reverse: a vectorized branchless IEEE
float->f16 round-to-nearest-even (the Giesen/float_to_half algorithm) for the
SIMD-safe source set, plus the int-widen front-ends that feed it.

New file DirectILKernelGenerator.Cast.ToHalf.cs:
  - FloatToHalfBits(Vector256<float>) -> 8x f16 bit patterns (low 16 of each i32
    lane): clear sign; blend normal / subnormal / inf-nan; RTNE via the
    +0xfff+mantOdd carry; rebuild the f16 NaN payload as 0x7c00|(mant>>13)|(pz).
    Two lanes truncating-Narrow to 16 contiguous u16.
  - SingleToHalfBits(float): scalar port for the <16 tail and strided conv,
    bit-identical to the vector path.
  - Per-source bulks: f32 direct; i32 cvtdq2ps; i16/u16/char/i8/u8/bool widen
    (vpmovsx/zx) -> i32 -> cvtdq2ps -> Giesen. Contig kernels = bulk + tail.
  - Strided kernels reuse StridedNarrowDriver (dstSize=2): inner-contig rows run
    the bulk, inner-strided/broadcast rows stage to a contig buffer then
    vectorize, scalar conv elsewhere.

    TryGetCastKernel (after halfToX) and TryGetStridedCastKernel (after
    halfStrided) in Cast.cs.

    sNaN / qNaN / +-inf / f32+f16 subnormals / all 65536 round-trips / the
    +0xfff rounding boundaries.

    f16 overflows to +-inf at 65504 << 2^24, so any int large enough for the f32
    step to round is already inf in f16 (sign-consistent). The small-int sources

perf(cast): SIMD u32/f64/c128 -> f16 — finish the f16 column except i64/u64 (Wave 11b)

Wave 11 left u32/i64/u64/f64/c128 -> Half on the scalar path. 11b adds the three
that AVX2 can serve, completing the f16 DST column down to just i64/u64 (which
need AVX512 for i64->f32). All proven bit-exact vs NumPy 2.4.2 and regression-free.

double -> f16 (the f64 + c128 enabler):
  cvtpd2ps double-ROUNDS, so a naive f64->f32->f16 diverges from NumPy's direct
  f64->f16 on values where the f32 step's rounding flips the f16 result. Fixed with
  round-to-odd (Boldo/Melquiond): round f64->f32 to ODD, then RTNE f32->f16 == direct
  RTNE f64->f16. SIMD RoundToOdd4 does cvtpd2ps then nudges the inexact-and-even lanes

  doubles/iter with a per-block scalar fallback when any lane is NaN. NaN payload is
  built directly from the double mantissa's top 10 bits (the (float) cast would quiet
  sNaN — same latent bug Wave 11 fixed for f32). Scalar DoubleToHalfBits mirrors it.
  Proven 0-diff vs NumPy over 1.88M cases incl. 63K f16-midpoint double-rounding
  hazards + all NaN/inf/subnormal edges.

u32 -> f16:
  cvtdq2ps reads the i32-reinterpret as signed, so high-bit-set lanes (u32 >= 2^31,
  always >= 65536 -> +inf in f16) are blended to +inf; the rest convert faithfully.
  Proven 0-diff vs NumPy over 2.07M cases. Scalar uses the correct C# (float)(uint).

  VPGATHERQQ of reals (idx hoisted outside the odometer) + round-to-odd, 8/iter, NaN

  cause (DoubleToHalfBits is slower per-element than the old (Half)(double)) AND turns
  the inner-strided cells into wins.

perf(cast): single-pass KEEPORDER same-type copy — kill the F-contig double-transpose (Wave 12)

Same-type astype(copy:true) on an F-contiguous (or transposed) source ran TWO
cache-hostile passes: TensorEngine.Cast's same-dtype branch returned nd.Clone()
(a C-order buffer — an F->C transpose), then NDArray.astype saw the result wasn't
F-contiguous and ran a SECOND copy('F') (a C->F transpose). For a sub-L3 array this
is catastrophic; for bool|F it showed up as the cast matrix's 0.18-0.20x cliff.

Two fixes:

1. NDIter.TryCopySameType — flat-buffer fast path (IsSameFlatLayout). The contig
   cpblk gate keyed off C-contiguity only, so an identical-stride F-contiguous src
   and dst (the i-th logical element at the same byte offset in both) missed it and
   fell to the per-element CopyGeneralSameType for the Vector-less dtypes
   (Boolean/Char/Half/Complex). Now any same-shape, identical-stride, C- OR
   F-contiguous pair takes the single cpblk. Differing orders (F-transpose src into a
   C-contig dst) have non-identical strides and are correctly excluded, keeping the
   real reorder on its strided path. Direct TryCopySameType(F-dst<-F-src) 0.56 -> 0.015ms.

2. DefaultEngine.Cast same-dtype branch — route the F-contiguous (non-C) source
   through CastCrossType (KEEPORDER: allocate an F-order dst, one NDIter.Copy that
   collapses to the flat cpblk above) instead of Clone()+copy('F'). C-contiguous /
   1-D / strided sources keep the lean direct Clone() (no CreateCopyState overhead),
   so the common path is unchanged.

Result (best-of-7, -c Release):
  - F-contiguous same-type astype now equals C-contiguous (F/C ~1.00; was ~14x for bool).
  - 10M (past L3, where the transpose dominates allocation): bool 31.9 -> 0.40ms (79x),
    i8 47.5 -> 0.46ms (103x), char 38.1 -> 0.56ms (68x), f64 96.7 -> 11.3ms (8.6x)
    vs the old two-transpose path.
  - At 1M the array fits in cache and per-call allocation dominates, so the sweep ratio
    is allocation-bound (NumPy pools 1MB buffers warm); the double-transpose elimination
    is what this fixes, and it pays off at scale.

Correctness: F/T/C/sliced/negcol same-type copy bit-identical across all 11 dtypes
(incl. bool/char/half/complex). Tests: 9956 passed / 0 failed (net10.0); net8.0's lone
failure is the pre-existing FuzzCorpus log1p/complex128 divergence (unrelated).

perf(cast): SIMD char->{i8,u8} contiguous narrow — close the generic emitter's char gap (Wave 13)

Measured at HEAD, char -> {i8,u8} lagged on every layout (~0.8x) while i16/u16 ->
{i8,u8} won outright (i16->i8 C 4.19x): the generic IL cast emitter SIMD-narrows the
arithmetic 2-byte ints but treats Char as non-arithmetic and emits a scalar per-element
cast. New ShortNarrow partial adds a 32-wide truncating Vector.Narrow contig kernel for
char -> {i8,u8}; i16/u16 contig keep the already-fast generic path.

  char->i8  C 0.82 -> 2.22   char->u8  C 0.84 -> 2.40   (NPY/NS, best-of-7, -c Release)

Truncating Vector.Narrow == unchecked (byte) low-byte == NumPy uint16->int8 wrap
(signedness-agnostic). Verified bit-exact vs the NumPy-wrap oracle for i16/u16/char ->
i8/u8 across C/sliced/negcol/strided/bcast/T.

    VPGATHER-eligible, and staging strided rows to a contig buffer (the StridedNarrowDriver
    path the float/Half->narrow kernels use) costs more than the one-cycle truncate it
    feeds: measured a REGRESSION (i16->i8 strided 0.82 -> 0.47, negcol 1.10 -> 0.39), so it
    was dropped. Staging only pays when the per-element convert is expensive (Giesen f16).
  - char non-contiguous (sliced/negcol/strided ~0.8x) shares the generic char gap but has
    no gather-free SIMD win; left on the generic path (unchanged, no regression).
  - *->bool for every src size (1/2/4/8-byte) is already SIMD (Waves 4/7b); the residual
    ~0.65x on the strided layout is near the staged-narrow limit.

    idx hoisted) for inner-strided rows.

perf(cast): bit-exact AVX2 f32/f64 -> u32 (Wave 15) — 16 cells 0.46-0.85 -> 1.04-2.22

float->u32 was the cast matrix's dominant laggard family: ~30 cells in the
u32 DST column at 0.48-0.85x because the conversion 'stayed scalar'. The
deferral reason (documented in Cast.FloatWideInt.cs) was that NumPy's float->u32
is a MODULAR wrap over the whole finite range, not a saturate:
    5e9 -> 705032704,  1e10 -> 1410065408,  -1 -> 4294967295,  -3e9 -> 1294967296,
    2^32 -> 0,  NaN/+-Inf/|x|>=2^63 -> 0
which the naive AVX2 'subtract 2^31' range-shift can't reproduce (it saturates
beyond [0,2^32)), and the AVX512 VCVTTPS2UDQ instruction ALSO can't (it saturates
too: 5e9 -> 0xFFFFFFFF). Both diverge from NumPy.

This lands a fully bit-exact AVX2 kernel (no AVX512 needed) covering the whole
finite range. Algorithm (Cast.FloatToUInt.cs), all in double space until the
final cvtt:
    t = trunc(x)                                  // VROUNDPD toward zero
    r = t - 2^32*floor(t*2^-32)                   // r = t mod 2^32 in [0,2^32), exact
    shifted = r - (r>=2^31 ? 2^32 : 0)            // -> [-2^31,2^31)
    i = cvttpd2dq(shifted)                        // signed int32 whose BITS are the u32
    result = (|x| < 2^63) ? i : 0                 // mask folds NaN/Inf/overflow -> 0
The mod-2^32 step (missing from the old range-shift) is what makes the wrap come
out exactly; the |x|<2^63 compare is false for NaN (unordered)/Inf/overflow -> 0.
f32->u32 widens each lane f32->f64 first (lossless): a direct-f32 reduction lands
negative results like 4294967295 that round to 2^32 in float, corrupting the cvtt.

Strided: ss==1 contig bulk; ss!=1 VPGATHER. f64 gathers 4 inline. f32's gather
feeds an 8-wide widen->convert chain that stalls on gather latency (0.69ms/500K),
so it STAGES the gather into a contig tile buffer first (gathers pipeline), then
converts at contig speed (0.30ms/500K, 2.5x). Bit-exact with the contig kernel.

Bit-exact vs NumPy 2.4.2 (proven 0 diffs over 800K values incl. every edge:
wrap, large +/- magnitudes, subnormals, NaN/+-Inf/overflow) AND via the real
astype path across C/F/T/sliced/negrow/negcol/strided/bcast (0 diffs vs numpy).
Scalar tail uses Converts.ToUInt32 (the NumPy-faithful reference).

Benchmarks (1M, best-of-7, NPY/NS, >1 = NumSharp faster):
  f32->u32: C 1.90 F 1.86 T 1.48 sliced 1.44 negrow 1.51 negcol 1.27 strided 1.04 bcast 1.75
  f64->u32: C 1.79 F 1.83 T 1.93 sliced 1.88 negrow 1.62 negcol 1.34 strided 1.29 bcast 2.19
All 16 cells now win (were 0.46-0.85). f16->u32 and c128->u32 (which route via
the half/complex kernels) follow next.

perf(cast): bit-exact vectorized f16 -> f32 widen (Wave 15c) — 8 cells 0.64-0.89 -> 0.92-3.75

f16->f32 was the last all-losing portion of the f16 SRC row (0.64-0.89x): it
stayed on the scalar (float)Half path because Giesen's widen mangles the NaN
payload — fine for ->int (NaN->INT_MIN regardless) but a user-visible divergence
for ->float.

Fix (HalfBitsToFloatExact): Giesen widens finite (normal/subnormal/zero) exactly,
then the inf/nan lanes are overridden with the IEEE widen
    sign | 0x7f800000 | (mant << 13)
via a single BlendVariable. This reproduces NumPy's f16->f32 bit-for-bit INCLUDING
the NaN payload and signaling NaNs. Proven EXHAUSTIVELY: 0 diffs over all 65536
possible f16 bit patterns vs numpy 2.4.2 astype(float32).

(0x7c01 -> 0x7fc02000 instead of 0x7f802000), so the previous scalar f16->f32
path diverged from NumPy on sNaN. The new path (and its matching scalar conv
HalfToFloatScalarExact, used by the tail / strided driver) preserves sNaN. Same
class of bug the X->Half wave fixed, here for the widen direction.

perf(cast): bit-exact AVX2 {f16,f32,f64,c128} -> u64 (Wave 15d)

Completes the u64 DST column. NumPy's float->u64 is trunc(x) mod 2^64 over
[-2^63, 2^64), with NaN/Inf/overflow -> 2^63 and negatives wrapping (-1 -> 2^64-1).
cvttpd2qq (float->i64) is AVX512-only, so this synthesizes the conversion on AVX2:

  DoubleToU64x4: split t = trunc(x) into hi=floor(t/2^32) and lo=t-hi*2^32, convert
  EACH 32-bit half with the Wave-15 f64->u32 kernel (which already wraps negatives
  correctly), then recombine (hi<<32)|lo. The hi half of a negative t wraps to the
  right high dword, so the whole 64-bit two's-complement wrap falls out. A
  |x| in [-2^63,2^64) range mask folds NaN/Inf/overflow -> 2^63.

  f32->u64 widens f32->f64 (lossless) then DoubleToU64x4. f16->u64 uses the Giesen
  widen (NaN payload irrelevant: inf/nan -> 2^63). c128->u64 deinterleaves reals.

Strided: f64 gathers 4 doubles then STAGES into a contig buffer before the (heavy,
hi/lo) convert — feeding the gather straight into DoubleToU64x4 stalls on gather
latency (negcol 0.78->0.84, strided 0.83->0.89). f32 stages floats; c128 uses the
real-gather Fused path; f16 reuses StridedNarrowDriver (2->8).

Bit-exact vs NumPy 2.4.2 via the real astype path across C/rev/str2/T/negcol for
all four src dtypes (0 diffs incl. wrap, negatives, NaN/Inf/overflow); the f64->u64
core proven 0 diffs over 500K random+edge values vs Converts.ToUInt64.

13/16 measured cells win; the 3 marginal (f64/f32 negcol/strided 0.84-0.89) are

perf(cast): bit-exact vectorized f16 -> i64 (Wave 15e) — 8 cells 0.73-0.81 -> 2.0-3.1x

f16->i64 was a systematic scalar laggard (all 8 layouts 0.73-0.81x): the Half
resolver covered i32/u32/u64/f32 but not i64, so it fell to the scalar
Converts.ToInt64(Half) path.

Every finite f16 (|v| <= 65504) fits in int32, so the conversion is just:
Giesen widen f16->f32 -> cvttps2dq -> sign-extend i32->i64 (exact). The only
special case is inf/nan: cvttps2dq yields 0x80000000 which would sign-extend to
0xFFFFFFFF80000000, but NumPy (and Converts.ToInt64(Half)) map inf/nan to
int64.MinValue (0x8000000000000000) — handled with a BlendVariable keyed on the
f16 inf/nan mask (expmant > 0x7bff). 8 halves/iter (two 4-wide i32->i64 widenings).

Bit-exact vs NumPy 2.4.2 via the real astype path across C/str2/T/negcol (0 diffs
incl. all NaN payloads, sNaN, +-inf -> int64.min, negatives, subnormals).
Strided reuses StridedNarrowDriver (2->8).

Benchmarks (1M, best-of-7, NPY/NS, >1 = NumSharp faster):
  f16->i64: C 3.02  T 3.12  negcol 2.02  strided 2.12  (were ~0.73-0.81)

Closes the sub-word `strided`/`negcol` same-type-copy cliff — the largest

target cells go from 0.53-1.30x to 1.10-2.67x NPY/NS (best-of-3 sweep):

  u8|strided  0.56 -> 2.51    i16|strided  0.59 -> 1.66
  char|strided 0.59 -> 1.49   u16|strided  0.66 -> 1.58
  f16|strided 0.55 -> 1.10

Matrix: 91.5% -> 92.3% >=0.9 (1448/1568), geomean 1.70 -> 1.72.

Root cause
  A same-type cast is pure byte movement (signed/unsigned/float-ness is
  irrelevant), but for a non-unit inner stride the generic MemoryCopy-strategy
  strided kernel falls to a SCALAR per-element inner loop. 2-byte/1-byte sources
  are not VPGATHER-eligible, and staging strided rows to a contig buffer costs
  more than the truncate it feeds (the ShortNarrow regression), so the float
  kernels' gather/stage tricks don't apply.

Kernel (DirectILKernelGenerator.Cast.SubwordCopy.cs)
  ONE size-parameterised StridedCastKernel covers all 7 sub-word dtypes
  (1B {bool,u8,i8}, 2B {i16,u16,char,f16}) since a same-type copy is byte-exact:
    * inner stride +2 ([:, ::2]) -> DEINTERLEAVE the even lanes: mask the odd
      half to 0, VPACKUSWB/VPACKUSDW the low bytes/shorts, VPERMQ to undo the
      pack's 128-bit-lane interleave (32/16 elems per iter).
    * inner stride -1 ([:, ::-1]) -> REVERSE: load forward, VPSHUFB within each
      128-bit lane, VPERMQ to swap lanes (generalises the double->int32 ss==-1
      precedent in InnerCastDoubleToInt32 to 1B/2B).
    * inner stride +1 -> per-row Buffer.MemoryCopy; else NumPy-faithful scalar.
  Routed first in TryGetStridedCastKernel, gated src==dst && size in {1,2}; so
  cross-type and 4/8/16-byte same-type keep their existing (already-winning)
  fast paths. Reached via both TryCopySameType (astype same-type) and the
  CloneData strided path.

PERF NOTE pinned during development (benchmark/poc/subword_structure_poc.cs):
  the inner SIMD loop MUST be inlined in the odometer body. Factoring it into a
  per-row helper costs ~6x (0.020 -> 0.125 ms stride-2 1B); the JIT will not
  inline a method containing a loop even with AggressiveInlining, and the call
  boundary wrecks the loop's codegen. The four inner cases are inlined per
  element-size; the ss/ds branch is per-row but perfectly predictable.

Validation

    negrow/negcol/strided/bcast) x 7 dtypes = 56/56 (subword_verify.cs); the

    deinterleave/reverse bug fails the check.
  * Standalone math proven 0-diff + benchmarked vs scalar and NumPy

    reverse 1B 0.370->0.031 ms.

perf(evaluate): fix np.evaluate F-order/transpose cliff (~15x) via F-aware iteration

The fused elementwise path (DefaultEngine.Evaluate.EvaluateCore) hardcoded
NPY_ORDER.NPY_CORDER for the NDIter pass AND always allocated the result
C-contiguous. On F-contiguous or transposed operands that forced a max-stride
step every element (cache miss per element) and strided output writes — the
operand-layout sweep just added to the fusion bench measured np.evaluate at ~16x
SLOWER than the unfused np.* chain and ~9x slower than NumPy's own unfused:
    [F] fused 64.28 ms  unfused 7.09 ms  (0.11x)
    [T] fused 63.72 ms  unfused 7.40 ms  (0.12x)

Root cause: the elementwise path never negotiated iteration order from the
operands. Both reduction paths right below it already used NPY_KEEPORDER; only
the elementwise MultiNew forced CORDER. The fast UNFUSED binary path
(TryExecuteBinaryOpViaNDIter) had long since solved this: when every non-scalar
operand is strictly F-contiguous it allocates the result column-major and passes
NPY_FORTRANORDER so the iterator coalesces all axes into ONE contiguous inner
loop. The fused path simply wasn't mirroring it.

Fix (mirrors the binary path exactly):
- New internal helper AreAllInputsStrictFContig(ops, resultShape) — the N-input
  analogue of AreAllOperandsStrictFContig: true when the result is multi-dim and
  every non-scalar input is pure-F (IsFContiguous && !IsContiguous), >=1 such.
- EvaluateCore: when all inputs are pure-F and we allocate the result (no out=),
  allocate it 'F'; pick NPY_FORTRANORDER iff the result buffer is actually
  F-contig (fresh F-alloc, or a provided F-contig out), else NPY_CORDER. C /
  strided / broadcast / mixed-C+F inputs are unchanged (C-order default).

Result (same box): F 64.28->4.33 ms (now 1.80x vs unfused, 3.2x vs NumPy);
T 63.72->4.28 ms (1.73x). No regression: C 4.37, strided 4.00, bcast 2.54x all
intact. As a NumPy-aligned bonus the result now PRESERVES input layout — an all-F
expression yields an F-contiguous array (verified: T->F, out=F kept, same
instance returned), matching np.multiply/np.add's layout behavior.

Verified: bit-exact (maxErr=0) value check of result[i,j] == a*b+c across
C/F/T/strided/bcast + F-contig out= + mixed-C+F on a non-square 200x137 (fresh

perf(reduce): collapse broadcast axes algebraically in flat reduction (bcast-reduce ~700x NumPy)

The flat reduction's broadcast handling (DefaultEngine.ExecuteElementReduction) folded each
stride-0 (broadcast) axis by ITERATING its D identical copies via ExecuteAxisReduction —
cache-hot but still O(D×unique), landing at ~1.0x NumPy (the prior "50x->0.9x" fix). A
stride-0 axis repeats its data exactly, so reducing over it is CLOSED-FORM — nothing to
iterate:
    sum -> *D,  prod -> ^D,  min/max -> identity   (mean = sum/count, in the caller).
Drop every broadcast axis to a non-broadcast view of the UNIQUE data (index 0 along each
stride-0 axis), reduce THAT once via the existing fast contiguous/IL-SIMD path, then apply
the collapsed multiplicity to the scalar. O(unique), not O(D×unique).

Measured (8192-unique x 1024 broadcast = 8.4M logical, -c Release, best-of-9):
  before (iterate fold) : 1.10   ms  (1.03x NumPy)
  after  (algebraic)    : 0.0016 ms  (~700x NumPy) — AT the floor: the SIMD sum of the
                          8192-row alone is 0.00149 ms; C# dispatch overhead is 0.11 us.
No per-element kernel can approach this: a perfect contiguous SIMD reduce of the
materialized 8.4M is 2.16 ms = 1350x slower — it pays O(D×N) while the collapse is
O(unique). IL/NDIter/IL-generation are throughput tools for that slower class and cannot
beat the algorithmic win; the inner unique-reduce already rides the IL SIMD kernel.

Correctness:
- Integer & min/max BIT-EXACT (modular */pow compose under truncation; min/max are
  order-independent). Float sum/prod differ only ULP-level — the summation-order class the
  codebase already documents here, well within the broadcast fuzz's 1e-5 tolerance.
- CombineWithCount applies the closed form in the accumulator dtype (IPowS/IPowU wrap like a
  materialized integer reduction; DPow throws on decimal overflow, matching np.prod).
- DropBroadcastAxes returns the unique view CONTIGUOUS (an O(unique) copy only when the

feat(sort): implement np.sort + np.argsort + ndarray.sort on NDIter with a radix line kernel

Closes one of the 8 documented Missing Functions (np.sort) and replaces the
pathological argsort. Sorting is structured exactly like NumPy's _new_sortlike /
_new_argsortlike (item_selection.c): an NDIter "IterAllButAxis" drive hands one
1-D line at a time to a high-performance inner sort kernel.

ARCHITECTURE
- Driver (AxisSort.DriveAllButAxis): NDIterRef.AdvancedNew with opAxesNDim=ndim-1
  and op_axes listing every axis EXCEPT the sort axis. Dropping the sort axis from
  the iterator stops it coalescing into the contiguous run (the bug that made an
  earlier EXTERNAL_LOOP+CORDER attempt hand the kernel count=20 into an N=5 buffer);
  the kernel then walks each line itself via the axis stride. Handles 1-D..N-D, any
  axis (incl. negative and None=flatten), and strided/transposed/F-contig inputs.
- Inner kernel = native-width LSD radix (RadixSort): u32 core for 1/2/4-byte dtypes,
  u64 core for 8-byte; 8-bit digits, one count + one scatter per byte, double-buffered,
  trivial-pass skip. Stable, so argsort ties resolve in ascending index order
  (== NumPy kind='stable'). Caller fills keys with a monotonic unsigned transform
  (so unsigned ascending order == NumPy value order) and un-transforms on the way out.
- Floats partition NaN to the end before radix (NumPy sorts NaN last); the float->key
  transform is the standard IEEE sign-flip so -inf<..<+inf orders correctly.
- Half/Complex/Decimal route to BCL introsort (Span.Sort) with exact NumPy comparators
  (npysort_common.h): real NaN-last; complex CDOUBLE_LT lexicographic real-then-imag,
  any-NaN-part last. Complex sorts at all now (it has no IComparable).
- argsort always returns int64 indices; the radix carries a parallel index column.

WHY RADIX (POC, i9-13900K, ratios are NumPy_ms/NS_ms, >1 = NS faster)
- int32 sort:    radix 164-217 M/s = 0.72-0.90x NumPy, 8-9x over BCL Span.Sort.
- int32 argsort: radix 87-135 M/s  = 2.1-4.3x FASTER than NumPy (NumPy uses slow
  indirect quicksort; radix carries indices for one extra scatter stream).
- Variation shoot-out @1M int32 sort: radix 197 M/s >> AVX2 vectorized quicksort
  52 M/s (correct, but out-of-place partition + no index path) >> Span.Sort 22 M/s.
  8-bit beats 11-bit (L1 thrash) and beats ulong-widened combined-histogram for
  <=4-byte. A SIMD quicksort could only edge radix on int *sort* and would forfeit
  the argsort win, so radix is the right max-perf, all-dtype, correct-and-stable choice.
  IL-generating the radix gives no gain (memory-bandwidth-bound, not dispatch-bound).

CORRECTNESS (all vs NumPy 2.4.2)
- 82/82 .npy round-trip parity: int32/int64/uint8/int16/float32/float64 x 1-D/2-D/3-D
  x every axis (incl. negative + None) x NaN/+-inf x empty/single/ties/constant.
- Half/Complex/Decimal verified (incl. the explicit complex lexicographic NaN-last case).
- 20 new unit tests (NpSortTests) incl. transposed-view, in-place ndarray.sort,
  3-D argsort-reconstructs-sort. Sort_ApiGap retagged [OpenBugs] -> [Fixed].
- Full suite: 9977 passed, 0 failed.

API
- np.sort(a, axis=-1, kind=null), np.argsort(a, axis=-1), ndarray.sort(axis=-1) in-place.
- ndarray.argsort<T> kept for source compat (delegates; element type from the array).
  Deleted the old LINQ implementation (per-element tuple + NDArray view allocation).

perf+fix(any/all): SIMD bool/char reductions + fix byte/sbyte any() AVX2 mask overflow

np.any / np.all on the two non-JIT-vectorizable dtypes (bool, char) fell through to
the scalar per-element loop in AnySimdHelper/AllSimdHelper because
Vector256<bool>/<char>.IsSupported == false. For the benchmarked any(all-false)
case at scale this was the 0.08-0.18x cliff (5-12x SLOWER than NumPy): a full
scalar scan of every element, no SIMD. bool/char are bitwise identical to
byte/ushort for a zero/non-zero test (bool: 0/1; char: UTF-16 code unit), so
reinterpret at the top of both helpers and run the existing vectorized integer
path. (Applies to the direct ReduceBool route AND the IL-emitted reduction route,
which both call these helpers.)

While fixing that, found and fixed a latent CORRECTNESS bug in AnySimdHelper: the
"all lanes zero" reference mask was `(1u << vectorCount) - 1`, which for
Vector256<byte>/<sbyte> (32 lanes) is `(1u << 32) - 1`. C# masks uint shift counts
to 5 bits, so `1u << 32 == 1u << 0 == 1`, making allZeroMask = 0 instead of
0xFFFFFFFF. An all-zero vector then hit `bits (0xFFFFFFFF) != 0` -> returned true on
the FIRST vector, so:
    np.any(np.zeros(1_000_000, dtype=byte)) -> True   (NumPy: False)
byte/sbyte any() was WRONG for any all-zero array >= 32 elements on AVX2 hardware.
Masked until now because the benchmark uses bool (scalar path) and arrays < 32 use
the Vector128 path where the shift doesn't overflow. Widened to
`(uint)((1UL << vectorCount) - 1)` (correct for all 4..32 lane counts). This is also
prerequisite for the bool->byte redirect, which now routes through the byte path.

Result (i9-13900K, Release, best-of-9, vs NumPy 2.4.2), np.any(bool all-false):
    100K  0.18x -> 1.90x     1M  0.08x -> 1.04x     10M  0.09x -> 1.04x
NumSharp now runs at 79-95 GB/s (memory-bandwidth-bound) -- at/above NumPy; the
block-unroll rewrite considered next was unnecessary once at the memory ceiling.

Verified: 33 correctness checks (bool/byte/sbyte/char/int x all-false/all-true/
early-hit/all-zero x sizes 1M/40/10 hitting V256 / V256+tail / scalar paths) pass,
incl. byte all-zero any=False at 1M; 19 NpAnyTest/np_all_Test pass on net8+net10;
broader reduction sweep green except 3 pre-existing [OpenBugs] (convolve int64,
var/std ddof>n) in unrelated kernels.

fix(reduce): root-fix NDIter strided sub-word accumulator drift; drop the broadcast-reduce copy

Follow-up to the broadcast-reduce algebraic collapse. That commit added a .copy() in
DropBroadcastAxes to dodge a "np.prod over a strided view returns 0" bug — a symptom patch.
This removes the copy and fixes the bug at its root so the strided unique view reduces
through NDIter directly (NDIter handles non-contiguous via coalesce + stride-ordered
axis-permute, and is the always-faster path — no materialization).

ROOT CAUSE — NDIter.Execution.DetermineAccumulatorType had a hand-rolled integer-widening
switch that had DRIFTED from the canonical NPTypeCode.GetAccumulatingType (the map the
direct/contiguous reduction path uses):
  - SByte and Char were MISSING -> fell through to `_ => src`, so a strided sub-word
    sum/prod/cumsum/cumprod accumulated in 1-/2-byte lanes and OVERFLOWED. np.prod over a
    strided sbyte/char view returned garbage (e.g. 47 for a true 3375) or 0.
  - Byte was mis-widened to Int64 instead of UInt64 (latent: a UInt64 TResult was returned
    through an Int64 accumulator; positive products happened to fit).
The contiguous path was unaffected because it never uses this method (it passes the
GetAccumulatingType result down explicitly). The bug was dormant until the algebraic collapse
started reducing strided unique views directly.

FIX:
- DetermineAccumulatorType now delegates the Sum/Prod/CumSum/CumProd widening to
  src.GetAccumulatingType() — single source of truth, can never drift again. (Mean/Var/Std
  -> Double and the pass-through for floats/decimal/complex are unchanged; GetAccumulatingType
  preserves Half/Single/Double/Decimal/Complex, so it is an exact drop-in.)
- DropBroadcastAxes drops the .copy(): returns the (possibly strided) unique view as-is; the
  flat reduction routes non-contiguous inputs through NDIter, now correct.

This also fixes strided sub-word reductions OUTSIDE the broadcast path (any np.sum/np.prod/
np.cumsum/np.cumprod over a strided/transposed sbyte/char view) — the fuzz improved 38 -> 37
fails (the remaining 37 are all pre-existing: 30 NaN-engine + 7 decimal argmax/argmin).

perf(cast): SIMD i64/u64 -> f16 via clamp-sentinel + low-32 pack (Wave 17, bucket A)

Closes the last large genuine cast laggard: i64->f16 and u64->f16 across all 8
layouts were the only AVX512-gated family left (was 0.68-0.89x NumPy on best-of-3,
falling to the scalar generic emitter). There is NO AVX2 i64->f32 (cvtqq2ps is
AVX512DQ, and this box is AVX2-only: Vector512 not accelerated, Avx512F/DQ/BW all
false), so synthesize the conversion exploiting f16's tiny finite range.

KEY INSIGHT: f16 saturates to +-inf at 65520, so EVERY finite i64/u64->f16 result
has |v| < 65520 << 2^17 -- which fits in i32 *exactly* (well under the 2^24 f32
mantissa limit, so the i32->f32 step never rounds, single RTNE at f32->f16). Any
|v| >= 65520 is inf regardless of the low bits.

KERNEL (DirectILKernelGenerator.Cast.ToHalf.cs):
  - Int64x8ToHalfBits / UInt64x8ToHalfBits: clamp out-of-range lanes to a +-70000
    sentinel (VPCMPGTQ + byte-granular VPBLENDVB; u64 uses the sign-bias unsigned
    compare), so the low-32-bit narrow is exact and the sentinel maps to +-inf.
    Pack 8 lanes' low words via PermuteVar8x32(RtoSel)+GetLower, then the exact
    cvtdq2ps and the already-proven Giesen FloatToHalfBits.
  - BulkInt64ToHalf / BulkUInt64ToHalf: 16-at-a-time contig bulk + scalar tail.
  - Int64ToHalfBits / UInt64ToHalfBits scalar ports (tail + strided conv); finite
    |v| < 2^24 so (float)v is exact, then SingleToHalfBits.
  - Contig (CastInt64/UInt64ToHalfContig) + strided (StridedInt64/UInt64ToHalf via
    the existing StridedNarrowDriver, srcSize=8) wired into TryGetXToHalfKernel /
    TryGetXToHalfStridedKernel (Int64/UInt64 switch cases). No Cast.cs routing
    change -- the X->Half resolvers were already in the chain.

fix(sort): eliminate O(N^2) blowup on 1-D / axis=None sort & argsort

np.sort, ndarray.sort and np.argsort were O(N^2) for every 1-D array and
every axis=None call - the most common cases. Root cause: AxisSort's
IterAllButAxis driver (DriveAllButAxis) drops the sort axis via op_axes,
so a 1-D input yields a 0-dimensional iterator (oa_ndim=0, op_axes=[[]]).
NDIter mis-drives that degenerate shape as `size` single-element
iterations instead of 1, and because each line kernel re-sorts the whole
line (it walks by LineCtx.n, ignoring the per-call count) total work is
N x O(N) = O(N^2).

Measured before fix (i9-13900K, Release), 1-D int32:
  N=10K   sort    514 ms   argsort    768 ms
  N=100K  sort 53,419 ms   argsort 83,132 ms   (~104x per 10x in N = quadratic)
1M+ effectively hung (minutes). Unit tests never caught it (5-12 element
arrays, N^2 trivial) and the radix POC benched RadixSort directly,
bypassing the driver.

Fix: at the single choke point DriveAllButAxis, promote a 1-D operand to
a (1, N) memory-sharing view (np.expand_dims aliases storage, so in-place
sort still mutates the original; a leading size-1 axis leaves the
data-axis stride - and thus LineCtx in/out strides - unchanged). Now
exactly one axis (size 1) is kept, so the iterator makes exactly one
line-kernel call. Multi-D was already correct (one call per line) and is
untouched.

Measured after fix:
  N=100K  sort 0.68 ms (147 M/s)  argsort 1.06 ms (94 M/s)  ~78,000x faster
  1-D throughput now flat across N (quadratic gone).
vs NumPy 2.4.2 argsort: int32 1.47x (1M) / 2.1x (4M) FASTER;
  int64 ~parity; f64 0.6x (1M) -> 0.96x (4M).

Correctness: NpSortTests 20/20 pass; validated 1-D sort/argsort, in-place
on strided a[::2] view, axis=None, int64/f64.

NOTE (separate latent bug, not fixed here): the underlying NDIter
0-dimensional / empty-op_axes iteration emits `size` iterations instead of
1; this still affects any other 0-dim op_axes use. The sort path now works
around it rather than relying on the iterator's 0-dim behavior.

perf(engine): route 7 strided ops through the kernel instead of materializing a contiguous copy

Removes the copy-to-contiguous anti-pattern (materializing a strided/transposed/
sliced/F-order/broadcast view because a kernel only handled C-contiguous data)
from seven compute paths, replacing each `.copy()`/`.copy('C')` with in-place
strided iteration — the same principle applied to the reduction fold earlier on
this branch ("must use NDIter, not copy"). Every element is now read through its
own strides in C-order (via a shared `FlatStrideOffset` odometer) or through the
existing IL strided kernel; results are bit-identical to the prior copy path and
verified against NumPy across all dtypes x layouts.

CumSum / CumProd flat (Default.Reduction.CumAdd.cs, CumMul.cs):
  - Both flat scans now share ScanElementwiseFlat, which drives the IL scan kernel
    directly on strided/transposed/sliced/reversed/F-order/3-D inputs. The flat
    scan generator already emitted a correct C-order strided walk
    (EmitScanStridedLoop); the old `cumsum_elementwise(arr.copy())` simply prevented
    it from ever being reached.
  - Enabled CumProd in the IL scan kernel (DirectILKernelGenerator.Scan.cs):
    EmitScanCombine now emits Mul, EmitScanHelperCall maps to a new
    CumProdHelperSameType. cumprod previously had NO IL kernel at all (TryGet
    returned null at generation, always falling to the scalar copy path).
  - Half/Complex accumulators can't be combined with il Add/Mul except same-type-
    contiguous, so for non-contiguous Half/Complex (and decimal cumprod) we keep a
    single C-order ravel — exactly what NumPy does — not a kernel-dodge copy.
  - Base address folds Shape.offset in (sliced views retain it; simple contiguous
    slices bake it into Address). NEP50 accumulator widening preserved.

Var / Std flat (Default.Reduction.Var.cs, Std.cs):
  - The fallback two-pass now iterates the input in place via FlatStrideOffset
    (var/std are order-independent, so any visiting order is valid — mirrors NumPy,
    which reduces strided arrays without copying). Shared moment helpers
    (VarMomentsReal<T> via INumberBase, VarMomentsDecimal, VarMomentsComplex) are
    used by both var and std (std = sqrt). Removes the old double-materialization
    (arr.copy() + Cast-to-double).

Integer Reciprocal (Default.Reciprocal.cs):
  - The 1/x integer loop reads the source through its strides instead of
    materializing sliced/strided/broadcast views (the comment admitted the previous
    raw read "THREW for views"). Broadcast stride=0 is handled naturally.
  - Pre-existing 1/0 semantics preserved verbatim (see known-bug note below).

Left / Right Shift (Default.Shift.cs):
  - Array-operand shift walks both the values and the per-element shift counts
    through their own strides (ExecuteShiftArrayStrided), so broadcast (stride=0),
    transposed, sliced and mixed-layout operands no longer get copied. The
    contiguous fast path still uses the IL scalar-loop kernel.

Clip (Default.ClipNDArray.cs, DirectILKernelGenerator.Clip.cs):
  - New ClipStrided reads src and (array) bounds through their own strides in
    C-order, writing a fresh C-contiguous result — eliminating the copy('C')
    normalizations in the general path, PrepareBound, and the @out path. The
    contiguous fast path still drives the IL SIMD kernel. One strided loop is
    shared across dtypes via Max/Min function pointers.
  - Clamp semantics mirror the IL kernel bit-for-bit: Math.Max/Min for sized
    numerics+decimal, the (now internal) Half/Complex NaN helpers, Char as UInt16,
    and NaN-propagating float/double Max/Min that resolve the signed-zero tie like
    hardware MAXPS/MINPD (maximum(+0,-0) = -0) rather than Math.Max (+0). np.maximum
    /minimum/fmax/fmin are implemented on top of clip, so this keeps their
    signed-zero/NaN results identical to the SIMD path and to NumPy.
  - Fixed a latent allocation bug: result buffers are now built from a fresh
    contiguous Shape, never np.empty(lhs.Shape) which would clone a strided/F-order
    layout and mis-address the linear dst writes.

Verification: per-op fuzz harnesses compare strided/transposed/sliced/reversed/
F-order/3-D/broadcast views against the contiguous ground truth and against live
NumPy across all dtypes (scan 308/308, var-std 660/660, recip+shift 220/220, clip
350/350). Full unit suite green (9987 passed, 0 failed); net8.0 + net10.0 build clean.

int32/int64/uint64 (uint64 -> 2^63); NumSharp uses MinValue for all signed and 0
for all unsigned, so reciprocal(int8/int16 0) and reciprocal(uint64 0) diverge.

rewrite; flagged for a separate fix.

fix(math): NumPy-exact integer reciprocal 1/0 (+ bool->int8) and clip/maximum signed-zero scalar tail

Two NumPy-parity bugs, both surfaced while removing the strided copy-hacks.

Integer reciprocal 1/0 (Default.Reciprocal.cs)
  Re-probed NumPy 2.4.2 bit-exact and deterministic across array sizes / lane
  positions: reciprocal(0) is the sign-bit sentinel 0x80..0 ONLY for the 32/64-bit
  loops (int32 -> int.MinValue, int64 -> long.MinValue, uint64 -> 2^63) and 0 for
  every narrower type (int8, int16, uint8, uint16, AND uint32). NumSharp returned
  MinValue for ALL signed (so int8 -> -128, int16 -> -32768) and 0 for ALL unsigned
  (so uint64 -> 0) — wrong for int8/int16/uint64. Fixed the three per-type 1/0
  results; the other five already matched. (A prior pin had mis-probed int8 1/0 as
  -128; corrected.)

  reciprocal(bool): NumPy promotes bool to the int8 loop -> int8 [True->1, False->0]
  (probed np.reciprocal([True,False]) -> int8 [1,0]). NumSharp took the float loop
  (Double [1, inf]). The dispatcher now maps a bool loop type to int8 and casts the
  input, so bool reciprocal returns int8 with the int8 1/0 = 0 rule. dtype was
  already preserved for the int types (the registry's "widen to float64" note was
  stale).

clip / maximum / minimum / fmax / fmin signed-zero scalar tail
  (DirectILKernelGenerator.Clip.cs, Default.ClipNDArray.cs)
  np.maximum etc. are built on clip. For float32/float64 the SIGNED-ZERO tie resolves
  to the SECOND operand (hardware MAXPS/MINPD: maximum(+0,-0) = -0) — the OPPOSITE of
  float16 (ties to the first operand) and of Math.Max (returns +0). The IL kernel's
  SIMD body already matched NumPy, but its SCALAR TAIL (EmitScalarClamp) used Math.Max
  and so diverged on a signed-zero tie landing in the last partial vector. Added
  NaN-propagating, tie-to-second FloatMaxNaN/FloatMinNaN/DoubleMaxNaN/DoubleMinNaN
  helpers and wired EmitScalarClamp to them for Single/Double; the engine's ClipStrided
  now shares the same helpers (dropping its local copies), so the contiguous SIMD body,
  contiguous scalar tail, and strided path all agree bit-for-bit with NumPy. The Half
  helper (tie-to-first) is correct for float16 and left unchanged.

  - NewDtypesCoverageSweep: corrected B36_SByte (int8 1/0 -> 0, not MinValue) and added

fix(nditer): 0-dim op_axes iterates once, not N times (root of sort O(N^2))

CalculateBroadcastShape gated the op_axes branch on `opAxesNDim > 0`, so an
explicit 0-dimensional iteration (opAxesNDim == 0, op_axes = [[]]) fell through
to natural broadcasting and returned the operand's own shape [N]. That made
IterSize = N, so a kernel driven without EXTERNAL_LOOP ran N times instead of
once. NumPy's NDIter_RemoveAxis leaves a 0-dim iterator with GetIterSize() == 1
(one iteration, data pointer = operand base; any dropped axis is the caller's
responsibility via its saved stride).

This is the ROOT of the 1-D / axis=None sort & argsort O(N^2) addressed at the
symptom level in b4d2128c: AxisSort's IterAllButAxis drops the only axis of a
1-D operand -> opAxesNDim == 0 -> the line kernel (which re-sorts the whole line
per call, ignoring the per-call count) was invoked N times.

Fix: treat opAxesNDim == 0 as an explicit 0-dim iteration and return an empty
iteration shape (IterSize == 1). The `> 0` -> `>= 0` gate plus an early
`return Array.Empty<long>()` leaves the opAxesNDim > 0 and the unspecified
(-1, natural-broadcast) paths untouched.

TDD (NDIterZeroDimOpAxesTests, 10 tests, direct NDIterRef.AdvancedNew):
- RED against the unfixed iterator: 7 fail / 3 pass, every failure the exact
  symptom (NDim 1 not 0; Calls/IterSize = 100000/1000/500/256/10/20 not 1).
- GREEN after fix: 10/10. Functional cases (single-call whole-line walk,
  in-place fill, two-operand lockstep copy, sliced-offset view) confirm the
  NDim=0 base pointer is offset-correct and read/write-valid; 3 regression
  guards (no-op_axes 1-D -> N calls; drop-axis-1 -> per-row; drop-axis-0 ->
  per-col) hold before and after.

Regression: 42/42 (NpSortTests 20 + NDIterZeroDimOpAxes 10 + AxisStride 12).

Note: AxisSort's (1,N) promotion workaround from b4d2128c is now redundant (the
sort path could rely on this root fix directly) but left in place; it is correct
and independent.

perf(binaryop): fix scalar-broadcast fast-path miss for weak-scalar literals (NEP50)

`a * 2`, `a + 5`, `a / 3.0` route through operator(NDArray, object) ->
np.asanyarray(literal), so a Python int literal is wrapped as an int32 0-d scalar
(a float literal as float64). For `f32[] * 2` the operands therefore arrive as
f32 x int32. resultType already reflects NumPy's weak promotion (f32), but the
fast-path gates key off the RAW operand dtypes:
  - TryTrivialContiguousBinaryOp: `if (lhsType != rhsType ...) return null;` bails
    BEFORE the scalar-broadcast arm, and
  - TryExecuteBinaryOpViaNDIter: sameDtype=false -> per-element-convert mixed loop
    (vector body null).
So the op fell to the heavy mixed path instead of the SimdScalarRight/Left
scalar-broadcast loop it should take. Measured (100K f32, Release):
  a * 2  (int32 scalar) 0.080 ms   vs   a * 2f (f32 scalar) 0.035 ms  -- 2.25x slower
for IDENTICAL work and an identical f32 result. This hit EVERY `array <op>
python-literal` and dominated the 100K-tier elementwise losses in the full benchmark
(`a * 2 (literal) f32 @100K` 0.067x was among the worst non-degenerate op-matrix cells).

Root cause is path-check ORDERING: the same-dtype gate is evaluated first, against
un-promoted operand dtypes, so a case that is effectively same-dtype after NumPy's
weak-scalar promotion never reaches the scalar-broadcast fast path.

Fix (ExecuteBinaryOp, before the trivial bypass): when exactly one operand is a
0-d/size-1 scalar, the OTHER (array) operand already IS resultType, and only the
scalar's dtype differs, materialize the scalar at resultType (one element -- exactly
what NumPy does, casting the scalar to the loop dtype). Both operands then share
resultType and the same-dtype SIMD paths (contiguous SimdScalarRight/Left and the
same-dtype NDIter SIMD loop, incl. strided) light up. When the ARRAY operand also
differs (e.g. int32[] * 2.5 -> float64) the guard skips: the array genuinely needs a
cast, which is the mixed path's job.

Value-identical: the mixed path converted the same scalar to resultType per element;
this converts it once up front. Verified across f32/f64/i16/i32/i64/u8/i8 (contig +
strided): (a * 2) == (a * same-type-scalar 2), every dtype eq=True; i32 * 2.5 still
-> float64 = 2.5 (guard correctly skips). Post-fix: a*2 ~= a*2f ~= a*s32 (gap closed).
778 binary/arithmetic/promotion/scalar/broadcast + 2345 math/reduction/statistics/
ufunc/comparison/evaluate tests pass on net8.0 + net10.0.

Settled while investigating (the suspected second ordering bug): DivergesFromNumpyCast
is a dead stub (returns false), so the cast *->bool slowness is NOT a gating-order bug
-- it is fixed overhead on a 1-byte output, like the same-type copy diagonal.

fix(complex): log1p(nan ± inf·i) → (+inf, nan) — port NumPy nc_log1p exactly

The FuzzMatrix UnaryExtra corpus gate (CI "Build and Release") failed with
19/4654 complex128 log1p cases diverging from NumPy: NumSharp produced
(NaN, NaN) where NumPy yields (+inf, NaN) for inputs whose 1+z has an
infinite component paired with a NaN (e.g. log1p(nan + inf·i), log1p(nan − inf·i)).

Root cause: Log1p delegated to the BCL Complex.Log(1+z), whose internal
Complex.Abs computes hypot(±inf, NaN) = NaN (then Math.Log(NaN) = NaN),
violating C99 hypot(±inf, anything) = +inf. NumPy's nc_log1p
(_core/src/umath/funcs.inc.src) instead computes real = log(npy_hypot(re+1, im)),
imag = atan2(im, re+1), and npy_hypot returns +inf whenever either part is
infinite.

Fix (matches NumPy's structure — a single npy_hypot feeds clog/csqrt/nc_log1p):
- Harden the shared NDComplexMath.Hypot into a faithful npy_hypot: return
  +inf if either arg is infinite (even when the other is NaN), then NaN if
  either is NaN, before the existing overflow-safe x*sqrt(1+(y/x)^2) core.
  Behavior for finite inputs is bit-identical, and Log/Sqrt already guard
  inf/NaN before reaching Hypot, so no other path changes.
- Rewrite Log1p to mirror nc_log1p directly (log of hypot + atan2) rather
  than routing through Complex.Log, keeping the naive magnitude log (NOT
  clog's near-|z|=1 refinement, so np.log1p(1e-10j).real stays 0, not 5e-21).

Result: 13/14 probed edge inputs are now bit-exact with NumPy 2.4.2 (every
inf/NaN special fixed); the lone residual (0.5-1j) is 1 ULP on the real part
from hypot correct-rounding — within the MisalignedRegistry's documented
3-ULP complex-unary excuse (imag bit-exact). Full unit suite on net8.0 and
net10.0: 0 failed / 9990 passed under the CI filter (was 1 failed: UnaryExtra).

fix(kernels): macOS/ARM64 signed-zero + integer-widening reduction parity

GitHub macos-latest (Apple Silicon / ARM64) failed 6 tests that pass on x86_64.
Root cause: three kernels relied on x86 instruction semantics that differ on ARM.
Reproduced locally by running the portable test IL under linux/arm64 via Docker+QEMU
(MSTest/testhost deadlock under qemu-user, so a single-process console oracle mirrors
the new MSTest assertions; both assert NumPy 2.4.2 truth). New committed suite:
test/NumSharp.UnitTest/Backends/Kernels/SignedZeroAndIntWideningParityTests.cs.

B1 maximum/minimum signed-zero (ARM-only) — DirectILKernelGenerator.cs
  EmitRawVectorMinOrMax's generic fallback used Vector{N}.Max/Min, which lower to ARM
  FMAX/FMINNM (IEEE maxNum/minNum: order-independent, +0 > -0) instead of x86 MAXPS/MINPS
  (second operand on a ±0 tie, = NumPy maximum/minimum). Added EmitFloatTieMinOrMax: an
  explicit strict-compare + ConditionalSelect (max = a>b?a:b, min = a<b?a:b) for the
  float/double generic path so every platform returns the second operand on a tie. The
  EmitVectorMinOrMax NaN-restore still runs, so NaN propagation is unchanged. x86 keeps
  its Avx/Sse intrinsic path untouched; integer min/max keep the bare hardware op.

B2 negate signed-zero (ARM-only) — DirectILKernelGenerator.Unary.Vector.cs
  Vector{N}.op_UnaryNegation lowers to Zero - x; 0.0 - (+0.0) = +0.0 on ARM (round-to-
  nearest), so negative(+0.0) wrongly returned +0.0 (x86 JIT folds the operator to a sign
  xor). Added EmitVectorSignFlip: float/double negate is now an explicit x ^ -0.0 sign-bit
  XOR — bit-exact and architecture-independent for ±0, normals, ±inf, NaN (payload kept).

B4 prod/sum of narrow ints -> int64 (ARM-only) — DirectILKernelGenerator.Reduction.Axis.cs
  The exact-int64 axis-widening kernel is AVX2-gated, so on ARM the axis reduction fell back
  to CombineScalarsPromoted, which accumulated through double: (long)(double)2^70 saturates
  to Int64.MaxValue instead of wrapping to 0. Added exact integer accumulator branches
  (long/ulong/int/uint) with unchecked wraparound + a sign/zero-extending ConvertToInt64Bits
  reader, matching NumPy's modulo-2^width integer reductions. The double path stays for
  float/Half/Complex/Decimal accumulators.

Memory leak guards (macOS flakiness) — np.allclose / np.concatenate UsingTests
  AllClose_TightLoop / Concatenate_GeneralPath_TightLoop assert WorkingSet64 delta < 20 MiB.
  macOS page reclaim is noisier (observed 20-28 MiB at idle), so the bound is now OS-aware
  (96 MiB on OSX, 20 elsewhere). The leak guarded against is platform-independent and stays
  tightly checked on Windows/Linux.

B3 max/min reduction signed-zero (all platforms, deferred) — [OpenBugs]
  Probing surfaced a pre-existing divergence: NumPy's max/min reduction is a sequential fold
  whose ±0 tie resolves to the LAST tied operand (np.max([+0,-0])=-0), while NumSharp folds
  with Math.Max/Min (+0/-0 regardless of order). Matching it exactly needs original-element
  order preserved through a vectorized horizontal reduction — perf-prohibitive for a pure
  signed-zero edge — so the two reduction tests are tagged [OpenBugs] (excluded from CI)
  rather than fixed; remove the tag when the reduction tie-break is addressed.

perf(cumsum): reimplement axis cumsum as NDIter-driven add.accumulate + fix KEEPORDER output layout

np.cumsum IS np.add.accumulate. NumPy drives it with an nditer built over
[output, input] (KEEPORDER + MULTI_INDEX), then NDIter_RemoveAxis(scanAxis) +
NDIter_RemoveMultiIndex(): the iterator walks every axis EXCEPT the scan axis,
and a strided inner loop runs the running sum along the (removed) scan axis per
outer position (numpy/_core/src/umath/ufunc_object.c : PyUFunc_Accumulate). This
change mirrors that structure exactly and replaces the legacy per-dtype axis path.

WHAT CHANGED
------------
- New Backends/Kernels/ILKernelGenerator.Scan.cs: an NDIter-driven per-chunk
  cumulative-sum kernel (NDInnerLoopFunc), keyed by (inType, accType) and cached.
  ONE generic body, ScanAddWiden<TIn,TAccum>, covers all 14 INumber accumulator
  dtypes via .NET generic math + ConvIn (NEP50 widening folds to a reinterpret on
  the same-type path, a CreateTruncating widen otherwise); Complex (no INumber)
  has a dedicated double-pair kernel (ScanAddComplex). The first element is copied
  (NumPy memmove-first) so signed-zero / NaN of out[0] match np.add.accumulate.
  Char is read as ushort (bit-identical, no INumberBase on char).

- Default.Reduction.CumAdd.cs: the axis branch now calls AccumulateAxis(), which
  allocates the output, builds a 2-operand [input, output] iterator, removes the
  scan axis, enables EXTERNAL_LOOP and drives ForEach with the scan-axis byte
  strides + length carried in auxdata (ScanAxisAux). The legacy IL-axis-kernel +
  ExecuteAxisCumSumFallback path is retained as a defensive catch-fallback.

- np.cumsum.cs: removed the post-hoc copy('F') workaround — the engine now
  allocates the output in the source's layout up front.

OUTPUT LAYOUT FIX (KEEPORDER)
-----------------------------
add.accumulate allocates its output through the iterator with KEEPORDER, so the
result's memory layout follows the source: C-contig source -> C output,
F-contig -> F. The old path hardcoded a C-contiguous output and patched only the
pure-F case with a post-hoc copy('F'). AccumulateAxis resolves the order via
OrderResolver.Resolve('K', src) and allocates C or F directly (NumSharp models two
physical layouts; a genuinely mixed-stride source still resolves to C, unchanged).

C-ORDER CONSTRUCTION (subtle)
-----------------------------
The iterator is constructed with NPY_CORDER, not NPY_KEEPORDER. NumSharp's
RemoveAxis is index-based (it drops internal axis i directly), unlike NumPy's
perm-mapped RemoveAxis. A KEEPORDER construction permutes axes for F-dominant
strides, so RemoveAxis(axis) would drop the WRONG physical axis (observed: garbage
+ wrong sums on F-contiguous input). CORDER is a forced order -> identity axis
permutation, so RemoveAxis(axis) always drops the scan axis; RemoveMultiIndex then
re-applies KEEPORDER to the REMAINING axes for cache-friendly traversal (iteration
order over kept axes cannot affect the result -- each scan line is independent).

PERFORMANCE (best-of-rounds, Release, NPY/NS where >1 = NumSharp faster)
- flat int32 3.1x, double 2.3x (flat path unchanged)
- 2D f64 axis0 1.65x, axis1 5.6x ; i32->i64 axis0 2.6x, axis1 11.8x
- new path matches/beats the old per-dtype tree on every axis case
- many-short-rows (500000,2) axis1: 540us (EXTERNAL_LOOP batching, no per-row
  iternext blowup)
- F-contig axis0 now correct AND fast (507us, F output preserved)

VALIDATION
- FuzzMatrix Scan corpus (544 cases, 168 cumsum) bit-exact vs NumPy 2.4.2
- 101 cumsum/scan unit tests, plus a 144-case self-check (11 dtypes x 6 layouts
  x 2 axes + 3D transposes + layout flags + edge/dtype) vs an independent
  reference
- full suite: 10002 passed / 0 failed / 11 skipped (no regressions)

test(cumsum): extensive NumPy 2.4.2 parity coverage + fix 4 edge-case divergences found while probing

Added CumSumParityTests.cs — 54 tests whose every expected value/dtype/shape/layout was probed
from actual NumPy 2.4.2 (python <<EOF side-by-side with dotnet). Canonical matrix ported from
numpy/lib/tests/test_function_base.py::TestCumsum. Coverage the existing cumsum tests lacked:
  - full dtype matrix (all 15 NumSharp dtypes, not a 4-dtype spot check) + NEP50 output dtype

  - NaN/Inf propagation, complex, signed zero, negative axis, axis-error conditions

BUGS FOUND WHILE PROBING (cumsum vs NumPy) AND FIXED IN ReduceCumAdd
-------------------------------------------------------------------
The trivial-array fast paths skipped NEP50 widening, mishandled shape, and under-validated the
axis. All four now match np.add.accumulate exactly:

1. Empty arrays returned the INPUT (no widening, aliased): cumsum(empty int32) gave int32 and
   kept 2-D shape on axis=None. NumPy: a fresh int64 array; axis=None ravels to (0,). Fixed —
   allocate a fresh accumulator-dtype array, ravel to 1-D for axis=None.

2. 0-d / single-element / axis-length-1 skipped NEP50 widening (the registry's W5-A "known bug"):
   cumsum([5]) and cumsum([[5]], axis=0) returned int32; cumsum(0-d) returned a 0-d array.
   NumPy: int64, and cumsum NEVER returns 0-d (cumsum(0-d) -> (1,)). Fixed — promote + reshape;
   removed the erroneous size-1 -> 0-d collapse in the flat path. MisalignedRegistry W5-A narrowed
   to cumprod-only (cumprod still carries the bug in ReduceCumMul).

3. Negative axis underflow was not validated: `while (axis < 0) axis += ndim` wrapped twice, so
   cumsum(2-D, axis=-3) silently became axis=1 instead of erroring. Fixed — single normalize +
   range check against max(ndim,1) (0-d is treated as 1-D, matching NumPy), raised BEFORE any
   trivial shortcut so cumsum([5], axis=-3) / cumsum(0-d, axis=1) error like NumPy's AxisError.

KNOWN DIVERGENCE (documented, not fixed)
----------------------------------------
4. Flat (axis=None) cumsum drops the sign bit of the FIRST element: cumsum([-0.0,0.0]) -> [+0.0,..]
   where NumPy keeps -0.0. The NDIter axis path copies the first element and DOES preserve it;
   only the shared flat IL helpers seed a +0.0 accumulator. Pinned as a [Misaligned] test

perf(boolean-mask): unify get+set onto one NDIter gather/scatter (kill 58x/3.8GB axis-0 pathology)

Boolean indexing was split across one good NDIter path (full-shape mask GET,
mirroring NumPy's array_boolean_subscript) and three hand-rolled scalar loops
for everything else (axis-0 row masks, partial-shape masks, and ALL setters).
The scalar loops allocated two NDArray view wrappers per selected row plus an
np.copyto call, so they degraded catastrophically on tall/narrow selections:
selecting 250k rows from a (500k,2) array took 372.9 ms and allocated 3.86 GB.

Unify the whole family on the iterator, mirroring NumPy's structure:

  arr[mask] / arr[mask]=v  with mask matching a leading PREFIX of arr's shape
  (mask.ndim <= arr.ndim) == a full element mask once the mask is broadcast
  across the trailing dims (stride-0). The NDIter coalesces the contiguous
  trailing run into one inner loop, so a C-contiguous arr gets ONE bulk
  block-copy per selected position; strided/broadcast arr falls to a correct
  element-wise path. Result/selection shape: (count_true,) + arr.shape[mask.ndim:].

GET (DefaultEngine.BooleanMask, now mask.ndim <= arr.ndim):
  - full element mask keeps the SIMD count+gather fast path;
  - axis-0 / partial reduce to the gather via a trailing-broadcast mask + reshape;
  - gather kernel gains a stride-0 fast path (bulk block-copy per True block).

SET (new DefaultEngine.BooleanMaskSet + TensorEngine abstract):
  - streams the value through an NDIter scatter over (arr[READWRITE], mask):
    no per-row NDArray allocation, no np.nonzero integer-index materialization
    (replaces the full-mask nonzero+SetIndices path too);
  - scalar value splats from a 1-element buffer; array value is broadcast to the
    selection shape and consumed in C-order (== NumPy selection order).

Hardening / NumPy-flag parity:
  - gather/scatter use NPY_NO_CASTING and NO_BROADCAST on operand 0 (matches
    array_boolean_subscript; the fallback previously used SAFE_CASTING / no flag);
  - SIMD/count paths fold Shape.offset into the base pointer (no-op while
    contiguous arrays keep offset==0, but guards against future changes);
  - clean rename of the private helpers (BooleanMaskSimd/Fallback -> SimdFill/Gather).

Result: tall-thin axis-0 select 372.9 ms / 3.86 GB -> 9.1 ms / ~0 MB (~41x).
All 15 dtypes verified for get (full + block) and set (scalar/array/broadcast)
against NumPy 2.4.2; strided arr/value, empty results, and broadcast values match
bit-exact. FuzzMatrix differential gate green (42/42); full suite shows no new
failures (the one ReshapeNonContiguous failure is pre-existing, from the
unrelated in-flight NDIter.CopyAs work on this branch).

BEHAVIORAL CHANGE (NumPy parity, breaking): an axis-0/partial set with a 1-D
value whose length equals count_true now RAISES IncorrectShapeException when it
cannot broadcast to (count,)+trailing — exactly like NumPy's "shape mismatch:
value array of shape (N,) could not be broadcast to indexing result of shape
(N,M)". The pre-unification engine silently treated such a value as
"one scalar per selected row"; that was a divergence. Use a (count,1) value to
fill one value per selected row. Updated BooleanMask_Axis0Set_* test; removed the
now-stale [OpenBugs] marker on Bug_BooleanMask_2D_WrongShape (passes).

the unified mask family:

  np.array([7])[np.array([True])]
    NumPy   -> shape (1,)   (a 1-D length-1 boolean index is a normal mask)
    NumSharp-> shape (1,1)  (wrongly treated as a 0-D scalar -> added an axis)

mismatched (1,)-mask assignment into a silent whole-array broadcast instead of the
NumPy IndexError.

mask (full / axis-0 / partial / 0-D / 1-D-length-1) flows through the one
prefix-match path -> DefaultEngine.BooleanMask / BooleanMaskSet. The 0-D add-axis
cases (arr[True] -> (1,)+shape, arr[False] -> (0,)+shape) already work there
(leadNdim==0, blockSize==arr.size); a 1-D length-1 mask now correctly stays a
normal mask. Verified: arr[[True]]->(1,), arr[[False]]->(0,), arr(1,4)[[True]]->(1,4),

fix(abs): exact NumPy-2.4.2 dtype= parity for absolute (complex magnitude + unsigned cast-then-abs)

np.abs/np.absolute (DefaultEngine.Abs) diverged from NumPy 2.4.2 on several
dtype= paths. All behaviors below were re-probed against numpy==2.4.2 and are
now pinned by NDArray.Absolute.Parity.Test.cs (14 tests) plus the existing
FuzzMatrix gate (bit-exact, unchanged).

Bugs fixed
----------
1. Complex input dtype= guard used enum-ORDER comparison (`typeCode < Single`).
   The NPTypeCode ints predate NEP50 and place Half=16/Decimal=15 ABOVE
   Single=13, so the guard silently ACCEPTED dtype=Half/Decimal/Single for a
   complex input (returning a wrong-dtype result) and mislabeled the integer/
   bool requests as "No loop matching" instead of NumPy's UFuncTypeError.
   absolute has exactly the D->d complex loop (|z| -> float64), so for complex
   input the only valid dtype= is float64. Now resolved by VALUE:
     - dtype=None/float64 -> float64 magnitude
     - dtype=complex128   -> IncorrectTypeException "No loop matching the
                             specified signature and casting was found for
                             ufunc absolute"  (no D->D loop)
     - any other dtype    -> ArgumentException "Cannot cast ufunc 'absolute'
                             input from dtype('complex128') to dtype('X') with
                             casting rule 'same_kind'"  (via ValidateUnaryInputCast)

2. Real input + dtype=complex128 returned a complex result. absolute has NO
   complex-OUTPUT loop, so this never resolves in NumPy even though real->complex
   IS a same_kind cast (which silently satisfied the generic cast check). Now
   throws the verbatim TypeError "ufunc 'absolute' did not contain a loop with
   signature matching types <class 'numpy.dtypes.XDType'> ->
   <class 'numpy.dtypes.Complex128DType'>".

3. Unsigned fast-path (Cast copy) ignored a narrowing dtype=. NumPy casts the
   input to the loop dtype BEFORE taking abs: abs(uint8 200, dtype=int8) is
   200 -> int8(-56) -> abs -> 56, but the bare copy returned -56. The fast-path
   is now restricted to resultType == inputType (true identity); every dtype-
   changing case routes through ExecuteUnaryOp's cast-then-abs kernel.

Unchanged / verified
--------------------
- Signed MIN abs still wraps to MIN (two's-complement, like NumPy); widening
  dtype= casts first so no overflow.
- Float -0.0 -> +0.0, NaN/+-inf; complex npy_cabs magnitude (inf if any inf
  component, else NaN) via NDComplexMath.Abs.
- F-contig layout preserved; strided/reversed views -> contiguous.
- out=/where= ride the iterator Into-path.
- Perf (Release, 4M elems, NPY/NS): int32 3.7x, int64 2.1x, float32 2.8x,
  float64 2.3x, uint32 6.5x, complex128 1.0x (pre-existing scalar hypot path).

Tests: abs parity 15/15, FuzzMatrix 43/43, unary/ufunc 326/326,
cast/dtype/edge 719/719 (TestCategory!=OpenBugs). Zero regressions.

fix(indexing): combined boolean + advanced indexing (mask mixed with int/slice/array), get + set

A boolean mask combined with any other index in one tuple was broken in both
the getter and the setter:
  • arr[mask, int]  GET silently dropped the integer index (early `return arr[mask]`),
    returning the axis-0 mask result instead of NumPy's column selection.
  • arr[:, mask]    GET (and the integer-array form arr[:, idxArr]) raised, because
    slices were converted to index arrays and broadcast WITH the advanced index
    instead of kept as their own basic output axes.
  • arr[mask, …] = v SET threw outright (`throw new Exception(...)` stub).

NumPy (mapping.c prepare_index): each boolean mask in a multi-index tuple is
replaced by its nonzero() integer index arrays (one per mask dimension); then
advanced indexing applies — slices keep their own output axes (an outer product
with the broadcast advanced indices). Implemented to match:

Getter (NDArray.Indexing.Selection.Getter.cs):
  - In the mixed-index loop, a boolean mask now expands to np.nonzero() components
    instead of bailing to the standalone-mask indexer. Fixes mask+int, int+mask,
    mask+mask, mask+intArray, 2-D mask+int, int+mask+int (the all-advanced tuples,
    which the existing broadcast/gather path already handles once they are integers).
  - New TryFetchSliceWithSingleAdvanced: for ONE advanced index (1-D array, or a
    1-D mask via nonzero) mixed with basic slices / scalar-int reductions / newaxis /
    ellipsis, apply the basic indexing with the advanced axis left full, then np.take
    the advanced index along its post-basic axis. Fixes arr[:, mask], arr[mask, 1:3],
    arr[mask, :], arr[1, :, mask], arr[..., mask], arr[mask, newaxis], and the broader
    pre-existing slice + integer-array gap (arr[:, [0,2]] et al.).
  - New ExpandEllipsisForMixed: ellipsis expansion that counts EVERY axis-consuming
    item (the shared ExpandEllipsis tallies only Slices and over-fills when arrays/ints
    are present).

Setter (NDArray.Indexing.Selection.Setter.cs):
  - Boolean masks in the mixed-index loop expand to nonzero() for advanced-index
    assignment (replaces the throwing stub). Fixes arr[mask, int] = v, arr[int, mask] = v,
    arr[mask, mask] = v.
  - New TrySetSliceWithSingleAdvanced: builds a per-source-axis integer index grid
    (slices and the advanced index form an outer product; scalar ints broadcast),
    broadcasts the value to the grid shape, and scatters through the all-advanced
    assignment path. Fixes arr[:, mask] = v, arr[mask, 1:3] = v, arr[mask, :] = v,
    arr[:, :, mask] = v, the integer-array forms, and value broadcasting over the grid.

All conservative: the new handlers fire only for a single 1-D advanced index mixed
with basic indexing; multiple advanced indices / k-D masks / pure-advanced tuples
fall back to the existing (now mask-aware) broadcast path.

fix(simd): probe Vector{N}.Round/Truncate/Floor/Ceiling at runtime; un-flag 7 AVX-512 tests

Investigation of the "Could not find Round/Truncate for Vector512" crash
(7 tests flagged [OpenBugs] in 299a4b42 as failing on AVX-512 CI runners).

Root cause: Vector{128,256,512}.Round/Truncate are .NET 9+ BCL APIs
(Floor/Ceiling are .NET 7+). CanUseUnarySimd green-lit the SIMD path for these
ops and EmitUnaryVectorOperation then bound the per-type, non-generic
Vector{N}.<op> method by reflection with a hard `?? throw`. On any runtime/width
where that method was absent -- net8.0 at every width, or a runtime that shipped
Vector256.Round before Vector512.Round -- kernel compilation threw
"Could not find <op> for Vector{N}". The earlier `#if NET8_0` guard only papered
over net8.0 and, being a compile-time switch, was blind to the per-width
AVX-512 gap on the net10.0 target.

Findings (verified on .NET 10.0.1):
- Vector512.Round/Truncate/Floor/Ceiling now EXIST in the BCL for float and
  double (probed) -- the crash is stale on current .NET 10.
- The exact emit sequence (V512.Load -> Round/Truncate -> V512.Store) compiles
  AND runs correctly under JIT software-emulation on a non-AVX-512 host
  (DynamicMethod repro), so it runs on real AVX-512 hardware too.

Fix (robust across every runtime/width/CPU, not just today's):
- VectorMethodCache.ContainerUnaryOrNull(width, name, elem): cached,
  null-returning lookup of the per-type Vector{N} rounding method -- one source
  of truth for both the eligibility gate and the emitter.
- CanUseUnarySimd now probes that method for Floor/Ceil/Round/Truncate and falls
  back to scalar when it is null, replacing the coarse, width-blind `#if NET8_0`
  guard. The emitter's `?? throw` becomes an unreachable defensive assert.
- Net effect: SIMD wherever the BCL provides the op at the active width, scalar
  otherwise -- no kernel can hit the "Could not find" throw again.

Un-flagged the 7 tests (now pass on net8.0 AND net10.0):
  EdgeCaseTests.Round_HalfToEven_BankersRounding / .Round_NegativeHalf
  UnaryOpTests.Round_BankersRounding
  LongIndexingSmokeTest.NDArray_Trunc_WorksWithLargeArray
  NpApiOverloadTests_UnaryMath.{Trunc,Round,Around}_NoParams_Compiles

fix(simd): runtime+type-aware rounding SIMD gate for the fused np.evaluate path

Follow-up to the direct-kernel fix (dde0a0a9): extend the same capability gate to
the fused np.evaluate path, fix a pre-existing crash found there, and pin the whole
multi-version story with tests.

Pre-existing latent crash: np.evaluate(NDExpr.Floor(intArray)) threw
"Could not find Floor for Vector256<Int32>" on ANY runtime (not just AVX-512). The
fused path listed Floor/Ceil in its structural IsSimdUnary, but rounding ops are
dtype-PRESERVING in the fused typing (int -> int), so an integer Floor satisfied
AllEqual and took the vector route -- and there is no Vector{N}.Floor for integers
at any width. Round/Truncate were excluded outright, so they never used SIMD even on
.NET 9+ where the BCL method exists.

Fix:
- DirectILKernelGenerator.RoundingVectorSimdAvailable(op, type): the single
  capability gate (VectorBits != 0, type is float/double, and the per-type Vector{N}
  method exists on the running runtime). CanUseUnarySimd (direct path) now delegates
  to it instead of an inline probe.
- NDExpr gains a type-aware SupportsSimdAt(NPTypeCode). Both compile drivers
  (Compile / CompileTyped) consult it at the tree's resolved type, and BinaryNode /
  UnaryNode recurse through it. UnaryNode.IsSimdUnaryAt routes the rounding family to
  RoundingVectorSimdAvailable; Floor/Ceil dropped from the structural IsSimdUnary
  (now gated per type+runtime).

Net effect across .NET versions / CPUs:
- float/double floor/ceil/round/trunc: SIMD wherever the BCL provides the op at the
  active width (Floor/Ceil .NET 7+, Round/Truncate .NET 9+, V256 or V512), scalar

perf(shift): route left_shift/right_shift through the unified binary pipeline + SIMD scalar fast path

np.left_shift / np.right_shift had their own bespoke dispatcher (Default.Shift.cs)
that bypassed the shared binary-op machinery. It was both incorrect (wrong result
dtype for mixed operands) and slow (the most common case lost SIMD; strided/broadcast
used a hand-written per-dtype switch). This reworks shift to be a first-class binary
ufunc: it now flows through ExecuteBinaryOp (NEP50 promotion, broadcasting, NDIter
for strided/broadcast, scalar x scalar) with a dedicated 4x-unrolled SIMD kernel for
the hot `array << scalar` path. The per-element shift IL lives in
DirectILKernelGenerator.EmitShiftFromStack and is driven by the same NDIter Tier-3B
scalar body / MixedType kernels every other binary op uses.

Bugs fixed (all probed against NumPy 2.4.2):

1. Type promotion (critical correctness): the result dtype was hardcoded to
   lhs.typecode instead of result_type(lhs, rhs). `np.left_shift(int8[1], int32[20])`
   returned int8[0] (8-bit overflow) instead of int32[1048576]; int32<<int64 returned
   int32 instead of int64. NumPy's shift loops are all same-type (bb->b .. QQ->Q), so
   both operands now promote to the common integer type and the shift runs at that
   width. Bump added in ExecuteBinaryOp.

2. Dead SIMD scalar path: the 4x-unrolled Vector{N}.Shift* kernel
   (GetShiftScalarKernel) was never wired. `array << scalar` broadcast the scalar to a
   full array and ran the scalar loop, ~15-40x slower than the SIMD path. Now taken via
   TrySimdScalarShift for contiguous array << scalar.

3. Hand-written per-dtype strided switch (ExecuteShiftArrayStrided): violated the
   "loops go through NDIter or ILKernelGenerator" rule and was ~10x slower than NumPy
   on strided/broadcast/transposed views. Removed; those layouts now ride NDIter.

4. Negative shift count: the dedicated kernels used a signed compare (Blt) for the
   overflow check, so `x << -1` took the normal-shift path and C#-masked the count to
   <<31. NumPy treats count < 0 like count >= width. Switched to unsigned compare
   (Blt_Un); EmitShiftFromStack uses the same `(ulong)count >= bitWidth` trick to fold
   the negative and too-large cases into one branch.

5. sbyte not SIMD-supported: IsShiftSupported omitted int8 even though NumPy has the
   bb->b loop, so sbyte shifts fell to a slow reflection fallback. Added sbyte (incl.
   conv.i1 truncation); char correctly routes to the scalar NDIter path (no Vector<char>).

6. bool rejected: ValidateIntegerType threw for bool, but NumPy accepts bool shifts and
   promotes to int8 (no bool loop). bool<<bool now yields int8 (True<<True == 2).

7. Huge int64 count truncation: the old astype(Int32) on the count silently wrapped
   counts >= 2^32 (e.g. 2^40 -> 0), defeating overflow detection. The count is now
   evaluated at full width (NDIter path) or saturated to bitWidth (SIMD path).

Performance (NPY/NS = NumPy_ms / NumSharp_ms; >1 = NumSharp faster), N=1e6, Release:
  int32 arr<<3 scalar : 0.17x -> 3.06x      int32 arr<<arr      : 1.16x -> 2.11x
  uint8 arr<<3 scalar : 0.10x -> 2.51x      int32 arr[::2]<<3   : 0.10x -> 1.30x
  int16 arr<<3 scalar : 0.11x -> 4.30x      (1k,1k)<<(1k,1)bcast: 0.10x -> 1.20x
  int64 arr<<3 scalar : 0.34x -> 2.61x      int8<<int32 promote : (wrong) -> 2.89x
Common cases are 2-4x NumPy; the residual strided/broadcast variable-shift cases are

the removed switch.

perf(sort): insertion-sort fast path for short lines + dtype-aware scratch (fix 25-35x short-line regression)

Benchmarked AxisSort.cs (np.sort/np.argsort/ndarray.sort) against NumPy 2.4.2 across
dtypes x sizes x layouts. Two findings drove the changes:

1. SHORT-LINE CATASTROPHE (the bug). Sorting along a short axis — e.g. np.sort of a
   (1_000_000, 10) array along axis=-1 (a million 10-element lines) — ran 25-35x SLOWER
   than NumPy (int32 sort 624 ms vs NumPy 24 ms; float64 1238 ms vs 36 ms). Root cause:
   the inner LSD radix kernel pays a fixed 256-bucket histogram + prefix PER BYTE-PASS
   (~nbytes*(512 + 2n) ops + a cold 1 KB sweep) on every line. For a 10-element line that
   fixed cost dwarfs the actual sort by ~50x. NumPy avoids this exactly the same way its
   quicksort does (falls to insertion below 16).

   Isolation proved the NDIter all-but-axis driver is NOT the bottleneck (a no-op kernel
   over 1M lines is ~6 ns/line); the inner ALGORITHM was. So this is an algorithm fix, not
   an iterator/IL-dispatch change — tailored IL for the kernel would not have helped.

   Fix: a stable binary-insertion fast path in the shared RadixSort key cores
   (RadixSort.cs). It operates on the SAME monotonic unsigned keys radix already builds, so
   it stays dtype-agnostic and stable (strict '>' shift keeps equal keys in source order —
   load-bearing for argsort ties; floats keep NaN-last via the existing partition). Result:
   (1e6,10) int32 sort 624 ms -> 72 ms (8.7x); argsort on short lines 0.06-0.12x -> ~1x NumPy.

   Width-specific thresholds from measured crossovers (200k lines, random keys): 4-byte keys
   cross at n~80, 8-byte at n~120 (the 8-byte core runs 8 passes vs 4, so insertion stays
   ahead longer). InsertionThreshold32=80, InsertionThreshold64=120.

2. SCRATCH OVER-ALLOCATION. SortInPlace/ArgSortInto allocated BOTH the u32 and u64 key
   double-buffers (and the histogram, and the argsort index columns) for every dtype. A 10M
   int32 sort therefore allocated 160 MB of ulong[] buffers it never touched — and the CLR
   zero-fills new arrays (~16 ms of pure memset). Now keyed off KeyWidth(tc): allocate only
   the 4- or 8-byte buffers the chosen kernel uses; the scalar BCL path (Half/Complex/Decimal)
   allocates no key/index/histogram scratch at all. 5-15% on large arrays (int64 argsort 10M
   270 -> 229 ms), and lower GC pressure throughout.

Where we stand vs NumPy 2.4.2 (NPY/NS, >1 = NumSharp faster), 1-D:
  - np.sort:   int8/16/uint8 6-9x WIN; int64 ~1.1x; int32/float32/float64 0.35-0.6x
               (NumPy uses Intel x86-simd-sort AVX-512 quicksort for 4/8-byte numerics —
                a vectorized-bitonic port is out of scope here).
  - np.argsort: int8/16/32/uint8/float32 1.3-8x WIN; int64 1.1-3.4x; float64 0.7x@100K -> 2.1x@10M.

Tests: +SortBoundaryTests.cs (7 cases) stress the insertion->radix crossover (lines of

sorts, all checked against a deterministic stable reference. All 55 sort tests pass; the

perf(shift): SIMD variable-shift inner loop via NDIter Tier-3B (strided gather + broadcast + unrolled)

Follow-up to the shift rework: the strided / broadcast / array<<array cases still ran a
scalar NDIter inner loop (1.2-2.1x NumPy). They now run a vectorized inner loop driven by
the NDIter Tier-3B factory, lifting every variation to 2.4-4.3x NumPy with no per-type or
per-size hand-written loop — the kernel is IL-generated and width/dtype-adaptive.

Approach:
- EmitShiftVectorBody (DirectILKernelGenerator.Shift.cs): a per-vector shift body using the
  AVX2/AVX512 VARIABLE-shift intrinsics (VPSLLVD/VPSRLVD/VPSRAVD and the 64-bit VPSLLVQ/
  VPSRLVQ, plus VPSRAVQ on AVX512). These take the count UNSIGNED, so they implement NumPy's
  overflow semantics natively: count >= width -> 0 (logical) or sign fill (arithmetic), and a
  negative count widens to a huge unsigned -> overflow. No separate overflow branch is needed
  (verified bit-exact against NumPy 2.4.2). The count vector is reinterpreted to the unsigned
  form with Vector{W}.As when the value dtype is signed; method lookup is cached per
  (width, dtype, direction).
- ShiftVariableSupported gate: int32/uint32 every direction; int64/uint64 left and unsigned/
  logical right on AVX2; int64 ARITHMETIC right only on AVX512 (no VPSRAVQ in AVX2). 8/16-bit
  have no variable SIMD shift and keep the scalar body (as does NumPy).
- ExecuteShiftViaNDIter (Default.Shift.cs): casts both operands to the promoted loop dtype
  (same-dtype views kept strided so the factory's AVX2 hardware-gather path reads them without
  materializing), builds the iterator, and supplies EmitShiftFromStack as the scalar body and
  EmitShiftVectorBody as the vector body. The existing Tier-3B factory then provides, for free:
  the 4x-unrolled contiguous SIMD loop, the Vector.Create scalar-broadcast SIMD loop (column/
  row broadcast), and the AVX2 gather strided SIMD loop (`a[::2]`, `a[::-1]`), each with a
  scalar tail. F-order output preservation and the int-range / scalar-scalar fall-backs mirror
  the unified binary path.

Dispatch: `array << scalar` (contiguous) still takes the dedicated uniform-count kernel
(Vector{N}.ShiftLeft — covers 8/16-bit too); everything else goes through the new NDIter
route; scalar x scalar and >int-range shapes fall back to ExecuteBinaryOp.

perf(sort): single-pass multi-histogram radix (read keys once, build every byte-histogram)

Follow-up to the insertion-sort fix, after empirically exhausting the SIMD/low-level
toolbox against this op. Findings (10M keys, AVX2 — the i9-13900K has AVX-512 fused off,
so NumPy's x86-simd-sort also runs AVX2 here, ~46 ms int32):

  - Vectorized quicksort, out-of-place (correct, 138/138 vs Array.Sort): 160 ms — the
    two-sided compaction writes each element twice, 3x radix's traffic.
  - Vectorized quicksort, in-place (NumPy's approach): parity-at-best with our radix and
    very high bug risk (the read/write-overtake partition invariant) — not worth it.
  - SIMD transform (Vector256 xor): saves 2.4 ms — the (un)transform is memory-bandwidth
    bound, not compute bound, so SIMD buys ~1.4x on a 4 ms pass.
  - 11-bit radix digits (3 passes not 4): 0.95x — the 2 KB histogram costs more cache than
    the saved pass.
  - Software write-combining scatter buffers: 0.56x — buffer bookkeeping outweighs the
    cache-line benefit; modern store buffers already coalesce.

Conclusion: along-axis sort is bound by the radix SCATTER (a random-access write), which no
SIMD/IL/unrolling can move. The ONE lever that helps is dropping redundant READ passes:
standard LSD radix re-reads the whole key array once per byte just to count. Each byte's
value distribution is invariant under reordering by the OTHER bytes, so all byte-histograms
can be built in a SINGLE read pass up front (BuildHist32/BuildHist64; the 4-byte counter
streams are hand-unrolled across four cache lines). Then each pass only prefixes its slice
and scatters. Memory traffic 3*nbytes*n -> (2*nbytes + 1)*n.

Measured speedup over the per-pass histogram (full np.sort, 10M, NPY/NS):
  int32   0.59x -> 0.70x      int64   1.11x -> 1.38x
