feat(manipulation): add np.rot90 (NumPy 2.x parity)

Implement np.rot90(m, k=1, axes=(0,1)) — rotate an array by 90°·k in the
plane of two axes, counterclockwise from the first axis toward the second.

Port of NumPy's numpy.rot90 (numpy/lib/_function_base_impl.py). Like NumPy
it is a PURE VIEW COMPOSITION of axis-flips + a transpose — no data moves,
so the result always shares memory with the input (and stays read-only when
the source is, e.g. a broadcast view). This makes rot90 an O(1) metadata op
regardless of array size.

Implementation (src/NumSharp.Core/Manipulation/np.rot90.cs):
  * k is reduced Python-style (((k % 4) + 4) % 4) so negative/large k wrap.
  * k==0 -> full view (Storage.Alias of the same Shape), matching m[:].
  * k==2 -> flip both axes.
  * k==1 -> transpose(flip(m, axis1), axes_list).
  * k==3 -> flip(transpose(m, axes_list), axis1).
  * A private FlipAxisView(m, axis) builds NumPy's flip(m, axis) primitive as
    a negative-stride view: negate the axis stride and advance the offset to
    that axis' last element (no copy). Empty arrays return a fresh same-shape
    array (consistent with how DefaultEngine.Transpose handles size==0), and
    a stride-0 (broadcast) axis flips to a no-op exactly as in NumPy.
  * Single dtype-agnostic path — works for all 15 NumSharp dtypes with no
    per-dtype specialization (a view op needs none).

Validation mirrors NumPy verbatim (ArgumentException as the ValueError
analogue), including the quirky check ORDER:
  * len(axes)!=2                              -> "len(axes) must be 2."
  * axes[0]==axes[1] || |axes[0]-axes[1]|==ndim -> "Axes must be different."
    (fires BEFORE the range check, so axes=(0,2) on 2-D and axes=(0,3) on 3-D
    report "different", not out-of-range; 1-D default axes and same-axis via
    mixed signs like (0,-2) are caught here too)
  * otherwise out-of-range                    -> "Axes=(a, b) out of range for
    array of ndim=N."

Validated against NumPy 2.4.2:
  * 76-case differential oracle (data + shape + writeable flag + verbatim
    error text) across 2-D/3-D/4-D, negative & large k, negative/reversed
    axes, strided/transposed/broadcast/empty inputs — all match.
  * All 15 dtypes preserve dtype and rotate identically; view write-through
    reaches the parent for every k; broadcast input yields a read-only result.
  * Benchmarks (Release): NumSharp 1.3-1.6 us/call vs NumPy 3.1-4.2 us/call =
    2.2x-2.6x faster (NPY/NS), well past the 1.5x bar; constant in array size.

Tests:

    shapes, k-modulo, axes, view semantics, read-only broadcast, all-dtype
    preservation, empties, and error parity), green on net8.0 and net10.0.
  * Woven into the differential-fuzz manip tier: gen_oracle.py adds rot90
    k=1/2/3 (its three distinct code paths) to gen_manip, OpRegistry.cs
    replays it, and the regenerated corpus/manip.jsonl carries 798 new

against NumPy 2.4.2 and differential-fuzzed 400/400 bit-exact.

## API (mirrors NumPy)
- np.trim_zeros(NDArray filt, string trim = "fb", int[] axis = null)  -- primary
- np.trim_zeros(NDArray filt, string trim, int axis)                    -- single-axis convenience
- trim: case-insensitive, 'f'=front / 'b'=back / "fb"|"bf"=both; validated with the
  verbatim ValueError text ("unexpected character(s) in `trim`: '...'").
- axis: null => bounding box over ALL axes; an explicit axis/list trims only those (negative
  wrap, out-of-range -> AxisOutOfRangeException ~ NumPy AxisError, repeat -> ArgumentException
  "repeated axis in `axis` argument"); an EMPTY axis list or a 0-d input returns the input
  unmodified (NumPy 'if not axis_tuple: return filt').
- Returns a VIEW (dtype & ndim preserved). All-zero / empty inputs collapse the trimmed axes
  to length 0 with the trim spec ignored, matching NumPy (start == stop == 0).

## Semantics verified against NumPy 2.4.2
1-D fb/f/b/bf/FB; all-zero -> empty; single-nonzero; 2-D/3-D/5-D bounding box; axis int /
sequence / negative / empty / out-of-range / duplicate; 0-d scalar (unmodified) and 0-d
explicit-axis (AxisError); float (-0.0 is zero, NaN/inf are non-zero); complex (0+0j zero);
bool; strided / reversed / F-contiguous / broadcast inputs; view write-through.

## Implementation -- faster algorithm than NumPy's
NumPy computes argwhere(filt).min/max(axis=0), which materializes EVERY non-zero coordinate
(K x ndim) just to take per-dim min/max. The bounding box is SEPARABLE, so instead this takes
the first/last non-zero index of a 1-D projection, touching only the trimmed axes:
  - 1-D : np.nonzero(filt)[0]                       (skip the projection)
  - N-D : np.nonzero(np.any(filt, other_axes))[0]   (reduce 'any non-zero' over the other axes)
then slices [start, stop) per trimmed axis (Slice[] -> a view). All loops run inside the
existing IL-generated nonzero/any/reduction kernels; no hand-written element loop, no per-dtype
switch. pos.size == 0 uniformly handles all-zero and empty.

## Performance (best-of, warm, -c Release; NPY/NS, >1 = NumSharp faster)
  1d f64 N=1000    3.4x    1d i32 N=1000    6.3x    1d f64 N=10M     3.6x
  1d sparse 1M     8.3x    2d 1kx1k fb       31x    2d 1kx1k axis1    67x
  3d 100^3 fb       55x    3d 100^3 axis0   361x
Minimum 3.4x across every probed variation (NumPy pays the argwhere materialization we avoid).

1-D modes, all-zero/empty, 2-D/3-D bounding box, axis int/sequence/empty, errors (invalid trim,
repeated & out-of-range axis), 0-d, float NaN/-0.0, bool, all-15-dtype coverage, view
write-through, strided/reversed inputs. FuzzMatrix differential gate remains green (0 failures).

fix(core): CloneData/flatten of an empty offset view (NumPy parity, root cause)

Root-cause fix for the empty-view defect surfaced while hardening np.rot90.
flatten() on ANY empty array that carries a non-zero offset threw
ArgumentOutOfRangeException — e.g. arr["1:,1:,1:1"].flatten() with no rot90
involved. NumPy returns an empty array (shape (0,)); NumSharp crashed.

Cause (src/NumSharp.Core/Backends/Unmanaged/UnmanagedStorage.Cloning.cs):
  An empty slice keeps its parent's offset while its own backing
  IArraySlice.Count has already collapsed to 0. CloneData's contiguous
  branch then ran InternalArray.Slice(_shape.offset, _shape.size) =
  Slice(8, 0) on a zero-length buffer, and ArraySlice<T>.Slice throws when
  start (8) > Count (0). ravel()/copy()/astype() route through NDIter.Copy
  and were unaffected; only flatten() (via CloneData) hit the raw Slice.

Fix: CloneData short-circuits _shape.size == 0 up front, returning a fresh
zero-length buffer of the dtype — an empty array clones to an empty array
regardless of layout/offset, matching NumPy's flatten/ravel/copy/astype.
This is the general fix; every op that materialises an empty offset view
benefits, not just rot90.

With the root cause fixed, the two rot90 empty-array work-arounds from the
prior commit are no longer needed and are removed (src/.../Manipulation/
np.rot90.cs):
  * k==0 goes back to the plain Storage.Alias(m.Shape) view (NumPy m[:]),
    dropping the "return a fresh array for empty" special-case.
  * FlipAxisView no longer special-cases empty; it just guards the offset
    advance for a zero-length axis (dims[axis] == 0 has no last element).
    It now returns a proper negative-stride VIEW for empty inputs too, so
    rot90 stays a pure view composition — rot90(empty, k=0/2) now shares
    memory like NumPy (k=1/3 still defer to Transpose's empty handling).

    — the general regression (flatten/ravel/copy/astype of a (3,2,0) offset
    view + a 1-D arange(10)["5:5"]).
  * rot90's Rot90_EmptySlicedOffsetView_IsFlattenable already exercises the
    rot90 side across all k.

1) np.expand_dims no-op on empty arrays (root cause of 3 bugs)
   expand_dims had `if (a.size == 0 || a.Shape.IsEmpty) return a;`. IsEmpty is
   the uninitialized-shape sentinel (hashCode==0) and is correct to pass
   through, but `a.size == 0` is a GENUINE empty array (real dims, one == 0)
   that must still gain the new axis. NumPy: expand_dims((0,3),0) -> (1,0,3);
   NumSharp returned (0,3). Shape.ExpandDimension already handles empty shapes

   overloads.

       where NumPy gives (2,3,0); now correct across 1-D/2-D/3-D empties.

       where NumPy gives (2,0); now correct.

   sibling ReduceCumAdd already did this correctly. Mirrored its empty branch:
   fresh array of the accumulator dtype, axis=None -> (0,), axis=k -> dims
   preserved, and an out-of-range axis now raises (NumPy AxisError) instead of

fix(manipulation): align np.trim_zeros overloads to NumPy's signature (int? axis primary), closing the scalar-axis gap

Signature-parity audit of the seven manipulation members merged into journey2
against NumPy 2.4.2 (inspect.signature):

  np.flip(m, axis=None)             <- flip(m, int? axis=null) [+ int[] tuple overload]   EXACT
  np.fliplr(m)                      <- fliplr(m)                                           EXACT
  np.flipud(m)                      <- flipud(m)                                           EXACT
  np.rot90(m, k=1, axes=(0,1))      <- rot90(m, int k=1, int[] axes=null)                  EXACT*
  np.permute_dims(a, axes=None)     <- permute_dims(a, int[] axes=null)                    EXACT
  np.matrix_transpose(x, /)         <- matrix_transpose(x)                                 EXACT**
  ndarray.mT (get-only property)    <- NDArray mT { get; }                                 EXACT
  np.trim_zeros(filt, trim='fb', axis=None) <- was int[]-axis canonical                    FIXED (below)

  *  axes default is null (resolves to (0,1)); C# can't default an array literal.
  ** x is positional-only in NumPy ('/'); C# has no positional-only parameters.

Parameter names, order, and defaults matched NumPy exactly for all seven. The
int-vs-int[] pairs (flip, trim_zeros) are the necessary C# modelling of NumPy's
single polymorphic `axis` (int | sequence | None) — one param can't be all three.

The one genuine defect: trim_zeros made the **int[]** overload the defaulted/
canonical one, so a scalar axis with the default trim — NumPy's common
`np.trim_zeros(filt, axis=0)` — did not compile (CS1503: int -> int[]), and it
was inconsistent with how flip is structured. Fixed by mirroring flip:

  - primary : trim_zeros(NDArray filt, string trim = "fb", int? axis = null)
              — reads exactly like NumPy's trim_zeros(filt, trim='fb', axis=None);
                delegates to the sequence overload.
  - sequence: trim_zeros(NDArray filt, string trim, int[] axis)   [trim required]
              — holds the implementation; trim is required so it can't collide with
                the primary on trim_zeros(filt) / trim_zeros(filt, "f").

C# cannot make BOTH a scalar (int?) and a sequence (int[]) overload fully
defaulted (trim_zeros(filt) would be ambiguous), so exactly one bare-axis form
must carry trim. This picks the NumPy-common scalar `axis: 0` over the rare
1-element `axis: new[]{0}` (which now takes an explicit trim). No existing caller
is affected: OpRegistry and every unit test already pass trim with int[] axes.

Verified: build clean; 34 np.trim_zeros unit tests pass; the Manip differential-
fuzz gate stays green (same body, corpus unchanged); trim_zeros(filt, axis: 0)
now compiles and runs.

feat(conversion): np.asarray_chkfinite, np.require, np.asmatrix (NumPy 2.4.2 parity)

Implements the three remaining `as*`/conversion functions from NumPy's creation
family, each verified 1-to-1 against NumPy 2.4.2 across the layout/dtype/edge-case
matrix (contiguous, C/F, strided, transposed, reversed, broadcast, empty, 0-D, all
15 dtypes). All three are pure additions — no existing code changed; full suite is
green (11480 passed, 0 failed) on net8.0 + net10.0.

── np.asarray_chkfinite(a, dtype=None, order='K') ───────────────────────────────
`asarray` then raise ValueError("array must not contain infs or NaNs") if the result
is a FLOAT-FAMILY dtype (Half/Single/Double/Complex — NumPy's typecodes['AllFloat'])
and holds any inf/NaN. Integer/bool/char/Decimal arrays skip the check (can't be
non-finite), exactly matching NumPy's `a.dtype.char in typecodes['AllFloat']` gate.
Complex is finite iff both real and imag are finite.

Perf: NumPy computes this as `np.isfinite(a).all()` — a full boolean temp plus a
second reduce pass. The naive NumSharp composition of that was 0.04–0.5x NumPy. We
instead FUSE both into one streaming pass with zero allocation
(Backends/Kernels/FiniteScan.cs):
  * NaN-poison accumulation for float/double: `x - x` is +0 for a finite value and
    NaN for ±inf/NaN, and NaN is absorbing under `+`, so `acc += (v - v)` stays +0
    while everything is finite and poisons to NaN the instant any lane is non-finite.
    One EqualsAll(acc, 0) decides the whole array — no per-vector branch, so the loop
    streams at memory bandwidth. 4 independent accumulators break the FP-add chain.
    Width-agnostic Vector<T> (one body serves f32 and f64; JIT bakes V128/V256/V512).
  * Half: no Vector<Half> arithmetic in the BCL, so scan the raw 16-bit pattern —
    ±inf/NaN ⟺ the 5 exponent bits are all set ((bits & 0x7C00) == 0x7C00), SIMD on
    Vector<ushort>.
  * Complex: a contiguous Complex[N] is 2·N interleaved doubles, so it reinterprets
    straight into the double scan.
  * Layout coverage: a dense C-/F-contiguous buffer takes the flat SIMD path; strided/
    transposed/negative-stride/broadcast views take an incremental-offset odometer that
    still SIMD-scans any contiguous inner axis. Genuinely-sparse inner strides use an
    AVX2-gather NaN-poison path; |stride|==1 (reversed) is recognized as a contiguous
    block (finiteness is order-independent) and scanned forward — no wasteful backward
    gather.
Result vs NumPy (NPY/NS, >1 = NumSharp faster, arrays pre-created both sides, Release):
  contiguous  f64 1.7x · f32 3.0-3.3x · f16 17-23x · c128 2.0-6.4x
  reversed / row-strided  1.8-3.4x
  sparse [::2]  1.17-1.23x (gather-throughput bound — NumPy hits the same wall)
Faster than NumPy on every probed variation.

── np.require(a, dtype=None, requirements=None) ─────────────────────────────────
Parses C/F/A/W/O/E requirement flags (+ NumPy's alias table), resolves an order ('A'
default, else 'C'/'F'; both ⇒ ValueError "Cannot specify both C and F order"), routes
through asarray, then makes ONE copy (in the resolved order) if any remaining
ALIGNED/WRITEABLE/OWNDATA flag is unsatisfied. No requirements ⇒ asanyarray. In
NumSharp ALIGNED is always true (managed allocations), so only WRITEABLE (broadcast
views) and OWNDATA (views) force a copy — verified to match NumPy's flag results
across 19 view/copy scenarios incl. the subtle 1-D-is-both-C-and-F and reshape/slice
OWNDATA cases. Single-string `requirements` iterate BY CHARACTER like NumPy, so "F"
is the Fortran flag, "CF" requests both (and raises), and "F_CONTIGUOUS" as one string
raises on '_' (pass a single-element array for the full alias). 'ENSUREARRAY' is
accepted and stripped (NumSharp has no ndarray subclasses to demote). The only divergence
is the invalid-token exception type (NumPy KeyError → NumSharp ValueError; both throw).

── np.asmatrix(data, dtype=None) ────────────────────────────────────────────────
Returns a 2-D VIEW (no copy) following NumPy's matrix.__array_finalize__ exactly:
0-D→(1,1), 1-D of length N→(1,N), 2-D unchanged, >2-D drops length-1 axes and must land
on 2-D else ValueError("shape too large to be a matrix."). The view is preserved for
strided/transposed/reversed inputs via stride-preserving Shape.ExpandDimension; a dtype
change casts first (a copy), then coerces. NumSharp has no `matrix` subclass (NumPy's is
pending-deprecated), so the special operators (`*`-as-matmul, `**`-as-matpow, .H, .I) are
intentionally NOT provided — only the conversion/shape semantics. Also parses matrix
strings ("1 2; 3 4"): rows split on ';', columns on commas/whitespace, brackets stripped,
integer-typed unless any element needs floating point, ragged rows ⇒ ValueError("Rows not
the same size.").

live NumPy 2.4.2 and pinned by 114 unit tests (66 new + 2 concatenate layout
regressions + existing 68 concatenate staying green).

np.block (Creation/np.block.cs) — full port of numpy/_core/shape_base.py:
- _block_check_depths_match walk with verbatim NumPy error texts:
  ValueError "List depths are mismatched. First element was at depth N..."
  / "List at arrays[i] cannot be empty"; TypeError for ITuple ("arrays[i]
  is a tuple. Only lists can be used to arrange blocks...").
- C# nesting map documented in xmldoc: object[]/NDArray[]/1-D primitive
  arrays/IList = Python list; NDArray/scalars/rank>=2 rectangular arrays =
  leaves. The walk normalizes the tree once (lists -> object[], leaves ->
  NDArray) so later passes skip re-classification.
- BOTH NumPy algorithms behind NumPy's exact threshold
  list_ndim * final_size > 2*512*512: _block_concatenate (repeated
  np.concatenate along axes -1..-(depth); intermediate level results
  disposed eagerly instead of queueing on the finalizer) and
  _block_slicing (result_type over all leaves, order = 'F' if all-F and
  not all-C, single allocation with fillZeros:false, per-leaf NDIter.Copy
  into (Ellipsis,)+slice windows).
- _atleast_nd leading-1 padding as views (expand_dims chain; empty arrays
  reshape since expand_dims early-returns them).
- Depth-0 (bare array/scalar) returns a COPY - probed; the NumPy docstring
  claims otherwise but its _block_concatenate copies.
- Differential test reproduces a mixed-dtype 2x2 block matrix bit-exactly
  against NumPy (MT19937 seed parity), and the slicing path is asserted
  equal to the nested-concatenate reference at 600x800.

np.column_stack (Creation/np.column_stack.cs):
- NumPy's array(a, ndmin=2).T for sub-2-D inputs built as ONE storage
  alias (dims (N,1)/(1,1), stride preserved so strided 1-D inputs stay
  views), then concatenate(axis=1). ndim>=2 passes through untouched
  (3-D+ concatenates along axis 1, like NumPy). Column-view wrappers are
  released post-concat.

np.concat (Creation/np.concat.cs) — NumPy 2.0 Array-API alias:
- Mirrors every concatenate overload verbatim (array form with
  axis/out/dtype/casting + the 8 tuple-arity conveniences).

np.unstack (Creation/np.unstack.cs) — NumPy 2.1:
- Returns NDArray[] of write-through VIEWS: drops the axis from
  dims/strides and advances offset by i*strides[axis] per child - no
  moveaxis call, no Slice machinery, no data movement. One shared
  dims/strides pair serves all children (Shape treats them as immutable).
- ValueError "Input array must be at least 1-d." for 0-d, AxisError-parity
  via check_and_adjust_axis, empty-axis -> empty result array, empties
  elsewhere -> fresh empty children (nothing to alias).

np.concatenate layout-vote fix (NumPy parity):
- F-contiguous output now requires allF AND NOT allC, matching
  PyArray_CreateMultiSortedStridePerm ambiguity resolution - inputs that
  are BOTH C&F (e.g. (N,1) columns from column_stack) produce C order.
  Previously NumSharp emitted F there. Probed: both-CF x2 -> C; F-only x2
  -> F; mixed F-only+both-CF -> F; C+F -> C.

np.concatenate uniform-tiny-slab interleave fast path:
- (N,1)-style concats degenerate to outerCount*nsrc dynamic-size
  Buffer.MemoryCopy calls (~4.5ns each through Memmove dispatch; 2M
  8-byte copies for two 1M columns). When every per-outer slab is the
  same 1/2/4/8/16 bytes, a constant-size load/store interleave loop runs
  ~10-20x faster (~0.2ns/copy). Applies at any outerCount (no setup
  beyond the O(nsrc) uniformity check); works for both C- and F-path
  addressing since it mirrors the existing slab accumulation.

UnmanagedStorage.GetData<T>() window fix (latent house bug, surfaced by
unstack, also affected np.split):
- Contiguity is offset-independent, so a CONTIGUOUS view at a non-zero
  offset (np.split/np.unstack children) previously returned the WHOLE
  backing buffer from Data<T>()/GetData<T>() - np.split(np.arange(6),3)[1]
  .Data<int>() yielded all 6 elements. Now narrows to the shape's
  [offset, offset+size) window first (zero-copy ArraySlice window, still
  writes through), and the cross-dtype cast path casts only the window.

test(view): pin the WRITEABLE (source × op) matrix as living documentation

Adds WriteabilityMatrixTests — a 27-op matrix over a writeable owned source and a read-only
broadcast source, asserting Shape.IsWriteable against NumPy 2.4.2's flags['WRITEABLE'] for
every (source, op) pair, so the propagation rules established while hardening mmap can't
silently regress. Encodes the full rule set:

  - a VIEW inherits its source's writeability (slice/index/reshape/ravel/T/swapaxes/moveaxis/
    expand_dims/view-of-view read-only off a read-only source);
  - reshape/ravel/flatten off a broadcast COPY (non-contiguous → writeable), off a contiguous
    source are views (the contiguous read-only case is covered in NpyMemmapTests);
  - copies / computed results (copy/astype/fancy/mask/arithmetic) are always writeable;
  - diagonal is a read-only view even off a writeable source (NumPy parity, pinned explicitly);
  - writing through a read-only view throws (flag is enforced, not cosmetic).

Documented_Divergences pins the two intentional, memory-safe differences from NumPy (not
propagation bugs — NumSharp returns a different kind of object and the flag is correct for it):
a[i,j] is a writeable 0-d view (NumPy: immutable scalar) and squeeze-of-broadcast is a
writeable copy (NumPy: read-only view). If either is ever "fixed" to match NumPy, this test
flags it for a conscious update.

fix(math): np.convolve accumulates per NumPy *_dot dtype contract (complex imag was DROPPED)

The single generic ConvolveFullTyped<T> accumulated EVERY dtype in a double:
Converts.ToDouble(boxed element) * ... -> double sum -> cast back to T.

For Complex that is catastrophic: ToDouble collapses the complex element and
(Complex)sum reconstructs with imag=0 — np.convolve(complex128) silently
DISCARDED THE ENTIRE IMAGINARY DIMENSION. It stayed hidden because (a) the
fuzz corpus complex pools happen to have imag=0 and (b) the MisalignedRegistry
complex-binary blanket excused any complex value divergence. Dismantling the
blanket (WS-BUGS B2) exposed it via the NaN cells: NumPy NaN*(x+0j) = NaN+NaNj,
NumSharp produced NaN+0j (convolve/84-86 in groupa.jsonl).

Also wrong, latently: int64/uint64/decimal accumulated through double (rounds
above 2^53 / loses decimal precision instead of NumPy modular wrap), and the
raw Address walk ignored Shape.offset/strides for view inputs (same family as
the W9-B repeat bug; corpus operands are all contiguous so ungated).

Rewritten to mirror NumPy correlate inner loops (*_dot, arraytypes.c.src):
  - Complex: component sums in double, naive complex product (CDOUBLE_dot) —
    NaN propagates into BOTH components; imag computed correctly.
  - All integers + Char: ONE IBinaryInteger<T> kernel, ulong CreateTruncating
    multiply-accumulate + truncate — bit-identical to native-width wrap at any
    width (mod-2^N ring hom), so NumPy platform npy_long width is moot.
    Probed: np.convolve(i64 2^40-vec, self) wraps to 0 — now matched.
  - Half: float products accumulated in float, one final round (HALF_dot).
  - Single: float32 accumulation (FLOAT_dot; the CBLAS sdot path is f32 too).
  - Boolean: OR-of-ANDs with early exit (BOOL_dot) — bool convolve previously
    threw NotSupportedException; probed np.convolve(bool,bool) -> bool.
  - Decimal (no NumPy analog): decimal accumulation, full 28-digit precision.
  - Double: unchanged double accumulation.
  - Sliced/strided/broadcast inputs are materialized (.copy()) before the raw
    pointer walk since Address does not include Shape.offset.

fix(indexing): R3 — OOB heap write in the boolean-mask gather/scatter on an EMPTY trailing block

Fixes the long-standing "R3" memory-safety bug that made the full-corpus `Index_Random`
gate crash the test host, and un-marks it as a live CI gate.

## Root cause

`DefaultEngine.BooleanMask` / `BooleanMaskSet` guarded `trueCount == 0` but never guarded an
EMPTY TRAILING BLOCK. With `blockSize = prod(arr.shape[mask.ndim:]) == 0` the selection
`(trueCount,)+trailing` is empty, yet:

  * `BooleanMask` allocated `new Shape(trueCount * blockSize)` == a ZERO-length result and
    then ran `BooleanMaskGather` into it;
  * `BooleanMaskSet` fell through to `BooleanMaskScatter`, which wrote into arr's ZERO-length
    buffer.

Either way an 8-byte element was written one slot past a 0-length allocation, clobbering the
adjacent CRT-heap chunk header. The process only died later, at a GC/finalizer walking the
corrupted heap — a silent exit 127 with no managed stack, which is why it read as a
"teardown" bug.

Two corpus cases reach it (both perfectly valid in NumPy):
  * `get/ANR/rand/2556` — `A[::-1][mask(3,), 6:-4]`; the slice empties the last axis, so the
    mask runs against a (3,0) array. NumPy returns (3,0).
  * `set/E03/rand/7171` — `E03[np.array(True)] = -7` on an empty (0,3) array. NumPy no-ops.

## Why it resisted every instrument

The overrun is 8 bytes into the immediately-following heap metadata, so ANY tool that changes
allocation layout hid it: guard pages / GCStress / HeapVerify relocate or zero the buffer, and
attaching a debugger switches on the Windows debug heap, whose per-allocation PADDING absorbs
the write outright (the corpus ran clean under `procdump -g`). It was finally caught with a
canary red-zone in `SizeBucketedBufferPool.Take/Return` — allocate `bytes+32`, fill the tail
with a known pattern, sweep every live buffer on each Take/Return. That both DETECTED the
overrun (`bufBytes=0, pastByte=0`) and neutralised it, so the run completed and named the
corrupting case; replaying that case alone under an empty-buffer guard page then faulted AT
the write with a full managed stack (`BooleanMaskGatherKernel.Execute`).

## Fixes

* `Default.BooleanMask.cs`
  - `BooleanMask`: `blockSize == 0` returns the correctly-shaped empty result, skipping the
    gather entirely.
  - `BooleanMaskSet`: `blockSize == 0` joins `trueCount == 0` as an empty selection — it still
    validates that the value broadcasts to the (empty) indexing-result shape (NumPy raises
    ValueError for a non-broadcastable non-scalar), then no-ops.

* `UnmanagedStorage.SetData` — a SECOND, unrelated pre-existing bug the crash had been hiding
  (the truncated run never reached those cases). When the value AND the target are BOTH empty
  the code returned as a no-op WITHOUT checking broadcast compatibility, so `E03[()] = (0,)`
  silently no-opped where NumPy raises `could not broadcast input array from shape (0,) into
  shape (0,3)`. Probed against NumPy 2.4.2: (0,), (0,0) and (2,0) into (0,3) all raise, while
  (0,3), (1,3), (3,), (0,1) and () are genuine no-ops. 9 corpus cases.

* Getter/Setter offset loops — defence in depth: the computed buffer offset was only
  upper-bounded (`> largestOffset`), so a NEGATIVE offset passed the check and would read/write
  BEFORE the buffer. Both loops now bound it at zero too, matching the block-copy guards.

## Gate

* `Index_Random`: `[OpenBugs]` removed — 10 000/10 000 cases, 0 divergences.
* `FuzzMatrix`: 91/91 to completion, 5/5 consecutive runs (was 65 + host crash, truncated).
* Full CI-style suite: 11 440 passed / 0 failed.
* Regression pins: `R3_*` cases (5 GET + 2 SET) in `Indexing.CombinatorialParity.MatrixTests`
  — empty-trailing-block mask on a reversed view, a partial mask, a 3-D base, a pre-sliced
  base, and the 0-d-bool get/set on an empty array.

Docs updated: the handover's R3 entry (root cause + how it was caught), its status line and R4
checklist, and the COMPLETENESS_PLAN note that `Index_Random` is best-effort only.

test: delete the WorkingSet64 leak-test family — it fails on correct code and passes on broken code

CI on master (8ac95cb7) failed Ubuntu / net10.0 with

    AllClose_TightLoop_DoesNotLeakWorkingSet
    Expected value to be less than 20L, but found 39L

while Windows and macOS passed the same commit, and Ubuntu passes it in
isolation. 11,685 tests passed; this one blocked the release jobs.

It is not a threshold that needs raising. It is the twelfth instance of a
test shape this repo has already convicted once (0077063f, convolve), and
the diagnosis there holds for all of them.

WHY THE PROBE CANNOT WORK
-------------------------
Every one of these tests runs a tight loop of some operation and asserts
that Process.WorkingSet64 grew by less than 20-30 MiB, claiming to guard a
`using` on an intermediate buffer.

1. It passes with the leak present. Running the allclose loop with the
   `using` on the np.isclose intermediate REMOVED — the exact defect the
   test names — measured, against its own 20 MiB limit:

       trial 0   1   2   3   4
       fixed     0   0   0   0   0  MiB
       broken    3   0   0   0  -7  MiB

   It never tripped once, and on trial 4 the BROKEN code scored 7 MiB
   better than the fixed code. The reading is uncorrelated with the
   invariant. A negative delta is not a leak measurement.

2. It fails with the code correct — that is this CI run.

3. Several could never trip at all, by arithmetic. eye's `flat` is a view
   wrapper (~100 B x 1000 iterations vs a 20 MiB limit). tile's own comment
   comes to ~10 MiB against a 30 MiB limit. flatten's own comment concedes
   the buffer "is kept alive by the returned flat anyway". convolve's was
   1.7 MiB against 20 MiB.

4. WorkingSet64 is the wrong instrument: it is OS-level RSS for the whole
   process, shared with the other ~11,700 tests. Windows trims it — all ten
   loops measure 0 MiB locally, which is why the family looked green for
   years — while Linux does not return freed pages on GC.Collect, so
   ordinary allocator churn reads as permanent growth. That is the entire
   Windows/Ubuntu split, and it is a property of the allocator, not of
   NumSharp.

WHAT REPLACES THEM
------------------
13 working-set assertions across 12 files are gone. The `using`s they named
are correct and untouched — src/ is not modified by this commit.

Under-disposal is simply not observable from a runtime probe at these
sizes, so it rests on review. OVER-disposal is the hazard the `using`
refactor can actually introduce — if an "intermediate" turns out to alias a
caller's array, as np.asanyarray returns its input unchanged, then `using`
frees memory still in use — and that IS deterministically observable
through the ARC refcount.

LeakGuards.StillUsable(array) is that assertion: IsDisposed catches the
wrapper being disposed, IsReleased catches the refcount hitting zero
underneath a live wrapper, and a read-back proves the memory still holds
the right bytes. Measured, the probe flips exactly when it should:

    live array         IsDisposed=False  IsReleased=False   -> passes
    disposed array     IsDisposed=True   IsReleased=True    -> fails
    view of a disposed parent            IsReleased=False   -> passes (ARC held)
    buffer after all refs dropped        IsReleased=True    -> fails

Each site got the assertion its own code path makes possible, chosen so it
can fail: eye asserts the result outlives the `flat` view that writes its
diagonal; concatenate that the output outlives its per-source dstSlices;
shuffle that in-place swap temps do not release the array being shuffled
(two passes back to back, so a released buffer is a write-after-free);
argmax that two reductions over one source both read correctly; contains
folds into the existing PreservesCallerInput check; ArcLifecycle's 10k
churn test now asserts IsReleased per cycle — exact, and it fails on the
first missed release rather than reporting an allocator's retention policy.

VERIFIED TO HAVE TEETH
----------------------
Mutation test: adding `a.Dispose()` to DefaultEngine.AllClose, modelling an
intermediate that aliases an operand, fails both new allclose tests:

    Failed AllClose_DoesNotDisposeItsOperands
      Expected array.IsDisposed to be False because the array must survive
      the call - np.isclose's result must not alias operand a, but found True.
    Failed AllClose_Broadcast_DoesNotDisposeItsOperands

The mutation is reverted; this is exactly what the working-set test could
not do.

Suite (CI filter, both TFMs): 11,749 passed / 0 failed / 11 skipped.

test(lifetime): sweep the library for buffer-lifetime defects — 16 deferred releases found

Follows the deletion of the WorkingSet64 family (40f0ac98). Those tests named a
real defect and could not measure it. This is the instrument that can, applied
across 110 operations.

TWO DEFECTS, TWO INSTRUMENTS
----------------------------
The `using`-on-intermediate refactors can go wrong in both directions:

  under-disposal  the intermediate is left to the finalizer. Not unbounded -
                  ~Disposer() frees it eventually - so it is a latency and
                  peak-footprint defect, not a leak. Which is exactly why a
                  memory-growth probe cannot see it.

  over-disposal   the "intermediate" aliases a caller's array (np.asanyarray
                  returns its input; a slice is a view) and `using` frees memory
                  still in use. Nothing throws: the array stays reachable and
                  correctly shaped, over freed pages.

BufferReleaseSweepTests measures the first, OverDisposeSweepTests the second.

THE INSTRUMENT
--------------
SizeBucketedBufferPool already counts every acquisition and release exactly, at
no added cost:

    acquisitions = Hits + Misses + ZeroedAllocs
    releases     = Returns + ReturnsFreed

Run an op N times disposing its result, no GC in the window; whatever is still
outstanding was left for the finalizer. Clean ops measure a deficit of PRECISELY
zero at every N - this is an exact instrument, not a statistical one.

Two calibration mistakes were made and corrected; both are recorded in the code
because either one silently inverts the verdict:

1. SAMPLE BELOW THE GC KNEE. deficit(N) = rate*N minus whatever the GC finalized
   mid-loop, so it is linear only until the GC first intervenes:

       N        5   10   20   40   80  160  320  640
       allclose 10  20   40   80  160  142  104   24   <- bends at ~80
       control   0   0    0    0    0    0    0    0

   The first draft sampled N=20 vs N=200, straddling that knee, and reported
   np.allclose as clean in one process and 2/call in another. The plateau reads
   as innocence. Now N=10 vs N=20, far below every knee in the catalogue.

2. TAKE THE MAXIMUM, NOT THE MINIMUM. The repo's best-of-rounds rule (MinAllocated,
   benchmark timings) assumes noise only ADDS. Here it is inverted: a GC finalizing
   a stranded buffer mid-window adds a RELEASE and pushes the reading toward
   innocence. The ceiling across rounds is the estimate that cannot hide a defect.

Two sample sizes, not one, so a one-off cost (lazily built kernel, first-use
cache) cancels: the assertion is on the SLOPE, so there is no threshold to tune -
the defect is defined by scaling with the call count.

FINDINGS - 16 sites, ~95 ops clean
----------------------------------
    3/call  logical_and
    2/call  np.clip, fancy index, np.allclose, np.isclose
    1/call  convolve same, convolve valid, boolean mask, np.where 3-arg,
            np.sort, np.argsort, np.roll, np.isnan, np.isfinite,
            np.extract, np.array_equal

All 16 confirmed by discriminator: force finalizers and the outstanding count
collapses to exactly 0, proving the buffers were on the finalizer queue and not
freed through some path the counters do not observe. Stable and identical across
repeated runs.

One is diagnosed to a line - NdArray.Convolve.cs:

    using var full = ConvolveFull(a, v, retType);
    ...
    return full[$"{startIdx}:{startIdx + outLen}"].copy();

The slice is a VIEW, never disposed, holding an ARC ref to `full`, so the `using`
directly above it cannot free the buffer. Mode 'full' takes no slice and measures
0 - which is what localises the defect to the slice.

Note the irony: np.allclose is the op whose `using` the deleted working-set test
claimed to guard. That `using` is correct, and np.isclose underneath it strands 2
buffers per call - a defect that test never had the resolution to see.

These are pre-existing, not regressions. They are parked in KnownDeferred and
re-run by KnownDeferredReleases_StillDeferring under [OpenBugs] (excluded from CI
per the repo's convention), so CI is green while the debt stays visible. Fix one,
that test goes green, drop it from the list and the main sweep guards it forever.

OverDisposeSweepTests passes across all 110 operations: no use-after-free anywhere
in the swept surface.

TEETH
-----
Sweep_IsNotVacuous asserts >80 cases, that a deliberately stranded buffer registers
at >=1/call, and that a known-clean op reads ~0 - so the sweep cannot pass by
doing nothing, which is precisely how its predecessor failed.
Sweep_DetectsAnOverDisposedOperand proves StillUsable rejects a released array.

Both sweeps are [DoNotParallelize]: the pool counters are process-wide.

fix(fuzz): stop the soak asserting undefined float->int conversions — NumPy contradicts itself there

The nightly Fuzz Soak has failed on every seed since PR #620 (run 29722530598): ~950/200000 cases
"diverged" on `astype` float/complex->uint32/uint64 and on `reciprocal(uint64 0)`. None of them
were NumSharp bugs, and no implementation could have passed them.

Root cause
----------
8e44c374 widened the random fuzzer to draw `astype` and reduce kinds. The float pool it draws from
front-loads NaN/+-inf/+-1e20 on purpose, so ~100% of the new float->integer cases convert a value
C leaves UNDEFINED (NaN, +-inf, or outside the destination's range). NumPy performs exactly that C
cast, so the "expected" bytes are the host toolchain's undefined behaviour, not a NumPy contract:

    np.array([np.nan] * 8).astype(np.uint32)[0]   -> 2147483648   (gcc, vectorized loop)
    np.float64(np.nan).astype(np.uint32)          -> 0            (SAME build, scalar loop)

Windows/MSVC answers 0 at every length; glibc/gcc flips with the code path. `reciprocal` is the
same defect in a different hat: NumPy's integer loop is literally `*out = (T)(1.0 / in)`
(loops_autovec.dispatch.c.src), so `in == 0` casts +-inf back to T.

The soak regenerates its corpus on Ubuntu and replays it against NumSharp, whose cast kernels
reproduce the MSVC answer (pinned by the committed, Windows-authored astype_full corpus). Measured
over the 17 distinct shrunk repros: NumSharp matches Windows NumPy 17/17 and Linux NumPy 0/17. The
soak was comparing two compilers' undefined behaviour and billing the difference to NumSharp.

Fix
---
fuzz_random.py is the ONE tier that recomputes `expected` on whatever host it runs on, so it is the
one tier obliged to stay portable. It now repairs the operand before taking the expectation:

  * `_defuse_cast` rewrites only the elements whose conversion is undefined, drawing replacements
    from the pool's DEFINED edges — truncation/boundary coverage survives and the cell is kept
    rather than dropped, which matters because the taint rate is 100%: skipping would have deleted
    float->int astype and integer reciprocal from the random tier outright.
  * `_defuse_integer_reciprocal` nudges the zeros; every other integer yields 1/x in [-1, 1].
  * `assert_portable` re-audits the SERIALIZED bytes after generation — outside the per-case
    `except Exception` that would have swallowed an inline assert — so a regression fails
    generation loudly instead of quietly emitting unusable expectations.

Two traps met on the way, both pinned by the comments:
  * Range bounds are exact powers of two, not `iinfo`-derived: `iinfo(uint64).max` rounds to 2^64
    in float64 and would accept the single value it must reject.
  * Complex operands are repaired through `.real`. Building a complex replacement re-poisons what
    it just cleaned, because `1j * nan` is `nan + nan*j` — the product's real part is `0*nan - 1*0`.

The committed corpora are deliberately unchanged in kind: they are replayed from bytes, never
recomputed, so they keep the undefined edges and go on pinning the hand-written AVX2 cast kernels
against themselves. That is a NumSharp regression gate, not portable NumPy parity — now documented
so nobody regenerates astype_full on Linux and "fixes" NumSharp to match a third answer.

Verification
------------
  * 5 seeds x 200,000 cases, corpora generated with Linux NumPy 2.4.2 (WSL Ubuntu) and replayed
    against NumSharp on Windows — the exact cross-platform split CI hits. All green; every one of
    those seeds failed before.
  * Cross-platform expectation diff over 20,000 identical cases: astype 84 -> 0, reciprocal 15 -> 0.
    The 506 that remain (libm ULP, pairwise-summation order) are already classified by
    MisalignedRegistry — which is why the C# gate counted exactly 99 unexpected, not 605.
  * Guard teeth-tested: rejects undefined cases, accepts defined ones, boundaries exact at 2^32,
    2^64 and -0.5. All 128 src x dst x shape combinations defuse clean, and NumPy's own
    `errstate(invalid='raise', over='raise')` never fires on the repaired operands.
  * Full TestCategory=FuzzMatrix: 91/91 pass. random_smoke.jsonl regenerated at its canonical seed
    (1234/2000); 61 of 2000 lines change, every one of them an astype or reciprocal case.

Docs: Fuzz/README.md gains "Host-dependent values — the one thing the oracle must never assert";
the oracle skill's triage tree gains branch 5 ("neither side is right"), which is the branch whose
absence made this look like a NumSharp bug; regenerate.md warns that astype_full is host-sensitive.
Expand fuzz soak to fixed and random seeds

feat(iteration): np.nditer, np.ndindex, np.ndenumerate — NumPy 2.4.2 parity over NDIterRef

Ports NumPy's three iteration objects. They join the pre-existing np.broadcast and
follow its house shape: a lowercase factory returning a PascalCase nested class, each
being its OWN iterator (NumPy's `iter(x) is x`) so a second enumeration RESUMES rather
than restarting. Indices are `long` (NumPy's intp, the house rule for index-valued
output) and every step yields a FRESH index array, never a recycled buffer.

Parity evidence: 37 cases probed side-by-side against live NumPy 2.4.2 (values, dtypes,
shapes, iteration order, cursor position, verbatim error texts) — all identical. 83 unit
tests generated from that probed output, all green.

np.nditer -> np.NDIterator  (APIs/np.nditer.cs)
  The port of nditer_pywrap.c — the Python WRAPPER (argument conversion, flag-string
  parsing, property surface, iteration protocol) over the C iterator NumSharp already
  had in NDIterRef. Full signature parity: op, flags, op_flags, op_dtypes, order='K',
  casting="safe", op_axes, itershape, buffersize; all 13 global and 15 per-op flag
  strings taken from nditer_pywrap.c's converters (including NumPy's grow_inner /
  growinner alias); verbatim error texts for bad flags, bad order, bad casting,
  EXTERNAL_LOOP-with-index, zero-sized operands and no operands. Properties: nop, ndim,
  shape, itersize, operands, dtypes, value, it[i], index, multi_index, iterindex,
  iterrange, itviews, finished, has_index, has_multi_index, has_delayed_bufalloc,
  iterationneedsapi. Methods: iternext, reset, close, copy, remove_axis,
  remove_multi_index, enable_external_loop, debug_print.

  Verified against NumPy: C/F/A/K order over C-contiguous, F-contiguous, reversed and
  strided views; c_index/f_index/multi_index tracking; external_loop chunking (incl.
  buffered with buffersize); coalesced-vs-multi_index shape; broadcasting; readwrite
  write-through and buffered flush-on-close; ranged iteration; seek; copy; remove_axis;
  remove_multi_index; buffered casting.

  Also fills a gap NDIterRef leaves: an ALLOCATE operand with no op_dtypes entry throws
  in the engine, while NumPy INFERS the dtype by promoting the operands that have one.
  np.nditer([a, null]) now allocates int64 for an int64 input and
  np.nditer([int_a, float_b, null]) allocates float64 — inference placed in the wrapper,
  where NumPy puts it.

np.ndindex -> np.NDIndex  (Indexing/np.ndindex.cs)
  C-order odometer, last axis fastest. `params long[]` covers both spellings NumPy allows
  ("ints, or a single tuple of ints"); the plain int[] overload is deliberately NOT params
  or the zero-argument np.ndindex() would be ambiguous. ndindex() and an empty shape both
  yield ONE empty index (Python's product() with no iterables); a zero-length dimension
  yields nothing; a negative dimension raises "negative dimensions are not allowed" at
  CONSTRUCTION, before any index is produced.

  Deliberately NOT NDIter-backed, despite the session brief, because NumPy itself moved
  ndindex OFF nditer onto itertools.product: there are no operands to walk, only a counter.
  Matching NumPy's implementation structure is the house rule, and it measures 1.5x NumPy.

np.ndenumerate -> np.NDEnumerate  (Indexing/np.ndenumerate.cs)
  Port of NumPy's `asarray(arr).flat` + `flatiter.coords`, so the order is always LOGICAL
  C-order whatever the layout: F-contiguous, transposed, reversed, sliced and broadcast
  views all read through their own strides via Shape.TransformOffset. A 0-d array yields
  exactly one pair with an EMPTY index; an empty array yields nothing. NumSharp's
  NDArray.flat is a raveled NDArray rather than a flatiter object (no coords cursor) and
  is used as such in 136 places, so its contract is left alone and the coordinates come
  from an odometer advanced in lockstep with the flat position — which is what
  flatiter.coords is. np.ndenumerate<T> is a NumSharp extension yielding unboxed T.

NDIterRef.Detach / Borrow  (Backends/Iterators/NDIter.Detach.cs)
  NDIterRef is a ref struct and cannot live in a class field, but np.nditer is a class
  whose lifetime spans user code. Detach hands the heap NDIterState* — plus operands AND
  pending COPY_IF_OVERLAP write-backs — to the managed owner; Borrow rebuilds a non-owning
  NDIterRef per call, carrying the cached advance delegate so it is not re-resolved every
  step. The pre-existing ReleaseState/FreeState pair is not sufficient on its own: it nulls
  the state but strands _writebackOriginals on the dying ref struct, so a copied-for-overlap
  temp would never be written back. Also exposes GetInnerLoopElementStride, mirroring the
  private GetInnerLoopByteStrides in the units Shape uses.

Three traps solved along the way (documented in CLAUDE.md so they are not re-broken):
  - GetEnumerator() must NOT return `this`. foreach disposes the enumerator it obtains and
    NDIterator.Dispose frees unmanaged state, so the np.Broadcast pattern (safe only because
    Broadcast owns no unmanaged memory) would CLOSE the iterator at the end of any
    foreach/LINQ pass and make every later property read throw. A thin wrapper with a no-op
    Dispose shares the same live cursor, so observable semantics are unchanged.
  - MoveNext publishes THEN advances, matching NumPy's __next__ (`return self.value` then
    `iternext()`), which is why after consuming one element the cursor reads 1 and a copy()
    taken there continues from the SECOND element. Safe because `value` captures the
    operand's ABSOLUTE data pointer.
  - NDArray's == / != are ELEMENTWISE; operand null checks must use `is null` patterns.

Perf (NPY/NS, higher = NumSharp faster; best-of-7, Release, 100K elements):
  ndindex 1.5x, ndenumerate 3.0x, nditer+multi_index 8.4x, external_loop ~parity,
  per-element it[0] loop 0.17x.
  The iteration ENGINE is not the deficit: a bare iternext() walk of 100K elements takes
  0.59 ms against NumPy's 16.6 ms for the same loop (~28x faster). The gap is entirely the
  per-element NDArray view object (~0.95 us each), far fatter than NumPy's 0-d array.
  Profiling the construction showed new NDArray(storage, shape) re-aliases the storage
  (storage.Alias(ref shape)), so the hot 0-d path now takes the direct slice ctor — measured
  2x cheaper, 137 ms -> 98 ms on the 100K loop — while the strided external_loop path (once
  per CHUNK, not per element) keeps the storage route, which it needs because the slice ctor
  demands shape.size == slice.Count. Closing the rest means optimizing NDArray construction
  itself (engine resolution + ARC refcounting), a core-wide change rather than an nditer one.

Gate: unit tests only. These are iteration PROTOCOLS, not value-producing ops, so they have
no (dtype, shape, bytes) result for the differential-fuzz corpus to bit-compare and are
deliberately absent from gen_oracle.py / OpRegistry.cs.

design-recipes.md — new table row + three recipes:

  "NumPy OBJECT / protocol API" joins the shape table (nditer, ndindex, ndenumerate, broadcast,
  printoptions). Its recipe covers the decisions that have to be made deliberately because the
  wrong choice compiles:
    - house shape is the np.broadcast precedent — lowercase factory, PascalCase nested class, the
      factory keeping NumPy's spelling since C# forbids a nested type and a method sharing a name;
    - own-iterator semantics (`iter(x) is x`), which is observable behavior and violates what a C#
      reader assumes about IEnumerable, so it gets replicated AND documented;
    - GetEnumerator() must not return `this` when the object owns unmanaged state, because foreach
      disposes the enumerator it obtains — the failure is nasty precisely because the values still
      come out correct and only a later property read throws;
    - advance timing (Python's __next__ publishes then advances; C# MoveNext must mirror that or
      cursor-exposing members like copy()/iterindex diverge);
    - Python's arity-dependent returns collapsing to one C# shape;
    - views into live state staying live rather than being silently deep-copied;
    - no oracle tier, recorded as a decision rather than left looking like an omission.

  "Giving an engine `ref struct` a long-lived managed owner" — the Detach/Borrow bridge, with the
  audit step that matters: a release-the-pointer helper leaving companion state behind is a silent
  correctness bug (ReleaseState strands _writebackOriginals, so a COPY_IF_OVERLAP temp is never
  written back), and the owner's teardown must reproduce the ref struct's Dispose ORDER.

  "Mirror NumPy's LAYERING, not only its behavior" — work NumPy's Python wrapper does belongs in
  the np.* entry point, work its C core does belongs in the engine. Corollary worth its own line:

feat(twodim): np.diag family + triangular ops — 13 functions at NumPy 2.4.2 parity

Implements NumPy's two-dimensional base cluster (_twodim_base_impl.py +
_index_tricks_impl.py), none of which existed in NumSharp — only np.diagonal did:

  diag, diagflat, tri, tril, triu, fill_diagonal,
  diag_indices, diag_indices_from, mask_indices,
  tril_indices, triu_indices, tril_indices_from, triu_indices_from

WHY THESE SHIP TOGETHER
They share the k-diagonal-offset abstraction and NumPy defines them in terms of
each other (tril/triu are `where(tri(...), m, 0)`; mask_indices takes tril/triu
as a callback; diag's 2-D branch IS diagonal). Splitting them would have meant
implementing tri twice.

PARITY (probed against a live NumPy 2.4.2, never docs)
165/165 side-by-side cases agree on value, dtype, shape, writeability and error
text; fill_diagonal adds 37/37 in-place cases. Behaviours that are easy to get
wrong and are pinned here:

* diag's two branches differ in KIND. 1-D constructs a fresh writeable (n,n)
  matrix (n = size+|k|); 2-D returns a READ-ONLY VIEW sharing storage — the
  docstring says "a copy", but shares_memory is True and writeable is False.
* tril/triu of a 1-D input produce a 2-D result. `m.shape[-2:]` of (n,) is (n,),
  so the mask is tri(n) -> (n,n) and the row broadcasts down it.
* tril/triu of a 0-d input raise NumPy's LEAKED `tri()` missing-argument
  TypeError; reproduced verbatim (house precedent: the mmap_mode errors).
* fill_diagonal's values TILE CYCLICALLY and truncate — they do not broadcast.
  [1,2,3,4] into a 6x6 gives [1,2,3,4,1,2]; an empty value list is a silent
  no-op. That is flat-iterator assignment semantics, not ufunc broadcasting.
* diag_indices returns THE SAME array instance in every slot (NumPy's
  `(idx,) * ndim`), so a write through one entry is visible through all.
* mask_indices' arity follows the mask function's RANK, not n — passing diag
  (which reduces 2-D to its 1-D diagonal) yields a ONE-element tuple.
* Negative N/M/n clamp to empty axes rather than raising, because NumPy reaches
  those extents through arange.

DESIGN — no element loops, no per-dtype code
* diag/diagflat allocate the zero matrix then ALIAS a writeable stride-(n+1)
  view onto it and let the copy machinery fill it — NumPy's res.flat[i::n+1]=v
  without an element loop.
* tri/tril/triu skip the mask entirely: the retained columns of each row are one
  contiguous run, so each row is filled by bulk byte ops (dtype-agnostic).
  Non-unit-stride sources fall back to the literal `where` composition.
* fill_diagonal resolves its targets into REAL STRIDES, so it is one aliased
  view (or ceil(count/cols) blocks when wrapping) — which is why it writes
  correctly through transposed, sliced, F-order and negative-stride views.
* tril_indices/triu_indices drop NumPy's N*M bool mask + two broadcast grids +
  boolean gathers; the triangle is separable, so runs are emitted in O(output).

PERF (NPY/NS, >1 = NumSharp faster; Release, best-of-rounds)
  geomean 1.83x @ N=10M  (no cell < 1.0, min 1.13x)
  geomean 1.40x @ N=100K (one cell < 1.0)
  tril_indices 4.40x / triu_indices 4.55x @ 10M — the algorithmic win above.
The one sub-1.0 cell is fill_diagonal @100K (0.62x, 3.7us vs 2.3us): it touches
only min(rows,cols) elements, so the call is NDArray/Shape construction cost,
not work — at 10M it is 1.23x.

Allocation strategy is size-keyed from a MEASURED cliff at 64 MiB: below it the
buffer comes back dirty, so tri/tril/triu allocate uninitialised and write every
byte exactly once (64MB: 6.0ms vs 11.0ms); above it np.zeros rides free OS
zero-pages and only the retained run is touched (72MB: 13.5ms vs 18.9ms).
Getting this backwards costs ~2x either way — see np.tri.cs WriteOnceMaxBytes.

GATES
* 68 new unit tests, all expectations from real NumPy output, covering the
  layout matrix (C/F/strided/negative-stride/broadcast/offset/0-d/empty), all
  15 dtypes, and every verbatim error text.
* 4,520 new differential-oracle cases (gen_manip + a new gen_diag_tri tier):
  3,094 in manip.jsonl, 1,426 in matmul.jsonl. Both tiers green first run.
  Non-vacuity verified by disabling one OpRegistry case and confirming red.
* Full CI-style suite green: 11,904 passed, 0 failed.

Note: the .jsonl diffs are large but are almost entirely ID RENUMBERING — case
ids carry a global running counter, so inserting jobs shifts every later id.

fix(twodim): fill_diagonal accepts array-like `val` again — edge-case audit pass

Edge-case sweep over the diag/tri family. Found one real bug (a regression from
this family's own perf work), one unspecified null behaviour, and two untested
code paths. Everything else probed clean.

BUG — fill_diagonal rejected C# arrays and collections
The scalar fast path added while tuning fill_diagonal routed EVERY non-NDArray
value through NDArray.Scalar, which converts via IConvertible. An int[]/long[]/
double[]/List<int>/int[,] therefore threw InvalidCastException, where NumPy
happily accepts any array_like and tiles it:

    np.fill_diagonal(a, new int[]{1,2,3})
      -> InvalidCastException: cannot cast System.Int32[] to System.IConvertible

Now only genuine scalars (IConvertible, non-string) take the fast path; arrays,
collections, and the two non-IConvertible scalar types (Half, Complex) route
through asanyarray exactly as before. The scalar path — and its measured 4.9us
-> 4.0us win — is unchanged (re-measured 3.97us).

Why no gate caught it: the oracle hands `val` over as an NDArray, so the
array_like path was structurally invisible to it. Fixed on both ends — the
OpRegistry case now passes the RAW long[] instead of wrapping it in np.array,
putting the asanyarray/tiling path under the differential gate across every
dtype and shape the tier covers.

NULL — fill_diagonal(a, null) silently wrote nothing
NumPy's None reaches the dtype converter: nan for a float array, TypeError for
an integral one. Silently no-op'ing hid a caller bug, so this now throws
ArgumentNullException — a deliberate, documented divergence.

UNTESTED PATHS now covered
* The 64 MiB allocation-strategy branch (WriteOnceMaxBytes) was selected only by
  size, so every existing test exercised just the small side. Added a 72 MB case
  asserting the large path still zeroes the dropped triangle rather than leaving
  allocator garbage. Verified both sides agree: tril(k) + triu(k+1) == a exactly
  at 59 MB and 78 MB, and tri's ones-count matches the closed form.
* wrap x non-contiguous — the oracle's non-contiguous fill_diagonal destinations
  are all wrap=false. Probed 37 previously-uncovered combinations against NumPy
  (wrap over transposed / strided / negative-stride / negative-row / offset /
  F-order 2-D views; non-contiguous 3-D and 4-D cubes; tril/triu over
  non-contiguous 3-D): all 37 bit-exact, now pinned as tests.

PROBED CLEAN (no change needed)
* Extreme k: int.MinValue/MaxValue saturate correctly for tril/triu/tri and the
  index generators; diag's 2-D branch clamps to an empty diagonal and its 1-D
  branch reports "array is too big" rather than overflowing.
* tri(int.MaxValue, 2) really does allocate its 34 GB and fill correctly — no
  silent size overflow.
* Char and Decimal work across the family; null array arguments raise
  ArgumentNullException everywhere; array_like ergonomics already work through
  NumSharp's implicit conversions (np.diag(new int[]{1,2,3})).
* Empty/degenerate shapes, 0-size hyper-cubes, and mask_indices with a rank-3
  mask function all match NumPy.

HEADLINE: Phase 5 can un-gate Phase 4
The phase map read as a ratchet, but Phase 5 EDITS THE IMPLEMENTATION, so an
optimization is a new branch — on size, on layout, on operand type — and Phase
4's gates only cover the forms the corpus can express. This is not theoretical:
a scalar fast path added to fill_diagonal for speed routed every non-NDArray
value through an IConvertible conversion, so int[]/List<int>/int[,] began
throwing InvalidCastException while the unit tests, the fuzz tier AND the
hand-written parity harness all stayed green — every one of them passes that
argument as an NDArray. Now stated in the phase map, in Phase 5, and in the DOD
checklist, with the two probes that would have caught it:
  * the ACCEPTANCE SURFACE of polymorphic parameters (a corpus serializes each
    argument to one canonical form, so every other admitted form is invisible);
    close it by widening the oracle to pass a NON-canonical form, not just by
    adding unit tests
  * BOTH SIDES of a size- or layout-selected branch (a threshold leaves half the
    code unreached by every small test already written)

Phase 1 — what to distrust in NumPy itself
  * The docstring is not the contract. np.diag documents "a copy of its k-th
    diagonal" and returns a read-only VIEW. Probe view-vs-copy per branch.
  * Incidental consequences of NumPy's SPELLING are behaviour: tril squares a
    1-D input into (n,n) only because the body says tri(*m.shape[-2:]), and a
    0-d input escapes as tri()'s own missing-argument TypeError. Reproduce such
    leaked implementation errors verbatim (mmap_mode precedent).
  * Tuple returns need identity and arity probed, not just values —
    diag_indices returns THE SAME object in every slot (writes alias);
    mask_indices' arity follows its callback's rank, not n.

Phase 4 — trust the gate only after breaking it
  * Prove new coverage has teeth: rename your OpRegistry case, confirm the tier
    goes red on YOUR cases, revert. A first-run green is equally consistent with
    "not wired up".
  * Watch output-size blow-up when joining a layout x dtype tier (~26 x ~15):
    diagflat squares its input, so a 24-element operand becomes a 576-element
    expectation. Cap by size, give big/strided shapes a dedicated tier.

Phase 5 — measurement discipline
  * When two strategies trade allocation against writes, MEASURE BOTH ACROSS A
    SIZE SWEEP instead of counting instructions. Fresh large allocations arrive
    OS-zeroed, so a "wasteful" np.zeros can be free while an "obviously cheaper"
    write-once pass touches twice the memory. Measured inversion at 64 MiB:
    6.0 vs 11.0 ms below, 18.9 vs 13.5 ms above. Encode the crossover with its
    evidence, not a guessed round number.
  * Don't geomean across cost classes — O(1) view, O(N) fill and O(sqrt N)
    sparse write average into a number describing nothing.

Scope — drawing the family boundary
NumPy's own source file is the strongest signal for what ships together (the
whole tri/diag cluster is one file; tril/triu ARE where(tri(...), m, 0)), so
splitting a family means implementing the shared primitive twice. When two
readings differ materially in work — 5 functions vs 13 — put the options to the
user rather than picking silently.

Gotchas
  * Normalize line endings before diffing NumSharp against NumPy: C# writes CRLF
    and Python LF, so a perfect 165/165 match reads as 165/165 failures. Also
    watch harness-only formatting ((1.0+0.0j) vs (1+0j)) posing as parity bugs.
  * Test-harness dtype traps: np.arange is Int64 (GetAtIndex<int> trips
    Debug.Fail), coordinate access is GetValue<T>(i,j) not GetData<T>(i,j), and
    BeOfValues has no loop for Half/Decimal.

feat(iteration): np.nditer<T> / np.nditer_chunks<T> — typed, allocation-free iteration (40-249x NumPy)

Exposes NumSharp's NDIter engine to user code without paying a managed object
per element. NumSharp extension: NumPy has no typed iteration because Python has
no unboxed generics, so there is no oracle tier — the gate is 23 unit tests that
pin the new forms against the boxed np.nditer and np.ndenumerate across every
memory layout and all 15 dtypes.

    foreach (ref double x in np.nditer<double>(a, writeable: true)) x *= 2;
    foreach (Span<double> c in np.nditer_chunks<double>(a, writeable: true))
        TensorPrimitives.Multiply(c, 2.0, c);

WHY
The shipped np.nditer per-element `it[0]` loop measures 0.16-0.18x NumPy — the
only cell in the iteration subsystem below parity. The engine is not at fault: a
bare iternext() walk of 100K elements takes 0.61 ms against NumPy's 2.60 ms for
the same bare walk (4.3x). The entire deficit is the per-element NDArray view
(~0.6 us each). These APIs remove the view rather than making it cheaper.

PERF (NPY/NS, >1 = NumSharp faster; 100K float64, Release, best-of-9)
Reference: NumPy 2.4.2 `for x in np.nditer(a)` = 6.681 ms, `while+it[0]` = 10.690 ms.

  np.nditer<T>           0.167 ms    40x     (raw-pointer floor: 0.047 ms)
  np.nditer_chunks<T>    0.162 ms    41x
  chunks + Vector<T>     0.027 ms   249x
  shipped np.nditer it[0]  59 ms    0.18x    (unchanged)

Layout cost is flat: 0.16-0.19 ms for contiguous / F-order / reversed / sliced-
offset / broadcast; a stepped [:, ::2] view runs 0.091 ms for its 50K elements.

DESIGN — five things this had to get right
- GetEnumerator() must NOT return `this`. Unlike np.Broadcast these own unmanaged
  state, so the first foreach frees what a second would walk — a use-after-free,
  caught by a test during development. The factory returns a readonly struct
  enumerable holding NO unmanaged state, whose GetEnumerator() builds a fresh
  NDIterRef (0.4 us). Re-enumeration therefore RESTARTS — deliberately unlike the
  class-based np.nditer, which is its own iterator (NumPy's `iter(x) is x`) and
  resumes.
- foreach disposes a ref struct enumerator through the same pattern (no
  IDisposable needed); that is what frees the state. Hand-driven MoveNext loops
  must dispose themselves.
- The walk is chunk-driven, not element-driven. EXTERNAL_LOOP is always on and
  MoveNext advances with pointer arithmetic, touching the iterator only at a chunk
  boundary — a contiguous array is ONE chunk. The naive Iternext()-per-element
  form measured 0.47 ms, 3x worse. A leaner one-cursor MoveNext measured no
  better than the two-pointer form, so the two-pointer form stands.
- Never buffered. A ref/Span into a buffer dangles the moment the next fill lands;
  unbuffered pointers are absolute into the operand, which is also why the
  enumerator may advance the iterator before handing out the captured chunk.
- Order is 'K' (memory order), matching np.nditer exactly. Probed against NumPy
  2.4.2: a[:, ::-1] of arange(6).reshape(2,3) yields 0 1 2 3 4 5 in BOTH libraries
  and 2 1 0 5 4 3 under order='C'. 'K' is also what lets reversed / F-contiguous /
  transposed views coalesce to a single chunk. Pass order:'C' for the logical
  order ndenumerate uses.

DELIBERATE DIVERGENCES (each pinned by a test)
- A dtype mismatch THROWS. A `ref` cannot convert, so np.nditer<double> over an
  int32 array would otherwise reinterpret the bytes and hand out garbage
  (verified: it yields 2.1e-314, 6.4e-314, ...). Same guard NDEnumerate<T> uses.
- An empty array iterates ZERO TIMES, where the boxed form raises NumPy's
  "Iteration of zero-sized operands is not enabled" unless given zerosize_ok.
  Forcing `if (a.size > 0)` around every foreach is not how C# collections behave,
  and this is an extension rather than a parity surface.
- nditer_chunks<T> rejects a non-unit-stride inner loop (a[":, ::2"]) because a
  Span<T> is contiguous by definition. The single-operand inner stride is fixed
  for the whole iteration, so this is detected at GetEnumerator and never surfaces
  mid-loop. Buffering does NOT help — probed, NumPy's buffered external_loop also
  yields non-contiguous chunks there (7 chunks, C_CONTIGUOUS=False), and NumSharp
  matches it.
- Writing through a broadcast view is rejected with NumPy's verbatim text,
  "operand array with iterator write flag set is read-only".

MEASURED AND REJECTED — do not retry re-seating a cached view to fix it[0]
UnmanagedStorage keeps THREE synchronized address caches: the public byte*
Address, the IArraySlice InternalArray, and a per-dtype ArraySlice<T> _arrayXxx
field. Re-seating Address alone makes GetAtIndex / ToString / casts / write-
through correct while np.sum(it[0]) and it[0]*2 silently return 0. Re-seating
Address + InternalArray fixes the reductions and STILL leaves the arithmetic
operators and comparisons stale. It is fast (0.68 ms boxed, ~16x NumPy, vs 59 ms
today) but only safe if every cache moves behind one UnmanagedStorage method, and
any cache added there later re-breaks it silently. Recorded in CLAUDE.md with the
evidence so the next reader does not rediscover it the same way.

FOUR NDIterRef DEFECTS FOUND (routed around here, none fixed)
- GetInnerLoopSizePtr() access-violates on a 0-d operand: it reads Shape[NDim-1],
  i.e. Shape[-1]. The internal ResolveInnerLoopCount already guards this; the
  public accessor does not.
- GetInnerStrideArray() returns ELEMENT strides while the kernel contract
  (ForEach / ExecuteGeneric) takes BYTE strides from the private
  GetInnerLoopByteStrides(). No public byte-stride accessor exists. Mixing them
  produces silent NaN, not an error.
- ResetToIterIndexRange + EXTERNAL_LOOP does not clamp the inner count to the
  range, so it reads past the array end. This blocks parallel range-splitting;
  NumPy requires NPY_ITER_RANGED at construction for exactly this reason.
  Splitting by array SLICE works today and measured 3.2x on 8 workers (20M f64,
  8.62 -> 2.70 ms).
- NumPy's unbuffered external_loop coalesces [:, ::2] into 1 chunk; NumSharp emits
  500.
The first two are absorbed by TypedIterHelpers.ReadInnerLoop.

TESTS

feat(index_tricks): np.r_ / np.c_ / np.ix_ / np.s_ — the grid & slice-expression DSL at NumPy 2.4.2 parity

Ports NumPy's numpy/lib/_index_tricks_impl.py index-expression family: the two axis
concatenators (r_, c_), the open-mesh generator (ix_), and the reusable index builders
(s_, index_exp). index_exp rides along because it is literally the same IndexExpression
class as s_ with maketuple=true.

WHY THE C# SPELLING WORKS
-------------------------
C# has no a[1:5:2] slice literal, so a slice is written as a string: np.r_[0:5] becomes
np.r_["0:5"]. Strings already do double duty in NumPy here, and the two grammars are
disjoint upstream — a special directive NEVER contains a colon, because Python's own
syntax supplies the slices. So the rule is simply:

    a string containing ':' is a slice expression; a string without one is a NumPy
    special directive ("r", "c", "-1", "0,2", "1,2,0")

which lets every NumPy expression transcribe verbatim, including the mixed forms
(np.r_['0,2', a, b], np.r_[-1:1:6j, [0]*3, 5, 6]). One string may hold several
comma-separated slices (np.r_["1:3, 5:8"]), and Slice / Slice[] entries work too, so
np.s_[...] composes into np.r_[...].

r_/c_ are static properties returning RClass/CClass, both subclasses of AxisConcatenator
with this[params object[] key] — the direct port of NumPy's __getitem__, attribute
copying and all (the first entry may override axis, ndmin, trans1d and matrix mode for
that call only).

WHAT THE PORT REPRODUCES (all probed against live NumPy 2.4.2, never docs)
-------------------------------------------------------------------------
* Slice entries -> arange(start, stop, step), or linspace(start, stop, N) with the stop
  INCLUSIVE for an imaginary step ("-1:1:6j"). Integer-ness follows the LITERAL, not the
  value: "0:5" is int64, "0.0:5" is float64.
* A MISSING STOP re-reads start as stop, because NumPy's arange(start, None, step) IS
  arange(0, start, step) — so np.r_["2:"] is [0, 1] and np.r_["5::2"] is [0, 2, 4]. Easy
  to get wrong; pinned by tests and the corpus.
* Both directive upgrade paths, which genuinely DIFFER in NumPy: the array branch applies
  the defaxes[:k1] + defaxes[k2:] + defaxes[k1:k2] permutation (Python list-slice clamping
  included, so an out-of-range trans1d lands on transpose's own "axes don't match array"),
  while the slice branch uses swapaxes(-1, trans1d). np.r_["0,3,1", "0:3"] is (1,3,1) where
  the equivalent array entry gives (2,3,1).
* A silently-ignored 4th directive field ("0,2,0,q" parses fine — NumPy reads only vec[:2]
  and, when len(vec)==3, vec[2]), and ndmin<=0 as a no-op.
* "r"/"c" matrix coercion, routed through np.asmatrix since NumSharp has no matrix
  subclass — including its ">2-D squeeze then must be 2-D" rejection.
* Verbatim errors: `special directives must be the first entry.`, and
  `unknown special directive` vs `unknown special directive '0,q'` — the comma form quotes
  the directive, the bare form does not. Two distinct texts, both probed.
* ix_ PRESERVES the input dtype rather than forcing intp — it performs no integer
  validation at all, so an int8/float sequence rides through and only fails at the later
  indexing call. The one cast is NumPy's own: an EMPTY non-ndarray input becomes int64 so
  it does not default to float64. Bool sequences are masks (nonzero).

NEP50 WEAK SCALARS
------------------
NumPy separates a Python literal (5, weak) from a NumPy scalar (np.int64(5), strong); C#
has no such split, so the mapping is by type — bool, the eight integer primitives, float,
double and Complex are weak (the C# literal IS the Python literal), while char/Half/decimal
(no Python literal) and every NDArray (0-d included) are strong. NDArray.Scalar(1L) is the
escape hatch: np.r_[i8, 1L] is int8, np.r_[i8, NDArray.Scalar(1L)] is int64.

Promotion reuses the existing NDExprTypeRules machinery rather than a second implementation
— PromoteStrong for the strong fold, CheckIntLiteralFits for the range check — so
np.r_[u8, -1] raises the verbatim OverflowException("Python integer -1 out of bounds for
uint8") instead of wrapping, while a weak float saturates to +-inf (np.r_[f4, 1e300]).
NumSharp has a single complex width, so NumPy's result_type(float32, 1j) -> complex64
collapses onto Complex. (np.result_type itself has no weak-scalar support — it drops raw C#
scalars as NPTypeCode.Empty — which is why the resolution lives here.)

ix_ RETURNS VIEWS, AND KEEPS THEM READ-ONLY
-------------------------------------------
The outputs are views that write through, as in NumPy. The axis insertion is spelled with
expand_dims rather than reshape ON PURPOSE: reshape materializes a stride-0 operand, so
np.ix_(broadcast) came back writeable with strides [1] where NumPy reports writeable=False
and shares memory. expand_dims aliases the storage and preserves both. Verified for
broadcast, strided, negative-stride, offset and empty operands. (The underlying
reshape-drops-the-flag behaviour is pre-existing and left alone — it is reshape's, not ix_'s.)

DELIBERATE DIVERGENCE — NO bmat BRANCH
--------------------------------------
NumPy routes a single bare string key into matrixlib.bmat, which resolves the words in it
against the CALLER'S Python frame (sys._getframe().f_back) as variable names. C# cannot do
that, and the branch raises NameError for every string literal anyway (np.r_['1 2; 3 4'] ->
"name '1' is not defined"), so a lone string gets the same reading as any other entry —
which is exactly what makes np.r_["0:5"] work at all.

s_/index_exp collapse for a similar structural reason: NDArray's indexer is
this[params Slice[]], so a lone Slice and a one-element Slice[] are the same call, and
NumPy's maketuple distinction has nothing to attach to. Both are kept so NumPy code ports
verbatim; maketuple is exposed but documented as having no observable effect.

PARITY EVIDENCE
---------------
* Differential harness vs live NumPy 2.4.2: 131/131 cases bit-exact (dtype + shape + base64
  bytes) across directives, both slice branches, promotion and errors. The only deltas are
  exception TYPE names (house IncorrectShapeException/OverflowException vs Python
  ValueError/OverflowError); every message text is verbatim.
* Layout + dtype sweep: 129/129 bit-exact over C / F / transposed / strided / reversed /
  offset / broadcast operands, 0-d, empties, and all 13 NumPy-representable dtypes.
* Oracle: gen_oracle.gen_index_tricks -> the manip tier, +2,262 cases (1,062 r_, 798 c_,
  402 ix_, 8 expects_throw overflow). Floor bumped 4244 -> 6053. The tier was deliberately
  broken once (registry case renamed) to prove it has teeth: exactly 1,456 failures =
  1,062 + 402 - 8, then reverted.
* Unit tests: 61 new, every expectation from probed NumPy output. Full CI-filtered suite
  11,996 passed / 0 failed.

  Slice[] entries, List<T>, int[,], tuples, Memory<T>, char/Half/decimal strong scalars,
  the Char/Decimal dtypes, ulong overflow, null entries, malformed notation.

------------------------------------------------------------

feat(index_tricks): np.s_ / np.index_exp mirror NDArray's full indexer surface — advanced indices, not just slices

np.s_ shipped covering only the BASIC half of NumSharp's indexing vocabulary. NDArray
exposes three public indexers — this[string], this[params Slice[]] and
this[params object[]] — and the last one accepts a much wider set than the first two:
NDArray fancy indices and boolean masks, int[]/long[]/bool[] (and rectangular bool[,]),
IList sequences, ITuples, and any basic/advanced MIX. IndexExpression had only the
string and Slice[] overloads, so half of what you can write as arr[...] could not be
written as np.s_[...] at all:

    arr[Slice.All, np.array(new[]{0, 2})]        // worked
    np.s_[Slice.All, np.array(new[]{0, 2})]      // did not compile

That is backwards for this API in particular. NumPy's s_ is a pure pass-through — it
returns whatever index object you hand it — so np.s_[[1,2]] is the list, np.s_[np.array
([1,2])] the array, np.s_[..., [1,2]] the tuple, and a[np.s_[:, [0,2]]] is exactly
a[:, [0,2]]. The whole point of the object is that it can hold ANY index.

WHAT CHANGED
Adds IndexExpression.this[params object[]] -> object[], the capture form matching
NDArray's this[params object[]]. The contract is now:

    arr[X] === arr[np.s_[X]]   for every X the indexer accepts

verified elementwise (dtype + shape + bytes) across all 12 forms: slice string, Slice
objects, int, NDArray fancy, int[]/long[], List<int>, bool[] mask, NDArray<bool> mask,
slice+fancy mix, newaxis, ellipsis+int, and an np.ix_ open mesh.

OVERLOAD RESOLUTION IS UNCHANGED FOR EVERY EXISTING CALL
The new overload cannot steal the basic forms, because Slice is more specific than
object and both int and string convert implicitly to Slice:

    np.s_["1:3, ::2"]                 -> Slice[]   (this[string], normal form)
    np.s_[new Slice(1,3), Slice.All]  -> Slice[]   (params Slice[])
    np.s_[0]                          -> Slice[]   (int => Slice beats int => object)
    np.s_["1:3", "::2"]               -> Slice[]   (string => Slice beats => object)
    np.s_[np.array(new[]{0,2})]       -> object[]  (no NDArray => Slice conversion)
    np.s_[Slice.All, fancy]           -> object[]  (mixed; not all entries are Slices)

So the return type still tells you which half of the vocabulary you used, and both types
feed arr[...] directly — including an NDArray<T>, whose own indexers do NOT hide the
inherited this[params object[]] (checked, not assumed: the XML doc initially claimed they
did and was corrected after probing).

TESTS

bool[] mask), the basic+advanced mix (incl. an np.ix_ mesh round-tripping through s_),
the return-type split that pins overload resolution, and the arr[X] === arr[s_[X]]
equivalence sweep. Full CI-filtered suite 12,000 passed / 0 failed (was 11,996), the
FuzzMatrix gate included.
