feat(blas): np.parity_matmul — byte-identical np.dot / np.matmul via NumPy's own BLAS

NumSharp's np.dot disagreed with NumPy's on 94.5% of the elements of a (128,784)@(784,128)
float32 product (max ~976,000 ULP), and on 45% at K=10. Both answers are correct matrix
products; they sum in different orders. That is fatal for issue #626 — train a net in both
stacks and byte-compare the weights — because the divergence compounds: 50 Adam steps spread
it to 73% of w1's bytes. The committed `matmul` fuzz tier never saw it: small integer operands,
deepest contraction K=4, where every summation order agrees exactly.

WHY NO PORTABLE ALGORITHM CAN FIX IT
Reading the in-repo clone (src/numpy/.../umath/matmul.c.src): for f32/f64 matrix@matrix NumPy
ALWAYS calls cblas — since gh-23588 it copies a non-blasable operand into a temp and calls BLAS
anyway, so the portable `matmul_inner_noblas` loop is unreachable in a stock wheel except for
zero-sized or >BLAS_MAXSIZE dims. NumPy's bits are therefore scipy-openblas' bits, and those
match NEITHER a sequential mul+add chain NOR a sequential FMA chain (8 per-element references
each) — the sgemm micro-kernel uses an arch-specific multi-accumulator register scheme. The
bits also change with the BLAS thread count: measured 1/2/4/24 threads give FOUR different
answers (35,540 / 39,055 / 45,091 elements differ from the 24-thread result on (512,784)@
(784,512) f32). Reimplementing that per micro-architecture in managed code was rejected.

WHAT THIS ADDS (strategy S-A of #626)
An OPT-IN backend that P/Invokes the very same BLAS binary the target NumPy calls, driven by a
route-for-route port of NumPy's two matrix-product dispatchers. Same binary + same route + same
flags => same bits by construction.

    np.parity_matmul(true);                       // auto-discover numpy's OpenBLAS
    np.parity_matmul(true, path, threads: 1);     // pin the binary and the thread count
    np.parity_matmul(false);                      // back to NumSharp's SIMD GEMM (the default)
    np.parity_matmul_enabled / np.parity_matmul_info()

NumSharp's GEBP/FMA SIMD GEMM is UNTOUCHED and remains the default; the two hooks are single
`if (Try...) return ...;` lines that only fire when the switch is on.

BOTH DISPATCHERS ARE PORTED, because np.dot and np.matmul are not the same C code and do not
always agree. Probed on 2.4.2 they are bit-identical across C/F/negative-stride/strided/sliced/
transposed/syrk layouts — EXCEPT in the special-shape routes when an operand is not blasable: a
stride-2 matrix times a vector gives np.dot a gemv-on-a-copy and np.matmul the portable loop,
and 278/300 elements differ. NumSharp funnels both APIs into one engine, so each keeps its own:
  - Default.Dot     -> cblas_matrixproduct (ndim<=2) + the dotfunc iterator tail (ndim>2, which
                       is NOT gemm: NumPy walks every (row, column-plane) pair and calls ?dot)
  - MultiplyMatrix  -> @TYPE@_matmul, the gufunc behind np.matmul/@ and every batch element
All five matmul routes are reproduced (noblas / row-column ?dot with NumPy's double accumulator
/ both gemv directions / gemm, incl. the a@a.T syrk shortcut with the mirrored triangle, the
copy-if-not-blasable rule with NumPy's |stride|-comparison transpose choice, and the
matmul(a,b,o)==matmul(b.T,a.T,o.T) equivalence), plus cblas_matrixproduct's own shape
classification, _bad_strides copy and ?axpy scalar branch. One unit change: NumPy's strides are
in bytes, NumSharp's in elements — every ported predicate works in elements, which is the same
logic with itemsize==1.

Scope: float32 + float64. Every other dtype silently keeps the native path — integer and bool
products are bit-exact by construction (modular integer addition is associative, so summation
order cannot change them); Complex (zgemm) and Half are the real gaps.

RESULTS
  110-case acceptance harness  (backend off: 20 exact)  -> 110/110 BIT-EXACT
  342-case matmul_parity corpus (backend off: 294 red)  -> 342/342 BIT-EXACT
  MLP twin Gate 2, all four np.dot sites                -> BIT-EXACT
  MLP twin Gate 4, 50 full training steps               -> weights byte-identical
Gate 4 also needs the float32 np.exp port (NDFloatMath.Exp, separate work-in-progress); with
both in place a 50-step float32 MLP train produces byte-identical w1/w2/b1/b2.

Performance (Release, best-of-rounds): the parity path is 1.7x-13x FASTER than NumSharp's own
GEMM (it is OpenBLAS) — 2048^3 f32 118ms vs 282ms, f64 293ms vs 3860ms. It stays opt-in anyway:
NumSharp ships no native binaries, and a backend that silently loaded whatever BLAS it found
would make results depend on the machine's Python installation.

A NAMED LIBRARY IS BINDING. An explicit path (or NUMSHARP_PARITY_BLAS) is used as given and
never falls back to auto-discovery — parity is a claim about ONE binary, so quietly substituting
another would produce confidently wrong bits. Caught by
MatmulParityBackendTests.NamedLibrary_IsBinding_NeverSilentlySubstituted, which failed on the
first implementation.

HOST PIN. matmul_parity.jsonl is the first corpus tier whose expected bytes are not reproducible
everywhere, so it ships matmul_parity.host.jsonl recording the numpy version, BLAS file name,
OpenBLAS build string, dispatched core name and thread count. MatmulParityPin compares before
judging: a host that cannot load that library, or loads a different one, is INCONCLUSIVE with
the reason — never red. A machine without the wheel has nothing to be wrong about. Same
precedent as the MSVC-pinned float->uint cast kernels.

fix(index_tricks): edge & extremes sweep over r_ / c_ / ix_ — ndmin hang, uint64 weak default, ix_(null)

Post-ship sweep along the Phase-5 dimension catalog (magnitude, structural, resource,
parameter/null, acceptance surface, adversarial combinations, call forms). Everything
here lives OUTSIDE what the corpus can express, which is why the tiers were green
through all three bugs.

BUG 1 — ndmin past NumPy's dimension ceiling HANGS
--------------------------------------------------
`ndmin` arrives from a user-typed directive string, so "0,2147483647" is a plausible
typo. NumSharp walked it: AtLeastNdView expands ONE axis per iteration, allocating a
fresh shape each time, so the cost is quadratic in ndmin. Measured 54 SECONDS at
ndmin=100_000; at int.MaxValue it never returns. NumPy validates against NPY_MAXDIMS
inside array(..., ndmin=n) and rejects instantly:

    np.r_['0,65', [1,2]]   ValueError: ndmin must be <= ndmax (64)

Adds the same guard at the same place — a single AtLeastNdmin wrapper now fronts all
three conversion sites (array entry, slice entry, scalar entry), because NumPy raises
for every entry kind, not just arrays (probed all three). A non-positive ndmin stays a
no-op, as it is upstream ('0,0' and '0,-1' still pass through untouched), and the
default ndmin of 1/2 for r_/c_ is unaffected.

BUG 2 — an all-literal integer past int64 threw instead of resolving to uint64
------------------------------------------------------------------------------
NumPy's weak-integer default is int64 only while the value FITS; result_type(2**63)
and result_type(2**64-1) are both uint64. NumSharp hard-coded Int64 for the all-weak
case, so np.r_[ulong.MaxValue] raised OverflowException("Python integer
18446744073709551615 out of bounds for int64") for a value that has an exact dtype.
ResolveDtype now lifts the all-literal default to UInt64 when any literal exceeds
long.MaxValue — which in C# can only be a ulong, the one type that carries it.

long.MaxValue still resolves to int64 (the lift is conditional, not unconditional), and
a STRONG operand still decides the dtype with the literal range-checked against it, so
np.r_[uint8Array, ulong.MaxValue] still raises — as NumPy does.

BUG 3 — ix_(null) leaked a bare ArgumentNullException
------------------------------------------------------
Triage rule: a raw .NET framework exception at the API boundary marks a guard nobody
wrote. np.ix_(null) surfaced ArgumentNullException("Value cannot be null.") from three
frames down inside asanyarray. NumPy reaches a typed, texted error by a different route
— asarray(None) is a 0-d object array, whose ndim is 0 — and reports
ValueError("Cross index must be 1 dimensional"). NumSharp has no object dtype, so the
OUTCOME is now reproduced directly at the top of the loop.

MATCHED — recorded so a later cleanup does not undo them
--------------------------------------------------------
* -0.0 keeps its sign bit through the concatenate (bytes 00..00 80, NumPy's
  0000000000000080); NaN, +-inf and the smallest subnormal all round-trip.
* Weak-integer boundaries are exact to +-1: i8+127 and i8+(-128) fine, +128 and -129
  raise. long.MinValue/MaxValue resolve to int64.
* "9e18:9e18+2" collapses to an EMPTY int64 array on both sides — 9e18+2 == 9e18 in
  double, so start == stop.
* Resource extremes are honest: a 9e18-element arange, a 1e12/1e18/1e30-point linspace
  all raise OutOfMemoryException rather than wrapping a byte count into a small
  allocation (the silent-OOB class the catalog warns about). A genuine 2e9-element
  arange succeeds.
* Error ORDER matches: a bad directive is reported before the (also invalid) shapes
  behind it, and a trailing directive is caught during the walk, before any concatenate.
* np.r_ / np.c_ are STATELESS singletons. axis/ndmin/trans1d look like instance state
  but Build copies them to locals, so a directive neither persists into the next call
  nor leaks across threads — checked under Parallel.For, 64 ways, both assertions.
* Acceptance surface: ArrayList, lazy IEnumerable, ReadOnlyMemory<T>, jagged int[][],
  NDArray<bool>, NDArray<long>, Half and Complex sequences all convert; DateTime is
  refused with a typed, texted NotSupportedException.
* trans1d at int.MaxValue produces NumPy's exact ValueError("axes don't match array");
  at int.MinValue it produces NumPy's exact (2,1).
* ix_ high arity builds the full-rank mesh (32 sequences -> 32-D, each keeping its own
  non-unit axis).

DELIBERATE DIVERGENCES (documented, not silent)
-----------------------------------------------
* A null ENTRY to r_/c_ throws. NumPy builds array([None], dtype=object); NumSharp has
  no object dtype. Same call as fill_diagonal's null.
* np.ix_("abc") is accepted as a char sequence — NumSharp converts strings to char
  arrays house-wide, where NumPy sees a 0-d <U3 and rejects it.
* A sub-1e-15 slice step reports np.arange's inherited "step can't be 0" (it also
  guards against a 10^300-element allocation). Left to arange, which owns it.
* np.r_[1L, ulong.MaxValue] succeeds as uint64 where NumPy raises OverflowError("int
  too big to convert") — a CPython conversion artifact with no C# analogue.

COVERAGE
--------
+8 unit tests: the ndmin ceiling (all three entry kinds, plus the no-op cases either
side), the uint64 lift, extreme float round-trips, the weak-integer +-1 boundaries,
per-call/cross-thread directive isolation, error ordering, ix_(null), and ix_ high
arity.

Oracle widened at both ends rather than only in the hand-written tests: the manip tier
gains 18 cases — the ndmin ceiling across {64, 65, 100000, 2**31-1} x {array, slice,
scalar} entries (the >64 rows as expects_throw), and the uint64 weak default. That
needed a new "u" scalar kind in the corpus, since a literal past long.MaxValue cannot
ride the existing "i" (GetInt64) path. Floor 6053 -> 6060.

TYPE-name rows differ, unchanged) and 129/129 layout x dtype.

perf(math): np.exp float32 is now BIT-EXACT with NumPy 2.4.2 - and 1.1-1.2x faster

Port NumPy's own float32 exponential kernel (simd_exp_FLOAT, from
numpy/_core/src/umath/loops_exponent_log.dispatch.c.src, the SIMD_AVX2_FMA3
instantiation) into Utilities/NDFloatMath.cs, replacing MathF.Exp in the IL
unary kernel for the float32 loop only.

WHY THIS IS A CORRECTNESS FIX, NOT AN OPTIMIZATION
--------------------------------------------------
NumPy's exp is deliberately NOT correctly rounded: Cody-Waite range reduction
plus a 5th-over-2nd-order Remez minimax ratio, with a documented worst error of
2.52 ULP (at x = 0xc2781e37). MathF.Exp routes to the platform libm and is
~correctly rounded - so it disagreed with NumPy on ~35% of all float32 inputs
by 1-2 ULP. Being "more accurate than NumPy" reads as a divergence in a project
whose contract is bit-for-bit parity, and the fuzz gate's blanket "unary ~ULP"
excuse (563 hits) was absorbing it silently. Reproducing NumPy means reproducing
its error, operation for operation, in the same order.

This is pillar P3 of issue #626 (byte-identical MLP training): np.exp sits on
the softmax path, so every weight downstream of it inherited the drift.

VERIFICATION - EXHAUSTIVE, NOT SAMPLED
--------------------------------------
All 2^32 float32 bit patterns (4,294,967,296 inputs) agree with NumPy 2.4.2,
through BOTH the SIMD kernel and the scalar entry point - a chunked-checksum
sweep (512 chunks x 8M, order-sensitive weighted sum + xor per chunk), with a
negative control proving the checksums detect the old kernel's differences.

Gates added:
  * exp_f32.jsonl corpus tier (22 cases / 2679 elements): every NaN spelling,
    both saturation boundaries +-1 ULP, the subnormal-output band, NumPy's own
    worst-error input, the FMA-contraction tie, and a quadrant sweep on which a
    correctly-rounded libm disagrees with NumPy for ~35% of elements; across
    contiguous / 2-D / F-view / strided / reversed / offset / broadcast / 0-d /
    empty / narrow-integer inputs.
  * MisalignedRegistry: the unary ~ULP branch now EXCLUDES exp at a float32
    result, so a 1-ULP regression turns the gate red instead of being excused.
    float16 exp (NumPy's separate loops_half kernel) and float64 exp (the
    platform's scalar npy_exp) stay excused, deliberately.
  * OpenBugs.FuzzGate B8: four tightness tests pinning that carve-out from both
    sides (f32 and int16->f32 not excused; f64 and other f32 transcendentals
    still excused).
  * np.exp.Float32Parity.Test.cs: 9 tests, every expectation a probed NumPy bit
    pattern (not a tolerance), incl. all three vector widths vs the scalar path.

Proven to have teeth: reverting the kernel to MathF.Exp turns ExpFloat32 red
(16/22 cases), Unary red (62/5278 - i.e. the narrowed excuse bites), and 4 unit
tests red. Restored, all green.

SPECIALS (probed, and a consequence of NumPy blanking NaN lanes BEFORE the
range compares, which makes the three masks mutually exclusive)
--------------------------------------------------------------
  * any NaN - quiet, signalling, either sign, any payload - returns the
    CANONICAL 0x7fc00000. Note .NET's own float.NaN is 0xffc00000, so returning
    float.NaN here would have been wrong.
  * x >= 88.72283935546875 (incl. +inf) -> +inf; x <= -103.97208404541015625
    (incl. -inf) -> +0; +-0 -> 1; the [-104, -87.3] band produces subnormals
    through NumPy's fma_scalef_ps exponent-split.
  * NumPy also raises the FP overflow/underflow status flags (a RuntimeWarning);
    NumSharp models no FP status word - pre-existing, not introduced here.

HOST PIN (same class as the MSVC-pinned cast kernels)
-----------------------------------------------------
The quadrant's mul+add is FUSED because MSVC 19.44 - the compiler of the pinned
numpy==2.4.2 win-amd64 wheel - contracted that intrinsic pair into a vfmadd.
It is observable at exactly one input, x = 0xc26d0e6c, where x*log2(e) is the
exact tie -85.5: fused rounds the quadrant to -85, unfused to -86, and the
results differ by 1 ULP. Documented in Fuzz/README.md alongside the existing
host-dependent cells. On Windows NumPy's AVX-512 variant is MSVC-gated and never
compiled, so the AVX2/FMA3 kernel is the only one the wheel can run.

PERFORMANCE (NPY/NS, higher = NumSharp faster; Release, best-of-25 warm, out=)
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------
  N        NumPy      before     after      NPY/NS before -> after
  1K       0.0009 ms  0.0027 ms  0.0013 ms  0.33x -> 0.69x
  100K     0.0614 ms  0.1709 ms  0.0502 ms  0.36x -> 1.22x
  10M      6.2294 ms  18.877 ms  5.4571 ms  0.33x -> 1.14x

2.1-3.4x faster than the MathF.Exp kernel it replaces, and NumSharp now BEATS
NumPy wherever throughput dominates. The win is vectorization: NDFloatMath.Simd
carries Vector{128,256,512}<float> overloads (the algorithm is purely
elementwise, so lane i is bit-identical to the scalar call - which is also why
NumPy generates its own kernel from one template for __m256 and __m512), gated
by DirectILKernelGenerator.ExpVectorSimdAvailable on hardware FMA exactly as
NumPy gates its own. Without FMA the scalar entry point runs - same bits, one
lane at a time - so the gate is about speed, never results.

Two perf findings worth keeping:
  * NumPy's whole-vector denormal branch is KEPT rather than folded into a
    branchless select. Folding it away costs a second vdivps on EVERY vector;
    measured, that was ~0.17 ns/element - a fifth of the whole kernel.
  * The vector overloads are AggressiveOptimization|AggressiveInlining. Without
    the former, tier-0 JIT made the first ~40 calls 27x slower than steady state
    (2.7 ms vs 0.10 ms at 100K).
The remaining sub-1.0 cell (1K, 0.69x) is fixed per-call dispatch overhead
(~0.8 us), not throughput: 1.30 ns/element at N=1K vs 0.50 ns at N=100K.

Sweep (Phase 5) clean across tail lengths N=1..40, rank-6, interior-zero dims,
unit dims, in-place out=input, strided out=, broadcast input, reversed input,
out=/where=/dtype= surface, and the fused np.evaluate path at N=3/8/17/1000.

perf(index_tricks): np.r_/np.c_ ndmin pads in ONE alias — NumPy's 64-dim cap is not imported

`np.r_["0,100000", x]` now builds the 100000-dimensional array in ~1.4 ms. It previously
raised `ValueError("ndmin must be <= ndmax (64)")` — a cap added in c4e27523 mirroring
NumPy's `NPY_MAXDIMS`. That was the wrong fix for a real problem; this replaces it.

The real problem
----------------
`ndmin` reaches `array(..., ndmin=n)` from a user-typed directive string (`np.r_["0,2", a, b]`
— the `2` is ndmin), so a typo like `"0,2147483647"` is reachable from ordinary use.
`np.AtLeastNdView` padded ONE AXIS PER ITERATION via `np.expand_dims(a, 0)`, and every step
clones both `dimensions` and `strides` and inserts into them — quadratic in `ndmin`.
Measured 27.6 s at ndmin=100_000 for the padding alone (~54 s end-to-end through `np.r_`),
and unbounded at 2**31-1.

Why the cap was the wrong answer
--------------------------------
NumSharp has no 64-dimension ceiling anywhere. The project's own edge-sweep reference
records `ndim=65` as accepted ("no cap"), and `np.ix_` builds a 200-way mesh fine. Capping
`r_`/`c_` at 64 made the DSL refuse ranks the rest of the library accepts — importing a
NumPy limitation NumSharp does not otherwise have, i.e. a regression in capability dressed
as a parity fix. Fix the COST, not the CAPABILITY.

The fix: Shape.PrependDimensions (View/Shape.Reshaping.cs)
----------------------------------------------------------
Repeated `ExpandDimension(0)` has a closed form, so the whole pad is one allocation:
  * prepending never touches an existing entry — dims/strides ride through verbatim;
  * every prepended axis takes stride `dimensions[0] * strides[0]`. The first insert
    computes exactly that; each later one recomputes `1 * that`, i.e. the same value.
  * a 0-d source degenerates to stride 0 via `ExpandDimension`'s `IsScalar` branch, and
    every later prepend propagates the 0 forward.
  * `bufferSize` (`> 0 ? bufferSize : size`) and `offset` are loop-invariant after step 1.
So the result is BIT-IDENTICAL to the loop it replaces — strides, cached `ArrayFlags`, the
BROADCASTED bit and the WRITEABLE bit included — at O(ndim) instead of O(ndim^2).

`np.AtLeastNdView` (Creation/np.block.cs) now does one `Storage.Alias(PrependDimensions(pad))`
instead of `pad` NDArray/Shape allocations. It stays a VIEW, which is the contract
(`array(a, ndmin=n, copy=None)`): verified that a stride-0 read-only broadcast operand keeps
BOTH its strides and its non-writeable flag — the trap `np.ix_` already fell into once when
`reshape` silently materialized a broadcast into a writeable copy.

`AtLeastNdmin` in `Creation/np.r_.cs` loses `MaxDims`/the throw and becomes a documented
one-liner; all three call sites (slice entry, array entry, scalar entry in
`Operand.Materialize`) stay routed through it, since NumPy applies `ndmin` to all three.

Verification
------------
Differential probe against the OLD implementation, transcribed verbatim and run side by side:
96 combinations (16 layouts x 6 target ranks) agree on dims, strides, offset, bufferSize,
size, the raw flags word, C/F contiguity, BROADCASTED, WRITEABLE and IsScalar — 0-d scalar,
1/2/3-D contiguous, F-order, transposed, `[::2]`, `[::-1]`, offset `[3:7]`, `[:, ::2]`,
both broadcast kinds, `(0,)`/`(0,3)`/`(3,0)` empties and `(1,1)`. Plus: a padded broadcast
stays `writeable=False, broadcasted=True`, and a padded live view writes through.

Timing (Release, `np.r_["0,N", x]` end to end):
    N          before                  after
    64         0.07 ms                 0.02 ms
    1_000      15.8 ms (pad only)      0.04 ms
    10_000     366 ms  (pad only)      1.16 ms
    100_000    27_603 ms (pad only)    1.43 ms
    1_000_000  (never measured)        7.4 ms (pad only)
`ndmin=2147483647` now fails in ~1.4 ms with `OutOfMemoryException` ("Array dimensions
exceeded supported range") — 2.1e9 dims is ~34 GB of shape metadata. That is the honest
answer and the same one every other oversized NumSharp allocation gives; it is an
allocation failure, not a policy cap.

Test / oracle
-------------
`R_NdminBeyondNumPysDimensionCeiling_Throws` -> `R_HighNdmin_IsSupportedAndCheap`: asserts
ndim 64/65/100000 are BUILT (not refused), that every entry kind (array/slice/scalar) takes
the same route, that 2147483647 is an `OutOfMemoryException`, and that the non-positive
no-ops (`"0,0"`, `"0,-1"`, `"0,-2147483648"`) still give ndim 1. It carries a `Stopwatch`
guard (< 5 s for ndmin=100_000, two orders under the 27.6 s O(n^2) cost) so the quadratic
behaviour cannot come back silently.

`gen_oracle.gen_index_tricks` now emits only `ndmin_cap/64/*` — the last rank NumPy and
NumSharp agree on. The `>64` rows were `expects_throw` because NumPy raises; NumSharp
deliberately does not, so there is no NumPy answer left to bit-compare and keeping them
would assert a limitation NumSharp does not have. The divergence is documented in the
generator (with a "do not re-add" note), in CLAUDE.md, and pinned by the unit test above.

fix(shape/alloc): kill raw framework exceptions at the API boundary — reshape -1, size×itemsize overflow, expand_dims axis

Error-parity sweep over the shape/allocation surface, applying the rule that a raw .NET
framework exception escaping a public np.* entry point marks a guard nobody wrote. Three
NumPy C functions are ported rather than re-hand-rolled, because in each case NumSharp's
approximation of them was where the bug lived. All expectations probed against NumPy 2.4.2;
81 new tests; full CI-filtered suite 12,078 passed / 0 failed, FuzzMatrix 93/93.

MEMORY SAFETY — `size × itemsize` overflow (Exceptions/AllocationGuard.cs, new)

  np.zeros((2^31, 2^31)) of float64 used to SUCCEED. The element count 2^62 is
  representable, but 2^62 × 8 = 2^65 wraps to exactly 0, so the allocator was asked for
  zero bytes and obliged: the array constructed, [0,0] read 0, and the last element read
  out of bounds. np.ones on the same shape wrote out of bounds and took the process down.
  One dimension over, (2^30, 2^33), the element count itself overflowed and `size`
  reported negative.

  AllocationGuard is the dimension-checking block of PyArray_NewFromDescr_int. Two of its
  behaviours are load-bearing and both are observable:
    - the running product starts at itemSize, so the quantity checked is BYTES — which is
      why zeros(2^60) f8 is rejected while the same shape of int8 is only an
      OutOfMemoryException (NumPy's MemoryError);
    - a zero dimension does NOT short-circuit the scan (NumPy keeps multiplying "as if" it
      were 1), so zeros((0, 2^62)) f8 still reports "array is too big" instead of quietly
      succeeding at zero bytes.
  Dims are scanned left to right, so the reported error follows NumPy's ordering:
  (-1, 2^62) is "negative dimensions are not allowed", (2^62, -1) is "array is too big".
  Negative dimensions previously surfaced as OutOfMemoryException.

  There are TWO distinct wrap points and a guard that sees only one misses the other:
  (2^31, 2^31) wraps the byte count, (2^62, 2^62) wraps the ELEMENT COUNT to 0. The guard
  therefore keys off DIMENSIONS, never shape.size. np.full / np.full_like / np.ones
  allocate from shape.size directly rather than through UnmanagedStorage.Allocate, so they
  carry the call explicitly — without it np.full((2^62,2^62), 1) silently returned an
  array claiming that shape over an empty buffer. UnmanagedMemoryBlock<T>'s two allocating
  ctors hold a byte-count backstop for any path that reaches an allocator without a Shape.

  ndarray.resize is deliberately NOT routed through this guard: PyArray_Resize_int is a
  different loop and differs on all three axes, all observable — it BREAKS at the first
  zero dim (so a.resize((0,-1)) is legal and yields shape (0,-1) while np.zeros((0,-1))
  raises), its text omits the "are" ("negative dimensions not allowed"), and an
  overflowing product is a MemoryError, not a ValueError. It now allocates by element
  count and relabels, exactly as NumPy mallocs newnbytes and only then writes the
  dimensions. Its own product was unchecked too, so resize((2^62,2^62)) had been
  relabelling the array over a buffer never allocated for it.

RESHAPE — DivideByZeroException, and a silently negative shape (View/Shape.Reshaping.cs)

  _inferMissingDimension is replaced by a port of _fix_unknown_dimension:
    - ANY negative dim is the unknown one, not just -1 (probed: reshape(-3) on size 6 is
      (6,), reshape(3,-5) is (3,2)). Matching only -1 let a SECOND negative ride through as
      a literal dimension, so reshape(-1,-2) silently produced the shape (-3,-2) — a
      negative-extent array, which is the worse failure class than a crash.
    - the zero product is tested BEFORE the division (s_known == 0 || size % s_known != 0),
      which is why np.zeros((0,3)).reshape(-1,0) no longer raises DivideByZeroException:
      a degenerate known dimension had been reaching the divisor.
    - the known dims' product is overflow-checked, as NumPy's npy_mul_sizes_with_overflow.

  Every rejection except the multiple-unknown one now carries NumPy's single verbatim text,
  "cannot reshape array of size {n} into shape {s}", replacing three different NumSharp
  messages (including a bare ArgumentException "Value cannot be an empty collection.").
  {s} comes from a port of convert_shape_to_string, whose three quirks are all visible in
  NumPy's own output: LEADING unknowns are dropped (reshape(-1,0) -> "(0)"), later ones
  read "newaxis" (reshape(0,-1) -> "(0,newaxis)"), and a one-element shape closes with ",)"
  (reshape(0) -> "(0,)") — so "(0)" and "(0,)" both occur and mean different things.
  Type stays the long-standing IncorrectShapeException (house convention: NumPy's ValueError
  maps to it across the shape APIs); the multiple-unknown case becomes ValueError
  ("can only specify one unknown dimension"), previously a bare ArgumentException.
  35/35 probed cases now byte-identical to NumPy, values and texts.

EXPAND_DIMS — three defects behind one missing bound (Manipulation/np.expand_dims.cs)

  Shape.ExpandDimension guards only the negative side, and does it against the ALREADY
  NORMALIZED value, so:
    - a positive overshoot fell through to Arrays.Insert and surfaced as
      "ArgumentOutOfRangeException ... (Parameter 'index')" — a parameter expand_dims does
      not have — from three frames down;
    - a negative overshoot reported the normalized axis ("Effective axis -1 is less than 0"
      for an axis of -3);
    - a 0-d input skipped the check entirely, so expand_dims(scalar, 5) silently returned
      shape (1).
  NumPy answers all three with "axis N is out of bounds for array of dimension {outNdim}",
  normalized against the OUTPUT ndim and reporting the axis AS GIVEN. The guard lives at
  the np.* boundary rather than in Shape.ExpandDimension because that method has internal
  callers (keepdims reductions, fancy-index shaping, asmatrix) not bound by NumPy's axis
  contract — the same placement decision as the np.ix_(null) fix. Text matches the sibling
  int[] overload exactly, so the two overloads now agree. 23/23 probed cases identical.

Recorded in .claude/CLAUDE.md, including the MATCHES (the manipulation family's values are
clean across degenerate split/repeat/tile/roll/squeeze/moveaxis inputs) and the remaining
text-only divergences, so the next audit does not re-prove them.

refactor(blas)!: the BLAS backend leaves Core — NumSharp.Interop.BLAS ships a DefaultEngine subclass

NumSharp.Core is 100% managed C#. The previous commit put P/Invoke in it, which is the wrong
place: an external BLAS is an ALTERNATIVE a user opts into by installing a package, never
something Core depends on. With no package installed NumSharp must — and now does — do all of
its own math.

CORE KEEPS ONE SEAM, AND IT IS THE ONE THE ARCHITECTURE ALREADY DOCUMENTED
"TensorEngine abstract | Pluggable computation backend behind one contract" was true in
principle and unusable in practice: BackendFactory hard-coded `EngineCache<DefaultEngine>.Value`
and the matrix-product members were `protected static`, so nothing could subclass in. Three
small changes make the seam real, and they are the ONLY BLAS-related lines left in Core:

  - BackendFactory.Default { get; set; }  — null means the built-in managed engine; GetEngine()
    returns `Default ?? DefaultEngine`. This is the static ModuleLoad setter: a package assigns
    it from a [ModuleInitializer], so referencing the package IS the wiring.
  - DefaultEngine.MultiplyMatrix / BatchedMatmul: protected static -> protected virtual.
  - InternalsVisibleTo("NumSharp.Interop.BLAS") — a subclass needs the same internal view of
    Shape (strides/offset) and the promotion helpers the built-in kernels have.

Core has NO BLAS vocabulary now: no ICBlasProvider, no parity switch, no np.parity_matmul (the
np.* API is deleted — a matrix product backend is not an np-level toggle). Deliberately general:
the same seam takes an MKL, CUDA or Accelerate engine later.

THE PACKAGE (src/NumSharp.Interop.BLAS, PackageId NumSharp.Interop.BLAS, co-versioned 0.60.0)
`BlasEngine : DefaultEngine` overrides exactly TWO members — Dot and MultiplyMatrix — and
everything else, every op/dtype/kernel/iterator, stays the managed code it inherits. Anything
the port cannot service (any dtype but float32/float64, or a shape outside the ported surface)
falls straight through to `base`, so installing the engine can only change WHICH implementation
computes a float matrix product, never WHETHER NumSharp can compute one. The route-for-route
port of NumPy's two dispatchers (unchanged from the previous commit, just relocated) lives here
too, because it is meaningless without a BLAS: gemm + the a@a.T syrk shortcut + copy rules,
both gemv directions, the row-column ?dot with NumPy's double accumulator, the portable no-blas
loop, batched matmul, and the N-D np.dot dotfunc route that is not gemm at all.

  Blas.Enable(library, threads) / Blas.Disable() / Blas.Enabled / Blas.Info / Blas.TryEnable()

A [ModuleInitializer] runs TryEnable() at load: found a CBLAS -> the engine is installed;
found none -> NOTHING changes and NumSharp keeps doing its own math. It never throws at module
load, so merely referencing the package cannot break an app on a machine with no native BLAS.
NUMSHARP_BLAS_AUTOINSTALL=0 opts out. NO native asset ships in the package — the BLAS is
whichever one the consumer already has, because bundling a second copy would only make results
depend on which one won the loader race, and parity is a claim about a SPECIFIC binary.

ENGINE BINDING IS AT CONSTRUCTION — an NDArray resolves `tensorEngine` in its ctor, and
np.dot(a,b) dispatches on `a.TensorEngine`, so the engine must be installed BEFORE the arrays
it should compute with are created. Documented on BackendFactory.Default, in the README, in
GEMM_PARITY.md, and enforced in the tests (which re-create their operands per engine).

TEST WIRING
The test project references the package so its gate can run, which means the module initializer
would install the engine for the WHOLE run — wrong twice over: every other tier asserts
NumSharp's own kernels, and the install would land at whatever unpredictable moment the first
parity type is touched, so tests before and after would use different engines. Fuzz/
BlasEngineAutoInstallGuard.cs is a [ModuleInitializer] in the TEST assembly (which loads first)
that sets NUMSHARP_BLAS_AUTOINSTALL=0; the parity tests enable and disable explicitly.

Also lands the gate wiring held back from the previous commit now that the files it shares with
concurrent work have settled: gen_oracle.py's `matmul_parity` mode (342 cases + the host pin),
FuzzCorpusTests.MatmulParity, the MinCases floor, and OpRegistry's dot_aat / dot_ata /
matmul_aat / matmul_ata (the corpus cannot express two operands sharing a buffer, so the op
name carries the transpose and the self-product is formed from one operand — which is what
keeps the syrk route reachable on replay).

refactor(blas): the backend is an IBlasBackend the engine HOLDS, not an engine subclass

Second correction to the same seam. Subclassing DefaultEngine put the extension point in the
wrong dimension: it made "use a BLAS" mean "be a different engine", when the only thing that
actually varies is who computes a matrix product. Core now exposes ONE abstraction and ONE
settable property, and the optional package fills it in:

    namespace NumSharp.Backends;

    public interface IBlasBackend                          // Backends/IBlasBackend.cs — the
    {                                                      // ENTIRE Core-side BLAS surface
        string Info { get; }
        bool TryDot(NDArray left, NDArray right, out NDArray result);
        bool TryMatMul2D(NDArray left, NDArray right, NDArray result);
    }

    public abstract class TensorEngine
    {
        public IBlasBackend Blas { get; set; }   // null (default) = NumSharp's managed kernels
    }

NumSharp.Interop.BLAS implements it (OpenBlasBackend) and assigns the property from its
[ModuleInitializer], so referencing the package remains the whole opt-in and assigning null
takes it back out. BlasEngine is deleted; BackendFactory.Default is reverted (no longer needed —
nothing swaps the engine any more); MultiplyMatrix/BatchedMatmul are plain instance methods
rather than virtual, since they now READ the property instead of being overridden.

WHY THE PROPERTY IS BETTER, NOT JUST DIFFERENT
An NDArray binds its engine when it is CONSTRUCTED (`tensorEngine = ... ?? BackendFactory
.GetEngine()`) and np.dot(a,b) dispatches on `a.TensorEngine`. So swapping the engine only ever
reached arrays created AFTERWARDS — a silent footgun that cost real debugging: the 110-case
acceptance harness kept recomputing its second pass with the first pass's engine until the
array cache was cleared between modes. Engines are cached singletons, so a property on one
takes effect for arrays that already exist. Enable/Disable is now genuinely live, and the test
that proves it computes the SAME two arrays both ways
(Backend_ProducesTheSameSHAPE_AndDTYPE_AsTheManagedKernel).

Both members are Try-shaped: a backend answers only for the operands it implements (an external
CBLAS: float32/float64) and returns false for everything else, which the engine then computes
itself. Installing a backend can change WHICH implementation runs, never WHETHER NumSharp can
compute the product. Two entry points rather than one because np.dot and np.matmul are NOT the
same dispatcher in NumPy and disagree on non-blasable operands (a stride-2 matrix times a
vector: 278/300 elements differ) — a backend claiming bit-parity has to reproduce that split.

feat(oracle): ufunc out=/where= tier — 3,727 cases over out x mask layouts

out=/where= are supported on ~40 ufuncs but the corpus reached them only through
maximum_out / minimum_out / clip_out: 11 cases each, contiguous out, no mask. None
of what the parameters actually promise was gated.

Every case records TWO slots (the tuple kind), which is what gives the tier teeth:

  slot 0  what the call returned
  slot 1  the ENTIRE base buffer behind `out`

The second slot is the point. `where` masking is defined by what does NOT change,
so the out array's PRIOR contents are recorded as an operand and re-checked after
the call; and a kernel that walks the buffer instead of the view corrupts elements
OUTSIDE a strided/offset/negstride window, which a view-shaped comparison cannot
see. Non-vacuity verified at generation: all 882 where=all_false cases leave the
base buffer byte-identical, 860/882 where=alternating cases change it.

Axes: 7 out layouts (c / f / strided / negstride / offset / transposed / broadcast)
x 9 mask layouts (none / all_true / all_false / alternating / checker /
row_broadcast / scalar_true / scalar_false / strided_mask) x 14 binary + 14 unary
ufuncs x 3 shapes. A read-only broadcast out must be REFUSED, so those land as
error cases carrying NumPy's message.

Results — out=/where= is largely correct, and the tier says so precisely:
  * ZERO out-of-window writes in any layout: strided, offset, negstride, F-order
    and transposed all leave the bytes outside the view intact.
  * masked-off slots retain their prior contents in every all_false case.

Found (scoped in MisalignedRegistry K10-K12, printed every run):
  K10  out= on a read-only BROADCAST view: NumSharp writes through it (587 cases)
       where NumPy raises — contradicting NumSharp's own rule that a broadcast view
       has Shape.IsWriteable == false
  K12  isnan into a STRIDED bool out= writes results onto the wrong elements; a
       contiguous bool out is correct, which is exactly why a strided-out axis was
       needed to surface it
  K11  OPEN QUESTION: exp(1.0f) in a (4,5) float32 array returns 0x402df854 from
       np.exp(x), np.exp(x, out) and np.exp(x, out, where) alike, while NumPy — and
       the committed unary.jsonl expectation for the same values, shape and dtype —
       say 0x402df855. The unary tier is green, so the same op on the same data
       disagrees depending on how the array was built. Points at kernel/path
       selection, not at out=; scoped only so this tier can gate the rest.

Also tightened K7 (NEP50 weak-scalar, error path) to exclude this tier: a 0-D
operand here is usually the `where` MASK (scalar_true/scalar_false), which has
nothing to do with promotion — without the guard it silently swallowed 60 mask
cases it had no business classifying.

layout_catalog's convention (describe() serializes base.tobytes(), a C-order walk,
while the recorded strides/offset are physical). An np.asfortranarray base made the
two disagree and reported 563 phantom F-order divergences — corpus bug, not a
NumSharp one; F-contiguity is now expressed as a transposed view over a C base,

perf(math): log/sin/cos float32 join exp as BIT-EXACT NumPy ports - and rad2deg's 79% drift

Follow-up to the exp port: a systematic scan for the REST of the float32/float64/float16 surface
that is not byte-identical to NumPy 2.4.2, then ports for everything the scan showed was portable.

THE SCAN (this is the part worth keeping)
-----------------------------------------
Two instruments, because neither alone is sufficient:
  * a divergence CENSUS over the whole committed corpus, tallying every excused case by
    (op, input dtype -> result dtype) rather than the harness's reason-only totals; and
  * a wide-sample differential scan (180K float32 / 300K float64 values spanning specials,
    subnormals, both tails and the interior, plus ALL 65,536 float16 values) - because the corpus
    value pool is dominated by magnitudes that saturate, and cannot see a polynomial's accuracy at
    all. That is the same blind spot the exp tier had to work around.

Result, measured (fraction of inputs whose bits differ from NumPy):
  float32   rad2deg 79.28%   log1p 33.64%   expm1 31.13%   tanh 9.73%   cos 7.84%   sin 6.88%
            log 4.72%   exp2 0.04%          (exp: already 0 after the previous commit)
  float64   expm1 30.72%   log1p 15.05%   tanh 8.13%   exp2 0.02%   (everything else exact)
  float16   17 elements out of 65,536 across six ops - already effectively clean

PORTED (all now bit-exact, each verified over ALL 2^32 float32 inputs)
---------------------------------------------------------------------
  * log   <- simd_log_FLOAT (loops_exponent_log.dispatch.c.src, the exp kernel's sibling):
    exponent/mantissa split with NumPy's 2^100 subnormal rescale, mantissa folded at 1/sqrt(2),
    a 5th-over-5th Remez ratio, then exponent*ln2 with a final FMA. NumPy documents 3.83 ULP of
    its own error here - which is exactly why a correctly-rounded MathF.Log could not match it.
  * sin/cos <- simd_sincos_f32 (loops_trigonometric.dispatch.cpp): Cody-Waite reduction against
    pi/2 in three fused steps, a sine and a cosine polynomial, selected and negated by quadrant.
    NumPy hands arguments past its Cody-Waite limits to libc - and uses a DIFFERENT limit per
    function (117435.992 for sine, 71476.0625 for cosine) - so the port does the same rather than
    extending the polynomial, which would move AWAY from NumPy.
  * rad2deg/deg2rad: NumPy's RAD2DEG macro is (180/PI) evaluated at the OPERAND's precision, so
    the float32 loop divides two float32 constants. NumSharp rounded the DOUBLE quotient instead -
    0x42652ee1 vs NumPy's 0x42652ee0, one ULP low - which shifted 79% of all float32 rad2deg
    results. Both the scalar and the VECTOR emitter carried the constant (EmitVectorScale took a
    double and cast it), so both are fixed; a test pins that contiguous and strided agree.

Specials, probed and pinned: log returns -inf at +-0 and a NEGATIVE NaN for a negative argument
(but a POSITIVE one for a NaN argument); sin(-0) keeps its sign through the reduction; every NaN
spelling collapses to the canonical 0x7fc00000 (.NET's own float.NaN is 0xffc00000, so returning
it would have been wrong).

    and BOTH Cody-Waite cutoffs +-1 ULP, and each NumPy-documented worst-error input.
  * MisalignedRegistry's unary ~ULP branch now skips a SET of ops at a float32 result

## Callbacks/ (Keras keras.callbacks port)

BaseCallback with OnTrain{Begin,End} / OnEpoch{Begin,End} / OnBatchEnd, plus a
TrainingContext carrying Layers, Optimizer and the StopTraining flag (Keras's
model.stop_training). Epoch and batch indices are 0-BASED as in Keras; the
console prints them 1-based. Log keys are Keras-named: loss, acc, val_loss,
val_acc, learning_rate.

- EarlyStopping — monitor/patience/min_delta/mode/baseline/restore_best_weights/
  start_from_epoch. Three upstream details reproduced deliberately, each with a
  matched-pair test because getting them wrong is silent:
  * min_delta is stored abs() and NEGATED in min mode, so the single comparison
    "current - min_delta vs best" means "improved by at least min_delta" in both
    directions. An unsigned delta inverts the test and stops immediately.
  * wait increments BEFORE the improvement check and resets only on an
    improvement, so patience counts epochs-since-best inclusive.
  * the stop test carries an "epoch > 0" guard, so patience:0 cannot fire on the
    first epoch.
  The baseline asymmetry is preserved too: an improvement that misses the
  baseline updates best but does NOT reset wait, so a run of genuine
  improvements can still exhaust patience.
- ModelCheckpoint — save_best_only, mode auto/min/max, and {epoch:D3} /
  {val_loss:F4} path placeholders ({epoch} expands 1-based, as Keras does).
  Weights-only by design: architecture is a separate JSON here, so Keras's
  save_weights_only has nothing to toggle.
- ReduceLROnPlateau — factor/patience/cooldown/min_lr/min_delta. Writes the
  optimizer's BASE LearningRate, which is legitimate: SGD/Adam derive each step
  as lr0/(1+decay*t) computed fresh from that field, so this reschedules without
  reintroducing the per-step compounding P0 fixed. Note its improvement test puts
  min_delta on the REFERENCE side (current < best - delta) where EarlyStopping
  puts it on the current side — the two genuinely differ upstream.
- CSVLogger — columns frozen at epoch 0 from the SORTED log keys (a later metric
  gets no column, a vanished one is written NA), and the epoch column is
  0-based because Keras writes the raw callback index there. Flushed per row and
  closed from OnTrainEnd, which the trainer invokes from a finally.

## Serialization/

ModelWeights: one .npz per model via core's byte-exact writer, so the file IS a
NumPy archive — verified by loading it in real numpy and getting float32 arrays
of the right shape for every key. Capture/Restore give detached in-memory
snapshots for restore_best_weights.

Two decisions worth keeping:

1. Keys are POSITIONAL — layer{i}/param/{name} and layer{i}/state/{name} — not
   by BaseLayer.Name. Name comes from Util.GetNext(), a process-global counter
   that never resets, so building the same architecture twice in one process
   yields fc_fused2/fc_fused3. A name-keyed checkpoint therefore cannot load into
   a freshly-built model, which is the entire point of a checkpoint.
2. Load/Restore validate EVERY tensor before writing ANY. The first cut checked
   shapes during assignment; the gate caught that a mismatch in a late layer left
   the model with layer 0 from the checkpoint and layer 1 from the initializer —
   it raises, but the caller's model is already corrupt, and it trains to garbage.

BaseLayer.NonTrainable was added now rather than in P4 so the archive format
needs no break when BatchNorm's running statistics arrive: optimizers demand a
Grads entry for every Parameters key, so gradient-less state cannot live there.

ModelArchitecture + LayerConfig: Keras to_json/model_from_json shape — a JSON
array of {class_name, config} rebuilt through a factory registry. A layer with no
registered factory is refused at SERIALIZE time rather than emitting something
that cannot be read back.

## Gradient clipping (BaseOptimizer)

ClipNorm (Keras's PER-PARAMETER norm), GlobalClipNorm (one norm over the whole
model = PyTorch clip_grad_norm_), ClipValue. Keras's precedence chain
(clipnorm > global_clipnorm > clipvalue, if/elif not composition) and its
rejection of clipnorm+global_clipnorm together, in either assignment order.

clip_by_norm is ported in its upstream SHAPE — v * c / max(|v|, c), multiply then
divide — rather than branching on norm > c. Under the threshold that is exactly
the identity in IEEE arithmetic (same c on both sides), which the gate pins with
a zero tolerance. global_clipnorm likewise uses Keras's c * min(1/norm, 1/c)
form, exactly 1 under budget, plus the "+ (norm - norm)" term that poisons the
scale on a non-finite norm instead of silently producing a finite update from
inf/NaN gradients.

Applied per-parameter inside SGD/Adam; the model-wide variant runs from
ApplyGlobalClipNorm, which the trainer calls once per step before the per-layer
updates (a single Update sees one layer and cannot compute a model norm).

## MlpTrainer

New optional arguments: shuffle (default TRUE, Keras's default), validationSplit,
validationData, callbacks, verbose (0 silent / 1 per-epoch / 2 per-batch).

- Shuffling draws one np.random.permutation(n) per epoch and gathers PER BATCH
  rather than materializing a shuffled copy of the whole set, so peak memory
  stays at one batch. All randomness goes through np.random (MT19937), so a
  seeded run is reproducible end to end — pinned by a spy layer that records the
  exact sample indices each batch received.
- validationSplit takes the LAST fraction BEFORE shuffling, as Keras does.
  The split point is computed in float32: (int)(10 * (1 - 0.2f)) is 8, the double
  promotion gives 7, and Keras gives 8 — the C# float literal's rounding lands on
  Python's answer where the widening does not.
- The partial final batch is now TRAINED ON instead of dropped (numBatches is a
  ceiling), and epoch loss/accuracy are SAMPLE-weighted so a short last batch
  counts proportionally — the gate pins 4/5, which a batch-mean would report as
  0.5. SoftmaxCrossEntropy.Backward already divided by preds.shape[0], so ragged
  batches were always gradient-correct.
- TrainResult gained EpochValLoss, EpochValAcc, EpochsRun and StoppedEarly;
  Epochs still means REQUESTED. EvaluateFull scores loss and accuracy in one
  pass. CountMatches no longer assumes Byte labels (a fancy-index gather or a
  hand-built array is often Int32/Int64).
- On an early stop the final test score is taken AFTER the callbacks run, since
  EarlyStopping may have just rolled the weights back.

NeuralNet keeps working and gained the same callback list, ApplyGlobalClipNorm,
and SaveWeights/LoadWeights/ToJson/FromJson.

- "dotnet run <script>.cs" caches on the SCRIPT hash, not the referenced project.
  After a source-only change a gate silently replays the old build — it reported

  Clear %LOCALAPPDATA%\Temp\dotnet\runfile\<name>-* before trusting a re-run.

## The contract change: BaseLayer.Training

Keras's training= / PyTorch's model.eval(), as a FLAG rather than a Forward
parameter — changing Forward(x) would break every existing layer, activation and
verification script for no behavioral gain. Defaults to false, so a bare Forward
is always inference. MlpTrainer sets it true around the training forward and
false in Evaluate/EvaluateFull; NeuralNet.Train sets true, NeuralNet.Predict
false.

The cost of a flag is that it must actually be SET, and both failure modes are
silent — Dropout that never drops, BatchNorm normalizing with stale running
statistics — so the gate spies on forward calls per mode instead of trusting the
trainer.

## Layers

- Dropout(rate) — inverted: survivors scale by 1/(1-rate) at training time so
  inference needs no compensation. The SCALED mask is cached, because backward
  must apply the identical scaling; a re-draw or re-scale there trains against a
  different network than the one it evaluates. rate=0 is the identity even in
  training.
- BatchNormalization(features) — 2-D (N,C). gamma/beta in Parameters,
  moving_mean/moving_variance in NonTrainable (the slot P1 added for exactly
  this: optimizers iterate Parameters and demand a Grads entry per key, so a
  running mean parked there either crashes the step or gets "optimized").
- LayerNormalization(features) — per-SAMPLE over the features. No running state,
  ignores Training, works at batch size 1 — pinned by a batch-independence pair.
- Embedding(inputDim, outputDim) — gather forward; backward is a scatter-ADD.
  The ADD is the entire point: a row appearing twice receives gradient from both
  occurrences, and an assignment loop keeps only the last, silently
  under-training every repeated token. Core has no np.add.at (ROADMAP backlog),
  so it is an explicit unsafe accumulate. InputGrad stays null — indices are not
  differentiable — and a 3-layer stack with an Embedding at its head is trained
  in the gate to prove the backward sweep tolerates that.
- Flatten / Reshape — shape algebra both ways; Reshape's target excludes the
  batch dim (Keras) and the batch is read per call, so one instance handles a
  partial final batch.

## Regularizers/ (L1, L2, L1L2)

Applied by the TRAINER, not by each layer's Backward: after the backward sweep
it calls ApplyRegularizerGradients() on every layer and adds
RegularizationPenalty() to the reported loss, as Keras does. Centralizing means a
layer author cannot forget to honour a regularizer someone attached to their
layer. The gradient call is deliberately NOT gated on `penalty != 0`, which
conflates "no regularizer" with "one that happens to score zero right now".

## Two things the probe/oracle corrected

1. **Keras's defaults are not the common ones.** BatchNorm AND LayerNorm use
   epsilon = 1e-3 — not the 1e-5/1e-6 everyone else uses — and the variance is
   the POPULATION (ddof=0) one, for both the normalization and the
   running-variance update. On a batch of 3 the sample variance shifts the output
   ~20%; on a batch of 256 it is invisible, which is how that bug survives casual
   testing. Embedding's default initializer is RandomUniform(+/-0.05), not
   Glorot. All probed against Keras 3.15 before implementing, not assumed.

2. **The oracle caught a real bug: L1's subgradient at w = 0.** np.sign(0) is 0,
   but jax.grad(jnp.abs) at +0.0 AND -0.0 is +1 — Keras/JAX's `x >= 0` branch,
   the same convention P2 found in LeakyReLU's gradient. w = 0 is exactly where
   an L1 penalty spends its time, so the wrong value stalls every weight the
   penalty has already driven to zero. Fixed via L1.SubGradient; do not
   "simplify" it back to np.sign.

## Backward derivations

BatchNorm and LayerNorm both use the folded form

    dx = invStd * ( dxhat - mean(dxhat) - xhat * mean(dxhat*xhat) )

which is algebraically identical to the textbook dvar/dmean chain once
Sum(x - mu) = 0 is substituted into dmean's second term, and stays exact with a
non-zero epsilon since epsilon only ever enters through sigma = sqrt(var+eps).
Four temporaries instead of nine. Both forms are written out in the source so the
equivalence is checkable rather than asserted.

The two layers differ in WHICH axis reduces: BatchNorm's input gradient reduces
over the batch and LayerNorm's over the features, while BOTH parameter gradients
reduce over the batch (gamma/beta are shared across samples). Mixing those up
produces gradients of the right SHAPE, so only a numeric check catches it — hence
the non-uniform upstream cotangent in every oracle case.

## Oracle extension (tests/gen_keras_oracle.py)

P4 layer gradients come from jax.grad over keras.Layer.stateless_call, so the
oracle differentiates the ACTUAL Keras implementation rather than a
re-derivation of it. Cases: BatchNorm train+inference forward, dx/dgamma/dbeta
and the running-stat update, plus a batch-of-1 case where the variance is exactly
0 so epsilon alone divides (the case that separates 1e-3 from 1e-5); LayerNorm
the same plus the batch-independence pair; Embedding with duplicate / all-same /
no-repeat indices and 2-D sequence input; Dropout's inverted-scaling contract
(the mask is RNG-specific, so what is pinned is the scale, the two-valued support
and the inference passthrough, with the kept fraction checked statistically at
>6 sigma); regularizer penalties with their gradients.

Two generator details are load-bearing: `training=` is forwarded only to layers
whose call() declares it (LayerNormalization and Embedding raise TypeError
otherwise), and an integer input is skipped for dx because jax.grad refuses to
differentiate it — the same fact our Embedding encodes with a null InputGrad.

## tests/verify_p4.cs

What a single-layer oracle cannot see: Training-flag plumbing through the trainer
and NeuralNet (a spy counts forwards per mode), running statistics updating in

fix(blas): the seam held, the plumbing did not — read-once hooks, a no-op failed Enable, and a per-STACK entry point

Design review of the IBlasBackend seam landed in a07f4e6c, done by probing rather than
reading: every load-bearing claim was attacked with a throwaway harness. The seam itself
survived intact. Three defects around it did not, and the entry-point granularity was
measurably wrong.

WHAT WAS PROVEN SOUND (do not re-derive; docs/GEMM_PARITY.md section 9 carries the table)

  * "A property on the cached engine reaches arrays that ALREADY exist, an engine subclass
    would not." 38 construction / operation / IO paths — ctors, slices, transposes,
    broadcast views, astype, flat, fancy/boolean index results, GetData(long[]) batch
    sub-views, np.load_npy, np.evaluate, operator results — all assert
    ReferenceEquals(arr.TensorEngine, BackendFactory.GetEngine()). 38/38. The only escape
    is the explicit public arr.TensorEngine = new DefaultEngine(), and even then a+b
    results land back on the singleton.

  * "Installing a backend changes bits and speed, nothing else." 52 calls — valid shapes
    across every layout, mixed dtypes, and 14 deliberately invalid ones — compared shape +
    dtype + exception TYPE + exception MESSAGE with the backend on vs off. 52/52 identical.
    The Dot hook sitting ABOVE Core's own validation is safe precisely because every
    misaligned route returns false rather than answering.

  * "Only a Core friend assembly can write a backend." REFUTED. A working IBlasBackend was
    written in an assembly absent from InternalsVisibleTo; it compiles, installs and
    computes correctly, strided views included. So was a Complex128 backend — the dtype
    NumPy sends to zgemm — with ZERO change to the interface, TensorEngine or any hook.
    There is one trap, now documented on IBlasBackend itself: the obvious-looking
    a.GetData<T>().Address DENSIFIES a non-contiguous view, so pairing it with the public
    Shape.Strides reads outside the buffer and silently returns wrong numbers on exactly
    the sliced/transposed operands a matrix product sees most. The correct public recipe is
    (T*)a.GetData().Address + a.Shape.Offset together with a.Shape.Strides.

FIX 1 — never test-then-call a settable property (Core)

Both hook sites read Blas twice: if (Blas != null && Blas.TryDot(...)). Blas is settable
from any thread, so a concurrent Blas.Disable() landing between the two reads dereferences
null inside np.dot. Not theoretical: 31,252 NullReferenceExceptions out of 1,562,291
products (~2%) with one thread flipping the property and eight multiplying, every stack
pointing at Default.Dot.cs. Reading into a local first — re-measured 0 of 1,553,695.
volatile would not have helped; reference reads are already atomic, the bug was the SECOND
read, not a torn one.

FIX 2 — a failed Blas.Enable must change nothing (Interop.BLAS)

CBlasNative.Load called Unload() — freeing the WORKING library — before it knew the new
candidate was any good, and Blas.Enable left OpenBlasBackend installed when the load then
threw. The result is the worst failure mode a parity feature has: Blas.Enabled reporting
TRUE while every product had silently reverted to the managed kernel. No exception at the
call site, and an answer that still looks like a matrix product. Reproduced from two
directions (a nonexistent path and a loadable non-CBLAS file).

  - Load binds the replacement completely before touching the incumbent, so a failed call
    is a no-op and an already-working parity setup keeps working.
  - Bind resolves all ten symbols into locals and commits the statics only on full success.
    The old order wrote _handle before the nine Require() calls, so a library exporting
    cblas_sgemm but missing e.g. cblas_dsyrk left IsLoaded true over a handle the caller
    had just freed: a later Enable() would skip loading and call into it, and a later Load
    would free it twice. (Found by reading — no partial-export library available here.)
  - Blas.Enabled now means installed AND bound. An installed-but-unbound backend declines
    every operand, so reporting true there claims a parity it is not delivering.
  - Unload is no longer on the Load path and says why: freeing a BLAS a thread may be
    executing in is a fatal AV, not a catchable error.

The shipped gate already asserted this invariant (NamedLibrary_IsBinding_...,
NotACBlasProvider_Throws) but only ever from a DISABLED start, which is the easy half.
Replaying both bodies from an ENABLED start flipped two passing assertions to failing;
those cases are now tests.

FIX 3 — TryEnable catches everything, deliberately (Interop.BLAS)

It runs from a [ModuleInitializer], where an escaping exception is not a failed opt-in but
a TypeInitializationException on every later touch of the assembly — merely REFERENCING the
package would break the app, the one thing the design promises it cannot do. Discovery
walks PATH and the filesystem, so the reachable failures were never limited to the three
loader exceptions it caught; an unreadable directory alone raises
UnauthorizedAccessException. Directory.GetFiles is additionally guarded at the call.

Also: every user-facing error message named np.parity_matmul, an API removed two commits
ago and present nowhere in the tree, and two dead <see cref>s shipped as live CS1574
warnings (parity_matmul, EnumerateCandidates). All now name Blas.Enable / AutoCandidates.

FIX 4 — the seam is per-STACK, not per-matrix: IBlasBackend.TryMatMulBatched

Granularity is a performance decision and this one was inverted. With only TryMatMul2D, a
stacked matmul called it once per batch element and the backend rebuilt NumPy's MatmulPlan
— route decision plus, for a non-blasable operand, a native scratch malloc — every time.
NumPy does that once, outside its gufunc outer loop, because the trailing strides cannot
vary within a stack. Measured (NPY/NS, Release, best-of-9):

    2000 x (8,8)   f32   managed 2.34ms   per-element 2.71ms -> hoisted 0.361ms   0.80x -> 6.47x
     500 x (32,32) f32   managed 1.93ms   per-element 1.39ms -> hoisted 0.850ms   1.28x -> 2.27x
       8 x (256^2) f32   managed 4.78ms   per-element 2.29ms -> hoisted 2.33ms    1.58x -> 2.05x
    single 512x784x512   managed 6.50ms                         2.89ms           2.25x (unchanged)
    2000 x (8,8) int32   declined by the backend                2.65ms           0.95x - seam is free

So per-element setup did not merely erode the advantage on many-small-matrix workloads, it
inverted it: an external OpenBLAS ran 20% SLOWER than NumSharp's own managed GEMM. The new
entry point is a pure performance change — the plan is a function of the trailing strides
and dims alone, so both routes reach the same MatmulCore call with the same pointers.
A/B'd through a decorator that declines the batched route: 25/25 stacked products
BIT-IDENTICAL across broadcast, transposed, sliced, negative-stride, 1-D-promoted,
degenerate-core (dm/dn/dp = 1), 4-D and 5-D, f32 and f64.

It is a DEFAULT INTERFACE METHOD, so a backend written against the original two members
compiles and runs untouched — verified with both third-party probe backends and pinned by
ABackendThatKnowsNothingOfBatching_StillWorks. Growing the interface without breaking an
implementer is itself the extensibility claim, executed.

TryMatMulBatched declines zero-sized extents on purpose. NumPy's own dispatcher excludes
them from its blas routes, and NumSharp's per-element loop currently THROWS on them, so
answering would make np.matmul succeed or fail depending on whether this package happens to
be referenced. A backend may change which implementation runs and how fast, never whether
the call works.

FOUND WHILE PROBING, NOT A BLAS DEFECT, LEFT OPEN

IBlasBackend members are operations (TryDot/TryMatMul2D/TryMatMulBatched), not BLAS

out=/where=/axis, a different contract shape — so a future ITranscendentalBackend belongs
beside it rather than inside it.

fix(matmul): stacked operands with a zero-sized extent — three defects, one shortcut, and the empty sum that is not nan

`np.matmul` threw on ANY operand of 3 dimensions or more carrying a zero-sized
dimension. Nothing to do with the optional BLAS package — it reproduced with
NumSharp.Core alone, `engine.Blas == null`:

    (0,3,4)@(0,4,5)  zero BATCH -> InvalidOperationException   [numpy: (0,3,5)]
    (2,3,0)@(2,0,5)  zero K     -> IndexOutOfRangeException    [numpy: (2,3,5) zeros]
    (2,0,4)@(2,4,5)  zero M     -> IndexOutOfRangeException    [numpy: (2,0,5)]
    (2,3,4)@(2,4,0)  zero N     -> IndexOutOfRangeException    [numpy: (2,3,0)]
    (0,3,4)@(4,5)    zero batch -> IncorrectShapeException     [numpy: (0,3,5)]
                     + broadcast

`np.dot` and the 2-D `np.matmul` path were both already correct, so the defect
was confined to `DefaultEngine.BatchedMatmul` — and it was THREE independent
defects, each with its own symptom, not one:

1. `BroadcastStackDims` resolved a stack pair with `Math.Max`, so `0` against
   `1` gave **1**. NumPy's rule is "the length-1 axis takes the OTHER extent",
   and that extent may be zero: `np.broadcast_shapes((0,), (1,))` is `(0,)`.
   Max turned an empty stack into a one-element stack and then demanded a
   `(0,3,4)` operand be broadcast to `(1,3,4)`, which is not a legal stretch —
   hence the `IncorrectShapeException` on the broadcast case. Now takes the
   extent that isn't 1. (`0` against `n > 1` still raises, as NumPy does.)

2. The batch odometer is constructed BEFORE the loop and rejects an empty
   iteration space, so a zero stack dim threw even though the loop body would
   never have run.

3. A sub-view of a zero-sized operand cannot be taken at all: `Shape.GetSubshape`
   bounds-checks `offset >= bufferSize`, and for a `(2,3,0)` array that bound is
   **0**, so even a valid index throws. This is why zero-K/M/N died in
   `lhsB.GetData(index)` before any kernel ran.

## The fix is NumPy's own structure

`any_zero_dim` forces `@TYPE@_matmul` off every blas route into
`matmul_inner_noblas`, where the answer falls out of the loop bounds. Two
outcomes, and neither needs the batch loop:

  * the RESULT is empty — an empty stack dim, or `n == 0` / `m == 0` — so there
    is nothing to write;
  * the result is non-empty but `k == 0`, in which case every entry is an
    EMPTY SUM.

The second is the subtle one and the easy one to get wrong: `(2,3,0)@(2,0,5)`
is NOT empty, it is a `(2,3,5)` of exact zeros, so the work cannot simply be
skipped. NumPy stores `0` into the output cell BEFORE its (zero-trip)
accumulation loop, which is why `nan(2,3,0) @ inf(2,0,5)` is `+0.0` and not
`nan` — probed, not assumed. NumSharp's own 2-D kernels already clear C the
same way (that is what makes the 2-D `(3,0)@(0,5)` case correct today), but on
the `k == 0` batched path no kernel runs at all, so the result is only as
correct as the allocation is zeroed. `new NDArray(dtype, shape)` does zero-fill
(`fillZeros` defaults true -> calloc), but the dependency was implicit and a
plausible future "the kernels overwrite C anyway" optimisation would break it
silently — so the argument is now spelled out at the call site and pinned by a
test that repeats the case 400 times interleaved with deliberately poisoned
allocations of the same size.

The shortcut sits AFTER the `TryMatMulBatched` hook, not before, so the seam
keeps its shape: the backend is still offered the whole stack and still
declines zero-sized extents — which it should, since NumPy excludes them from
its blas routes too. Verified 81/81 identical (shape, dtype, and result BITS)
with a real scipy-openblas backend enabled vs disabled, across float32 /
float64 / int32 and the whole degenerate + non-degenerate pair matrix.

feat(blas): ship NumPy's own OpenBLAS in the package — and pin the two variables the binary does not

The package promised results "bit-identical to a NumPy that calls the same binary" and then left
finding that binary to the consumer: discovery walked PATH looking for a python whose numpy.libs
held an OpenBLAS. A .NET user with no Python got the managed GEMM and no parity at all.

It now BUNDLES the binary, as `runtimes/<rid>/native/` NuGet assets for 8 RIDs (62 MB packed).

docs/GEMM_PARITY.md §6 argued the opposite — "bundling one would make results depend on which copy
won the loader race, and parity is a claim about a specific binary". That objection was to bundling
AN OpenBLAS. It dissolves because the bundled one is NumPy's:

  * NumPy 2.x builds no OpenBLAS. Its wheels bundle the prebuilt scipy-openblas32/64 artifacts from
    PyPI (openblas-libs), pinned in numpy's requirements/ci_requirements.txt at 0.3.31.22.0 and
    consumed by tools/wheels/cibw_before_build.sh.
  * The DLL in that wheel is BYTE-IDENTICAL to the one in numpy 2.4.2's numpy.libs/ — both sha256
    74a408729250596b0973e69fdd954eea…, and NumPy's mangled filename IS that hash's first 32 hex
    chars, because delvewheel names the file by its content.
  * So "bundle a binary" and "call the binary NumPy calls" became the same act. Verified end to end:
    12/12 products bit-exact vs numpy 2.4.2 through the bundled asset (the same 12 were 8-divergent
    on the managed kernels — the control came free from a bug in my own probe).

Discovery order is now fixed and documented rather than incidental: explicit path /
NUMSHARP_PARITY_BLAS (binding, never substituted — not even by the bundled copy) -> BUNDLED ->
numpy.libs on PATH -> bare loader names. Bundled deliberately outranks a discovered numpy.libs: a
library's numeric output must not change because an unrelated `pip install` ran, and an app with no
python must not get a different backend from one that has it. Matching some OTHER numpy stays
possible and is now an explicit act (name it). NUMSHARP_BLAS_BUNDLED=0 drops the bundled entry.

win-arm64 is scipy-openblas32, not 64, because NumPy's own build selects LP64 there. It exports
scipy_cblas_sgemm — prefix, no suffix, 32-bit BLAS int — a scheme CBlasNative.Bind did NOT have, so
binding a win-arm64 numpy's BLAS would have failed outright with "exports no recognizable
cblas_sgemm symbol". Added, ahead of the bare LP64 scheme.

BUNDLING PINS THE BUILD, NOT THE ANSWER. OpenBLAS is DYNAMIC_ARCH and picks a micro-kernel from the
running CPU. Probed, same binary, 1 thread, (512,784)@(784,512) f32:

    unset -> Haswell b9ea5057…    Haswell -> Haswell b9ea5057…  (identical to unset)
    Nehalem -> b6bb0f58…          Sandybridge -> 1903e357…       Core2 -> Katmai 0da21438…
    SkylakeX -> process killed, Illegal instruction

Four consequences, all load-bearing:
  1. OPENBLAS_CORETYPE works, so Blas.ParityCoreType ("Haswell") reproduces the corpus bits on any
     x86-64 with AVX2+FMA.
  2. It is NOT safe to set blindly — it overrides OpenBLAS' capability detection, so naming a kernel
     above the CPU's ISA executes an unsupported instruction. Uncatchable, therefore refused up front
     (PlatformNotSupportedException) for the families with a known ISA floor.
  3. It must be set BEFORE the library loads; OpenBLAS reads it once while initialising.
  4. Thread count is independent — with the core pinned, 1/2/4/24 threads still give four answers.

It is opt-in, not the default: the default must match the NumPy on the same machine, and that NumPy
dispatches by CPU too, so pinning unilaterally would CREATE divergence on any host newer than
Haswell.

Two silent-failure bugs found while building it, both the same class as the ones the last review
caught — the parity feature reporting success while not delivering parity:

  * Environment.SetEnvironmentVariable does NOT reach a native getenv. .NET keeps its own table, so
    setting OPENBLAS_CORETYPE that way reads back correctly and changes nothing: OpenBLAS still
    dispatched Haswell after being told Nehalem. Going through the CRT (ucrtbase!_putenv_s,
    libc!setenv) works. Windows' own SetEnvironmentVariableW does not either — it updates the
    process environment block, not the CRT copy getenv reads.
  * Blas.Enable skipped CBlasNative.Load when a library was already loaded, so a coreType passed on
    any call after the first was DISCARDED WITHOUT A WORD. Found by its own new test. It now either
    already holds (idempotent) or throws.

The host pin identifies the library by CONTENT, not filename. Bundling forced this and it is
strictly stronger. A filename is a poor proxy in both directions: delvewheel mangles it per build
(libscipy_openblas64_-74a4….dll) while the bundled copy of the same bytes is plainly
libscipy_openblas64_.dll — so name-matching skipped the whole 342-case tier on a host that was
genuinely bit-identical (observed the moment bundled discovery landed), and would equally have
ACCEPTED a differently-built library that happened to share a name. matmul_parity.host.jsonl now
carries blas_library_sha256 and MatmulParityPin hashes what it actually loaded; the name check
remains only as a fallback for corpora generated before the field existed. Note the direction: the
excuse got narrower, not wider. Regenerating produced a byte-identical matmul_parity.jsonl.

Packaging mechanics:
  * tools/openblas-manifest.json is the checked-in pin (per-RID wheel URL + sha256, member path,
    extracted library sha256). tools/fetch_openblas.py downloads and verifies BOTH hashes per RID,
    so a re-pointed URL or mutated artifact fails loudly instead of quietly changing the bits.
  * Binaries are gitignored (186 MB unpacked). Building without them staged is fine and produces
    today's asset-free package (warning); -p:RequireOpenBlasAssets=true makes it a hard error for
    release builds; -p:BundleOpenBlas=false skips them entirely. All three paths verified.
  * PackagePath names the full destination FILE. Naming a directory made pack append the recursive
    path on top, silently producing runtimes/linux-x64/native/linux-x64/native/lib… — a path no RID
    resolution matches, so the package would have looked complete and loaded nothing. The current
    RID also has to be packed by the Content item rather than the None glob: a file carried by two
    item types gets one set of pack metadata, and Pack="false" won, dropping the host's own RID.
  * License expression is now compound (Apache-2.0 AND BSD-3-Clause-Attribution AND BSD-2-Clause AND
    (GPL-3.0-or-later WITH GCC-exception-3.1)) with THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.txt, rather than hiding
    native payload behind the managed project's license. The libgfortran exception is what permits
    redistribution here, and is the same basis on which NumPy and SciPy ship it in every wheel.

perf(math): tanh joins exp/log/sin/cos as a BIT-EXACT NumPy port — and is the first to also replace a float64 loop

np.tanh was the last PORTABLE divergence in NumSharp's float unary surface. MathF.Tanh/Math.Tanh
(the platform libm, ~correctly rounded) differed from NumPy 2.4.2 on 9.7% of float32 and 8.1% of
float64 inputs — all of it inside the blanket `unary ~ULP` fuzz excuse, so it was being absorbed
silently. Both widths are now ports of the kernel NumPy actually runs.

WHAT NUMPY RUNS
  numpy/_core/src/umath/loops_hyperbolic.dispatch.cpp.src — simd_tanh_f32 / simd_tanh_f64,
  converted by NumPy from Intel SVML's svml_z0_tanh_{s,d}_la. tanh is odd, so the kernel works on
  |x| and ORs the sign back at the end. [0, SATURATION_THRESHOLD) splits into 32 subintervals at
  f32 / 16 at f64; the exponent field of |x| indexes a table of per-subinterval minimax
  coefficients plus a recentring offset b, and the answer is a degree-6 / degree-16 Horner
  evaluation of P(|x| - b). The top subintervals hold 1 + 0*y + 0*y^2 ..., which is how the
  saturated range returns exactly +-1 through the same arithmetic instead of a branch.

  tanh is the ONLY one of these ports that also replaces a float64 loop. exp/log/sin/cos fall
  through to the platform's scalar npy_* at f8 and already agreed bit-for-bit there; NumPy ships
  its own tanh at BOTH widths, so both BCL calls diverged and both are replaced.

  Unlike exp/log/sincos the FMA here is NOT a host pin: this kernel spells its Horner steps as
  hn::MulAdd — an explicit fused multiply-add — so FusedMultiplyAdd is a literal transcription
  rather than a bet on MSVC contracting a separate mul+add.

THE COEFFICIENT FETCH IS A TRANSPOSE, NOT A GATHER
  The one deliberate departure from the shape of NumPy's own AVX2 code, and it is what makes the
  port fast. A subinterval's 8 f32 coefficients are 8 CONSECUTIVE floats — exactly one Vector256 —
  so the whole table read is 8 contiguous row loads plus an 8x8 transpose that lands each
  coefficient across the lanes, where a gather-per-coefficient issues 8 vgatherdps: 64 separate
  element loads for the same 8 rows. Both were implemented and measured, bit-identical against the
  same table: transpose 0.071 ms vs gather 0.124 ms at 100K, and 7.41 vs 12.87 ms at 10M — 1.7x,
  the difference between losing to NumPy and beating it.

  float64 stays SCALAR on purpose: its lookup would cost 18 gathers per 4 lanes, and the scalar
  kernel already outruns NumPy by ~1.5x. Vector512 is composed from two verified Vector256 halves
  rather than an AVX-512 gather that cannot be tested on this host. Vector128 keeps the simple
  gather — the emitter picks 128 only when 256 is NOT accelerated, which on x86 means no AVX2 and
  therefore the scalar path anyway.

VERIFICATION
  float32: ALL 2^32 bit patterns agree with NumPy 2.4.2, through BOTH the emitted SIMD kernel and
  the scalar entry point (chunked-checksum sweep, 512 chunks). A negative control proves the
  checksums are not vacuous — the pre-port MathF.Tanh differs in 34 of the 512 chunks (the rest of
  the space saturates to +-1 or is NaN, where libm already agreed), while the port matches in 512.
  float64 admits no exhaustive sweep, so: 4.83 billion values — 2^32 covering every
  sign x exponent x 2^20 mantissa prefix, plus 5.4e8 full-width splitmix64 patterns — all matching
  through both paths.
  Every np.tanh route re-checked bit-exact: contiguous SIMD, f64 scalar, strided ::2, out=, and
  the fused np.evaluate path at both dtypes (a miss on the CanUseUnarySimd or NDExpr seam would
  have shown here as the old kernel silently surviving).

SPECIALS (probed): any NaN — quiet, signalling, either sign, any payload — returns the canonical
  0x7fc00000 / 0x7ff8000000000000 (note .NET's own float.NaN is 0xffc00000); +-inf and every |x|
  past the saturation cut return +-1; +-0 returns +-0 with the sign bit intact (subinterval 0 has
  b = c0 = 0 and c1 = 1, so the polynomial collapses to |x| and the sign is OR-ed back).

GATES
  - numpy_f32_kernels.jsonl 120 -> 140 cases: tanh's 32 subinterval seams +-1 ULP, the saturation
    cut, every NaN spelling, across the same 20-layout sweep the other kernels get.
  - NEW numpy_f64_kernels.jsonl (24 cases) — the f8 seams, +-0/+-inf/NaN, and the int32-and-wider
    dtypes that promote INTO this loop. A separate tier rather than more rows in the f32 one,
    because the dtype axis genuinely differs.
  - MisalignedRegistry: tanh carved out of the unary-ULP excuse at BOTH widths
    (NumPyPortedFloat32Kernels + the new NumPyPortedFloat64Kernels), so a 1-ULP drift is now a hard
    failure rather than an excused algorithm difference.
  - OpenBugs.FuzzGate B8: tanh moved out of the "still excused" list into the ported carve-out,
    plus a float64 tightness test and a companion pinning that f8 exp/log/sin/cos KEEP the
    envelope — both directions, so the carve-out cannot silently widen.
  - Teeth test: sabotaging the kernel turns both tiers red; restored, green.

PERF (NPY/NS, higher = NumSharp faster; Release, best-of-21 warm, out=, 100K / 10M)
  float32   0.18x / 0.19x  ->  1.78x / 1.82x    (9.9x / 9.7x faster than the MathF.Tanh it replaces)
  float64   0.70x / 0.68x  ->  1.90x / 1.92x    (2.7x / 2.8x faster than Math.Tanh)

REMAINING, measured and documented but NOT ported: exp2 (0.04% / 0.02% of inputs, 1 ULP) and
expm1/log1p (31.1% / 30.7% and 33.6% / 15.1%). None is portable — NumPy calls the CRT for all
three — but expm1/log1p additionally carry a genuine accuracy defect independent of parity:
NumSharp computes them as Exp(x)-1 / Log(1+x), so expm1(1e-8) returns exactly 0 where NumPy
returns 1e-8, and expm1(-0.0) loses its sign. .NET's own float.ExpM1/double.ExpM1/LogP1 are
themselves just Exp(x)-1 / Log(1+x) and do not help.
