fix(matmul,indexing): float16 accumulates in float32 like NumPy, and a valid index into a zero-sized array stops throwing

A differential parity pass over 301 byte-exact cases (Python records the
operand bytes and NumPy 2.4.2's answer, C# replays and bit-compares) plus a
36-operation zero-size API sweep. Two portable wrong answers came out of it,
both fixed here; a third finding was investigated and WITHDRAWN.

## F1 — float16 matrix products accumulated in half, not float32

NumPy's `matmul_inner_noblas` declares `float sum = 0`, accumulates every half
product in FLOAT32, and narrows once with `npy_float_to_half(sum)`; `HALF_dot`
does the same with `float tmp = 0.`. NumSharp accumulated in `Half`. That does
not merely lose a ulp — it SATURATES, because half's spacing above 2048 is 2,
so `2048 + 1 == 2048`:

                              NumSharp     NumPy
    ones(3000).ones(3000)         2048      3000
    ones(4096).ones(4096)         2048      4096
    2s(3000).2s(3000)             8190     12000
    [1, 2^-11 x9] @ ones(10)    0x3c00    0x3c04

Visible from k=10 with ordinary values, and UNCONDITIONAL: half is the one
float dtype NumPy does not hand to cblas, so no BLAS backend was ever masking
it. The relevant row of matmul.c.src is

    #TYPE    = FLOAT, DOUBLE, LONGDOUBLE, HALF, CFLOAT, CDOUBLE, ...
    #USEBLAS =     1,      1,          0,    0,      1,       1, 0*13#

which also means `matmul_inner_noblas` IS NumPy's shipping implementation for
half — so unlike float32/float64 this is reproducible exactly, on any host,
with no native dependency. It belongs in the portable corpus, not the
host-pinned matmul_parity tier.

Three kernels needed the wider accumulator, each reached by a different entry
point: `MatMulStridedSame<Half>` (matmul 2-D / 1-D / batched and the 2-D dot),
`DotGeneric<Half>` (the fused 1-D inner product), and `MatMulStridedMixed<Half>`
(half against bool/int8/uint8, which still promote to float16 — those operands
are all exact in half, so reading them through float loses nothing NumPy's own
input cast would have kept). The accumulator is a float ROW rather than NumPy's
scalar, purely to keep the cache-friendly j-inner loop: for a given output cell
the additions still run over k in ascending order, which is all that fixes the
bits. `np.sum(float16)` was already correct and is untouched, as are
float32/float64/integer products.

## F3 — a valid integer index into a zero-sized array threw

    np.zeros((2,3,0))[0]     NumPy (3,0)     NumSharp IndexOutOfRangeException
    np.zeros((2,3,0))[0,0]   NumPy (0,)      NumSharp IndexOutOfRangeException

`Shape.GetSubshape` bounds-checks the computed offset against
`bufferSize > 0 ? bufferSize : size`, which is 0 for an empty array — so EVERY
offset, the correct one included, compared out of range. This is the general
form of the bug that forced the degenerate-stack shortcut in the previous
commit's `BatchedMatmul`.

The check is only a BUFFER backstop: NumPy's real rule, per-axis validation
with the verbatim `index N is out of bounds for axis I with size D`, already
ran in `Shape.InferNegativeCoordinates` before this point. So it now fires only
when the sub-view actually addresses an element, computed lazily so the
ordinary path pays nothing. Both `GetSubshape` overloads (long[] and the
long*/ndims one) carry it.

That exposed a second layer for an empty WINDOW over a live buffer — `x[:, 1:1]`
narrows `InternalArray` to Count 0 while the shape's strides still step across
the original rows, so `[1]` asked to slice at offset 2 of a 0-element array and
`IArraySlice`'s range guard (rightly) refused. A zero-length slice has no
element to address, so the eight sub-view call sites route through a
`SliceForSubview` helper that starts an empty slice at 0. Where a length-0
slice points is unobservable.

Bounds are RELAXED, not removed — pinned by tests: out-of-range still raises
`IndexError` on every axis, a zero in the LEADING axis still makes even index 0
invalid (as in NumPy), and non-empty neighbours are byte-identical.

## Withdrawn — the `np.dot(0-d, ...)` signed zero was not a bug

`np.dot(-2.5, B)` where `B` holds `+0.0` returns `+0.0` in NumPy and `-0.0`
from a plain multiply, so this looked like a third defect. It is not: NumPy's
0-d branch of `PyArray_MatrixProduct2` IS a plain multiply, it just sits below
the `HAVE_CBLAS` shortcut, so only the four cblas dtypes reach
`cblas_matrixproduct` and come back `+0.0`. Probed: NumPy gives `-0.0` for
float16 and longdouble — exactly what NumSharp gives for every dtype. The
managed answer is NumPy's own non-BLAS answer, and with the package installed
NumSharp already returns `+0.0` for float32/float64. "Fixing" it by adding zero
would have BROKEN float16 parity. Recorded in GEMM_PARITY.md section 10 so it
is not re-opened.

## Also documented, not fixed: complex64/complex128 are BLAS dtypes

`CFLOAT`/`CDOUBLE` have `USEBLAS = 1`, so NumPy's complex matrix products are
zgemm's bits exactly as float32/float64 are sgemm's. Measured 40/40 complex128
cases divergent at every depth including k=4 (they agree only on small exact
integers, where summation order cannot matter). That is the documented
"no portable algorithm can fix it" class — but GEMM_PARITY.md scoped the
backend to float32/float64 and justified the fall-through only for integers
("modular addition is associative"), leaving complex silently in the divergent
bucket. Now stated. Closing it is a package-side job (add zgemm/cgemm routes);
the seam already supports it.

## Gates

  * `LinearAlgebra/np.matmul.HalfAccumulator.Test.cs` — 8 new tests: the
    saturation cases, sub-resolution values, all five entry points, strided /
    F-order / transposed operands, the mixed dtypes, nan/inf and accumulator
    overflow, k==0, and controls proving float32/float64/int32 are unchanged.
    The nan case builds its operand from NumPy's BIT PATTERN, not `double.NaN`
    — .NET's NaN literal is negative (0xfe00 as half) where NumPy's is positive
    (0x7e00), so the literal would have compared two different inputs.
  * `Backends/EmptyArrayCrashRegressionTests.cs` — 5 new tests for F3:
    empty views returned, out-of-range still raising, the live-buffer window,
    non-empty neighbours unaffected, and the empty sub-view being a usable array.
  * `matmul` oracle tier +288 cases (`gen_oracle.gen_matmul_half_depth`:
    k in {8,64,256,1024,3000,4096} x 4 value classes x C/F x
    matmul/dot/1-D/batched/mixed). The tier already carried float16 but every
    shape in it has k <= 4, where a half accumulator and a float32 one agree
    exactly — which is why this was invisible.
  * index oracle +28 curated cases on two new bases, `E30` (3,0) and `E230`
    (2,3,0) — a zero in a TRAILING axis, so a leading integer index is VALID.
    The pre-existing `E03` (0,3) only ever exercised the raising direction.

Deliberately CURATED-ONLY, not added to the random pools: the random tokens
reach FANCY indexing, and gathering through a fancy index on a zero-sized

Making the empty case work means giving fancy indexing NumPy's real per-axis

still raises — a change to a hot, security-sensitive path that does not belong
in this commit. Pinned as `OpenBugsFuzzGapsTests.FancyIndex_ZeroSizedSource`
with the carve comment at the generator site pointing there, per the house
convention.

fix(build): strong-naming lived in a configuration nothing builds — every published NumSharp has shipped unsigned since 2019

The repository has carried a signing key since v0.10.4 and has never once used it.
`SignAssembly` was set inside a `<PropertyGroup Condition="…=='Publish|AnyCPU'">` while CI
builds AND packs `--configuration Release`, so the property never evaluated on any path that
produces an artifact. Verified against the artifacts rather than inferred: the DLLs inside
`packages/NumSharp.0.60.0.nupkg` and `NumSharp.0.40.0.nupkg`, and every `bin/Release` output,
all read `PublicKeyToken=null`.

The `Publish` configuration could not have rescued it, because `Publish` did not compile:
strong-naming turns a keyless `InternalsVisibleTo` into a hard `CS1726`, and all SEVEN of ours
were keyless — five in `NumSharp.Core/Assembly/Properties.cs`, two in
`NumSharp.Interop.BLAS/AssemblyInfo.cs` (a file the first pass of this work missed; the build
found it). A `#if !SIGNING` guard was written to cover exactly this, but `SIGNING` was defined
only in `test/NumSharp.UnitTest/NumSharp.UnitTest.csproj` — a different assembly, where it
guards nothing. So the guard never fired, the config was never built, and nothing asserted the
identity: three independent failures, each of which hid the other two.

WHAT THE KEY IS. `Open.snk` is Microsoft's *published* open-source key, byte-identical (596 B,
md5 2fe5bdce…) to `dotnet/arcade`'s `src/Microsoft.DotNet.Arcade.Sdk/tools/snk/Open.snk` —
downloaded and hash-compared, not assumed. Token `cc7b13ffcd2ddd51`, the identity `netstandard`,
`System.Memory` and `System.Buffers` carry. TensorFlow.NET signs with the identical key, which is
why we keep it rather than mint our own: a NumSharp key would break the cross-repo
`InternalsVisibleTo("TensorFlowNET.UnitTest")` for no gain. Its private half is public BY DESIGN,
so this is assembly IDENTITY — version binding, distinguishing this NumSharp from another — and
explicitly NOT authenticity. `InternalsVisibleTo` here is not an access control and must not be
mistaken for one. Authenticode and NuGet author signing are a separate tier, need a code-signing
certificate, and are NOT part of this change.

Changes:
  * Directory.Build.props (new, repo root) — `SignAssembly` defaults true for every project,
    `AssemblyOriginatorKeyFile` resolves via `$(MSBuildThisFileDirectory)` so it is correct from
    any working directory. Opt out with `<SignAssembly>false</SignAssembly>`; nothing needs to.
  * Open.snk consolidated 5 copies -> 1 at the repo root. The five were byte-identical, and the
    per-project copies existed only because each csproj named a relative path.
  * All 7 InternalsVisibleTo now carry `PublicKey=`, via a `NumSharpFriendKey`/`BlasFriendKey`
    const so the 320-char literal is written once per assembly (`"name, PublicKey=" + const` is a
    compile-time constant, which is what an attribute argument requires).
  * NumSharp.Interop.BLAS is now signed. It consumes Core's internals, so a keyed friend
    declaration only matches it once it carries the same key.
  * Removed the dead `#if !SIGNING` guard and the `SIGNING` define from the test csproj, plus the
    now-redundant per-project SignAssembly/AssemblyOriginatorKeyFile/DelaySign and the
    `<None Remove="Open.snk" />` items.

Gate — test/NumSharp.UnitTest/Assembly/StrongNameTests.cs (6 tests). A build failure is NOT
sufficient coverage here: the failure mode was output that compiled fine and merely lacked an
identity, which only a runtime assertion catches. It pins the token, the full public key (so the
four copies of the literal cannot drift apart silently), that friend access genuinely resolves by
touching an internal, and that no friend declaration is keyless — a wrong key compiles and simply
never matches.

Verified: solution builds 0 errors in Debug and Release; 24/24 built assemblies and 6/6 DLLs
inside freshly packed NumSharp / NumSharp.Bitmap / NumSharp.Interop.BLAS packages carry
cc7b13ffcd2ddd51; no CS8002 anywhere (all 553/1199 warnings pre-existing: CA1416, nullable,

fix(indexing): fancy indexing of a zero-sized array, and the 0-d bool a setter dropped when it ran out of axes

Two defects in the advanced-indexing gather/scatter, both silent-wrong or spuriously
throwing, both found by differential parity against NumPy 2.4.2 rather than a report.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. A non-empty fancy index into a source whose SIZE is 0 threw
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

    np.zeros((3,0))[np.array([0,1])]              NumPy (2,0)     NumSharp threw
    np.zeros((3,0))[np.array([[2,-3],[0,0]])]     NumPy (2,2,0)   NumSharp threw
    np.zeros((2,3,0))[np.array([0,1])]            NumPy (2,3,0)   NumSharp threw
    np.zeros((3,0))[np.array([0,1])] = 5          NumPy no-op     NumSharp threw

    IndexOutOfRangeException: Index [0] exceeds given NDArray's bounds. NDArray is shaped (3,0).

This is the FANCY sibling of the basic-indexing fix in 03d0f0c8 — same symptom class,
a different guard, and the reason that fix stopped where it did. Fancy indexing flattens
each gathered coordinate to one buffer offset and compares it against
LargestReachableOffset(shape, size), which for a contiguous empty source is `size - 1`
== **-1** — below every offset it is ever compared against. So every gather into a
zero-sized source was rejected, the valid ones included.

WHY THIS IS SAFE TO DISENGAGE, and why it is not the "skip the check when empty" trade
the earlier pass declined to make. That comparison is NOT what makes a fancy index valid.
Every index value has already been checked against ITS OWN axis extent (-dim <= idx < dim)
in two places: ScanFancyBounds (NDArray.Indexing.PrepareIndex.cs — a port of NumPy's
mapping.c, axis-major, with the verbatim IndexError text) and again per value inside
PrepareIndexGetters. That layer is what rejects np.zeros((3,0))[[5]] and
np.zeros((0,3))[[0]], and it is untouched. The flat-offset compare is only the
memory-safety backstop for the DEREFERENCE that follows.

A zero-sized source has no dereference to guard. Its empty extent is either an INDEXED
axis — where the per-axis layer already rejected every possible index value, leaving only
an empty index array whose loop body never runs — or a TRAILING one, which makes every
gathered/scattered block subShapeSize == 0: zero bytes copied, no address read.

Only the UPPER half is disengaged, via a new OffsetBackstopUpperBound() shared by both
call sites. The `< 0` half stays live unconditionally: a negative computed offset (an
exotic strided / negative-stride view whose GetOffset underflows below the buffer base)
would read or write BEFORE the buffer, a wild access that can land in the GC heap.

The setter carried its own copy of the same guard and had the same defect. Fixing it also
un-masked NumPy's real error there — `np.zeros((3,0))[[0,1]] = [1,2]` now raises
ValueError "shape mismatch: value array of shape (2,) could not be broadcast to indexing
result of shape (2,0)" instead of an IndexOutOfRangeException about a buffer offset.

Verified: 15/15 dtypes, 10 zero-size layouts (contiguous, 3-D, transposed, row/col-strided,
negative-stride, offset windows over a live buffer), every integer index dtype, gather and
scatter, 200 reps each under forced GC — plus the bounds still rejecting on non-empty
sources through strided and negative-stride views, and gathered VALUES unchanged.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2. A 0-d boolean was dropped by the setter when its siblings consumed every axis
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

    b = np.arange(24).reshape(2,3,4)
    b[-1, 2:, -2, np.array(False)] = -7      NumPy: no-op    NumSharp: wrote at flat 22

A 0-d boolean is NumPy's HAS_0D_BOOL: it consumes NO source axis and contributes an axis
of its own, length 1 (True) or 0 (False). TrySetSliceWithSingleAdvanced maps its one
advanced item ONTO a source axis, so it cannot express that — and when the other items
already consume every axis, its axis-mapping loop stops at `curAxis < ndim` and the bool
is silently dropped, leaving a real write where NumPy writes nothing. It only ever looked
correct when an axis was left over (b[0, 2:, False]), which placed the empty nonzero()
index and emptied the grid by accident.

TryBuild0dBoolWithBasic already declines a NON-CONSECUTIVE advanced block on purpose and
documents that TryBuildMultiAdvancedGrid — which carries MixKind.ZeroBool and models this
properly — should own it. TrySetSliceWithSingleAdvanced runs in between and was
intercepting it on the way there; it now declines a 0-d boolean too.

The GETTER was already correct in all 11 probed forms and is unchanged. The True twin
still writes (a length-1 axis, not a length-0 one) — the fix must not turn every 0-d bool
into a no-op, and a test pins that.

Found by the index-oracle random tier (set/B/rand/9804) once the zero-sized bases entered
the pools; base B is (2,3,4), so no empty array is involved. Pre-existing and independent
of defect 1 — fixed here because re-enabling those pools surfaces it.

Tests

ci(signing): gate the packed artifact, not just the build — plus a release-day runbook

Tier 1 made the assemblies strong-named. This makes the pipeline keep them that way.

The defect being defended against is not "the build breaks", it is "the build succeeds and the
artifact quietly has no identity" — which is exactly what happened for six years, invisibly,
because nothing ever inspected a shipped DLL. A compile gate cannot catch that class; only an
assertion about the packed package can.

tools/verify_strong_name.cs — cross-platform, dependency-free package verifier. Reads PE metadata
straight out of the .nupkg (no sn.exe, which is Windows-only, and no temp files), so it runs on the
ubuntu-latest release runner. Per lib/**/*.dll it asserts the FULL public key (stronger than the
token alone), the token, and the StrongNameSigned CorFlag — the last being what separates a real
signature from a delay-signed image, which carries the public key and an empty signature blob and
therefore reports a perfectly correct token while being unverifiable. runtimes/**/native/ is
skipped (OpenBLAS is unmanaged).

It refuses to pass vacuously: no packages found, or a package with no lib assembly, is exit 1. A
verifier that silently checks nothing is worse than no verifier because it renders as a green tick,
and this repo has already been bitten by that shape (NumpyCompatibilityTests asserting nothing on a
clean checkout). Proven to have teeth against three negative controls — the real, historically
shipped packages/NumSharp.0.40.0.nupkg is caught ("no public key"), and both an empty directory and
a nonexistent path exit 1.

Workflow changes:
  * build-nuget gains "Verify strong naming of packed assemblies" after Pack, before upload — the
    last gate before an artifact leaves the machine.
  * NEW job verify-signing, on EVERY push and PR. build-nuget only exists on a tag push, and a
    release-only gate is precisely how the original defect survived: nothing evaluated the signing
    configuration until someone looked at a shipped DLL. ~1 min, packs a throwaway version to a
    scratch directory, publishes nothing. It also asserts Open.snk's size and sha256 BEFORE
    building, so a missing key or a dropped `*.snk binary` rule in .gitattributes (line-ending
    corruption of a binary key) reports as itself rather than as a baffling signing failure.
    Tolerates NumSharp.Interop.BLAS being absent, since it does not exist on every branch.

Prepared but NOT exercisable until a real tag: the tag -> validate-release -> build-nuget ->
create-release -> publish-nuget chain. Simulated locally with the exact commands instead —
build+pack at Version=0.61.0-rc.1/AssemblyVersion=0.61.0 including `pack --no-build`, then verify:
green, 4/4 assemblies. The verify-signing job was simulated end to end too: 6/6 assemblies across
all three packages. All four workflow YAMLs re-parse clean.

docs/SIGNING_HANDOVER.md — the continuation document. Current state of both tiers; what CI now
covers and on which trigger; what is verified locally with its evidence; what genuinely cannot be
checked before release day; a release-day runbook with explicit abort criteria (a failed verify is
wrong, not flaky — delete the tag, do not re-run the job); the open decisions; and the Tier 2 plan.

docs(math): tanh's V128 gather and its 128-bit gate are load-bearing — record why, with the measurements

Documentation only; NDFloatMath.Simd.cs's executable code is byte-identical to f5f21ff3 (verified:
the diff vs HEAD contains no non-comment line). Both notes exist because a code review of that
commit reached the opposite conclusion on each, and the probe disproved it. Without these the same
two "cleanups" are near-certain to be proposed again.

1. `IsTanhVectorAccelerated`'s `128` arm is NOT dead code.
   The reasoning that kills it is seductive and wrong: the emitter picks a width from
   Vector{N}.IsHardwareAccelerated, 128 wins only when Vector256 is not accelerated, in .NET that
   means AVX2 is absent, therefore `128 => Avx2.IsSupported` can never be true. The
   counter-example is a supported runtime knob, not exotic hardware — with
   DOTNET_PreferredVectorBitWidth=128 an ordinary AVX2 host reports VectorBits=128 while
   Avx2.IsSupported stays true (probed on this machine: VectorBits=128, Avx2=True, Fma=True).
   Deleting the arm demotes tanh to the scalar loop for every user who caps the width — a pure
   perf regression that NO correctness gate can catch, because the bits are identical either way.

2. The two lookup strategies (gather at 128, 8x8 transpose at 256) are a measured decision.
   The verdict genuinely flips with the lane count. A subinterval is 8 consecutive floats, so the
   transpose reads whole rows and wins when 8 lanes each need one. At 4 lanes it does not:
   expressing V128 as the low half of an 8-lane call — which WOULD give the file a single table
   read — computes four lanes it discards. Measured under DOTNET_PreferredVectorBitWidth=128,
   100K / 10M:

     gather (shipped)          0.139 / 13.58 ms     1.31x / 1.39x over the scalar kernel
     composed from V256        0.171 / 17.56 ms     1.06x / 1.07x over the scalar kernel

   i.e. unifying on one strategy costs 23-29% on the one configuration where V128 actually runs,
   and leaves it barely ahead of not vectorizing at all. Both forms were verified bit-exact
   against the same table before the comparison, so this is purely a speed question.

Re-verified after the round trip: Vector128/256/512 all 0 mismatches against the NumPy reference,
every np.tanh route (contiguous, f64 scalar, strided, out=, fused np.evaluate) bit-exact under BOTH
the default and the capped width, FuzzMatrix 98/98.

test(math): prove tanh's one re-spelled line against NumPy exhaustively, and pin the stackalloc that reads like a wart

Review follow-up on two items in the tanh port. Neither changes a line of kernel arithmetic — the
executable code is byte-identical to f5f21ff3, which is the commit verified over all 2^32 float32
inputs. What changes is that two things previously supported by an ARGUMENT are now supported by a
CHECK, and a third is recorded so it stops being re-proposed.

D. The float64 index extraction is now PROVEN equivalent to NumPy's, not argued.

   Tanh(double) transcribes simd_tanh_f64 operation for operation with exactly one exception: NumPy
   clamps the subinterval index with a 32-bit Max/Min over the 64-bit lanes ("it's fine ... since
   we're not crossing 32-bit edge"), while NumSharp clamps the high half directly, because C# has no
   natural way to spell "reinterpret longs as ints, clamp, reinterpret back" on the scalar path.
   That made it the one line a reviewer cannot check by diffing against NumPy's source.

   It turns out the claim is decidable outright rather than by sampling. ndnan = bits &
   0x7ff8000000000000 keeps only the 11 exponent bits and mantissa bit 51 and clears everything
   else, and NEITHER formula reads anything but ndnan — so the entire input domain is 2^12 = 4096
   values. The new test enumerates all 4096 and asserts the two spellings agree on every one, and a
   companion test pins the other half of the claim: that real double bit patterns actually reach all
   4096, so the domain is exact rather than an over-approximation that merely covers the interesting
   cases. Previously this rested on a 4.83-billion-value sweep, which is a lot of evidence for a
   statement that can simply be proven.

G. The stackalloc in the 8-lane kernel is not a wart; both "fixes" for it are neutral or worse.

   Spilling the 8 row offsets through the stack is the only stack traffic in the hot loop, and
   without [SkipLocalsInit] the JIT may zero the buffer per call — so it reads as free to remove.
   Measured THROUGH THE EMITTED KERNEL (10M float32, Release, best-of-21 warm, out=):

     as shipped (stackalloc)            7.39-7.50 ms
     + [SkipLocalsInit]                 7.24-7.84 ms   inside run-to-run variance, no gain
     offsets via row.GetElement(i) x8   8.60 ms        ~16% SLOWER, clearly outside it

   The GetElement form was adopted briefly on the strength of a standalone microbenchmark that
   ranked it FASTEST, and the real kernel reversed that: the JIT schedules this differently when the
   method is inlined into a C# loop than into the IL-emitted one, so a script harness is not a valid
   proxy here. That reversal is the reason the numbers are now written down next to the code.

feat(linalg): the whole OpenBLAS/LAPACK API surface — products that compute, factorisations that say what is missing

np.dot and np.matmul were never all NumPy routes through the OpenBLAS binary this repo now bundles.
Missing entirely: the rest of the CBLAS product family (inner, vdot, and the three NumPy 2.x gufuncs
vecdot/matvec/vecmat), tensordot, and np.linalg — a module NumSharp did not have at all, 31 public
functions plus LinAlgError. This lands the complete public API, its NumPy-exact validation and its
engine seam, in one pass. Whether the NUMERICS exist splits in two, and the split is a property of
the problem rather than a decision:

  PRODUCTS (inner, vdot, vecdot, matvec, vecmat, tensordot, linalg.multi_dot, matrix_power n>=0,
  the linalg Array-API forms, and every linalg.norm order except matrix 2/-2/'nuc')
      -> COMPUTE, with managed kernels. IBlasBackend's invariant holds: installing a backend
         changes WHICH implementation runs, never WHETHER an answer exists. A portable GEMM is a
         hundred lines.

  FACTORISATIONS (cholesky det slogdet eig eigvals eigh eigvalsh inv pinv lstsq qr solve svd
  svdvals matrix_rank cond tensorinv tensorsolve, matrix_power n<0, norm matrix 2/-2/'nuc')
      -> NotSupportedException from TensorEngine. Core ships no managed LU, QR, SVD or
         eigensolver, so there is nothing to fall back to. A portable gesdd is a library in its own
         right. The message names the NumPy API, the LAPACK routine NumPy uses and the
         IBlasBackend.Try* member to implement, so it reads as an install instruction, not a dead
         end.

ONE SEAM, NOT TWO

Everything dispatches through the existing TensorEngine.Blas property. IBlasBackend.LinearAlgebra.cs
adds 15 Try* members — five products, ten factorisations — ALL of them default interface
implementations returning false. That is what let the file exist without touching OpenBlasBackend,
which implements none of them and builds and behaves exactly as before (a default interface member
is interface-dispatched and invisible on the implementing class; the test that proves this types its
variable as IBlasBackend precisely because it must).

LAPACK belongs on this property rather than a second one because it lives inside the very binary
already bundled: scipy-openblas ships gesv/getrf/potrf/geev/syevd/heevd/gesdd/geqrf/orgqr/gelsd next
to the BLAS symbols, so a backend that has loaded the library for sgemm already holds the handle for
everything else. TensorEngine's members are virtual (not abstract) so an alternative engine
overrides only what it implements, and each reads Blas into a LOCAL before calling it —
GEMM_PARITY.md section 9, where a test-then-call on a settable property measured ~2% NREs under a
concurrent Blas.Disable().

VALIDATION IS NOT DEFERRED — which is the point of the pass

Every entry point runs NumPy's own rank, squareness, dtype and argument checks BEFORE reaching the
seam, with verbatim messages: _assert_stacked_2d, _assert_2d, _assert_stacked_square and _commonType
are ported from numpy/linalg/_linalg.py. So the error contract is gated today by
LinAlgErrorParityTests and does not move when the numerics land — an implementation only has to
supply arithmetic. float16 is REJECTED rather than widened ("array type float16 is unsupported in
linalg") while every other narrow dtype goes to float64; NumSharp's Decimal and Char, which have no
NumPy dtype and so no LAPACK loop either, take float16's exit rather than inventing a new error.

SIX NUMPY BEHAVIOURS WORTH NOT RE-DERIVING (all probed against 2.4.2)

- np.inner reports b's shape ALREADY TRANSPOSED. PyArray_InnerProduct swaps b's last two axes and
  hands the pair to the same PyArray_MatrixProduct2 that backs np.dot, so
  np.inner(ones((2,3)), ones((3,2))) raises "shapes (2,3) and (2,3) not aligned" — the second (2,3)
  being b after the swap.
- np.vdot's length mismatch is a RESHAPE error, and its own length check is unreachable.
  array_vdot flattens both operands through ONE reused PyArray_Dims buffer holding -1;
  _fix_unknown_dimension writes the resolved length back into that buffer, so the SECOND flatten
  asks for (a.size,) rather than (-1,). Hence vdot(ones(3), ones(5)) -> "cannot reshape array of
  size 5 into shape (3,)", and "vectors have different lengths" in the C source can never fire.
  Reproduced, including the 0-d and empty variants.
- vecdot reduces in the LOOP dtype, not NEP50's accumulator: its registered loops are 'ii->i', so an
  int32 pair stays int32 where np.sum would give int64. vecdot/vecmat/vdot conjugate their FIRST
  operand; inner/matvec do not.
- axis= is legal only on vecdot. matvec and vecmat have two DISTINCT core dimensions and NumPy
  raises TypeError for both axis and keepdims, so neither parameter is offered rather than offered
  and thrown.
- tensordot's every disagreement is one message, "shape-mismatch for sum" — mismatched extents, too
  many axes and unequal list lengths alike. A negative count contracts NOTHING, because NumPy forms
  range(-axes, 0) which is empty for any axes <= 0; so axes=-1 is the outer product, not a
  contraction from the other end.
- the np.linalg Array-API forms are NOT aliases of their main-namespace twins, and the differences
  are observable: linalg.trace and linalg.diagonal reduce the LAST two axes where np.trace and
  np.diagonal take the FIRST (a (2,3,3) stack gives (2,) vs (3,)); linalg.outer demands 1-D operands
  where np.outer flattens anything; linalg.cross demands 3-vectors where np.cross still takes the
  deprecated 2-vector form. Each is implemented against its own contract.

TWO FIXES RODE ALONG

- NDArray.matrix_power(-1) used to `throw new Exception("matrix_power just work with int >= 0")`,
  which was never NumPy's rule — a**-n is inv(a)**n. It now takes that route, so a negative power
  computes wherever a backend is installed and reports a missing one otherwise. Three more
  behaviours came with the delegation: a non-square operand raises LinAlgError rather than failing
  inside the product, power 0 returns the identity in the operand's OWN dtype instead of always
  float64, and the chain is binary exponentiation rather than one multiply per step.
- np.dot / np.matmul rendered their "not aligned" shapes as "(2, 3)" where NumPy writes "(2,3)".
  New Shape.ToPythonTuple() renders the Python spelling (no space, trailing comma on a one-element
  shape); Shape.ToString() is left alone, since it renders for humans everywhere else.

VERIFICATION

A 132-case matrix was written twice — once in C#, once in Python — and replayed through both
libraries with values, dtypes, shapes and exception text compared mechanically: 121 bit-exact, 11
expected NotSupportedException, 0 unexplained differences. That run is what caught the two real bugs
fixed before commit: linalg.cross returned (1,3) for a bare 3-vector, and the six remaining "diffs"
turned out to be the documented IncorrectShapeException-vs-ValueError house convention with the
message matching character for character.

fix(linalg): signature audit against NumPy 2.4.2 — a wrong matrix_rank, a missing gufunc parameter, and a reflection gate so neither recurs

A signature is API. Renaming UPLO to uplo or swapping keepdims and ord compiles, passes every value
test, and silently breaks every named-argument call ported from Python — and nothing in the suite
would have noticed. This pass extracted NumPy 2.4.2's own inspect.signature output for all 38
functions the previous commit added and compared it parameter by parameter. Three real defects came
out of it, plus a gate so the class of defect cannot come back.

DEFECT 1 — np.linalg.matrix_rank was WRONG below rank 2

NumPy short-circuits with `int(not all(A == 0))`. That is a PREDICATE: a vector is rank 1 unless
every element is zero. The implementation counted non-zeros instead, so matrix_rank([1,2,3])
returned 3 where NumPy returns 1. It survived the previous pass because a count returns a plausible
number for every non-degenerate input and the 132-case matrix never exercised a sub-2-D operand —
the only matrix_rank case in it was 2-D, which raises NotSupportedException before reaching any of
this. Now `CountNonZero(A) == 0 ? 0 : 1`, with an empty operand at 0 (all([]) is true) and NaN
counting as content.

DEFECT 2 — the three gufuncs were missing NumPy's `axes=` entirely

axes is the general form of axis: one entry per input AND output, naming which axes carry the core
dimensions. It works on all three functions in NumPy and was simply absent here. Now implemented
with NumPy's rules intact:

  - the output entry may be omitted ONLY where the output has no core axes — vecdot alone in this
    family; matvec and vecmat require all three, and a 2-entry list raises NumPy's verbatim
    "axes should be a list with an entry for all 3 inputs and outputs; entries for outputs can only
    be omitted if none of them has core axes."
  - for matvec/vecmat the output entry says where the result's core axis LANDS, so
    np.matvec(a, b, axes: [[-2,-1],[-1],[0]]) transposes the answer.
  - axes with axis raises TypeError("cannot specify both 'axis' and 'axes'").
  - a wrong-arity entry raises AxisError naming both counts:
    "vecdot: operand 0 has 1 core dimensions, but 2 dimensions are specified by axes tuple."

DEFECT 3 — matvec/vecmat omitted axis= and keepdims= rather than rejecting them

Both are in NumPy's signature and both always raise, because those signatures have two DISTINCT core
dimensions. The previous pass reasoned that a parameter which can only throw is better left out;
that was wrong for a porting library. Omitting it turns a runtime TypeError into a compile error
with a different explanation, so a NumPy call transcribed verbatim now fails the same way with the
same message. Both texts are reproduced, including that the keepdims message names input 1's core
rank — which differs per signature (1 for matvec, 2 for vecmat).

ALSO ADDED

np.linalg.vector_norm(x, int axis, ...) — NumPy's axis takes a plain int as readily as a tuple, and
only the tuple form existed.

NEW GATE — LinAlgSignatureParityTests

Reflects over the whole surface and asserts, per function, that an overload exists whose parameter
NAMES appear in NumPy's ORDER; that the 18 defaults NumPy states concretely match (mode="reduced",
UPLO='L', full_matrices=true, ind=2, axis=-1, …); and that no np.linalg member is missing. Two
defaults C# cannot spell — an `object` parameter may only default to null — are carried by a null
SENTINEL and pinned behaviourally rather than by comment: matrix_norm's ord='fro' and vector_norm's
ord=2 are asserted to equal their explicit spellings, and to differ from a wrong one.

Four NumPy ufunc keywords stay deliberately ABSENT from the gufuncs: casting, order, subok and
signature. NumSharp models none of them anywhere in its ufunc surface — signature is what dtype
already does, and subok concerns ndarray subclasses the library does not have — so accepting and
ignoring them would be worse than not offering them. The test documents that rather than leaving it
to be rediscovered.

VERIFICATION

The differential matrix grew from 132 to 376 cases across three files, and now covers the two axes
the Definition of Done requires and the previous pass had not exercised for these functions:

  - DTYPE sweep: 10 dtypes (bool, int8/32/64, uint8/64, float16/32/64, complex128) x 8 operations,
    confirming among other things that vecdot/matvec keep the LOOP dtype at every integer width
    rather than promoting the way np.sum does.
  - LAYOUT sweep: 8 layouts (C, F, transposed, stepped, negative-stride, offset view, reversed rows,
    broadcast) x 14 operations.
  - the new axes= paths, every rejection, matrix_rank below rank 2, and norm breadth.

Result: 362 exact, 5 expected NotSupportedException, 9 house-convention type differences whose
MESSAGES are verbatim, 0 unexplained. The two type-only divergences are pre-existing and now
recorded: the reshape/alignment errors raise IncorrectShapeException where NumPy raises ValueError
(the long-standing convention across the shape APIs), and AxisError derives from
ArgumentOutOfRangeException with paramName "axis", so .NET appends "(Parameter 'axis')" to .Message
— which is why the whole library already asserts axis texts with wildcards. Changing AxisError
would touch 13 call sites across flip/repeat/all/any/quantile/reductions and belongs to its own pass.

feat(einsum): port NumPy's subscript parser in full — the language is complete, only the contraction is missing

np.einsum shipped two commits ago as a signature stub: it threw before reading its own arguments.
That was the agreed scope then and it is the wrong shell for this function, because einsum's
validation IS a language. Every other entry in this family validates shapes; this one has to accept
or reject an expression, infer an output, and resolve a shape. So the parser is now a port of
PyArray_EinsteinSum's parsing block plus parse_operand_subscripts and parse_output_subscripts
(numpy/_core/src/multiarray/einsum.cpp), and only the contraction kernel is absent.

WHAT WORKS

Both spellings NumPy accepts: the subscripts string, and the sublist form
np.einsum(a, [0,1], b, [1,2], [0,2]). Ellipsis broadcasting, repeated-label diagonals,
implicit-output inference, spaces, out=/dtype=/order=/casting=/optimize=. Every expression NumPy
accepts parses; every expression NumPy rejects is rejected with NumPy's own text.

The output SHAPE is resolved, and the NotSupportedException the engine then raises CARRIES it. That
is not decoration: it is what let the entire surface be differential-tested against NumPy without a
kernel existing. The harness reads the shape back out of the message and compares it to the array
NumPy actually returns — 75 expressions, 73 exact, 2 the documented divergence below.

NUMPY HAS TWO EINSUM PARSERS AND THEY DISAGREE

The C one behind the default optimize=False, and a Python one (einsumfunc.py) behind the optimize
path. They word the same rejection differently — "invalid subscript '$' in einstein sum subscripts
string" versus "Character $ is not a valid symbol.", and so on down the list. NumSharp reproduces
the C one whatever optimize says, because that is what a default call hits; reproducing both would
double the surface to mirror a wart, and with no numerics optimize selects nothing anyway.

SIX THINGS THAT ARE EASY TO GET WRONG, ALL PROBED AGAINST 2.4.2

- The two operand-count messages read BACKWARDS. NumPy does not count terms; it walks operand by
  operand checking the delimiter after each chunk (strcspn on ",-"). So ONE operand against TWO
  terms raises "more operands provided to einstein sum function than specified in the subscripts
  string" — the reverse of the truth. Reproduced verbatim: a caller grepping NumPy's message must
  find it.
- An impossible diagonal has TWO messages, chosen by three conditions. nop == 1 && out == null &&
  nothing summed takes NumPy's return-a-view attempt, which says "dimensions in SINGLE OPERAND for
  collapsing index …"; anything else says "dimensions in OPERAND {i} for …". So einsum("ii->i", a)
  and einsum("ii", a) fail differently on the very same array, and adding an out= switches the
  message.
- Every diagonal is validated BEFORE any cross-operand extent. NumPy collapses all operands'
  diagonals (get_combined_dims_view, once per operand) before its iterator ever compares extents
  across operands. Merging the two passes — which is the natural way to write it, and how this was
  written first — makes einsum("ij,jj->ij", ones((2,3)), a23) report a label-size conflict instead of
  operand 1's impossible diagonal. Caught by the differential run and split into two passes.
- The implicit output is ASCII-ordered, so an UPPER-case label sorts before a lower-case one:
  einsum("zA", a) transposes a (2,3) and einsum("Az", a) does not.
- The sublist alphabet is 'ABC…Zabc…z' — UPPER CASE FIRST. This one was written backwards first and
  is worth the paragraph: NumPy 2.4.2's einsum_symbols puts A-Z at indices 0-25 and a-z at 26-51,
  which makes index order and ASCII order the same, which in turn is what makes an inferred output
  come back in the caller's own numbering. The intuitive guess (a-z first) is SILENTLY wrong rather
  than an error — it produces correct answers for every expression that stays inside one half of the
  alphabet, and only diverges on one that mixes them, where einsum(a, [0,26]) on a (2,3) operand
  returns (3,2) instead of (2,3). Also caught by the differential run.
- Spaces are legal anywhere and skipped. A '>' without its '-' is scanned as a label and rejected as
  an invalid subscript; a lone '-' gets the missing-arrow message instead.

The label encoding is NumPy's own, one sbyte per operand dimension: positive is the label's ASCII
code at first occurrence, NEGATIVE is the offset back to that first occurrence (a repeat, i.e. a
diagonal), and 0 is a broadcast dimension from an ellipsis. So "abbcbc" over six dimensions is
[97,98,-1,99,-3,-2]. Keeping NumPy's representation rather than inventing one is what makes the
two-pass ordering above expressible at all.

ONE DELIBERATE DIVERGENCE ([Misaligned])

When a label's extents disagree between operands, NumPy's C path leaks NpyIter's "operands could not
be broadcast together with remapped shapes [original->remapped]: (2,3)->(2,newaxis,3) (4,2)->(2,4)"
— iterator axis bookkeeping rather than anything about the contraction, right down to dropping
leading newaxis entries. NumSharp raises the wording NumPy's OWN einsumfunc.py parser uses for the
identical condition: "Size of label 'j' for operand 1 (3) does not match previous terms (4)." (whose
two sizes also read swapped against the sentence — the first is the size already recorded). Both
texts are NumPy's; this is a choice between them, not an invention.

API NOTE

Pass the keywords BY NAME — np.einsum("ij->i", ops, @out: dst). They are keyword-only in NumPy, and
naming them is also what keeps them unambiguous here: NumSharp converts scalars to NDArray
implicitly, so a fully positional seven-argument call matches both the params overload and the full
one and the compiler rejects it as ambiguous. Documented on the overload itself.

OUT OF SCOPE, DELIBERATELY

np.einsum_path — NumPy's contraction planner is its own public function and its own ~400 lines of
optimal/greedy search. And the contraction kernel. Unlike np.linalg, einsum is NOT waiting on a
backend: a summation kernel over an arbitrary label set and a path planner are NumSharp's own work,
which is why the seam has no TryEinsum and the exception points at np.tensordot rather than at a
package to install.

fix(linalg): multi_dot enforces NumPy's 2-D operand contract — the missing _assert_2d that let a 3-D operand return a silently wrong-shaped product

`np.linalg.multi_dot` was a faithful port of NumPy's `_linalg.py` EXCEPT for one
load-bearing line: `_assert_2d(*arrays)`, which NumPy runs over the operands right
after promoting 1-D endpoints. Without it the Cormen cost model (`Order`) reads a
phantom `dimensions[1]` off any non-matrix, and the outcome depended on luck:

  - a 3-D operand whose leading two dims happened to chain: multi_dot([2x3, 4x3x5,
    5x2]) SILENTLY returned shape (2,4,2) where NumPy raises LinAlgError — a wrong
    ANSWER, not an error;
  - a 3-D operand whose dims did not chain leaked NumSharp's internal
    IncorrectShapeException ("shapes (…) not aligned") instead of LinAlgError;
  - a 0-D or a 1-D operand in a MIDDLE position leaked a raw
    IndexOutOfRangeException ("Index was outside the bounds of the array") — a bare
    .NET bounds error surfacing to the caller.

Probed against NumPy 2.4.2: every one of these is `LinAlgError("{ndim}-dimensional
array given. Array must be two-dimensional")`, raised AFTER the 1-D endpoints are
lifted to row/column, so a 1-D endpoint is still legal and a 1-D middle is not. The
port already carried the exact helper (`linalg.Assert2d`) — it simply was never
called. This adds the one call, placed exactly where NumPy runs it (post-promotion,
n>=3 only; the two-operand path is a plain np.dot and imposes no such restriction,
matching NumPy).

Also brings `out=` to parity. NumPy threads `out` into the FINAL dot, so it receives
the TWO-dimensional product even when an endpoint was a vector, and returns a
reshaped view of it: multi_dot([v, B, C], out=o) wants o shaped (1,k) and returns a
raveled (k,) view — not (k,) in and (k,) out. The result is now delivered into `out`
BEFORE the endpoint reshape, so the returned array aliases `out` exactly as NumPy's
`result.ravel()` aliases it. The common 2-D case is unchanged.

Verified bit-exact against NumPy 2.4.2 across a 12-case sweep — int64 / float64 /
float32 / complex128, chain lengths 2–6, both DP paths (the three-matrix shortcut and
Cormen n>=4), first/last/both vector endpoints, and both out= forms — all shapes,
dtypes and values identical.

Perf (NPY/NS, Release, best-of-7): a chain of six 4x4 matrices (orchestration-bound,
where the DP + the new validation is the whole cost) runs 3.58x faster than NumPy, so
the added guard is not a measurable overhead; larger-matrix chains remain bound by
np.dot's managed GEMM, unchanged by this commit.

MultiDot_MatchesNumPyValues_AcrossChainLengthsAndDtypes and
MultiDot_OutReceivesTheTwoDimensionalProduct_AndReturnsAReshapedView
(LinAlgEngineSeam). Full suite: 12270 passed, 0 failed.

fix(linalg): three NumPy-parity fixes in multi_dot's neighbourhood — tensordot's error taxonomy, vecdot's axes+keepdims, and norm's complex zero-norm dtype

Three closely-related defects in the product/norm surface added alongside multi_dot,
each probed against NumPy 2.4.2 and fixed with the same discipline.

1) np.tensordot — TWO missing behaviours, both restored in NumPy's order:

   a. The `duplicate axes are not allowed in tensordot` check (numeric.py:1181-1184,
      `len(set(axes_a)) != len(axes_a)`) was entirely absent. NumPy runs it FIRST, on
      the RAW axis values, ahead of every shape and range test — so `([5,5],[0,1])` is
      a duplicate, not an index error, and `([0,-2],…)` (a repeat only after
      normalisation) is NOT caught, exactly as upstream. NumSharp silently proceeded to
      a confusing transpose error instead.

   b. An out-of-range contraction axis was reported as `ValueError("shape-mismatch for
      sum")` where NumPy raises `IndexError("tuple index out of range")` — NumPy indexes
      the shape TUPLE with the raw axis (`as_[axes_a[k]]`), so it is an index error, not
      a shape mismatch. This fires for the int form too (`tensordot(a2d, b2d, 3)`, whose
      generated axes `[-3,-2,-1]` are out of range on a 2-D operand). The extent
      comparison still short-circuits the loop, so a mismatch found earlier HIDES a
      later out-of-range axis (`([0,1],[0,5])` settles as the shape mismatch because
      a[0]!=b[0] is reached first) — reproduced exactly via per-k resolve-then-compare.

   The old code folded both into one `equal=false → shape-mismatch` path; the doc/test
   claim that "every disagreement is one message" was therefore wrong for the true
   too-many-axes case (which is IN range only when both operands have that rank). Added
   `HasDuplicateAxis` and `ResolveContractionAxis`; the existing test is renamed and
   extended to cover all three rejection kinds.

2) np.vecdot — `axes=` combined with `keepdims=True` was rejected outright with a
   hard-coded AxisError, refusing input NumPy computes. NumPy keeps the reduced core
   dimension as size 1 under keepdims, so the output's EFFECTIVE core rank becomes 1: a
   PROVIDED output entry must then be length 1 and names where the kept axis lands
   (`[[1],[1],[1]]`→(2,1), `[[1],[1],[0]]`→(1,2)), while an OMITTED entry (`[[1],[1]]`)
   is still legal and lands it at the END (→(2,1)). Only an explicit empty output entry
   (`[[1],[1],[]]`) contradicts the kept dimension and is the AxisError "operand 2 has 1
   core dimensions, but 0 dimensions are specified" — its mirror without keepdims is
   "has 0 … but 1 specified". The output axis is validated against the output rank
   (`axis N is out of bounds for array of dimension M`). Implemented via one optional
   `outputCoreRankOverride` on `GufuncGuard.NormalizeAxes` (the omit-check still keys off
   the SIGNATURE rank, so the entry may be omitted; only the provided-entry length uses
   the effective rank) plus a unified kept-axis placement that also subsumes the bare
   `axis=` and default cases. matvec/vecmat reject keepdims before NormalizeAxes and pass
   no override, so they are unchanged. Verified bit-exact across the whole 2-D/3-D
   placement matrix (shapes AND values) and every range/length rejection.

3) np.linalg.norm — the zero "norm" (ord=0 vector) cast the non-zero mask to
   `x.dtype`, so a COMPLEX operand returned a complex count. NumPy casts to
   `x.real.dtype` (`(x != 0).astype(x.real.dtype).sum(...)`), i.e. float64 for a complex
   operand; every real dtype's real component is the dtype itself, so only Complex needs
   the substitution. `norm([3+4j,0,1j], ord=0)` is now float64 2.0, matching NumPy;
   real/integer operands and every other order are untouched.

Perf: no hot-path change. tensordot's duplicate check is O(k²) over the k≤~3 contraction
axes (measured 0.96x NumPy on a 3-D contraction, i.e. parity); vecdot's keepdims logic
runs only when keepdims=true; norm changed one dtype selection. LinearAlgebra suite 240
passed; full suite 12271 passed, 0 failed.

feat(creation): port np.ogrid — the open-mesh grid constructor (NumPy 2.4.2 parity)

Implements `np.ogrid`, NumPy's open (sparse) mesh-grid — the `sparse=True`
instance of `nd_grid` in `numpy/lib/_index_tricks_impl.py`. It was absent from
NumSharp (only the legacy 2-arg `np.mgrid(NDArray, NDArray)` existed, which is a
different, non-slice-indexer API and is left untouched to avoid a name clash /
removing existing code).

WHAT IT DOES (all probed against NumPy 2.4.2, bit-exact):
- Single slice  -> a bare 1-D array: `arange(start, stop, step)`, or `linspace`
  (stop INCLUSIVE) for an imaginary `Nj` step. `np.ogrid["-1:1:5j"]` = [-1,-.5,0,.5,1].
- Multiple slices -> an OPEN MESH: N arrays, each shape 1 in every axis but its
  own (`(1,…,size,…,1)`), built arange -> (astype) -> reshape. Broadcasts to a
  dense grid, so `g[0] + g[1]` reconstructs meshgrid.
- Shared dtype across a multi-slice mesh (NumPy's single `result_type` over every
  slice bound): int64 iff every field of every slice is an integer literal, else
  float64 — an imaginary step or any float literal floats the WHOLE mesh
  (`np.ogrid["0:2","0.0:2"]` -> two float64 arrays, not one int64 + one float64).

SLICE GRAMMAR: reuses the DSL primitives `AxisConcatenator.ParseSliceToken` /
`SliceSpec`, so a Python slice literal is spelled as a string exactly as for
`r_`/`c_` (`np.ogrid["0:3", "0:5"]` ≙ `np.ogrid[0:3, 0:5]`); one string may carry
comma-separated slices; `Slice` objects work as entries. Unlike `r_`, ogrid has
NO directives — every entry is a slice.

EDGE CASES matched to NumPy:
- Single slice may omit its stop (`np.ogrid["5:"]` = arange(0,5)); a MULTI slice
  may not — NumPy sizes each axis from `stop-start` and leaks an AttributeError,
  so NumSharp raises a clear ValueError. An imaginary step always needs a stop.
- Empty ranges / zero point-counts / empty mesh axes / start==stop imaginary all
  match (`np.ogrid[":"]` empty, `np.ogrid["0:0","0:3"]` -> (0,1)&(1,3), etc.).
- Non-slice entries and colon-less strings raise ArgumentException; a multi-slice
  result used as a bare NDArray raises InvalidOperationException (ambiguous).

RETURN TYPE: NumPy's ogrid is polymorphic (bare ndarray for one slice, tuple for
many), which one C# indexer cannot express, so it returns a new `OGridResult`
struct that converts implicitly to `NDArray` (single) and `NDArray[]` (mesh),
supports `Deconstruct` (`var (y, x) = np.ogrid["0:3","0:5"];`), indexing, Length
and ToArray. This collapses NumPy's bare-array-vs-1-tuple trailing-comma
distinction into one value.

CORRECTNESS: verified against NumPy 2.4.2 across single/multi × int/float ×
imaginary × empty × missing-stop × 1-3D; imaginary/float grids are bit-exact
(same linspace/arange code path as `r_`). 18 unit tests in
`Creation/np.ogrid.Test.cs`, all green; the shared `r_`/`c_`/`ix_` machinery is

feat(indexing): implement np.select + fix np.take/np.put negative indices under mode='raise'

## np.select (new) — port of numpy.select (numpy/lib/_function_base_impl.py)

`np.select(condlist, choicelist, default=0)` draws each output element from the choice
whose condition is true, the FIRST matching condition winning; positions where every
condition is false take `default`. Ported as NumPy's OWN structure — allocate a
default-filled result, then `np.copyto(where=cond)` each choice onto it in REVERSE order
so the first condition wins — so every masked write rides NumSharp's existing SIMD
masked-cast kernel and the whole op is a composition of tested primitives.

C# API shapes (NumPy is keyword-only; C# is statically typed):
  - condlist : NDArray[]  (boolean arrays)
  - choicelist : object[]  (an NDArray[] binds via array covariance; scalar choices need
    `new object[]{…}`)
  - default : object  (null ≙ NumPy's 0)

Behavioural parity, all probed against NumPy 2.4.2 and pinned:
  - NEP50 weak scalars, select's OWN rule — only int/float/double/Complex literals are
    weak (adopt the other operands' dtype); bool/char/Half/decimal/arrays/NDArray are
    strong (NumPy's `type(x) in (int,float,complex) else asarray(x)`). A weak-int default
    that overflows the resolved dtype WRAPS (int8 choice + 1000 → int8, 1000→-24) rather
    than raising — select fills via copyto, it does not range-check like np.r_. Result
    dtype = result_type(*choices, default) folded via NDExprTypeRules.PromoteStrong.
  - first-match precedence; default fill; broadcasting (conditions and choices broadcast
    as two SEPARATE groups); all-false → default everywhere; empty; 0-d.
  - errors verbatim: length mismatch / empty condlist → ValueError; non-bool condition →
    TypeError("invalid entry {i} in condlist: should be boolean ndarray").

Deliberately does NOT materialise the intermediate broadcast VIEWS: it computes only each
group's broadcast SHAPE (dimensions) and hands the ORIGINAL operands to copyto, which
broadcasts each to the result shape via broadcast_to. This both avoids needless allocation
AND sidesteps broadcast_arrays's single-array path (Shape.Clean(), which resets a
non-contiguous operand's strides to contiguous — it would read a transposed/strided/
reversed condition through the wrong elements).

Perf: a fused single-pass kernel (SIMD reverse-ConditionalSelect blend chain, keyed by
(dtype,nCond,scalarMask)) was implemented and MEASURED SLOWER than the composition — the
SIMD bool-mask expansion has no early-out and the scalar reverse-overwrite evaluates every
condition, whereas the composition's copyto short-circuits false lanes. It was therefore
reverted. The shipped composition is at parity with NumPy at scale and overhead-bound
(NDArray/Shape construction) for tiny arrays; NumPy's copyto-based select is already
efficient and the op is memory-bound, so the >1.5x target is not reachable here.

## np.take / np.put — negative indices under mode='raise' (bug fix)

The IL kernels (DirectILKernelGenerator.{Take,Put}.cs) rejected EVERY negative index in
raise mode — `np.take(a, [-1])` / `np.put(a, -1, v)` threw instead of addressing the last
element. NumPy's check_and_adjust_index normalizes a negative index ONCE (idx += n) before
the bounds test; an index still out of range after the shift raises, with the ORIGINAL
value left in indices[] for the diagnostic. Both raise-mode branches now do the same. This
is a genuine correctness bug the take/put oracle missed (it only tested positive indices).

## Gates

  - Indexing/np.select.Test.cs (19): weak-scalar dtype resolution, errors, strong-vs-weak
    split, broadcasting, transposed operands, empty/0-d — what the corpus cannot encode.
  - SelectionTests.cs: Take/Put_Raise_NegativeIndices_Normalize + _TooNegative_Throws.
  - Differential-fuzz (groupa tier, bit-exact vs NumPy 2.4.2): 11 `select` cases (dtype
    sweep × precedence × broadcast × transposed/all-false) + negative-index take/put +
    take wrap/clip; OpRegistry wires `select` and the take/put `mode` param. FuzzMatrix
    (98) green, full selection suite (136) green, CI-filtered indexing suite (1834) green.

feat(creation): port np.mgrid — the dense mesh-grid indexer (NumPy 2.4.2 parity), replacing the legacy 2-arg method

Implements NumPy's `np.mgrid` — the `sparse=False` instance of `nd_grid` — as
the slice-indexer it actually is (`np.mgrid[0:5, 0:3]`), the dense twin of the
`np.ogrid` shipped in the previous commit.

BREAKING CHANGE: replaces the legacy non-NumPy `np.mgrid(NDArray, NDArray)` method
(and its `NDArray.mgrid(rhs)` instance twin, `NdArray.Mgrid.cs`). A C# property
named `mgrid` cannot coexist with a method of the same name, and NumPy's mgrid is
an indexer, not a 2-arg call. The legacy method computed a 2-operand 'ij' grid
from two explicit arrays — a misnamed, limited meshgrid with no NumPy analogue.
In-repo callers migrated: the ShallowWater example now uses `np.mgrid[$"0:{n}",
$"0:{n}"]`; NdArrayMGridTest is replaced by np.mgrid.Test.cs.

WHAT IT DOES (all probed against NumPy 2.4.2, bit-exact):
- Single slice  -> a bare 1-D array (identical to ogrid single: arange, or the
  inclusive-stop linspace of an imaginary `Nj` step).
- Multiple slices -> ONE dense stacked array of shape `(N, size_0, …, size_{N-1})`;
  `result[k]` is the k-th coordinate broadcast across the whole grid, so
  `result[0] + result[1]` reconstructs a meshgrid.
- Shared dtype across the mesh (NumPy's single result_type over every slice bound):
  int64 unless any field is a float literal or the step is imaginary, then float64.

SHARED WITH ogrid: the parsing and dtype rules are factored out of np.ogrid.cs into
`np.ParseGridSpecs` / `GridMeshDtype` (same string-slice grammar, same missing-stop
and imaginary `ValueError`s, now carrying the caller's name). mgrid keeps its OWN
build because it genuinely diverges from ogrid on sizing:

- Built NumPy's way: `np.indices(sizes, typ)` then each NON-trivial axis (start≠0 /
  step≠1 / imaginary) is rescaled by overwriting its layer with the 1-D line
  broadcast across the grid (`np.copyto`). A pure `0:n` axis is already correct, so
  the common `np.mgrid[0:a, 0:b]` is a single fused indices fill with no post-pass —
  and the overwrite reuses SliceSpec's exact arange/linspace values instead of a
  dtype-branching multiply-add.
- CRUCIAL divergence from ogrid, now correct: NumPy sizes each axis by
  `ceil((stop-start)/step)`, which may be NEGATIVE. `np.mgrid[5:0, 0:3]` therefore
  raises "negative dimensions are not allowed" (via indices) where
  `np.ogrid[5:0, 0:3]` clamps to an empty axis; a zero step is a divide-by-zero.
  An arange-line-based mgrid would have silently papered this over.

RETURN TYPE: NumPy's mgrid is a single array, so `MGridResult` converts implicitly
to `NDArray` (the stack) and additionally `Deconstruct`s
(`var (x, y) = np.mgrid["0:5", "0:3"];`) and indexes into the per-axis grids —
mirroring how `X, Y = np.mgrid[…]` iterates the array's first axis in Python.

CORRECTNESS: a 13-case differential matrix (single/multi × int/float × imaginary ×
step/offset/reversed × empty × 3-D) is bit-exact vs NumPy 2.4.2 — shape, dtype and
every double bit; negative-size and step-0 raise. 15 unit tests in
np.mgrid.Test.cs; the shared machinery leaves ogrid/r_/c_/ix_ green (106 combined).

PERFORMANCE (NPY/NS, Release, best-of, warm): FASTER than NumPy on every measured
variation — 1.5x (100x100) to ~13x (1000x1000) to 7.6x (tiny 5x5), geomean ~6x.
The open/dense grids are O(output); the pure-int case is a single fused indices fill.

feat(logic): implement np.iterable — NumPy's pure iterability predicate

np.iterable(y) is NumPy's whole `try: iter(y); return True; except
TypeError: return False` (numpy/lib/_function_base_impl.py). It is a
PREDICATE, not an iteration op: it never touches element data, only asks
whether iteration is possible. It therefore needs NO kernel / NDIter /
loop of any kind — an O(1) rank/type check living beside np.isscalar in
Logic/np.is.cs. (The task framing asked which of NDIter / np.fromfunction /
np.evaluate could "power" it; the correct answer is none — there is no
element traversal to run.)

Parity (probed against NumPy 2.4.2; C# object -> bool mapping):
- null                                 -> false  (iter(None) raises TypeError)
- NDArray                              -> ndim != 0
    * A 0-d array is the ONLY non-iterable array: iter() on it raises
      TypeError("iteration over a 0-d array"), exactly as
      NDArray.GetEnumerator() already does; every rank>=1 array (empties
      included) is iterable. This is the one surprise NumPy documents —
      isinstance(a, Iterable) is True but np.iterable(a) is False.
- string                               -> true   (Python strings are iterable)
- IEnumerable (arrays/List/Dictionary/HashSet/...) -> true
- scalar value types
  (int/double/bool/char/Half/decimal/Complex/...) -> false

The NDArray case precedes the IEnumerable catch because NDArray implements
IEnumerable — a 0-d NDArray would otherwise be misclassified as iterable.

Because iterability is purely a rank property, the memory-layout matrix
(contiguous/strided/broadcast/transposed/...) collapses to a single axis
here: no data is read, so only 0-d vs rank>=1 matters — both covered.

Being a bool predicate over an arbitrary object rather than a value-
producing kernel over array data, it is unit-test-only and deliberately
absent from the differential-fuzz corpus — same rationale as
isscalar/nditer/ndindex.

Validated 22/22 against a live NumPy 2.4.2 table; gated by
Logic/np.iterable.Test.cs (30 cases, all green). CLAUDE.md supported-API
list updated.

perf(indexing): fuse np.select into a single-pass IL kernel for the contiguous array-choice case

np.select shipped as NumPy's own composition — np.full(default) then one masked
np.copyto per condition in REVERSE so the first match wins. That is (n+1) full
passes over the result: every masked copyto re-reads AND re-writes the whole
buffer to preserve its masked-off lanes, so the result alone sees (2n+1) touches.
The composition already beat NumPy 1.2–8.5x everywhere EXCEPT the 8-byte
(int64/float64) all-array-choice large arrays, which sat at 1.22–1.54x: there the
op is pure memory bandwidth and that redundant result traffic dominates.

Add a fused single-pass kernel (DirectILKernelGenerator.Select.cs) for exactly
that case — every condition and choice C-contiguous at the full result shape and
dtype (no broadcast, no cast). np.select is elementwise a chain of np.where, so
the kernel is a reverse Vector.ConditionalSelect chain (seed = default; overlay
choices n-1 -> 0 so the first true condition wins), 4x-unrolled with four
independent accumulators, reusing np.where's exact EmitInlineMaskCreation
bool->lane expansion, with the scalar default hoisted once via CreateBroadcast.
Each condition and choice is read once and the result is written once. Generated
per (dtype, n, defaultIsScalar) and cached; a scalar tail covers the remainder
and non-SIMD platforms.

np.select routes to it via TrySelectFused; every other shape (broadcast / strided
/ cast / scalar-choice) declines the gate and keeps the copyto composition, which
already outruns NumPy there. Operand pointers are taken as base + Shape.offset so
contiguous offset slices address logical element 0 correctly.

Result: the sub-1.5x cells rise to 1.6–2.4x (min 1.60x at int64 n=1 10M with an
ARRAY default — the irreducible 4-array-traffic memory-bound floor); no measured
cell below 1.5x. Perf (NPY/NS, Release, best-of-rounds), array choices:
1K 3.3–5.0x, 100K 8–18x, 10M 1.6–5.8x; scalar choices (composition) 3.3–3.8x.

This supersedes the earlier "fused kernel measured slower, composition ships"
note from fc10404d — that rested on a broken prototype; a correctly vectorised
single pass is strictly less memory traffic and wins.

Gates: Indexing/np.select.Test.cs grows to 21 — a 1000-element reference-oracle
sweep over every element size x n x scalar/array default that exercises the SIMD
body + 4x unroll + 1-vector remainder + scalar tail, plus a contiguous-offset
slice. Full CI-filtered suite green (12326); FuzzMatrix bit-exact vs NumPy on
net8.0 + net10.0. (The matching CLAUDE.md docs already landed via ce560796.)

feat(creation): complete np.meshgrid to full NumPy 2.4.2 (variadic + indexing/sparse/copy), replacing the 2-arg Kwargs stub; audit np.ix_

Completes NumPy's `np.meshgrid` — the coordinate-grid cousin of the just-shipped
`mgrid`/`ogrid` and of `ix_`. The old implementation was a 2-input stub with a
non-NumPy `Kwargs` options-bag, 2-D only, and a `copy` flag that did nothing.

WHAT IT DOES (all probed against NumPy 2.4.2, differential bit-exact):
- Variadic: N coordinate vectors -> N coordinate grids (NumPy returns a tuple).
  Each input is flattened (C-order) onto its own open-mesh axis.
- `indexing`: "xy" (Cartesian, default) swaps the first two axes vs "ij" (matrix)
  — 2-D outputs are (N, M) under xy and (M, N) under ij; 3-D (N,M,P) vs (M,N,P).
- `sparse`: keep the open-mesh (1,…,Ni,…,1) shapes instead of broadcasting to the
  full grid (they still broadcast to the same dense result).
- `copy` (default true): independent C-contiguous grids; false returns the dense
  broadcast VIEWS (non-contiguous, may alias — NumPy-verbatim).
- Each grid PRESERVES its input's dtype (grids are NOT promoted to a common type).
- Bad `indexing` -> ValueError "Valid values for `indexing` are 'xy' and 'ij'."

API (C#): `meshgrid(x1, x2[, x3], string indexing="xy", bool sparse=false, bool
copy=true)` for the common arities, plus `meshgrid(NDArray[] xi, …)` for 4+. The
keyword-only NumPy args become C# optional named params.

RETURN TYPE: `MeshgridResult`, consistent with `OGridResult` — NumPy's tuple made
usable in C#: implicit to `NDArray[]`, `Deconstruct` (`var (xx, yy) =
np.meshgrid(x, y);`) and indexer. Replaces the fixed `(NDArray, NDArray)` tuple
(which could not be variadic) and removes the non-NumPy `Kwargs` class.

-> `[0]/[1]`, `Kwargs` -> named params), the old weak `np.meshgrid.test.cs`
replaced by a comprehensive `np.meshgrid.Test.cs`. The fuzz `OpRegistry` meshgrid
case keeps compiling via `Deconstruct` (meshgrid is not in the corpus).

ValueError — all matching, and it is already the green differential-fuzz `ix_`
tier. The int32-vs-int64 literal difference is language-wide, not an ix_ behaviour.

Tried to break np.iterable (prev commit) with adversarial inputs probed

feat(indexing): port np.take_along_axis — the per-slice gather (NumPy 2.4.2 parity)

Implements numpy.take_along_axis(arr, indices, axis=-1) — the inverse companion
to argsort/argmax(keepdims): take_along_axis(a, a.argsort(axis), axis) == sort(a, axis).
NumPy implements it as advanced indexing (arr[_make_along_axis_idx(...)]); this port
reproduces the identical semantics as ONE whole-array strided-odometer IL gather kernel
rather than routing through the general fancy-index path (whose boxing ScanFancyBounds
value-scan is O(indices.size) and would miss the 1.5x-vs-NumPy bar).

Semantics (all probed against NumPy 2.4.2; 24,000+ differential-fuzz cases bit-exact):
  * axis default -1 (NumPy 2.3+); axis=None flattens arr in C (logical) order and
    requires 1-D indices.
  * indices must be an INTEGER array (issubdtype(dtype, integer) — bool/float/complex
    raise IndexError "`indices` must be an integer array") whose ndim equals arr's
    (else ValueError "`indices` and `arr` must have the same number of dimensions").
  * The axis dim of indices supplies J (need NOT equal M = arr.shape[axis]); every
    OTHER dim broadcasts BOTH arr and indices — a stride-0 broadcast source view (on a
    non-axis dim OR on the axis itself) is read fine; a non-axis conflict raises NumPy's
    fancy-index "shape mismatch: indexing arrays could not be broadcast together with
    shapes ..." listing each arange-grid shape verbatim (trailing space included).
  * A negative index normalizes ONCE (idx += M, advanced-indexing semantics); anything
    still out of range raises IndexError "index {orig} is out of bounds for axis {axis}
    with size {M}" reporting the ORIGINAL (pre-wrap) value.
  * Result is a fresh writeable C-contiguous copy of arr's dtype; any source layout
    (C/F/strided/reversed/sliced/transposed/broadcast) is read through its own strides,
    no materialisation.

Kernel (Backends/Kernels/Direct/DirectILKernelGenerator.TakeAlongAxis.cs):
  A DynamicMethod-emitted whole-array gather, cached per element width (1/2/4/8/16 bytes)
  so the per-element copy is a typed load/store, not a variable-size cpblk. The traversal
  is an OUTER odometer over dims [0, ndim-1) wrapped around a TIGHT inner loop over the
  innermost dimension (usually the take axis), so the multi-level carry runs once per
  1-D slice rather than once per element. arr is read at its own (possibly negative) axis
  stride with the resolved index; broadcast dims are stride-0 entries; indices is cast to
  int64 once and read strided. No per-dtype switch, no struct kernel.

Perf (NPY/NS, Release, best-of): >=1.5x faster than NumPy on EVERY measured variation
(geomean ~3.7x; the outer/inner restructure lifted the 1M cases from ~2.3x to 4.6-5.6x
and the compute-bound 16M axis=-1 from 1.37x to 2.03x). The tightest cell is a random
16M axis-0 gather at 1.54x, which is memory-latency-bound (NumPy is 241ms, NumSharp 156ms).

Gates:
  * Indexing/TakeAlongAxisTests.cs (36 tests) — core semantics, index/source broadcasting,
    all six memory layouts, all 15 dtypes, result independence, empty results, and every
    error path with verbatim NumPy messages.
  * 44 take_along_axis cases added to the `groupa` differential-fuzz tier (11 per dtype x
    int32/float64/uint8/complex128) — argsort/argmax reconstruction, axis=None flatten,
    J!=M, negative-wrap, non-axis index broadcast, and a transposed (non-contig) source;
    replayed bit-exact by FuzzCorpusTests + OpRegistry.

perf(indexing): specialize take/put/place element copy, add gather prefetch + values counter-wrap; fix float-index acceptance

The take/put/place IL kernels copied each element with cpblk sized by a RUNTIME
elemBytes — a per-element memcpy where a single MOV belongs (measured ~2x slower;
it made take LOSE to NumPy at 0.68x). Three performance levers plus a correctness fix:

1. Element-copy specialization. CopyKindFor + EmitElementCopy pick a typed
   Ldind/Stind of the dtype width (two 8-byte MOVs for 16-byte Complex/Decimal),
   keyed into the kernel cache; cpblk survives only for multi-element take axis
   slabs. Every NumSharp itemsize is in {1,2,4,8,16}, so put/place never cpblk.

2. Software prefetch in the take gather (Sse.Prefetch0 of the slab
   PrefetchDistance=32 indices ahead), gated at emit-time on SSE and at the call
   site on the gathered footprint exceeding IndexPrefetchThresholdBytes = 2 MiB —
   below that it is pure overhead (~1.6x slower at 100K), so a separate
   (copyKind, prefetch) kernel is cached and the small path stays lean. NumPy does
   not prefetch in take, so this is a clean win at scale.

3. A wrapping values cursor in put/place replacing the per-element
   'i % valuesCount' integer division (NumPy's iterator model) — the dominant cost
   for cyclic values, and why place was stuck at ~1.0x (one idiv per True).

Perf (NPY/NS, Release, best-of-rounds): take flat 100K 1.0-1.3x / 10M 1.7-2.5x,
axis-slab 4-byte 2.4-2.6x; put 100K 2.0-3.1x / 10M 1.2-1.4x; place 100K 2.0-4.5x /
10M 4-byte 2.5x. take went from LOSING (0.68x) to winning everywhere. The remaining
sub-1.5x cells are memory-latency / bandwidth / allocation-overhead bound (random
scatter, 8-byte slabs, tiny-array result alloc) — the same walls NumPy hits.

Correctness: take/put silently truncated a float index array where NumPy raises.
CastIndicesToInt64 now rejects a non-castable index dtype with NumPy's verbatim
TypeError, reproducing NumPy's subtle rule split — take converts under 'same_kind'
(uint64 allowed), put under 'safe' (uint64 rejected), each leaking its own rule
name. Integer/bool pass; float/complex refused.

Gates: SelectionTests grows by 7 (float-index rejection x2, take/put uint64
divergence, 16-byte Complex fidelity x2, put/place cyclic-wrap); full CI-filtered
suite green (12407) + FuzzMatrix bit-exact vs NumPy on net8.0 + net10.0.

harden(indexing): np.take_along_axis — adversarial stress, OOB-order divergence, branch-light resolve

Follow-up to the take_along_axis port: break it, widen edge-case coverage, and
optimise (evaluating SIMD). Outcome — implementation is correct across every layout
combination; one cosmetic error-message divergence found, characterised and documented;
a hardware-gather SIMD path measured and rejected; the resolve made branch-light.

STRESS / EDGE CASES (18,000 new adversarial cases, on top of the 24,000 value cases):
  A layout-fuzzer rebuilds the EXACT operand views from raw (dtype, shape, strides,
  offset, buffer) descriptors — the FuzzCorpus.Reconstruct mechanism — so it stresses
  the strided odometer reading BOTH arr AND indices at arbitrary strides, which the
  first round (contiguous indices) never did: non-contiguous SOURCES × non-contiguous
  INDICES (C / F / reversed / strided / swapped / broadcast / offset) across ranks 1-6
  and all 5 element widths. Result: values, shapes, dtypes and error TYPE/axis/size are
  100% bit-exact vs NumPy 2.4.2 — zero real bugs.

DELIBERATE DIVERGENCE (documented, [Misaligned] test):
  The ONLY mismatch found — when a NON-contiguous indices array holds MULTIPLE
  out-of-range values, NumSharp reports the first in the RESULT's C-order while NumPy
  reports whichever its fancy-index NpyIter (PyArray_MapIterCheckIndices) visits first.
  Probing NumPy shows the order follows the INDEX array's memory/axis layout with
  negative-stride flipping (C-contig->7, F-contig->8 for identical logical values) — an
  internal-iterator artifact that is NEITHER pure min-address (fails on 1-D negative
  stride, 97.2% match) NOR pure logical C-order (fails on F-layout, 86.6% match), so it
  is not cleanly reproducible without replicating NpyIter's multi-operand axis ordering.
  Only the offending index VALUE differs; TYPE, axis and size always match, and it never
  arises from argsort/argmax output (C-contiguous -> byte-identical). Documented at the
  throw site, in CLAUDE.md, and pinned by Misaligned_OobReportOrder_NonContiguousIndices.

SIMD — MEASURED AND REJECTED:
  A hardware VPGATHERQD/QQ gather was benchmarked against the scalar loop for the hot
  4/8-byte, axis=last, contiguous case: only ~1.16x on this host (AVX2; AVX-512 gather
  unavailable) — and that is BEFORE the SIMD bounds-validation and scalar OOB-fallback a
  raise-mode gather still needs. Not worth a per-width gather kernel, its correctness
  surface, or its CPU-dependence (gather is at/below parity on several microarchitectures);
  NumPy's own advanced-index gather is likewise scalar. Rationale recorded in the kernel
  header so it is not re-litigated.

OPTIMISATION THAT DID LAND — branch-light resolve:
  The per-element bounds check folds its two signed compares (< 0 and >= axisLen) into
  ONE unsigned compare ((ulong)resolved >= (ulong)axisLen catches both), dropping the hot
  loop from three conditional branches to two. The wrap stays a BRANCH rather than a
  branchless sign-shift+and+add ON PURPOSE: take_along_axis indices are overwhelmingly
  non-negative (argsort/argmax), so the wrap predicts not-taken for ~free, whereas the
  branchless form spends ALU on every element for a wrap that almost never fires (measured
