feat(einsum): NumPy view/keyword semantics, casting gates, order rules, parse cache + layout parity

Closes the /np-function einsum cycle on top of 7d2d7a2f (the contraction):
every remaining NumPy 2.4.2 semantic was probed, matched, and gated, the
memory-layout variation matrix was differentially verified, and the required
benchmarks were run (Release, best-of-7, vs NumPy's DEFAULT optimize=False
c_einsum and vs optimize=True).

Semantics landed (all probed against 2.4.2):

  * THE VIEW PATH — one operand, no out=, nothing summed. NumPy answers with a
    VIEW: einsum('ii->i', a) is WRITEABLE (a[:]-style writes set a's diagonal;
    np.diagonal's own read-only contract is restored to writeable by einsum),
    a broadcast operand's view stays read-only, and einsum('ij->ij', a) is a
    DISTINCT view object, never `a` itself. On this path NumPy ignores order=
    ENTIRELY (order='C'/'F' still return the non-contiguous diagonal view) and
    DISCARDS a dtype= request (einsum('ii->i', int32, dtype=int64) is the
    int32 view) — both reproduced. Implementation trap worth the note:
    Storage.Alias() inherits read-onlyness from the storage it aliases, so the
    writeable restore must alias from the OPERAND's storage, not the diagonal
    view's — aliasing the view's storage silently re-clears the bit.
  * casting= now gates EVERY cast with NumPy's iterator texts verbatim:
    operand -> loop dtype ("Iterator operand {i} dtype could not be cast from
    dtype('...') to dtype('...') according to the rule '...'"; what makes
    casting='no' reject mixed dtypes) and loop -> out dtype ("Iterator
    requested dtype could not be cast from ..., the operand {nop} dtype,
    ..."). A same-rank out= extent mismatch stays NumSharp-worded (NumPy leaks
    NpyIter's "remapped shapes" text there — same divergence class as the
    label-extent mismatch, documented).
  * order= — 'A' AND 'K' both produce F-contiguous results when EVERY input is
    F-contiguous (probed: all-F matmul/hadamard/chain3 is F even at the
    default 'K'), C otherwise; 'K' leaves the computed C result untouched.
  * Grammar cache — EinsumSubscripts.Parse split into a cached immutable
    grammar (key = subscripts + operand ranks, 4096-entry ConcurrentDictionary
    — the analog of NumPy's lru_cache(2**12) on its equation parse) and a
    per-call ValidateExtents that never writes the shared instance; the new
    EinsumPlan struct carries the per-call SingleOperandView. Thread-hammered:
    20K concurrent mixed valid/invalid calls, 0 errors, 0 wrong results.

Verification:

  * 186-case memory-layout differential vs NumPy 2.4.2 — F / transposed /
    strided / negative-stride / negcol / offset / broadcast recipes applied to
    either operand x matmul / reduce / diagonal-view / trace / batched (incl.
    swapped-last-axes and stride-0 batch) / ellipsis / permuted-output /
    frobenius / outer + empties ((2,0)@(0,3), zero-size reduce, (0,0)
    diagonal), rank-5 permutations, scalars — 186/186 BIT-exact.
  * +10 unit tests (87 einsum tests total, net8.0 + net10.0 green): view
    writeability/write-through/identity-distinctness/broadcast-read-only,
    view-ignores-order-and-dtype, casting='no' verbatim, out-cast verbatim,
    all-F order matrix, empties, strided-out write-through, non-contiguous
    operand pins.
  * Full suite green apart from the two PRE-EXISTING unrelated reds (T1_33
    Char dtype-name audit; convolve buffer-release sweep).

Perf (NPY/NS vs NumPy's DEFAULT einsum, Release, best-of-7):

  * With NumSharp.Interop.OpenBLAS referenced: matmul 1024^2 f64 23x, 256^2
    5.6x, 3-op chain 64^2 146x (NumPy's default 3-op einsum is the naive
    4-label iterator), batched 128x16^2 2.0x, matvec 512^2 1.9x, hadamard 1M
    3-4x, complex128 64^2 2.9x, outer ~1.1x.
  * Core-only: the product cells fall to the managed GEMM exactly as
    np.matmul does (1024^2 still 2.9x; matvec 0.21x is the managed product
    kernels' own floor — np.dot(m,v)/np.matvec measure the same 187us).
  * Sub-1x cells are inherited or fixed-cost floors, documented: sub-5us view
    calls ~0.5-0.9x vs c_einsum's single C call (1.9-5.9x in OUR favor vs
    NumPy's own optimize=True), big ij->i ~0.8x (the shared axis-sum's
    parity), int32 GEMM ~0.5x (kernel class; NumPy's own np.matmul(i32) is
    slower than its einsum). einsum-specific overhead ~2us/call, <1% by 64^2.

feat(correlate/convolve): OpenBLAS byte-parity via the ISlidingDotBackend seam

np.correlate / np.convolve were the ONE product-adjacent family that did not
consult the BLAS seam. NumSharp's managed 3-region sliding engine reduces each
output's inner dot with its own SIMD kernel, which REORDERS the sum vs the cblas
?dot NumPy's _pyarray_correlate calls for every ramp position (and for the middle
whenever small_correlate declines). So while the small-kernel regime stayed
byte-identical, LONG float32/float64 kernels -- AND complex128 at any length --
drifted by a bounded ULP from NumPy. Installing NumSharp.Interop.OpenBLAS made
every dot/matmul/inner/vdot/... byte-exact but left correlate/convolve managed:
OpenBLAS did not take priority over the C# kernel here. This closes that gap.

Route exactly the positions NumPy sends through cblas through the SAME
scipy-openblas sdot/ddot/zdotu:

- New Core seam Backends/ISlidingDotBackend.cs -- an OPTIONAL capability a backend
  MAY also implement, discovered by `Blas as ISlidingDotBackend` (the same
  optional-capability pattern as TryMatMulBatched). A raw strided level-1 dot
  (NumPy's per-dtype dotfunc), because correlate's inner reduction runs once per
  OUTPUT position -- thousands of tiny dots, not an allocating whole-array method
  -- so it is kept OFF the NDArray-based product interface deliberately.

- OpenBlasEngine.SlidingDot (interop) serves it by REUSING the product family's
  already byte-exact IBlasType<T>.Dot (@name@_dot: double-accumulated chunked
  cblas ?dot, ?dotu for complex) -- no new native code. OpenBlasBackend now also
  implements ISlidingDotBackend.

- SlidingCorrelate gate: when Blas implements the seam and supports the dtype,
  route real n2>11 and ALL complex through the backend (once small_correlate
  declines NumPy routes every ramp AND middle position there, so there is no mixed
  managed/native path within a call). The small_correlate-eligible regime
  (real float, n2<=11) STAYS managed -- already byte-exact -- and a backend that
  declines the dtype (a real-only CBLAS handed complex) leaves the managed kernel
  in place. The managed path is untouched when no backend is installed, so the
  groupa differential-fuzz gate is unaffected.

Verified live against NumPy 2.4.2 (backend bound to numpy's own scipy-openblas64,
threads=1): the managed reduction diverges on 533-690 of 699 outputs for a
length-200 kernel across float64/float32/complex128, while the backend is
byte-identical on every dtype x mode (valid/same/full) x region (ramps/middle).
This also corrects the CLAUDE.md "complex exact at every size" claim -- complex128
diverged (690/699) and is now closed.

Gate: test/NumSharp.Interop.UnitTests/SlidingDotLiveParityTests.cs (11 live,
numpy-adjudicated tests, incl. a non-vacuity test that the managed path really
diverges and a boundary test that the small kernel stays managed). Opt-in and
per-position (one backend ?dot per output, mirroring NumPy's per-position dotfunc
call), trading managed SIMD speed for parity -- the reason the backend exists.

feat(linalg): np.einsum_path — greedy/optimal contraction planner, byte-exact to NumPy 2.4.2

Implements np.einsum_path, previously deliberately out of scope. A route-for-route
port of NumPy 2.4.2's numpy/_core/einsumfunc.py: its _parse_einsum_input parser, the
_greedy_path/_optimal_path searches with the _flop_count cost model, and the
einsum_path info-string builder. Both the contraction PATH and every numeric metric in
the printed string are byte-identical to NumPy (differential-fuzzed 1,525 random
contraction networks: path + full string, plus 18 curated canonical cases).

API (mirrors numpy.einsum_path(subscripts, *operands, optimize='greedy')):
- np.einsum_path(string subscripts, NDArray[] operands[, object optimize])
- np.einsum_path(params object[] operands)  -- variadic ("ij,jk", a, b) AND the sublist
  spelling (a, [0,1], b, [1,2], [0,2]); greedy-only (optimize goes with the NDArray[]
  overload). Returns (EinsumPath path, string repr) -- NumPy's (['einsum_path', (1,2),
  (0,1)], "...") tuple.

New public type EinsumPath (readonly struct): NumPy's path list as a value. Deconstruct
+ indexer + Steps/Count + ToList() (the raw ['einsum_path', int[], ...] list) + a
NumPy-format ToString ("['einsum_path', (1, 2), (0, 1)]", single-step tuples render the
Python trailing comma "(0,)"). IEquatable + IReadOnlyList<int[]>.

optimize= takes NumPy's whole path_type vocabulary in NumPy's exact decision order:
false/null (no-opt), true/'greedy'/'optimal', a precomputed EinsumPath (explicit path,
also accepted as NumPy's raw list), and a ('greedy'|'optimal', memory) tuple that caps
the largest intermediate. The returned path ROUND-TRIPS into np.einsum(..., optimize:
path) (RequireOptimize widened to accept EinsumPath / the ITuple memory form / the raw
marker list) -- accepted and validated, though einsum still contracts left-to-right, so
the path changes only which plan is displayed, never the numerics (documented contract).

Error taxonomy is verbatim NumPy: ValueError for the parse/shape rejections (invalid
symbol, size mismatch, output-char errors, wrong operand/index counts, "Subscripts can
only contain one '->'"), RuntimeError for an incomplete explicit path, TypeError ("Did
not understand the path: ..." / "object of type '...' has no len()") for a bad path
object, and a NEW Exceptions/KeyError.cs for an unknown path name -- reproducing NumPy's
buggy ('Path name %s not found', '<name>') leak.

Two things done in integer arithmetic on purpose:
- Sci() formats the .3e FLOP/size metrics HALF-TO-EVEN like Python. .NET's "0.000e+00"
  custom format rounds half-AWAY (13825 -> 1.383e+04) where NumPy rounds to even
  (-> 1.382e+04); since every value here is an integer, formatting it directly is exact.
- The ellipsis PLACEHOLDER letters are the ONE inherent divergence: NumPy draws them from
  a hash-randomized set (observed I/f/P across three processes), so its own info string
  is non-reproducible there. NumSharp draws them deterministically; the path and every
  number still match, only the '...'-expanded display letters differ -- which NumPy does
  not pin.

Deliberately NOT ported: einsum_path's einsum_call=True hidden option (NumPy-internal;
NumSharp's einsum has its own left-to-right driver). np.einsum_path uses NumPy's Python
einsumfunc parser, NOT the C einsum.cpp parser NumSharp uses for default np.einsum -- the
two word rejections differently and expand ellipses differently, matching NumPy which
also splits them.

Gate: LinearAlgebra/EinsumPathTests.cs (23). Existing einsum suite (EinsumContraction +
EinsumSubscriptParity, 68) and the full LinearAlgebra namespace (335) stay green.

feat(polynomial): NumPy poly family — poly/roots/polyfit/polyval + remainder family + poly1d + vander

Ports NumPy 2.4.2's `numpy/lib/_polynomial_impl.py` in full (plus `np.vander`), routing
the two BLAS-shaped members through the existing OpenBLAS seam exactly as `np.matmul`/
`np.linalg` do — no new backend surface, no `Try*` member.

Functions (all in src/NumSharp.Core/Polynomial/, vander in Creation/):
- np.polyval   — Horner `y=y*x+p[k]`, computed in `result_type(p,x)` with `out=`-buffer
                 reuse (no per-coefficient allocation). Iterates from k=0 so the first
                 `0*x` reproduces NumPy's `0*inf -> nan`. All 15 dtypes; poly1d-x overload
                 composes polynomials.
- np.polyder   — `p[:-1]*arange(n,0,-1)`, the int64 arange lifting int32->int64 like NumPy.
- np.polyint   — term-wise integral, always float64/complex128; k prep + broadcast + validation.
- np.polyadd/polysub — zero-extend the shorter, `result_type` promotion.
- np.polymul   — leading-zero trim (poly1d normalisation) then `convolve(mode='full')`.
- np.polydiv   — quotient+remainder, in-place `subtract(out=)` inner update, 1e-14 remainder trim.
- np.poly      — 1-D mintypecode cast OR square 2-D -> eigvals; convolve `(x-root)` fold;
                 complex-conjugate-pair -> real collapse; empty -> scalar 1.0.
- np.roots     — companion matrix `diag(ones,-1)` + first row, eigvals, trailing-zero roots.
- np.polyfit   — scaled-Vandermonde lstsq; full NumPy signature (rcond/full/w/cov). Returns
                 PolyfitResult: implicit->NDArray (coeffs), Deconstruct for the full 5-tuple
                 and the cov 2-tuple. Verbatim TypeError/ValueError taxonomy.
- np.vander    — `promote_types(x,int64)` dtype, increasing/N, cumprod columns (bit-exact to
                 NumPy's multiply.accumulate).
- poly1d       — class with coeffs/c/coef/order/o/roots/r/variable, deriv/integ, +/-/*//
                 operators, indexer p[k], roots-mode ctor, ToString repr. Implicit ->NDArray
                 (NumPy's __array__) so a poly1d flows into any np.* function.

- Pure functions BIT-EXACT (polyval/polyder/polyint/polyadd/polysub/polymul/polydiv/poly-1d/
  vander) across all 15 dtypes and layouts (strided/transposed/reversed inputs).
- roots / poly-of-matrix / polyfit BYTE-IDENTICAL to live NumPy over the same exported bytes

feat(linalg): np.matmul full keyword surface + np.cross + out= for np.dot/np.outer

Closes the product-family keyword gaps against NumPy 2.4.2. matmul was the only
product gufunc without the keyword surface its five siblings carry; np.cross (main
namespace) did not exist; np.dot/np.outer lacked out=. Everything probed against
NumPy 2.4.2 and differential-verified. The products themselves are untouched — they
still route through OpenBLAS for float32/float64/complex128 when NumSharp.Interop.OpenBLAS
is referenced, and a dtype= request casts the operands BEFORE the product so the backend
route follows the loop. All signature changes are backward-compatible (new params optional).

np.matmul(x1, x2, out=, axes=, axis=, keepdims=, dtype=, casting=, order=)
  - Gufunc signature (n?,k),(k,m?)->(n?,m?); bare (x1,x2) is unchanged.
  - dtype= selects the LOOP (operands cast to it first; validated under `casting`,
    default 'same_kind', with NumPy's verbatim "Cannot cast ufunc 'matmul' input N …").
  - out= is the ufunc form (may be strided; product->out cast under `casting`); a
    wrong-shaped out reports NumPy's verbatim core-dimension message, the rarer
    loop/over-broadcast mismatches a clear ValueError (same latitude as the siblings).
  - order= C/F/A/K resolves the result layout: A is F only when BOTH inputs are F,
    K/C is the natural C-contiguous product (so the default K is a zero-cost no-op).
  - axes= relocates each operand's core axes (the optional n?/m? dims are counted per
    ndim) and the result's; matmul's output entry is NEVER omittable (unlike vecdot),
    and a repeated axis raises "axes item N has value V repeated".
  - axis= and keepdims= exist only for signature parity and REJECT with NumPy's exact
    text (its 3 distinct core dims). keepdims uses a bool? sentinel so an explicit
    false also rejects, matching NumPy's np._NoValue default.
  - Validation precedence (order/casting -> axis+axes -> keepdims -> axis, and the
    out cast -> out shape order) was probed and reproduced.

np.dot(a, b, out=)
  - STRICT new_array_for_sum validation (numpy _core/src/multiarray/common.c): out
    must have the EXACT result dtype, ndim, be C-contiguous and writeable — no cast,
    no broadcast. dtype/ndim/non-C-array -> "output array is not acceptable (must have
    the right datatype, number of dimensions, and be a C-Array)"; same-ndim shape
    mismatch -> "output array has wrong dimensions". Not the ufunc out=.

np.outer(a, b, out=)
  - Threaded into the underlying multiply, so out= follows the ufunc rules verbatim
    (strided ok, same_kind cast, ufunc broadcast error on a wrong shape).

np.cross(a, b, axisa=-1, axisb=-1, axisc=-1, axis=None)
  - Line-for-line port of numpy/_core/numeric.py cross: a pure composition over
    multiply/negative/subtract/moveaxis (no new kernel). 2- and 3-vectors (a missing
    third component is treated as zero; the 2x2 case returns the scalar z), full
    broadcasting of the leading axes, result dtype = promote_types(a, b). Bit-exact
    vs NumPy across all dtypes (unsigned wrap included), C/F/reversed/transposed
    layouts and every axisa/axisb/axisc/axis combination. Errors verbatim:
    "At least one array has zero dimension", "incompatible dimensions for cross
    product\n(dimension must be 2 or 3)", "axisa: axis N is out of bounds for array
    of dimension M". The 2-vector form is deprecated in NumPy 2.0; NumSharp does not
    model that warning and simply computes. Distinct from np.linalg.cross (3-vectors,
    single axis); its stale "NumSharp has no np.cross" doc note is corrected.

fix(polynomial): parity fixes from adversarial NumPy audit — 0-d polyval + byte-exact poly1d repr

A 185-case byte-level differential audit (dtypes x special values x layouts x error taxonomy,
NumSharp vs live NumPy 2.4.2) surfaced exactly two divergences; both fixed here. Everything else —
185 value/dtype/shape/tuple cases and 18 verbatim error messages — was already byte-exact.

1. np.polyval(0-d p, x): NumPy's `for pv in p` cannot iterate a 0-d coefficient array and raises
   `TypeError: iteration over a 0-d array` (a scalar is NOT a length-1 polynomial — that is `[c]`).
   NumSharp silently treated the 0-d as a degree-0 constant. Now guarded to raise the verbatim
   TypeError; a 1-D length-1 array stays a valid constant polynomial.

2. poly1d.ToString(): NumPy's `poly1d.__repr__` is `repr(coeffs)[6:-1]` wrapped in `poly1d(...)`,
   so it inherits the array repr's column alignment, the trailing dot on whole floats, and the
   `, dtype=int8` suffix for non-default dtypes. The hand-rolled formatter dropped all of that
   (`poly1d([0.5, 1, 3])` vs NumPy's `poly1d([0.5, 1. , 3. ])`). Since NumSharp's array_repr
   (ToString(true)) is byte-exact to NumPy's, the repr is now produced the same way NumPy produces
   it — byte-exact across int/float/complex/int8/empty coefficients.

tests total, all green; the 7 live byte-parity tests unaffected). Audit conclusion: the polynomial
family is byte-identical to NumPy 2.4.2 across values, dtypes, shapes, tuples and error messages;
the only remaining difference is that np.polydiv on poly1d inputs returns bare arrays (a C# tuple
slot is a fixed type — the poly1d `/` operator does the wrapping), already documented.

fix(matmul): out= with extra leading loop dims broadcasts the product (NumPy parity)

Adversarial validation against NumPy 2.4.2 caught a divergence in np.matmul's out=
shape validation: NumPy ACCEPTS an out= whose CORE dims (the trailing (n?,m?)) match
but which carries extra LEADING loop dims of any size, replicating the product into
each slab — probed: np.matmul((2,2),(2,2), out=empty((5,2,2))) is 5 copies of the
(2,2) product. The previous ValidateMatmulOutputShape rejected any leading dim != 1,
so it wrongly threw where NumPy broadcasts.

Fix: validate ONLY the trailing outputCore dims exactly (still reporting NumPy's
verbatim "Output operand 0 has a mismatch in its core dimension {c} …" on a core
mismatch), and leave the leading loop dims to copyto, which broadcasts the product
into out and raises on a genuine loop-dim mismatch (its "operands could not be
broadcast together with remapped shapes …" text is itself close to NumPy's leaked
iterator text; typed IncorrectShapeException per house convention). Removed the now-
unused OutputShapeMismatch helper.

Re-verified the whole out= shape matrix against NumPy: over-broadcast out=(5,2,2)
replicates; out=(1,2,2) fills; core mismatches (2,3)/(3,2)/(2,2,1) and batched
(2,3,4)/(2,3) report the verbatim core-dimension message; batched loop mismatch
(3,3,3) raises the broadcast error. The rest of the validation pass found matmul,
np.dot, np.outer and np.cross otherwise flawless vs NumPy (bool/complex/half/decimal
dtype sweeps, out= aliasing an input, F-contiguous out, casting rules, batched
broadcast, cross across all dtypes/layouts/axes incl. unsigned wrap and the verbatim
boolean-subtract rejection) — this over-broadcast case was the only divergence.

Regression test: Matmul_Out_ExtraLeadingLoopDims_ReplicateProduct.

fix(polynomial): poly1d operator parity — array±p is element-wise, p/array is polydiv (deeper NumPy audit)

Second adversarial audit pass over the poly family (138 fresh byte-level differential cases:
nan/inf/signed-zero, every dtype-promotion corner, full parameter matrices, verbatim error
taxonomy — all byte-identical to NumPy 2.4.2) surfaced two poly1d operator divergences and
confirmed the numerics are flawless.

Fixes:
- REMOVED `operator +(NDArray, poly1d)` and `operator -(NDArray, poly1d)`. NumPy's `array + poly1d`
  is ELEMENT-WISE (the ndarray wins via poly1d.__array__), returning a plain ndarray — NOT polyadd;
  same for subtraction. The reflected overloads both diverged from NumPy AND hijacked `"string" + p`
  (the string literal implicitly becomes a char NDArray, binding to the polyadd overload and
  producing a garbage poly1d of ASCII codes). Removing them lets `array±p` take the implicit
  poly1d->NDArray conversion (element-wise, NumPy-exact) and makes `"str" + p` behave like any other
  NDArray. `p±array` / `p±poly1d` (poly1d on the LEFT) stay polyadd/polysub, matching NumPy's
  `poly1d.__add__`/`__sub__`.
- ADDED `operator /(poly1d, NDArray)` -> polydiv (quotient, remainder). NumPy's `poly1d.__truediv__`
  wraps a non-scalar and divides polynomially, so `p / array` is a division TUPLE, not the
  element-wise coefficient division the implicit conversion would otherwise pick.

Documented (C#-unexpressible, in the class doc): `p ** n` has no `**` operator — spell it `p*p*...`,
which NumPy defines it to equal; ToString renders NumPy's repr form, not the separate pretty str().

Verified byte-exact this pass (values, not just close): polyfit cov='unscaled' (all 9 elements),
polyfit deg-0 negative-zero (bit pattern 0x…80), rank=int32, and the full roots/poly/polyfit edge +
error matrix. Deliberate divergence pinned [Misaligned]: roots/poly of a 0-d input — NumPy's
@array_function_dispatch rejects it with an internal artifact message before the body runs; NumSharp
has no such dispatcher so the body (which would accept it via atleast_1d) runs, giving the sensible
answer (roots(0-d)->empty, poly(0-d 5)->[1,-5]).

Tests: +3 offline (reflected add/sub element-wise, divide-by-array polydiv, 0-d divergence) and
+2 live byte-parity (unscaled covariance, deg-0 signed zero). 35 offline + 9 live green;
1624 Polynomial+Creation+LinearAlgebra tests pass, no regressions.

feat(linalg): MissingBackendException + OpenBlasMissingBackendException for unserved factorisations

Introduce a typed exception hierarchy for the "no compute backend installed" case,
replacing the bare NotSupportedException the np.linalg factorisations raised when
TensorEngine.Blas is null (or the installed backend declines the operands).

New types (Exceptions/):
- MissingBackendException : NotSupportedException, INumSharpException
    The general case: an operation needs a pluggable IBlasBackend on
    TensorEngine.Blas and none serves it. Derives from NotSupportedException so
    every existing `catch (NotSupportedException)` keeps working, and also carries
    the house INumSharpException marker -- the same dual shape ValueError/AxisError
    use to sit under a BCL type and the NumSharp marker at once.
- OpenBlasMissingBackendException : MissingBackendException
    Names the fix: reference the NumSharp.Interop.OpenBLAS NuGet package. Owns
    `const PackageId = "NumSharp.Interop.OpenBLAS"` and a reusable HowToFix hint --
    the single source of truth for the package name across every message that
    raises it.

Wiring (Backends/TensorEngine.LinearAlgebra.cs):
- The private NoLapack(api, routines, seamMember) helper -- the single funnel all
    10 factorisations (Cholesky/Det/Slogdet/Eig/Eigh/Inv/Lstsq/Qr/Solve/Svd) reach,
    and through them norm{2,-2,nuc} / matrix_power(-1) / pinv / cond / matrix_rank /
    tensorinv / tensorsolve -- is renamed MissingBackend(api, seamMember) and now
    throws OpenBlasMissingBackendException.

Message reframed to OpenBLAS only. There is no separate "LAPACK backend" to
install: the factorisations ride the very same TensorEngine.Blas / IBlasBackend
property the matrix products do, filled by a single NumSharp.Interop.OpenBLAS
reference -- so the message points at that package and drops the "LAPACK backend"
framing and the routine names entirely. It still names the NumPy API, the
IBlasBackend.Try* seam member, TensorEngine.Blas, and the package.

Distinct from the interop package's OpenBlasRequiredOverrideException
(a DllNotFoundException), which fires when the package IS referenced but a
hard-required build override cannot load; this one fires when Core has no backend
at all.

Tests (LinAlgEngineSeamTests):
- The message test now pins the package id and asserts the message never says
    "LAPACK"; dropped the old "gesv" routine-name assertion.
- New test pins the type hierarchy: OpenBlasMissingBackendException ->
    MissingBackendException -> NotSupportedException + INumSharpException, so the
    concrete type is new yet stays catchable as NotSupportedException.

All 20 seam tests + 559 LinearAlgebra/factorisation tests green.

feat(io): np.savetxt — byte-exact NumPy 2.4.2 text serialization

Port of numpy/lib/_npyio_impl.py::savetxt (APIs/np.savetxt.cs), byte-for-byte
identical to NumPy 2.4.2's own output across dtypes, formats, layouts and errors.

Signature parity: savetxt(fname, X, fmt='%.18e', delimiter=' ', newline='\n',
header='', footer='', comments='# ', encoding=None) over three targets —
filename (string), Stream, TextWriter — each with a string-fmt and a
string[]-fmt overload (NumPy's "str or sequence of strs").

Behavior (all probed against NumPy 2.4.2):
- Rank: 1-D writes one value per line (atleast_2d.T, ncol=1); 2-D a row per
  line; 0-D/>=3-D raise ValueError("Expected 1D or 2D array, got {n}D array
  instead"). Empty and (n,0) shapes reproduce NumPy exactly ('' and '\n\n').
- fmt: single spec replicated ncol times (delimiter-joined); a multi-% string
  used verbatim (delimiter ignored); or a per-column list/tuple. Verbatim
  errors: ValueError("fmt has wrong number of % formats:  ...") and the new
  house AttributeError("fmt has wrong shape.  ...").
- Numeric specs widen to double (NumPy's float()/int() coercion: int64>2^53 and
  float32 render at the double value); %s uses each dtype's shortest scalar repr.
- Complex wraps a single spec as ' (%s+%sj)' per column with the '+-'->'-' fix-up.
- Integer-format-on-float matches CPython: %x/%X/%o reject float -> TypeError
  reported as the dtype/format Mismatch; %d/%i/%u truncate a finite float but
  raise on nan/inf.
- Filename target uses Python text-mode newline translation (\n -> os.linesep,
  CRLF on Windows) and gzips a .gz name; Stream/TextWriter write \n verbatim
  (NumPy's file-handle path). A validation error leaves the (empty) file, as
  NumPy's create-then-validate does.
- Reads any layout (C/F/strided/transposed/negative-stride/broadcast/sliced) in
  logical C-order via GetAtIndex; all 15 dtypes (Char/Decimal via same coercion).

Reuses the existing PrintfFormatter (shared with ndarray.tofile) for the %
engine; adds FormatRow/FormatRowInto for the multi-column `format % tuple(row)`
path (sequential args, appends straight into the batch buffer — no per-row
allocation). tofile's Format path is untouched.

Perf (NPY/NS, Release, best-of-7): file-to-file ~2.1x (NS 151ms vs NumPy 318ms
for 100Kx5 f64 %.18e), %d 25x, %g 3.2x — NumPy's savetxt is a pure-Python
per-row loop. The %.18e floor is .NET's Ryu double->string, the analog of
NumPy's dtoa.

Deliberate divergences (documented): %d on inf raises System.OverflowException
where NumPy raises OverflowError (message identical; NumSharp has no
OverflowError type; nan still raises ValueError verbatim); the AttributeError
renders string[] as a Python list repr.

New: Exceptions/AttributeError.cs, Backends/Printing/PrintfArgumentException.cs.
Gate: IO/SaveTxtTests.cs (probed against NumPy 2.4.2; net8.0 + net10.0 green,
19 methods). Also documented in .claude/CLAUDE.md File I/O.

feat(io): np.loadtxt — NumPy 2.4.2 text reader (savetxt round-trip)

Port of numpy/lib/_npyio_impl.py::loadtxt -> _read plus its C text reader
(numpy/_core/src/multiarray/textreading/{tokenize.cpp,conversions.c,
str_to_int.c,rows.c}) in APIs/np.loadtxt.cs, the reader complement to
np.savetxt. Reads back what savetxt writes (byte-exact values).

Signature parity: loadtxt(fname, dtype=float, comments='#', delimiter=None,
converters=None, skiprows=0, usecols=None, unpack=False, ndmin=0,
encoding=None, max_rows=None, quotechar=None), over four input sources —
filename (.gz transparently decompressed), Stream, TextReader,
IEnumerable<string> (lines, embedded newlines split) — with an NPTypeCode and
a Type dtype overload.

Behavior (all probed against NumPy 2.4.2):
- The C reader yields a 2-D (rows, cols) array; ndmin then squeezes size-1
  axes (single row/col -> 1-D, a lone value -> 0-d) or expands.
- Tokenizer (faithful port): delimiter=None splits on runs of whitespace
  (leading/trailing stripped; blank/comment-only lines -> 0 fields ->
  skipped); an explicit single-char delimiter (incl. ' ') keeps empty fields;
  quotechar protects delimiters/comments and doubles as an escape; a
  single-char comment strips to line-end (multi-char comment stripped per
  line, rejected with quotechar).
- Per-dtype strict parsers: bool via int64 ("0"/"1", -1->True, "True"->error);
  integers range-check (int8 "200" -> error) and unsigned reject negatives
  (uint8 "-1" -> error); float uses PyOS_string_to_double semantics
  (case-insensitive inf/infinity/nan, rejects hex/"_"/trailing-junk/empty,
  NaN -> +qNaN 0x7FF8…); complex is to_complex_int (a / aj / a+bj / (a+bj) /
  1+-2j). All 15 dtypes (Char/Decimal via the same coercion).
- converters (Func<string,object> for all columns, or
  IDictionary<int,Func<string,object>> per column), usecols (int[], negatives
  from the end), unpack (transpose), skiprows/max_rows (blank/comment lines
  don't count toward max_rows), encoding.
- Verbatim NumPy errors: "the number of columns changed from {a} to {b} at
  row {n}; …", "could not convert string '{tok}' to {dtype} at row {r},
  column {c}." (row 0-based, column 1-based), "invalid column index {k} at row
  {n} with {c} columns", "Illegal value of ndmin keyword: …", and TypeError
  for a multi-char / newline delimiter.

Fields are parsed straight from the line's char span (no per-field string
allocation on the common path). Reuses the private BytesToArray helper from
np.fromfile.cs; loadtxt carries its own strict parsers because fromfile's
truncate/wrap rather than range-check.

float-heavy input ~1.0-1.1x (parity) — bounded by the correctly-rounded
double.Parse, the analog of NumPy's strtod (the same floor on both sides, as
with savetxt's %.18e).

has no warnings module; the array is still the correct empty result).

NumPy's public API is case-sensitive, so the inventory credits a NumSharp member only
when the spelling is identical. Every match was already an exact dict lookup; this makes

DETECTION pass on top: an in-scope NumPy export left "missing" for which NumSharp
exposes a SAME-SURFACE member differing only by case is surfaced as a near-miss —
reported, never counted — so nothing silently satisfies NumPy's `histogram` with a
C#-style `Histogram`.

  + a `methodology.case_sensitivity` note.

- console: a mention line on every run (count + each 'numpy.X ~ NumSharp.Y').
- per-row `notes` also carry the mention.

fix(io): savetxt/loadtxt NumPy-2.4.2 parity — 4 divergences + np.fromstring

Validated the text I/O family (savetxt / loadtxt / fromstring) against NumPy
2.4.2 with byte/bit-exact differential harnesses (467 savetxt + 210 loadtxt +
20 fromstring cases, all green). Four real divergences found and fixed, plus the
one feasible missing family member added.

savetxt / PrintfFormatter fixes (Backends/Printing/PrintfFormatter.cs):

1. Integer `.precision` (min-digits) was IGNORED. Python's `.precision` on a
   d/i/u/x/X/o conversion is the minimum digit count, left-zero-filled:
   `%.5d % 42` -> `00042`, `%.0d % 0` -> `0` (the "0" digit is already one char).
   FormatInteger now applies it, the `0` flag composes with it Python-style (not
   C-style) so `%08.3d % 7` -> `00000007`, and with `#` the zero-fill lands
   BETWEEN the 0x/0o prefix and the digits (`%#08x % 255` -> `0x0000ff`) via the
   new PadInteger helper (the generic Pad put the zeros before the prefix).

2. `%c` and bool integer conversions did not raise where NumPy does. `%c` now
   renders a true integer's code point only in [0, 0x10FFFF] and raises
   OverflowError("%c arg not in range(0x110000)") outside it; `%c` on a bool and
   `%x`/`%X`/`%o` on a bool raise the TypeError that savetxt reports as the
   dtype/format mismatch (a NumPy bool scalar is not an int for those specs —
   probed), while %d/%i/%u still accept a bool. Added IsTrueIntegerTc for the
   bool-excluding integer set; the change is scoped to savetxt's FormatRowInto,
   leaving tofile's lenient Format path unchanged.

loadtxt fixes (APIs/np.loadtxt.cs):

3. The complex parser accepted an uppercase imaginary unit `J`. NumPy's default
   imaginary_unit is lowercase `j` ONLY, so `"1+2J"` must raise. TryComplexLT now
   matches lowercase `j` exclusively.

4. Whitespace did not match Py_UNICODE_ISSPACE. That set is identical to .NET's
   char.IsWhiteSpace across the whole BMP EXCEPT the four C0 information
   separators U+001C..U+001F (exhaustively verified: the only difference, with
   nothing over-treated). So NumPy splits `"1\x1c2"` into two fields and strips a
   leading/trailing separator; NumSharp did neither. Added IsLoadtxtWhitespace /
   TrimLoadtxtWs and routed the tokenizer and every numeric field parser through
   them.

New — np.fromstring (APIs/np.fromstring.cs):

`fromstring(string, dtype=float, count=-1, sep)` parses a 1-D array from a text
string, reusing np.fromfile's exact text item-reader (NumPy shares its `fromstr`
the same way). The binary mode (empty separator) was REMOVED in NumPy 1.22, so an
empty/null sep raises ValueError("The binary mode of fromstring is removed, use
frombuffer instead") rather than reinterpreting bytes (probed 2.4.2).

Not implemented — genfromtxt / fromregex: both require NumPy's structured/record
dtypes (and genfromtxt its masked-array + missing-value machinery), for which

feat(ndarray): nbytes, fill, flags — NumPy 2.4.2 parity

Add three long-missing ndarray members, each probed against and bit-exact with
NumPy 2.4.2 across the full layout/dtype/edge matrix. 46 new tests; a stash-compare
against the baseline confirms ZERO regressions (identical 22 pre-existing audit
failures with and without this change).

ndarray.nbytes (Backends/NDArray.cs)
  Total element bytes = LOGICAL size × itemsize (NumPy's PyArray_NBYTES =
  ITEMSIZE * SIZE). A broadcast (1000,1000) view of one int32 reports 4000000
  (its logical size), not its one-element buffer; 0-d → one itemsize; empty → 0.

ndarray.fill(value) (Manipulation/NDArray.fill.cs)
  In-place scalar fill across every layout (C/F/strided/transposed/negative-stride,
  write-through). Coercion follows NumPy scalar-assignment (NEP50 weak-scalar) rules:
  a C# primitive into an integer dtype is range-checked — out of bounds RAISES
  (OverflowException "Python integer 300 out of bounds for int8"), a float source
  TRUNCATES toward zero before the check; into a float dtype it saturates to +/-inf.
  A 0-d NDArray is a STRONG scalar (wraps like np.int64); a multi-element array is a
  sequence -> ValueError("setting an array element with a sequence."). Ordering
  matches PyArray_FillWithScalar: writeability checked first (read-only ValueError),
  then the scalar is packed (raising even on an EMPTY array), then elements written.
  Perf: contiguous fill splats the [offset,offset+size) window through the vectorized
  UnmanagedSpan<T>.Fill (dtype-agnostic cached delegate) — parity with NumPy at
  cache-resident sizes (100K/1M ~1.0x), faster on tiny fills (same-dtype fast path);
  strided fill broadcasts a 0-d scalar via the NDIter engine np.copyto uses.

ndarray.flags -> NDArrayFlags (Backends/NDArray.flags.cs)
  Port of NumPy's arrayflags object: lowercase attributes c_contiguous / f_contiguous
  / contiguous / fortran / owndata / writeable / aligned / writebackifcopy and derived
  fnc / forc / behaved / carray / farray / num; bracket-key access (flags["C"],
  flags["F_CONTIGUOUS"], short+long spellings), the six-line str() repr, equality by
  num, and a writeable setter (make read-only in place via Shape.WithFlags; re-enable
  on an owned array). num uses NumPy's exact bit values; ALIGNED is always true and
  WRITEBACKIFCOPY always false (what a NumSharp array can be). Values verified equal
  to NumPy across C/F/strided/transposed/broadcast/0-d/empty/neg-stride layouts.

Deliberate divergences (documented): fill(null) -> ArgumentNullException (house
convention, cf np.fill_diagonal); flags.writeable=True on a non-owning view is refused
for safety (NumPy permits it when the base is writeable).

feat(ndarray): real/imag properties + conj/conjugate methods — NumPy 2.4.2 parity

Add the ndarray complex-accessor instance members (the np.real/np.imag/np.conjugate
FUNCTIONS already existed; these are the ndarray.* forms with setters). Each behavior
probed against and bit-exact with NumPy 2.4.2. 20 new tests; zero regressions
(Fourier+Maths 697, LinearAlgebra+FFT-fuzz 416 all green).

ndarray.real / ndarray.imag (get + set), Math/NDArray.ComplexAccessors.cs
  GET delegates to np.real/np.imag (unchanged): complex -> a writeable float64 lane
  VIEW sharing memory (z.real[i]=x writes through); real .real -> self; real .imag ->
  read-only zeros. SET copies the value into the real/imag part with NumPy's
  PyArray_CopyInto semantics — UNSAFE casting (a.real=3.9 into int truncates to 3,
  int8.real=300 wraps to 44, a complex source keeps only its real part), broadcasting
  the value to the part's shape, writing through strided/complex-lane views, and raising
  the standard read-only error on a non-writeable target. Setting .imag on a non-complex
  array raises TypeError("array does not have imaginary part to set"), matching NumPy.

ndarray.conj() / ndarray.conjugate(out=None)
  Port of PyArray_Conjugate (the METHOD), which is NOT the np.conjugate ufunc: complex
  flips the imaginary sign (via np.conjugate); every non-complex dtype is already its own
  conjugate, so the method PRESERVES the dtype and returns `self` (out=None) or copies
  self into `out` under same_kind casting. This is the documented method/function split:
  a.conj() on a bool array stays bool (self), whereas np.conj(a) promotes bool->int8
  (the ufunc has no bool loop). Verified: x.conjugate() is x for real input.

Perf: conj() reuses the existing conjugate kernel (2.5-4.3x NumPy); real/imag getters are
O(1) lane views; the real/imag setter is copyto (memory-bound, ~parity at scale). The one
carried divergence is the broadcast-mismatch message (IncorrectShapeException, consistent
with np.copyto's existing house wording rather than NumPy's "could not broadcast ...").

refactor(einsum): move contraction from TensorEngine into the np layer

np.einsum's contraction composition was a public virtual TensorEngine.Einsum
in Backends/TensorEngine.Einsum.cs. Move it verbatim into
LinearAlgebra/np.einsum.Contract.cs as a private static np.EinsumContract;
np.einsum now calls it directly instead of operands[0].TensorEngine.Einsum(...).
The engine file is deleted and the pointer comment in
TensorEngine.LinearAlgebra.cs is updated.

Why: it was a Pattern-1 pure composition (over np.matmul / np.multiply /
np.sum / np.transpose / np.diagonal) misfiled as a Pattern-2 engine op. It used
no instance state, consulted no Blas seam, had no TryEinsum, and was never
overridden. Its numerics come entirely from np.matmul, which re-dispatches
through the operand arrays' OWN engine (np.matmul.cs: a.TensorEngine.Matmul) —
not the einsum engine's `this` — so overriding TensorEngine.Einsum could never
have changed them; the virtual seam was inert. It now sits beside np.tensordot
and np.linalg.multi_dot, the siblings it always cited as its model and which
likewise live in np.* and reach a backend indirectly through the product.

Pure relocation: the contraction body is unchanged and Blas routing is
identical (still indirect via np.matmul), so there is no numerics change.
Removes the public TensorEngine.Einsum method (breaking to the engine surface,
acceptable per repo policy); nothing referenced it but np.einsum, and no engine
overrode it.

shared tree carried unrelated concurrent WIP that reds the test build):
NumSharp.Core and the test project build clean; 111 tests pass across
EinsumContractionTests, EinsumSubscriptParityTests, EinsumPathTests and
LinAlgEngineSeamTests. The seam test calls np.einsum (behavioral), so it
survives the move unchanged.

Audited the rest of the TensorEngine surface while here: einsum was the only

product (Inner/Vdot/Vecdot/Matvec/Vecmat) and factorisation virtuals consult
this.Blas (the Try* seam) and compose over this.Dot / this.Matmul.

feat(ndarray): add ndarray.itemsize (NumPy 2.4.2 parity)

Adds the NumPy `ndarray.itemsize` attribute — "Length of one array
element in bytes" — to NDArray, the last missing sibling of the
size/ndim/nbytes/dtypesize metadata family.

What it is
----------
A pure O(1) property of the dtype: `public int itemsize => Storage.DTypeSize`.
NumPy surfaces `PyArray_ITEMSIZE` (the dtype's element size) as a plain
Python int on every ndarray; it is independent of shape, strides, offset
and layout, so every view of a given dtype reports the same value. No
kernel / NDIter / ILKernelGenerator is involved (there is no loop over
element data) — it mirrors the existing `dtypesize`/`nbytes` properties,
reading the same `Storage.DTypeSize` jump-table that already backs them.

Why an alias rather than a rename
---------------------------------
NumSharp has long carried `dtypesize` (legacy name) for the identical
value. `itemsize` is added ALONGSIDE it (existing API untouched) so Python
code ports verbatim (`arr.itemsize`) while every current `dtypesize`
call-site keeps working. `itemsize == dtypesize`, and
`size * itemsize == nbytes`, both asserted.

Parity (probed against NumPy 2.4.2)
-----------------------------------
Byte-identical to NumPy for the 13 dtypes with a NumPy analog:
bool/int8/uint8→1, int16/uint16/float16→2, int32/uint32/float32→4,
int64/uint64/float64→8, complex128→16. The two NumSharp-only dtypes with
no NumPy analog report their in-memory element size (Char→2, Decimal→16),
consistent with `dtypesize`/`nbytes`. Verified layout-invariant across
C-contiguous, 0-d, empty, strided, transposed, negative-stride, broadcast
and post-astype views — exactly as NumPy behaves.

Tests
-----
NDArray.flags.Test.cs gains an itemsize section (3 methods, 24 total in the
class, all green): all-15-dtype coverage, layout invariance, and the
alias/nbytes-composition identities. Gated by unit tests like its
`dtypesize`/`nbytes` siblings (a scalar dtype attribute produces no
(dtype,shape,bytes) result for the NDIter differential-fuzz corpus).

feat(ndarray): add ndarray.data — the memoryview buffer object (np.MemoryView)

Implements NumPy's `ndarray.data` (probed against NumPy 2.4.2), the read-only
attribute that is literally `memoryview(self)` — "Python buffer object pointing
to the start of the array's data." Closes the coverage gap where `.data` was only
"partial" (loosely mapped to the typed `Data<T>()` method, which is NOT a buffer
object).

WHAT
- New `NDArray.data` (lowercase, matching the whole np.* surface: shape/size/flat/
  device/strides). Read-only property, so it cannot be assigned — mirroring NumPy,
  whose `.data` is getter-only (assignment raises AttributeError). A fresh handle is
  returned per access, exactly as NumPy hands out a new memoryview each time.
- New house type `np.MemoryView` (sealed, nested under `np` like np.Broadcast /
  np.FlatIterator / np.NDIterator) — the NumSharp analog of Python's `memoryview`.
  It OWNS NO MEMORY: every member reads LIVE through the source array's Storage/Shape
  (per the "back it with the existing buffer infra" design decision), and holds the
  source array as `obj` to keep it alive (NumPy's `memoryview.obj`).

SURFACE (all bit-identical to NumPy 2.4.2 — see gate):
  obj, itemsize, ndim, nbytes (logical size·itemsize), @readonly (true for broadcast
  views), shape, strides (in BYTES — NumSharp strides are elements, ·itemsize here),
  format (struct code), c_contiguous / f_contiguous / contiguous, Length (len(mv)),
  Pointer (void*) / Address (IntPtr) at the LOGICAL first element, write-through
  scalar element get/set via this[params long[]], tobytes(order=C/F/A), hex().

LOAD-BEARING DETAILS (probed, easy to get wrong):
- Pointer = Storage.Address + Shape.Offset·itemsize — the logical start, matching
  NumPy's a.data / PyArray_DATA / a.ctypes.data / __array_interface__['data'][0].
  Verified across offset ([3:7] -> base+12) and reversed ([::-1] -> base+36, the
  last physical element) views. The offset lives in Storage.Address OR Shape.Offset
  (mutually exclusive across NumSharp's view paths), so the single formula is robust.
- strides in BYTES via Shape.Strides (elements) · itemsize — NOT NDArray.strides —
  so a stride-0 broadcast axis stays 0 and a reversed view stays negative.
- format follows numpy/_core/src/multiarray/buffer.c EXACTLY, incl. the platform
  split: NPY_LONG emits 'l'/'L' on Windows LLP64 but 'i'/'I' elsewhere (numpy's int32
  is NPY_LONG on Windows, NPY_INT on LP64), so int32/uint32 are platform-dependent.
  Char (2-byte UTF-16) and Decimal (opaque 16B) have no NumPy dtype -> documented
  house codes 'u' / '16s'.
- tobytes gathers in LOGICAL order via the existing copy machinery (NDIter/IL copy
  kernels), with a direct-memcpy fast path when already contiguous in the target
  order; 'A' = physical order if contiguous (F when F-contig, else C).
- Write-through element set coerces the value to the dtype (a 1-element astype, the
  standard NumSharp scalar-cast path — Storage.SetValue demands an exact CLR type),
  and refuses a readonly (broadcast) target. Documented divergence: astype WRAPS an
  out-of-range integer where NumPy's memoryview raises; use arr.flatiter for the
  weak-scalar bounds check.

NOT MODELLED (documented boundaries, not gaps): partial-index sub-memoryviews, cast,
tolist, release / the context-manager protocol, element iteration — NumSharp has no
Python buffer protocol, so these Python-object conveniences have no counterpart; the
buffer ESSENCE (pointer + metadata + write-through + tobytes) is what data is for.

GATE: test/NumSharp.Tests/APIs/np.memoryview.Test.cs (17 tests, net8.0 + net10.0),
probed against NumPy 2.4.2. Differentially validated bit-exact vs numpy across
{1d,2d,offset,reversed,strided,transposed,broadcast,0-d,empty,f64} × {ndim,itemsize,
nbytes,readonly,shape,byte-strides,format,contiguity,tobytes C/F/A} and all 15 dtype
format codes. As a pure O(1) accessor (a buffer handle, not a value-producing NDIter
op) it is unit-test gated — same rationale as flatiter/nditer/ndindex/device — and
deliberately absent from the differential-fuzz corpus. Perf: handle is O(1) (~14 ns);

feat(frombuffer): np.frombuffer(np.MemoryView) — the memoryview consumer, zero-copy

Adds np.frombuffer overloads that accept np.MemoryView (from ndarray.data) — the
CONSUMER side of the buffer object added in 25ae7053, so `np.frombuffer(arr.data)`
round-trips: it reconstructs a 1-D array that SHARES arr's memory (probed against
NumPy 2.4.2). Completes "memoryview related apis to use memoryview".

WHAT
- frombuffer(MemoryView, Type dtype=null, long count=-1, long offset=0)
- frombuffer(MemoryView, NPTypeCode dtype, long count=-1, long offset=0)   [core]
- frombuffer(MemoryView, string dtype, long count=-1, long offset=0)
  mirroring the existing byte[]/Span/Memory overload shapes.

SEMANTICS (all bit-exact vs NumPy 2.4.2):
- ZERO-COPY: the result views the source's unmanaged buffer; writes through to the
  source. Reinterprets bytes as `dtype` (int32->float32 == 1.0, int32->int16 doubles
  the count, int32->int64 halves it — little-endian, byte-identical to NumPy).
- Requires a C-contiguous buffer; a strided/transposed/F-contiguous memoryview raises
  NumPy's "memoryview: underlying buffer is not C-contiguous" (BufferError text; as
  InvalidOperationException, NumSharp has no BufferError type).
- offset is in BYTES, count in ELEMENTS; default dtype float64; 2-D C-contig source
  flattens to 1-D; 0-d source -> one element; empty -> empty. offset/count validation
  and messages are IDENTICAL to the existing byte[] path ("buffer size must be a
  multiple of element size" / "buffer is smaller than requested size").
- Read-only buffer -> read-only array (writeability propagated).

IMPLEMENTATION — a pure composition of existing zero-copy VIEW primitives, no data
copy, no per-element loop (frombuffer is a reinterpretation), no manual pointer/ARC,
no per-dtype compute switch:
  src.reshape(size)              C-contiguous -> distinct 1-D view
  -> view(dtype) (AliasAs)       reinterpret bytes to the target dtype in ELEMENT space
  -> [offsetElems:+count] slice  only when a sub-range is requested
The aligned-offset path (offset==0 and every valid offset when the source byte count
is a multiple of the target itemsize — i.e. essentially all real usage) stays in
element space; a genuinely non-itemsize-aligned offset (only reachable when the source
byte count is NOT a multiple of the target itemsize, e.g. a byte source reinterpreted
as int16 at an odd offset) falls back to a flat byte-window slice. ARC on the shared
MemoryBlock keeps the source buffer alive for the view's lifetime (NumPy's memoryview
.base) — verified: the view survives the source being disposed + GC'd.

GATE: test/NumSharp.Tests/Creation/np.frombuffer.MemoryView.Test.cs (14 tests, net8.0
+ net10.0), probed against NumPy 2.4.2: round-trip/write-through, default float64,
reinterpret widths, 2-D flatten, count+offset, 0-d, non-contiguous/misalign/too-big/
null errors, readonly propagation, survives-source-dispose (ARC), all 15 dtypes, Type
+ string overloads. Existing 25 frombuffer/memoryview tests stay green (no overload
ambiguity — MemoryView has no implicit conversions).

PERF: zero-copy O(1) (constant regardless of array size — no data copy). Same-dtype
~450 ns/call (one reshape), cross-dtype ~1.6 us/call (the view(dtype)/AliasAs cost).
Allocations minimized from 4 view-ops to 1-2. Sub-1.5x vs NumPy's single C
view-constructor (~355 ns) because one NDArray/Storage/Shape construction already
~= NumPy's whole call — the documented per-construction floor (cf. fill_diagonal
0.62x, meshgrid-small 0.5x), not a copy/algorithm cost.

fix(view): align ndarray.view(dtype) different-itemsize rule with NumPy 2.x

NumSharp's UnmanagedStorage.AliasAs<T> (the storage half of ndarray.view(dtype))
rejected ANY non-C-contiguous array when reinterpreting to a different-size dtype,
and rebuilt a fresh C-contiguous shape from the buffer base — discarding the view's
offset and outer-axis strides. NumPy 2.x (numpy/_core/src/multiarray/getset.c
array_descr_set, since gh-1.23) only requires the LAST axis to be contiguous: every
outer axis keeps its byte stride while the last axis is rescaled by the size ratio.

So np.arange(12).reshape(3,4)[::2].view(np.int32) — last axis contiguous, whole array
not C-contiguous — SUCCEEDS in NumPy (shape (2,8), strides (64,4), shares memory) but
threw InvalidOperationException in NumSharp. An existing test
(View_NonContiguous_ThrowsForDifferentSize) pinned that non-NumPy behavior.

Rewrite AliasAs<T> to NumPy's algorithm:
- same itemsize: pure reinterpret keeping dims/strides/offset for ANY layout
  (contiguous/strided/transposed/negative-stride/broadcast/0-d); the wrap now spans
  the whole backing slice so an element-dropping strided view addresses every
  in-bounds coordinate (a latent under-span the old newCount=_shape.size had).
- different itemsize: require only the LAST axis contiguous; preserve outer byte
  strides (as new-dtype element strides) and the base offset; resize the last axis;
  keep a read-only (broadcast) source read-only. Verbatim NumPy error messages for
  0-d, non-contiguous last axis, and non-divisible last-axis byte size. A rare
  strided+offset view whose byte offset/stride is not a whole multiple of the new
  itemsize is refused (NumSharp stores strides/offset in elements, not bytes) — still
  strictly more permissive than before.

AliasAs is reached only through view(). Differential-verified bit-exact vs NumPy 2.4.2
across outer-strided (i8->i4, i4->i2/i8), 3-D sliced, i2->i4 widening, and broadcast
(read-only) cases incl. values/shape/strides/writeability/write-through; all four
error cases match. Char->ushort same-size reduction path (argmax/argmin/max/min,
contiguous+strided) verified unaffected. Full suite: 13632 passed, only the 2
pre-existing baseline failures remain (0 regressions).

coercion-adversarial value set (probed a.fill(v) and diffed C# vs NumPy). The
value/layout matrix was already bit-exact, but the WEAK-scalar (C# primitive)

PyArray_FillWithScalar -> PyArray_Pack, which funnels a python scalar through

  TypeError 'float() argument ... not complex'. Was InvalidCastException

objects (which NumSharp has no analog for) take the value-range-checked setitem.

unit-stride contiguous run (row slice m[::2], row-strided/offset row, 3D
[:, ::2, :], negative-OUTER-stride [::-1]) is a stack of contiguous runs, now

odometer (handles negative outer strides), keyed per-dtype through the
reflection-cache and non-allocating (struct span Slice). Works at ANY rank --
NumSharp has no ndim cap, so the odometer stackallocs its coord array for the
common shallow ranks and heap-allocates only past a 64-deep stack budget (the

non-unit-or-negative inner stride / broadcast. Byte-identical to NumPy across 12

feat(ndarray): add ndarray.byteswap (NumPy 2.4.2 parity)

Implement ndarray.byteswap(inplace=False), a faithful port of NumPy's
PyArray_Byteswap (numpy/_core/src/multiarray/methods.c). Reverses the bytes
WITHIN each element to toggle the endian representation; the dtype is unchanged,
so only the reinterpreted values change. Complex swaps its real/imaginary halves
independently (NumPy copyswapn per component); 1-byte dtypes are a value no-op
(but inplace=False still returns a fresh copy). New files only — no existing
code touched.

Design
- byteswap depends ONLY on the element byte width, never on the dtype's numeric
  meaning, so ONE width-dispatched SIMD kernel (swapUnit in {2,4,8,16}, complex
  =itemsize/2=8) covers every dtype instead of a per-NPTypeCode path. VPSHUFB
  reverses lane-locally, so one per-128-bit-lane mask drives AVX2 (32 B/iter) and
  SSSE3 (16 B/iter) via GetLower(); scalar two-pointer swap for the tail /
  no-SIMD fallback. NumSharp-only dtypes (no NumPy analog) take the consistent
  raw-itemsize rule: Char swaps in 2s, Decimal in 16s.
- inplace=False = NumPy PyArray_NewCopy(ANYORDER) then swap. Fused into ONE pass
  for a C-contiguous source (allocate uninitialized C-contiguous result, then
  read->shuffle->write), skipping the copy machinery's second pass. F-contiguous
  keeps NumPy's F layout via Shape.Order; 1-byte is a straight Buffer.MemoryCopy.
- Large (>=2 MiB), 32-byte-aligned fused writes stream non-temporally
  (Avx.StoreAlignedNonTemporal + StoreFence) to skip the read-for-ownership a
  fresh destination would otherwise pay (what Buffer.MemoryCopy avoids). Large
  fresh buffers are page-aligned, so no alignment prefix is needed. NT does NOT
  help the in-place path (the read already owns the line).
- inplace=True on a non-contiguous (strided/transposed/reversed) view drives a
  single-operand EXTERNAL_LOOP + READWRITE + KEEPORDER NDIter whose kernel swaps
  each chunk (unit-stride chunk -> SIMD block; else per-element) - NumPy's
  IterAllButAxis inplace path. One-segment (C or F contiguous) swaps the whole
  contiguous byte block wholesale. A non-writeable array (broadcast / read-only)
  raises ValueError("array to be byte-swapped is read-only"), verbatim.

Verification
- 117-case in-process differential vs NumPy 2.4.2: 13 dtypes x 9 layouts
  (1d / 2d / F-contig / strided / reversed / transposed-3d / 0-d / empty /
  broadcast), both not-inplace and in-place (the strided in-place path exercises
  the EXTERNAL_LOOP writeback), plus 13/13 broadcast -> ValueError. C# dumps
  input+swap+inplace bytes; Python reconstructs the identical input via
  frombuffer and validates. All bit-exact.
- Char/Decimal self-consistency (double-swap identity, raw byte reversal),
  strided-inplace base-integrity (only viewed elements touched), read-only guard,
  and large-array SIMD+non-temporal correctness.
- 23 unit tests (Casting/NDArray.byteswap.Test.cs), green on net8.0 and net10.0;
  full Casting namespace (843) + FuzzMatrix gate green.

Perf (NPY/NS, best-of-21, Release, GC-clean)
- inplace 1.25-8.8x (only 10M int64/float64 at 1.39-1.49x, the DRAM-bandwidth
  wall - both sides saturate memory, NumSharp the faster side).
- not-inplace 1.9-9.7x at every non-trivial size; sub-1.5x only at n=1000 fresh
  allocation (the per-NDArray construction floor).

fix(reductions): remove NDAxisIter's 64-dim cap (unlimited ndim, NumSharp parity)

NDAxisIter is the axis-reduction FALLBACK for non-contiguous / sliced / broadcast
arrays (var / std / cumsum / cumprod / all / any along an axis). Its state struct
embedded a `fixed long[64]` outer-dimension scratch and threw
NotSupportedException("NDAxisIter currently supports up to 64 dimensions.") for any
raw ndim > 64 -- a hard cap that contradicts NumSharp's unlimited-dims design (the
contiguous DirectILKernelGenerator axis path is already uncapped, and NDIter uses
NativeMemory for unlimited dims). Found while sweeping for other ndim caps after the
ndarray.fill fast-path cap; it was the one genuine structural one (einsum's nop>32 /
MaxDims=64 are intentional NumPy einsum parity; NDMemOverlap's <=32 all heap-fall-back).

Reachable and proven: np.all(np.arange(...).reshape([2,3,1,...,1,4]).T, axis=0) with
ndim=65 threw NotSupportedException, even though the array is mostly size-1 padding
(the check keyed off raw ndim, but the scratch only ever stores NON-unit outer dims).

Fix: NDAxisState's three `fixed long[64]` buffers become caller-provided `long*`
(OuterShapePtr / SourceOuterStridesPtr / DestinationOuterStridesPtr). Each of the four
entry points (ExecuteSameType, ReduceDouble, ReduceBool, ReduceNumeric) stackallocs the
scratch sized by ndim -- `stackalloc long[Math.Max(1, ndim)]`, exactly NDIter.Execution.cs's
idiom -- and CreateState/CreateReductionState fill it; the ndim>64 throw is gone. No fixed
cap, and the by-value state shrinks (3 pointers vs 1536 embedded bytes).

Verified: values bit-identical to NumPy 2.4.2 at ndim=64 (its max rank) for var/std/

refactor(reductions): make NDAxisState a ref struct (stack-pointer safety)

Follow-up to 8f34e8ff. That commit moved NDAxisState's outer scratch from an
embedded `fixed long[64]` to raw `long*` pointers into caller-stackalloc'd
(non-pinned) stack memory. A plain struct holding such pointers can be boxed,
stored in a heap field, or captured by a closure/async frame — any of which would
outlive the entry method's stack frame and leave the pointers dangling (the
compiler does NOT lifetime-track raw pointers). Making NDAxisState a `ref struct`
enforces the stack-only contract at compile time, exactly as Span<T> and NDIterRef
do. All uses already comply (returned by value from Create{State,ReductionState},
local in the 4 entry methods, `ref` params to the loop helpers — no escape), so it
compiles unchanged. Also dropped the now-purposeless [StructLayout(Sequential)]
(it existed for the fixed arrays; the type is now pure stack, never marshalled).
Behavior identical (ref-struct is a compile-time constraint); axis reductions green.

feat(ndarray): add ndarray.getfield / ndarray.setfield (NumPy 2.4.2 parity)

Implement NumPy's byte-field view methods on NDArray, byte-exact with NumPy
2.4.2 across every layout, dtype and offset (152-case dtype-matrix differential
+ 34 unit tests, both TFMs green; verified in an isolated HEAD worktree amid
concurrent Core churn, committed only-my-files-by-path).

getfield(dtype, offset=0) returns a byte-reinterpreting VIEW: it reads `dtype`
out of the `offset`-th byte(s) of each element while keeping EVERY byte-stride
and dimension verbatim (unlike view(dtype), which rescales the last axis). So a
complex128 array's real/imag parts are getfield(f64, 0) / getfield(f64, 8), and
an int32's low/high halves are getfield(i16, 0) / getfield(i16, 2) — the narrow
field of a contiguous array is a strided view that SHARES memory (writes
through, unless the source is read-only). setfield(val, dtype, offset=0) is
getfield + an assignment: it writes `val` (unsafe-cast, broadcast) into that
field, leaving the rest of each element intact; returns void, in place.

Implementation (2 new Core files + 1 test file, no existing code touched):

- UnmanagedStorage.GetFieldAlias<T>(offset) / (NPTypeCode, offset) — the storage
  half, modelled on AliasComplexLane/WrapReinterpreted. NumPy carries strides in
  bytes; NumSharp in ELEMENTS, so each stride is recomputed as
  oldByteStride/newItemsize — always exact, because every NumSharp itemsize
  (1/2/4/8/16) divides every larger one, so an old byte-stride is always a whole
  multiple of the new. The one representation gap is a sub-element byte OFFSET
  (e.g. int32.getfield(i16, 1) starts mid-element, which element-granular
  Shape.offset cannot express): the remainder r = offset % newItemsize is
  absorbed into the WRAP POINTER (shifted r bytes) while Shape.offset carries the
  aligned part — so EVERY in-range offset is representable, matching NumPy's raw
  byte pointer. Contiguity flags recompute from the resulting strides (a same-
  size field of a C-contiguous array stays contiguous, a narrower one does not);
  a read-only source yields a read-only field view. Validation is NumPy's
  PyArray_GetField verbatim texts/order: "new type is larger than original
  type" / "offset is negative" / "new type plus offset is larger than original
  type".

- NDArray.getfield / NDArray.setfield — the instance methods (Type / NPTypeCode /
  generic<T> overloads, matching the view() convention). setfield checks SELF
  writeable FIRST (ValueError "assignment destination is read-only"), before the
  dtype/offset validation, exactly as PyArray_SetField does; the value is coerced
  like fill_diagonal (scalar -> NDArray.Scalar, else asanyarray) and written via
  np.copyto(..., casting:"unsafe") (float->int truncates toward zero).

Parity verified: complex real/imag, int low/high halves, all three misaligned
byte-offset cases (incl. combined with a non-zero base offset from a sliced
source), same-size reinterpret, strided/F-contig/transposed/negative-stride/
sliced sources, 0-d, empty, read-only (view stays read-only; setfield raises),
all 15 field dtypes dispatched (Char/Decimal/Complex have no NumPy analog but
plumb correctly by size). Sole divergence is the broadcast-mismatch error TYPE
(setfield of a wrong-shaped array -> IncorrectShapeException vs NumPy's
ValueError) — the pre-existing library-wide house convention inherited from
copyto/broadcast_to, not specific to this feature.

feat(ndarray): add ndarray.setflags + close flags gaps (NumPy 2.4.2 parity)

Implements ndarray.setflags(write=, align=, uic=) — the port of NumPy's
array_setflags (methods.c) — and fixes the three gaps the existing
NDArrayFlags object had against NumPy, every behavior probed live on 2.4.2.

setflags semantics (all probed, messages verbatim):
- Processing order align -> uic -> write, with NumPy's flagback ROLLBACK:
  an error (uic=True, or a refused write=True) restores the entry state,
  so a same-call align change never survives a failed call.
- write=True follows _IsWriteable (common.c), evaluated UNCONDITIONALLY
  (a still-writeable view whose base went read-only is refused and stays
  writeable): owner of ordinary memory -> always; view -> iff its base is
  writeable; foreign read-only memory -> never. So np.broadcast_to views
  CAN be re-enabled (writes then alias across stride-0 axes and reach the
  source, matching NumPy exactly), while an 'r' memmap and a frombuffer
  over a read-only buffer refuse with ValueError('cannot set WRITEABLE
  flag to True of this array').
- align=False observably clears ALIGNED (flags.aligned/num/behaved/
  carray/farray and the repr all follow; num 1287->1031 on owned 1-D);
  align=True restores. NumPy's mis-aligned refusal is unreachable here
  (element strides/offsets - data can never sit mis-aligned), documented.
- uic=True raises verbatim; uic=False is a deliberate no-op divergence:
  NumPy also SEVERS the view's base (v.base -> None, data can dangle) -
  NumSharp's base chain roots the owner for the view's lifetime, and
  detaching it would be a use-after-free with no writeback state to
  resolve ([Misaligned]-pinned).

flags gaps closed:
- NDArrayFlags.writeable setter now routes through setflags (as NumPy's
  arrayflags setters literally call arr.setflags), replacing the old
  refuse-all-views rule with the real _IsWriteable rule. flags['W'/'A'/
  'X'] setters route the same way, so flags['A']=false is now LIVE
  (aligned was a hardcoded const true with a no-op setter).
- ALIGNED reads live from Shape flags; fresh views/copies of an
  align-cleared array re-report aligned=True (NumPy recomputes alignment
  per new array object): re-set at the _Allocate funnel (covers GetData's
  identity-subshape and sliced-view storages) and in the verbatim-shape
  alias factories (Alias/Alias(Shape)/Alias(ref)/WrapReinterpreted).

Write-protection plumbing (the memory-safety half of _IsWriteable):
- UnmanagedStorage.WriteProtected marks storages wrapping foreign
  read-only memory; CanEnableWriteable() is the _IsWriteable analog.
- NpyFormat memmap 'r': the WRAP storage (the owner) is now marked AND
  shape-cleared BEFORE the F-order reshape/transpose views are taken -
  previously only the FINAL view's shape was cleared, leaving the wrap
  storage writeable underneath; with the new base-chain re-enable rule
  that hole would have let a write reach PROT_READ pages (access
  violation, not an exception). The empty-'r' branch is marked too
  (NumPy refuses setflags(write=True) on an empty 'r' memmap).
- np.frombuffer over a read-only MemoryView marks the boundary storage,
  so the direct re-enable refuses like NumPy's writable-buffer probe;
  memmap 'r+' round-trips (writable buffer), 'c' stays writeable.

Perf (NPY/NS, Release, best-of-9): setflags write pair 9.9x (21.9 vs
217.9 ns), align pair 7.5x, no-op call ~94x, flags.writeable/num reads
30-36x, 3-D write pair 10.6x - metadata ops with no Python dispatch.

from the parent's flags (parentC && (axis==0 || sameLen), mirrored for F),
which cannot express NumPy's size-1 contiguity relaxation:

feat(np): np.bmat — block-matrix assembly (NumPy 2.4.2 parity)

Port of numpy.bmat (numpy/matrixlib/defmatrix.py). Builds a 2-D array from
blocks by concatenation — it performs NO matrix multiplication, so there is no
BLAS/OpenBLAS path; the numerics come entirely from the already-fuzzed
np.concatenate + np.asmatrix (matching NumPy, whose bmat is literally
`matrix(concatenate(...))`). NumSharp has no matrix subclass, so the result is a
plain 2-D NDArray (no `*`-as-matmul / `.H` / `.I`).

Overloads (mirroring NumPy's polymorphic `obj` as typed C# arrays):
- bmat(NDArray[][])               nested [[A,B],[C,D]]: each row concat axis=-1,
                                  rows concat axis=0, then coerce to 2-D
- bmat(NDArray[])                 flat [A,B]: single side-by-side row (axis=-1)
- bmat(NDArray)                   single array -> 2-D COPY (NumPy matrix() copies)
- bmat(string, ldict, gdict=null) "A,B; C,D": each token resolved as a NAME via
                                  the dicts (ldict first, then gdict)

Behaviours verified 1-to-1 against NumPy 2.4.2:
- two-stage per-row-then-across-rows concatenate -> identical NEP50 promotion
- 1-D blocks coerce to a (1,N) row; 0-D single -> (1,1)
- single-array form copies (result never aliases the input)
- string tokens are NAMES: a numeric literal "1" raises NameError just like a
  missing name, matching NumPy verbatim ("name '1' is not defined")
- ragged width / per-row height mismatch raise the concatenate shape error

Deliberate divergence (documented): the string form REQUIRES a name dictionary.
NumPy resolves bare tokens against the caller's Python frame
(sys._getframe().f_back) when gdict is None; C# has no frame, so at least one of
ldict/gdict must be supplied — the same reason np.r_/np.c_ omit the bmat branch.

KeyError), mirroring the KeyError port added for einsum_path.

perf(quantile): pivot-stack block-partition quickselect — 2.5–5× NumPy on percentile/median/quantile

np.percentile(a, 50) float32 10M measured 0.596× NumPy (whole family 0.5–0.85×);
the shared QuickSelect partition that backs median/percentile/quantile/nan* was the
bottleneck (~90% of the call). Two root causes, both fixed in the value-only
QuickSelect.PartitionAtMany<T> (also the np.partition value path):

1. Branch misprediction. The scalar Hoare inner loop mispredicts ~50% of its
   data-dependent comparisons on random data, so a single 10M float32 median cost
   ~65ms. Replaced with a branchless BLOCK-HOARE partition (BlockQuicksort/pdqsort
   scheme): each outer edge is scanned into a fixed 128-wide byte[] of misplaced-element
   offsets with a data-independent write (numX += cmp ? 0 : 1), then paired offsets are
   swapped. NumPy's median3_swap sentinels (v[low+1] ≤ pivot ≤ v[high]) let the scan run
   unguarded and are preserved by the block swaps, so the sub-block middle is finished by
   a scalar unguarded crossing. Single 10M float32 select: 65 → 21ms (3.1×).

2. Multi-kth work sharing. percentile/median partition around adjacent prev/next kth
   PAIRS; the old driver only narrowed `lo`, re-selecting the min of a half-array per
   pair. Ported NumPy's introselect_ PIVOT STACK (store_pivot): every placed pivot ≥ the
   current kth is recorded so the next kth narrows from BOTH ends. even-median and
   perc[25,50,75] now share one array's worth of work (3.1× / 3.5×; 11-quantile 4.4×).

Critical generic-perf detail: the by-value LtV<T>(T a, T b) takes &a/&b, forcing a
per-element stack store+reload that erased the block-scan win (generic stayed ~78ms).
Added a pointer form LtPtr<T>(T* a, T* b) reading array elements in place with the
pivot's address hoisted once — the float32 instantiation now matches a hand-written
typed loop (0.93–0.99× of direct float). PartitionAtMany carries AggressiveOptimization
(tier-1 from first call, so the per-row InsertionSort/IntroSelectBlock inline in the hot
axis-reduce loop) and SkipLocalsInit (the pivot stack is written-before-read, so the
per-row 256-byte stackalloc zero-init is skipped) — both matter for many-tiny-rows axis
reductions and keep that shape at parity.

Also SIMD-vectorized the plain-path NaN prescan (Vector<T> self-equality: a NaN lane
fails v==v) for float/double, now a meaningful share since the partition is ~3× faster.

Worst-case O(n log n) guarantee (heap-sort at the depth limit), insertion-sort small
windows, and dumb tiny-window handling are preserved. NaNs are still stripped before
partitioning, so the raw LtPtr ordering is total in the hot loop. The Comparison<T>
(complex) and index-tracking (argpartition) overloads are unchanged.

  float32  perc50 2.77× · [25,50,75] 2.52× · median 3.43×
  float64  perc50 3.37× · [25,50,75] 3.51× · median 3.08×
  int32    perc50 5.2×  · [25,50,75] 3.34× · median 3.5×
  int64    perc50 4.5×  · [25,50,75] 3.9×  · median 2.7×

fix(random): np.random.bytes byte[] ceiling — clear error + boundary fix, shared core

Addresses the byte[] size limit for np.random.bytes / Generator.bytes.

Facts: NumPy's bytes(length) takes a 64-bit npy_intp and returns a Python
bytes object (max ~2^63), so it can exceed 2 GiB. A .NET byte[] cannot —
Array.MaxLength is 2,147,483,591 (~2.0 GiB). byte[] remains the correct
NumPy-faithful return: NumPy's bytes() is a byte STRING, deliberately distinct
from a uint8 ndarray (for a >2 GiB array of random bytes use an NDArray path
such as default_rng().integers(0, 256, size, np.uint8), which NumSharp backs
with unmanaged storage). This 2 GiB byte[] ceiling matches np.save/np.savez.

Two bugs fixed:
- Requests past the byte[] limit threw a raw "Arithmetic operation resulted in
  an overflow" from `new byte[...]`. Now a clear OverflowException fires BEFORE
  any allocation, naming Array.MaxLength and the integers(0,256,...,uint8)
  alternative.
- Boundary over-allocation: the old code allocated nUint32*4 (up to 3 bytes more
  than length) then sliced, so a length within 3 of Array.MaxLength failed even
  though the result would fit. The shared BytesCore now allocates exactly `end`
  bytes and stores only the first `end` little-endian bytes while still drawing
  all ceil(length/4) words (unchanged stream consumption).

byte-exact vs NumPy 2.4.2 across lengths {0,1,2,3,4,5,7,8,10,13,100,-1,-2,-4,-5}

perf(argpartition): pivot-stack block-partition quickselect — up to 3.7× the old scalar index path

np.argpartition was the lone straggler in the select/partition family: the value-only
quickselect (median/percentile/quantile/nan*, commit 8a1376ff) was rewritten to a branchless
block-Hoare partition + NumPy introselect_ pivot stack and reached 2.5–5× NumPy, but the
SEPARATE index-tracking overload behind argpartition was left on the old scalar Hoare loop,
measuring ~0.30× NumPy on 2M random f32/i32. This ports that exact edge to the index path.

WHAT
Rewrote QuickSelect.PartitionAtMany<T>(T* buf, long* idx, int n, int* sortedKs, int nKs) — the
IComparable<T> argpartition path — from the scalar `IntroSelect(buf, idx, lo, hi, k)` + `lo=k+1`
narrowing to the shared pivot-stack driver, and added index-threaded mirrors of the value-only
block internals: IntroSelectBlock / PartitionBlock / Median3Swap / ScalarPartitionFinish, each
carrying the parallel `long* idx` column through every Swap. StorePivot / LtV / LtPtr / Log2 and
the BlockSize(128)/PivotStackMax(64) constants are shared with the value path unchanged. The
Comparison<T> index overload (complex128) stays on the old scalar path (niche, CDOUBLE_LT).

This is faithful to NumPy: `introselect_<Tag, arg>` (selection.cpp) is ONE template; `arg=true`
threads the `tosort` index array through the identical swaps and shares the identical
`store_pivot`/`pivots`/`npiv` stack — exactly the mirror added here.

WHY IT IS SAFE
Every comparison reads `buf` alone (LtV/LtPtr), so `idx` never steers control flow — it is a
passive passenger recording the permutation the value partition performs. The control flow, and
hence each placed kth's final sorted position, is bit-identical to the already-validated
value-only path; only the parallel idx permutation rides along. NaN is stripped into an
encounter-order tail by the argpartition line kernels (AxisPartition.ArgPartLineF{16,32,64})
BEFORE this runs — identical to how the quantile kernel strips NaN — so the raw `<` ordering is
total here and never sees a NaN. The oracle compares argpartition by its DERIVED kth-values
(take_along_axis(a, g)[ks]), which are deterministic for any multiset; the arrangement BETWEEN
kth anchors is introselect-implementation-specific on both sides and is not contractual, so the
new block/pivot-stack arrangement is bit-exact where it must be. Every exact-arrangement unit
assertion is on n<=4 arrays, which route to InsertionSort identically in both paths.

CORRECTNESS (all green)
- 201,600 adversarial kernel trials (int32/int64/double x random/dup-heavy/all-equal/sorted/
  reverse/binary/mixed x sizes 1..5000 spanning InsertionSort/median-of-3/block-scan x single/
  min/max/adjacent-pair/spread/multi kths): idx a permutation, orig[idx[i]]==buf[i] (faithful),
  buf[kth]==sorted[kth], two-sided invariant — 0 failures.
- 13,800 public np.argpartition trials (NaN tail encounter-order, strided views, 2D axis=0/1,
  float16/float32/int/byte/short) — 0 failures.
- Oracle Sort tier (bit-exact vs NumPy 2.4.2 derived kth-values) — PASS.
- 47 partition/argpartition unit tests + Sorting namespace 241/241 (CI filter) — PASS.
- Value-path consumers untouched: oracle Stat + NanReduce tiers (percentile/median/quantile/
  nan*) — PASS.

PERF (NPY/NS = NumPy_ms / NumSharp_ms; higher = NumSharp faster; Release, best-of-9/15 warm)
No-degradation BEFORE(old scalar)->AFTER, same machine — improvement everywhere, no regression:
  100K  f64 1.95x  f32 3.10x  i32 1.91x  i64 2.06x  | multi3 f64 2.76x  i32 3.03x
  2M    f64 1.83x  f32 1.96x  i32 1.60x  i64 2.05x  | multi3 f64 3.70x  i32 2.90x
  10M   f64 1.33x  f32 1.17x  i32 1.27x  i64 1.00x  | multi3 f64 1.25x  i32 1.27x
vs NumPy (AFTER): multi-kth 1.19–2.75x (>=1.5x at 100K/2M) — the pivot stack shares selection
work across kths where NumPy re-runs its SIMD select per region. Single-kth 0.40–1.21x, lifted
from ~0.30x toward parity but BOUNDED by NumPy's x86-simd-sort SIMD argqselect (idx is a second
int64 column NumPy moves with vectorized permutes; our scalar swaps move it element-by-element)
— the same documented ceiling as np.partition. A risky SIMD-gather argqselect port was NOT
attempted; the win here is the branchless partition + both-ends pivot narrowing.
