perf(unique): route np.unique family through the radix sort core — 5–74× NumPy

The np.unique family (np.unique + return_index/inverse/counts, and the Array-API
unique_values/unique_counts/unique_inverse/unique_all) sorted through System.Array.Sort —
the .NET BCL introsort, a COMPARISON sort (~n·log n comparisons, ~50% branch-mispredict on
random data). Every sort-path cell lost to NumPy: np.unique int-low/med + ALL floats
0.14–0.77×, all-float unique_values/unique_counts 0.12–0.61×, unique_counts int-high 0.25×.

Reuses machinery that already shipped — no new sort/select core:

1. Radix replaces the BCL sort (new NDArray.unique.Radix.cs). RadixSortValues<T> /
   RadixArgSortKeysPerm<T> route the flat sort/argsort through the SHARED LSD RadixSort
   (Backends/Default/Sorting/RadixSort.cs, the axis-sort kernel): O(n·nbytes), comparison-free,
   single-pass histogram + trivial-pass skip (magnitude-adaptive — small ints do 1 pass, not 4).
   The per-dtype monotonic key transforms (ToKey32/64, FromKey32/64) are generic typeof(T)-const
   dispatch + Unsafe.As reinterpret (the HashKey<T> pattern), byte-identical to AxisSort's
   IKey32/IKey64/FKey adapters, so ascending key order == NumPy value order and -0.0 sorts before
   +0.0 exactly as Array.Sort's float comparer. Two additive RadixSort.ArgSortU32/U64 overloads
   expose the co-sorted key buffer alongside the sorted index column, so the perm path recovers
   sorted values through the key's inverse with NO gather.

2. Integer values-only / counts-only route to the hash path (already used by unique_values):
   np.unique(int) and np.unique(int, return_counts) were on the sort path; the hash beats any sort
   at low/medium cardinality (equal_nan is irrelevant for ints — identical result).

3. High-cardinality radix bail-out in the hash (UniqueHashSortedInt). Past ~L2 the open-addressing
   table is a cache miss per insert — exactly where NumPy's own std::unordered_set thrashes
   (int32 2M-distinct: NumPy 1540ms). Rather than guess cardinality up front (a cheap sample can't
   distinguish 100k-distinct-in-1M from all-unique), the loop OBSERVES growth: once uniqueCount
   reaches 1<<17 (131072, table past L2) it abandons the hash and radix-sorts the extracted buffer.
   Low/medium cardinality never reaches the threshold (the array's own distinct count is the
   ceiling), so it keeps the hash. This turns int-high from a loss inherited from NumPy's algorithm
   into 74× (2M-distinct: 1540ms → 21ms).

4. Counts-only skips the perm argsort (EmitValuesAndCountsFloat + generic/float branches). counts
   are run-lengths of the sorted values, derived from the mask alone — the perm is only read for
   index/inverse. Floats now sort values-only; ints route to the hash. Flipped all-float
   unique_counts from 0.12–0.70× to 1.2–2.6×.

Bit-parity is by construction: everything around the sort is unchanged (NaN partitions to the tail
with original bits preserved, IEEE-Equals mask, min-perm-within-run first-occurrence, inverse
reshape, run-length counts); radix yields the same total order as the BCL comparer for every
non-NaN value, so the mask/dedup output is identical. Half/Complex/Decimal (no monotonic radix key)
keep the scalar BCL path — the same three dtypes AxisSort routes to its scalar kernel.

Measured (NPY/NS, 2M elems, best-of-9 × min-of-3-runs, Release; >1 = NumSharp faster):
  np.unique       0.14–14×  → 0.98–74×   (int32 high-card 14→74×; all floats now ≥0.98×)
  unique_values   0.18–16×  → 1.10–69×   (float32-low 0.18→1.10×; int32 high 8→69×)
  unique_counts   0.12–14×  → 1.22–15×   (int-high 0.25→3.25×; all floats 0.12→≥1.2×)
  unique_inverse  1.14–7.9× → 4.67–14×
  unique_all      1.00–14×  → 3.27–38×
81/90 cells ≥1.5× NumPy; 0 degradations vs the pre-change baseline; the single sub-1.0 cell is
np.unique float32-low at 0.98× (parity, bounded by NumPy's SIMD vqsort — the out-of-scope follow-on
lever that would also lift np.sort/argsort/partition/searchsorted).

perf(isin): hash-set membership replaces sort+searchsorted — float64 0.28×→2.55×, wide-int 3.3×→11×

np.isin's non-table path (SortedSearchMembership) sorted the test set then ran one binary
searchsorted per element — n binary searches over the m-element sorted array. Profiling isin on
1M×1M float64 showed searchsorted was the entire cost (~317ms of the call; the sort was only 23ms),
because each of 1M lookups is ~20 cache-miss comparisons into a 1M array. NumPy's in1d is itself
sort-based here, so this lost badly (float64 0.28×).

Replaced with an open-addressing hash-set membership (O(n+m) — build the test table once, probe each
element once): TryHashMembership handles the hashable dtypes (integer-family + char + float32/
float64), declining (→ sort path) for Complex/Half/Decimal (Decimal needs value-equality: 1.0m ==
1.00m by value, not bits) and for a test set too large to index. Bit-exact with NumPy by
construction: integer bit patterns are exact; floats normalize -0.0→+0.0 (so signed zeros share a
bucket, -0.0 == +0.0 as NumPy) and exclude NaN (NaN never equals itself → never a member, matching
isin([nan],[nan])==False). Reuses the splitmix64 finalizer. This BEATS NumPy (which does not hash
floats here).

The integer counting-table fast path (TryTableMembership, modest-range integers) is unaffected —
the hash only replaces the sort+searchsorted fallback it declines to. setdiff1d (built on
isin(invert=True)) inherits the win. Reads through offset-free contiguous buffers (copy-if-sliced,
the bincount pattern, since .Address ignores Shape.offset).

Measured (NPY/NS, 1M×1M, >1 = NumSharp faster):
  isin float64 med   0.28× → 2.55×  (213ms → 25ms; searchsorted bottleneck eliminated)
  isin int32  high   3.28× → 11.1×  (wide range declines the table → was sort+searchsorted; 464ms→42ms)
  isin int64  med    1.36× → 1.52×
  isin int32  med    1.17× → 1.35×  (modest range still uses the counting table)

Validation: oracle GroupA tier (the 22 isin cases) bit-exact; 129 isin unit tests + 30 set-ops
tests green; a 4-dtype × 200k differential vs a reference HashSet (NaN/-0.0/inf injected) is
0-mismatch. Edge cases probed against NumPy 2.4.2 (NaN never a member, -0.0==+0.0 both directions,
±inf, invert, wide int64/uint64).

feat(random)!: np.random.bytes / Generator.bytes return NDArray<byte>, not byte[] — supports >2 GiB (NumPy npy_intp parity)

NumPy's `bytes(length)` takes a 64-bit `npy_intp` and returns a Python `bytes`
object, so on 64-bit it can exceed 2 GiB (memory permitting). A managed .NET
`byte[]` cannot — `Array.MaxLength` (~2.0 GiB) is a hard ceiling — so the old
implementation THREW `OverflowException` for any request past it, deliberately
refusing what NumPy accepts. This changes the return type to a 1-D uint8
`NDArray<byte>` backed by unmanaged memory (addressed by `long`), so NumSharp
now matches NumPy's capability: a >2 GiB request succeeds instead of raising.

BREAKING (accepted per NumPy-parity policy): `np.random.bytes(long)` and
`Generator.bytes(long)` now return `NumSharp.Generic.NDArray<byte>` instead of
`byte[]`. The array is a 1-D uint8 array (NumSharp's analogue of NumPy's `bytes`);
to recover a managed array from a small result use `bytes(n).ToArray<byte>()`
(itself capped at Array.MaxLength).

Validated against NumPy 2.4.2 — every edge case preserved byte-for-byte (the
word-draw + little-endian packing + slice arithmetic is unchanged; only the
destination buffer moved from managed byte[] to unmanaged NDArray<byte>):
  * `bytes(0)` -> empty result but STILL draws one uint32 word (NumPy's
    n_uint32 = (length-1)//4+1 == 1; both mtrand.pyx and _generator.pyx set
    cdivision=True, so `//` truncates toward zero and C# integer division matches).
  * `bytes(-1)` -> first 3 bytes, draws 1 word (NumPy `tobytes()[:-1]`);
    `bytes(-2)` -> 2 bytes; `bytes(-3..-5)` -> empty, draws 0 words;
    `bytes(-8)` -> ValueError "negative dimensions are not allowed" (n_uint32 == -1).
  * Byte-exact in the region PAST int.MaxValue: bytes(2_147_483_700)[2_147_483_690]
    == 114 == NumPy's MT19937 word stream (verified by replaying NumPy's own
    n_uint32 uint32 words, avoiding the tobytes() copy).

Perf (NPY/NS, Release, best-of-9): bytes(100M) 1.49x — and the gap widens with N,
because NumPy's `randint(...).astype('<u4').tobytes()[:length]` pays extra
full-size copies while NumSharp writes once into the unmanaged buffer (so at the
multi-GB sizes that motivate this change NumSharp is both faster and ~half the
peak memory). Small sizes are 0.71-0.77x, bound by the per-word MT19937 draw where
NumPy bulk-fills; this is the pre-existing floor, unchanged by the refactor.

BytesCore keeps fillZeros:false (the loop writes all `end` bytes exactly once) and
takes the raw `(byte*)result.Address` write path.

fix(bench): stop Decimal cumprod overflow and np.imag OOM in the op matrix

Two benchmark cells crashed during the official run, each leaving a hole in
the op/dtype/N matrix ("No Workload Results were obtained from the run").

1) CumulativeBenchmarks.np.cumprod(a) — Decimal, all three sizes:
   System.OverflowException "Value was either too large or too small for a
   Decimal" (Scan_Cum_CumProd_Decimal -> DecCalc.ScaleResult). The class fed
   np.cumprod full-range random data ([-50, 50), via CreateRandomArray). The
   running product grows without bound; Single/Double/Half saturate to +/-inf
   and complete, but System.Decimal has no infinity, so the scan kernel throws
   at every size. Fix: bound the inputs to [0.5, 1.0] so the running product
   monotonically shrinks toward 0 (underflow) and stays finite for every size
   and dtype — the exact technique ProdBenchmarks already uses for the same
   reason. The NumPy twin run_cumulative_benchmarks is bounded identically, so
   both sides measure the same non-degenerate scan instead of one that
   collapses to inf after a handful of elements.

2) UnaryFamilyBenchmarks.np.imag(a) — Single/Double/Half at N=10M:
   System.OutOfMemoryException. np.imag(real) has no imaginary lane to view,
   so it returns a fresh, owned, lazily-allocated zeros array — O(1)-fast.
   BenchmarkDotNet then runs thousands of invocations per iteration, and on
   Windows every committed-but-untouched buffer charges commit, exhausting
   memory before finalizers can reclaim the discarded results. (np.real does
   not hit this: its real-input result is a view, so it allocates nothing.)
   Fix: dispose the result per invocation — the pattern and rationale already
   documented on CreationBenchmarks for np.zeros/np.empty, and matching the
   NumPy twin's discard-each-result loop. Safe because inputs here are always
   real (Half/Single/Double), so the result is a fresh owned array that never
   aliases _a.

Verified in an isolated worktree (Core untouched): bounded Decimal cumprod
runs clean at 1K/100K/10M while the old full-range data still throws
(confirming the cause); np.imag(real) returns zeros, leaves its source array
intact after 400 imag+dispose iterations, and keeps private bytes flat where
the undisposed loop would reserve ~32 GB. Benchmark-only change.

perf(openblas): stop wasted result-zeroing before full-overwrite BLAS/LAPACK calls

The degraded OpenBLAS LinearAlgebra benchmarks (np.matmul/multi_dot/linalg.vecdot
/cholesky/inv at 0.31x-0.68x NPY/NS) all shared one root cause: the result buffer
was allocated ZEROED (the NDArray ctor's fillZeros:true default) immediately before
a native routine that fully overwrites it. That is not merely a wasted memset — a
freshly calloc'd / VirtualAlloc'd zero buffer hands the native call demand-zero
pages it then faults in on first write, so the page-fault/TLB cost lands on (and is
mis-attributed to) the BLAS call. Measured on 128x128 f64 gemm: 0.090 -> 0.059 ms
(31 us) just from switching the result to a warm pooled fillZeros:false buffer. The
standalone zeroing looks free (~1.6 us) because VirtualAlloc reserves lazily; the
cost only materialises when the native write touches the pages, which is why the
double-zeroing hid in plain sight.

Every route that produces these results writes 100% of the output before returning,
so pre-zeroing is provably redundant:
  - matmul.c.src @TYPE@_matmul never memsets (gemm beta=0 / syrk+mirror overwrite;
    the managed SIMD/generic kernels Clear() C themselves).
  - cblasfuncs.c cblas_matrixproduct allocates UNINITIALISED (new_array_for_sum) and
    does exactly ONE memset; NumSharp's port zeroed TWICE (ctor + explicit Zero).
  - potrf/gesv results are fully written by DelinearizeTriangle/Delinearize.

Fixes:
  - Default.MatMul.2D2D.cs: 2D matmul result -> fillZeros:false (mirrors matmul.c.src,
    which never memsets). Also speeds the managed GEMM path (it already Clear()s C).
  - OpenBlasEngine.Dot.cs (np.dot / multi_dot): allocate uninitialised + keep the
    single Zero, faithfully matching cblasfuncs.c's lone memset (was double-zeroing).
  - OpenBlasEngine.Cholesky.cs / Lapack.cs (inv): result -> fillZeros:false.
  - np.vecdot.cs: skip the no-op moveaxis when the named axis is already the last one
    (np.linalg.vecdot's axis=-1 default always resolves there), which kept it ~2x
    slower than a bare np.vecdot on the same 1-D operands. Validation still runs.

Results (NPY/NS, official backend_profiles harness, threads=1):
  np.matmul 128            0.682x -> 1.002x
  np.linalg.matmul 128     0.732x -> 1.034x
  np.linalg.multi_dot 128  0.672x -> 0.972x
  np.linalg.vecdot 100K    0.545x -> 0.808x
  np.linalg.inv 32         0.550x -> 0.593x
  np.linalg.cholesky 96    0.553x -> 0.651x
  np.linalg.cholesky 32    0.307x -> 0.335x  (8KB result; the <10 us fixed managed
                                              per-call floor dominates at N=32, not
                                              the zeroing — amortises away by N>=96)
  np.einsum ij,jk 128      2.823x -> 3.913x  (bonus: contracts via matmul)

moveaxis skip is a no-op): fuzz tiers Matmul/MatmulParity/LinalgParity/Products/
DecimalMatmul, 30 MatmulParityBackendTests, BlasBackendDelta, 407 LinearAlgebra +
157 vecdot/matmul/moveaxis/dot/gufunc unit tests all green; identity checks
(L@L.T==spd, A@inv==I) hold to machine precision.

perf(openblas): batch sliding-dot middle + force tier-1 on LAPACK copy loops

Fixes the degraded OpenBLAS benchmarks by removing two managed-overhead
pathologies, both leaving the numerics BYTE-IDENTICAL to NumPy 2.4.2 (verified
against live NumPy: 444 interop parity tests + 70 core unit tests + the
linalg/matmul oracle tiers all green; correlate/convolve/cholesky/inv/solve/
slogdet re-checked bit-exact by hand).

Measured NPY/NS (single-thread, warm; was -> now):
  correlate same 100K   0.51x -> ~1.13x   (2443us -> 976us)
  convolve  same 100K   0.45x -> ~1.14x   (2486us -> 984us)
  cholesky  n=32        0.31x -> ~1.9x    (8.5us  -> 2.5us)
  cholesky  n=96        0.55x -> ~1.22x
  inv       n=32        0.55x -> ~1.26x
  polyfit   1000 deg3   0.23x -> ~0.49x   (lstsq/Linearize gain; still bound by
                                           the vander/scale np.* composition)

1) Sliding dot (np.correlate / np.convolve) — per-position interface dispatch.
   NumPy declines small_correlate for a kernel > 11 (arraytypes.c.src: nk>11)
   and reduces every fully-overlapping middle position through cblas ddot in a
   double accumulator (DOUBLE_dot), so byte parity genuinely requires ~100K
   per-position ddot calls — the same work NumPy does. The managed loop paid the
   ISlidingDotBackend.Dot cost (interface virtual dispatch + dtype switch, not
   inlinable) once PER OUTPUT: profiled at 2.35ms of which 1.45ms was pure
   dispatch (the native ddot loop itself is 0.84ms, matching NumPy's ~1ms).
   Fix: hoist the uniform middle behind ONE call. New
   ISlidingDotBackend.DotBatch (default impl = the old per-position loop, so any
   backend keeps working) that the OpenBLAS backend overrides to switch on the
   dtype once and run the tight DoubleBlas.Dot loop directly. Bit-identical
   (same NumPy @name@_dot), dispatch paid once instead of 100K times.

2) LAPACK small-matrix factorisations — tier-0 JIT of the copy/transpose leaves.
   dpotrf(32) is 1.1us but the whole backend cholesky-32 was 8.5us. The generic
   Linearize<T>/Delinearize<T>/DelinearizeTriangle<T>/IdentityColMajor<T> had no
   MethodImpl, and a linalg op on a small matrix finishes in far less than
   tiered compilation's ~100ms background-promotion delay, so those loops ran at
   TIER-0 for the entire call -- measured ~12x slower than tier-1 on a 32x32
   transpose (2.5us vs 0.2us), which was essentially all of the managed
   overhead. Fix: [MethodImpl(AggressiveOptimization)] on those four leaves
   (forces immediate tier-1, matching NumPy's precompiled-C 'always warm' for
   the cold/few-call usage a linalg op typically sees -- same rationale as
   NDFloatMath.Simd). Also strength-reduce the strided pointer walks and split
   DelinearizeTriangle into a kept run + a contiguous zeroed run (no
   per-element branch, ~2x faster). Helps every LAPACK op (cholesky/inv/solve/
   det/slogdet/qr/tensorsolve/tensorinv all improved).

Note: AggressiveOptimization is deliberately NOT applied to *Blas.Dot -- there
it blocks inlining into the sliding/product loops and made correlate ~2x slower
(measured); leaf loops want it, inline-hot helpers do not.

Rejected: rewriting np.vander to NumPy's lean 4-op in-place form -- NumSharp's
strided-view writes make it SLOWER than the current contiguous composition
(38.9us vs 32.6us, measured), so polyfit stays composition-bound.

perf(openblas): close the last degraded small-N benchmarks (tensordot/eig/dot memset)

Follow-up to 9cf599c4, which forced tier-1 on the tier-0-STUCK generic LAPACK copy
leaves (Linearize/Delinearize) and thereby fixed 5 of the 7 degraded OpenBLAS cells.
The remaining two — np.tensordot / np.linalg.tensordot at 128 (0.72x / 0.74x NPY/NS) —
are NOT tier-0-stuck: np.tensordot is a plain managed wrapper (List/transpose/reshape
+ np.dot) that JIT-warms normally. The ad-hoc backend/openblas benchmarks warm with a
single body() call and then time 3-7 rounds, so they measure that wrapper while it is
still tier-0, against an always-warm native NumPy — a cold-vs-warm comparison. Measured:
tensordot's own steady state is 0.0634 ms == NumPy's own tensordot 0.0643 ms (1.01x),
i.e. there is no warm code gap to close, only a measurement one.

Root causes and fixes (all byte-identical to NumPy 2.4.2):

- benchmark harness (backend_profile_bench.{cs,py}, openblas_bench.{cs,py}): warm the C#
  Best() to JIT steady-state (tier-1) before timing — loop to a call-count AND wall-clock
  floor, capped so a slow op does not warm forever — and floor the timed rounds at 21
  (best-of-21, the repo perf convention) on BOTH harnesses. A min over 3-7 samples of a
  ~60us-1.5ms op has ~15-20% jitter and swings a single cell 0.7x<->1.3x run-to-run; 21
  rounds report the steady-state minimum. NumPy is native/always-warm so the Python side
  needs no JIT warmup, but takes the same best-of-21 floor for a symmetric statistic.

- OpenBlasEngine.Dot.cs (np.dot): drop the redundant output memset on the matrix-matrix
  route. cblas_matrixproduct memsets the output unconditionally, but that zero is only
  OBSERVABLE where the routine accumulates into it (the scalar/axpy Level-1 path) or
  returns the zeros as the answer (l == 0, an empty contraction). gemm/syrk (beta == 0)
  never read C, so pre-zeroing the whole result before a full overwrite is a wasted second
  write — the exact lever np.matmul's kernel already drops. Every other route keeps the
  memset, so their bytes are unchanged. dot now matches matmul (immeasurable at 128, real
  at large N: 32 MB fewer bytes written at 2048^2), and tensordot inherits it via np.dot.

- np.linalg.eig.cs (CollapseEig): use astype(result_t, copy:false), NumPy's exact
  `w.astype(result_t, copy=False)`. np.real already yields the float64 real-lane VIEW, and
  the complex branch's w/v are already the complex128 the geev seam returned, so copy:false
  avoids re-materialising the (up to n x n) eigenvector buffer whenever the dtype already
  matches. This also FIXES a latent layout divergence: NumPy's eig returns the strided
  real-lane views (w.strides == (16,), non-contiguous), where the old astype forced a
  contiguous copy. Only float32's real collapse and a genuine width change still cast.

np.random singleton: `seed`, `rnd`, `set_state` and `get_state` each called

of np.random.*. The global singleton is never touched.

Add [MethodImpl(OptimizeAndInline)] (= AggressiveInlining |
AggressiveOptimization) across the hot SIMD/scalar kernel code so it skips
the tiered-JIT tier-0 penalty (the documented ~27x-slower first calls) and
inlines the small lane/bit helpers. Value-neutral: MethodImpl only affects
JIT tiering/inlining, never computed results. NumSharp.Core builds clean.

Two target classes, matching the convention the reduction kernels
(SimdDot / FiniteScan / NanReplace) already follow:

1. Small loopless lane / bit-reinterpret transforms (the FloatToHalfBits
   archetype), annotated for inline + tier-1:
   - Half cast bit-fiddle: FloatToHalfBits, HalfBitsToFloat(Exact),
     Single/HalfToFloatScalarExact, RoundToOdd4, {Int64,UInt64,Double}
     ToHalfBits, Half<->{i32,u32} lane loads, AnyNaN, NegateHalf
   - f->u32/u64 lanes: DoubleToU32x4, SingleToU32x8, DoubleToU64x4
   - complex deinterleave: ComplexReals4, ComplexRealsToInt32, ComplexNonzero4
   - byteswap MaskFor; NDFloatMath.Simd MulAdd (V128/256/512)
   - radix/hash/isin bit keys: FKey/FVal32/64, ToKey/FromKey32/64, HashKey,
     HashKeyComplex, Splitmix, NormalizeZeros, KeyBits

2. Non-inlinable SIMD loop kernels (Bulk*, Fused*, Cast*Strided,
   ReduceStridedAxis*, *SimdHelper, ScanRun*), annotated for the tier-0 skip.
   Inlining is a structural no-op here (most are invoked through CastKernel /
   StridedCastKernel delegates and &Bulk*V function pointers, through which
   the JIT cannot inline), but AggressiveOptimization removes the cold-start
   penalty and the inline hint is harmless. Applied via a Roslyn rewrite
   (token-position insertion, formatting-preserving) after a dry run.

Scope notes:
- The FFT butterfly helpers and the scalar NumPy-exact float32 math
  (Exp/Log/Sin/Cos/Tanh) got the same treatment but landed in a prior commit.
- Excluded: vendored Utilities/SpanSource helpers (kept in sync with the
  .NET runtime), FFT Pass/Radf codelets (Cmplx-struct math, not hardware
  intrinsics), and setup-time capability predicates (IsExpVectorAccelerated,

fix(reduce): float16 sum via a float32 widen-compute-narrow shadow (NumPy HALF_add parity)

np.sum(float16) accumulated in the wrong precision and diverged from NumPy. NumPy's
HALF_add reduce widens each float16 to float32 on read, accumulates with the FLOAT
pairwise_sum, then narrows per inner-loop call (npy_float_to_half) — so the accumulator
saturates PER ORIENTATION. NumSharp's flat path summed in Double and its axis Direct
kernel accumulated in Half (a real ~3.5% error): np.sum(ones((4096,3), f16), axis=0)
returned [4096,4096,4096] where NumPy returns [2048,2048,2048], and the Double flat path
could differ in the last ULP.

Fix: reproduce NumPy exactly in a FLOAT32 SHADOW accumulator — the reduce output is
allocated Single and narrowed to Half once at the end (ReduceAdd), never accumulating in
Half.

New kernel (ILKernelGenerator.Reduction.Half.cs):
  - PairwiseFoldHalf — NumPy's HALF_pairwise_sum: widen each f16->f32 (Giesen, proven
    0-diff vs npy_half_to_float over all 65536 patterns) and accumulate in float32 with
    the pairwise tree (blocksize 128, eight accumulators, split kept a multiple of 8). The
    AVX2 leaf maps the eight accumulators onto one Vector256<float>; the strided leaf keeps
    the scalar eight-accumulator block. Bit-for-bit np.add.reduce(float16).
  - HalfSumKernel — per-chunk reduce into the float32 shadow. PINNED (contiguous inner
    reduced axis / flat): fold the stripe pairwise, RoundToF16 the running slot, so
    sum(ones(4096)) == 4096. SLAB (reduced axis outer): each kept slot accumulates across
    the outer steps with a per-step RoundToF16, so it SATURATES like NumPy —
    sum(ones((4096,3)), axis=0) == [2048,2048,2048]; 4x-unrolled AVX2 body, bit-identical
    to the scalar per-element round.
  - RoundToF16 == widen(narrow(x)) computed in float32 (no half<->memory round-trip),
    verified bit-exact to HalfToFloatScalarExact(SingleToHalfBits(v)) over 8M floats incl.
    specials.

Routing:
  - Default.Reduction.Add.cs — the Half AXIS sum now accumulates in Single (was Double)
    and narrows to Half; the NDIter gate accepts (Sum, Half, Single). Half MEAN stays on
    the Double accumulator; an explicit dtype request is honored by the normal path.
  - ILKernelGenerator.Reduction.cs — routes (Half, Single, Sum) to HalfSumKernel; the
    (Half, Double) route stays for MEAN.
  - DefaultEngine.ReductionOp.cs — the flat SumElementwiseHalfFallback folds the whole
    array in float32 (C-/F-contiguous in memory order; strided/transposed/broadcast via
    ascontiguousarray then C order) and narrows once with SingleToHalfBits; empty -> +0.

Scope: SUM only (flat + axis). Half PROD/MIN/MAX unchanged (Direct path); Half MEAN
unchanged (Double accumulate). Reuses the already-internal Giesen widen/narrow helpers
(HalfToFloatScalarExact / HalfBitsToFloatExact / SingleToHalfBits) from the cast kernels.

Greens the PR #628 failures that the numpy-pin / vendored-deps / macOS-OpenBLAS-wheel fixes
(5e70a9de, b3ba6bc7) had UNMASKED once the `test` job stopped short-circuiting at the Half test.
Every remaining red is one of two classes: a host/arch bit-exactness artifact no numpy pin can
remove (handled with the established Inconclusive-off-pinned-host model), or one genuine Core bug.

## Core bug — power with a negative integer exponent (ALL OS; ErrorsFull red)

Two defects, both in Default.Power.cs:

1. ContainsNegative's per-type scans read the exponent with nd.GetInt32(long) — the COORDINATE
   overload (params long[]) — so a flat index i is read as the 1-D coordinate [i] into axis 0. For a
   2-D/(4,5), strided, or broadcast exponent this walks off axis 0 and trips
   Debug.Fail("index < Count, Memory corruption expected"): an out-of-bounds read (a real
   memory-safety bug in RELEASE, where the assert is compiled out) instead of NumPy's clean
   ValueError. Now reads by FLAT index through Storage.GetAtIndex<T> (Shape.TransformOffset), correct
   for contiguous / strided / broadcast / non-zero-offset layouts.

2. The negative-exponent guard keyed "integer loop" off lhs.IsInteger() && rhs.IsInteger(), which is
   FALSE for a bool base — so power(bool, negative_int) skipped the guard and returned a result where
   NumPy raises. The loop is the PROMOTED type (bool**int32 -> int32, bool**bool -> int8). Now keyed
   off ResolvePowerResultType (the same promotion the compute path uses), which also keeps the
   uint64**signed -> float64 NEP50 case non-raising (power(uint64,-1)=0.5).

Retires the now-obsolete MisalignedRegistry K6/K8 excuses (bool-loop-missing-guard;
int-path-trips-assert): all 88 errors_full power cases now raise the clean ValueError bit-for-bit.

twiddles, and Vector<T> var/std coalesce differently under glibc (Linux) and clang/NEON (macOS-arm64).

feat(lifetime): NDScope ambient reclamation scope — eager buffer release with original site bodies

The disposal sweep's goal (return transient NDArray buffers to the SizeBucketedBufferPool
synchronously instead of stranding them on the finalizer queue — a 1.6x-3x win at small N /
hot loops) is now carried by ONE instrument instead of per-temp bookkeeping: NDScope, an
ambient allocation scope (the TorchSharp DisposeScope pattern).

Mechanism
- NDScope (Backends/NDScope.cs): [ThreadStatic] scope stack; every NDArray constructed while
  a scope is open is tracked via a single hook in NDArray.InitializeArc (the funnel all ctors
  pass). Disposing the scope disposes every tracked array not yielded via scope.Returns(..).
  Disposal is ordinary ARC release (frees only at refcount 0), so releasing a base whose view
  was yielded never corrupts — the manual sweep's exact safety, with registration automated.
- Returns(x) / Returns(x[]) yield the result (O(1) via a TrackingScope back-pointer on
  NDArray) and re-track it into the PARENT scope, so an enclosing scope reclaims a dropped
  inner result. Returns on an UNTRACKED array (input passthrough, caller's @out) is a
  provable no-op — "wrap every egress" is a safe blanket rule. Out-params egress via
  result = scope.Returns(temp). NDScope.Detach(x) for arrays cached past every scope.
- Ownership rules become structural: inputs are constructed before the scope opens and are
  never tracked (rule R2 with no ReferenceEquals guards); the return is the one egress (R1).
  Scopes nest per thread; worker threads without a scope degrade safely to the finalizer.

Sites (bodies restored to their ORIGINAL minimal form + Open/Returns only)
- np.logical_and/or/not/xor, np.roll, np.isin (helpers 100% scope-free), np.ptp (both
  overloads), np.cov, np.corrcoef, QuantileEngine.Compute (median/percentile/quantile/nan*),

  expand_dims promotion views for sort/argsort/partition alike), engine BooleanMask get+set,
  NonZero (tuple yield via Returns(T[])), ClipNDArray, the fancy-index FetchIndices/
  SetIndices 15-way dispatchers, and the typed generics surface (&, |, ^ operators, string/

THE WEAVER (tools/NumSharp.Weaver — Mono.Cecil 0.11.6 console tool):
- Transform per [NDScoped] method: scope = NDScope.Open() into a fresh local
  BEFORE the protected region (the C# using shape); the whole original body
  becomes the try of a try/finally whose finally is scope.Dispose(); every
  original ret is rewritten — the CLR forbids ret inside a protected region,
  so wrapping the body forces every return through a rewritable seam. Each ret
  is MUTATED IN PLACE into the first replacement instruction (branches and
  nested-handler boundaries that referenced it stay valid): return value to a
  local, NDArray-like values routed through scope.Returns<T>(T)
  (Returns<T>(T[]) for tuple-style array returns; generic instantiation uses
  the method's own return type, so NDArray<TDType> operators inside the open
  generic type weave correctly), each out-NDArray/out-NDArray[] parameter's
  FINAL value yielded on the success path, then leave to a single epilogue
  ([ldloc ret;] ret) after the handler. SimplifyMacros before, OptimizeMacros
  after; existing try/using blocks nest inside the new outer handler (appended
  last = innermost-first table order the CLR requires).

harden(lifetime): NDScope out-of-order Dispose safety + thread asserts + [NDScoped] weave coverage gate

Audit pass over NDScope and the [NDScoped] IL weaver for robustness and API
completeness. Findings verified sound: the tracking model is one Track per object
(every concrete NDArray ctor funnels InitializeArc exactly once; the storage-less
base ctors don't Track, the allocating/derived ctors do), so Dispose can never
reclaim a Returns-yielded array; the weaver correctly handles every ret/out/void/
scalar/array shape including recursive, view-returning (roll) and generic-type
operator methods. Three hardening changes:

- NDScope.Dispose is now out-of-order safe. Open() hands out a raw IDisposable, so a
  hand-managed scope can be disposed off the weaver/using LIFO path. Dispose keeps the
  in-order fast path (this IS t_current -> pop to parent) but, when disposed out of
  order, splices itself out of the middle of the thread's scope chain, so t_current is
  never left pointing at -- or through -- a disposed scope. Reclamation correctness is
  unchanged; this only keeps the ambient stack coherent under public-API misuse.

- Debug thread-affinity asserts on Returns/Attach/Detach (matching the existing one on
  Dispose). These mutate per-scope Lists that are single-thread by contract; the asserts
  trip a cross-thread touch in Debug instead of racing. Zero false positives under the
  8-thread NDScopeStressTests load.

- New gate NDScopeWeaveTests: reflects the shipped assembly and asserts every [NDScoped]
  method (and property accessor) carries an NDScope local -- a necessary consequence of
  scoping, woven or hand-written. Turns a silently un-run weave (broken NDScopeWeave
  target, or a -p:SkipNDScopeWeave=true build) red instead of letting those methods
  quietly revert to the finalizer backstop; a non-vacuity floor guards against the
  attribute being stripped. A reflection probe confirms 53/53 attributed methods woven,
  matching the weaver's own report.

test(lifetime): verify manual Dispose() inside a scope is flawless (no double-free)

Covers the interaction of a hand-written NDArray.Dispose() on a TRACKED array with the scope's
later reclamation sweep, which disposes the same array again. Load-bearing property: freed EXACTLY
once -- Dispose is CAS-idempotent, so the sweep's second dispose is a no-op and the buffer is never
double-returned to the pool (a double-free would hand the same buffer to two later allocations =
silent aliasing corruption). Seven cases, asserting via pool-counter deltas + IsReleased + IsDisposed:

- ManualDisposeOfTrackedTemp_ScopeSweepIsNoOp_FreedExactlyOnce: manual Dispose frees the buffer and
  leaves the temp STILL tracked; the sweep visits it again and must add ZERO further releases.
- DoubleManualDispose_ThenScopeSweep_FreedOnce: two hand disposes + the sweep = one free.
- ManualDisposeBase_YieldedView_StaysValid_FreedOnceAtViewDispose: dispose a base whose reshape view
  is yielded; ARC keeps the buffer alive, the view reads correctly, freed once at the view's dispose.
- ManualDisposeThenReturnsSame_Graceful_NoCorruption: disposing what you return (a user bug) yields a
  disposed array gracefully, never a crash/double-free; the input stays untouched.
- ExceptionAfterManualDispose_ScopeFinallySweep_FreedOnce_InputUntouched: throw after a manual dispose;
  the finally sweep must not free the temp again; input untouched.
- MixedManualAndScopeReclaim_Balanced_NoDoubleFree_NoLeak: the §6 mid-method direct-Dispose pattern
  mixed with scope reclaim over 200 cycles; deficit >= 0 (no double-free = Releases > Acquisitions)
  AND <= 8 (no leak).
- ManualDisposeThenScopeSweep_NoAliasing_HostileProbe: churn the pattern 100x, then allocate two
  arrays, fill with distinct values, and prove no cross-corruption (the strong aliasing detector).

Result: flawless. All freed exactly once; a fixed exact-count assertion had to account for the
scalar transient that 'input * 2' allocates (the sweep correctly reclaims it) -- switched that case
to arange (one buffer, no hidden transient). 3 net8.0 runs + net10.0 green; Lifetime suite 63/63.

- NDArrayTuple: a System.ValueTuple of 2..4 NDArray-likes (modf/polydiv/qr/eig/svd/lstsq/
  average_returned/...). Emits `scope.Returns((a,b[,...]))` through new NDScope.Returns<T1,...>

  which would have mis-bound the tuple overloads onto ReturnsOne).
- Carrier: a result struct implementing the new internal interface NumSharp.INDArrayCarrier

each struct field directly. It throws FieldAccessException at RUNTIME — the CLR grants a nested type

unsupported carriers (object/collection field, >4-arity or mixed tuple, struct without the
interface), and a hand-scoped supported carrier with [NDScoped] is skipped rather than erroring.

fix(lifetime): ~NDArray abandons its buffer ref instead of freeing — close the aliased-base use-after-free (SlicingWithNegativeIndex1, macOS CI)

Symptom: intermittent red on test (macos-latest) — SlicingWithNegativeIndex1
read 0L where 8L was stored. The test builds
`new UnmanagedStorage(np.arange(10).GetData(), shape)`: the arange NDArray
temp dies immediately while its buffer is aliased by a bare UnmanagedStorage,
which holds NO counted ARC reference (only NDArray ctors AddRef). When GC ran
between construction and the reads, ~NDArray -> InternalArray.Release() ->
refcount 1 -> 0 -> claim-free CAS -> buffer returned to
SizeBucketedBufferPool UNDER the live alias; the next same-size allocation
overwrote it. Deterministic repro on Windows (forced GC + same-size
np.full(7777) thief): 2000/2000 iterations freed, 1999/2000 read 7777
instead of 8. Green-at-7e6c1279 / red-at-edc946c4 (a data-only commit)
proved the GC-timing race.

Root cause: the finalizer path claimed the eager free. An NDArray being
UNREACHABLE proves nothing about OTHER reachable aliases of the same block —
bare UnmanagedStorage / IArraySlice handles from GetData() are invisible to
the refcount. Freeing at refcount-0 is only sound where a caller asserts
lifetime, i.e. the deterministic Dispose()/NDScope path.

Fix: split the drop in two.
- Disposer.Abandon() (new, plumbed as IArraySlice.Abandon ->
  ArraySlice<T> -> UnmanagedMemoryBlock<T>): decrement WITHOUT the 0 -> -1
  claim-free transition; count rests at live-zero, so a later TryAddRef
  (a new NDArray wrapping a still-live alias) legitimately revives 0 -> 1,
  and a stray call on a released block self-heals exactly like Release.
- ~NDArray now calls Abandon() instead of Release(). Dispose() (and with it
  NDScope eager reclamation and ndarray.resize) is untouched and keeps the
  eager free-and-pool at refcount 0.

Why this is safe and leak-free: the block's inner Disposer has its own
finalizer that frees regardless of refcount, gated only on reachability —
exactly the right authority for the non-deterministic path. An abandoned
buffer whose aliases all died is freed (and pool-returned) in the following
GC cycle; an abandoned buffer with a live alias stays valid for as long as
the alias is reachable. Verified: fixed build 0/2000 UAF hits; pool-reuse
probe 49/49 buffers still recycle through SizeBucketedBufferPool after
finalization; buffer readable under the alias, refcount drained to 0.

Test updates (ArcLifecycleTests): three tests pinned the OLD contract —
each held the slice (a reachable alias!) and asserted IsReleased==true
after finalization, i.e. asserted freed-memory-reachable-through-a-live-
alias, the exact hazard fixed here.
- Finalizer_ReleasesUnmanaged_WhenDisposeMissed ->
  Finalizer_AbandonsRef_ButNeverFreesUnderALiveAlias: asserts the buffer
  survives finalization while the alias is held (and stays readable), the
  counted ref drains to 0, and — via a WeakReference to the inner Disposer —
  that the block IS reclaimed once the last alias dies. Every touch of the
  slice box is confined to NoInlining helper frames: a single-shot test
  method JITs at tier-0, whose untracked eval-stack temps root the box until
  method end (measured: the drop-phase probe never dies inside the test's
  own frame, dies immediately when confined to a helper frame).
- UndisposedNDArray_BecomesCollectable_ViaFinalizer: same contract flip
  (buffer NOT freed under the held alias, refcount 0).
- ReshapeNonContiguous_AllocatesNewOwningBuffer: the orphan intermediate now
  abandons at finalization — assert refcount drains to 0 and the buffer
  stays alive under the held c_slice.
- NEW AliasedBaseBuffer_SurvivesFinalizerOfItsLastNDArray: the CI failure
  made deterministic — 200 iterations of the exact SlicingWithNegativeIndex1
  idiom with forced GC + a same-size allocation that would steal a wrongly
  pooled buffer.

feat(lifetime): weave bare IArraySlice/UnmanagedStorage returns with counted-ref protection

Support [NDScoped] on a boundary method that RETURNS a lower-layer buffer (IArraySlice /
UnmanagedStorage) not wrapped in an NDArray — the third "other return kind" beyond tuples/carriers.

The hazard this addresses: the scope's reclamation unit is the NDArray, which owns the single counted
ARC reference on its buffer; NDScope reclaims tracked NDArrays via the DETERMINISTIC Release path
(eager free at refcount 0, "asserting no alias outlives" — see the ~NDArray ABANDON contract, commit
09b47a49). A bare IArraySlice/UnmanagedStorage is an UNCOUNTED alias, so a scoped method returning one
would have its buffer freed out from under the caller the instant the scope Releases the intermediate
NDArray that shares it (the SlicingWithNegativeIndex1 UAF class).

NDScope: add Returns(IArraySlice) and Returns(UnmanagedStorage) — each takes a counted reference
(TryAddRef, a stable ARC API) on the returned buffer so the scope's Release can no longer reach 0; the
buffer survives, and the reference is deliberately abandoned (never Released), so the block's finalizer
reclaims it on unreachability — the same non-deterministic backstop a bare buffer already relies on.

Weaver: new RetKind.Storage — a return typed exactly NumSharp.Backends.Unmanaged.IArraySlice or
NumSharp.Backends.UnmanagedStorage emits `ldloc scope; ldloc retVar; callvirt Returns(slice/storage);
stloc retVar`. ResolveRefs finds the two overloads by their zero-generic parameter type.

Deliberately DEFERRED (documented): auto-TRACKING intermediate bare buffers for eager reclamation —
hooking bare-buffer construction would double-count against the NDArray's reference, lands in the
parallel ARC rework, and has no consumer (compositions own NDArrays, whose transients are already
reclaimed transitively). Only the RETURN is protected.

No in-tree method returns a bare buffer, so (like the ITuple/out-param branches) the semantics are
pinned on the NDScope methods the weaver targets: NDScopeWeaveCarrierTests proves a yielded slice/
storage survives the scope's Release of its NDArray (readable afterward), with a control showing an
un-yielded bare alias IS freed (the hazard the counted ref fixes). Full Lifetime suite (75) green.

test(lifetime): prove woven [NDScoped] storage-touching methods never double-dispose

Adds NDScopeDoubleDisposeTests, pinning that the woven [NDScoped] np.* methods which touch
UnmanagedStorage internally — those that explicitly Dispose() a transient (np.diff, np.ediff1d, and
nonzero's documented `materialized?.Dispose()` ARC-release) or alias a buffer into a returned view
(np.nonzero, np.einsum diagonal) — never release a buffer twice.

The concern: the weaver injects a scope that reclaims every tracked NDArray at method exit, so a
method that ALSO disposes one of those transients itself would, if unguarded, release the same buffer
reference twice — a double-free / premature-free under a live view.

It cannot happen, for two audited reasons this gate exercises at runtime:
 1. NDArray.Dispose is idempotent (an Interlocked _disposed guard), so an explicit dispose followed by
    the scope's dispose releases the buffer's one reference exactly once.
 2. No [NDScoped] method releases a buffer DIRECTLY — none call InternalArray.Release()/DangerousFree()
    (verified by source audit); every release goes through the idempotent NDArray.Dispose. The .Storage
    accesses in [NDScoped] methods are read-pointer / reshape-metadata / alias-view / fill — never a
    release.

Tests:
 - ExplicitTransientDispose_PlusScopeDispose_ReleasesBufferExactlyOnce — the mechanism made observable:
   a scope tracks a base, the base is explicitly disposed (the np.diff/nonzero pattern), and a view
   sharing its buffer is yielded; the buffer must survive scope exit (proving no double-release under
   the live view) and free exactly once when the view — the last owner — drops.
 - YieldedViewOntoDisposedBase_SurvivesBothDisposes — a yielded column view outlives both the explicit
   dispose and the scope (the nonzero shape).
 - WovenStorageMethods_UnderGCPressure_NoDoubleFree — 12k iterations of np.diff/ediff1d/nonzero(non-
   contiguous)/where/einsum under forced GC, the exact conditions Default.NonZero documents as
   reproducing a double-free AccessViolation in Release; a double-release would crash or read garbage.

Green on net8.0 + net10.0.

perf(storage): collapse the 15 per-dtype ArraySlice<T> fields into one explicit-layout union (-896 B per UnmanagedStorage)

Every UnmanagedStorage carried 15 strongly-typed 64 B ArraySlice<T> fields of
which exactly ONE was ever populated (the lane matching the array's dtype) --
960 B embedded per instance, ~896 B of it permanently default. They are now a
single [StructLayout(LayoutKind.Explicit)] nested struct TypedSlices whose 15
lanes all overlap at [FieldOffset(0)], accessed as _slices.Int32 / _slices.Double
etc. Pure mechanical rename on every read/write site; the getter read path is
byte-for-byte identical (_slices.X[_shape.GetOffset(indices)]).

Why the overlap is CLR-legal: ArraySlice<T>'s layout is identical for every T
(T occurs only behind pointers: T*/void*/long/bool), and its single managed
reference -- the non-generic Disposer inside UnmanagedMemoryBlock<T> -- sits at
the same offset with the same type in all 15 lanes, so the GC ref map is
well-formed. A malformed map would be a TypeLoadException at first touch (the
loader's own check), never silent corruption. Aliasing is never crossed: only
the _typecode-matched lane is written or read over a storage's lifetime. The
ARC refcount is untouched -- TryAddRef/Release flow entirely through the boxed
InternalArray, which is kept verbatim.

feat(weaver): ship NumSharp.Weaver as an installable build-time weaver NuGet package

NumSharp.Weaver now packs as a tools-only NuGet package that WEAVES the project it is
installed on instead of becoming a dependency of it: install it, mark methods
[NDScoped], and the packaged NDScopeWeave target rewrites the intermediate assembly
after each per-TFM compile exactly like NumSharp.Core's own self-weave.

Not-a-dependency, by construction:
- IncludeBuildOutput=false + SuppressDependenciesWhenPacking: the nupkg carries NO lib/
  and NO dependency entries (Mono.Cecil rides inside tools/net8.0/any/, never expressed
  to the consumer's graph).
- DevelopmentDependency=true: `dotnet add package NumSharp.Weaver` writes
  PrivateAssets="all" on the consumer's PackageReference by itself, so the weaver never
  flows into the consumer's own package as a dependency.
- build/ only (deliberately NOT buildTransitive/): weaving applies exactly where the
  package is installed, never to projects that merely reference a woven library.
- The tool payload is the PUBLISH output (weaver + Cecil + runtimeconfig with
  RollForward=Major so an SDK-10-only box runs the net8.0 tool; UseAppHost=false).
  TRAP: PrivateAssets="all" on the Mono.Cecil PackageReference EXCLUDED it from the
  publish output (the SDK treats such packages as non-published dev dependencies) --
  keeping Cecil out of the consumer's graph is SuppressDependenciesWhenPacking's job,
  so the reference deliberately carries no PrivateAssets.

Cross-assembly weaving (a consumer's NDScope lives in the REFERENCED NumSharp):
- WeaverAssemblyResolver: exact-path map built from the compiler's own reference list
  (@(ReferencePathWithRefAssemblies) written as a response file, passed via --refs)
  plus directory-probing fallback; reference assemblies are fine because the weaver
  imports member SIGNATURES, never bodies.
- ResolveRefs falls back from module.GetType to the assembly references (NumSharp-named
  refs first, type forwarders honoured) and IMPORTS every member into the woven module
  (an identity pass-through for the in-module self-weave).
- Classification guards relaxed from name-prefix to resolver-backed resolution:
  consumer-defined INDArrayCarrier result structs, NDArray subclasses and consumer/BCL
  enums classify exactly like in-module ones (System./Microsoft. fast-skip avoids
  opening BCL ref packs for answers the classifier already knows).
- New error NDW001: [NDScoped] methods present but NDScope unresolvable -- a loud
  configuration error instead of silently shipping unwoven methods.
- An assembly with no [NDScoped] methods (or whose targets are all hand-scoped
  already) is left byte-for-byte UNTOUCHED: no rewrite, so its compile-time signature
  and determinism id survive. Program: --refs <rsp>; an empty --snk is tolerated
  (unsigned consumers); the summary reports 'assembly unchanged' when nothing wove.

Consumer-facing surface: NDScopedAttribute and INDArrayCarrier go PUBLIC in
NumSharp.Core -- the ndscoped docs already promise both to consumers, and the woven
cross-assembly YieldTo/Returns calls must pass the CLR's runtime accessibility check.
Without the package the attribute stays inert metadata: adding/removing the weaver
never changes results, only WHEN transient buffers are reclaimed.

it encodes, mapped each against NumSharp.Weaver, and adopted the three that apply.

Adopted (all three verified end-to-end):
- HOST SELECTION, no bare-PATH assumption: the Exec ladder now prefers
  $(DOTNET_HOST_PATH) (set by the dotnet CLI / .NET-Core MSBuild for exactly this
  hand-off; the SDK-documented discovery for a build step's own host) and falls back to
  PATH 'dotnet' only where it is unset (VS devenv / Full-framework MSBuild, whose SDK
  installer registers dotnet machine-wide). Overridable via $(NumSharpWeaverDotnetHost).
  Applied to BOTH the packaged build/NumSharp.Weaver.targets and NumSharp.Core's own
  inline NDScopeWeave target. Proven live in both regimes: a dotnet-CLI build resolves
  to the full 'C:\...\dotnet.exe' path, and a REAL VS 2022 MSBuild.exe consumer build
  with DOTNET_HOST_PATH scrubbed falls back to 'dotnet', weaves, and the app verifies
  its own NDScope local at runtime.
- ANCHOR SET: BeforeTargets grows _TimeStampAfterCompile;AfterCompile (AspectInjector's
  own anchors) so the SDK's post-compile timestamping stays consistent with the
  rewritten assembly and AfterCompile-hooked IL rewriters (MAUI XamlC and friends) see
  the WOVEN assembly instead of racing it. MSBuild ignores anchors naming targets a
  project never defines, so this is inert elsewhere. Mirrored into Core's inline target.
- CONTENT PRE-SCAN (their '__a$_instance' marker-scan technique): using [NDScoped]
  compiles a TypeRef whose name lands as an ASCII run in the metadata #Strings heap,
  and ASCII runs survive lossy UTF-8 decoding of arbitrary binary intact — so
  File.ReadAllText(...).Contains('NDScopedAttribute') is a reliable was-it-used probe
  on fresh CoreCompile output. Attribute-free consumers (and rebuilds where a foreign
  rewriter bumped the assembly past the marker) now skip the tool spawn entirely; a
  false positive (the name in a user string literal) merely spawns the tool, which
  no-ops. No false negative exists on compiler output. The gate's step 12 accepts the
  new skip message alongside the tool's own nothing-to-do line.

Scars audited and NOT applicable — the design is already immune, now deliberately so:
- their PART 1 core bug (in-process task leaks Cecil ReadWrite handles into reused
  MSBuild nodes; CreateAppHost then dies on the locked dll): we are out-of-process by
  construction with InMemory reads, and the OS closes everything at tool exit — their
  fix converges on our architecture (their -nodeReuse:false child-MSBuild machinery is
  unnecessary for a plain console child);
- the CULTURE/CALENDAR scar (%(ModifiedTime) formats with the current culture's
  CALENDAR while Touch parses Time invariant → Persian/Umm-al-Qura locales die with
  'Not a valid Win32 FileTime'; their ToString('o') round-trip fix): our Touch stamps
  bare AlwaysCreate (no Time string round-trip at all), the targets format no dates or
  numbers, and the tool runs InvariantGlobalization=true with ordinal comparisons;
- ADVICE STACKING on re-weave (their measured one-save-becomes-N bug behind both the
  content check and the XamlC restamp target): our transform is per-method idempotent
  (an already-scoped body is skipped) and a nothing-woven pass does not rewrite the
  file — live-proven this session: deleting the marker and rebuilding reports
  'woven 0, already-scoped 90, assembly unchanged' where AspectInjector would have
  double-woven;
- RE-SIGN-AFTER-STAMP re-weave loop (sn -R bumps the assembly past the marker): our
  re-sign happens inside the tool's single write, BEFORE the marker touch — the
  ordering hazard cannot exist;
- sn.exe discovery / Windows-only re-sign / warn-when-missing: Cecil signs the blob
  in-process, cross-platform, no external tool;
- command-line overflow of reference lists: already a response file (--refs);
- semicolon-in-path property tearing (their NJS1007): we pass quoted ARGUMENTS to a
  console tool, never -property: values through a child MSBuild command line.

perf(pool): GC pacing + coarse pressure + burst-sized buckets — fix small-N elementwise 0.2-0.3x floor

The 1K/100K elementwise cells (np.copy/np.abs/np.trunc/a*a*a at float32 and
every other dtype) sat at 0.2-0.33x NumPy because dropped, undisposed result
buffers return to SizeBucketedBufferPool only via the block Disposer's
FINALIZER, which runs only after a GC — and the pool's own per-Take
GC.AddMemoryPressure made every one of those collections a FULL gen-2.

Instrumented root causes (live-idle, Release, Stopwatch):
1. Per-Take/Return GC.Add/RemoveMemoryPressure pair: 55 ns/call AND drove
   pressure-triggered FULL gen-2 collections every ~24 calls at 100K
   (~12 us/call of GC time; every observed collection was gen2 — 84/84/84).
2. Finalizer returns arrive in one burst per collection; the flat cap of 8
   per bucket discarded ~95% of each burst (20K-call 1K loop: 3.3K pooled,
   16K freed) — the next window ran cold: 16.8% hit-rate at 1K.
3. Misses re-pay cold NativeMemory.Alloc + first-touch page faults: ~35
   us/op at 100K float32 (kernel itself: 5.6 us).

Fixes (all in SizeBucketedBufferPool; EnvVars gains the knobs):
- COARSE PRESSURE: pressure now tracks net outstanding bytes (taken -
  returned) in 64 MiB chunks — the hot path pays two interlocked adds
  instead of Add/RemoveMemoryPressure per call; the GC only hears about
  net growth at chunk granularity, so the gen-2 storms are gone while the
  issue #501 protection (process holding GBs of native arrays still pushes
  the GC) is preserved. Warm Take+Return: 96 -> 57 ns.
- GEN-0 PACING: when a Take misses (or a bucket drains to its low-water
  slack) after >= 16 MiB handed out since the last paced collection, the
  pool requests ONE forced blocking non-compacting gen-0 collection
  (~4-6 us) — the .NET stand-in for CPython's refcount-prompt free. The
  dropped wrapper graphs are still gen 0 (allocated inside the window), so
  gen 0 suffices; the finalizer thread drains and the returns refill the
  buckets. Deterministically-disposing workloads (Dispose/NDScope) keep
  buckets stocked and never trip the trigger. Knobs:
  NUMSHARP_POOL_GC_PACING=0 opt-out, NUMSHARP_POOL_GC_PACING_MB window
  (default 16; swept 1/2/4/8/16/32/64/128 — 16 is the measured optimum:
  smaller starves on finalizer-drain latency, larger rotates the warm set
  past L3).
- BURST-SIZED BUCKETS: per-bucket cap = one pacing window of bytes plus
  ~25% low-water slack (clamped 8..4096 entries below 1 MiB, floor 2 at/
  above), so a whole finalizer burst fits; the low-water mark triggers the
  paced collection while slack buffers still cover the asynchronous drain.
  Buckets+depth maps merged into one Bucket object (single probe per op).
- New diagnostic counter PacedCollections; all existing counters unchanged
  (Lifetime/NDScope test contract intact).

Measured (live-idle, Release, best-of-rounds, NPY/NS — higher is better):
- 1K float32: copy 0.29->0.57x, abs 0.29->0.67x, cube 0.29->0.61x,
  absolute 0.30->0.68x, trunc 0.30->0.69x; abs f64 0.20->0.65x;
  abs i32 -> 1.00x. Hit-rate 16.8% -> 99.7%, returns-freed ~16K -> ~0.
- 100K float32: abs 41.9 -> 12.4 us (0.25->0.46x), cube -> 1.14x,
  abs f64 -> 0.86x, abs i32 -> 2.21x. GCs: full-gen2 every ~24 calls ->
  gen0-only every ~43 calls.
- 10M float32: no regression — abs 8.1 -> 6.0 ms (1.21x), copy 1.35x,
  cube 1.31x (pacing returns the 40 MB buffers promptly instead of waiting
  on pressure-driven full GCs).
- The remaining sub-1.0 1K/100K float32 cells are bounded by the finalizer
  pipeline (~0.2 us/op amortized) and NumPy's single-warm-buffer reuse
  (refcount-immediate free); the disposed path (using/NDScope) already
  BEATS NumPy there (0.376 vs 0.411 us at 1K) and stays the guidance for
  hot loops. Measured-and-rejected: suppressing the transient NDArray's
  finalizer buys only ~15% — not worth an ARC-contract change.

perf(predicates): SIMD isnan/isinf/isfinite kernels for float32/float64 — 0.10x -> 0.9-1.3x

np.isnan/np.isinf/np.isfinite over Single/Double ran SCALAR at every size:
the generic unary SIMD gate (CanUseUnarySimd) requires input dtype == output
dtype, and a predicate is inherently float->bool, so the ops fell to the
per-element float.IsNaN/IsInfinity/IsFinite body — measured 40.6 us vs
NumPy's 4.1 us on 100K float32 isnan (0.10x), 25.9 vs 5.1 for isfinite
(0.20x). NumPy vectorizes exactly these in loops_unary_fp_le.dispatch.c.src.

Port of NumPy's kernel structure into two dedicated IL kernels in
DirectILKernelGenerator.Unary.Predicate.cs (dispatched from
DefaultEngine.UnaryOp.cs; every other dtype keeps its existing route —
NumPy's own HALF/CFLOAT predicate loops are scalar too):

- CONTIGUOUS (GetPredicateContiguousKernel, UnaryKernel-shaped, 4x-unrolled
  + 1-vector remainder + scalar tail): lane logic all in the float domain,
  no reinterpret casts —
    isnan(v)    = NOT Equals(v, v)      (npyv_notnan)
    isinf(v)    = Equals(Abs(v), +inf)  (Abs(NaN) stays NaN; NaN==inf false)
    isfinite(v) = LessThan(Abs(v), +inf) (false for +-inf and NaN)
  then the comparison kernels' mask->bool store (ExtractMostSignificantBits
  + BMI2 PDEP -> one sized store per vector; per-lane fallback without BMI2),
  parametrized by output-arg slot and SIMD width. Served from the
  trivial-contiguous bypass for C- AND F-contiguous inputs.
- STRIDED 1-D (GetPredicateStridedKernel, StridedUnaryKernel-shaped) — the
  NCONTIG->CONTIG loop: each vector assembled from lane-count strided scalar
  loads (VectorMethodCache.CreateElements = npyv_loadn; NumPy prefers
  insert-builds over hardware gather for these cheap lane ops), 2x unroll
  (4x measured WORSE — register pressure on the insert chains), predicate
  mask + PDEP store to the fresh contiguous bool result. Single is pinned to
  128-bit vectors exactly as NumPy pins this file (NPY_SIMD_FORCE_128): the
  cost is the strided assembly, and a 4-lane insert chain beats a cross-lane
  8-lane build (measured 9.4 -> 8.8 us). Replaces the scalar gather-to-tile
  route for predicates, which paid ~1 ns/element on the gather alone
  (70 us vs NumPy's 4.9 on a 50K stride-2 isnan); the buffered route stays
  as fallback and TryBufferedStridedUnaryOp now also accepts the predicate
  kernel for shapes the fused path declines.

perf(predicates): isnan/isinf/isfinite return via AsGeneric (shared storage) not MakeGeneric (alias) — close the float→bool double-alloc

The float-classification predicates np.isnan/np.isinf/np.isfinite wrapped their
freshly-produced bool engine result with `result.MakeGeneric<bool>()`, whose
`Storage.Alias()` allocates a SECOND UnmanagedStorage + ArraySlice per call on
top of the result NDArray. Their sibling bool-output family — the comparisons
(np.less/greater/...) — allocate `NDArray<bool>` directly and pay ONE object.
So every predicate call carried an extra alias + object that comparisons did not.

Root-cause of this session's investigation ("why can't f32 isnan clear >1.0x?"):
the predicate KERNELS already beat NumPy at every size (pure isnan f32 kernel:
1K 7.6x, 100K 1.05x, 10M 1.14x vs NumPy's own out= loop). The reported sub-1.0x
ratios were entirely per-call OVERHEAD — NDArray/ARC construction + dispatch +
the bool wrap — not compute. This MakeGeneric alias was a removable slice of that
overhead specific to the predicate family (measured ~0.08 us; alloc+MakeGeneric
0.547us -> alloc+AsGeneric 0.470us, vs comparison's direct NDArray<bool> 0.419us).

AsGeneric is the intended path for freshly-produced engine results (its own
doc-comment): the result is already owned, so it wraps the storage in place
(new NDArray<bool>(Storage), one AddRef) instead of aliasing it. Combined with
the existing `using var result`, the ARC pattern is identical to the prior code
minus the alias — result AddRef'd to 2, disposed back to 1, wrapper returned
owning the last ref. Verified: returned array is still a typed NDArray<bool>,
owns its data (IsView=false, base==null), writeable, contiguous; writing the
result does not touch the input.

  isnan    f32 100K: 0.87x -> 1.06x disposed (0.83x -> 0.97x nondisp)
  isinf    f32 100K: ~0.9x -> 1.37x disposed (1.23x nondisp)
  isfinite f32 100K: ~0.9x -> 1.32x disposed (1.18x nondisp)
  10M all three 1.49-1.86x; 1K 0.62-0.70x (NumPy's ~0.36us C-struct floor — the
  irreducible small-N allocation wall, unchanged: that is the systemic per-call
  overhead, not fixable without the ARC/finalizer rewrite).

bit-exact vs NumPy 2.4.2) + 929 isnan/isinf/isfinite unit tests, both net8.0/net10.0.

per-element NaN-aware walk (ArgMax/MinFloat/DoubleNaNHelper), the documented
"~12x behind NumPy" gap. Integer types already used a SIMD two-pass helper; only

Ported NumPy's simd_argmax_@sfx@ / simd_argmin_@sfx@
(numpy/_core/src/multiarray/argfunc.dispatch.c.src): a single-pass, 4x-unrolled
tournament that carries the winning lane's ABSOLUTE index in a companion integer
vector (int32 for f32 / int64 for f64), with the NaN branch handled the NumPy way
— (x == x) notnan masks, and the FIRST NaN in encounter order returns immediately.
Strict >/< keeps the LOWEST index on ties (acc overwritten only on a strict win),
so first-occurrence holds across lanes and across blocks. f32 caps the vectorized
region at int.MaxValue so the int32 index vector cannot overflow on a >2^31-element
(8 GB) array; the scalar tail finishes the remainder. Half stays scalar (no
Vector256<Half> arithmetic in the BCL, and NumPy's f16 argmax is scalar too);
integer types keep their existing generic two-pass helper.

loop: an in-loop compare-direction branch is free at 100K but measured 2.26x
SLOWER at 10M (it blocks the JIT from streaming the memory-bound loop) — exactly
why NumPy generates them as separate functions via its repeat macro.

perf(exp2): SIMD float32 exp2 kernel — hybrid double-2^r + float scale; 0.19x -> 1.82-3.12x NumPy

np.exp2(float32) computed (float)Math.Pow(2,(double)x): a double `pow` per element,
~5x slower than NumPy's own scalar loop (0.19x NPY/NS at 100K live-idle) and 1 ULP off.
Replace it with a vectorized NDFloatMath.Exp2, the fast sibling of the exp/log/sin/cos/
tanh ports — wired identically (CachedMethods SingleExp2/SingleExp2Vector; the scalar
route in Unary.Math, the vector case in Unary.Vector, the shared FMA gate in Unary.cs).

Not a bit-for-bit NumPy port, by necessity. NumPy's SIMD exp2 (simd_exp2 in
loops_umath_fp.dispatch) is SVML, gated NPY_HAVE_AVX512_SKX && NPY_CAN_LINK_SVML =
Linux/AVX-512 only, so the numpy 2.4.2 win-amd64 wheel this repo targets runs the SCALAR
fallback npy_exp2f (the MSVC CRT exp2f). There is thus no reproducible float kernel to
match, and a pure-float polynomial cannot reach the CRT's near-correctly-rounded result
(float rounding of the Horner chain alone leaves ~1 ULP on ~4.5% of inputs, any degree).

Algorithm: 2^x = 2^n * 2^r with n = rint(x), r in [-0.5, 0.5]. 2^r is a degree-8 minimax
evaluated in DOUBLE (2^-37.7 relative error, ~13 bits below float precision), narrowed ONCE
to float and then scaled by the integer power 2^n straight in the exponent field — exact,
so it adds no second rounding for a normal result. The n <= -125 denormal branch reuses the
exp kernel's ScalefDenormal split. The vector form widens each float register to two
Vector{}<double> halves (WidenLower/WidenUpper), runs the poly per half, and Narrow packs
2^r back; the 2^n scale stays in cheap float int-ops. A full-double scale via
Vector256.ConvertToInt64 was measured at 343us/100K (SLOWER than NumPy) because that convert
is AVX2-emulated — the hybrid is what makes it fast.

Accuracy: <= 1 ULP vs NumPy on every input, ~0.2% differ (all subnormal outputs, where the
narrow + denormal split double-rounds) — the same accuracy class as the Math.Pow bridge it
replaces. Scalar entry point is lane-identical to the vector kernel (verified 0-diff over
~7M inputs). Stays under the <= 2-ULP `unary ~ULP` fuzz excuse; deliberately NOT added to
the bit-exact NumPyPortedFloat32Kernels carve-out. Specials match NumPy (probed): NaN ->
0x7fc00000, x >= 128 -> +inf, x <= -150 -> +0, +-0 -> 1, integer x exact (exp2(10)=1024).

Perf (NPY/NS, Release, best-of, warm, 1K / 100K / 10M): 1.82x / 2.40x / 3.12x — up from
~0.2x (the Math.Pow bridge), ~12x faster at 100K. Other dtypes unchanged (double/int/Half
via Math.Pow, complex via NDComplexMath.Exp2).

contract, <= 2-ULP envelope, fused NDExpr) + the unary_extra/specials differential-fuzz
tiers (FuzzMatrix 88/88 green). CLAUDE.md math section updated: exp2 moved out of the
"still platform libm / NOT ported" list into its own port paragraph.

perf(openblas): thread-local retained scratch pool — LAPACK factorisations 0.44-0.50x -> parity

Every OpenBLAS LAPACK core (inv/solve/det/slogdet/svd/eig/eigh/qr/cholesky/lstsq)
allocates its native scratch each call — the column-major operand copy, the LAPACK
workspace, the U/VT/eigenvector temporaries — with a fresh NativeMemory.Alloc, and frees
it at the end. Under real heap pressure (a program that has already run other
large-workspace factorisations) the CRT stops keeping those blocks resident, so LAPACK's
first write to a freshly malloc'd workspace demand-zero-faults its pages — and because the
fault lands INSIDE the timed native call it ~doubles a small factorisation. Measured
96x96 f64: det/inv/eigh/pinv/svd all ~0.44-0.50x NumPy, the fault cost ~= the whole native
compute. NumPy never pays this: its process keeps the same-sized malloc blocks hot.

Root-caused by decomposition: coalescing all scratch into ONE malloc does NOT help
post-churn (a single ~450 KB alloc faults just the same); only RETAINING the pages across
calls does — a warm reused buffer measures 0.70 ms where a fresh one is 1.60 ms.

Fix: route Alloc<T>/Free<T> through a thread-local pool that retains freed blocks
(power-of-two buckets; a 16-byte size header lets Free re-bucket from the pointer alone;
per-thread so no lock; idle retention capped at 32 MiB/thread so a one-off huge
factorisation is not pinned). Pure allocation change with ZERO change to any core's
numerics — a pooled block is uninitialised exactly as a fresh malloc is, and every core
already fully writes its scratch before reading it (Linearize fills the column-major copy,
LAPACK fills the workspace/outputs, IdentityColMajor zeroes what it needs).

Result (NPY/NS, best-of-21, threads=1, live idle, 96x96 f64): the whole factorisation
family lifts from ~0.48x to parity — cholesky 1.11x, det 0.98x, inv 1.04x, solve 1.08x,
slogdet 1.05x, eigh 0.97x, eigvalsh 0.98x, eigvals 0.95x, eig 0.94x, qr 1.03x, lstsq 0.99x,
pinv 0.95x, cond 0.98x, matrix_rank 1.00x.

Bit-exact preserved: 97/97 live-numpy byte-compares (Lapack/Svd/Eig/Cholesky/Qr/Products/
Matmul/SlidingDot LiveParity) + the host-pinned FuzzMatrix linalg_parity/matmul_parity
corpus tiers all green.

Documented residual (a benchmark-measurement artifact, NOT an op cost): in the single
long-lived openblas_bench process a gen2 GC on the grown heap issues an OS working-set
trim (EmptyWorkingSet) that evicts even the retained pages, so the LAST ops measured
(svd/svdvals/tensorinv/tensorsolve/matrix_power/matrix_norm/norm) re-fault mid-timing —
the same gesdd is fast at op #2 (cond) and slow at op #16 (svdvals). Each is at parity in
isolation (svd 0.70 vs NumPy 0.82 = 1.16x; matrix_power 0.079 vs 0.079 = 1.01x). Neither
VirtualLock (capped by the process min working set, regresses under churn) nor a hard
min-working-set floor (too intrusive for a library, overridden by EmptyWorkingSet) is a
clean library-level fix, so it is left to the harness.

feat(weaver): [NDScoped] weaves async/iterator state machines + Task/ValueTask returns

The weaver previously refused async and iterator methods outright (NDW004: the
visible body is a state-machine stub) and Task-shaped returns as unsupported
carriers (NDW003). Both are now first-class:

  - async methods    Task / Task<T> / ValueTask / ValueTask<T> / async void /
                     custom [AsyncMethodBuilder] task-likes
  - iterators        IEnumerable[<T>] / IEnumerator[<T>] (yield return)
  - async iterators  IAsyncEnumerable<T> (await + yield)
  - NON-async methods returning Task/ValueTask[<T>]
  - T = any already-supported shape (NDArray, NDArray[], NDArray tuples,
    ITuple mixes, INDArrayCarrier structs, IArraySlice/UnmanagedStorage,
    scalars) - an unsupported T stays the same loud NDW003.

Design: ONE scope per logical invocation, stored in a weaver-added state-machine
field '<>ndscope'. A scope-per-segment is unsound - 'await Bar(t)' hands tracked
temps to an in-flight callee that outlives the segment - so the scope SURVIVES
suspension and every segment re-installs it:

  - MoveNext prologue: scope = NDScope.OpenOrResume(ref this.<>ndscope)
    (opens on the first segment; re-installs + re-stamps the owning thread on
    every resumption - segments are sequenced, so the handoff is race-free).
  - BEFORE each Await[Unsafe]OnCompleted: suspended = true; NDScope.Suspend(scope)
    - after the schedule call the continuation may already be resuming on
    another thread, so the scope must be off this thread's chain first; the
    'suspended' flag is a LOCAL because the finally must not read scope state a
    concurrent resumption mutates (mutate-call-in-place keeps branch targets
    correct; the insert is stack-neutral under the pending call args).
  - BEFORE builder.SetResult/SetException: the result is yielded through the
    ordinary Returns/YieldTo egress, then NDScope.DisposeSlot(ref slot) -
    disposal precedes the completion signal because the signal can run the
    CALLER's continuation inline on this thread, which must not execute under
    (and track into) a dying scope; it also makes 'temps are gone when the
    await returns' deterministic (observed live: finally-only disposal lagged
    the caller by ~50ms). The finally remains as a no-op backstop.
  - Iterators: suspension IS 'return true' and the consumer only regains
    control after MoveNext returns, so the finally decides single-threadedly
    (retVar ? Suspend : DisposeSlot); every stfld <>2__current routes through
    Returns (the consumer owns yielded elements); the enumerator's Dispose()
    gets DisposeSlot before each ret, so 'foreach { break; }' reclaims
    deterministically. Async iterators run ExitIterator(ref slot, hasMore)
    BEFORE promise.SetResult(hasMore) - the consumer can re-enter MoveNext the
    instant the promise is signalled - and dispose before promise.SetException.
  - Consequences needing NO per-field instrumentation: parameters (constructed
    pre-scope, never tracked - an aliased 'var x = input' hoisted local cannot
    be reclaimed), hoisted locals and containers (correctly tracked for the
    whole invocation), exception paths (SetException disposes eagerly).

Non-async Task-shaped returns get a deferral egress: retVar =
scope.ReturnsTask(retVar) yields a COMPLETED task's result immediately, and for
an INCOMPLETE task suspends the scope and defers both the result yield and the
disposal to a completion continuation (ExecuteSynchronously) - protecting
tracked operands a still-running callee holds ('return BarAsync(t)'). The
finally becomes CloseUnlessDeferred (the throw path never defers, so exceptions
still reclaim eagerly). An incomplete ValueTask is single-consumption and
cannot be observed (IVTS GetResult resets pooled sources) - it is Preserve()d
and the CALLER RECEIVES THE PRESERVED (multi-observable) form; plain-value and
task-backed ValueTasks preserve to themselves at zero cost.

NDScope additions (src/NumSharp.Core/Backends/NDScope.cs): OpenOrResume(ref),
Suspend, DisposeSlot(ref), ExitIterator(ref,bool), CloseUnlessDeferred,
ReturnsTask/ReturnsTask<T>, ReturnsValueTask/ReturnsValueTask<T>, private
Resume/YieldBoxed/UnlinkFromChain (extracted from Dispose, behavior identical)
and the _deferred flag (reset in Open; written only on the opening thread -
the completion continuation only reads task state and re-stamps _threadId
before disposing, sequenced by task completion). All seam members carry NEW
NAMES deliberately: the shipped weaver keys the 'Returns' family by generic
arity alone (last-write-wins), so a new Returns<T>(Task<T>) OVERLOAD would
silently re-bind an OLD weaver's ReturnsOne against a new NumSharp and emit
invalid method refs - distinct names make both skew directions safe, and a new
weaver against an old NumSharp reports the new NDW008 only when an
async/task-shaped target actually exists.

Weaver (tools/NumSharp.Weaver/ScopeWeaver.cs): RetKind.TaskLike + the
StateMachineKind Async/Iterator/AsyncIterator routing (the attributed stub's
[AsyncStateMachine]/[IteratorStateMachine]/[AsyncIteratorStateMachine] names
the SM type; its MoveNext is what gets woven). Roslyn's generated-name pins
(<>t__builder, <>2__current, <>v__promiseOfValueOrEnd,
ManualResetValueTaskSourceCore) are compat-stable upstream (debugger/EnC parse
them); any miss is a LOUD NDW004 ('unrecognized state-machine shape'), never a
silent mis-weave. Await/SetResult call sites are matched by name AND the
builder field's declaring type, so a user method merely named
AwaitUnsafeOnCompleted cannot trigger a spurious suspend. Generic state
machines (generic async methods/iterators, SMs in generic types) get field
tokens on the self-instantiated GenericInstanceType, as Roslyn emits its own.
SM idempotence keys on OpenOrResume in MoveNext - a hand-written segment-inner
NDScope.Open must NOT skip the weave. The async seam is resolved LENIENTLY so
older NumSharp references still weave every synchronous target unchanged.

test(oracle): outside-pool allocation detection — runtime bypass verdict + static chokepoint gate

Completes the scope gate with the class it could not see: an op that
allocates its buffers OUTSIDE SizeBucketedBufferPool and frees them outside
it reads as takes=0/returns=0 — a perfect zero balance — while paying a cold
NativeMemory alloc + first-touch page faults on every call with no warm
reuse (the allocator tax the pool exists to remove). Two complementary
detectors close it, because the two halves of the class need different
instruments:

RUNTIME (UndisposedIntermediateTests sweep): ScopeAudit gains MeasureTraffic
(takes AND returns, not just the balance); the sweep inspects each result
BEFORE disposing it and computes its fresh bytes — arrays that are not an
operand instance, whose data pointer lies outside every operand's
base-buffer byte range (corpus Operand offset/bufferSize reconstruct the
exact ranges), and larger than a StackedMemoryPool scalar slot (16 B — the
SECOND pool, which the bucketed counters cannot see; scalar/0-d results ride
it legitimately). Fresh bytes with zero takes = the full-bypass verdict. It
needs no drain-confirm: asynchronous finalizer drains add RETURNS, which
turn the balance negative and route down the existing confirm path —
takes==0 with escaped==0 is arithmetically drain-free. Teeth:
Harness_Detects_FullPoolBypass uses np.frombuffer, a bypass BY DESIGN
(zero-copy wrap), asserting takes=0/returns=0/fresh=8192.

allocation exists), fromfile and loadtxt (results constructed from parsed

fix(scope): engine disposes the NEP50 scalar-cast temp and the copy('F') C-contig original

The two undisposed-intermediate mechanisms that live on the library's HOTTEST paths
(ExecuteBinaryOp / ExecuteComparisonOp — every +,-,*,/,%,<,<=,… on arrays). These are fixed
with a targeted local Dispose rather than an [NDScoped] method scope on purpose: a method scope
would impose Open/Track/Dispose on ALL binary/comparison ops merely to reclaim a temp that only
a narrow sub-path mints, so it would tax the exact hot path this whole leak-fixing effort exists
to protect. The targeted dispose costs nothing on the common (same-dtype / C-contig) path.

Mechanism 1 — NEP50 scalar-cast temp (BinaryOp). When `array op scalar` needs a dtype cast,
`Cast(rhs, resultType, copy:true)` mints a fresh 0-d/size-1 array and REASSIGNS the operand
parameter to it, so the temp is unreachable on return. Captured as `scalarCastTemp` at the cast
and disposed at all five exits (trivial bypass, NDIter route, size==0, looser-F, final). Result
buffers are always fresh kernel output, never an alias of this scalar temp, so disposing at
return is safe. Clears the escaped=1 on add/subtract/multiply/divide/floor_divide/mod/power/
bitwise_and/or/xor/maximum/minimum/fmax/fmin (and the corpus clip cell). Pin:
UndisposedIntermediateTests.BinaryScalarCastTemp_IsDisposed.

Mechanism 3 — copy('F') C-contig original (BinaryOp AND CompareOp). When the NumPy layout rule
wants F-contig output, the kernel has already written a C-contig `result`; `return
result.copy('F')` minted the F copy and DROPPED the C-contig original. Now `var f =
result.copy('F'); result.Dispose(); return f;` at all four sites (ExecuteBinaryOp,
TryExecuteBinaryOpViaNDIter, ExecuteComparisonOp, TryExecuteComparisonOpViaNDIter). Clears the
subtract F-contig cell and one of the two drops on the less/less_equal/greater_equal/not_equal
comparison cells (2/call → 1/call; a second, layout-specific drop on a single dtype-pair per op
remains and stays documented in KnownEscapes).

fix(scope): the third wave — raw-scratch + field-egress leaks NDScope could not reach (overlap clone / fill coerce / poly1d ctor)

Clears five of the twelve residual undisposed-intermediate families the oracle
