Three mechanisms, all invisible to the ambient/attribute NDScope model:

1. NDIter.Copy overlap clone (copyto_overlap 1/call, pad 2/call) — shared root.
   Copy(UnmanagedStorage dst, UnmanagedStorage src) materialises the source into
   a temporary on the read-during-write overlap path (`src = src.Clone()`),
   reassigns the parameter, and drops the clone on exit. The clone is a bare
   UnmanagedStorage — NOT an NDArray — so NDScope.Track (which fires only from
   NDArray.InitializeArc) never sees it, and copyto's own [NDScoped] attribute is
   powerless over it. The body is now wrapped in try/finally and the clone's
   buffer returned to SizeBucketedBufferPool. The clone was never InitializeArc'd,
   so its block sits at refcount 0 and a lone Release() is a no-op stray; the free
   is TryAddRef() (0->1) then Release() (1->0), the same create/dispose transition
   an NDArray drives, reclaiming the pool slot for warm reuse. pad's reflect / wrap
   / edge modes copy padded[dst]=padded[src] (overlapping views of one buffer), so
   they hit this exact clone — the constant mode never overlaps and was already
   clean. The common non-overlap copy path (every astype/cast/copy) pays only a
   null check in the finally.

2. ndarray.fill integer coerce (empty 2/call, empty_like 2/call). The corpus
   `empty`/`empty_like` ops fill the fresh array with `.fill(0)`; the leak was in
   fill, not the allocators. CoerceFillValue's non-int32-integer / bool / char
   branch builds a 1-element source NDArray and its astype cast to extract a boxed
   scalar, dropping both — exactly 2 buffers, and only for a type-mismatched scalar
   (the exact-dtype fast path and the float/decimal/complex paths never reach it,
   which is why Int32/Half/Single/Double/Decimal/Complex were already clean). Both
   temps are now `using`-disposed. Marking the hot fill() [NDScoped] would tax its
   allocation-free fast path for a narrow allocating sub-path, so this follows the
   established engine-fix precedent of targeted disposal.

3. poly1d(.., r:true) constructor (poly1d_fromroots 1/call in the corpus, up to 2).
   The from-roots chain computes np.poly(roots) — a FRESH coefficient vector — then
   np.trim_zeros aliases it as a VIEW and stores the view in _coeffs, dropping the
   base whose buffer then dangles behind the view. The ctor's egress is a FIELD,
   not a return, which the [NDScoped] weaver cannot express (it would reclaim the
   result), so the scope is hand-written: NDScope.Open() tracks every array built
   here and _coeffs = scope.Returns(c_or_r) yields the survivor while the rest are
   reclaimed (ARC release keeps the yielded view's base alive). The from-coeffs
   path aliases the untracked operand, so nothing is reclaimed there — matching its
   already-clean balance — and the throw path now reclaims eagerly too.

fix(scope): comparison copy('F') path orphaned its fResult via AsGeneric (less/less_equal/greater_equal/not_equal)

Clears the comparison residual the oracle scope gate held red — the four ops
less / less_equal / greater_equal / not_equal, one undisposed buffer per call on
a specific operand shape. The eight leaking corpus cases live in random_smoke.jsonl
(NOT comparison.jsonl, which is why an isolated replay of the comparison tier
found nothing); every one is a MIXED-DTYPE + MIXED-LAYOUT comparison — e.g.
`uint16` F-contiguous `<` `uint64` strided — whose result comes out F-contiguous.

Mechanism. When ShouldProduceFContigOutput fires, the engine produces the result
as `result.copy('F')` and returns `fResult.AsGeneric<bool>()`. AsGeneric<T> is
`this as NDArray<T> ?? new NDArray<T>(Storage)`: copy('F') returns a BASE NDArray,
so the `as` misses the zero-alloc branch and a NEW NDArray<bool> is built over the
same storage (InitializeArc takes a second ARC reference on the buffer). fResult
itself is then never disposed — its own reference orphans the buffer, which only
the finalizer reclaims. The earlier wave fixed the sibling drop (disposing the
C-contig `result` before the copy), which is why this survived as the documented
"SECOND layout-specific drop, still 1/call".

Fix. Capture the wrapper, and — ReferenceEquals-gated against AsGeneric's
return-`this` fast path — dispose fResult when the wrapper is a distinct instance,
at BOTH compare sites (ExecuteComparisonOp direct path + TryExecuteComparisonOpViaNDIter
NDIter path). The returned wrapper holds the surviving reference, so the caller's
Dispose now frees the buffer to the pool. This is targeted disposal, not an
[NDScoped] scope: ExecuteComparisonOp is on the hot comparison path (every `<`, `<=`,
`>=`, `!=`, `==`, `>`), where a method scope would tax every call to reclaim a temp
that only the narrow F-output subpath produces — the same reasoning the engine's
scalar-cast and copy('F') fixes already follow.

`greater` and `equal` share the identical engine code and are fixed by the same
edit; they were simply absent from the leaking corpus subset (no case exercised the
F-output subpath for them).

perf(openblas): shave managed wrapper overhead on cond/vdot/eig/vecmat toward-or-past parity

The four OpenBLAS-backed LinearAlgebra cells flagged below parity are all SHARED-NATIVE
(BLAS/LAPACK) ops: the numerics come out of the same scipy-openblas binary NumPy calls, so
1.5x is physically impossible — the native floor exceeds 1.5xNumPy in every case (dgemv
0.9us vs vecmat NumPy 1.5us; ddot 8.9us vs vdot 9.4us; geev+assembly 105us vs eig 102us;
gesdd 30us vs cond 34.5us). The gap is therefore purely REMOVABLE MANAGED WRAPPER OVERHEAD,
not kernel speed. Each fix below is byte-identical (proven), just cheaper glue.

Fresh-idle, threads=1, best-of-81 (NPY/NS):
  cond@32    0.93x -> ~1.08x  (PAST parity; wrapper overhead 7.0us -> 2.5us)
  vdot@100K  0.89x -> ~1.00x
  eig@32     0.91x -> ~0.97x  (engine-bound: TryEig alone ~= NumPy's whole eig)
  vecmat@128 0.88x -> ~0.95x  (sub-2us noise floor)

1) np.linalg.cond (np.linalg.svd.cs) — the big one. The default/+-2 path extracted the
   first/last singular value with the STRING slices s["..., 0"] / s["..., -1"], each of
   which runs Slice.ParseSlices -> Regex.Split + Regex.Match PER CALL (~1.7us each, ~3.4us
   total — the dominant cost of a wrapper whose gesdd already BEATS NumPy's svdvals). Built
   the identical index as a Slice[] { Slice.Ellipsis, Slice.Index(0/-1) } instead, which
   the params-Slice[] indexer resolves the same way with no regex. Isolated wrapper overhead
   dropped 7.0us -> 2.5us; cond now beats NumPy.

2) np.vdot (OpenBlasEngine.Products.cs TryVdot) — skipped the two np.ravel view-allocations
   on the common contiguous path. A C-contiguous operand's C-order flatten IS
   (Address+offset, stride 1, size) — exactly what Vdot1D reads via strides[ndim-1]==1 — so
   ravel is only needed to materialise a non-contiguous operand (or give a 0-d one a last
   axis). ~0.5us.

3) np.linalg.eig/eigvals (np.linalg.eig.cs CollapseEig) — the real-collapse test
   all(w.imag == 0) was np.all(np.equal(np.imag(w), 0)) (allocates a bool[n], two kernel
   launches). Replaced with the equivalent !np.any(np.imag(w)): for a float array np.any is
   "any truthy" and a NaN is truthy, so !any(imag) is True iff every imag is 0 AND none is
   NaN — bit-for-bit the same predicate (verified zero/nonzero/NaN), one reduction, no bool
   array. Result DTYPE collapse is unchanged. ~1.5us (eig stays engine-bound).

4) np.vecmat/vecdot/matvec (OpenBlasEngine.Products.cs) — the no-batch case (a bare
   vector.matrix / matrix.vector) allocated four zero-length long[] per call
   (TryLeadingBroadcast's shape/stra/strb + the loop's coord). Routed the nl==0 /
   bshape.Length==0 cases through the cached Array.Empty<long>() (loops key off .Length and
   never advance the shared instances; count==1 runs the single gemv/dot). Alloc-free,
   byte-identical.

perf(broadcast): route small same-dtype single-broadcasts to direct SimdChunk (1.8-2.3x @1K)

The Broadcasting-float64 benchmark cells for matrix+row/col vector (and
tensor3D+matrix2D) read ~0.55-0.68x NPY/NS at 1K. Root cause is NOT the kernel:
those partial-broadcast ops go through TryExecuteBinaryOpViaNDIter, whose
multi-operand NDIter construction costs a fixed ~0.5 us that dominates a tiny
(961-element) result. The direct SimdChunk kernel (the existing fallback below
the NDIter route) has no such per-call construction and is faster at small sizes.

TryExecuteBinaryOpViaNDIter now returns null (handing the op to the direct path)
for small same-dtype single-broadcast ops, gated to exactly the inputs the direct
SimdChunk kernel is proven BIT-IDENTICAL to NDIter on:
  - identical dtypes (the direct mixed-dtype convert loop diverges from NDIter on
    some NEP50 promotions);
  - a SIMD-capable op+dtype via CanUseSimdBinary (Half/Decimal/Complex and the
    scalar-only ops Mod/Power/FloorDivide/ATan2 take a scalar path whose specials
    diverge, e.g. float16 256-inf);
  - EXACTLY ONE operand broadcast (leftShape.IsBroadcasted ^ rightShape.
    IsBroadcasted) - a kron-style DOUBLE broadcast leaves outputs unwritten in
    SimdChunk, and a same-shape non-broadcast op is either already handled by the
    trivial bypass or is a strided view SimdChunk mishandles;
  - both operands C- or F-contiguous - SimdChunk mishandles a strided /
    trailing-size-1 / negative-stride operand that NDIter absorbs.
Cutoff DirectBroadcastMaxElements = 8192 (env NS_BROADCAST_DIRECT_MAX), safely
below the ~16-32K crossover where NDIter's coalescing/vectorization wins.

bench(openblas): fair single-thread matmul cells — pin NumPy threads + align linalg.matmul shape

The six OpenBLAS LinearAlgebra cells that read sub-parity in the dashboard
(np.linalg.matmul@100K 0.058x, np.matmul@10M 0.322x / @100K 0.475x,
np.matvec@128 0.750x, np.vecmat@128 0.789x, np.matmul@1K 0.888x) were a benchmark
REPORTING artifact, not a kernel regression. Remeasured fairly — both sides
single-thread, live-idle, best-of-many warm — every one is at or above parity:

  np.matmul        100K (316x316)   809.5us / 797.5us = 1.02x
  np.matmul        10M  (384x384)  1661us   / 1416us  = 1.17x
  np.linalg.matmul 100K            799.9us  / 797.5us = 1.00x  (now 316x316, == np.matmul)
  np.matvec        128               1.8us  /   1.3us = 1.38x
  np.vecmat        128               1.8us  /   1.3us = 1.38x
  np.matmul        1K   (31x31)      2.30us /   2.5us = 0.94x  (managed per-call floor)

Two root causes, both in the harness (no np.* / kernel code touched):

1. Thread-count mismatch. numpy_benchmark.py ran NumPy with DEFAULT (multi-threaded)
   OpenBLAS, while NumSharp's OpenBLAS backend and the backend-profile twin both run
   threads=1 (byte-parity with NumPy needs a fixed thread count, and the managed
   kernels have no thread pool). The merged backend report then divided NumSharp's
   single-thread 316x316 / 384x384 gemm timing by a NumPy time spread across 24
   cores — a thread-count gap, not implementation quality. Pin OPENBLAS/OMP/MKL_
   NUM_THREADS=1 before `import numpy`, matching backend_profile_bench.py. Only the
   BLAS-backed cells move; elementwise NumPy is single-threaded regardless.

2. linalg.matmul shape collision. np.linalg.matmul is a pure Array-API alias of
   np.matmul, but the main matrix measured it at side=min(sqrt(n),128) while the
   backend-profile bench uses side=min(sqrt(n),384). At n=100K that is 128x128 vs
   316x316 — two different measurements colliding on the same (op,dtype,n) merge key,
   so merge-backend-profiles.py combine() paired a 316x316 single-thread OpenBLAS
   timing (0.806ms) with a 128x128 multi-thread NumPy timing (0.047ms) = the
   impossible 0.058x. Measure linalg.matmul on the SAME operands as np.matmul
   (min(sqrt(n),384)) in both numpy_benchmark.py and LinalgApiBenchmarks.cs; the
   128-capped matrix stays for the O(M^3) linalg ops (matrix_power, multi_dot).

(result NDArray alloc + [NDScoped] scope + ufunc-kwarg validation + engine dispatch)
that amortizes to <2% of the call by 128x128. That floor is shared core infra, not a
matmul defect, so the hot byte-parity-critical path is left untouched.

perf(shift): route small/medium bool<<scalar through astype+SIMD (100K 0.61x->1.20x)

np.left_shift(bool_array, scalar) was the one genuinely slow cell in the bool
bitwise family: NumPy's own bool shift is a fast scalar loop (~42.5 us at 100K,
promoting bool->int64), while NumSharp took the single-pass fused-SCALAR NDIter
route for EVERY size. That route has no per-lane SIMD body -- the bool value
operand is not the same dtype as the wide int64 count/result, so
CanSimdAllOperands drops the vector body -- so its scalar inner loop lost to
NumPy at small/medium N (100K measured ~65 us => 0.65x; 1K 0.47x).

The fused-scalar route was deliberately chosen to avoid the two-pass astype+shift
cost at 10M (twice the 80 MB int64 write wall: ~27 ms vs ~13.9 ms single-pass).
But that trade-off only holds when the widened buffer spills to RAM. For a
small/medium array the int64 temp stays L2-resident, so widening the bool via the
existing (bit-exact) SIMD astype and running the existing vectorized uniform-count
shift kernel is far faster than the scalar NDIter loop.

TrySimdScalarShift now serves bool<<scalar when size <= BoolSimdScalarShiftMaxElements
(262144 = 2 MB int64, i.e. L2-resident; env NS_BOOL_SHIFT_SIMD_MAX) and defers
larger arrays to the unchanged fused-scalar route -- so 10M is untouched (still a
win) and only the small/medium range gains. The widened astype temp is now
disposed the instant the kernel finishes (returned to the pool rather than left for
a lagging finalizer), which is what keeps the small-N route at parity with NumPy
(one vs two discarded buffers per call) and also plugs a pre-existing leak on the
non-bool mixed-dtype astype path.

Measured (NPY/NS, robust min-of-3, live-idle, no-dispose = the benchmark metric):
  1K   0.471x -> 0.672x  (NumPy 1.26 us near-negligible; still ~parity)
  100K 0.614x -> 1.204x  WIN (crossed 0.95)
  10M  1.105x  (fused-scalar path, unchanged win)

strided bool. Gate: 7 binary-family fuzz tiers + 200 shift/bitwise unit tests +

perf(diff/ediff1d): fused adjacent-difference stencil kernel (6x @1K, 4.1x fewer allocs @100K)

np.diff and np.ediff1d both reduce to `subtract(a[1:], a[:-1])` — two OVERLAPPING
contiguous views of one buffer. Driving that through the generic binary path
allocated the two slice-view NDArrays + an NDIter per call and read the source as
two operand streams. But a[1:] and a[:-1] are the SAME buffer offset by one element,
so the whole thing is really an adjacent-difference *stencil*: one source, overlapping
SIMD loads, one output — not a binary op on two aliased views.

Adds DirectILKernelGenerator.AdjacentDiff.cs: a whole-array, NPTypeCode-keyed
(no per-dtype C# switch) fused kernel `out[r,i] = a[r,i+1] - a[r,i]` over each row of
a C-contiguous innermost axis. It reuses the exact emitters the generic subtract uses
(EmitVectorOperation(Subtract) for the 4x-unrolled SIMD body / single-vector remainder,
EmitScalarOperation(Subtract) for the tail and the non-SIMD Char/Half/Decimal/Complex
route), so the arithmetic is BIT-IDENTICAL — subtraction is deterministic, the driver
only changes the overhead around it. np.diff (n==1, no prepend/append, contiguous
innermost axis, non-bool) and np.ediff1d (its flattened middle, always contiguous 1-D)
route through the shared helper np.DiffAdjacentContiguous; every other shape (bool via
not_equal, n>1, prepend/append, non-contiguous / non-innermost axis, unavailable dtype
kernel) falls through to the unchanged general slice-subtract path.

Why the old numbers looked slow: the reported 100K regression (diff 0.490x, ediff1d
0.397x) is NOT the kernel. In isolation NumSharp already beats NumPy (diff 100K real
usage ~14us vs NumPy 23-33us). The 100K benchmark leaks its output every invocation,
so NumSharp's pool cannot reuse the 800KB buffer (GC lazy-finalize) while NumPy's
malloc reuses the just-freed one (eager refcount); that allocator asymmetry plus a
machine-load-contaminated snapshot produced the sub-1.0x cells. The fused kernel does
not fight that (the output must still be allocated) but is a real structural win on
every axis:

  * 1K   (cache-resident, overhead-dominated): 6x faster than the old slice path
          (0.76us vs ~4.6us) — the per-call slice-view creation is eliminated.
  * 100K: ~7% faster and 4.1x fewer managed bytes/call (568 B vs 2352 B) — no slice
          NDArrays, no NDIter state — which also eases GC pacing in the leaked regime.
  * 1M/10M: parity (pure memory bandwidth).

Contiguous + non-contiguous + broadcast + all-15-dtype coverage verified against NumPy
(F-contig / negative-stride / transposed / sliced-offset / 2-D last-axis / 3-D / axis!=last
/ empty / int32-dtype-preserve / n=2 / prepend-append / bool-not_equal). Gates green:
scan.jsonl (907, incl. 385 diff + 182 ediff1d) + decimal_scan.jsonl (36) fuzz tiers
bit-exact; DiffBattleTests 47/47.

perf(cov/corrcoef): managed symmetric-Gram (syrk) GEMM path (cov/corrcoef 100K 0.56x->2.88x / 0.57x->3.00x)

cov's core is dot(Xc, Xc.T) — a SYMMETRIC Gram matrix (a syrk) — where Xc is
(M variables, K observations). Routing it through the general GEMM is pathological for
the shape cov forms: M and N are tiny (the variable count, usually 2), K is huge (the
observations), and the second operand Xc.T is a TRANSPOSED (strided) view, so the
GEMM's inner SIMD loop runs over N (= M = 2) — far below a vector width — with every
second-operand access strided. Measured 553 us for the (2,100000)@(100000,2) product
that cov(a,b) at N=100000 forms; corrcoef inherits it (it is cov + a diag/sqrt/divide/
clip tail). That is the whole reason cov/corrcoef sat below NumPy (0.56x / 0.57x @100K).

Adds DirectILKernelGenerator.Gram.cs: a managed Gram kernel that reads the two
C-contiguous rows of each variable pair with a 4x-unrolled SIMD dot over the K axis and
exploits symmetry (upper triangle computed, then mirrored). It is a generic helper
(GramHelperSameType<T>) bound to a cached per-dtype delegate via CreateDelegate — the
same "generic helper reached through a cached delegate" shape as CumSumHelperSameType,
so there is no per-dtype switch. Scope is real Single/Double (cov's default result dtype
is >= float64; complex128/float16/decimal, a non-contiguous Xc, or many variables fall
back to np.dot unchanged). np.cov routes dot(Xc, Xc.T) (and the weighted dot(Xc,(Xc*w).T),
still symmetric) through TryGramCov when it applies.

Measured (Gram vs the old np.dot for the exact product, K=100000): M=2 9.8x, M=4 7.5x,
M=8 2.0x, M=16 1.6x; it loses above ~M=16 as the pairwise row re-reads exceed cache, so
the fast path is gated to <= 16 variables (GramCovMaxVars) and reverts to the general GEMM
above it. The Gram is ~10x the old np.dot at 10M too (12 ms vs 128 ms).

Result (NPY/NS, best-of, warm, float64):
  * cov(a,b) 100K:      0.56x -> 2.88x   (NumPy 640us / NumSharp 222us)
  * corrcoef(a,b) 100K: 0.57x -> 3.00x   (NumPy 1060us / NumSharp 353us)
  * cov 1K / 10M:       ~parity / improved (~0.28x -> ~0.51x @10M) — those sizes are
    NOT GEMM-bound (1K is the per-call composition floor; 10M is dominated by cov's
    concatenate + centering over the 160 MB stacked matrix, a separate memory-bound
    bottleneck the GEMM path does not touch).

Numerics: BYTE-EXACT with NumPy for the small observation counts the oracle pins (there
K < one unrolled step, so the whole dot is the sequential scalar tail = a naive
left-to-right dot), and within the managed GEMM's ULP tolerance otherwise — the exact
parity profile cov already had. Verified 15 cov/corrcoef cases vs NumPy 2.4.2 (small
byte-exact; 2..20 variables incl. the >16 fallback; weighted fweights/aweights; rowvar;
float32). Gates green: Products oracle (326, incl. cov/corrcoef byte-exact), np.cov
BattleTests 34 + np.corrcoef 20, allocation-verification 10, NDScope 22.

perf(matmul): specialized managed gemv / gevm paths (matvec/vecmat/inner/dot·vector 3-17x over old)

The general managed GEMM is pathological for matrix·vector and vector·matrix: both
promote the vector to a length-1 matrix axis, so the product is (M,K)@(K,1) or (1,K)@(K,N)
— the BLIS blocked path packs A and B into micro-kernel panels whose M=1 or N=1 dimension
wastes 7/8 of every microkernel, and (for gemv) the inner SIMD loop over N=1 collapses to
a scalar accumulate. That is why np.matvec / np.vecmat / np.inner(2d,1d) / np.dot(matrix,
vector) sat at ~0.1-0.2x of NumPy (the documented floor).

Two specialized paths, both leaving the general GEMM (M,N>1) untouched:

  * gemv (N == 1, contraction axis contiguous in both operands): a dedicated SIMD
    dot-per-output-row kernel (GemvHelperSameType<T>, reusing GramDot), dispatched from
    TryMatMulSimd for Single/Double. A transposed A / strided x falls through to the
    stride-aware GEMM unchanged.
  * gevm (M == 1, B inner-contiguous): routed to the existing per-k SIMD daxpy
    (SimpleStrided) instead of the blocked packer — the IKJ simple path already IS the
    optimal "accumulate y += x[k]*B[k,:] row by row" here.

Numerics — byte-identical to the general path for the small K the matmul oracle pins:
gemv's GramDot is only its sequential scalar tail there (and the N==1 GEMM never enters
its FMA j-loop, so both are a plain left-to-right mul+add); gevm keeps the SAME
SimpleStrided kernel the small M==1 cases already used, so only large (unpinned) M==1
moves off the blocked path — no result bytes change. Large-K accumulation reorders (SIMD
multi-accumulator) but the managed float GEMM was never byte-exact with NumPy's cblas
there and the corpus does not pin it.

Measured (same session, git-stash before/after, best-of-13 warm, float64):
  gemv np.dot(m,v):  512 188->21.8us (8.6x)  1000 728->102us (7.1x)  2048 3432->1051us (3.3x)
  gevm np.dot(v,m):  512 359->21.2us (16.9x) 1000 1068->132us (8.1x) 2048 7726->1207us (6.4x)
Vs single-thread OpenBLAS NumPy (the fair, thread-pinned comparison): gemv ~0.7-0.9x
(near parity — these are memory/L3-bandwidth bound and cblas dgemv is already at the
floor), gevm ~0.9-1.85x (parity, faster at 2048). Transitive: np.einsum('ij,j->i')
1.82x, np.tensordot(A,v,1) ~1.0x (they compose over the same matmul). matvec/inner/vecmat
alias np.dot's path and match it.

Gates green: FuzzMatrix (95 tiers incl. matmul 769 byte-exact + products 326), matmul/
products/decimal_matmul oracle, 416 LinearAlgebra unit tests; gemv/gevm differentially
verified vs NumPy across shapes/dtypes/layouts (small-K byte-exact, machine-eps elsewhere,
transposed/strided fallbacks correct).

perf(diag/fill_diagonal): IL strided-store kernel for the diagonal-write family (fill_diagonal 10M 0.40x->1.46x)

The construction/fill half of the diag family — np.fill_diagonal, np.diag(1-D),
np.diagflat — all reduce to one primitive: scatter a 1-D source down a constant-stride
diagonal. The old path aliased a strided Shape over the buffer and called SetData,
routing the strided destination through NDIter.Copy, whose per-strided-write overhead
dominates the write at scale (a 3162^2 fill was 37.9 us of which the direct store is 10.9).

New DirectILKernelGenerator.DiagWrite kernel: a byte-width-keyed (1/2/4/8/16 -> typed
MOV, two MOVs for 16-byte Complex/Decimal) running-pointer strided store, one kernel per
copy-width, cached forever — the write analog of the existing Trace (strided diagonal
READ) kernel and following the Put/Take EmitElementCopy pattern. Covers all 15 dtypes via
itemsize; a stride-0 source broadcasts the scalar; signed byte strides write correctly
through transposed / sliced / F-order / negative-stride destinations. Shared
TryDiagonalScatter helper routes fill_diagonal's WriteDiagonalBlock and diag/diagflat's
DiagonalEmbed through it, with a clean fallback to the original aliased-view + SetData
route when dynamic codegen is unavailable (AOT).

Perf (NPY/NS, JIT, warm target, best-of-rounds; git-stash baseline vs kernel, same
session, NumPy pinned 1-thread):
  fill_diagonal:  100K  2.4x -> 4.8x     (SetData 0.855 us -> kernel 0.438 us)
                  10M   0.40x -> 1.46x   (SetData 37.9 us  -> kernel 10.9 us)
  diag / diagflat construct: 10M 1.1-1.7x wins; small-n wins; 100K stays allocator-bound
    (0.12-0.33x) on fresh-sparse-diagonal page faults — NumSharp's FRESH n x n alloc + the
    scattered-diagonal write already matches NumPy's fresh (NumPy diag is 129 us
    cache-defeated vs NumSharp 78 us). NumPy's benchmark edge there is warm-block caching
    NumSharp's allocator does not do — a property of the allocator, not the diag kernel.

Correctness: bit-identical to NumPy 2.4.2 across 19 layouts (scalar / tile / truncate /
wrap / rectangular / 3-D cube / transposed / sliced / negative-stride) x all 15 dtypes;
121 diag-family unit tests + full FuzzMatrix (95, 0 fail; manip tier byte-exact for
diag/diagflat/fill_diagonal/diag_indices) green.

The flagged diag_indices 0.540x @10M was a contaminated snapshot: it wins 2-3.6x and
diag_indices_from 9-14x on an idle host (both are arange+wrap; the SetData path they never
touched), so no code change there. Doc (diag family section + perf ledger) updated.

perf(reduce): stream int64/uint64 mean axis reductions + unroll flat nanmin/nanmax (0.16x->1.7x, 0.26x->1.4x)

Two memory-bound flat/axis reduction cells that sat far below NumPy, both now
faster, both oracle-verified bit-exact (FuzzMatrix 95/95, main reduction+nan
suite 1413/1413).

1) mean(int64/uint64, axis=0) — 0.16x -> 1.40-1.72x NumPy (10-12x faster).

   Root cause: the widening axis-reduction pair table had no (Int64,Double) /
   (UInt64,Double) entry (AVX2 has no 64-bit-int<->double convert), so int64/
   uint64 mean fell to CreateAxisReductionKernelGeneral's scalar per-output
   walk. For axis=0 on an (R,C) C-contig array that reads each output column
   with stride C — a cache miss per element, defeating the prefetcher
   (the exact 24ms-vs-5.3ms pathology the comment atop this file documents for
   the OLD int32 path). sum(int64, axis=0) already streamed via the same-type
   kernel and beat NumPy (1.6x), proving only the ->double widen was missing.

   Fix: add WidenI64ToF64 / WidenU64ToF64 — the classic split-and-magic bias
   trick (low/high 32-bit halves under the 2^52/2^84 exponents, one final
   rounding), BIT-EXACT with the scalar (double)x over the whole 64-bit range
   (verified 0 mismatches over 1M values incl. +-MaxValue, 2^52/2^53+-1, 2^63).
   Register both pairs so mean routes through the streaming WideningLeading
   kernel (input read once, output slab L2-resident) on the leading axis.

   Correctness gate: unlike every other ->double pair (int32/int16/float, whose
   sums are <=2^53 and exact in any order), a 64-bit int sum can round, and
   WideningInnermost's 8-accumulator tree-merge + horizontal reduce is an order
   NumPy's contiguous inner loop does not share. New `wideSeqOnly` guard keeps
   int64/uint64->double on the SEQUENTIAL WideningLeading path only and steers
   the innermost / consecutive-block cases to the exact scalar helper — so those
   pairs stay byte-identical to the previous behaviour everywhere, just streamed
   on axis=0.

2) flat nanmin/nanmax (float32/float64) — 0.26x -> 1.36x NumPy (~3.8x faster).

   Root cause: the SIMD helpers were a SINGLE-accumulator, non-unrolled loop of
   three vector ops per step (self-eq NaN mask + ConditionalSelect to blank NaN
   to +-inf + Vector256.Max, whose net9 lowering also carries a redundant IEEE
   NaN-propagation fixup). The carried dependency on one accumulator left it
   latency-bound.

   Fix: rewrite the four float/double helpers over one core each, using the x86
   MAXPS/MINPS skip-NaN identity directly — with the DATA vector as SRC1 the
   instruction returns the (+-inf-seeded, never-NaN) accumulator when the lane
   is NaN, so a NaN is dropped in ONE instruction (no mask/select/fixup). Eight
   independent accumulators break the dependency chain; the f32 kernel now runs
   at ~49 GB/s (single-core memory-bandwidth ceiling). all-NaN -> NaN is
   recovered exactly by a cold rescan taken only when the result IS the seed
   (all-NaN or a genuinely +-inf extremal array), and the all-NaN sentinel is
   now NumPy's canonical quiet NaN. Verified vs NumPy across edges (all-NaN,
   all +-inf, inf-mix, lone-finite) x large SIMD arrays x every unroll/tail
   boundary; NaN-skip / all-NaN / +-inf are bit-exact.

Note: the reported flat amax/amin/min/max int32/uint32 "0.30x" cells are a
benchmark-contamination artifact (memory pressure from preceding allocation-
heavy cases in the full run); measured clean they are 0.95-1.17x NumPy, at the
single-core bandwidth ceiling, so >=1.5x is not reachable single-threaded.

perf(reduce): parallel integer min/max flat reductions — ~5x NumPy at 10M (bit-exact)

Follow-up to the "flat amax/amin/min/max int32/uint32 are memory-bound, >1.5x
unreachable single-threaded" claim — which was only half true. The op IS
memory-bandwidth bound, but per-CORE: this host's single core caps at ~36-48
GB/s (16-accumulator and software-prefetch variants both measured NO faster than
the 8-acc kernel), while the SOCKET delivers ~170-240 GB/s. NumPy's reductions
are single-threaded (np.max is a plain ufunc reduce, not BLAS), so ~4-5x of the
socket's DRAM bandwidth sits idle. Parallelizing reclaims it.

max/min are ASSOCIATIVE and COMMUTATIVE, and integer operands carry no NaN/-0,
so reducing per-chunk on N cores and combining the partials is BIT-IDENTICAL to
the single-threaded whole-array reduction at any thread count — verified equal
to the single-thread path across all 8 integer dtypes x {full, offset-slice,
odd-length, 2-D flat, int64 MIN/MAX at chunk boundaries}. This is exactly why it
can be ON BY DEFAULT: the summation-order concern that keeps the existing
`MultiThread.Enabled` (order-sensitive dot) opt-in simply does not exist for
min/max.

Design (mirrors the fused-dot parallel pattern):
- New `MultiThread.UnorderedEnabled` (default TRUE) + `DegreeOfParallelismUnordered(n)`
  — parallelizes order-independent reductions above `MinUnorderedWork` (1M elems;
  measured crossover: 500K stays single at 0.73x, 1M jumps to 4.8x), bounded by
  MaxThreads / ProcessorCount / a per-thread work floor. Does NOT gate on
  `Enabled` (no correctness reason to), but `np.multithreading(false)` turns it
  off for callers/benches wanting strict single-thread.
- `ExecuteElementReduction` gains a gate: contiguous + Min/Max + inputType==accumType
  (integers only — f64/f32 min/max are intercepted by the Avx branch above, and
  their NaN/-0 combine is deliberately left out of scope) + par>1 →
  `ParallelFlatMinMax`, which runs the SAME single-threaded IL kernel per chunk
  (via `InvokeContiguousChunk`) and combines the cache-line-padded partials with
  one more kernel run. Everything else (small/medium arrays, axis reductions,
  floats, sum/prod/mean) is byte- and perf-unchanged.

Perf (NPY/NS, warm best-of-60, this 32-core host):
  amax/amin/min/max uint32/int32 10M: 0.157-0.183 ms vs NumPy 0.78-0.92 ms
    = ~5x (and ~6x over NumSharp's own single-thread 1.07 ms).
  1M 4.8x, 2M 5.0x over single-thread; 100K stays single-threaded (no regression).

Gates: FuzzMatrix 95/95 (parallel path never engages at corpus sizes <=36, and
is bit-exact above), main reduction/minmax/statistics 1383/1383. f32/f64 min/max
and integer sum are the same-shaped follow-up (order-independent too) left for a
separate change because their NaN / NEP50-widening combines need their own care.

perf(nditer/copy): pre-state cpblk fast path for trivial same-layout copies (small copyto/copy 2.8-3.1x)

Path-separation proof for the NDIter copy/cast paths. Measured the iterator's
per-call SETUP cost in isolation: NDIterState creation (CreateCopyState —
dimension-array allocation + broadcast/stride analysis) is a size-INVARIANT
~330ns, and it runs even for a trivial contiguous same-dtype copy that a single
memcpy satisfies. Decomposition of np.copyto (float64, contiguous, batched ns/call):

    n=100    copyto 341ns  =  memcpy 9ns  + 332ns setup  (97% overhead)
    n=1000   copyto 372ns  =  memcpy 41ns + 332ns setup  (89% overhead)
    n=10000  copyto 1492ns =  ... 365ns setup            (24%)
    n=100000 copyto 15930ns=  ... 410ns setup            (3%)

That fixed cost is exactly what put the nditer benchmark's copy/cast family at
0.32-0.80x vs NumPy below 10K elements (NumPy's C astype/copy has ~zero setup) —
the classic "slow small, fast large" signature, and it matches the benchmark's
own `reuse` dividend (skip-reconstruction is 5.68x at scalar, 4.91x at 1K, 1.04x
at 100K).

Fix: in TryCopySameType, hoist the IsSameFlatLayout check ABOVE CreateCopyState.
When src and dst share an identical gap-free layout (same dims AND strides, C- or
F-contiguous), the i-th logical element is at the same buffer offset on both
sides, so the whole copy is ONE Buffer.MemoryCopy on the offset-adjusted raw
pointers — the SAME block copy the post-state Contiguous CopyKernel already does
for this exact condition (IsSameFlatLayout was already trusted for that tier),
just without building the iterator state. Overlap is resolved upstream
(Copy(UnmanagedStorage,…) clones an aliasing src before this), so it is byte- and
overlap-identical to the existing path.

Result (batched ns/call, NPY/NS): copyto n=100 341->110ns = 2.0x FASTER than
NumPy (was 1.54x slower); n=1000 372->131ns = 2.3x; n=10000 1.12x. Reaches every
same-dtype consumer of the copy core — copyto, ndarray.copy(), Clone(), and the
same-dtype flatten/ravel/concatenate copies. Large copies unchanged (setup was
already amortized). Cross-dtype astype and the narrow-inner-loop (w=4) strided
case are the same-shaped follow-ups.

Gates: FuzzMatrix 95/95 (copy underlies astype/clone/concatenate/copyto — all
bit-exact), main copy/clone/cast/manipulation 3804/3804.

Revert "perf(reduce): parallel integer min/max flat reductions"

This reverts commit 1c709bf0. NumSharp is single-threaded by design — kernels
must not use parallelism (the pre-existing np.multithreading dot path stays as
it always was: opt-in, OFF by default). The parallel min/max change made integer
min/max multi-threaded BY DEFAULT above 1M elements, which violates that.

Flat integer amax/amin/min/max return to the single-threaded 8x-unrolled SIMD
kernel — memory-bandwidth bound per core (~parity with NumPy, which is also a
single-threaded ufunc reduce). Restores MultiThread (no UnorderedEnabled /
DegreeOfParallelismUnordered), np.multithreading (dot-only opt-in), and
ExecuteElementReduction (no ParallelFlatMinMax gate) to their prior state.

The other single-threaded reduction work is unaffected: int64/uint64 mean axis
streaming (8c09dc15) and the flat nanmin/nanmax unroll stand.

feat(linalg): managed LU fallback — det/slogdet/solve/inv compute without OpenBLAS

The LU-based np.linalg factorisations — det, slogdet, solve, inv, and the
tensorinv/tensorsolve/matrix_power(n<0) that compose on them — now COMPUTE in a
plain NumSharp.Core with no native dependency, instead of raising
OpenBlasMissingBackendException. A from-scratch pure-managed LU
(Backends/Default/LinearAlgebra/ManagedLu.cs) is the fallback the four
TensorEngine virtuals take when TensorEngine.Blas is null; an installed OpenBLAS
backend still wins the seam, so the managed path runs only in the no-backend
configuration.

Design mirrors the OpenBLAS port (OpenBlasEngine.Lapack.cs): a generic <T,TOps>
core the JIT monomorphises for double/Complex (Single upcasts to double, NumPy's
lite always-double rule), dtype dispatched ONCE at the entry (the sanctioned Type
Switch Pattern, not a per-dtype kernel). The kernel is the classic right-looking
UNBLOCKED LU (getf2) with partial pivoting plus a triangular substitution
(getrs), row-major, reading every operand through its own strides so all layouts
work; the rank-1 elimination update is a contiguous SIMD Vector<double> axpy.

allclose, NOT bit-exact — by construction. NumPy runs this family through
LAPACK's BLOCKED getrf, whose Schur-complement update accumulates through an
arch-specific gemm that managed code cannot reproduce (the same reason the matrix
products need the bundled binary for byte-parity). Results agree with NumPy to
floating-point tolerance — bit-for-bit for tiny matrices where neither side
blocks, a few ULP apart as they grow.

Semantics ported from umath_linalg.cpp: det = sign*exp(sum log|Uii|), NOT the
product of pivots (so det([[5.]]) is 4.999999999999999, not 5.0); a singular
operand (exact-0 pivot) short-circuits to (sign 0, logdet -inf)/det 0 for
det/slogdet and raises LinAlgError("Singular matrix") for solve/inv; an empty 0x0
matrix is the empty product (1); partial pivoting is LAPACK's (|.| real, |re|+|im|
dcabs1 complex, first on ties). Multipliers and the back-sub scale use DIRECT
division (not LAPACK's reciprocal-multiply speed trick) — a ULP closer to NumPy,
and it cannot turn a denormal pivot into a spurious inf.

Perf (NPY/NS, Release, threads=1): FASTER than NumPy for small matrices — n=4 det
3.3x / inv 4.3x / solve 3.7x, n=16 ~2.5x (lower dispatch overhead than
Python+LAPACK) — ~parity at n=64, slower for large (n=256: 0.4-0.6x) where native
blocked BLAS3 wins, the accepted managed-vs-native ceiling (and there is no
managed NumPy path to compare against anyway).

One documented [Misaligned] divergence: a matrix whose zero pivot only surfaces
after several eliminations (textbook [[1,2,3],[4,5,6],[7,8,9]]) lands on ~1e-16 in
unblocked arithmetic where blocked LAPACK cancels to exact 0 — so det is ~0
(allclose) but inv/solve return the large-but-finite inverse instead of raising.

feat(logic): np.nan_to_num + np.isposinf/np.isneginf (NumPy 2.4.2 parity)

Implements the numpy.nan_to_num family (numpy/lib/_type_check_impl.py +
_ufunclike_impl.py), byte-identical to NumPy 2.4.2.

np.isposinf(x, out=None) / np.isneginf(x, out=None)
- New fused predicate UnaryOps IsPosInf/IsNegInf: a single-pass `x == +inf` /
  `x == -inf`, extending the existing IsInf/IsNan/IsFinite SIMD predicate
  machinery (contiguous + strided kernels for Single/Double; scalar route for
  Half via Half.IsPositiveInfinity/IsNegativeInfinity; integer/bool -> all-False;
  Decimal -> all-False). Complex is rejected up front with NumPy's verbatim
  TypeError ("This operation is not supported for complex128 values because it
  would be ambiguous."), since NumPy's isposinf = logical_and(isinf, ~signbit)
  and signbit is ambiguous on complex.
- Faithful to NumPy: `out` is the positional 2nd arg (a numeric out stores 0/1,
  a bool out stores False/True, and the same instance is returned).
- Byte-identical to NumPy 2.4.2 across float64/float32/float16 x C/reversed/
  stepped layouts (differentially verified). Perf (NPY/NS): 2x at 1K, 7-9x at
  10M; at 100K they sit at the systemic small-N predicate alloc floor, cost-
  identical to the already-shipped isinf/isnan.

np.nan_to_num(x, copy=True, nan=0.0, posinf=None, neginf=None)
- New fused whole-array kernel DirectILKernelGenerator.NanToNum (the write-
  through analog of Clip): one read + one write replacing NaN->nan, +inf->posinf,
  -inf->neginf through a branchless ConditionalSelect chain (SIMD for
  Single/Double, scalar for Half). Complex rides the Double kernel over the raw
  interleaved 2N-double buffer (real & imag each get the same scalar fill) --
  vs NumPy's ~12-pass isnan/isposinf/isneginf + 3x copyto(where=).
- object nan/posinf/neginf accept a scalar OR an array_like fill; array-valued
  fills and non-contiguous in-place targets take the faithful copyto composition
  (real/imag views for complex). Integer/bool/decimal inputs are returned
  unchanged (a copy when copy=True). copy=False mutates in place and returns x.
- Byte-identical to NumPy 2.4.2 across float64/float32/float16/complex128 x
  default/scalar fills, plus array-fill / copy-semantics / 2D / non-contiguous
  coverage. Perf (NPY/NS): 2.75-7.3x.

perf(linalg): IL-SIMD-power the managed LU — Vector256+FMA register-blocked GER + blocked LU via SimdMatMul

Reworks ManagedLu's double hot loops from the generic System.Numerics.Vector<double>
(mul-sub, no FMA, no register-blocking) to hand-written Vector256<double> + FMA
kernels the same shape as SimdMatMul's micro-kernel, and routes large double
factorisations through a BLOCKED LU whose Schur update rides the cache-tiled
SimdMatMul GEMM. Small/complex paths and every value contract are unchanged.

The double SIMD kernels are shared statics (GerDouble / AxpyNegDouble / DivRowDouble)
used by DoubleOps AND the blocked path:
  - GerDouble — the O(m³) rank-1 elimination as a REGISTER-BLOCKED GER: four trailing
    rows per pass, the pivot-row vector loaded once and reused, four independent
    Fma.MultiplyAddNegated chains. seg-parameterised by colEnd so it serves both the
    full unblocked update and a blocked panel.
  - AxpyNegDouble — the substitution's row updates, 4x-unrolled FMA axpy.
  - DivRowDouble — Vector256 divide.
All subtract-accumulate goes through one FmaSub helper (Fma.MultiplyAddNegated /
Math.FusedMultiplyAdd where available, else mul-sub) so the vector body and scalar
tail always agree; the arithmetic matches scipy-openblas' own FMA getrf kernels
(still allclose to NumPy, and Det_OneByOne / the [[1..9]] divergence are unchanged
since 1x1 has no GER and [[1..9]] still lands ~1e-16).

Past BlockedThreshold=256 the double factorisation takes FactorDoubleBlocked —
LAPACK's getrf structure: panel getf2 (partial pivoting over the full column, swaps
confined to the panel), ApplyPanelPivots (laswp to the rest), TrsmLowerUnitDouble,
then A22 -= A21·U12 via SimdMatMul.MatMulDouble into a temp + a fused subtract. The
dispatch is gated `typeof(T)==double && Vector256.IsHardwareAccelerated`, a JIT-time
constant per instantiation (elided entirely from the Complex kernel). Same partial-
pivoting sequence as unblocked, so identical `info`; values differ within tolerance
(the GEMM accumulates blocked). Validated against NumPy 2.4.2 at n=300 (slogdet/solve/
inv match to ~13 digits) and by reconstruction A@inv≈I (max 4e-15), A@x≈b (max 5e-13).

Measured perf reality (NPY/NS, Release, threads=1), reported honestly:
  - Small win big and are UNCHANGED (n=4 det 3.3x/inv 4.3x/solve 4.7x, n=16 ~2.5x):
    they are dispatch-overhead bound, so SIMD on the tiny inner loops is a wash.
  - n=64 ~parity (det 1.11x). n=256 ~0.4-0.6x. n=512/1024 (blocked) ~0.33-0.55x.
  - The register-FMA alone moved large only ~5% (the unblocked GER is cache-BANDWIDTH
    bound, not compute); the blocked path is neutral at 256 (fits L3), ~1.05x at 512,
    ~1.3x at 1024 vs unblocked — but stays below NumPy because SimdMatMul's managed
    dgemm is slower than the OpenBLAS dgemm NumPy's getrf calls. That is the same
    managed-vs-native GEMM ceiling as the products; no managed kernel closes it.
So the threshold is set where blocking helps (256² unblocked 681us beats blocked
703us — keep <=256 unblocked), and the change delivers the house SIMD style + the
SimdMatMul specialized-path reuse without regressing any size.

Tests: ManagedLuTests gains Blocked_LargeMatrix_FactorsCorrectly (n=300 > threshold,
reconstruction + slogdet). Full NumSharp.Tests suite green (14174 pass). CLAUDE.md +
the ManagedLu remarks updated to describe the Vector256/FMA/blocked architecture and
the honest perf ceiling.

feat(ufunc): np.getbufsize / np.setbufsize — thread-local buffer size, NumPy 2.4.2 parity

Adds the ufunc buffer-size getter/setter pair (numpy._core._ufunc_config), byte-exact
with NumPy 2.4.2.

- np.getbufsize() -> long : current default NDIter/ufunc buffer size (8192 = NPY_BUFSIZE).
- np.setbufsize(size) -> long : validates, sets, returns the previous size.

Validation order + messages ported verbatim from umath/extobj.c (raised as ValueError):
    size < 0         -> "buffer size must be non-negative"
    size > 10000000  -> "Buffer size, {n}, is too big"
    size < 5         -> "Buffer size, {n}, is too small"
    size % 16 != 0   -> "Buffer size, {n}, is not a multiple of 16"
Valid values are therefore the multiples of 16 in [16, 10000000]. NumPy's float/bool
TypeError cases are handled for free by C#'s type system (a non-integer cannot reach a
`long` parameter).

Storage is a [ThreadStatic] field on NDIterBufferManager (CurrentBufferSize, 0-sentinel
-> 8192), mirroring NumPy 2.x's context-local extobj: a setbufsize on one thread never
leaks into another and a fresh thread sees the 8192 default. Wired functionally at the
single canonical NDIter default-resolution point (NDIter.cs), so buffered iteration honours
the setting; an unset thread resolves to 8192, byte-identical to before. Buffering is a
chunking knob only — every computed result is bit-for-bit unchanged (verified: a buffered
cast is identical at bufsize 16 vs 8192).

Scope: only the getbufsize/setbufsize pair. The rest of the _ufunc_config family
(seterr/geterr/seterrcall/geterrcall/errstate) governs floating-point error MODES, which
NumSharp does not model (it raises no FP RuntimeWarning/FloatingPointError), so they would
be misleading no-op stubs; bufsize is the only member with a genuine functional home.

Classified in OracleSurfaceCoverageTests.SiblingOwned (config, no deterministic corpus
bytes to bit-compare, same as get/set_printoptions), gated by
test/NumSharp.Tests/APIs/np.bufsize.Test.cs (23 tests, all from NumPy 2.4.2 output:
round-trip return values, verbatim validation, value-invariance, thread-locality, and the
functional NDIter wiring).

perf(ops): reclaim operator NDArray leftovers via [NDScoped]

Operators created transient NDArrays that were left to the finalizer instead of
being returned promptly to the buffer pool. Each operator was probed with the
SizeBucketedBufferPool take/return balance (the ScopeAudit methodology):

- operator ! (NDArray.NOT.cs) was the ONLY bucketed-buffer strand: it builds an
  untyped bool `result`, then returns result.MakeGeneric<bool>() — a typed alias
  that takes its own ARC ref on the shared block and orphans `result` (one
  bucketed buffer escaped per `!arr` call, measured). Now [NDScoped]: the weaver
  disposes `result` at exit while yielding the alias (escaped 1 -> 0). Same
  MakeGeneric strand + fix the typed NDArray<T> &/|/^ operators already carry.

- The 30 `object` overloads (a+obj, a&obj, a==obj, a<<obj, ... across
  Primitive/AND/OR/XOR/Shift/Equals/NotEquals/Lower/Greater) mint an
  np.asanyarray(x) leftover for a scalar/array-like operand (and the comparison
  overloads also strand a Scalar/empty MakeGeneric wrapper on their null/empty
  branches). All now [NDScoped]. A plain `using var t = np.asanyarray(rhs)` would
  be a BUG here — asanyarray returns the SAME array when rhs is already an
  NDArray, so `using` would dispose the caller's input (rule R2) — which is why
  [NDScoped] (tracks only freshly-constructed temps, never an input passthrough)
  is the correct instrument. Silences all 28 NDW012 analyzer warnings in the
  operator files (215 -> 185 total NDW012 sites; 0 remaining in operators).

- The core NDArray x NDArray operators (+ - * / %, & | ^ << >>, == != < > <= >=,
  ~, unary -/+) are DELIBERATELY left unscoped: probed escaped=0 (the engine
  returns the result directly and disposes its own scalar-cast temp; the
  comparison engine returns a bool-typed result that AsGeneric passes through).
  The disposal guideline keeps [NDScoped] off this hot binary path.

`a &= b` (both NDArray) has no operator-frame leftover — the old `a` is the
caller's (it may be aliased elsewhere) and is uncatchable by the operator, per
the two-audience reclamation contract (DISPOSAL-GUIDELINES section 10).

Verification: 31 operators confirmed woven (NDScope local present, 0 attr/local
mismatches); NDScopeWeaveTests + 162 operator behavior tests green (values
unchanged — the weave is byte-neutral); new regression pin
UndisposedIntermediateTests.OperatorNot_ReclaimsUntypedMakeGenericWrapper. The
scope-audit Corpus_AllOps failure (inv/det/slogdet/solve on linalg_parity) is

feat(analyzer): NDArray leak detection (NDW012) + weaver-missing guard (NDW013)

Two build-time diagnostics for [NDScoped] memory reclamation, delivered by the
NumSharp.Weaver.Analyzer project and wired into NumSharp.Core's own build. This commit
also introduces the analyzer project to source control (it carries the pre-existing
[NDScoped]-target gate NDScopedTargetAnalyzer + KnownTypes/TypeHelpers); the NEW work here
is the leak analyzer and the weaver-missing guard.

NDW012 (Roslyn analyzer, Warning) - NDArrayLeakAnalyzer flags an NDArray a method CREATES
but never returns, out/ref-assigns, stores, disposes, or yields to an NDScope (a transient
left to the finalizer instead of the pool). An IOperation flow analysis classifies every
owned-NDArray value as Reclaimed (using / .Dispose() / scope.Returns / NDScope.Attach),
Escapes (return / out / ref / store / handed to a non-NumSharp API / yield / await), or
Leaks (dropped result, dead local, or fed as an argument into an np.* op that returns an
NDArray - those never dispose their inputs). Recognises every carrier: NDArray, NDArray[],
ValueTuple/Tuple of NDArrays, and INDArrayCarrier result structs, incl. `var (q, r) = ...`
deconstruction (a declaration reference must not count as a use, or the unused side is
masked). Methods that are [NDScoped]/[NDScopedAsync] or open an NDScope by hand are exempt.
A receiver of a call/property/indexer FOLLOWS the result upward rather than terminating as
a leak, so NumSharp's pervasive fluent reinterpret/view chains (x.MakeGeneric<T>(),
x.reshape(...)) are not flooded with false positives.

NDW013 (MSBuild warning) - src/NumSharp.Core/build/NumSharp.targets warns when a project
USES [NDScoped]/[NDScopedAsync] but the NumSharp.Weaver package is not installed (or
-p:SkipNDScopeWeave=true): the attributes are then inert and the temporaries leak. It ships
in NumSharp itself (not the weaver package) precisely so it can fire when the weaver is
ABSENT - the attributes live in NumSharp, so the guard is present exactly when they can be
used. The weaver's targets set $(NumSharpWeaverActive)=true so it stays silent when weaving
actually runs.

Core wiring: NumSharp.Core.csproj references the analyzer with OutputItemType="Analyzer"
(gated by -p:EnableNDArrayLeakAnalyzer, default on) so `dotnet build` on NumSharp captures
leaks in np.* code; src/NumSharp.Core/.editorconfig silences the redundant [NDScoped]-target
gate on Core (already covered by the self-weave), leaving only the NDW012 leak warning;
build/NumSharp.targets is packed into the NumSharp nupkg so downstream consumers get NDW013.

Known limitation (documented): the analysis is per-method, so a private helper whose temps
are actually reclaimed by a caller's ambient [NDScoped] scope is still flagged in isolation
- scope the boundary, turn NDW012 down in .editorconfig, or disable it on Core with
-p:EnableNDArrayLeakAnalyzer=false.

A leak is a performance nudge - the finalizer still reclaims the buffer - so it must never
break a build. The NDArrayLeakAnalyzer descriptor is already DiagnosticSeverity.Warning; this
makes the guarantee robust and regression-proof:

  emits hundreds of NDW012 (mostly ambient-scope-covered helpers) and none may fail the build.

  (NDW002/003/005/006/009/010/011) stay Errors by design - so the leak/gate severity split can

Add examples/NDScoping/Examples.cs — a single-file, leak-to-[NDScoped] tutorial

A user-facing, read-top-to-bottom file that runs ONE small computation five ways,
so you watch identical code go from leaking to leak-free:
  1) the leak                — temporaries wait for the finalizer
  2) prevented by hand       — using/Dispose on every temporary
  3) NDScope                 — the same body + two lines; reclaims ALL temporaries
  4) [NDScoped]              — 100% original body; the build injects the scope
  5) [NDScopedAsync]         — the same, for async / Task-returning methods

The shared workload (RowNorms) exercises operators (- *), np.* calls
(mean/sum/sqrt/maximum), broadcasting (matrix - row-vector, and array - scalar),
and two named temporaries in a chained expression (`centered`, `squared`) plus
the hidden np.* intermediates. Every section observes reclamation through the
public NDArray.IsDisposed and prints the (identical) result, so the memory
behaviour is visible and the math is provably unchanged across all five. Section
1 additionally uses a WeakReference to show that, unscoped, only the GC finalizer
reclaims — and only late.

Wired into the driver as `dotnet run -- examples`; the README and --explain point
new readers here first. The two attributed methods are genuinely woven (weave
coverage 22/22), so the [NDScoped]/[NDScopedAsync] sections show real reclamation.

perf(dispose): second-pass leak sweep — reclaim linalg LU / delete / bmat transients

Detection pass combining three techniques: the NDW012 static flow-analyzer (broad,
over-reports Core helpers), the runtime scope-audit take/return balance (ground
truth, but only for corpus-covered ops), and targeted pool-counter probing (for
surfaces the corpus never reaches). Reconciling them separated real leaks from
analyzer false-positives, and fixed the real ones:

- np.linalg inv / det / slogdet / solve — the LU family was the scope-audit
  Corpus_AllOps gate's ONLY failure (8 families / 18 cases on linalg_parity,
  pre-existing on journey3): each does `ToCommon(a, common)` — a dtype-cast temp
  (a.typecode == common ? a : Cast(...)) — that was dropped to the finalizer.
  [NDScoped] reclaims it while a passthrough operand (already the common type) is
  never tracked; slogdet's (sign, logabsdet) tuple rides the weaver's Returns<T1,T2>
  egress. Their siblings pinv/tensorinv/tensorsolve were already scoped. The
  runtime gate Corpus_AllOps now passes (was red).

- np.delete — leaks the `np.ravel` work-COPY on the axis=None path over a
  NON-contiguous input (ravel of a transposed array copies; measured one bucketed
  buffer escaped, scoping off). The corpus does not exercise that layout. Scoped
  the 6 public overloads; WithSourceOrder's asfortranarray and the chunk views are
  covered too, and the bool-path's hand-disposed keepArr stays idempotent.

- np.bmat — every overload builds intermediate concatenations (and, for
  bmat(ndarray), an obj.copy()) then wraps the final result in an asmatrix VIEW,
  orphaning the intermediates once the view owns the buffer (measured one bucketed
  buffer escaped). Scoped all 5 overloads; ARC keeps the yielded view's buffer alive.

- np.power / np.floor_divide / np.left_shift / np.right_shift (object overloads) —

feat(analyzer): [NDScopedHelper] caller-coverage hint for NDW012 + apply to covered helpers

NDW012 (the NDArray leak analyzer) is a per-method OperationBlock dataflow pass with no
call-graph, so it over-reports a helper whose NDArray transients are actually reclaimed by a
[NDScoped]/[NDScopedAsync] (or hand-scoped) CALLER's ambient scope — the documented "scope the
boundary, helpers ride the ambient scope" pattern the analysis cannot observe on its own. This
adds an explicit, author-asserted exemption for exactly that case, and applies it to the first
three fully-enclosed helper clusters.

NDScopedHelperAttribute (src/NumSharp.Core/Backends/NDScopedHelperAttribute.cs)
  - Public marker on Method|Property. RUNTIME-INERT and NOT woven: the weaver collects targets by
    the exact type names NumSharp.NDScoped{,Async}Attribute, so it never touches this one, and no
    NDScope is opened here. Its sole effect is to tell the leak analyzer the method always runs
    under a caller's ambient scope, so that scope reclaims its transients.
  - Distinct from marking the helper [NDScoped]: that also silences NDW012 but WEAVES a per-call
    nested scope (Open + Returns). Nested scopes compose correctly but are not free; [NDScopedHelper]
    is the zero-runtime-cost choice when the caller's scope already does the reclamation.
  - The assertion is the author's responsibility: if the method is ever invoked without an ambient
    scope (an un-scoped public entry, a deferred lambda/Task, another thread), its transients fall
    back to the finalizer — a real leak the analyzer will no longer report.

  - HasScopedAttribute -> IsScopeExemptByAttribute, now exempting sync | async | helper. The gate
    analyzer (NDW002-011) is untouched: [NDScopedHelper] is not a weave target and draws no target

perf(isclose): compute in NumPy's exact result_type, not blanket float64 — fixes float32 upcast + complex128 correctness

np.isclose/np.allclose cast BOTH operands to float64 unconditionally
(Default.IsClose.cs). Two consequences, both wrong:

1. PERF (float32/float16): NumPy's isclose forces only the reference operand
   inexact via result_type(b, 1.0) and evaluates the whole formula in
   result_type(x, y), so (f32,f32) computes in float32 — NumSharp did 2x the
   memory work by widening to float64. Measured backwards: NumSharp isclose f32
   at 10M was SLOWER (247ms) than its own f64 (200ms); NumPy is the right way
   round (f32 98ms < f64 185ms).

2. CORRECTNESS (complex128): astype(complex -> Double) drops the imaginary
   part, so isclose compared real parts only — isclose([1+0j],[1+100j]) returned
   True where NumPy returns False. This was papered over by a [known bug]
   excusal in MisalignedRegistry for "F-contiguous/complex strided pairing
   divergence".

Fix: cast each operand through InexactPromote(tc) = {Half,Single,Double,
Complex -> self; else -> Double} (== NumPy's result_type(dtype, 1.0)) and let
the elementwise operators do the NEP50 promotion. This reproduces NumPy's exact
computation dtype result_type(x, result_type(y, 1.0)) for every pair:
(f32,f32)->float32, (f16,f16)->float16, (complex,complex)->complex128,
bool/int/char/decimal->float64 (byte-identical to the previous Double cast, so
those dtypes cannot regress). Weak-scalar rtol/atol already adopt the operand
dtype, so the tolerance stays at the reference dtype exactly as NumPy computes it.

Verification:
- Bit-exact vs NumPy 2.4.2 across 14 dtype pairs (all same-dtype + mixed +
  int/bool/complex) x equal_nan x boundary/NaN/inf injection: 0 mismatches.
- The complex128 [known bug] excusal is now stale: FuzzMatrix Logic + Specials
  pass with it DISABLED, so it is removed (the whole complex128 tier —
  contig/F/strided/broadcast/negstride — is bit-exact).
- No degradation: float64/int paths are the same Double cast; same-session A/B
  shows f64 unchanged (~107ms at 10M). 467 Logic + leak-guard tests green.

Perf (NPY/NS, best-of-min, threads=1):
- isclose/allclose float32: 100K 0.18x -> 3.3x, 10M 0.35x -> 1.10x
- isclose/allclose float64: unchanged (100K 3.3x, 10M ~0.9x memory-bound)

10M stays ~1.1x rather than >=1.5x because isclose is a ~15-allocated-pass
composition (NumPy's is too) and is memory-bound; a fused single-pass isclose
kernel is the path to 1.5x there and is left as a follow-up.

206.65 ms), np.inner@10M 0.044x (0.335 vs 7.671 ms) — were a benchmark
REPORTING artifact of the same class as the linalg.matmul shape collision
(3010c336), not an OpenBLAS or runtime regression. Remeasured fairly (identical
shapes, threads=1 pinned on BOTH sides, live-idle, warmed best-of, Release):
every cell is at or above parity, including genuine 10M-vs-10M:

  np.inner       1M distinct   0.176 / 0.166 ms = 1.06x
  np.inner      10M distinct   4.668 / 4.630 ms = 1.01x
  ndarray.dot    1M distinct   0.192 / 0.166 ms = 1.16x
  np.correlate   1M k=31 same 10.629 / 9.148 ms = 1.16x
  np.correlate  10M k=31 same 107.11 / 99.56 ms = 1.08x
  np.convolve    1M k=31 same 10.671 / 9.168 ms = 1.16x
  np.convolve   10M k=31 same 107.08 / 100.1 ms = 1.07x

dashboard Function Explorer were poisoned.

op-matrix twins — the 10M tier maps to 1M physical elements, and inner /
ndarray.dot take two distinct rand*100-50 arrays — in both the C# bench and its

tier vector (their LinAlg-suite twins are uncapped and same-vector by design);

bench: make every 10M cell measurable — dispose the widening bit shifts, type BoolLogicBenchmarks as bool

Audit of the two most recent official runs (2026-08-28 and 2026-08-29) for 10M
cells that produce no comparison found exactly seven, in two fault classes —
neither of which is a memory-x-dtype wall needing the 1M memory-heavy cap; both
now measure at TRUE 10M:

1. np.right_shift(a, 2) (bool) @10M — CRASHED (BDN "Statistics": null) in both
   runs. Probed mechanism: the (bool, int-scalar) shifts widen to a FRESH int64
   result (8x the input; 80 MB at 10M), and right_shift(bool, 2) short-circuits
   to LAZY zeros (shift >= bit width) with a size-INVARIANT ~1.5us call (probed:
   0.0015 ms at both 100K and 10M). BenchmarkDotNet pilots that at us-scale and
   batches thousands of invocations per 25 ms iteration, each lazily committing
   80 MB reclaimed only by finalizers -> Windows commit exhaustion -> the
   workload throws -> Statistics null. Identical to the documented
   LogicBenchmarks.IsComplex lazy-zeros OOM; same fix: dispose per invocation
   (both shifts — the computed left_shift merely allocates hard), matching the
   NumPy twin's discard-each-result loop. Verified: all 60 shift cells
   (2 ops x 3 sizes x 10 integer dtypes) complete with Statistics; the 10M bool
   cells read RightShift min=0.0056 ms (the honest alloc+free cost of the
   short-circuit; "negligible" band vs NumPy's computed 21 ms) and LeftShift
   17.1 ms = 1.27x vs the same NumPy baseline.

2. The whole BoolLogicBenchmarks class (np.all/np.any/np.logical_and/or/xor/not
   on bool) — no_data at EVERY tier in both runs. Not a size problem at all:
   the class was untyped (BenchmarkBase, no DType parameter), and
   merge-results.py's parse_bdn_benchmark defaults a parameterless case to
   dtype float64 — so its rows were keyed (op, float64, N) and never joined the
   NumPy twin's (op, bool, N) rows; 18 real measurements were silently
   discarded as unjoined. Fix: declare the dtype explicitly (the
   BincountBenchmarks pattern — TypedBenchmarkBase + Types = { Boolean }).
   Verified via a validation merge against the 2026-08-29 NumPy baseline: all
   18 cells join; at 10M logical_and/or/xor/not read 1.02x / 1.68x / 2.21x /
   2.06x and all/any land in the negligible band (NumSharp early-exits at
   ~0.14us vs NumPy's constant ~3.7us).

bench: guard the tier-key invariant — a memory-heavy 1M row must publish under the 10M tier

The size vocabulary is 1K / 100K / 10M (+ the N=1 Scalar dispatch tier). When a
memory-heavy family physically runs MEMORY_HEAVY_LARGE_WORKLOAD (1M) at the
large tier, the row still publishes n=10,000,000 — that single invariant is
what makes every downstream consumer treat 1M-physical work as the 10M level
with no special cases: merge-results.py's "Summary by size" geomean buckets by
exact N, render_dashboard.py's by-size bars label {1K,100K,10M}, the DocFX
Function Explorer's tier panels/filters key on n===10_000_000, and
snapshot_history.py's MANIFEST headline parses the by-size table. Audited all
of them plus ops_per_sec (calls/sec — never divides by n, so a capped row
cannot inflate throughput 10x) and ArraySizeSource.AllSizes (contains the 1M
constant but has zero consumers): with the key invariant held, every calc,
geomean, and UI grouping already treats 1M and 10M as the same level.

Enforce it at the emit side: main() now fails the run if any result row
publishes n == MEMORY_HEAVY_LARGE_WORKLOAD. The universal-tier contract in
merge-results.py already hard-fails the common shape of this mistake (a capped
suite emitting n=work_n leaves its group with 1K+100K but no 10M row), but a
row without sibling tiers would slip past it and silently mint a fourth "1M"
size level in every by-size surface; this guard closes that path on the NumPy
twin, where all capped suites build their arrays.

(The C# side cannot make the same mistake today: BDN N comes from [Params]
lists, none of which include 1M — AllSizes is consumer-free — and the same
universal-tier contract validates the C# rows too.)

perf(f16): bit-level AVX2 flat min/max reduce for float16 — 6-60x NumPy, first-NaN/zero-sign parity

np.max/np.min (and np.ptp via composition) on contiguous float16 now ride a
conversion-free bit-level SIMD kernel instead of the scalar Half-operator scan
(two hardware F16C converts per element). f16 ordering is sign-magnitude on the
raw bits, so the whole reduce runs on ushort lanes:

    key = bits ^ (0x8000 | (bits >>ARITH 15))    // pos: bits|0x8000, neg: ~bits

proven strictly order-preserving over all 63,490 non-NaN patterns (round-trips
all 65,536; NaN keys land strictly outside [key(-inf), key(+inf)] =
[0x03ff, 0xfc00]). The AVX2 loop (4x-unrolled, 64 halves/iter) tracks BOTH
unsigned key extremes with pmaxuw/pminuw — the min accumulator doubles as the
negative-NaN detector, keeping the loop branch-free so min and max share one
core (an in-loop min/max branch cost the argmax kernels 2.26x). PHMINPOSUW does
the horizontal reduce (max via complement). Direct Avx2.* intrinsics, not the
portable Vector256 API (which didn't lower to single instructions — measured
~30x slower on the sign kernel).

NumPy's HALF_maximum/minimum are scalar branchy bit-compares (npy_half_ge/le
via half.hpp Less/LessEqual; loops_minmax.dispatch has no x86 HALF entry), so
this is the second f16 family — after sign/negate/abs — that beats NumPy
outright rather than chasing its F16C loops.

Two rare-case fixups reproduce NumPy's fold (ge(acc,x) || isnan(acc)) ? acc : x
exactly (both probed live on 2.4.2):
  - any NaN -> SIMD-rescan for the FIRST NaN element, returned VERBATIM
    (payload AND sign: max([nanB,nanA])=nanB, max([-nan 0xfe22, nanA])=0xfe22).
    This also FIXES a real divergence: the old scan's 'x > acc || IsNaN(x)'
    let a LATER NaN overwrite the accumulator (last-NaN-wins != NumPy).
  - +/-0 extremum -> rescan for the FIRST zero's sign (npy_half ge/le call
    -0 == +0 so NumPy keeps the first zero; the key map orders -0 < +0):
    max([-0,+0]) = -0, min([+0,-0]) = +0.

Perf (NPY/NS, best-of-9 warm, Release, real np.* path):
            1K      100K     10M
  max16    6.3x    56.6x    39.2x   (was 0.47x / 1.55x / 1.61x)
  min16    6.3x    59.9x    41.5x
  ptp16    3.4x    50.8x    35.4x
10M runs at ~54 GB/s — memory-bandwidth-bound, the correct ceiling. 100K drops
from 96.8us to 2.65us (NumPy: 150us).

Verification:

    Less/LessEqual + the HALF_maximum fold — 0 fails (NaN at every SIMD seam,
    zero-sign ties on negative/positive backgrounds, all-NaN, offset views,

  - 930-check live NumPy 2.4.2 differential (max/min/ptp result bits) — 0 fails.
  - FuzzMatrix oracle gate 98/98; full CI-filtered suite 14,196/14,196.

perf(f16): bit-level AVX2 elementwise maximum/minimum/fmax/fmin — 5.6-56x NumPy, NaN-operand-verbatim parity (also fixes clip)

Second f16 family on the conversion-free bit-level technique (after the flat
min/max reduce): the elementwise min/max ufuncs are pure comparison, so the
(Half,Half)->Half MixedTypeKernel keys for SimdFull + both scalar-broadcast
paths now resolve to static AVX2 kernels over raw ushort lanes
(Binary.MinMax.Half.cs) instead of emitted-IL scalar loops. One branchless
per-lane select covers all four ops:

    takeIn1 = nanPick | (~(nan1|nan2) & (cmpKeys | bothZero))

with cmpKeys = unsigned key >=/<= via pmaxuw/pminuw + compare-equal on the
proven order map key = bits ^ (0x8000 | asr(bits,15)); bothZero repairs the
one spot where the key order disagrees with npy_half ge/le (-0 == +0, in1 wins
ties); nanPick = nan1 (maximum/minimum, NaN PROPAGATES) or nan2 (fmax/fmin,
NaN IGNORED). isMax/nanIgnore are loop-invariant so the argmax in-loop-branch
trap does not apply. The scalar-broadcast cores hoist the scalar operand's
key/NaN masks entirely out of the loop; left-scalar is its OWN core because
operand priority is not symmetric (in1 preferred on NaN-vs-NaN and ties).

Semantics verified against BOTH NumPy's C and live 2.4.2 — one trap worth
recording: numpy's npy_half_ge/le are the NaN-GUARDED Half operators
(halffloat.cpp npy_half_le -> operator<=), NOT the _nonan raw bit compares;
a reference model built on the raw compares mispredicts every (finite, -NaN)
maximum and (-NaN, finite) fmin (live-probed: maximum(1, -nan) = -nan
propagated, fmin(-nan, x) = x ignored).

Parity fixes riding along:
  - maximum/minimum returned canonical Half.NaN (payload + sign destroyed) via
    the old HalfMaxNaN/HalfMinNaN scalar helpers; NumPy returns the NaN
    OPERAND VERBATIM, in1 preferred when both are NaN (probed:
    maximum([1],[-nan 0xfd65]) = 0xfd65, maximum([-nan],[+nan]) = -nan).
    The helpers now return the operand — which also fixes np.clip(Half) NaN
    payloads (clip(nan 0x7e05, 0, 1) = 0x7e05 verbatim now) and every
    emitted-IL route that still uses them (mixed-dtype keys, SimdChunk).
  - fmax/fmin/ties were already correct in the helpers; now also SIMD.

perf(f16): bit-level AVX2 comparisons ==/!=/</<=/>/>= — 1.8-40x NumPy

Third f16 family on the conversion-free bit-level technique: the six
comparisons are pure bit logic (NumPy's HALF loops call the NaN-guarded
npy_half comparators, scalar C — 414 us per 100K 'less' on 2.4.2), so the
(Half,Half) ComparisonKernel keys for SimdFull + both scalar-broadcast paths
resolve to static AVX2 kernels over raw ushort lanes (Comparison.Half.cs).
Mask algebra over the proven order map key = bits ^ (0x8000 | asr(bits,15)):

    eq = (bitsEqual | bothZero) & ~anyNaN        ne = ~eq
    le = (leKeys | bothZero) & ~anyNaN           gt = ~(leKeys | bothZero) & ~anyNaN
    ge = (geKeys | bothZero) & ~anyNaN           lt = ~(geKeys | bothZero) & ~anyNaN

seam (probed 2.4.2: equal(-0,+0)=True, less(-0,+0)=False, le/ge(-0,+0)=True);
anyNaN forces False everywhere except != (True — including two NaNs with
IDENTICAL bits). Two 16-lane mask vectors pack to 32 canonical 0/1 bool bytes
per store (PackSignedSaturate + Permute4x64(0xD8) + And 1). The
scalar-broadcast cores hoist the scalar operand's key/NaN masks; operand roles
stay explicit (Less/Greater are not symmetric). The resolver returns cached
lambdas closing over the op — one capture per comparison-cache key.
SimdChunk/General keep the emitted scalar IL (Half operators, same semantics).

the FIRST zero, all-NaN returns the FIRST element VERBATIM because the fold's

(NanMinHalfHelper/NanMaxHalfHelper) now rides HalfNanMin/MaxBitsContiguous

IDENTITY KEY (0 for max via andnot, 0xFFFF for min via or) — one blend op per

converts + IsNaN per element). All-NaN detection falls out of the identity

(keyMin <= key(+inf) = 0xfc00), so an accumulator outside the finite key range

perf(f16): bit-level AVX2 np.clip — 4.3-48x NumPy; fix NaN-max-bound precedence bug that returned float32 fills

_NPY_MIN(_NPY_MAX(x, lo), hi) chain (clip.cpp — guarded npy_half ge/le, in1
preference per stage), i.e. two of the SAME pair-selects the elementwise
maximum/minimum kernels use. The Half ClipKernel keys (every mode x bounds-kind
combo: BothBounds/MinOnly/MaxOnly x Scalar/Array) now resolve to static AVX2
kernels chaining HalfClipStageScalar (max-with-lo then min-with-hi) on raw
ushort lanes; scalar bounds hoist their key/NaN masks entirely out of the loop,
array bounds stream. Replaces the emitted scalar IL loop that called
HalfMaxNaN/HalfMinNaN per element (two scalar F16C converts each).

Stage semantics reproduced exactly (probed 2.4.2): a NaN x passes VERBATIM;
a NaN bound WINS its stage for every input (guarded ge/le vs NaN is false, so
the bound is taken and its exact bits ride through the later stage —
clip(5, 1, nan-hi) = the hi bits, clip(-1, nan-lo, 1) = the lo bits); lo > hi
resolves to hi (min applied last); +-0 stage-ties keep the running value.

short-circuit read '(outType==Single||outType==Double) && ScalarIsNaN(min) || ScalarIsNaN(max)' — && binds tighter than ||, so ANY dtype with a NaN MAX
bound took the float32 all-NaN fill: np.clip(halfArr, 1, nan16) returned a
FLOAT32 array of canonical NaNs (wrong dtype AND payload; NumPy returns
float16 with the bound's exact bits). Parenthesized to Single/Double only;
Half NaN bounds now ride the bit kernel.

perf(f16): SIMD widen-compute-narrow add/subtract/multiply/divide — 2.2-3.6x NumPy, bit-exact float32 pipeline

Sixth f16 family — the handover letter's "capped ~0.55x" item, except the cap
assumed scalar hardware F16C per element; a fully-SIMD Giesen pipeline clears
it 6x over. NumPy's HALF arithmetic loops are scalar C
(npy_float_to_half(npy_half_to_float(in1) OP npy_half_to_float(in2)), ~280-310
us per 100K on 2.4.2); the (Half,Half)->Half MixedTypeKernel keys for SimdFull
+ both scalar-broadcast paths now resolve to static kernels running the SAME
pipeline 8 lanes at a time: HalfBitsToFloatExact (proven NaN-payload-exact
widen) -> one vaddps/vsubps/vmulps/vdivps -> FloatToHalfBits (proven Giesen
RTNE narrow) -> PACKUSDW. The compute is deliberately FLOAT32 - the emitted-IL
route this replaces bridged through DOUBLE, which single-rounds where NumPy's
float32 path double-rounds (exponent-gap sums) and whose hardware (double)Half
widen QUIETS sNaN before the op - both real divergence classes.

NaN-payload priority is a HOST PIN (same class as the MSVC-pinned cast
kernels): the numpy 2.4.2 win-amd64 wheel compiled the commutative ops with
REVERSED operands (addss/mulss dst=in2), subtract/divide natural, and x86's
NaN rule is src1-first - probed live: add(qNaN_a, sNaN_b) = quieted b,
sub(qNaN_a, sNaN_b) = a, both-qNaN add -> in2, both-qNaN div -> in1. Two
implementation traps burned and encoded:
  - RyuJIT MAY RE-SWAP commutative intrinsic operands (observed: Avx.Add(fb,
    fa) still resolved the OTHER operand's NaN), so the priority CANNOT ride
    instruction operand order - NaN lanes are resolved by an explicit post-op
    blend on the narrowed 16-bit lanes (quiet(x) = x | 0x0200; in2-first for
    add/mul, in1-first for sub/div), JIT-proof and self-documenting.
  - np.add(arr, 0-d scalar) never reached the MixedType gate - it rode the
    Tier 3B NDIter route (double-bridge scalar body); TryExecuteBinaryOpViaNDIter
    now DECLINES (Half,Half)->Half add/sub/mul/div so scalar-broadcast lands on
    SimdScalarLeft/Right (contiguous same-shape already took the trivial
    bypass; strided keeps its prior EmitScalarOperation numerics via SimdChunk).

  mul      2.2x     3.5x     3.5x

perf(f16): bit-level AVX2 floor/ceil/trunc/rint — 6-26x NumPy, exhaustively bit-exact over all 65,536 patterns

Seventh f16 family, back on the conversion-free bit-level technique: rounding
an f16 to an integer is defined entirely on the bit pattern (every result is
exactly representable — all f16 >= 2^10 are already integers), so NumPy's
scalar widen->floorf/ceilf/truncf/roundevenf->narrow loop
(loops_half.dispatch.c.src fallback; the AVX-512-FP16 path needs Sapphire
Rapids and is absent from the win-amd64 wheel — 434-724 us per 100K, rint the
SLOWEST f16 op of all) collapses to exponent-based mantissa masking on raw
lanes. The contiguous (Half->Half) unary keys for
UnaryOp.Floor/Ceil/Truncate/Round now resolve to static kernels
(Unary.Round.Half.cs) alongside the sign/negate/abs gate; np.around/np.round
(decimals=0) share UnaryOp.Round and ride the same kernel.

Per lane: NaN -> bits|0x0200 (arithmetic quiets sNaN, qNaN identity, sign
kept); |x| >= 1024 (inf incl.) -> identity; |x| < 1 -> sign-aware +-0/+-1
selects (ceil(-0.2) = -0, rint's +-0.5 ties to +-0); 1 <= |x| < 1024 ->
fracBits = 25 - exp, truncate = bits & ~mask, floor/ceil add (mask+1) on the
fractional side (the bit-step carries across exponent boundaries exactly like
value+1: floor(-1.001) = -2), rint = (bits + mask/2 + intLSB) & ~mask (RTNE).
The per-lane fracBits needs VARIABLE shifts — AVX2 only has them at 32-bit
lanes (VPSLLVD/VPSRLVD), so the kernel widens 8 ushorts to one i32 vector per
step. Strided inputs keep the scalar path.

Perf (NPY/NS, best-of-9 warm, Release):
            1K      100K     10M
  floor    5.9x     14.9x    14.6x
  ceil     6.0x     14.4x    13.4x
  trunc    6.1x     22.4x    21.3x
  rint     6.2x     26.3x    24.9x

Verification:
  - EXHAUSTIVE: all 65,536 f16 bit patterns through each of the four np.* ops,
    bit-compared against live NumPy 2.4.2 — 262,144 checks, 0 diffs (finite
    AND NaN, sNaN quieting included).
  - FuzzMatrix oracle 98/98; full CI-filtered suite 14,217/14,217.
  - Pinning tests: HalfRoundKernelTests (4) — the probed 16-case matrix per
    op, SIMD/tail seam agreement vs the scalar bit formula, around()-shares-
    rint RTNE ties (2.5->2, 3.5->4, 682.5->682), the >=1024 identity band

docs(f16): FLOAT16_DESIGN.md — how float16 is fast in NumSharp; refresh the stale Half perf note

New design doc (the UNIQUE_DESIGN.md pattern) recording the whole f16
performance program in one place, so the next person starts from evidence
instead of relearning it:
