feat(np): logaddexp, logaddexp2, nextafter, interp (NumPy 2.4.2 parity)

Implements four NumPy functions with full API/behavioral parity, all-dtype
coverage, and NumPy-differential + oracle-corpus gates.

## np.logaddexp / np.logaddexp2 / np.nextafter — binary float-tier ufuncs

Float-tier binary ufuncs whose loop signatures (ee->e, ff->f, dd->d, gg->g) and
dtype promotion are IDENTICAL to arctan2 (bool/i8/u8 -> f16, i16/u16 -> f32,
i32+/i64+/char -> f64, floats preserved), so the DefaultEngine reuses ATan2's
promotion / path-classification / kernel-dispatch machinery (Default.LogAddExp.cs
-> PromoteATan2Binary / ClassifyATan2Path / ExecuteATan2Kernel). The only
op-specific piece is the scalar kernel: BinaryOp.{LogAddExp,LogAddExp2,NextAfter}
are intercepted at the top of EmitScalarOperation (before the Half/Decimal
routing, like min/max) and emit ONE Call to the matching (op, resultType) static
helper in Utilities/NDLogAddExpMath.cs — operands already arrive in the loop dtype.

Full ufunc surface: f(x1, x2, out=None, where=True, dtype=None) + positional-dtype
convenience overloads, mirroring NumPy. out=/where= ride the shared
ExecuteBinaryUfuncInto path. Complex inputs and non-float dtype= raise NumPy's
verbatim "not supported for the input types" / "No loop matching" TypeErrors.

Numerics (verified against NumPy 2.4.2 via ucrtbase P/Invoke probes — NOT in the
library):
  - nextafter is BIT-EXACT: Math.BitIncrement/BitDecrement compose to exactly
    ucrtbase nextafter/nextafterf (0-diff over 6M random pairs). Half is a straight
    port of npy_half_nextafter on the raw 16-bit pattern (NumPy's half returns x on
    x==y, unlike the C99 double/float path returning y).
  - logaddexp/logaddexp2 are <=2 ULP. Math.Exp / double.Exp2 / MathF.Exp are already
    bit-identical to ucrtbase exp/exp2/expf; the only divergence is log1p — NumPy's
    ucrtbase log1p is closed, so an fdlibm log1p/log1pf port agrees to <=1 ULP (5%
    of evaluations differ by 1). float64 logaddexp <=1 ULP, logaddexp2 <=2 ULP (the
    LOG2E*log1p product), float32 logaddexp bit-exact, logaddexp2 <=1 ULP. This
    RECOVERS the catastrophic small-value case a naive log(1+exp(-tmp)) loses
    (logaddexp(0,-50) = 1.93e-22, not 0). Half computes in float32, matching NumPy's
    ee->e half loop.

## np.interp — 1-D linear interpolation

Port of compiled_base.c::arr_interp + the _function_base_impl.py wrapper
(Math/np.interp.cs). Bit-exact with NumPy. x/xp/fp cast to float64 (fp complex ->
complex128 path); returns a scalar (0-d) if x is a scalar, else x's shape. Core is
a tight unsafe managed loop (QuickSelect/sort precedent, not IL): monotonic
binary_search_with_guess, slope precompute (lenxp<=lenx heuristic), NaN-x -> NaN,
dx[j]==x -> dy[j], and NumPy's "try the other direction" NaN fixup. left/right
default to fp[0]/fp[-1]; period preprocessing normalizes/sorts/wrap-extends via
np.mod/argsort/concatenate. Error taxonomy verbatim ("array of sample points is
empty", "fp and xp are not of the same length.", "period must be a non-zero
value", "object too deep for desired array"). complex128 fp + complex left/right
overload supported.

## Verification

  - Differential vs NumPy 2.4.2: 441 ufunc cases (2817 values) across every dtype
    pair x special values (inf/-inf/nan/+-0/subnormal) — 0 dtype mismatches, 0 value
    mismatches beyond the <=2 ULP bound; layouts (strided/negstride/transposed/
    broadcast), out=/where=/scalar/empty; full interp matrix incl. period + complex.
  - Oracle corpus: logic.jsonl +189 (63 each op), stat.jsonl +13 interp cases;
    OpRegistry + gen_oracle wired; MisalignedRegistry excuses logaddexp/logaddexp2
    <=2 ULP (nextafter/interp bit-exact, no excuse). Surface gate green.
  - 35 unit tests (LogAddExpNextAfterTests + InterpTests), net8.0 + net10.0.

## Perf (NPY/NS, best-of-9, Release)

nextafter WINS (10M 1.6x, 100K 1.1x — pure bit ops, tight loop). logaddexp ~parity
(10M 1.16x — bound by the SAME scalar Math.Exp+log1p NumPy calls). interp ~parity
(memory/search-bound like NumPy's own C loop). logaddexp2 0.5-0.66x: .NET
double.Exp2 is 2.3x slower than ucrtbase exp2 (a BCL weakness; can't P/Invoke, and
Math.Exp(x*ln2) blows to 264 ULP). 1K is <1.0x everywhere (systemic small-N alloc
floor). Universal 1.5x for scalar transcendentals needs SIMD exp/log1p ports (a
separate effort); parity is the honest ceiling for the compute/memory-bound ops.

## Also lands: f16 half-via-float32 unary WIP

This branch's HEAD (Unary.cs) already referenced HalfSignContiguous /
EmitUnaryHalfViaFloat whose definitions lived only in the uncommitted
DirectILKernelGenerator.Unary.Decimal.cs / .cs working-tree changes, so the branch
did not build without them. That in-progress f16 unary path (Sinh/Cosh/Tanh/
ASin/ACos/ATan/Asinh/Acosh/Atanh/Tan/Cbrt/Log2/Log10/Exp2/Reciprocal/Square on
Half via the (Half)Xf((float)h) F16C round-trip that mirrors NumPy's npy_half loop)
is committed here alongside the new functions to restore a buildable HEAD. Oracle
unary/unary_extra/specials tiers pass.

feat(np): copysign — IEEE sign-copy ufunc (NumPy 2.4.2 parity)

Adds np.copysign, the closest binary sibling of the nextafter family shipped in
043370e0. Returns the magnitude of x1 carrying the sign of x2 (the sign of x2
includes its sign bit, so copysign(3, -0.0) == -3).

copysign is a float-tier binary ufunc with arctan2's exact promotion
(bool/i8/u8 -> f16, i16/u16 -> f32, i32+ -> f64), so it reuses the nextafter /
logaddexp machinery verbatim: BinaryOp.CopySign is intercepted in
EmitScalarOperation and dispatched to one static helper per (op, resultType), and
the engine goes through the shared ExecuteFloatTierBinary path
(PromoteATan2Binary / ClassifyATan2Path / ExecuteATan2Kernel). Full ufunc surface
(out=/where=/dtype=) + positional-dtype overloads.

BIT-EXACT with NumPy: Math.CopySign / MathF.CopySign are the IEEE bit op NumPy's C
copysign performs; Half is done on the raw 16-bit pattern
((hx & 0x7fff) | (hy & 0x8000)); Decimal (no NumPy analog) uses magnitude-of-x /
sign-of-y. The only divergence is copysign(nan, nan), whose NaN payload/sign
differs (.NET's canonical NaN is 0xfff8 vs NumPy's 0x7ff8) — tokenized by the
oracle, so no MisalignedRegistry excuse is needed.

Verification: 63 logic.jsonl corpus cases (gen_binary over arctan2's dtype pairs x
pair layouts, bit-exact), 6 unit tests (LogAddExpNextAfterTests), surface gate
green.

Perf (NPY/NS, best-of-15, Release): WINS at every size — 1K 1.38x, 100K 1.08x
(memory-bandwidth-bound: copysign is a cheap bit op so both sides saturate
bandwidth), 10M 1.31x. NumPy SIMD-vectorizes copysign; NumSharp's scalar
Math.CopySign loop still beats it.

The rest of the IEEE-manipulation family (spacing, signbit, ldexp, frexp) was
investigated (algorithms understood: spacing = signed _next(x,1)-x for f32/f64 but
the npy_half_spacing magnitude algorithm for Half; signbit = unary->bool sign-bit
predicate; ldexp = Math.ScaleB over float x int; frexp = unary two-output with an
int32 exponent) but deferred: they need the unary / two-output emission paths,
which are currently mid-refactor for the f16 half-via-float32 unary work, and
warrant their own focused session once that settles.

build(packaging): the NDW analyzer ships inside the NumSharp package; NumSharp.Build becomes weaver-only

Package-role split, decided and now enforced by the gates:

  NumSharp        = the library + analyzers/dotnet/cs/NumSharp.Build.Analyzer.dll
                    + build/NumSharp.targets (NDW013). No dependency entries.
  NumSharp.Build  = the post-compile IL weaver ONLY (tools/ payload + the
                    NDScopeWeave targets). developmentDependency, no lib/, no
                    dependencies - and now NO analyzers/.

WHY. The [NDScoped]/[NDScopedAsync] attributes live in NumSharp.Core, so the
compile-time diagnostics that validate their use - the [NDScoped]-target gate
(NDW002/003/005/006/009/010/011, compile ERRORS) and the NDW012 leak nudge -
belong to the package that makes the attributes reachable: referencing NumSharp
alone now turns them on, before any weaver is installed. Keeping the analyzer
OUT of NumSharp.Build (rather than shipping it in both) means installing the
two packages together can never double-apply it: two copies at different paths
only dedupe when their MVIDs happen to match, which version skew breaks, and
duplicated NDW errors/warnings would be the result. Weaving is unchanged:
NumSharp.Core self-weaves via the in-repo tools/NumSharp.Build, and consumers
opt in with `dotnet add package NumSharp.Build` exactly as before.

Mechanics (NumSharp.Core.csproj):
- _NumSharpCorePackAnalyzer, hooked on TargetsForTfmSpecificContentInPackage,
  stages the analyzer DLL into analyzers/dotnet/cs/. GetTargetPath (no rebuild,
  so pack-with-no-build stays valid, matching CI's build-then-pack flow) with
  RemoveProperties="TargetFramework" (the inner net8.0/net10.0 global would
  point GetTargetPath at the analyzer's non-existent per-TFM output). Gated to
  the net8.0 pass only: analyzers/ is TFM-agnostic and both passes staging the
  same file draws NU5118. A missing DLL is a loud pack <Error>, not a silently
  analyzer-less nupkg.
- The analyzer ProjectReference is now two conditional ItemGroups: the default
  keeps OutputItemType="Analyzer" (NDW012 on Core's own compile, as before);
  -p:EnableNDArrayLeakAnalyzer=false now leaves a plain build-ordering P2P so

fix(analyzer): composite producers (tuple/array/conditional) + store-escape coverage; two real Core leaks fixed

NDW012's ProducesOwnedNDArray previously recognized only direct producers
(object creation, operators, calls), so an owned temp WRAPPED in a composite
value silently leaked:
  var t = (a + b, c - d);          // dropped tuple literal — both temps stranded
  var g = new[] { a + b };         // dropped array literal
  var t = p ? a + b : c - d;       // dropped ternary of temps (CF-4)
  var t = n switch { ... };        // dropped switch expression (CF-11)
  var (q, r) = (a + b, c - d);     // deconstructed literal, unused side

The fix adds composite-producer classification with two DELIBERATELY
asymmetric rules (see COVERAGE_PLAN §10 — do not unify them):
  - tuple literal / array creation: producer iff AT LEAST ONE element is a
    producer. It holds all elements at once, so a produced element is
    definitely in the dropped value; a tuple/array of plain inputs owns
    nothing and must stay silent (R2 — (a, b) / new[]{ a, b } are the
    caller's values).
  - conditional values (ternary / switch expression / coalesce): producer
    iff EVERY branch produces. Only one branch is held, so a single
    aliasing branch makes demanding reclamation unsafe — the same
    conservatism as the CF-3 mixed if/else rule. Mixed x ?? (a + b)
    remains a documented false negative (pinned Misaligned).

CF-4/CF-11 move from KnownLimitationScenarios (Misaligned FN pins) to
ControlFlowScenarios as tagged warns — the pin design working as intended:
the fix flipped them and the pins were updated consciously.

Rebuilding Core with the sharper analyzer surfaced TWO REAL leaks
(1 -> 3 NDW012 sites), both fixed here, restoring Core to exactly the one

  - np.setops CanonicalizeSetOpNaN: the canon scalar (ternary of two
    NDArray.Scalar producers handed to np.where, never disposed). All three

  - np.interp PreparePeriodic: the wrap-extend temps xpLast-period /

fix(analyzer): four leak-exit fixes (cast-dispose FP, collection exprs, deconstruct-into-existing, throw branches) + body-kind coverage + RB-5 property fuzz

Probe batch 4 swept the remaining leak-exit space — method-body kinds,
exotic reclaim spellings, newer syntax, deconstruction forms — and
surfaced one false positive and three false negatives, all fixed:

1. FALSE POSITIVE — ((IDisposable)t).Dispose() flagged t. IsDisposeCall
   required the containing type to be owned, so a dispose through an
   interface cast was invisible (the conversion is transparent in the
   receiver walk, but IDisposable.Dispose failed the type check). The
   receiver walk only ever arrives from an owned value, so ANY
   parameterless Dispose on it disposes that buffer — the containing-type
   constraint is dropped.

2. FALSE NEGATIVE — C# 12 collection expressions: NDArray[] g = [a + b];
   was silent (a new operation kind, not a recognized producer). Joined
   the any-element composite rule — matched by SYNTAX
   (CollectionExpressionSyntax), because the analyzer compiles against
   Roslyn 4.8 (the .NET 8 SDK floor), which has the language feature but
   not ICollectionExpressionOperation (CS0246); the syntax match works on
   a 4.8 host (unrecognized/None operation) and newer hosts (typed
   operation) alike, reading elements from ChildOperations. Aliases
   [a, b] and returned/escaping forms stay silent (probe-verified).

3. FALSE NEGATIVE — deconstruction into EXISTING locals:
   (q, r) = Split(a); with r unused was silent. The local references
   inside the deconstruction TARGET counted as uses (IsDeclarationReference
   only recognized the "var (q, r)" declaration form), so the unused
   side looked consumed by its own assignment. The helper now walks
   tuple wrappers tracking the child and treats a reference under the
   assignment's Target as a write. Both-sides-used stays clean.

4. FALSE NEGATIVE — throw-expression branches: p ? a + b : throw ... was
   silent because the throw branch failed the every-branch-produces rule.
   A throw branch never completes, so it can never be the held value —
   BranchProduces treats IThrowOperation as vacuously true. The result is
   owned on every path that yields one; an ALIAS completing branch
   (p ? a : throw) still wins the conservatism and stays silent.

fix(ndscope): close the egress gap between the leak analyzer's carrier model and what [NDScoped]/[NDScopedAsync] actually yields

The leak analyzer (docs/LEAK_ANALYZER.md) models an owned carrier as "NDArray,
NDArray[], a ValueTuple containing any NDArray (ANY NESTING), an INDArrayCarrier
struct" and Sec.9 promises a scoped boundary handles every class automatically.
Probing showed the EGRESS side of that promise had holes: a gate-clean,
successfully-woven method could hand its caller DISPOSED arrays. 11 live runtime
reproductions + a 6-shape weaver matrix confirmed before fixing; all closed.

RUNTIME (NDScope.cs) - one fix covers every route:
- Returns(ITuple) now dispatches each component by its RUNTIME type through
  YieldBoxed: nested tuples (recursively), NDArray[] elements, INDArrayCarrier
  structs (YieldTo) and bare IArraySlice/UnmanagedStorage (counted ref) are all
  yielded; previously only bare NDArray components were, so ((a,b),c) returned
  a and b disposed. Covers sync tuple returns, async SetResult, yield return'ed
  elements, task-carried results (YieldBoxed -> Returns(ITuple)) and
  [NDScopedExit] tuple params - every route funnels through this method.
- Detach(ITuple) recurses the same way (NDArray / NDArray[] / nested ITuple),
  so a retained ((a,b),c) argument detaches ALL THREE arrays.
- Rest-packed 8+ tuples already flattened through ITuple (verified, pinned).

WEAVER (ScopeWeaver.cs) - support what the runtime can express, gate the rest:
- out-parameter escape extended from bare NDArray/NDArray[] to the full carrier
  vocabulary: ND-carrying tuples (ldobj+box -> Returns(ITuple); reference Tuple
  via ldind.ref), INDArrayCarrier structs (constrained. YieldTo THROUGH the
  byref - the out param IS the managed this-pointer, no box), and bare
  IArraySlice/UnmanagedStorage (counted ref). Emission reworked into
  BuildOutEscape (fresh per-ret sequences, mutate-in-place head preserved).
- NEW error NDW015: an ND-carrying out shape the escape cannot yield
  (out List<NDArray>, out Task<NDArray>, out NDArray[,], out T : NDArray) is
  refused loudly - previously silently swept (caller received disposed arrays).
- NDW002 widened from IsNDArrayCarrying to CarriesNDArray: ref/in over ANY
  ND-carrying shape (a tuple with an NDArray component, a carrier struct,
  a List<NDArray>, a T : NDArray) - all previously slipped through silently.
- Classify: a general tuple (RetKind.Tuple) validates its components - an
  ND-carrying component the Returns(ITuple) dispatch cannot see through
  (List<NDArray>, Task<NDArray>, T : NDArray) is NDW003 instead of
  weave-then-corrupt; components carrying no NDArray constrain nothing
  (object components dispatch dynamically at runtime). A nested
  Task<Task<NDArray>> non-async return is refused (TaskLike unwrap rejects a
  task-like result - the SM path already did; the deferral cannot ride an
  inner task, whose completion outlives the scope lifecycle).
- ClassifyExitParam applies the matching component rule for [NDScopedExit]
  tuples (undetachable ND-carrying component -> NDW014); nested tuples and
  NDArray[] components are legal and detach recursively.
- Dead narrow IsNDArrayCarrying helper removed (both call sites now use the
  widened predicates).

GATE ANALYZER (NDScopedTargetAnalyzer/TypeHelpers) - exact weaver mirror (T4):
- TypeHelpers.CarriesNDArray + IsSupportedOutCarrier + recursive
  IsSupportedTupleCarrier; IsSupportedCarrier's task unwrap rejects a nested
  task; tuple support is component-validated.
- NDW015 descriptor added; NDW002 check widened; out params checked.
- GT-8 closed: an async method returning a custom [AsyncMethodBuilder]
  task-like is DEFERRED to the weaver (which validates the real SM result type
  from SetResult's argument at IL time) instead of the old NDW003 false
  positive on a shape the weaver weaves fine.

fix(half): strided/broadcast float16 add/sub/mul/div — coalescer negative-stride bug + bit-exact odometer kernel

The oracle FuzzMatrix gate had two red cases, both float16-only, both silent
garbage (wrong elements read, not rounding):

  • FuzzRandom  subtract/random/237  — 40/72 elements wrong on a 4-D
    negative-stride view pair (strides [48,16,4,-2] / [-24,-8,-2,-1]).
  • Products    kron/{1d_2d,2d_1d,3d_2d}/float16 — every output row past the
    first was garbage; kron is bit-exact for Single/Double/Int32.

Root cause (shared): DefaultEngine.MergeStride merged an adjacent dim pair by
SMALLER VALUE (`strideW < strideR`). For a valid C/F-order merge the merged
axis walks the pair via its INNER (fastest) stride — the one of SMALLER
MAGNITUDE. Smaller-value is only correct for non-negative strides: a reversed
view whose merged pair is (-24,-8) kept -24 (the OUTER stride) instead of -8,
so every direct-path kernel then addressed the wrong elements. This never
surfaced for any other dtype because non-contiguous binary ops on every dtype
EXCEPT float16 coalesce inside NDIter — float16 add/sub/mul/div deliberately
decline the NDIter route (to keep the bit-exact SIMD widen-compute-narrow
kernels), so float16 is the ONLY dtype that reaches this direct-path coalescer
and its SimdChunk/General kernels, and thus the only one that exposed the bug.
kron(float16) hit the same path via its broadcast-multiply of two operands
stretched on complementary axes.

Fixes (both needed for byte-exact NumPy parity):

1. MergeStride: resolve the merged stride by smaller MAGNITUDE, and make it
   shape-aware so a size-1 axis (whose coord is always 0) defers to its
   neighbour's stride rather than contributing a phantom stride. Root-cause
   fix; feeds correct coalesced strides to every direct-path kernel.

2. TryGetHalfArithKernel now serves the SimdChunk/General paths with a new
   HalfArithStrided — a per-element coordinate odometer (EmitGeneralLoop's
   address model) driving the bit-exact scalar HalfArithBits. Required
   because the emitted chunk/general IL computes float16 arithmetic through a
   DOUBLE bridge, which double-rounds vs NumPy's float32 HALF loop on
   exponent-gap add/sub and on divide, and quiets sNaN — so correct strides
   alone would still diverge ≤1 ULP. The odometer reuses HalfArithBits (NumPy's
   exact HALF pipeline incl. the operand-order NaN pin), so it is byte-exact
   for every layout: contiguous, broadcast (stride 0), negative, or step>1.
   The contiguous SimdFull/SimdScalar paths keep the SIMD kernels.

Verification: oracle FuzzMatrix 98/98 (was 96/98) — FuzzRandom subtract/237 now
0/72 diffs, all kron float16 cases bit-exact; main suite 14266 passed / 0
failed; both net8.0 and net10.0. kron(float16) row values now identical to
Single/Double/Int32 and to NumPy.

fix(logic): np.isreal/np.iscomplex inspect the imaginary part (+ fix strided-real garbage)

np.isreal and np.iscomplex never looked at the imaginary component: for a complex
input isreal returned ALL True and iscomplex ALL False regardless of value, and on a
strided/broadcast REAL input the same ops emitted GARBAGE BYTES (np.ones/np.zeros were
handed the view's Shape — strides+offset — so they read past the logical window). Two
[OpenBugs] pins reproduced both: OpenBugsDtypeCoverageTests.IsReal_IgnoresImaginaryPart
and IsComplex_IgnoresImaginaryPart.

Ported to NumPy 2.4.2's own structure (numpy/lib/_type_check_impl.py):
  * isreal(x)   = imag(x) == 0
  * iscomplex(x)= imag(x) != 0 for a complex dtype, else zeros(shape, bool)

Implementation (Logic/np.isreal_iscomplex.cs):
  * Complex input -> np.equal/np.not_equal(np.imag(a), 0). np.imag yields the strided
    float64 imaginary-lane VIEW (AliasComplexLane, correct for C/F/strided/reversed/
    broadcast/sliced/0-d), and IEEE ==/!= gives NumPy's exact specials: -0.0 counts as
    real (== 0 True), NaN/Inf are NOT real (== 0 False, != 0 True). Both loops run
    through the existing kernel-backed imag + comparison ufuncs (NDIter/IL), matching
    NumPy's own composition rather than a bespoke per-dtype kernel.
  * Non-complex input -> a fresh C-contiguous bool ones/zeros built from the DIMENSIONS
    only (new Shape(a.shape)), never the view's Shape — fixes the strided-real garbage.

Parity: bit-exact vs NumPy 2.4.2 across 17 layouts x 2 funcs (formal diff — contiguous/
2-D/reversed/step/broadcast/0-d/empty/transposed, incl. -0.0/NaN/Inf imag) and the full
differential-fuzz logic tier, now widened from the old carve (REAL dtypes x contiguous
only) to FULL coverage: ALL dtypes incl. complex128 x EVERY layout (676 isreal/iscomplex
cases, all green on net8.0 + net10.0). The complex pool carries nonzero imaginary parts,
so it directly exercises the imaginary inspection.

Perf (NPY/NS, Release, best-of, warm): float64 isreal 18-37x (NumPy allocates a float64
zeros + compares; we allocate a bool ones), float64 iscomplex competitive-to-faster.
complex128 is memory-bandwidth-bound — NumPy's vectorized strided compare already sits at
the bandwidth ceiling, so it is ~parity-bound (>1.5x not physically reachable, the
memcpy-ceiling class); we match NumPy's imag+compare structure.

fix(reduction): preserve F-contiguity through axis reductions via KEEPORDER allocation (issue #610)

Axis reductions (sum/mean/prod/min/max/std/var + all nan* variants) flipped an
F-contiguous input to a C-contiguous result, where NumPy preserves the layout.
Root cause: the reduction executors allocated the output C-contiguous
unconditionally, and the keepdims step reshaped through a fresh C-shape which
also reset the strides to C.

NumPy does NOT copy to fix this — its reduce iterator allocates the output
operand in KEEPORDER and the reduction loop writes directly into that (already
F-strided) buffer. NumSharp now does exactly the same, with no post-hoc copy:

- New DefaultEngine.AllocateReductionResult(outputType, outputDims, inputShape)
  allocates the result in OrderResolver.Resolve('K', inputShape) order — F for a
  strictly-F-contiguous input, C for C-contiguous / general-strided (matching
  NumPy for pure-C and pure-F; the same C/F-only 'K' model cumsum, np.copy and
  empty_like already use). AllocateReductionZeros is the zero-filled sibling for
  the degenerate size-1-reduced-axis std/var paths.
- keepdims now re-inserts the reduced axis with Storage.ExpandDimension(axis),
  which preserves the layout, instead of Storage.Reshape(new Shape(ks)), which
  reset it to C.

Every output-writing mechanism already honours the result's strides, so filling
an F-strided buffer needs no copy and no kernel change: the IL axis kernels write
via outputStrides (their C-contiguous fast paths are gated on a C-contiguous
INPUT, so an F input never reaches them), the scalar and nan-scalar paths via
SetAtIndex -> Shape.TransformOffset, the np-layer nan loops via SetDouble(coords),
and NDAxisIter via dstOuterStrides.

argmax/argmin are deliberately excluded — NumPy allocates their index output
C-order regardless of input layout (probed 2.4.2).

Converted executors: ExecuteAxisReduction, ExecuteAxisReductionNDIter,
HandleTrivialAxisReduction (Add), ExecuteAxisStdReductionIL + fallback + trivial
(Std), the Var equivalents, ExecuteNanAxisReduction + ExecuteNanAxisReductionScalar
(Nan), and the hand-rolled np.nan{mean,std,var} axis paths.

Verification: 0 flag divergences vs NumPy across 392 C/F x op x axis x keepdims
cases (incl. the size-1-axis edge), 0 value mismatches across 312 F-vs-C checks
(all 13 ops), FuzzMatrix 98/98 bit-exact, 1592 statistics/reduction tests green.
Known residual (documented, not a regression): a genuinely transposed
neither-C-nor-F input reduces to a C result where NumPy's full stride-sort
KEEPORDER may pick F — values are byte-correct, only the flag differs, and it is
invisible to the oracle (which serializes ascontiguousarray on both sides).

-> all-True bool; clip(bool,False,True) -> identity).

strided result is bit-identical to the contiguous 0/1 scalar select, for scalar
AND array (incl. broadcast stride=0) bounds. No new per-dtype path, no struct
kernel: it reuses the Byte case's kernel verbatim. All 15 dtypes are now handled
on the strided clip path (bool was the only gap).

fix(hashset): correct 35 composite entries in HashHelpersLong prime table + drop int-era growth cap

Fixes the two [OpenBugs] tests HashsetLongIndexingTests.HashHelpersLong_GetPrime
and HashHelpersLong_ExpandPrime_ProgressiveGrowthTest, both annotated
"HashHelpersLong.primes array contains non-prime values".

HashHelpersLong is the long-indexed port of .NET's System.Collections.HashHelpers
that backs Hashset<T> (consumed by ConcurrentHashset<T> and np.unique's hash path).
Its capacity table must be all-prime: prime bucket counts are what keep the modulo
hash distribution collision-free. Two defects broke that contract.

Root cause 1 — composite table entries. The 47-entry "Extended primes for large
collections" section (indices 72..118, values ~8.6e6 .. ~37.9e9) was generated as a
~1.2x geometric progression whose members were never verified prime: 35 of the 47
are composite (e.g. 8639243 = 7*1234177, 10581492263, 37915399963). GetPrime returns
the first table entry >= min, so GetPrime(1e10) returned the composite 10581492263 and
the test's IsPrime(result) assertion failed. (In DEBUG this also tripped the latent
Contract.Assert(IsPrime(newSize)) in SetCapacity for those sizes.)
Fix: each composite bumped up to nextprime(value). Values stay >= the original (so the
">= min" and growth guarantees hold) and strictly increasing; the 84 already-prime
entries — including the base-72 block and the two the IsPrime test pins (7199369,
4252464407) — are byte-identical.

Root cause 2 — the MaxPrimeArrayLength cap. It was 0x7FFFFFC7 (~2.147e9), the 32-bit
Array.MaxLength copied verbatim from the int-based original and never adjusted for the
long retrofit. In ExpandPrime it fires when oldSize < cap < newSize, so an oldSize of
2e9 (past the 1e9 large-growth threshold) capped to ~2.46e9 instead of reaching its
33%-growth target of 2.666e9 — failing ProgressiveGrowthTest. It also wasn't prime.
The table already returns up to ~38e9 for larger oldSize (e.g. 5e9 -> 7.3e9), proving
the ceiling was meant to track the table, not the 32-bit array limit.
Fix: MaxPrimeArrayLength = 37915399967L, the largest table entry (now prime). Beyond
the table GetPrime computes as before.

Validation: both target tests plus all 28 HashsetLongIndexingTests pass (incl. the 1M
-element stress test, which drives the real Initialize/IncreaseCapacity/ExpandPrime/
GetPrime/SetCapacity resize path). 133 unique + Hashset/ConcurrentHashset consumer
tests pass — the corrected bucket sizing changes collision behavior only, never the
set of values a consumer produces. Verified against the compiled NumSharp code that
all 119 entries are prime, strictly increasing, and MaxPrimeArrayLength is prime.

fix(shape): OWNDATA flag now maintained on Shape — audit T1.29/T1.64 closed

The ArrayFlags.OWNDATA bit (0x0004) was declared since the flags enum landed but
never set by any code path, so Shape.OwnsData and (Shape.Flags & OWNDATA) always
read false — while the REAL ownership tracking lived only on UnmanagedStorage
(_baseStorage is null && !ExternalBase). The two AuditV2 OpenBugs pinning this
(T1_29_OWNDATA_Flag_Never_Set, T1_64_Flags_OWNDATA_Always_False) now pass and
run in CI as regression pins.

Design — mirror NumPy's array-object flags word (probed against the source):
numpy ctors.c PyArray_NewFromDescr_int raises NPY_ARRAY_OWNDATA when IT
allocates (line 923) and clears it when data is passed in (line 931), and
common.c's _IsWriteable asserts base != NULL => !OWNDATA. Shape._flags is
already NumSharp's array-object flags word (WRITEABLE and ALIGNED are
maintained statefully through the same funnels), so OWNDATA joins them as the
third stateful flag, kept in lockstep with the storage truth:

- UnmanagedStorage.SyncOwnDataFlag() (new): reconciles _shape's OWNDATA bit
  with OwnsData. Called at every funnel where ownership or _shape transitions:
  * _Allocate (allocating constructors set the bit),
  * the ~30 codegen'd scalar/vector ctors (via pre-owned ScalarOwnedShape /
    OwnedVectorShape statics — zero per-construction cost; codegen template
    comments updated in lockstep),
  * every _baseStorage assignment (all 3 Alias overloads, WrapReinterpreted,
    AliasComplexLane, CreateBroadcastedUnsafe, 4x GetData view overloads,
    GetView's empty+contiguous branches, GetFieldAlias) — a view borrows the
    parent's shape struct, which carries the parent's bit and must drop it,
  * ExternalBase raises in NpyFormat (memmap 'r'/'r+'/'c'; 'r+' takes no later
    shape swap, so the explicit sync is the only thing clearing the wrap bit),
  * SetShapeUnsafe / ExpandDimension / the ReplaceData family — in-place shape
    swaps assign freshly built shapes that never carry the bit, which would
    otherwise silently strip it from an owner (NumPy: in-place mutation never
    changes OWNDATA; methods.c re-enables it after in-place resize).

- NDArrayFlags.O now reads _arr.Shape.OwnsData (was Storage.OwnsData), so the
  1104-case flags oracle + 210-case layout-parity oracle gate the MIRROR: any
  future funnel that drops or fails to set the bit turns the corpus red
  instead of leaving Shape.OwnsData silently wrong. np.require keeps reading
  the storage truth; tests assert the two never disagree.

- Shape.WithFlags now routes through the no-walk 7-arg ctor: dims/strides are
  unchanged so size/hash are carried verbatim instead of recomputed — the
  pre-existing WRITEABLE/ALIGNED fixups in the alias hot paths lose two
  O(ndim) walks per call, more than paying for the new OWNDATA reconcile.

Verified against live NumPy 2.4.2 on an ~80-case probe matrix (owndata + base
+ flags.num for creation/views/copies/in-place/memmap): NumSharp's storage
truth already matched NumPy on all rows except the 5 KNOWN open op-level

perf(nditer): cut the iterator's fixed cost — single recycled state block, packed kernel key, direct EXLOOP advance, SIMD comparison out=, eager overlap-temp dispose

NDIter's per-call setup tax was the dominant cost of every NDIter-routed op below ~10K
elements, and the ufunc out= route was slower than NumPy at n=1 on every op. Measured
(Release, `dotnet run -c Release` probes vs NumPy 2.4.2 in the same session):

  three-operand 1-D construction         161 ns, of which 3 calloc/free pairs = 78 ns
  per-call kernel-cache key string        45 ns + 96 B garbage (4 enum formats + concat)
  Broadcast + ResolveUfuncIterationShape  55 ns + 2 Shape allocations (identity work)
  per-chunk driver (iternext + dispatch)  5.6 ns
  np.less(f64, f64, out=bool) @100K       43.4 us vs NumPy 11.4 (scalar-only inner loop)
  np.add(a, b, out=a) (COPY_IF_OVERLAP)   forced-copy temp leaked to the finalizer per call

Six changes, all behaviour-preserving (14,446/14,446 main suite, FuzzMatrix 98/98 bit-exact,
net8.0 + net10.0 build):

1. Single-block state + per-thread recycling (NDIter.State.cs, NDIter.cs).
   NDIterRef.AllocateStateBlock allocates the header and a 1536-byte inline arena in ONE
   native block; AllocateDimArrays carves the dimension and per-operand arrays from the
   arena (falls back to the separate blocks when ndim x nop outgrows it; stack states from
   CreateCopyState/CreateReductionState have no arena and keep the old path). Dispose /
   FreeState / Copy's failure path return the block through ReleaseStateBlock, which parks
   it in a bounded [ThreadStatic] 4-slot cache after ResetForRecycle re-zeroes the header and
   only the carved bytes — every array the iterator hands out must start zeroed (BaseOffsets
   is +=-accumulated by FlipNegativeStrides; Coords/Buffers/BufStrides too).
   Construction: New 1-op 146 -> 62 ns, 3-op EXTERNAL_LOOP 161 -> 93, ufunc flags 197 -> 113.
   AdvancedNew's catch now tears down through FreeState (also frees buffers a failed
   Initialize had allocated).

2. Packed kernel-cache key (Backends/Kernels/InnerLoopKernelKey.cs, InnerLoop.cs).
   InnerLoopKernelKey packs family/op/dtypes into one ulong; a struct-keyed front cache
   (_innerLoopKeyCache) sits over the string-keyed _innerLoopCache, and ToCacheKey()
   reproduces the legacy "npy_binop_{op}_{l}_{r}_{res}" string byte-exactly on a miss, so
   DynamicMethod names, kernel identity and GeneratedDelegates.InnerLoopCount are unchanged
   (ClearInnerLoop clears both). NDIterRef gains packed-key ExecuteElementWise /
   ExecuteElementWiseBinary / ExecuteElementWiseUnary overloads whose cache hit allocates
   nothing; the nine production sites (BinaryOp, CompareOp, UnaryOp x2, UfuncOut x4, Shift)
   use them. The string overloads stay for user kernels (Tier 3A/3B/3C).

3. Direct EXTERNAL_LOOP advance (NDIter.Execution.cs, NDIter.cs). ForEach,
   ExecuteGenericMulti and ExecuteReducing call ExternalLoopNext directly (inlined, state
   array pointers hoisted into locals so the JIT stops reloading them per operand per axis)
   instead of through the cached NDIterNextFunc delegate when IsPlainExternalLoopAdvance()
   — the production ufunc configuration. Per-chunk driver overhead 5.6 -> 4.7 ns on
   4-element rows; buffered and non-EXLOOP iterators keep the delegate path untouched.

4. SIMD comparison for out= (NDIter.Execution.cs TryExecuteComparison, UfuncOut.cs).
   ExecuteComparisonUfuncInto compiled a scalar-only Tier-3B body for EVERY layout. When the
   inputs share a dtype and the bool out is contiguous in iteration order it now runs the
   whole-array SIMD comparison kernel (Vector.Compare + mask packing — the kernel the no-out
   route already uses for contiguous inputs) through the iterator's post-coalesce strides;
   mixed dtypes, cast outs and strided/F outs keep the scalar body.
   np.less(f64, f64, out=) @100K: 43.4 -> 9.3 us (NumPy 11.4).

5. Same-dims fast path on the three *UfuncInto routes (UfuncOut.cs). When lhs/rhs/out have
   identical dims the input broadcast and the out join are identity transforms that cannot
   raise (Shape.Equals compares dims only), so Broadcast + ResolveUfuncIterationShape are
   skipped: -55 ns and two Shape allocations on np.add(a, b, out=o).

6. Eager COPY_IF_OVERLAP temp dispose (NDIter.cs ResolveWritebacks, NDIter.Detach.cs
   ResolveDetachedWritebacks). After the write-back the operand slot reverts to the user's
   original (NumPy's operands revert once WRITEBACKIFCOPY resolves) and the forced-copy temp
   is disposed instead of dropped to the finalizer — one leaked pooled buffer per in-place
   ufunc call before. inplace np.add(a, b, out=a) @1: 282 -> 154 ns (NumPy 570).

Net at n=1 (ns, NumSharp before -> after | NumPy 2.4.2): add(out=) 411 -> 168 | 289,
less(out=) 366 -> 140 | 300, sqrt(out=) 338 -> 183 | 258, negative(out=) 329 -> 153 | 267,
positive(out=) 332 -> 141 | 257; add(out=) @1K 510 -> 233 | 438; less(out=) @1K 794 -> 232
| 417. Managed garbage per add(out=) call 552 -> 200 B. Every out= op measured is now faster
than NumPy at n=1 (all were slower). Official nditer benchmark sections (NPY/NS, fresh both
sides): construction geomean 2.73x -> 5.8x (ctor.3op_exl 8.6x, ctor.ufunc 9.3x), lessbool
0.71/0.49/0.18/0.60x -> 2.07/1.82/1.25/1.06x across 1/1K/100K/1M, inplace@1 0.62x -> 3.7x,
zerodim 0.62x -> 3.2x, chunkwidth w=4 0.48x -> 0.82x, w=16 1.02x -> 1.13x.

np-function: caveat against inlining large scripts in <<'EOF' heredocs

The command taught 'dotnet run <<'EOFDOTNET'' / 'python <<'EOFPYTHON''
as the general probe/validate/benchmark mechanism with no size caveat.
A large or quote-dense script inlined in a heredoc is emitted as one
giant single-command string that can corrupt in transport and fail with

case is the worst).

(probe.cs / probe.py) and redirect it in (dotnet run -c Release - <
probe.cs / python probe.py); short snippets can stay inline. Aligns with
the benchmark skill, which already mandates file-based timing scripts
(dotnet run -c Release - < script.cs, fresh filename per rebuild). Small
python twins (measure-verify / O1_EXCLUSIONS) are legitimate small
heredocs and were left as-is.

perf(nditer): 2-D block kernel for narrow strided rows — 0.82x→1.4-2.5x NumPy

The per-chunk ForEach route drives a (rows, w) view with a contiguous inner axis
one row at a time under EXTERNAL_LOOP, paying the odometer advance AND the
per-chunk kernel's own SIMD-viability prologue on EVERY row — so a narrow w sat at
~0.82x NumPy (np.positive) while a hand-written 2-D loop (prologue once, inner
SIMD run, per-row pointer bump) measured 1.7-2.1x. The whole gap was per-row
overhead, not memory traffic; buffering the strided rows into a contiguous window
was measured SLOWER (the inner runs are already SIMD-able in place). This is
docs/NDITER_PERF_DISCOVERY.md §7 angle 2.

ND2DElementwiseKernel (DirectILKernelGenerator.InnerLoop2D.cs) loops the outer
axis itself with per-operand outer byte strides, called once per coalesced 2-D
block — neither the odometer nor the prologue runs per row. It reuses the SAME
scalar/vector emit bodies as the per-chunk kernel, so results are byte-identical
(elementwise ops carry no cross-element state). Dispatched by
NDIterRef.{Is2DElementwiseShape,TryExecute2DElementwise}, wired into the three
packed-key ExecuteElementWise* entry points so it serves both out= and allocating
unary/binary routes. Gate: unbuffered, no where= mask, EXTERNAL_LOOP, inner axis
element-contiguous for every operand, all operands the same SIMD-capable dtype.

NumSharp's NDIter does not coalesce outer axes (a 3-D x[:,:,:w] stays NDim=3), so
the gate also flattens mutually contiguous outer axes
(stride[d]==stride[d+1]*shape[d+1], true for any trailing-narrow N-D slice) into
one (outerCount, outerStride) and reuses the same kernel — covering N-D
trailing-narrow AND routing it off a pre-existing malformed-output crash in the
ForEach 3-D odometer path.

positive had no vector body (CanUseUnarySimd(Positive) was false), so it was
scalar even contiguously and could not engage — an identity vector body was added
(EmitUnaryVectorOperation Positive branch + the gate), which also gives contiguous
positive a SIMD copy (1.59x NumPy).

Measured (NPY/NS, 2M f64): 2-D positive 1.95-2.18x, sqrt 2.11-2.52x, add
1.82-2.29x; 3-D trailing-narrow 1.37-2.26x — every cell a win.

    that one layout and strided_2d_cols / negstride_2d_offset are gated bit-exactly.
  * ND2DElementwiseKernel contract gains innerByteStrides; the kernel dispatches ONCE per call
    on the inner-mode pattern — unary {C, S}, binary {CC, SC, CS} — each a full 2-D loop with
    the S (broadcast-along-the-row) operand loaded and Vector.Create'd once per row. The gate
    accepts inner stride 0 on inputs (output must be element-contiguous).
  * Masked sub-vector rows and tails: on a 256-bit AVX2 host with 32/64-bit lanes the row
    remainder innerCount % lanes — and the whole row when innerCount < lanes — is one MaskLoad
    per C input -> the same vector body -> one MaskStore (vmaskmov, NumPy's npyv_load_tillz /
    store_till). The mask is built once per call (GreaterThan(Create(tail), {0,1,..})).
    Masked-off lanes are never touched in memory; integer masked-off lanes are filled with 1
    after the load so a software Vector.Divide cannot throw on a 0 lane. Other hosts and
    1/2-byte lanes keep the scalar tail.

    otherwise) — exp/log/power/mod/mixed-dtype/Half/Decimal/Complex no longer pay the per-row
    route.
  * Leading axes that do not fold into the block (x[::2, :, :w]) are walked in
    TryExecute2DElementwise by a per-BLOCK odometer, never per row.

NumSharp indexes with int64/long everywhere; a narrower index path is admissible only if it
measurably increases performance. Measured the idx32 take/put/flat kernel variants (index array
read in place at 4 bytes, sign-extended on load, all index arithmetic int64) against the

  native int64 / in-place: 0.97–1.13x (an int32 index costs the same as an int64 one).

feat(analyzer): NDW016/NDW017 type-level NDArray ownership, contagion into NDW012, [NDBorrowed]

Why
- NDW012 is per-method and treats "stored into a field/property" as a clean escape, so
  ownership silently evaporated at every field boundary: a class could hold NDArrays until
  the finalizer and nothing ever asked it to be IDisposable or to dispose them. Eli's rule:
  a type that stores NDArrays in any way must be disposable and dispose them, and a type
  storing such a disposable must dispose it too (contagious disposing responsibility).

What — a third analyzer in tools/NumSharp.Build.Analyzer (same DLL, same package payload)
- NDArrayHolderAnalyzer.cs over the shared OwnershipModel.cs (memoized, concurrent-safe):
  * NDW016 (warning, one per type): a class/struct declares instance fields / auto-properties
    (positional record properties included; a computed property is a view) whose type HOLDS
    NDArrays — NDArray(<T>)/subclass, arrays of any rank, tuples with a holding component,
    generics instantiated over a holder (List/Dictionary/Lazy/Task/a consumer's Box<NDArray>,
    and types nested in such containers), INDArrayCarrier structs, T : NDArray, and ANOTHER
    type that stores them (own members or base — ownership is contagious) — yet implements
    neither IDisposable nor IAsyncDisposable (a ref struct: no public void Dispose()).
  * NDW017 (warning, one per member): the type is disposable but the holder is not disposed
    on any path from Dispose/Dispose(bool)/DisposeAsync/DisposeAsyncCore. Reachability runs
    over same-type callees (methods, property accessors, delegates over methods; local
    functions are in-tree). Disposal is recognised when a Dispose/DisposeAsync/Close/close
    receiver ROOTS at the member (through conversions, ?., tuple/field/property/indexer/
    element chains, call results, and derived locals: declarators, assignments, foreach loop
    variables incl. deconstruction, deconstruction — to a fixed point), the member is a
    `using` resource, it is handed as an argument to any method/ctor (type-gated: the
    argument itself must hold NDArrays and not be a call result, so Log(x.size) and
    Log(_a.ToString()) are not disposals), or a call on it carries a disposing lambda
    (_list.ForEach(x => x.Dispose())). Not disposal: `= null`, Clear(), a finalizer (the
    backstop, deliberately not a root), an unreachable helper. Message hints name an
    inherited base Dispose (override Dispose(bool)) or a non-disposable inner type (make it
    disposable first).
  * Exempt: static classes, interfaces, INDArrayCarrier types (transient result packaging the
    scope yields through), [NDBorrowed] types. Never owners: static members, delegates,
    comparers/IEquatable/IComparable/IObservable/IObserver/IProgress, WeakReference<T>,
    unconstrained type parameters, object/IDisposable, any type from an assembly that cannot
    name NDArray (BCL answered without a member scan). Metadata types are consulted (visible
    fields/properties/indexers, so np.NDIterator and NpzFile count), never reported.
- NDArrayLeakAnalyzer (NDW012) contagion: an NDArray-owning disposable (a consumer holder
  class, np.NDIterator, NpzFile) or a rank-1 array of them is an owned value — a dropped/dead/
  discarded/factory instance warns; Dispose/DisposeAsync/Close/close reclaim; return/store/
  hand-off escape; a foreach over a PRODUCED NDArray or owning disposable is a leak (C#
  disposes the enumerator, never the enumerable — foreach (var x in np.nditer(a)) leaves the
  iterator open) while a produced NDArray[]/tuple/carrier stays conservatively consumed. The
  message names the kind ('Batch' instance / 'NDIterator' instance / 'Batch' array).
- [NDBorrowed] (src/NumSharp.Core/Backends/NDBorrowedAttribute.cs; Field|Property|Class|
  Struct; runtime-inert like [NDScopedCovered]): "this references an array owned elsewhere"
  — excludes a member, or exempts a whole type and removes it from the contagious set. The
  name contains neither NDW013 scan token (NDScopedAttribute/NDScopedAsyncAttribute).
- KnownTypes: BorrowedAttr, IDisposable, IAsyncDisposable.

Core triage (fresh -t:Rebuild: 18 NDW016 types + 9 NDW017 members + 9 new NDW012 sites →
exactly 1 NDW012, the documented indexer false positive, 0 NDW016, 0 NDW017)
- [NDBorrowed] on genuine borrowers: FlatIterator, MemoryView, NDRefIter<T>/NDChunkIter<T>,
  NDEnumerate(<T>), NDFlatIterator, NDExpr ArrayNode/NDExprBindContext, NDArrayFlags, the
  debugger proxy, _Unsafe/_Pinning, r_'s Operand, SplitContext, IndexOp/PreparedIndex,
  NpzFile.BagObj, NDIterRef._operands/_writebackOriginals (an iterator never owns its
  operands; the COPY_IF_OVERLAP temp is resolved by ResolveWritebacks — this also stops the
  five Borrow() handle drops from reading as leaks), NDIterator.Current + its foreach
  Enumerator, NDArray.TrackingScope (the scope owns the array, not vice versa),
  Broadcast._ops, NpzFile._cache (an array is the reader's the moment it is handed out;
  disposing the cache on Close would break `using var z = np.load_npz(p); var a = z["a"];`).

  * poly1d owned its coefficient array (the ctor yields it into the field via
    scope.Returns) yet was not disposable → poly1d : IDisposable; the copy-constructor now
    COPIES (+ NDScope.Detach, a field egress) instead of sharing one array between two

    temps are `using`; polyval(poly1d, poly1d) disposes its Horner product and superseded

    so results are unaffected).

fix(complex): byte-identical NaN sign for all complex128 unary ufuncs + oracle gate

Closes the NaN byte-identity divergences in docs/bugs/nan-byte-identity-vs-numpy.md
(now deleted) and closes the oracle blind spot that hid them.

## Root cause (one line, proven on x86-64 SSE)

.NET double.NaN is the NEGATIVE-signed quiet NaN 0xfff8...; NumPy's NPY_NAN is the
POSITIVE 0x7ff8.... On win-amd64 NumPy's complex ufuncs run through MSVC's UCRT C99
complex functions, which emit the positive NaN in their "produce a NaN" special
paths. Both engines lower to the SAME deterministic SSE2 ops, so NaN PROPAGATION
already matched - every divergence came only from NumSharp's NaN SEED constants
(double.NaN), from inf-inf/0/0 arithmetic where NumPy uses the constant, or from
BCL Complex.Exp delegations for non-finite inputs.

Verified: inf-inf/0-div-0/inf*0 -> 0xfff8 on BOTH engines (kept as arithmetic); a
positive-NaN operand propagates through +,-,*,/,sqrt unchanged; an explicit negate
flips the sign - so a per-path fix (positive-NaN constant where NumPy canonicalises,
arithmetic where it produces a signed result) makes NumSharp bit-identical to NumPy.

## The fix (NDComplexMath.cs) - per-path, NOT a blanket canonicalize

- positive-NaN constant NAN (0x7ff8...) replaces the double.NaN seeds in
  HypotNonFinite, CasinhNonFinite, CacosNonFinite, Catanh, ExpSpecial.
- sqrt/log/log1p: HypotNonFinite now PROPAGATES the present NaN's sign
  (IsNaN(x)?x:y) - so sqrt(2.5,-NaN).real is -NaN like NumPy, while clog's pre-abs'd
  operands keep giving +NaN.
- reciprocal: rewritten as the exact CDOUBLE_reciprocal ufunc loop
  (1/d, -r/d, r/d, -1/d). NumPy's imaginary term is a DIVISION (-1.0)/d, not the old
  Smith -scl negate - a negate flipped a positive NaN d.
- square: true vfmaddsub via Fma.MultiplySubtractScalar (real) +
  Fma.MultiplyAddScalar(im, re, re*im) (imag). The fused subtract keeps the
  subtrahend's NaN sign (the old -(im*im) negate flipped it); re*im in the addend
  slot matches NumPy's product-NaN on mixed-sign-NaN inputs. Finite results (incl.
  square(1e300+1e300i).real = -inf) are identical.
- exp/exp2: Complex.Exp now only serves fully-finite inputs; ExpSpecial reproduces
  MSVC cexp (PROPAGATES an input NaN's sign; +NaN for an Inf input; +0 imaginary
  zero for a NaN y at -inf).
- sinh/cosh: CANONICALISE every NaN slot to +NaN (MSVC csinh/ccosh do too, verified
  csinh(-NaN,y)=+NaN) - which is what makes the derived csin/ccos match after their
  -Re transform negate; also fixes the cos(+-0,NaN) zero-sign.
- tanh: PROPAGATES the NaN sign (ctanh(x,-NaN)=-NaN); both-NaN follows y.

Result: bit-exact over the FULL +-0/+-inf/+-NaN x +-0/+-inf/+-NaN grid (BOTH NaN
signs) for sqrt log log2 log10 log1p exp exp2 expm1 square reciprocal sin cos tan
sinh cosh tanh arcsin arccos arctan arcsinh arccosh arctanh conjugate negative
positive. Only the pre-existing finite-interior <=1-ULP residuals remain (documented,
excused). float16 sign/maximum and complex/float16 NaN preservation were already
byte-exact.

## The oracle gate (was blind - BitDiff tokenized every NaN to "NaN")

- BitDiff.Compare(..., nanBitExact) overload compares NaN by RAW bytes; new
  DiffHasSignFlip distinguishes a pure NaN-sign / signed-zero flip from a value
  change (WithinUlp reports NaN-vs-NaN and +-0 as "0 ULP", which would swallow it).
- FuzzCorpusTests.CompareArray turns nanBitExact ON for ComplexNanContractOps (the
  complex-unary set) and HARD-FAILS a sign flip before any ULP/pathological excuse
  runs. Everything else keeps the tokenizing compare (a differing NaN payload is
  non-contractual elsewhere).
- The corpus already carried NumPy's exact NaN bits; the gate immediately caught the
  -NaN-input exp/exp2 cases my first pass missed (now fixed). FuzzMatrix 98/98 on
  net8.0 + net10.0.

## float32 sum NaN sign - ACCEPTED as documented (policy decision)

sum(float32 NaN-laced) is 0xffc00000 vs NumPy's 0x7fc00000: an order-dependent
NaN-BIT difference (value is NaN either way). Matching NumPy's pairwise NaN tree
would abandon the multi-accumulator SIMD reduction for a non-contractual sign bit -
not worth it. The oracle correctly tokenizes float NaN, so it never false-fails.

Gates: FuzzMatrix 98/98 (Unary+Specials complex-unary NaN now raw-byte compared);
complex/math unit tests 819/0; Math/Fourier/Kernels/Statistics 3502/0.

The Oracle FuzzRandom tier failed on macОS/arm64 (square/random/88 et al, ~4096 ULP)
because NDComplexMath.Square only FMA-contracts re*re-im*im on x86 (Fma.IsSupported):

vs the Fma intrinsic). Only a NaN im*im's sign differs from the x86 ADDEND-preserving
form, and that is host-dependent off x86 and tokenized by the oracle (nanExact is

per-function Type / NPTypeCode / NPTypeCode? dtype overloads with ONE overload whose dtype
parameter is the unified DType, and move the TensorEngine ufunc/reduction surface onto DType too.
Because Type / NPTypeCode / NumPy dtype string all convert to DType implicitly, every existing
KEYWORD call site keeps working unchanged; the only behavioral change is that dtype is now
KEYWORD-ONLY (NumPy-faithful) for the out/where ufuncs — positional `f(x, typeof(T))` /
`f(x, NPTypeCode.X)` become `f(x, dtype: ...)`.

Engine (TensorEngine + DefaultEngine):
- The ufunc/reduction ops now take `DType dtype = null` instead of `Type dtype = null`
  (~70 DefaultEngine op files + TensorEngine.cs abstract decls). `null` == None/infer, so the
  existing `dtype?.GetTypeCode()` / `dtype == null` idioms are untouched — only the parameter
  type flips. Non-ufunc `Type` params (GetStorage / Cast / astype / storage / allocation on
  UnmanagedStorage + NDArray) are deliberately left as `Type` (they are concrete element types,
  not the optional loop dtype).

Public np.* (Math — the ufunc/reduction slice):
- Collapsed every Math dtype-taking function to a single `DType` overload: the unary ufuncs
  (sqrt/sin/cos/tan/exp*/log*/sign/floor/ceil/trunc/rint/reciprocal/cbrt/deg2rad/rad2deg/
  conjugate/positive/negative/invert/... incl. arc/hyperbolic aliases), the binary ufuncs
  (add/subtract/multiply/divide/true_divide/mod/power/floor_divide/arctan2/logaddexp/logaddexp2/
  nextafter/copysign/maximum/minimum/fmax/fmin/bitwise_*), square, clip and modf. `round_`/`around`
  fold to one `(x, decimals=0, out=null, DType dtype=null)` each (the engine's decimals=0 path
  already delegates to the no-decimals round, so behavior is identical). power/floor_divide keep
  their no-dtype `object`/`in NDArray` scalar-rhs perf overloads and drop only the dtype duplicates
  (scalar-rhs + dtype is served by the NDArray-rhs overload via implicit scalar->NDArray).

Tests: ~90 positional-dtype call sites across 9 test files rewritten to the `dtype:` keyword
(the NumPy-faithful form). The ValueType-scalar power/floor_divide cases now pass the scalar via
np.asanyarray (the object-rhs dtype convenience is intentionally gone).

Validated: full solution builds; migrated-area suite 1202/0; FuzzMatrix (bit-exact NumPy 2.4.2
oracle) 99/0. Remaining np.* dtype surface (Statistics reductions, Creation, IO, Logic, linalg
array-API) still carries Type/NPTypeCode overloads that compile unchanged via the implicit
conversion to the DType engine — migrating those to DType is the next step.

feat(build): [NDScoped] on a virtual/abstract/interface member is a contract every override and implementation inherits

Before this change the scope attributes were read off each method's OWN metadata, so
`[NDScoped]` on a virtual member scoped only that body: an override without its own
attribute was silently left unwoven (finalizer backstop), `[NDScoped]` on an abstract
member was a hard NDW005 build error, and the `[NDScopedExit]` collector's doc comment
spelled the rule out — "the CONCRETE override must re-declare the attribute". Core itself
carries the shape (`TensorEngine.Vdot/Vecdot/Matvec/Vecmat` are `[NDScoped] virtual`, and
every `DefaultEngine` override of an abstract engine member re-declares `[NDScoped]` by
hand), and any consumer engine or subclass overriding a scoped member got nothing.

Now the attribute is declaration-site: `[NDScoped]` / `[NDScopedAsync]` /
`[NDScopedCovered]` on a virtual, abstract or interface member — and the `[NDScopedExit]`
parameter attribute — is a CONTRACT. Every override and implementation is woven exactly as
if it carried the attribute itself, keeping its 100% original body; the scoping is stated
once, where the API is declared.

The rules (what the CLR's own slot resolution implies), identical in the weaver and the
analyzer:
- What inherits: class overrides through any number of levels (a base that does not declare
  the slot is climbed past), implicit interface implementations (a public method matching
  the member's name and signature; the base interfaces of a listed interface included),
  explicit interface implementations and covariant-return overrides (the `.override`
  MethodImpl table), generic instantiations (`Derived : Base<int>` matches
  `Base<T>.M(T)` against `M(int)` through a positional generic-argument chain), and a
  property-level attribute on a base property reaching its getter override. The
  declaration may live in ANOTHER assembly — a consumer overriding a NumSharp member, or a
  member of any library that used the weaver — walked through the compile's reference list
  (`WeaverAssemblyResolver`). Framework types are never climbed into.
- Nearest declaration wins; an explicit scope-family attribute on the override wins over it:
  `[NDScoped]`/`[NDScopedAsync]` re-state or change the model, `[NDScopedCovered]` opts the
  override OUT of the inherited weave (covered on the author's assertion, as any helper).
- The declaration is the contract, not a target: an abstract/interface attributed
  declaration is skipped (verbose: "contract"), never NDW005 — that error is now an
  `extern`'s alone (no body, no inheritors). Its SIGNATURE is still gated: a hidden `ref`
  egress on the contract is NDW002 on the declaration AND on every override inheriting it.
  A declaration carrying both attributes (NDW011) propagates nothing.
- `[NDScopedExit]` inherits by parameter position; an override that marks any parameter
  itself uses only its own marks.

Weaver (tools/NumSharp.Build):
- New `ScopeInheritance` (Mono.Cecil): `EffectiveScope(method)` / `EffectiveExitParameters(
  method)` memoized per MethodDefinition; the walk visits explicit `.override`s, the
  implicit interface implementations at each level, then the class base chain, with
  structural signature equality under the base's instantiation (`SameType` + `GenericContext`).
  Held on `Refs.Inheritance`; created before the seam is resolved so a target-free module
  still exits without resolving NDScope or rewriting the file.
- `CollectTargets` / `CollectExitTargets` / `ValidateExitParams` / `InjectParameterDetaches`
  read the effective attribute; `Validate`'s NDW005 text names extern only; every diagnostic
  and verbose line carries " (inherited from T::M)".

MSBuild targets:
- `build/NumSharp.Build.targets`: the ASCII pre-scan is blind to an override-only assembly
  (its metadata names the base type, never the attribute), so the tool is ALSO spawned when
  the compile references NumSharp; the tool is the precise probe and exits without
  rewriting when nothing inherits. Consumers that do not reference NumSharp keep the
  spawn-free path. Both targets files expose `NumSharpBuildActive` /
  `NumSharpDisableWeaverMissingWarning` as `CompilerVisibleProperty` items.
- `src/NumSharp.Core/build/NumSharp.targets`: `NumSharpBuildActive` defaults to `false` so
  declared-but-inactive and never-declared stay distinguishable to the analyzer (verified:
  `build_property.NumSharpBuildActive = false|true` lands in the generated editorconfig).

Analyzers (tools/NumSharp.Build.Analyzer):
- New `ScopeInheritance` (Roslyn twin): `ExplicitInterfaceImplementations` →
  `FindImplementationForInterfaceMember` at each level → `OverriddenMethod`, recursing into
  the base declaration.
- `NDScopedTargetAnalyzer`: gates inherited targets under the declaration's attribute (label
  names the source), NDW005 only for a non-abstract body-less target, and reports the ONE
  inherited case the MSBuild NDW013 text scan cannot see — an override inheriting the
  attribute from a declaration in ANOTHER assembly — as NDW013 (a warning, at the override)
  when `build_property.NumSharpBuildActive` is declared and not `true` (absent = unknown =
  silent; same-assembly inheritance stays the MSBuild scan's).
- `NDArrayLeakAnalyzer`: an inheriting override is NDW012-exempt like an attributed one.

Attributes: `Inherited = true` on all four, with the contract documented in the XML docs;
`NDScopeWeaveTests` reads them with `inherit: true` (and skips abstract declarations).

Gates:
- `InheritanceScenarios.cs` fixture + `InheritanceAnalyzerTests` (exact tag match; five
  unscoped controls leak, every inheriting member is clean; NDW002 on declaration and
  override; NDW005 gone for abstract; explicit-wins; a wrong-model declaration rejected on
  both; cross-assembly inheritance via a base library compiled to a MetadataReference;
  NDW013 honours the build knobs; same-assembly never draws the analyzer's NDW013).
- `WeaverInheritanceBuildTests` (AnalyzerBuild): a real two-project build — Lib declares
  the contracts (woven 2: its two attributed bodies), an attribute-FREE App overrides and
  implements them (woven 7: abstract/virtual/async-state-machine/property-getter/interface/
  generic-base scopes + an inherited `[NDScopedExit]` detach), verified by NDScope locals,
  a Detach call in IL, and running the woven code (values, retained argument survives).
- `GateScenarios.cs`: NDW005 is now an extern; the abstract declaration beside it is a clean
  contract. `AnalyzerContractTests`: NDW013 is a warning. `AnalyzerTestHarness`: extra
  references + `build_property.*` options provider.
- `tools/verify_build_package.sh` step 12: the tool now runs for a NumSharp-referencing
  attribute-free consumer and reports "no [NDScoped]/[NDScopedAsync]/[NDScopedExit]
  methods; nothing to do" — the regex accepted the OLD wording only; also asserts the
  assembly was not rewritten. ALL 18 STEPS OK.
- Core self-weave unchanged (woven 264 per TFM; Core has no inherited-only target today).
  NumSharp.Tests.Build.Analyzer 238/238 (net8.0 + net10.0), Lifetime 113/113.

Docs: numsharp-build-compiler.md (attribute table row + "Inheritance" section, NDW005/NDW013
rows and section, build-step note), tools/NumSharp.Build/README.md, COVERAGE_PLAN.md.

and a separate change).

fix(core): drop (int)size truncation in flat argsort/argpartition/cum-scan output shapes

The flat (axis=null) branches of np.argsort, np.argpartition and the
cumsum/cumprod empty-result path built their 1-D output shape with
new Shape((int)a.size) / Shape.Vector((int)shape.size). For an array
whose total element count exceeds int.MaxValue the (int) cast overflows
(e.g. 3e9 -> negative), so the output shape was garbage/negative even
though the adjacent reshape(a.size) already used the long overload.

Storage is long-capable (UnmanagedMemoryBlock<T>.Count / UnmanagedStorage.Count
are long) and Shape carries long dims/strides/size, so these casts were
gratuitous: Shape.Vector(long) and Shape(params long[]) already exist.
Switched all five sites to Shape.Vector(a.size)/Shape.Vector(shape.size).

The cum-scan sites are only reached with size==0 (harmless today) but are
corrected for consistency; the argsort/argpartition sites are reachable
non-empty flat paths and were genuine >int.MaxValue truncation bugs.

UnmanagedStorage.ToArray()/GetSpan() guard with OverflowException/
InvalidOperationException before casting; Char->string, tobytes, nditer<T>

fix(core): chain inner exceptions when re-wrapping into NumPy-style errors

Every catch block that translates a low-level failure into a NumPy-shaped

so the original stack trace and root cause were lost — a broadcast ValueError
gave no hint which internal step actually failed.

- Default.BooleanMask           -> ValueError
- DefaultEngine.UfuncOut        -> ArgumentException (out= and where= broadcast)

- NDArray.Indexing.PrepareIndex -> IndexError (index overflow)
- EinsumSubscripts / linalg.norm -> TypeError (subscript / ord parse)
- NpyFormat                     -> UnicodeEncodeException, InvalidOperationException (latin-1 header)
- np.savetxt                    -> TypeError (row format)

NpyFormat.UnicodeEncodeException (ValueError already had one).

test(longindexing): add byte >int.MaxValue oracle sweep across np.* ops

Adds ByteHugeArrayOracleTests: a self-checking long-indexing oracle that runs
np.* functions on a uint8 array of N = int.MaxValue + 16 (~2.0 GB, the minimum
that crosses 2^31) and CONFIRMS, per function, whether it honours > int.MaxValue
elements or silently truncates to a 32-bit index/length. Goal: all should.

Why not the committed differential-fuzz corpus: a single >2 GB case cannot be
committed and NumPy generating 2B+-element arrays is impractical, so expected
answers are known analytically from a few sentinel values -> no Python at test
time, the same 'confirm the long path' role expressed the only way >2 GB allows.

The load-bearing design is that every sentinel a check reads back sits ABOVE
int.MaxValue (Over = 2^31, Last = N-1): index-returning ops (argmax/argmin/
nonzero/flatnonzero/argwhere/where) return an index > int.MaxValue, so a 32-bit
truncation is caught even though the result is tiny. This closes the gap in the
existing LongIndexingMasterTest, whose argmax/argmin sentinels sat BELOW
int.MaxValue (LargeSize/2, /3) and so could not catch a 2^31 truncation, and it
adds the flat .size ops that test missed (argsort/argpartition/sort/partition).

Two methods, both [LongIndexing][HighMemory] (CI-excluded), each RAM-guarded to
go Inconclusive rather than OOM:
 - BoundedOutputOps (~6 GB peak): creation, get/set, reductions, arg/search,
   element-wise, comparison, where/take, shape/view, sort/partition.
 - WideOutputOps (~18 GB peak): argsort/argpartition/cumsum/cumprod/astype whose
   result is int64/double at full size -- the exact class fixed by dropping the
   (int)a.size output-shape truncation in AxisSort/AxisPartition.

Each large array is disposed eagerly (NDArray.Dispose frees synchronously; the
finalizer only abandons, so relying on GC would OOM the sweep). Op logic +
expected values were validated at small N (49/49) so the >2 GB run yields
trustworthy pass/fail rather than false failures.

fix(core): 64-bit the sort/select core so sort/argsort/partition/argpartition support > int.MaxValue

The byte >int.MaxValue oracle caught np.sort returning UNSORTED data (silent) and
np.partition throwing OverflowException on a 2.1-billion-element flat array. Both
traced to the value-side sort family being int-indexed end to end:

  * AxisSort.SortInPlace/ArgSortInto took the line length as int N = (int)shape[axis]
    (negative for a >2^31 axis -> sort early-returned unsorted); their radix scratch was
    managed uint[N]/ulong[N]/long[N], whose element count caps at ~2^31.
  * AxisPartition built new byte[N*elsize] (byte[] caps at ~2^31 -> the OverflowException)
    and ctx.n = (int)N; PrepKth truncated kth positions to int.
  * RadixSort and QuickSelect indexed every element with int (n, lo/hi, positions, the
    pivot stack); RadixSort's histogram was int* though one byte-bucket can hold up to N
    counts (> int range).

Converted the whole core to 64-bit:
  * RadixSort: n -> long, hist -> long* (bucket counts can exceed int), positions -> long.
    The insertion-sort fallbacks stay int (they run only for n <= 120).
  * QuickSelect: every element index (n, lo/hi/left/right/mid/p, block bounds, the pivot
    stack) -> long; block-local counters (numL/numR/startL/startR, the 0..BlockSize scan),
    npiv and depthLimit stay int. Added a thin int-taking PartitionAtMany overload that
    widens onto the stack and forwards, so the quantile IL kernels (line length always
    <= int.MaxValue) are unchanged.
  * AxisSort/AxisPartition: long N, and the radix key/idx/histogram + partition value/idx
    scratch moved to UNMANAGED NativeMemory (long-capable). The scalar comparison path
    (Half/Complex/Decimal) still uses managed Span/Array.Sort and so throws a clear
    NotSupportedException for a > int.MaxValue axis (documented, rather than truncating).
  * NDArray.unique.Radix.cs: histogram widened to long* to match RadixSort (its managed
    key buffers keep it <= int.MaxValue, unchanged otherwise).

Validated: bounded byte oracle now 49/49 on the real 2.1e9 array on net8.0 AND net10.0
(np.sort 25s, np.partition 68s, previously silent-wrong / OverflowException); a 200K
differential vs Array.Sort across the radix-scatter, block-Hoare, SortU64, NaN-last, byte
and 2-D axis paths (8/8); 638 sort/partition/quantile/median/percentile/unique/nanargmax/
lexsort unit tests; and the FuzzMatrix sort/partition/scan/nanreduce/lexsort/stat
bit-exact-vs-NumPy tiers (9/9). argsort/argpartition ride the same converted cores (their
output-shape (int)a.size truncation was fixed in 85891751).

feat(threading): TensorEngine.Threading — unified, per-module threading config

Add `TensorEngine.Threading`, a single process-wide surface for every threading
knob NumSharp and the native BLAS/OpenMP ecosystem expose, and integrate
`np.multithreading` with it. Motivated by the incoherence that
`np.multithreading` today governs ONLY the managed fused 1-D dot
(`Default.Dot.Fused.cs` via `MultiThread.DegreeOfParallelism`) — the exact op
`blas.TryDot` bypasses — so it is a no-op the moment the OpenBLAS backend serves
f32/f64/c128 products. There was also no place to configure the native thread
env vars from one API, and the managed side had no env var at all.

Design
- `TensorEngine.Threading` (Backends/TensorEngine.Threading.cs): a registry of
  named, env-var-backed `Variable` knobs, each with an optional live `reader`
  and an `applier`. Well-known knobs registered out of the box: NumSharp
  (NUMSHARP_NUM_THREADS), OpenBLAS (OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS), OpenMP
  (OMP_NUM_THREADS), MKL, BLIS, NumExpr, vecLib.
- Extensible per module: `Register(name, envVar, reader, applier)` upserts, so a
  module attaches its own reader/applier to a knob Core already declared. This is
  the "extend further per module" hook.
- API: Register / Get / TryGet / Variables / GetThreads / SetThreads /
  TrySetDefault / SetAll.

Two invariants (as requested)
- Source of truth: a variable already set in the environment when a knob is
  first observed seeds it (`IsEnvSourced`) and is pushed to the applier; a
  module default (`TrySetDefault`) never overwrites it. An explicit
  SetThreads/SetAll is a deliberate in-process override and does take effect.
- Writes only apply to the process: every env write targets
  `EnvironmentVariableTarget.Process` — the persistent User/Machine environment
  is never modified.

np.multithreading integration
- `np.multithreading(enabled, max_threads)` now routes the cap through the
  NumSharp knob (`SetThreads(NumSharp, max_threads)` → sets
  `MultiThread.MaxThreads` via the applier and writes the process-scoped
  NUMSHARP_NUM_THREADS), while the enable flag still sets `MultiThread.Enabled`.
- `MultiThread` seeds itself from NUMSHARP_MULTITHREADING / NUMSHARP_NUM_THREADS
  at startup (source of truth); its cctor is self-contained so a dot workload
  that never touches Threading is still correctly seeded.
- `EnvVars` gains typed `NumSharpMultithreading` / `NumSharpNumThreads`
  accessors and a `GetIntOrNull` helper.

OpenBLAS module (the concrete per-module extension)
- `OpenBlasEngine.EnsureThreadingRegistered()` upgrades the OpenBLAS knob with a
  live reader (`openblas_get_num_threads`) and a native applier
  (`OpenBlasNative.ApplyThreadCount`) that pushes a change through the CRT
  (`_putenv_s`, which a native getenv actually reads — Environment.Set does not)
  AND `openblas_set_num_threads`. Registered from the module init path (via
  Enable) and idempotent.
- `OpenBlasEngine.Enable(threads:)` routes thread-setting through
  `TensorEngine.Threading.SetThreads(OpenBlas, threads)` so the two surfaces
  agree; the native effect is unchanged (still openblas_set_num_threads(threads)),
  and the source-of-truth OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS is honoured at load as before.

Verification
- Isolated in a detached worktree at HEAD (the shared working tree carries other
  sessions' in-progress, non-compiling edits): Core, OpenBLAS and the test
  project build clean; 15/15 threading + multithreading tests pass.
- Tests (test/NumSharp.Tests/Backends/TensorEngineThreadingTests.cs): well-known
  knob registration, live binding to MultiThread.MaxThreads, the np.multithreading
  integration, process-scoped writes, null-clears-env, source-of-truth seeding +
  applier push, TrySetDefault precedence, and the upsert extension point.

refactor(ndscope): drop redundant/misplaced [NDScoped] from pure-delegation np.* methods

[NDScoped] opens an NDScope whose only job is to reclaim the NDArray temporaries a
method constructs IN ITS OWN FRAME (NDScope.Returns re-parents the result to the
enclosing scope, then the finally disposes what is left). A method that creates no
temporary of its own gains nothing from it: a pure delegation to an already-[NDScoped]
method, or a view-returning wrapper, adds an empty scope + try/finally + a redundant
Returns round-trip while the wrapped call's own scope already reclaims its temps and
hands back a detached result.

Verified each against the actual NDScope re-parenting semantics AND the target's own
scoping, then removed the attribute from seven such methods:

- np.fft.rfft2  => rfftn   (target [NDScoped])
- np.fft.irfft2 => irfftn  (target [NDScoped])
- np.conj       => conjugate ([NDScoped]); pure alias, no temp
- np.vdot       => TensorEngine.Vdot (the [NDScoped] engine boundary that already
                   reclaims its ravel/reshape/conjugate temps)
- np.linalg.norm(int? axis) => norm(int[] axis) ([NDScoped]); only wraps the axis in
                   an int[] (no NDArray temp)
- np.pad(int pad_width) => PadImpl ([NDScoped]); this matches the file's own
                   "Scoped here (not per-overload)" note and the four sibling
                   value-mode overloads, which were already unscoped
- np.reshape(int[]) => nd.reshape (a view op, no temp); matches the three unscoped
                   sibling overloads

Also MOVED repeat's scope onto the overloads that actually calculate. It sat on the
delegating repeat(int) (an int->long cast) while the calculating repeat(long) and
repeat(NDArray) -- which build ravel/ascontiguousarray temps -- were unscoped, so a
direct call to those leaked their temporaries to the finalizer. Now repeat(int)
delegates unscoped and the two calculating overloads carry [NDScoped].

The removals are behaviour-neutral (the targets already scope their own temps); the
repeat move additionally reclaims temps eagerly for direct repeat(long)/repeat(NDArray)
callers. NumSharp.Core builds 0 warnings / 0 errors (0 warnings also confirms the
ownership analyzer draws no NDW012 on the now-unscoped methods).

fix(einsum_path): arbitrary-precision (BigInteger) cost model to match NumPy bignum

np.einsum_path's greedy/optimal planner computed element counts and FLOP
counts in `long`, which OVERFLOWS on large contraction networks where NumPy
uses arbitrary-precision Python ints. For e.g. `ea,fb,abcd,gc,hd->efgh` with
every dimension 100000 (naive FLOP count 5e40, largest intermediate 1e20) the
`long` cost model wrapped to a NEGATIVE count, printed garbage (naive FLOP
`-6.788e+18`), and derailed the greedy/optimal cost comparisons — it gave up to
the single naive contraction (`Optimized scaling 8`, speedup `1.000`) instead of
finding the real path.

NumPy's `_compute_size_by_dict`/`_flop_count` (einsumfunc.py) are Python bignum,
so the only way to be byte-identical for these networks is BigInteger.

Fix — the cost model only:
- EinsumPathPlanner: ComputeSize/FlopCount, sizeList/costList/outSizeList,
  maxSize/memoryArg/naiveCost/optCost/maxIntermediate, the greedy Candidate
  (SortRemovedNeg/SortCost) and TryParseContraction, the optimal path's cost
  tuples and MinByCost, and Sci() are all BigInteger now. Sci() keeps the exact
  round-half-to-even behavior (Python's `%.3e` on an int), just over BigInteger.
- np.einsum_path: the `("greedy", N)` memory-limit tuple parses to BigInteger
  (ToBigInteger) so Directive.MemoryLimit is BigInteger?.

Deliberately NOT widened (all correct as-is):
- Individual DIMENSION extents stay `long` — a single array dimension always
  fits int64, as in NumPy's intp shapes; only the PRODUCTS need bignum.
- EinsumPath contraction-step POSITIONS stay int[][] — operand indices, capped
  tiny, exactly the small ints NumPy returns.

Scope — audited ALL einsum managed code; the fix was needed ONLY in the planner:
- np.einsum.Contract.cs / EinsumSubscripts.cs / np.einsum.cs already use `long`
  for every dimension/extent/product, and every product is bounded by the
  operand's Shape.size (which must fit `long` for any array that can exist), so
  the contraction CANNOT overflow. The planner is the sole einsum code that
  reasons about hypothetical, un-allocated contraction sizes/costs, hence the
  sole place that can exceed `long`.

Verified byte-identical to NumPy 2.4.2:
- Planner overflow (long->bignum): naive 5.000e+40, optimized 8.000e+25, speedup
  625000000000000.000, intermediate 1.000e+20, path (0,2)(0,3)(0,2)(0,1) — exact
  for greedy AND optimal.
- Public API overflow (ij,jk,kl->il, all dims 2e9): 4.800e+37 / 3.200e+28 /
  1500000000.000 / 4.000e+18, path (0,1)(0,1) — exact.
- Sizes past int32 (i=3e9): 1.800e+11 / 6.000e+09 — exact.
- View path with >int.MaxValue dims (transpose/diagonal): correct shapes.

Writing and running the tour against the live bridge found two things worth fixing:

1. PyTorch test gate was an exact-line pin. `PyTorchTestGate` required `torch.__version__` to start
   with "2.13." — so on any host with a different stable PyTorch (this one: 2.12.1+cu126) all 27
   Torch tests reported Inconclusive: the whole PyTorch bridge was green-by-skipping, the exact
   failure mode PythonSession's own docs warn about. The gate is now a version FLOOR,
   `MinimumTorchVersion = 2.3.0` (the release whose torch.from_numpy accepts the unsigned 16/32/64-bit
   dtypes the tests pin), with a `Parse()` that strips CUDA local-version and pre-release tags
   ("2.12.1+cu126", "2.14.0a0+git1234"). `Runtime_IsLatestStablePyTorch213` became
   `Runtime_IsAtLeastTheGateFloor_AndTheFloorParserHandlesLocalVersions` (also pins the parser).
   Result: 28/28 Torch tests pass on 2.12.1+cu126, including the real CUDA->CPU accelerator cell;
   the interop suite goes from 497 passed / 27 skipped to 526 passed / 0 skipped.

2. ToNumpy(Decimal) leaked its float64 temporary to the finalizer. The Decimal export builds the numpy
   view over `source.astype(Double)`, a temporary nothing could ever dispose; ~NDArray only ABANDONS
   its buffer reference (no free at zero — the block is reclaimed a collection after the finalizer
   runs), so each Decimal export left a float64 buffer to two GC cycles' worth of finalizer latency
   after Python let go. `ExportKeeper` now takes `ownsSource` and disposes the temporary in
   `Release()` (CLR-only, safe under the GIL / on the orphan sweep); `ToNumpyCopy` `using`s its own
   temporary; the empty-array and TryAddRef-failure early exits dispose it too. Test seam:
   `PythonRuntimeInterop.LiveExportKeepers` + `ExportKeeper.Source/OwnsSource`. Gates:
   `ExportTests.Decimal_Export_OwnsItsFloat64Temporary_AndFreesItTheMomentPythonLetsGo` (the
   temporary's slice is released synchronously inside Python's `del`, no GC) and
   `ExportTests.ExportKeeper_Release_DisposesAnOwnedSource_AndLeavesABorrowedOneAlone`.

Docs: pytorch.md records the floor + the 2.12.1+cu126 validation and the renamed gate; the package
README and pythonnet-numpy.md link the examples.

Traps pinned while writing the scripts (encoded in their comments/README): pythonnet DEFERS the decref
of GC-finalized wrappers (the arguments of a `dynamic` call, notably) until `Finalizer.Instance.Collect()`
runs, so counters only drain after flushing it; `np.float64(x).reshape(())` is a READ-ONLY 0-d array
(a numpy scalar's buffer) — `np.array(x)` is the writable form; pyarrow buffers export format 'b'
(SByte) and may be padded to 64-byte multiples; a PyObject must never be touched after
PythonEngine.Shutdown() (the scaffolding's PyScope.Dispose checks PythonEngine.IsInitialized).
